claim: Hunter Biden had no experience in Ukraine or in the energy sector when he joined the board of Burisma.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: When Hunter Biden joined Burisma’s board in April 2014, his background was in law, lobbying, finance, and corporate governance (e.g., counsel at Boies Schiller, co-founding an investment firm, serving on Amtrak’s board). Public records and contemporary reporting note he had no specific experience in Ukraine or in the energy/oil-and-gas industry. Defenders pointed to his governance and compliance expertise, but not sectoral or Ukraine-specific experience. (Minor caveat: his investment work sometimes touched broadly on international deals, but not established energy or Ukraine expertise.)

claim: Donald Trump delivered the largest tax cuts in American history.
response_text: FALSE.  The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was not the largest in U.S. history by standard measures. As a share of the economy, it reduced revenues by roughly 0.8–0.9% of GDP in its early years—smaller than the 1981 Reagan tax cut and major post‑WWII cuts (often around 2–3% of GDP). Analyses by JCT/CBO and independent groups have consistently found Trump’s cut was not the largest.

claim: In Nigeria … in terms of revenue share, 20% goes to the local government.
response_text: TRUE (roughly). Under Nigeria’s current Federation Account vertical allocation formula, local governments receive 20.60% (after the 13% derivation is set aside), so “20%” is a rounded figure. Note: other pools like VAT use a different split (LGAs get 35%).

claim: Biden has pledged to stop border wall construction and give amnesty and health care to all illegal immigrants.
response_text: FALSE.  - Biden did pledge to halt new border wall construction (e.g., “not another foot” during the 2020 campaign). - He did not pledge “amnesty to all” undocumented immigrants; his plan proposed a conditional, multi‑year pathway to citizenship with background checks and cutoff dates—not blanket amnesty. - He did not promise to “give health care to all” undocumented immigrants; he proposed allowing them to buy into coverage (e.g., a public option/ACA marketplaces) without federal subsidies, not free universal coverage.  Overall, the claim overstates and distorts his positions.

claim: After the police shooting of Jacob Blake, Gov. Tony Evers & Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes did not call for peace or encourage calm.
response_text: FALSE.  Both did. Examples: - Aug. 24, 2020, Gov. Tony Evers: “I ask everyone who chooses to exercise their First Amendment rights to please do so peacefully and safely,” while deploying the National Guard and condemning violence and property damage. - Aug. 24, 2020, Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes urged protesters to remain nonviolent, saying the hurt and frustration “cannot turn into violence or destruction” and calling for peaceful demonstrations.  These statements were noted in contemporaneous press releases, briefings, and coverage (e.g., PolitiFact Wisconsin).

claim: The Common Law Admission Test (CLAT) 2020 will not be conducted on September 7, 2020, as planned
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Consortium of National Law Universities announced in early September 2020 that CLAT 2020, slated for September 7, was postponed due to COVID-19-related restrictions. It was rescheduled to September 28, 2020.

claim: 35% of revenue goes to states. (In Nigeria)
response_text: FALSE.  Under Nigeria’s current vertical revenue allocation formula, states receive 26.72% of the Federation Account (federal 52.68%, local governments 20.60%, with a separate 13% derivation to oil-producing states off the top). Even proposed revisions have put states under 30%, not 35%. If referring to VAT, states get 50%, not 35%.

claim: Biden will take away the Second Amendment.
response_text: FALSE.  A U.S. president cannot “take away” a constitutional amendment. Repealing or altering the Second Amendment would require a new constitutional amendment passed by two‑thirds of Congress and ratified by three‑quarters of the states. Biden has advocated gun-safety measures (e.g., background checks, assault‑weapons ban) while stating he supports the Second Amendment, not its repeal.

claim: Biden has pledged to defund the police
response_text: FALSE.  Joe Biden has repeatedly said he does not support defunding the police. In June 2020 he wrote “I do not support defunding the police,” advocating reforms and conditional federal aid. He has proposed increased funding for training and community policing and said in his 2022 State of the Union, “The answer is not to defund the police. It’s to fund the police.” He has endorsed redirecting some resources toward mental health and social services, but that is not a pledge to defund.

claim: 45% of Nigeria's revenue goes to the federal government.
response_text: FALSE.  Under the current revenue allocation formula for Nigeria’s Federation Account, the federal government receives about 52.68% (states 26.72%, local governments 20.60%), with a 13% derivation to oil-producing states taken off the top. A ~45% federal share has been proposed in reviews but not adopted.

claim: Joe Biden voted for the Iraq War and he supported wars in Serbia, Syria, and Libya.
response_text: TRUE.  - Iraq: As a senator, Biden voted in 2002 for the Authorization for Use of Military Force against Iraq. - Serbia: He supported NATO’s 1999 intervention in the Kosovo conflict (air campaign against Yugoslavia/Serbia). - Libya: As vice president, he backed the 2011 NATO intervention in Libya. - Syria: As vice president, he supported U.S. military action in Syria, including the anti-ISIS air campaign begun in 2014 (and signaled support for limited strikes after Assad’s 2013 chemical attacks).  Note: “Supported” refers to backing U.S./NATO military interventions, not necessarily advocating a full-scale ground war.

claim: President Muhammadu Buhari sign a new Police bill to allow officers arrest without a warrant
response_text: FALSE.  Buhari did sign the Police Act 2020, but it did not newly “allow” warrantless arrests. Nigerian police already had limited powers to arrest without a warrant under earlier laws; the new Act largely restated and regulated those powers rather than creating them.

claim: Plant Seeds Can Restructure Their Own DNA Through Human Saliva
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that human saliva can cause plant seeds to “restructure” their DNA. Saliva contains enzymes and microbes but no mechanism to direct genomic changes in plants. Seeds can change gene expression or epigenetic marks in response to environment, but that’s not DNA restructuring, and it isn’t guided by human saliva. Horizontal gene transfer from humans to plants via saliva does not occur under natural conditions. Any effect of saliva would be limited to moisture or microbial contamination, not genomic alteration.

claim: We actually saw revenues to the Treasury increase after we lowered taxes in 2017. Rest assured the Democrats do not want you to know that.
response_text: TRUE (but misleading).  - Total federal receipts in nominal dollars did tick up after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act: about $3.33T in FY2018 vs $3.32T in FY2017, and ~$3.46T in FY2019. - However, revenues fell as a share of GDP and declined in real (inflation‑adjusted) terms in 2018; corporate income tax receipts dropped by roughly a third. Relative to prior-law baselines, CBO and other analyses conclude the tax cuts reduced revenues and widened deficits.

claim: In 2019 the US Police were 20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal
response_text: TRUE.  - FBI LEOKA reports 48 U.S. law enforcement officers were feloniously killed in 2019. - The Washington Post database counts 999 fatal police shootings in 2019.  999 ÷ 48 ≈ 20.8. Note: this uses fatal police shootings (not all causes of death by police); including all police-caused deaths would make the ratio slightly higher.

claim: The Edo Modular Refinery is Governor Obaseki's project.
response_text: FALSE.  The Edo Modular Refinery (Edo Refinery and Petrochemicals Company Ltd., at Ologbo) is a privately owned project developed by AIPCC Energy (with technical partners), not Governor Obaseki’s personal project. The Edo State Government under Obaseki facilitated and supported it (including policy support and some financing), but it is not his project or personal property.

claim: In Kenya now with a population of about 48 million, there is one judge serving over 300,000 people.
response_text: TRUE  Kenya’s population was about 48 million around 2018–2019. At that time the total number of judges (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court, Environment and Land Court, and Employment and Labour Relations Court) was on the order of roughly 150–180. That yields about 1 judge per 270,000–320,000 people, so “over 300,000” is a reasonable approximation depending on the exact count used. Note: if magistrates are included, the ratio would be much lower.

claim: The Kenyan judiciary does not even get 1% of the national budget.
response_text: TRUE.  In recent budgets, Kenya’s Judiciary has received roughly KSh 20–26 billion against total national budgets around KSh 3.6–4.0 trillion—about 0.5–0.7%. That’s below 1%. Percentages vary slightly by fiscal year and how the “national budget” is defined, but allocations have consistently been under 1%.

claim: Kenya only disposes of about 300,000 cases.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Kenya’s Judiciary reports typically show annual disposals well above 300,000 cases in recent years (often roughly 350,000–450,000+). There was a pandemic dip toward ~300,000, but as a general statement “only about 300,000” understates current performance. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by year.

claim: The judiciary of Kenya have an average of 400,000 cases being filed in our courts every year.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Kenya’s State of the Judiciary annual reports typically show roughly 350,000–450,000 new cases filed each year, with pandemic-era dips and post-pandemic rebounds. That yields an average close to “about 400,000” filings per year. (Exact figures vary by year, so this is an approximate but reasonable average.)

claim: There is an average of 400,000 cases being filed in Kenya's courts every year.
response_text: TRUE.  Kenya’s Judiciary reports show new case filings typically in the high hundreds of thousands each year—roughly 350,000–450,000, with several recent years near 400,000 (e.g., about 402k in FY 2018/19). So “about 400,000 per year” is a reasonable average, though it varies by year.

claim: The Kenya judiciary have one magistrate serving over 77,000 people.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Kenya’s population is about 50–55 million, while Judiciary reports list roughly 600–650 magistrates. That implies around 80,000–90,000 people per magistrate on average—i.e., over 77,000. Figures vary by year, but the ratio remains above 77,000.

claim: The judiciary does not even get 1% of the national Kenyan budget.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent Kenyan budgets allocate well under 1% to the Judiciary. For example: - FY2023/24: total budget about KSh 3.68 trillion; Judiciary roughly KSh 23–24 billion (~0.6%). - FY2021/22: total budget about KSh 3.3–3.6 trillion; Judiciary about KSh 18–20 billion (~0.5–0.6%).  These figures show the Judiciary’s share is consistently below 1%.

claim: All government schools in India are being privatised.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no nationwide policy to privatize all government schools in India. Over a million government schools continue to operate, and the government is investing in them through programs like Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI. While some states have experimented with limited public–private partnerships or NGO support, these do not amount to “all government schools being privatized.”

claim: If one gets the Spanish flu you have a 50% chance of dying
response_text: FALSE.  The 1918 “Spanish flu” was deadly, but the risk of death if infected was far below 50%. Best estimates put the case/infection fatality on the order of a few percent (roughly 2–5%, with some estimates up to about 10% in certain analyses), though it varied by age and region. Some communities were hit unusually hard, but not half of those infected died.

claim: Ghana's economy previously grew at 3.4% under the form President Mahama's government and on average, for three successive years, at 7% per year with the current administration.
response_text: TRUE (with minor caveat)  - Ghana’s real GDP growth in 2016 (Mahama’s last year) was about 3.4% (World Bank/Ghana Statistical Service). - Under the succeeding Akufo-Addo administration, real GDP growth was about 8.1% (2017), 6.3% (2018), and 6.5% (2019), averaging roughly 7% over those three years.  Caveat: The 3.4% figure refers to 2016 specifically, not the average for Mahama’s entire term.

claim: Kenya settles  about 300,000 court cases each year.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Kenya’s State of the Judiciary reports show annual case disposals in recent years are generally above 300,000 (often around 350,000–450,000+), with only some COVID-affected years near that 300,000 mark. So “about 300,000 each year” understates typical recent output. (Exact figures vary by fiscal year and whether tribunals are included.)

claim: Kenya's judiciary does not even get 1% of the national budget
response_text: TRUE.  - In recent budgets, the Judiciary’s allocation has been roughly KSh 18–26 billion against a total national budget of about KSh 3.3–3.9 trillion—about 0.6–0.7%. - Example: FY 2023/24 allocation ~KSh 23–25 billion vs a ~KSh 3.7–3.9 trillion budget, well under 1%. - Even measured against discretionary (ex‑CFS) spending, the share has still been below 1%.  Minor uncertainty on exact figures by year, but all recent ratios are clearly under 1%.

claim: In Kenya, one Magistrate serves 77,000 people.
response_text: TRUE (approximately)  Reason: Kenya’s 2019 census put the population at about 47.6 million. Judiciary reports around 2018–2020 show roughly 600–650 magistrates in post. That gives a ratio near 47.6M ÷ ~620 ≈ 76,800—about 77,000 people per magistrate. The exact figure varies by year and staffing, but 77,000 is a reasonable estimate.

claim: In Kenya now, with a population of about 48 million, they have one judge serving over 300,000 people.
response_text: TRUE  Kenya’s population is about 48 million (2019 census ~47.6m). The number of judges (Superior Courts: Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court, ELRC, ELC) has been roughly in the 150–170 range in recent years, which yields a ratio around 280,000–320,000 people per judge—i.e., over 300,000 in many estimates. Note: including magistrates would lower the per–judicial officer ratio, but the claim specifies “judge.”

claim: No Democrats have condemned the rioting that has occurred alongside recent protests.
response_text: FALSE.  Many Democrats have explicitly condemned rioting and violence alongside protests. Examples: - Joe Biden (Aug. 31, 2020): “Rioting is not protesting. Looting is not protesting.” He repeated in 2024 that protests don’t include violence or property damage. - Nancy Pelosi (June 2020): said there is “no excuse for the violence, looting, [or] destruction.” - Democratic mayors/governors (e.g., Atlanta’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, Minneapolis’s Jacob Frey, New York’s Andrew Cuomo) publicly condemned rioting and urged nonviolence.

claim: A pizza place in Washington, D.C. -- Comet Ping Pong has ties to Hillary Clinton and other leading Democrats
response_text: TRUE.  Comet Ping Pong’s owner, James Alefantis, is a Democratic donor who has hosted Democratic political events/fundraisers, had social/contact links with John and Tony Podesta (appearing in the leaked Podesta emails), and previously dated Democratic operative David Brock. These are ordinary political/social connections; there’s no evidence of any wrongdoing.

claim: South Africans that drink are amongst the top drinkers in the world.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO reports show South Africa’s average alcohol consumption per drinker is very high (around 27–30 liters of pure alcohol per year), placing South African drinkers among the highest globally, with high rates of heavy episodic drinking as well. While overall per-capita consumption is moderated by many abstainers, among those who do drink, intake is among the world’s highest.

claim: South Africans are among the top drinkers in the world.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO/Our World in Data figures show South Africa’s total alcohol consumption is well above the global average (around 11–12 liters of pure alcohol per adult 15+ per year vs ~6–7 globally), putting it in the higher ranks worldwide. Because many adults abstain, consumption among those who do drink is among the highest globally (roughly 25–30+ liters per drinker annually), and heavy episodic (binge) drinking rates are also very high. Rankings vary by metric/year, but the claim is broadly accurate.

claim: South African consume more alcohol per person on average than anywhere else in Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  South Africa is among the higher-consuming countries in Africa, but not the highest. WHO/Our World in Data estimates (e.g., 2016–2019) show per‑adult alcohol consumption around 9–10 liters of pure alcohol per year in South Africa, while countries like Seychelles, Gabon, Namibia, and sometimes Uganda are higher (roughly 10–12+ liters). Rankings vary slightly by year and method, but South Africa is not number one.

claim: South Africans drink more per person than anywhere else in Africa
response_text: FALSE.  On standard measures (liters of pure alcohol per adult, 15+), WHO data show several African countries consume more per person than South Africa. Recent WHO Global Status Reports place Seychelles and Uganda (and often Namibia, Equatorial Guinea) above South Africa, which is around 9–10 L per adult per year versus ~11–12 L in the highest countries. Rankings vary slightly by year/metric, but South Africa is not No. 1.

claim: South Africans drink more per person than anywhere else in Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO estimates show several African countries have higher per‑capita alcohol consumption than South Africa (e.g., Seychelles, Gabon, Namibia, Equatorial Guinea, Uganda). South Africa is high but not the highest. Note: rankings vary by year and whether measured per total adults or drinkers only, but South Africa is not number one on common measures.

claim: world bank currently rates Nigeria as one of ten top performing countries on its Doing Business Index.
response_text: FALSE.  Nigeria has not been ranked among the top 10 countries in the World Bank’s Doing Business (ease-of-doing-business) rankings. In recent editions before the index was discontinued in 2021, Nigeria ranked far lower (e.g., around 131 in Doing Business 2020). It was at times listed among the “top 10 improvers,” but not among the top 10 performers. Moreover, the Doing Business index is no longer current.

claim: South Africans are among the top drinkers in the world
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: By WHO and other international data, South Africa’s adult per-capita alcohol consumption is above the global average, and among those who do drink, average consumption and heavy episodic (“binge”) drinking rates are among the highest worldwide. While it’s not at the very top by total per-capita liters (Eastern Europe typically leads), South Africa is in the higher tier globally—so the claim is broadly accurate. (Depends on metric.)

claim: Only 31% of South Africans drink alcohol
response_text: TRUE.  WHO estimates show about 31% of South Africans aged 15+ are current drinkers (past-12-month use), with men much higher than women. Figures vary by year and definition, but multiple WHO/South African sources consistently report roughly one-third as current drinkers. (Uncertainty: depends on survey year and “current drinking” definition.)

claim: Only 31% of South Africans drink alcohol.
response_text: FALSE.  Most recent estimates put current alcohol use in South Africa at roughly 40–45% of people aged 15+ (WHO and national survey data). The “about 31%” figure appears in some older or narrower definitions, but as a general statement it understates the share who drink. Note: prevalence varies by definition (past month vs past 12 months) and year.

claim: Democratic Arizona Superintendent of Public Instruction Kathy Hoffman is “pushing” for sex education that would teach kindergartners about masturbation and sexual positions.
response_text: FALSE.  - Arizona doesn’t have a statewide sex‑ed curriculum; local districts set it, and any sex education is opt‑in by parents. - There’s no evidence Hoffman “pushed” lessons for kindergartners on masturbation or sexual positions. The materials cited by critics were optional resources, with any mention of masturbation aimed at older students, and “sexual positions” are not part of Arizona standards. - Multiple fact‑checks and state policy confirm this. Uncertainty: low.

claim: The interface of the COVID-19 Exposure Notification System, a contact tracing programme developed by Apple and Google has been secretly inserted onto phones and tracks user’s location.
response_text: FALSE.  - Apple and Google added an Exposure Notifications setting/API via regular OS updates (iOS and Android), not a secretly installed app. It is off by default and only works if a user explicitly opts in (via a public health app or EN Express). - The system does not track or collect location data. It uses Bluetooth Low Energy to exchange rotating random identifiers to estimate proximity, not GPS.

claim: Democratic Arizona Superintendent of Public Instruction Kathy Hoffman was sworn into office on a Dr. Seuss book.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a debunked meme. Official photos and local reporting show Kathy Hoffman did not use a Dr. Seuss book for her oath; she took the oath without a book (and in a later ceremonial setting used the U.S. and Arizona Constitutions), not Dr. Seuss. Slight uncertainty on which text was present in the later ceremony, but it was not a Dr. Seuss book.

claim: India's Supreme Court recently changed its motto from ‘Satyamev Jayate’ to ‘Yato Dharmastato Jai’.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: “Satyameva Jayate” is India’s national motto (on the State Emblem), not the Supreme Court’s. The Supreme Court’s own motto has long been “Yato Dharmastato Jaya(h)” (“Where there is Dharma/righteousness, there is victory”) from the Mahabharata, and there has been no recent change.

claim: Democrats recited the US Pledge of Allegiance tonight and took out "under God".
response_text: FALSE.  At the 2020 Democratic National Convention, the official, televised recitations of the Pledge included “under God” each night. Two separate caucus/assembly meetings had individual participants omit the phrase, but the DNC did not “take it out” of the pledge. (AP, Reuters, PolitiFact)

claim: Democratic VP candidate Kamala Harris called young voters stupid.
response_text: FALSE.  In a 2015 speech as California attorney general, Harris said “18- to 24-year-olds are stupid” while discussing young people’s decision-making and criminal justice. She was not talking about voters or voting, and she was not a VP candidate at the time. The “young voters” framing is misleading.

claim: Israel has developed super-quick saliva test for COVID-19.
response_text: TRUE.  Several Israeli groups developed rapid saliva-based COVID-19 tests. For example, Sheba Medical Center and Newsight Imaging prototyped a spectrometry-based saliva/mouthwash test reporting results in about 20 seconds, and Israeli startup Salignostics developed a saliva antigen rapid test (SaliCov) with results in roughly 10–15 minutes.

claim: Children are silent super-spreaders of coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence from household, school, and community studies shows children—especially under 10—are generally less susceptible to infection and less likely to transmit SARS‑CoV‑2 than adults. While many children have mild or no symptoms (“silent”), they do not disproportionately seed large outbreaks and are not “super‑spreaders.” Adolescents can transmit at rates closer to adults, and highly transmissible variants raised rates across all ages, but the “silent super‑spreader” label for children is not supported overall.

claim: Candace Owens was fired from her show at One America News after a  racist outburst.
response_text: FALSE.  Candace Owens did not host a show on One America News Network, nor is there credible reporting that she was fired from OANN for a “racist outburst.” Her notable departures include leaving Turning Point USA (2019) and being let go by The Daily Wire (2024) after disputes over her commentary—unrelated to OANN. The claim likely confuses her with other conservative hosts (e.g., Tomi Lahren previously had an OANN show but was not fired from OANN).

claim: President Trump is the most pro-gay president in American history.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump made some symbolic gestures (e.g., appointing Richard Grenell, a global push to decriminalize homosexuality), but his administration rolled back multiple LGBTQ protections: rescinded guidance for transgender students, banned transgender military service, sought to narrow “sex” discrimination protections in health care and education, supported broad religious-exemption policies, and argued at the Supreme Court that federal job-bias law didn’t cover sexual orientation or gender identity (Bostock). By contrast, Obama and especially Biden advanced and restored protections (repeal of “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” support for marriage equality, restoring and expanding nondiscrimination rules, ending the trans military ban, signing the Respect for Marriage Act).

claim: Messages in Google Earth show the "Deep States New Home," which shows up on the map as "Setatspeed Emohwen Gardens" near Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
response_text: FALSE.  “Setatspeed Emohwen Gardens” (which reads “Deepstates Newhome” backward) is not an official Google Earth/Maps place label. It appeared in screenshots from a user-created layer/list sometimes called “Messages in Google Earth,” which allows anyone to place custom pins with arbitrary names. The base Google map near Guantánamo Bay has no such feature, and fact-checks (e.g., Reuters/USA Today) found the label was user-generated, not a hidden Google message or evidence of a “Deep State” site. Uncertainty: low.

claim: USA is the only major industrial economy to have it unemployment rate triple.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The claim lacks a timeframe. Historically, other advanced industrial economies have seen unemployment rates triple. For example, Spain’s unemployment rose from about 8% in 2007 to around 26% by 2013 (more than triple), and Ireland’s rose from roughly 4–5% to ~15% after the 2008 crisis. While the U.S. unemployment rate did more than triple at the onset of COVID-19, it was not uniquely the only major industrial economy ever to experience such a jump. Uncertainty: if the claim intended a very specific window (e.g., among G7 in early 2020), it would be closer, but as stated it’s false.

claim: The USA has only 4% of the worlds population but has 25% of the worlds Covid-19 Cases.
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. has about 4% of the world’s population. - Its share of cumulative reported COVID-19 cases is not 25% overall. By 2023–2025, the U.S. recorded roughly 100+ million cases out of about 750–770 million globally (≈13–15%). - The “25% of cases” figure was roughly true only during parts of mid-2020, not as a general or current statement.

claim: Donald Trump is trying to take away the health care by getting rid of the Affordable Care Act.
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump repeatedly sought to repeal the Affordable Care Act: he backed 2017 repeal bills, supported litigation to invalidate the law, and as recently as 2023 said he wanted to “terminate” Obamacare. Nonpartisan analyses (e.g., CBO on the 2017 House bill) projected tens of millions would lose coverage if repeal went through. While he often said he’d “replace” it, his efforts aimed to end the ACA, which would have taken coverage from many.

claim: Mughal Gardens Renamed To Dr. Rajendra Prasad Garden
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Mughal Gardens at Rashtrapati Bhavan were renamed “Amrit Udyan” in January 2023. There is no official announcement renaming them to “Dr. Rajendra Prasad Garden.”

claim: Trumps January 2018 travel ban was unlawful.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The travel restrictions in effect in January 2018 were those of Presidential Proclamation 9645 (issued Sept. 2017). Although some lower courts found it likely unlawful, the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately upheld the proclamation in Trump v. Hawaii (June 2018), making it lawful. If the claim intended the first January 2017 order, that one was largely blocked by courts, but that was 2017, not 2018.

claim: Drinking vodka protects an individual against COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that drinking vodka or any alcohol prevents COVID-19. WHO and CDC state alcohol does not kill the virus inside the body and does not protect against infection. Only alcohol-based sanitizers work externally on hands/surfaces. Drinking alcohol can harm health and may weaken immune defenses. Uncertainty: none.

claim: BJP MP and former Union Minister Alphons Kannanthanam  sent his mother's dead body from Delhi to Kerala for the funeral without revealing she died of Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In May 2020, Alphons Kannanthanam’s mother died in Delhi and her body was flown to Kerala with official permissions. Kerala officials and Alphons stated she had tested negative for COVID-19, and the transport followed then-applicable SOPs for non-COVID deaths. Multiple fact-checks (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today) and local authorities (Kottayam district) clarified there was no concealment and she was not a COVID-19 case.

claim: Drinking traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) or steroids, along with antibiotics at the onset of symptoms cures COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  - COVID-19 is caused by a virus; antibiotics do not cure it and are only indicated for confirmed bacterial coinfection. - Systemic steroids (e.g., dexamethasone) benefit severe/critical cases requiring oxygen; early use in mild disease can be harmful and is not recommended by WHO/NIH. - Traditional Chinese medicine has no high‑quality evidence of curing COVID‑19; some products may relieve mild symptoms but are not proven to clear the virus or prevent progression.  Evidence‑based early treatment for eligible patients is with antivirals (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir), not routine antibiotics, steroids, or TCM.

claim: The Sarang Jeil Church of Jesus took preventative measure against coronavirus but the government spread the virus to prevent Rev. Jeon Kwang-hun attending the anti-government demonstration on August 15th.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence supports the claim that the government “spread the virus.” In August 2020, South Korea’s health authorities traced a large COVID-19 outbreak to Sarang Jeil Church, reporting hundreds of cases linked to the church and its attendees. Officials also said the church obstructed contact tracing and violated prevention guidelines (e.g., crowded services, poor compliance), and Pastor Jeon Kwang-hun himself tested positive shortly after the Aug. 15 rally. The assertion that the government seeded infections to block the demonstration is a baseless conspiracy theory.

claim: In 2016, 33 million Americans voted by mail.
response_text: TRUE.  About one-quarter of 2016 ballots were cast by mail. With roughly 136–137 million total votes, that translates to about 33 million mail ballots (per the U.S. Election Assistance Commission’s 2016 EAVS and other analyses).

claim: In Michigan, US one of the three key states that enabled Donald Trump to win the presidential election in 2016, the winning margin averaged out to just over two votes per precinct.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Donald Trump’s certified 2016 Michigan margin was 10,704 votes. Michigan has about 4,800–4,900 precincts, which yields roughly 10,704 ÷ 4,800 ≈ 2.2 votes per precinct—i.e., just over two. (This is a simple average; actual precinct margins varied.)

claim: The Trump administration disbanded the pandemic response team that was given to them.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2018, under National Security Adviser John Bolton, the Trump administration dissolved the National Security Council’s Directorate for Global Health Security and Biodefense—an NSC “pandemic response” unit created after Ebola during the Obama administration. Its lead (Adm. Timothy Ziemer) left and the team was dispersed, with some functions folded into other NSC offices. Other agencies (CDC, HHS) still had pandemic roles, so the broader federal capacity wasn’t eliminated, but the NSC pandemic team that the administration inherited was disbanded.

claim: Auto workers across Michigan could have lost their jobs if not for Barack Obama and Joe Biden
response_text: TRUE  Reasoning: In the 2008–09 crisis, GM and Chrysler were on the brink of collapse, threatening massive job losses in Michigan’s auto sector and supply chain. The Obama-Biden administration provided extensive support and guided the companies through structured bankruptcies, actions that independent analyses (e.g., Center for Automotive Research, White House Council of Economic Advisers) estimate preserved around 1–1.5 million U.S. jobs, with large effects in Michigan. Note: The Bush administration initiated emergency loans in late 2008, so credit is shared, and the exact number is a counterfactual estimate.

claim: Vice President Biden and President Obama assembled a pandemic playbook to make sure that America was prepared and protected.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During the Obama–Biden administration, the National Security Council’s Directorate for Global Health Security and Biodefense produced a 69-page “Playbook for Early Response to High-Consequence Emerging Infectious Disease Threats and Biological Incidents” (2016), developed after the Ebola crisis. It outlined roles, triggers, and actions for federal pandemic response. While Obama and Biden didn’t personally write it, it was created under their administration to guide preparedness and response.

claim: Nigeria is the largest producer of rice in Africa, ranking 14th in the world.
response_text: FALSE.  Nigeria is among Africa’s top rice producers and in recent FAO data is often the largest, but its global rank is not fixed at 14th; it typically falls roughly around 13th–16th depending on the year and dataset. Hence the specific claim “largest in Africa, ranking 14th in the world” is not reliably correct. (Some years Egypt has also led Africa, adding to the uncertainty.)

claim: There are many scientific studies saying masks should be worn only in enclosed spaces, such as in elevators and conference rooms, and not outdoors
response_text: FALSE.  Studies consistently show transmission risk is far higher indoors than outdoors, but they do not say masks “should be worn only” indoors or “not” outdoors. Evidence indicates outdoor transmission is rare but can occur, especially in crowded, close-contact settings, and public health guidance has recommended masks outdoors in such situations. Examples: Qian et al., 2020 (outbreaks overwhelmingly indoors) and Bulfone et al., 2021 (systematic review: outdoor transmission uncommon but possible).

claim: In the US, envelopes used for mail-in ballots in general elections reveal the party affiliation of the voter allowing postal workers to toss votes.
response_text: FALSE.  - In U.S. general elections, mail‑ballot return envelopes do not display a voter’s party. Ballots are secret, and the outer envelope typically shows name, address, signature line, and tracking/barcodes (for precinct/ballot style), not party affiliation. - Some states’ primary election materials may indicate party choice (since primaries are party-run contests), but that does not apply to general elections. - Tampering with mail, including ballots, is a federal crime (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1703), and there’s no evidence of systematic discarding based on party.

claim: In one of the states that determined the outcome" of the 2016 presidential race, "the winning margin averaged out to just two votes per precinct — two votes.
response_text: TRUE.  - Michigan, one of the pivotal 2016 states, was won by 10,704 votes. - Michigan has roughly 4,800 precincts, so the margin averaged about 10,704 ÷ 4,800 ≈ 2.2 votes per precinct. - Describing that as “just two votes per precinct” is a reasonable rounding, though slightly understated.

claim: Social Security beneficiaries count on the post office to get their checks.
response_text: FALSE.  Since March 2013, federal law requires Social Security and SSI benefits to be paid electronically (direct deposit or Direct Express debit card). Only rare exceptions receive paper checks, so most beneficiaries do not rely on the post office for their payments.

claim: Vice President Biden and President Obama assembled a pandemic playbook to make sure that America was prepared and protected. The Trump administration disbanded the pandemic response team that was given to them.
response_text: TRUE.  - Obama’s NSC produced and handed to the Trump transition a detailed “Playbook for Early Response to High-Consequence Emerging Infectious Disease Threats and Biological Incidents” in 2016–2017. - In 2018, the Trump White House eliminated the NSC’s dedicated Directorate for Global Health Security and Biodefense (often called the pandemic response team), folding its functions into other offices. While some responsibilities continued elsewhere, the standalone team was disbanded.

claim: Sweden, which does not require the wearing of masks in public, has had few deaths due to COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  Sweden did not impose a broad public mask mandate, but it did not have “few” COVID-19 deaths. Its per-capita death rate was high compared with its Nordic neighbors and substantial by international standards, with tens of thousands of deaths (roughly 20–25k total, about 2,000+ per million), especially high in 2020–2021.

claim: Beijing government announced that Chinese people should not travel to the United States or buy American-made products.
response_text: FALSE.  China has issued safety/travel advisories about the U.S. (e.g., warnings about crime or study risks) and some agencies restricted certain foreign devices at work, but there has been no official nationwide announcement telling Chinese citizens not to travel to the United States or not to buy American-made products. In fact, China resumed group tours to the U.S. in 2023–2024.

claim: MS Dhoni has exited the cricket team for refusing to campaign for BJP in Jharkhand election.
response_text: FALSE.  MS Dhoni did not leave the Indian cricket team over politics. He retired from Tests in 2014 and from international cricket on August 15, 2020, after a long break following the 2019 World Cup. There’s no credible evidence he exited because he refused to campaign for the BJP in Jharkhand. His non-selection post-2019 and eventual retirement were framed as cricketing decisions; he has continued playing in the IPL.

claim: warm water is effective in curing joint pain
response_text: FALSE.  Warm water/heat (e.g., warm baths, warm compresses, hydrotherapy) can temporarily relieve joint pain and stiffness by relaxing muscles and improving blood flow, but it does not cure the underlying causes of joint pain (such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, or injuries). Evidence supports short-term symptom relief as an adjunct therapy, not a curative treatment. Heat may also be inappropriate for acutely inflamed or swollen joints.

claim: Walmart stores have stopped accepting cash payments.
response_text: FALSE.  Walmart still accepts cash in its stores. Some self-checkout stations or certain services (e.g., online pickup/delivery) may be card-only, and during the 2020 coin shortage some locations encouraged card use, but Walmart has not ended in-store cash payments.

claim: warm water is effective in curing asthma
response_text: FALSE.  Asthma has no cure. Evidence-based management relies on controller and reliever medications (e.g., inhaled corticosteroids, bronchodilators). Warm water or warm fluids may temporarily soothe the throat or help loosen mucus, but they do not treat the underlying airway inflammation or “cure” asthma.

claim: Facebook deleted a photo of Melania Trump with her sister and mother.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence shows Facebook deleted such a photo. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) found the claim was an engagement-bait rumor; the image of Melania with her mother and sister circulated widely and remained available on Facebook. Uncertainty: none beyond lack of any documented takedown.

claim: UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson apologised for colonial rule in India.
response_text: FALSE.  Boris Johnson did not issue an official apology for British colonial rule in India. During his tenure, UK leaders reiterated regret over specific events (e.g., the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre), but stopped short of a formal apology for colonialism, and no such apology from Johnson exists.

claim: Cold water affects the internal walls of the stomach. It affects the large intestine and results in cancer
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no scientific evidence that drinking cold water damages the stomach or large intestine or causes cancer. Major cancer organizations do not list cold beverages as a risk factor. By contrast, very hot drinks (above about 65°C/149°F) have been linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer. Cold water may transiently trigger spasms or discomfort in some people, but it does not cause cancer.

claim: warm water is effective in curing migraine
response_text: FALSE.  Warm water (drinking it or using heat) is not an evidence‑based cure for migraine. While hydration and heat on tense neck/shoulder muscles may provide comfort for some people, there’s no robust evidence that warm water treats the migraine process itself. Effective migraine management typically involves specific acute and preventive medications and trigger management.

claim: Sweden, despite never having had lockdown, has a lower COVID-19 death rate than Spain, Italy, and the United Kingdom.
response_text: TRUE.  By cumulative COVID-19 deaths per capita, Sweden ended the pandemic with fewer deaths per million than the UK, Italy, and Spain (e.g., OWID/WHO totals through 2023–2024 put Sweden ~2,3k per million vs Spain ~2.5k, Italy ~3.2k, UK ~3.3k). Sweden did not implement a nationwide stay-at-home lockdown, though it did use targeted restrictions.

claim: warm water is effective in curing epilepsy
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that warm water treats or cures epilepsy. Effective treatments include anti-seizure medications, certain diets (e.g., ketogenic), neurostimulation, and surgery in selected cases. In fact, hot or warm water can trigger reflex seizures in some people (“hot-water epilepsy”), so it may be a risk rather than a remedy.

claim: The United States Postal Service advises customers to never send cash in the mail.
response_text: TRUE.  USPS (including the Postal Inspection Service) explicitly advises customers not to send cash in the mail due to theft/loss risk, recommending money orders, checks, or electronic payment instead. While mailing cash isn’t illegal, USPS guidance says “don’t send cash”; if unavoidable, use Registered Mail and insurance.

claim: Tricolour to be hoisted for first time at Niagara Falls to mark 74th Indian Independence Day.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2020 (74th Independence Day), Niagara Falls was illuminated in the Indian tricolour—something that had already been done in earlier years (e.g., 2017). The “first time” flag-hoisting news pertained to Times Square in New York, not Niagara Falls.

claim: Former U.S. President George W. Bush supports the Democratic presidential ticket of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.
response_text: FALSE.  George W. Bush did not endorse or publicly support the Biden–Harris ticket. His spokesman said he would not be getting involved in the 2020 presidential race, and he made no endorsement. While some alumni from his administration backed Biden (“43 Alumni for Biden”), Bush himself did not.

claim: The United States has reached herd immunity for COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 continues to circulate in the U.S. with recurring waves driven by highly transmissible, immune-evasive variants and waning protection. While population immunity reduces severe disease, it has not been sufficient to stop sustained transmission, and no public health authority has declared herd immunity achieved.

claim: The Annabelle doll escaped from the Warren's Occult Museum on 14th August 2020 at 3am.
response_text: FALSE.  This was an internet hoax that trended on August 14, 2020. Tony Spera, the Warrens’ son‑in‑law and curator of the collection, posted a video that day showing the Annabelle doll still secured in its case. The Warren’s Occult Museum had also been closed since 2018, so there was no “escape,” and the specific “3 a.m.” detail is fabricated.

claim: Vitamin D prevents COVID-19 infection and reduces severity.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Large randomized trials and meta-analyses have not shown that vitamin D supplementation prevents SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, and treatment trials have not demonstrated consistent reductions in hospitalization, ICU admission, or mortality. Health agencies (e.g., NIH, NICE/WHO) advise there is insufficient evidence to use vitamin D specifically to prevent or treat COVID‑19, though maintaining adequate vitamin D for general health is still recommended. Some small, biased studies suggested benefit, but overall evidence does not support the claim.

claim: The media is ignoring the tragic death of a 5-year-old boy who was fatally shot by a neighbor in Wilson, North Carolina, on August 9, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  The case — the Aug. 9, 2020 shooting death of 5-year-old Cannon Hinnant in Wilson, N.C. — received significant local and national coverage. Local outlets (WRAL, Wilson Times, News & Observer) reported it immediately, and national outlets soon followed, including AP (syndicated widely), CNN, NBC News, ABC News, Fox News, USA Today, People, and the New York Post. Fact-checkers also debunked claims that the story was ignored. Coverage may not have been wall-to-wall, but it was not ignored.

claim: The murder of Oscar Grant, by a police officer in the United States, was never prosecuted by the DA.
response_text: FALSE.  Alameda County’s District Attorney charged BART officer Johannes Mehserle with murder for the 2009 shooting of Oscar Grant. He was prosecuted, tried (venue moved to Los Angeles), and the jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter in 2010. He served a jail sentence.

claim: Former president Pranab Mukherjee from India has passed away.
response_text: TRUE — Pranab Mukherjee, former President of India, died on 31 August 2020.

claim: Kamala Harris called Joe Biden 'A Racist And A Rapist'
response_text: FALSE.  Harris did not call Biden “a racist” or “a rapist.” In the 2019 primary debate she explicitly said, “I do not believe you are a racist,” while criticizing his past positions on busing. She never labeled him a rapist; when asked about allegations, she said accusers should be heard and later said she believed Biden. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, PolitiFact) have debunked the “racist and rapist” quote as fabricated.

claim: COVID-19 has caused more casualties than WWI; the Korean, Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan-US wars; and 9/11.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: In war statistics, “casualties” usually means killed plus wounded. World War I caused about 37–40+ million casualties (roughly 15–20 million deaths and ~21 million wounded). COVID-19 has caused about 7 million confirmed deaths worldwide, with excess-mortality estimates around 15–30 million—well below WWI’s total casualties. COVID deaths do exceed the death tolls of the Korean, Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan wars and 9/11 individually. Uncertainty: If one uses “casualties” to mean deaths only, COVID may exceed WWI deaths, but not WWI total casualties.

claim: Creativity is contagious. Pass it on was said by Albert Einstein
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is widely misattributed to Albert Einstein. No reliable source (Einstein’s writings, speeches, or early biographies) contains it, and references tie it to much later aphoristic usage (echoing “Kindness is contagious; pass it on”). Wikiquote and Quote Investigator list it as misattributed.

claim: Kamala Harris said "And once Trump’s gone and we have regained our rightful place in the White House, look out if you supported him and endorsed his actions, because we’ll be coming for you next".
response_text: FALSE.  Fact-checkers (Reuters, PolitiFact, Snopes) found no record of Kamala Harris ever saying this. It appears to be a fabricated quote circulated in memes; no speech, interview, or transcript supports it.

claim: Russia has successfully developed a vaccine for Covid-19 and it has passed all checks.
response_text: FALSE.  Russia announced Sputnik V in August 2020 before completing large Phase 3 trials, so it had not passed the standard checks at the time. Although later data showed efficacy, Sputnik V never received WHO Emergency Use Listing or EMA approval due to outstanding data/manufacturing issues. Thus it cannot be said to have “passed all checks.”

claim: Kamala Harris was descended from enslavers, and this is an inconvenient part of her history and this is a deep dark secret.
response_text: FALSE.  - Harris’ father, Donald J. Harris, wrote in 2018 that their Jamaican family lineage includes a slave owner (he named Hamilton Brown). Genealogists and fact-checkers have noted the specific link is unproven, though plausible. - Regardless, it is not a “deep dark secret”: her father publicly disclosed it, and it has been reported in the press.

claim: Democratic California Sen. Kamala Harris was the Alameda County district attorney when Oscar Grant, a 22-year-old black man, was shot and killed in Oakland, California.
response_text: FALSE.  Kamala Harris was San Francisco’s district attorney in 2009. Oscar Grant was shot on Jan. 1, 2009 in Oakland; the Alameda County DAs then were Tom Orloff (who filed the case) and, later that year, Nancy O’Malley—not Harris.

claim: Sarah Huckabee Sanders said "it's not the government's job to protect my health" and that "when you trade liberty for safety, you end up losing both"
response_text: FALSE.  Those lines are widely misattributed to Sarah Huckabee Sanders. They trace to conservative writer Bethany S. Mandel, who tweeted in 2020: “It’s not the government’s job to protect my health… When you trade liberty for safety, you end up losing both.” Sanders has criticized COVID mandates, but there’s no reliable record of her saying this exact quote.

claim: President Trump Says He Hopes The NFL Season Gets Canceled Due To Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  Trump repeatedly said he wanted sports to return and expected the NFL season to start on time during the early COVID-19 period (e.g., April 2020 briefings). The claim that he hoped the NFL season would be canceled traces to satirical/fake-news posts and lacks credible sourcing.

claim: Russia has developed a new vaccine to fight COVID-19.
response_text: TRUE.  Russia developed multiple COVID-19 vaccines, notably Sputnik V (Gam-COVID-Vac) in 2020, and later Sputnik Light, EpiVacCorona, CoviVac, and others (e.g., nasal and adolescent formulations). Hence the claim is accurate.

claim: All regular Indian Railways trains cancelled till 30th September, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: During COVID-19, Indian Railways suspended regular time‑tabled passenger services “until further notice,” not specifically till 30 September 2020. Meanwhile, special trains (e.g., Rajdhani specials and other pairs of special trains) continued to operate, so not all trains were cancelled. Some reports mentioned 30 September, but the official status was suspension until further notice with special services running.

claim: COVID-19 virus is airborne.
response_text: TRUE.  Briefly: SARS‑CoV‑2 spreads through inhalation of virus‑laden aerosols that can remain suspended in the air and travel beyond close contact, especially indoors with poor ventilation. Major health agencies (e.g., WHO/CDC) recognize airborne (aerosol) transmission as a key route, though not the only one.

claim: LITTLE CAESARS IS OFFERING FREE PIZZA TO ANYONE WHO SHARES AND COMMENTS ON A FACEBOOK POST
response_text: FALSE.  This is a common Facebook “engagement bait” scam. Impostor pages posing as Little Caesars post fake giveaways that promise free pizza if you share and comment. Little Caesars has not run a legitimate promotion that gives free pizza to anyone for sharing/commenting; fact-checkers have debunked these posts, and Facebook’s rules prohibit requiring shares for entry. Only trust offers announced on Little Caesars’ verified website/app or official social accounts.

claim: Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos has offered free one-day Prime shipping for all mail-in ballots.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible announcement or reporting that Jeff Bezos (who hasn’t been Amazon’s CEO since 2021) offered free Prime one-day shipping for mail-in ballots. Prime shipping applies to Amazon purchases, not general mail. U.S. ballots must be returned via official channels (USPS or designated drop-off sites) per state rules, and Amazon doesn’t handle ballot return.

claim: The NZ Green Party should have delivered 16,000 KiwiBuild houses by now (10/08/2020). They’ve only managed just around 400. And so to promise 5,000 extra houses a year is nothing more than just wishful thinking and is destined to go the same way as KiwiBuild.
response_text: FALSE.  - KiwiBuild was a Labour-led policy (Ministers Phil Twyford then Megan Woods). The Green Party was not responsible for delivering KiwiBuild. - The original ramp-up targets were 1,000 homes in year 1, 5,000 in year 2, and 10,000 in year 3—i.e., 16,000 cumulatively by around July 2021, not by August 2020. Those interim targets were scrapped in the September 2019 “reset.” - By mid–late 2020, KiwiBuild homes delivered were in the hundreds (roughly 500–600), not “16,000,” so the benchmark used in the claim is wrong on both responsibility and timeline.  Uncertainty: exact delivered count in August 2020 varies by source/month, but it was far below thousands and closer to ~600 than “around 400.”

claim: Vaccines have caused deaths in the Philippines.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: While deaths after vaccination are usually coincidental, Philippine reviews of the 2016–2017 Dengvaxia program found a small number of pediatric deaths consistent with vaccine‑related severe dengue in children without prior dengue infection. Most reported post‑vaccination deaths were not causally linked, but a few were judged likely related. (Causality assessments are complex, so exact numbers remain debated.)

claim: Amid the coronavirus pandemic, Facebook has changed its privacy rules, allowing it to use pictures and posts shared by users in lawsuits against them.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a recycled hoax. During the COVID-19 pandemic, posts falsely claimed Facebook (and Instagram) changed privacy rules and could use your photos/posts “in lawsuits against you.” Facebook did not make such a change. Its longstanding terms grant a license to host and display user content, but they did not newly authorize using your content “against you” in court. Copy‑paste “privacy notices” have no effect. Major fact-checkers (Reuters, AP, Snopes) debunked this claim.

claim: A video shows people in Pakistan are uprooting the trees planted as part of Imran Khan’s plantation campaign because they consider planting trees as "unIslamic".
response_text: FALSE  Briefly: The video was miscaptioned. Fact-checks traced it to a local sapling collection/removal incident unrelated to religion or Imran Khan’s campaign; people were taking or relocating newly planted saplings, not calling tree-planting “un-Islamic.” There’s no credible evidence of a religious motive, and planting trees is in fact encouraged in Islam. (Some uncertainty on the exact location/date of the clip, but consistent debunks show the “un-Islamic” claim is false.)

claim: Donald Trump's payroll tax deferral could leave American workers liable for thousands of dollars during tax season and could potentially leave programs like Social Security and Medicare weakened.
response_text: TRUE.  - The 2020 executive action deferred (did not forgive) the employee share of Social Security payroll tax (6.2%) for many workers from Sept–Dec 2020. Those amounts were still owed in 2021, typically via increased withholding, leaving some workers “on the hook” for up to roughly $2,000+ depending on earnings—i.e., potentially “thousands” of dollars.  - Payroll taxes fund Social Security (and a separate payroll tax funds Medicare). While the deferral itself didn’t include Medicare and was temporary, Trump also said he wanted to forgive the deferred taxes and pursue permanent payroll tax cuts. Forgiveness or permanent cuts without replacement funding could weaken Social Security’s finances (and broader payroll-tax-funded programs), as SSA’s actuary warned.   Note: The deferral by itself didn’t cut Medicare’s tax, but the concern about weakening such programs is reasonable if cuts were made permanent.

claim: Choluteca bridge withstood a hurricane in 1998 but the river changed course and no longer flows under the bridge.
response_text: FALSE.  Hurricane Mitch (1998) did destroy the approach roads to the new Choluteca Bridge, and the river’s main channel shifted during the floods. But the idea that the river no longer flows under the bridge is a popular myth/misinterpretation. Water continued to pass under parts of the bridge, and subsequent works reconnected the highway; the bridge remains in use with the river beneath it. (Some uncertainty stems from photos taken right after Mitch that made the river’s temporary side channel look like a full relocation.)

claim: T cells may play a role in the body’s immune response against the virus SARS-CoV-2
response_text: TRUE.  T cells are a key part of adaptive immunity to SARS-CoV-2. Infected and vaccinated individuals develop SARS‑CoV‑2–specific CD4+ T cells (which help B cells and coordinate responses) and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (which kill infected cells). These responses have been repeatedly documented and are linked to viral control and protection.

claim: According to Harry Roque, even if 10,000 people die, 10 million COVID-19 cases in the country will not be a loss.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Harry Roque saying this. The quote circulated as a fabricated/misattributed meme on social media and has been debunked by Philippine fact-checkers. No credible transcript, briefing, or news report supports that he said “even if 10,000 people die, 10 million COVID-19 cases … will not be a loss.”

claim: The Australian govt is handing out $25,000 to all nursing homes who label covid as the main cause of deaths on death certificates.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no Australian government program that pays nursing homes $25,000 for listing COVID-19 as the main cause of death. - Aged care facilities do not complete death certificates; doctors or coroners do, following strict WHO/ABS guidelines. - Government COVID supports for aged care have reimbursed outbreak-related costs or supported staff, not cause-of-death coding. - The $25,000 figure likely stems from confusion with the unrelated HomeBuilder grant.

claim: Massive international study shows a much lower COVID-19 mortality rate in countries where hydroxychloroquine was prescribed to patients.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: No credible “massive international” study has shown lower COVID-19 mortality from hydroxychloroquine. Large, well-run randomized trials (e.g., the WHO Solidarity trial across many countries and the UK RECOVERY trial) found no mortality benefit and led to stopping HCQ arms for futility. A widely publicized international observational analysis (Surgisphere/Lancet) was retracted, and country-level ecological comparisons are confounded and not evidence of causation.

claim: Balbir Singh converted to Islam after he participated in the demolition of Babri Masjid
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reports (e.g., Indian Express, Scroll) document that a Haryana man named Balbir Singh, who says he took part in the 1992 Babri Masjid demolition, later converted to Islam (taking the name Mohammad Aamir) out of remorse and worked to build mosques. Note: his precise role in the demolition is based largely on his own account rather than a court finding.

claim: 82% of the public are wearing face masks on Translink buses and trains.
response_text: TRUE.  Translink (Northern Ireland) reported in mid-2020, shortly after face coverings became mandatory, that roughly 82% of passengers on its buses and trains were wearing masks. Note: this was an observational estimate at that time, not a permanent or current figure.

claim: 330,000 people a day are being tested for Covid-19 under the Test and Trace programme in the United Kingdom
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: - The “330,000” figure referred to tests processed UK‑wide, not unique people. - It also included tests outside the NHS Test and Trace system (e.g., surveillance/antibody). - NHS Test and Trace operates in England only, so citing a UK-wide number is misleading. - The number of people tested under NHS Test and Trace was substantially lower than 330,000 per day.  Minor uncertainty: exact daily totals varied by date, but the claim conflates tests with people and UK with England.

claim: Madagascar has found a coronavirus medicine that can wipe out the virus at any stage within a period of six days.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The claim refers to Madagascar’s herbal tonic “COVID-Organics” (Artemisia annua–based). In 2020 the WHO and researchers noted there was no credible clinical evidence that it cures COVID-19, let alone “wipes out the virus at any stage within six days.” Subsequent evaluations and trials did not demonstrate proven efficacy or regulatory approval as a curative treatment.

claim: The GOP lawyer who helped Kanye West get on the ballot in Wisconsin USA is actively working for Donald Trump's campaign.
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2020, GOP attorney Lane Ruhland was filmed delivering Kanye West’s nomination papers to Wisconsin election officials. At the same time, court filings show she was representing Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. in an active lawsuit in Wisconsin. (Kanye ultimately was kept off the Wisconsin ballot for late filing, but the lawyer’s concurrent work for Trump’s campaign is documented.)

claim: Communist government in Kerala India impose a blackout on August 5 to prevent people from watching the Ram Mandir bhoomi pujan ceremony.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no state-imposed blackout in Kerala on August 5, 2020. Kerala State Electricity Board officials and multiple fact-checks reported no government order or deliberate power cut to block the Ram Mandir bhoomi pujan telecast; any outages were localized/weather-related.

claim: Large country-randomized controlled trial in 2.7 billion people shows 79.1% lower death rate in COVID-19 patients treated with hydroxychloroquine
response_text: FALSE.  There has been no country‑randomized controlled trial of hydroxychloroquine involving 2.7 billion people. The figure and “79.1% lower death rate” claim trace to non-randomized, ecological country comparisons (e.g., websites like c19study/hcqmeta), which are highly confounded and not RCTs. Large, well-conducted randomized trials (e.g., RECOVERY and WHO SOLIDARITY) found no mortality benefit of hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19, and systematic reviews conclude it is ineffective for reducing death.

claim: The U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar's visit to Taiwan in August 2020 is a breach of international rules.
response_text: FALSE.  Azar’s 2020 visit did not breach international law. The United States maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan under its One China policy and the Taiwan Relations Act, and U.S. law (the 2018 Taiwan Travel Act) encourages high-level visits. China condemned the trip as violating its One China principle and bilateral communiqués, but those are political/bilateral positions, not binding international rules prohibiting such visits.

claim: The USA has more COVID-19 cases, because they do more tests
response_text: FALSE.  More testing finds more infections, but it doesn’t create them. The U.S. repeatedly had high test-positivity rates, hospitalizations, deaths, and seroprevalence, indicating genuinely higher transmission—not just more testing. In parts of the pandemic the U.S. didn’t even test the most per capita, yet still had high case and death rates.

claim: France approves the use of HCQ for treatment of Covid 19. After trials proved successful. 800 hospital have commenced using it.
response_text: FALSE.  France did not “approve” hydroxychloroquine after successful trials. In late March 2020, France temporarily allowed HCQ only in hospitals and under strict medical supervision for certain COVID-19 patients while trials were ongoing—not because trials had proved it effective. The claim that “800 hospitals” began using it is unsupported. France later halted its use for COVID-19 outside clinical trials due to lack of proven benefit and safety concerns.

claim: At Trump’s Tulsa rally there were 12000 people, not 6000 as reported by Axios and others.
response_text: FALSE.  The Tulsa Fire Department’s official count for Trump’s June 20, 2020 rally at the BOK Center was about 6,200 people inside the arena. The 12,000 figure was a campaign claim and not corroborated by local officials. Axios and others accurately reported the roughly 6,000–6,200 attendance.

claim: Angela Merkel is the daughter of Adolf Hitler, Justin Trudeau is the son of Fidel Castro and Barbara Bush is the daughter of Aleister Crowley.
response_text: FALSE.  - Angela Merkel: Born 1954 to Horst and Herlind Kasner; Adolf Hitler died in 1945 and had no acknowledged children. - Justin Trudeau: Born 1971 to Pierre Trudeau and Margaret Sinclair; the Trudeaus first met Fidel Castro in 1976. No credible evidence (or DNA) supports the Castro claim. - Barbara Bush: Born 1925 to Marvin Pierce and Pauline Robinson; no credible evidence links her mother to Aleister Crowley.  These are debunked conspiracy theories.

claim: There is now a 10-year rule. If you damage a federal property such as courthouse, you go to jail for 10 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Federal law (18 U.S.C. § 1361) has long provided that willfully damaging U.S. government property is punishable by up to 10 years in prison if the damage exceeds $1,000 (otherwise up to 1 year). It is not a new “10-year rule,” and the sentence is not automatic or mandatory; it’s a maximum penalty subject to judicial discretion and the facts of the case.

claim: Trump did more for the Black community than anybody with the possible exception of Abraham Lincoln.
response_text: FALSE.  - The claim is hyperbolic and not supported by historians. Many figures clearly did more for Black Americans than Trump, including Lyndon B. Johnson (Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965, Fair Housing Act 1968), Ulysses S. Grant (enforcement acts against the KKK), Harry Truman (desegregated the military), and leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall. - Trump’s notable actions (First Step Act, HBCU funding bill, Opportunity Zones, low pre-pandemic Black unemployment) are significant but bipartisan/long‑running efforts with mixed or limited measured impact compared to the transformative civil-rights milestones above.

claim: With African Americans, Trump is doing very well. They had the best employment numbers they’ve ever had. ... They were making more money than they ever made.
response_text: TRUE.  - BLS data show the Black unemployment rate fell to its lowest on record in 2019 (since the series began in 1972). - Census data show real median income for Black households hit a record high in 2019, and Black poverty fell to a record low.  Caveats: These gains were part of a long post‑Great Recession recovery and many were disrupted by the 2020 pandemic; also, “doing very well” with Black voters politically is debatable.

claim: The late Rep. John Lewis, D-Ga., didn't come to Trump's inauguration. He didn't come to Trump's State of the Union speeches.
response_text: TRUE.  - John Lewis publicly boycotted Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration. - He skipped Trump’s State of the Union addresses: he boycotted in 2018 and 2019, and did not attend in 2020 while undergoing cancer treatment.

claim: California is going to send tens of millions of ballots to California, all over the place.
response_text: FALSE.  In 2020, California mailed ballots to all registered voters (about 21–22 million) at their registered addresses, not “all over the place” or to “anyone.” They were not sent “to California” from elsewhere; they were sent within the state to voters on the official rolls with standard verification safeguards.

claim: Covid deaths are way down from where it was … It spiked, but now it's going down again. It's going down in Arizona. It's going down in Florida. It's going down in Texas.
response_text: FALSE.  Context matters: This quote was made in late July 2020. At that time, COVID-19 deaths were not “going down” in Arizona, Florida, or Texas; they were rising. Seven-day averages of daily deaths in all three states, as well as nationally, were climbing through late July and into early August 2020 (per Johns Hopkins/NYT/COVID Tracking Project data). Any declines came later. Uncertainty: exact daily figures vary by source, but the trend was clearly upward then.

claim: Ghislaine Maxwell's boyfriend Jeffrey Epstein died in jail and people are still trying to figure out how did it happened, was it suicide, was he killed.
response_text: TRUE.  Jeffrey Epstein died in jail in August 2019. The New York City medical examiner ruled it a suicide by hanging, and multiple investigations found serious security failures but no evidence of homicide. However, public debate and speculation continue. Note: Epstein was Ghislaine Maxwell’s longtime associate and former boyfriend.

claim: COVID-19 has infected fewer people than H1N1 virus, but “media hysteria” has prompted an overblown response.
response_text: FALSE.  - COVID-19 has infected far more people than the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. Confirmed COVID cases exceed 700 million, with serology indicating billions infected; reported deaths ~7 million (excess deaths likely >15 million).   - The 2009 H1N1 pandemic is estimated to have infected roughly 11–21% of the global population (hundreds of millions to ~1.4 billion) with 151,700–575,400 deaths.   - “Media hysteria” is an opinion, not a verifiable fact; public-health responses reflected COVID-19’s higher severity and mortality.  Note: Exact infection counts are estimates, but the direction is clear—COVID-19 infected more people and caused far more deaths than H1N1.

claim: The violence in Portland is getting better since federal agents went in. They've arrested a lot of people.
response_text: FALSE.  Reporting during the July 2020 Portland protests shows the arrival of federal agents coincided with larger crowds and more intense nightly clashes around the federal courthouse, not an improvement. Local and national outlets, as well as city/state officials, said the federal presence escalated tensions. As for arrests, federal authorities reported only dozens of arrests during that period—significant but not “a lot” relative to the scale and duration of the protests. (Timing of the claim isn’t specified, but this reflects the period when federal agents were deployed.)

claim: Millions of ballots are being mailed, nobody even knows where they’re going.
response_text: FALSE.  Election officials mail ballots to specific registered voters at the addresses on file, not randomly. States maintain and update voter rolls, verify addresses (e.g., via DMV/USPS data), and use barcodes or unique identifiers to track each ballot. While occasional mail issues or outdated addresses can cause some ballots to be returned undeliverable, it’s not the case that “nobody knows where they’re going.”

claim: South Korea have spikes of Covid cases and nobody knows if they only had 300 deaths.
response_text: FALSE.  South Korea did see spikes in COVID-19 cases, but its reporting has been transparent and widely trusted. The country’s cumulative COVID deaths are far higher than 300 (in the tens of thousands), so it’s not true that “nobody knows” or that they “only had 300 deaths.”

claim: Devender Sharma fabricated false covid-19 positive reports for patients  in order to get them admitted for kidney harvesting.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Devender (Devinder) Sharma, the so‑called “Doctor Death,” ran an illegal kidney transplant racket and committed murders in the 1990s–early 2000s. He was arrested in 2004 and re-arrested in 2020 after jumping parole. Credible reports do not show he fabricated COVID‑19 positive reports or harvested kidneys from COVID patients; that allegation appears to conflate his earlier crimes with pandemic-era rumors.

claim: "Depending on which study you look at," he said, "either 68% or 5 out of 6 individuals ... are making more on unemployment than they did on the job."
response_text: TRUE  - A May 2020 University of Chicago analysis (Ganong, Noel, Vavra) found about 68% of eligible unemployed workers received benefits exceeding their lost wages due to the $600/week CARES Act supplement. - A June 2020 CBO analysis estimated that, if the $600 supplement were extended, roughly five out of six unemployment recipients would receive weekly benefits exceeding what they could expect to earn from work during that period.  Caveat: These figures apply to recipients/eligible workers during the pandemic’s $600 top-up and use assumptions about wages and benefits; they don’t mean “all individuals” generally.

claim: US Washington mayor exempted members of Congress from the mandatory 14 day quarantine, after travelling to a coronavirus high risk area to attend the funeral of John Lewis.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In July 2020, D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser issued a 14‑day quarantine requirement for travelers returning from “high‑risk” areas (which included Georgia). The order contained an exemption for “essential” government travel, including travel to maintain federal government operations. Bowser’s office said that members of Congress traveling to Rep. John Lewis’s funeral in Atlanta qualified under that exemption and thus were not required to quarantine on return. This was not a special carve‑out created after the fact, but an application of the standing exemption.

claim: Devender Sharma ran an illegal kidney racket on the pretext of coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Dr. Devender (Davinder) Sharma was convicted for running an illegal kidney transplant racket in the late 1990s–early 2000s and for multiple murders of taxi drivers. He was re-arrested in 2020 after jumping parole, but there is no credible evidence that he ran a kidney racket using the coronavirus as a pretext. His kidney racket predates COVID-19 by many years.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech will be available on the market on August 15, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Bharat Biotech’s COVID-19 vaccine (Covaxin) was not available on August 15, 2020. That date was an aspirational target mentioned in an ICMR letter that drew criticism. Covaxin received emergency use authorization in India on January 3, 2021, with rollout starting mid-January 2021.

claim: Kenya's judiciary does not get even 1% of the national budget.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent Kenyan budgets allocate well under 1% to the Judiciary. Examples: - 2022/23: about KSh 18.9 billion out of ~KSh 3.3 trillion (~0.6%). - 2023/24: about KSh 22–23 billion out of ~KSh 3.68 trillion (~0.6%). - 2024/25 (proposed): roughly KSh 23–24 billion out of ~KSh 3.9–4.0 trillion (~0.6%).  Across recent years the Judiciary’s share has consistently been below 1% of the national budget.

claim: In 2018, South African police service officers were accused of 217 cases of torture and 3,661 cases of assault
response_text: TRUE.  According to South Africa’s Independent Police Investigative Directorate (IPID) 2018/19 annual report, there were 217 complaints of torture and 3,661 of assault against SAPS members. Note: these are complaints for the 2018/19 financial year (not strictly the calendar year 2018).

claim: A married couple in Florida, Tito and Amanda Watts, was arrested for selling fake golden tickets to heaven to hundreds of people.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a long-running hoax from fake/satire sites. No credible news or police records support such arrests, and the mugshots used with the story were misattributed from unrelated cases. Debunked by Snopes as false.

claim: There is a ‘global average’ for the number of judges and magistrates to number of people
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: While datasets (e.g., UNODC’s Crime Trends Survey) report judges/magistrates per 100,000 population by country, there is no single, authoritative “global average” that is standardized and accepted. Definitions differ across legal systems, data coverage is uneven, and any computed average (weighted or unweighted) would be arbitrary and not officially recognized.

claim: Michigan Senator Gary Peters is known for doing nothing, where he has skipped 84% of small business hearings and 89% of hearings on China.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Those percentages come from a 2020 attack that cherry‑picked and miscounted hearings (including many from committees/subcommittees Peters didn’t serve on or that conflicted with other duties). There’s no authoritative metric showing he “skipped 84%” of small‑business hearings or “89%” of China‑related hearings. Independent fact‑checkers (e.g., Washington Post Fact Checker, PolitiFact, Detroit Free Press) rated the claim false/misleading. Also, the “known for doing nothing” line is opinion; Peters has a high voting attendance and has been recognized for legislative effectiveness. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Kenya's courts dispose of about 300,000 cases every year
response_text: TRUE  Reason: Judiciary of Kenya annual reports show courts dispose of several hundred thousand cases per year, typically in the 300,000–400,000+ range (pandemic year lower, recent years higher). So “about 300,000” is a reasonable ballpark, though figures vary by year. Uncertainty: exact totals differ annually.

claim: In Kenya now with a population of about 48 million, we have one judge serving over 300,000 people
response_text: TRUE (roughly). - Kenya’s population was about 48 million around 2016–2018. - The total number of judges (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court, Employment and Labour Relations Court, and Environment and Land Court) was roughly 150–170, giving a ratio near 1 judge per 280,000–320,000 people—i.e., “over 300,000” is broadly accurate. - Note: This excludes magistrates; including them would lower the ratio.
