claim: Soon Ram Mandir will also have a kitchen and Bhojanalya, where devotees visiting the town will be offered free meals and the ‘Raghupati’ laddus as Prasadam
response_text: TRUE  Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra officials (notably Champat Rai) have said the Ayodhya Ram Mandir complex will include an Annapurna kitchen and a Bhojanalaya to serve free meals to visiting devotees, and that “Raghupati laddus” will be the temple’s prasadam. These facilities were announced as part of the temple’s planned amenities following the inauguration.

claim: Kenya has one magistrate serving over 77,000 people
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Recent Judiciary data put Kenya’s magistrates at roughly 500–600, while the population is about 50–55 million. That yields roughly 80,000–110,000 people per magistrate—i.e., well over 77,000. Exact figures vary by year, but the ratio remains above 77,000.

claim: With a population of about 48 million, Kenya has only one judge serving over 300,000 people
response_text: TRUE.  Kenya’s superior courts have only around 150–170 judges. With a population near 48 million, that works out to roughly one judge per about 280,000–320,000 people—i.e., “over 300,000” is a fair approximation. Note: this counts judges, not magistrates; including several hundred magistrates would make the ratio much lower. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by year and appointments.

claim: 1.110,000 Delicious Laddus are being prepared for the Bhoomi Poojan Ceremony at Sri Ramachandra Janmabhoomi Ayodhya
response_text: FALSE  Multiple news reports around the August 2020 Bhoomi Pujan in Ayodhya said about 1.11 lakh laddus (111,000) were being prepared/distributed. The claim’s figure “1.110,000” reads as 1,110,000, which is not supported. If the intent was 1.11 lakh (111,000), that would be accurate, but as written it overstates the number.

claim: Kenya has an average of 400,000 cases being filed in our courts every year
response_text: TRUE.  Judiciary of Kenya annual reports in recent years typically show roughly 350,000–470,000 new cases filed per year, which averages out to about 400,000. Exact figures vary by year (and dipped during COVID), but “about 400,000” is a reasonable average. Minor uncertainty arises from the specific years included in the “average.”

claim: Kenya has one magistrate serving over 77,000 people
response_text: TRUE.  Rough math from recent figures suggests this is accurate: with Kenya’s population around 55 million and roughly 650–750 magistrates, that’s about 1 magistrate per 73,000–85,000 people—i.e., over 77,000 in many years. Exact ratios vary by year as staffing changes, but the claim is broadly consistent.

claim: an average of 400,000 cases being filed in Kenya's courts every year
response_text: TRUE.  Kenya’s Judiciary annual “State of the Judiciary” and statistical reports typically show roughly 350,000–450,000 new cases filed each year, with several years reporting just over 400,000. While the exact figure varies by year (and dipped during COVID), the multi-year average is around 400,000.

claim: Kenya President Uhuru Kenyatta said that health experts had “indicated that levels of the positivity rate countrywide have fallen from a high of 13% in June to 8% in August” and described this as “very encouraging”.
response_text: TRUE.  In his 26 August 2020 national address on Covid-19, President Uhuru Kenyatta said health experts indicated Kenya’s test-positivity rate had declined “from a high of 13% in June to 8% in August,” calling the trend “very encouraging.” (State House Kenya presidential address; widely reported by Kenyan media at the time.)

claim: The judiciary does not even get 1% of the Kenyan national budget.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent Kenyan budgets allocate well under 1% to the Judiciary. For example: - FY 2023/24: about KSh 23 billion out of roughly KSh 3.6–3.7 trillion (~0.6%). - FY 2024/25: about KSh 24–26 billion out of roughly KSh 3.9–4.0 trillion (~0.6–0.7%).  Thus, the Judiciary’s share has been below 1% of the national budget. (Exact figures vary by source, but the share remains under 1%.)

claim: Since 2002 South Africa’s police force has grown by 50%
response_text: TRUE  SAPS headcount rose from roughly 120–130k in 2002/03 to about 198–200k by 2011/12—an increase of around 50–60%. Note: numbers declined somewhat after that peak, so the increase versus 2002 depends on the endpoint, but the “since 2002 … 50%” claim is supported by the 2000s–early 2010s data.

claim: face coverings/masks became “mandatory” in shops and indoor public spaces in Northern Ireland on 1 August 2020
response_text: FALSE.  In Northern Ireland, face coverings became legally mandatory in shops and certain indoor public areas on 10 August 2020. From 1–9 August there was only an advisory “grace period” encouraging use, not a legal requirement. (Masks on public transport had already been mandatory since mid-July.)

claim: Social distancing, to prevent the spread of coronavirus was not practiced at the funeral of civil rights icon, John Lewis.
response_text: FALSE.  Reporting and photos from John Lewis’s July 30, 2020 funeral at Ebenezer Baptist Church show COVID-19 precautions were in place: attendance was limited to invited guests, seating was spaced for distancing, and most attendees wore masks. While brief exceptions occurred (e.g., pallbearers and speakers at the podium), social distancing was generally practiced.

claim: In the UK the new daily allowance for peers in the House of Lords in 2020 is £323.
response_text: TRUE.  In February 2020 the House of Lords agreed to uprate the attendance allowance by 3.1%, raising the higher (maximum) rate from £313 to £323 per sitting day (with an optional lower rate, about £162).

claim: Walt Disney's Characters Mickey and Minnie Mouse Were Twins
response_text: FALSE.  Mickey and Minnie Mouse are romantic partners, not siblings. Walt Disney even noted in a 1933 interview that “in private life” Mickey is married to Minnie (while on-screen they often appear as boyfriend and girlfriend). There is no canon in which they are twins.

claim: COVID-19 cases in the Baranguay UP campus increased due to the SONAgkaisa rally held there on July 27 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Quezon City’s epidemiology unit and the DOH said they found no cases or clusters traced to the July 27, 2020 SONAgkaisa rally at UP Diliman. Any rise in cases in Barangay UP Campus around that time was not linked by contact tracing, and immediate post-rally increases would also be inconsistent with COVID-19’s incubation period. (It’s impossible to rule out an isolated case with absolute certainty, but official data showed no evidence of a rally-driven spike.)

claim: Ratneshwar temple leans at an angle higher than the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
response_text: TRUE.  Ratneshwar Mahadev (Kashi Karvat) temple in Varanasi is widely reported to lean by about 9°, which exceeds the Leaning Tower of Pisa’s current inclination of roughly 4° (about 5.5° at its worst before stabilization). Note: the temple’s exact angle is based on reports rather than a widely cited formal survey, but the consensus is that it leans more than Pisa.

claim: 3.8% of Wisconsin’s coronavirus funding has been spent.
response_text: FALSE.  The 3.8% figure refers to a narrow slice (early “expended” totals for ARPA State Fiscal Recovery Funds at one point in time). Wisconsin had already spent large portions of other COVID-19 funds (notably CARES Act money) and had obligated/committed much of its ARPA funds. As a blanket claim about Wisconsin’s overall coronavirus funding, 3.8% spent is misleading and incorrect.

claim: Ghislaine Maxwell tested positive for Covid-19 in jail.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In July 2020 rumors spread that Ghislaine Maxwell had tested positive for COVID-19 while in federal custody, but prison officials and her attorneys indicated she was in quarantine due to standard intake protocols, not a positive test. Fact-checks by outlets such as Reuters and USA Today found no evidence she tested positive.

claim: Taylor Swift says we should remove the Statue of Liberty.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record—no interviews, social media posts, or reputable news coverage—of Taylor Swift calling for the Statue of Liberty to be removed. This appears to be a fabricated or satirical claim.

claim: COVID Outbreak Discovered in Oregon Minks
response_text: TRUE.  In November 2020, the Oregon Department of Agriculture reported a COVID-19 outbreak at an Oregon mink farm: workers and minks tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2. Shortly after, a free-ranging mink near the farm also tested positive, confirming local spread linked to the outbreak.

claim: The Philippines, during the Marcos dictatorship, developed a missile system before China did.
response_text: FALSE.  China fielded indigenous missile systems by the early–mid 1960s (e.g., DF-1/DF-2 ballistic missiles and the SY-1 anti-ship missile), well before the Philippines’ Marcos-era Project Santa Barbara in the 1970s, which produced experimental rockets (“Bongbong” missiles) and did not become an operational missile system. Minor uncertainty lies in how one defines “missile system” for the Philippine project, but China’s predates it regardless.

claim: Tint Tint Htun, a former Myanmar actress and singer who became a Buddhist nun, has died.
response_text: FALSE — I can’t find reliable reports confirming Tint Tint Htun’s death. Sources up to my Oct 2024 knowledge note she left entertainment to ordain as a Buddhist nun, but no verified obituary. If this is a very recent event, I may be outdated.

claim: Congress-led government closed Rafale deal in 2012.
response_text: FALSE.  In January 2012, the Congress-led UPA government selected Dassault’s Rafale as the lowest bidder for the 126-aircraft MMRCA tender and began negotiations, but no contract was signed. The MMRCA process was later withdrawn in 2015. The only concluded Rafale contract was a 36-aircraft government-to-government deal signed in September 2016 under the BJP-led government.

claim: Russia offered bounties to the Taliban to kill U.S. troops in Afghanistan.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: In 2020, reports said U.S. intelligence suspected Russia’s GRU offered payments to Taliban-linked militants to target U.S./coalition troops. But the intelligence community later characterized this as a low-to-moderate confidence assessment, based largely on detainee reporting, with no confirmed link to specific U.S. casualties. The Pentagon said it found no corroborating evidence. So the claim remains unproven, not an established fact.

claim: The South Sudan government has teamed up with the world bank to offer grants worth 41.4$ million to entrepreneurs
response_text: FALSE  I can’t find any credible World Bank or government record of a $41.4 million grant program for South Sudanese entrepreneurs. Recent World Bank support to South Sudan includes other amounts (for example, larger IDA grants for safety nets and a $70 million women’s economic empowerment project), but not a $41.4 million entrepreneur grant. If you have a source, I can re-check. Uncertainty: low to moderate due to lack of matching official documentation.

claim: John Mahama presided over higher inflation. Nana Akufo-Addo has reduced inflation.
response_text: FALSE.  - Under John Mahama (2013–2016), annual inflation mostly ranged about 11–18%, peaking below 20%. - Under Nana Akufo-Addo (from 2017), inflation fell to single digits by 2018–2019, but later surged to a multi-decade high of about 54% in late 2022 before easing in 2023–2024.  So Mahama did not preside over higher inflation than Akufo-Addo, and while Akufo-Addo initially reduced inflation, it later rose far above Mahama-era levels. (If the claim refers only to 2017–2019, it would be partly true.)

claim: John Mahama presided over a decline in Ghana's agriculture. Nana Akufo-Addo increased Ghana's agricultural output.
response_text: FALSE.  - Under John Mahama (2012–2016), Ghana’s agriculture sector did not generally contract; it recorded modest positive real growth most years. Some subsectors (notably cocoa around 2014–2015) dipped, but the overall sector did not “decline” across his tenure. - Under Nana Akufo-Addo (from 2017), output rose in the early years (e.g., PFJ boosted maize/rice; record cocoa in 2020/21), but gains were not consistent—later years saw setbacks and declines in key crops like cocoa amid input and disease shocks.  Note: Exact rates vary by data series (Ghana Statistical Service, World Bank/FAO), but the blanket framing is misleading.

claim: Uttar Pradesh Police, in India, took several goats into custody for not wearing masks.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a viral, misleading story from July 2020 in Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh. Police briefly took a goat to the station because it was roaming unattended during COVID restrictions, not for “not wearing a mask.” Police clarified there is no mask rule for animals and the goat was returned to its owner. Fact-checked by outlets like AFP, BOOM, and India Today.

claim: Republican bill says no medical malpractice suits until 2024.
response_text: FALSE.  Context: In 2020, Senate Republicans proposed the SAFE TO WORK Act, which would temporarily limit COVID-19–related liability (including certain medical malpractice claims) through roughly October 1, 2024. It did not ban all medical malpractice suits: non–COVID cases were unaffected, and even COVID-related cases could proceed for gross negligence or willful misconduct. It also never became law.

claim: The New York state Labor Department is giving essential workers $4,800 in hazard pay.
response_text: FALSE.  New York State’s Department of Labor has not announced or administered a $4,800 “hazard pay” program for essential workers. The closest statewide COVID-era payments were: - Healthcare and Mental Hygiene Worker Bonus (up to $3,000), administered by the Department of Health, not DOL. - Excluded Workers Fund (up to $15,600) for workers who lost income, also not “hazard pay.”  No official NYS DOL program offers a $4,800 hazard pay.

claim: Actor Sonu Sood launched a toll-free number on May 26 to facilitate migrants to reach their home. Through this toll-free number, one can easily reach out to Sonu Sood’s team for help.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple news reports from May 26, 2020 state that Sonu Sood announced a toll‑free helpline so stranded migrant workers could contact his team for assistance in reaching home during the COVID-19 lockdown. The number connected callers to his team to coordinate help. (Widely reported by outlets such as The Indian Express, NDTV, and Times of India.)

claim: Hetero is selling 6 vials of Remdesivir at Rs 32,400 at Kukatpally
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: While Hetero initially priced its Remdesivir (Covifor) at Rs 5,400 per vial (making a 6‑vial course Rs 32,400), the company clarified it was not selling directly to the public from its Kukatpally office. Distribution was through hospitals/authorized channels, not retail at Kukatpally.

claim: John Mahama presided over low industrial growth during his four years in office. Nana Akufo-Addo has increased industrial growth.
response_text: TRUE.  - Under John Mahama (2013–2016), Ghana’s industry sector was weak and often negative. Ghana Statistical Service data show the industry sector contracted in multiple consecutive years (e.g., around 2014–2016) amid power shortages and oil/mining headwinds. - Under Nana Akufo-Addo, industry rebounded strongly in the early years (2017–2019), with double‑digit growth driven largely by higher oil and mining output. Growth fell back in 2020 due to COVID‑19, but compared to Mahama’s period, industrial growth initially increased.  Note: Exact rates vary by data series/rebase, but the pattern is consistent across official and World Bank sources.

claim: Reports as recent as 2017 reported 92% prevalence of blood lead poisoning in children from some villages in the Nigerian state of Zamfara.
response_text: TRUE.  Several 2017 publications summarizing the Zamfara lead-poisoning crisis reported extraordinarily high rates of elevated blood lead levels among children in certain affected villages—on the order of 90%+, including figures around 92%. These reports referenced outbreak measurements from the early 2010s (e.g., villages like Dareta/Yar Galma), not necessarily 2017 conditions, but the statistic was indeed reported in sources published as late as 2017.

claim: Tom Hanks went on on national TV to say he had COVID 19
response_text: FALSE.  Tom Hanks announced he had COVID-19 via an Instagram post on March 11, 2020, while in Australia. He did not initially “go on national TV” to reveal it, though he later discussed having had COVID-19 in televised appearances (e.g., SNL) after the news was already public.

claim: USA is largely out of Afghanistan.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: The U.S. ended its military mission and withdrew forces from Afghanistan in August 2021, closed its Kabul embassy, and has no permanent military bases or large footprint there. Any remaining involvement is limited to over‑the‑horizon counterterrorism, sanctions/diplomacy from outside the country, and humanitarian aid via partners. (Some covert or episodic operations are possible, but the U.S. is “largely out.”)

claim: Four Ukrainian soldiers died after taking part in Covid-19 vaccine trials conducted by USA.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that any U.S.-run COVID‑19 vaccine trials were conducted in Ukraine, nor that Ukrainian soldiers died from such trials. Ukraine’s health authorities and Ministry of Defense denied the claim, and clinical trial registries showed no COVID‑19 vaccine trials in Ukraine at the time. The story traces to pro‑Kremlin/disinformation outlets and has been debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, AFP, StopFake).

claim: Smartphone apps can measure blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels by asking you to press your index finger on the camera.
response_text: FALSE.  - Heart rate: Yes—camera/flash can estimate pulse via photoplethysmography. - Blood pressure: No—camera-only apps are not reliable or clinically validated; cuffless BP requires specialized, calibrated sensors and no FDA‑cleared phone-camera app exists. - Oxygen saturation: Camera-based SpO2 estimates are experimental and variable (skin tone, lighting); no FDA‑cleared smartphone camera app for this.  So while heart rate is feasible, blood pressure and oxygen levels via just pressing a finger on the camera are not reliably or clinically approved.

claim: Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan had said he  (water burial)would take jalsamadhi if he was not invited for the Bhumi Pujan of the Ram Temple in Ayodhya on August 5, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible record of Azam Khan saying he would take “jalsamadhi” if not invited to the August 5, 2020 Ram Temple bhoomi pujan. At that time he was lodged in Sitapur jail (arrested in February 2020), and no mainstream reports or verified statements support this claim. Fact-checks traced such posts to social media rumors, not to any attributable quote from him.

claim: The United Nations delivered a formal stand down order to the Trump administration in July 2020, ordering the President to stop Federal officers from using non-lethal force against peaceful protesters in Portland.
response_text: FALSE.  UN human rights officials issued non-binding statements in July 2020 urging U.S. authorities to stop excessive force and protect protesters’ rights in Portland. The UN did not (and generally cannot) issue a “formal stand down order” to the U.S. President, nor did it order a halt to all non-lethal force.

claim: Too much exposure to 5G, can literally fry the human central nervous system.
response_text: FALSE.  - 5G uses non‑ionizing radiofrequency (RF) waves. At levels from phones and base stations that comply with safety limits (ICNIRP, FCC/FDA), RF exposure does not “fry” tissue or damage the central nervous system. - Millimeter‑wave 5G (e.g., 24–40 GHz) penetrates only fractions of a millimeter into the skin; it does not reach the brain or spinal cord. Sub‑6 GHz 5G also operates far below intensities needed to cause harmful heating. - Only unrealistically high, uncontrolled RF power could cause thermal injury—and that would burn superficial tissues first, not “literally fry” the CNS.  Minor uncertainty only in the sense that any electromagnetic source at extreme, unsafe power could cause burns, but this is not relevant to real‑world 5G exposure.

claim: Nigeria recorded 1.25 million abortion cases in 2012 alone, but that this figure represented double the 1996 figures.
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence: A Guttmacher Institute study estimated about 1.25 million induced abortions occurred in Nigeria in 2012—more than double the estimated 610,000 in 1996. Note: these are research estimates, not officially “recorded” cases, given Nigeria’s restrictive law and underreporting.

claim: Your face will become exposed to the virus if you wear your mask on your chin.
response_text: TRUE.  A mask worn on the chin doesn’t cover the nose and mouth, so it provides no filtration against respiratory droplets and aerosols. It can also transfer contaminants from the mask’s outer surface to your chin/face. Proper protection requires covering both nose and mouth snugly.

claim: Florida is doing over five times better” than New Jersey and New York in COVID-19 deaths per million people
response_text: FALSE.  “Over five times better” would mean Florida had less than one‑fifth the COVID-19 deaths per million of New York and New Jersey. That was only true very early in 2020. By mid‑to‑late 2020 Florida’s cumulative deaths per million were about 2–3 times lower than NY/NJ (not 5x), and by 2021–2022 they were roughly similar. So the claim does not hold in general. (Timeframe ambiguity noted.)

claim: UNICEF stated that Coronavirus (COVID-19) is large in size where the cell diameter is 400-500 micro and for this reason any mask prevents its entry.
response_text: FALSE.  - UNICEF never issued such a statement; it’s a misattributed WhatsApp/viral rumor debunked by multiple fact-checkers. - The SARS‑CoV‑2 virus is about 0.06–0.14 micrometers (60–140 nanometers), not 400–500 micrometers (which would be visible to the naked eye). - Masks don’t guarantee “any mask prevents entry.” They reduce risk by blocking virus‑laden droplets and aerosols; effectiveness depends on material and fit (e.g., N95/FFP2 > surgical > cloth).

claim: 5G towers unleash severely damaging level of radiation to DNA
response_text: FALSE.  - 5G uses non‑ionizing radiofrequency waves (sub‑6 GHz and some millimeter waves). Their photons carry far too little energy to break chemical bonds or directly damage DNA (e.g., ~0.0001 eV at 28 GHz vs. several eV needed for ionization). - Measurements around base stations show public exposures are typically hundreds to thousands of times below international safety limits (ICNIRP/FCC). Millimeter waves are mostly absorbed in the outer skin, not deep tissues. - Major reviews (WHO, ICNIRP, FDA, UK health agencies) report no established adverse health effects or DNA damage from 5G base‑station exposures within these limits.  Note: A few laboratory studies claim effects, but overall evidence is inconsistent and not supportive of “severe” DNA damage at real‑world exposure levels.

claim: Those most susceptible to the radiation from 5G technology are fetuses in utero and children.
response_text: FALSE.  Major health authorities (WHO, ICNIRP, FDA) report no established adverse health effects from 5G’s non‑ionizing radiofrequency (RF) exposures when they comply with safety limits, which are set with large margins to protect all people, including children and pregnant individuals. Dosimetry shows 5G millimeter waves penetrate only superficial tissues (skin/eyes) and fetal exposure is further attenuated by maternal tissues. There is no credible evidence that fetuses or children are “most susceptible” to 5G RF at compliant exposure levels, though research continues. Uncertainty: ongoing study, but current consensus does not support the claim.

claim: Due to their exterior anatomy, male testicles are especially susceptible to 5G radiation, which lowers sperm count. Just the same, cellular radiation kills off irreplaceable eggs in females.
response_text: FALSE.  - 5G/cellular radiofrequency (RF) waves are non‑ionizing; they don’t have enough energy to damage DNA or “kill” eggs. Established harm to ovarian reserve is from ionizing radiation (e.g., X‑rays, radiation therapy), not RF. - 5G millimeter‑wave signals penetrate only the outer skin millimeters; sub‑6 GHz bands penetrate more but typical exposures are far below limits set to prevent tissue heating. The testes’ external location makes them sensitive to heat, but there’s no solid evidence that everyday 3G/4G/5G RF exposure lowers sperm count. - Major health agencies (e.g., WHO, FDA, ICNIRP) report no confirmed causal link between typical mobile/RF exposure and male or female infertility. Some small or biased studies report associations, but overall evidence is inconsistent.  Uncertainty: Research continues, but current data do not support the claim.

claim: US healthcare workers still don't have enough PPE during the COVID-19 pandemic
response_text: FALSE.  Early in 2020 there were severe PPE shortages for U.S. healthcare workers, but supply chains and stockpiles largely stabilized from late 2020 onward. By 2022–2023, widespread PPE shortages were no longer the norm, and the federal COVID-19 public health emergency ended in May 2023. While occasional localized or specialty-item shortages can occur, the claim of ongoing general PPE insufficiency is not accurate. Uncertainty: specific facilities may have intermittent issues.

claim: APC is luring Abubakar Shekau with Vice Presidential ticket  as an inducement to end Boko-Haram War.
response_text: FALSE.  - There are no credible reports that Nigeria’s APC offered Abubakar Shekau a vice-presidential ticket. - APC’s actual VP nominees were Yemi Osinbajo (2015, 2019) and Kashim Shettima (2023). - Abubakar Shekau, the Boko Haram leader, was reported dead in 2021, making such an offer impossible thereafter.  This claim appears to be a baseless rumor/disinformation.

claim: BLM injures 1000 police officers, kills36 people and does $8 billion in damage .
response_text: FALSE.  - Damage: Insurance industry estimates put insured losses from the 2020 racial‑justice unrest around $1–2 billion (PCS/Insurance Information Institute), not $8 billion. Total economic damage is hard to quantify, but credible sources don’t support $8B. - Deaths: Compilations generally count roughly 25–30 deaths linked to the 2020 unrest, not a confirmed 36. - Police injuries: A Major Cities Chiefs Association survey reported over 2,000 officers injured nationwide—so “1,000” isn’t a solid figure, and attributing all injuries to “BLM” is imprecise since incidents involved varied actors and circumstances.  Some figures vary by definitions and time frames, but the claim’s numbers are not supported by the best available data.

claim: Ghanan government presented inconsistent data about the Free Senior High School programme in the 2020 Mid-year review budget.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Independent fact-checkers in Ghana (e.g., Fact-Check Ghana/GhanaFact) noted that the 2020 Mid-Year Budget Review carried conflicting figures for Free SHS beneficiaries. The narrative and tables/graphics cited different totals for the same period, and some breakdowns did not sum to the stated totals, indicating internal inconsistencies in the document. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by source, but the presence of inconsistencies in that review was documented.

claim: Clint Eastwood endorsed Donald Trump.
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2016, Clint Eastwood told Esquire he’d “have to go for Trump,” indicating he would vote for him—widely reported as an endorsement. (He later said in 2020 he preferred Mike Bloomberg over Trump.)

claim: Wisconsin Democrats say lawmakers in neighbouring states have implemented more safety precautions against the spread of COVID-19 than state GOP.
response_text: TRUE — with a caveat. During 2020–21, several neighboring legislatures (Illinois, Minnesota, Michigan) adopted stronger COVID-19 precautions than Wisconsin’s GOP-run Legislature, including mask requirements, remote/hybrid sessions, distancing, and screening. Wisconsin Republicans generally declined to require masks or adopt robust chamber-wide rules. Iowa was an exception, with fewer requirements, but overall the claim that neighboring states implemented more precautions is broadly accurate.

claim: Jim Carrey said,  'Hollywood Elites Eat Whole Babies For Christmas' - 'The More They Suffer - The Better They Taste'
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Jim Carrey ever saying this. The quote originated on a known disinformation site (The People’s Voice/NewsPunch) and has been debunked by fact-checkers. No interviews, verified social media posts, or reputable news sources contain this statement.

claim: US drug prices in 2019 went down for the first time in 51 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI for prescription drugs did fall slightly in 2019 (about −0.4%), which was the first calendar‑year decline in roughly 46 years (since the early 1970s), not 51 years. Moreover, other measures of drug prices did not show a broad decline. So “first time in 51 years” is inaccurate. (Some uncertainty stems from which price index and timeframe are used, but none support 51 years.)

claim: PM Modi has not imposed President’s rule even a single time since 2014.
response_text: FALSE.  Since 2014, President’s Rule has been imposed multiple times under the Modi-led Union government (the President proclaims it on the Union Cabinet’s recommendation). Examples include: - Maharashtra (2014; again Nov 2019) - Arunachal Pradesh (Jan 2016) - Uttarakhand (Mar 2016) - Jammu & Kashmir (Dec 2018–2019, after a period of Governor’s Rule) - Puducherry (2021)  So the claim that it hasn’t happened even once is incorrect.

claim: County governments in Kenya have continued to adhere to the two-thirds gender principle. Three counties of Kilifi, Nyeri and Migori have gone higher and have a 50/50 representation of male and female CECs (county executive committee members).
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: - Compliance with the two‑thirds gender principle among Kenyan counties has been uneven; several counties failed to meet it in recent CEC appointments, so it is not accurate to say county governments “have continued to adhere.” - While Kilifi was reported to have achieved a 50/50 split in its CECs after the 2022 appointments, Nyeri did not reach 50/50 (reports indicated fewer than five women), and Migori was flagged for non‑compliance (fewer than one‑third women) in the same period.  Note: Exact figures can change with reshuffles, but available watchdog and media reports contradict the claim as stated.

claim: Target ended its “Heroes & Helpers” program that pairs children with police officers for holiday shopping trips
response_text: TRUE.  Target discontinued its corporate “Heroes & Helpers” program after 2020–2021 as it shifted community-giving priorities and paused in‑person events during the pandemic. Multiple police departments and local news reports said Target notified them the program was ended, and a Target spokesperson has confirmed it was retired. Note: some “Shop with a Cop” events still occur at Target stores, but those are typically organized/funded by local groups rather than through Target’s former Heroes & Helpers program.

claim: Federal High Court has restrained Godwin Obaseki, the incumbent Edo state governor, from participating in the Peoples’ Democratic Party’s gubernatorial primaries in the state.
response_text: TRUE.  Briefly: In June 2020, shortly after Godwin Obaseki joined the PDP, a Federal High Court in Port Harcourt granted an interim injunction (in a suit by PDP aspirant Omoregie Ogbeide-Ihama) restraining Obaseki from participating in the PDP governorship primary. The order was later vacated/settled, and Obaseki eventually contested and won the PDP ticket. Note: this was a temporary 2020 order.

claim: Counties in Kenya have over the past year sustained an average allocation of 24% of their total budgets to the health sector
response_text: TRUE  Available analyses of recent county budgets (e.g., Controller of Budget and independent budget reviews) show counties, on average, allocate roughly a quarter of their total budgets to health, with the latest year around 24% (typically in the 24–27% range). Minor variation by source/year exists, but the claim is consistent with recent averages. Uncertainty: exact percentage varies slightly across reports and fiscal years.

claim: Kenyan Counties allocated an average of 7.3% of budgets to agriculture.
response_text: TRUE (with slight uncertainty)  Multiple budget analyses of Kenyan county governments since devolution report that counties, on average, allocate about 7% of their budgets to agriculture—typically around 7.0–7.5% and below the 10% CAADP/Malabo target. Figures such as 7.2–7.3% are commonly cited for mid-2010s periods, though the exact share varies by year and county.

claim: Counties in Kenya are striving to reach the 10% budget allocation to agriculture recommended by the Malabo declaration.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Malabo Declaration (2014) calls for governments to allocate at least 10% of public spending to agriculture. In Kenya—where agriculture is largely a county function—national and county policies and advocacy (e.g., CAADP/Malabo commitments, ASTGS, Council of Governors communiqués, and donor-supported budget-tracking initiatives) have pushed counties to work toward this 10% target. Most counties still allocate less than 10% in practice, with only a few meeting it in some years, but the stated aim and ongoing efforts make the “striving to reach 10%” characterization broadly accurate. Note: effort and compliance vary by county.

claim: Study Concludes that Mask Wearers Have Lower IQ
response_text: FALSE.  No credible, peer‑reviewed study has concluded that mask wearers have lower IQ. Viral claims misrepresent papers about CO2 levels or discomfort with masks; those studies did not measure IQ and don’t show cognitive decline. Physiologic studies find no harmful changes in oxygen/CO2 for healthy mask users, and there’s no evidence that wearing masks lowers IQ.

claim: In Kenya, Water coverage now stands at 63% from 57%.
response_text: TRUE.  Estimates for Kenya’s access to at least basic drinking water have risen to about 62–63% (around 2022–2023), up from roughly 57% in the mid‑ to late‑2010s, per WHO/UNICEF JMP and national reporting. Note: figures vary by definition (e.g., “safely managed” is lower), so the exact percentage depends on the metric used.

claim: Kenyan counties allocated an average of 7.3% of budgets to agriculture.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple analyses of Kenyan county budgets put agriculture’s share around 7–8% on average; IBP Kenya reported roughly 7.3% in recent fiscal years (e.g., around FY 2018/19–2019/20). Exact figures vary by year and what sub-sectors are included, but 7.3% is consistent with published averages.

claim: Kenya's county governments have continued to adhere to the two-thirds gender principle. Four counties, Mombasa, Kilifi, Nyeri, and Migori, have gone higher and have a 50/50 representation of male and female CECs.
response_text: FALSE.  - County governments have not “continued to adhere” to the two‑thirds gender principle overall; multiple audits and media reports after the 2017 and 2022 CEC appointments flagged many counties as non‑compliant and some were challenged in court. - The specific 50/50 claim is also inaccurate. While Mombasa has been reported with a balanced (5 men/5 women) CEC at one point, Kilifi, Nyeri, and Migori did not all have 50/50 CEC line‑ups (typically 3–4 women out of 10), depending on the term and appointments.  Note: Exact compositions vary over time with reshuffles, but the broad claim is not supported.

claim: Two-thirds of the debt in the Australian budget was borrowed before the start of the pandemic
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Using the standard “gross debt” measure in the budget, Australia’s debt just before COVID (early 2020) was about $540–560 billion. Recent budgets put total gross debt around $900 billion to ~$1 trillion, so roughly 55–62% of the debt predates the pandemic—well short of two-thirds. (On net debt, shares vary by date but don’t reliably reach two-thirds either.) Conclusion: the claim overstates the pre‑pandemic share. Uncertainty: exact percentage depends on the measure and date used.

claim: The allocation to agriculture is an increase of 0.6% from what was reported last year in Kenya.
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: In Kenya’s FY2024/25 national budget, the agriculture allocation rose to roughly 3.8% of total spending from about 3.2% in FY2023/24—an increase of about 0.6 percentage points. Note: exact figures vary slightly depending on which agriculture-related functions (e.g., irrigation, cooperatives) are included.

claim: Modi Govt Make 'Country Of Origin' Label Mandatory on Products For GeM Platform.
response_text: TRUE.  In June 2020, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) made it mandatory for sellers to declare the “Country of Origin” for all product listings. New listings required this field, and existing products had to be updated. GeM also introduced filters and preference features to promote “Make in India.”

claim: Joe Biden owns island next to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s hideaway.
response_text: FALSE.  Jeffrey Epstein owned Little St. James (and later Great St. James) in the U.S. Virgin Islands. There is no record that Joe Biden owns any island there. A viral rumor wrongly claimed he owned nearby Water Island; in reality Water Island is owned by the U.S. Virgin Islands government and isn’t adjacent to Epstein’s islands. Multiple fact-checks (Reuters, AP, PolitiFact, Snopes) have debunked the claim.

claim: Counties allocated an average of 7.3% of budgets to agriculture in 2019/20
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: Analyses of Kenyan county budgets show that, on average, counties allocated about 7.3% of their total budgets to the agriculture sector in FY 2019/20. This figure is reported in public expenditure reviews (e.g., Tegemeo Institute and similar budget-tracking studies) and is below the 10% CAADP/Malabo target. Minor variation can occur depending on which sub-sectors (e.g., fisheries, cooperatives) are included, but 7.3% is a widely cited average.

claim: [The allocation to agriculture] is an increase of 0.6% from what was reported last year.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: This phrasing conflates “percent” with “percentage points.” Budget shares typically change by percentage points (e.g., from 3.3% to 3.9% is a 0.6 percentage-point increase), not by 0.6%. A 0.6% relative increase would be tiny and not equivalent to a 0.6-point rise. (Context is limited, but this is the common error.)

claim: Little girl shown lying in a casket in a photo died from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely shared photo of a little girl in a casket has been repeatedly miscaptioned. Fact-checks (e.g., Reuters, AFP, Snopes) traced the image to a death that occurred before the COVID-19 pandemic/from other causes, not from COVID-19. (Exact cause varies by report, but it was not COVID.)

claim: Mandatory vaccinations is in direct violation of the Nuremberg Code.
response_text: FALSE.  The Nuremberg Code governs ethical standards for human experimentation, requiring voluntary consent to participate in research. Vaccine mandates for licensed/authorized vaccines are public health measures, not human experiments, and do not compel participation in research. Courts have repeatedly upheld vaccine mandates (e.g., Jacobson v. Massachusetts; ECHR’s Vavřička v. Czech Republic) as lawful public health policies, not violations of the Nuremberg Code.

claim: Kenyan counties have over the past year sustained an average allocation of 24% of their total budgets to the health sector.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Recent Controller of Budget and independent budget analyses show Kenyan counties typically allocate about a quarter of their total budgets to health. In the last fiscal year, the average county health allocation hovered around 23–26%, making “about 24%” a fair characterization. Minor variation by county and year exists.

claim: Man dies at the R N Cooper Hospital in Mumbai due to medical negligence.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The claim is unspecific and not backed by any credible, verifiable report or official finding linking a man’s death at R. N. Cooper Hospital to proven medical negligence. Without details (date, name, inquiry outcome), it remains unsubstantiated. Uncertainty: could reference an unspecified incident, but no confirmed evidence available.

claim: There Is An Upcoming Shortage Of Dr. Pepper Because Of The Coronavirus
response_text: TRUE  During 2020, Dr Pepper publicly acknowledged nationwide shortages linked to COVID-19–related supply chain disruptions and increased at-home demand, compounded by an aluminum can shortage. So warnings of a coronavirus-related shortage were accurate at that time, though “upcoming” quickly became “current.”

claim: New Zealand has authorised troops to enter homes to enforce COVID-19 quarantine.
response_text: FALSE.  New Zealand used Defence Force personnel to support border and managed isolation/quarantine facilities, but they were not authorised to enter private homes to enforce COVID-19 rules. Enforcement powers rested primarily with police under the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act, which specifically excluded warrantless entry into private dwellings and did not grant such powers to military personnel.

claim: US Home Health workers receive low pay, Limited benefits and 40% of them are on SNAP or Medicaid.
response_text: TRUE  - Pay: BLS reports home health/personal care aides earn low wages (median roughly $15–16/hour in recent years), far below the overall U.S. median. - Benefits: Research (PHI, EPI) shows many lack employer-provided health insurance, paid leave, or retirement benefits. - SNAP/Medicaid: Multiple analyses (PHI/EPI) find roughly 40% or more of home care workers rely on public assistance; about 35–45% are on Medicaid and roughly a quarter to a third receive SNAP, with overlap—so around 40% are on SNAP or Medicaid. Figures vary by year/definition, but the claim’s magnitude is supported.

claim: Indiana woman charged for mail in voter fraud, delivered 400 ballots with Democrat box prechecked
response_text: FALSE.  What actually happened: In 2020 an Evansville, Indiana Democratic activist, Janet Reed, was charged for mailing roughly 400 absentee ballot applications for the primary with the Democratic Party preference preselected. They were applications, not ballots. No ballots with a “Democrat” box prechecked were delivered. Sources at the time included the Evansville Courier & Press and Associated Press.

claim: Mel Gibson accused Hollywood of child sacrifices and paedophillia.
response_text: FALSE.  The quotes about Mel Gibson claiming Hollywood engages in child sacrifice and pedophilia originate from fabricated articles (notably on YourNewsWire/NewsPunch) and misattributed “interviews.” Credible records of his public statements do not show him making these accusations, and multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, Reuters, PolitiFact) have debunked the claim.

claim: Greenhouse gases emitted into the ocean are causing more holes in the ozone layer; the ozone layer has holes in it, causing global temperatures to rise.
response_text: FALSE.  - Ozone depletion is mainly caused by ozone‑depleting substances (CFCs, halons, etc.) released into the atmosphere, not by “greenhouse gases emitted into the ocean.”  - While nitrous oxide is both a greenhouse gas and an ozone‑depleting substance, it acts in the atmosphere, not via the ocean. - The ozone “hole” allows more UV to reach the surface but is not a driver of global warming; global temperature rise is driven primarily by increased atmospheric greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O). Stratospheric ozone loss actually causes a small net cooling at the surface.

claim: A rare yellow turtle was spotted in Balasore, Odisha.
response_text: TRUE.  In July 2020, a bright yellow (albino) Indian flapshell turtle was rescued in Balasore district, Odisha. Forest officials and an Indian Forest Service officer shared photos and confirmed the rare coloration due to albinism.

claim: US space agency NASA has added a 13th star sign named "Ophiuchus" to the zodiac.
response_text: FALSE.  NASA didn’t add a new zodiac sign. In a 2016 explainer, NASA noted that the Sun’s path actually crosses 13 constellations (including Ophiuchus) and that Earth’s axial precession has shifted the sky since ancient times. But NASA doesn’t manage astrology, and it didn’t change or “add” zodiac signs; Ophiuchus has long been an ecliptic constellation that astrologers traditionally exclude.

claim: Medical experts from the World Health Organization (WHO), US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and The New England Journal of Medicine have warned against wearing face masks because they can cause “severe health issues”.
response_text: FALSE.  - WHO and CDC have consistently recommended masks to reduce respiratory virus transmission and explicitly state that properly worn masks do not cause CO2 poisoning or oxygen deprivation; they caution mainly about use in children under 2 or for people with certain medical conditions. - The often-cited NEJM piece (2020) did not warn of “severe health issues” from masks; its authors later clarified they support public masking. No authoritative guidance from WHO, CDC, or NEJM warns against masks on the basis of severe health risks.

claim: Former President of the United States, Theodore Roosevelt once said "To anger a conservative, lie to him. To anger a liberal, tell him the truth."
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Theodore Roosevelt saying this in his speeches, writings, or the comprehensive “Works of Theodore Roosevelt.” Quote-investigation sites (e.g., Quote Investigator/PolitiFact/Snopes) have found the line only in much later internet-era appearances, decades after Roosevelt’s death, with no credible primary source. It’s a modern misattribution.

claim: As of July 2020 Covid-19 vaccines are not safe, because of the accelerated pace of their development
response_text: FALSE  Reason: Speed alone doesn’t make a vaccine unsafe. By July 2020, COVID-19 vaccine candidates were undergoing standard phase 1/2 trials with early data showing acceptable safety profiles (e.g., no serious adverse events in early Moderna, Pfizer/BioNTech, and Oxford/AstraZeneca studies). Regulators stated safety standards would not be lowered; the timeline was accelerated by funding and overlapping trial/manufacturing steps, not by skipping safety evaluations. Uncertainty note: Long‑term safety was still being studied at that time, but there was no evidence that vaccines were “not safe.”

claim: The WHO has said that cats and dogs cannot contract Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Early in 2020, WHO said there was “no evidence” pets such as cats and dogs were being infected at that time—not that they “cannot” be. Later, WHO and other health bodies acknowledged that cats and dogs can contract SARS‑CoV‑2 (usually from infected humans), though cases are relatively rare and typically mild.

claim: United States space agency NASA has added a 13th Zodiac sign named “Ophiuchus” to the list of existing 12 Zodiac signs.
response_text: FALSE.  NASA didn’t add a new zodiac sign. Ophiuchus is a long-recognized constellation, and astronomers note that the Sun actually passes through 13 constellations due to Earth’s axial precession. But astrology’s 12 zodiac signs are not set or changed by NASA; NASA simply explained the astronomy behind the constellations and said they didn’t change the zodiac.

claim: Netflix will end its Turkish service after the production of an upcoming local drama that was blocked by the country’s government over a gay character.
response_text: FALSE.  In 2020, a planned Turkish Netflix series (“If Only”) was blocked from filming in Turkey reportedly due to a gay character. Netflix canceled/relocated that specific project (later produced in Spain) but explicitly said it would stay in Turkey and has continued operating and commissioning Turkish content.

claim: COVID-19 vaccine is DNA-altering and has been fast-tracked through safety qualifications.
response_text: FALSE.  - COVID-19 vaccines do not alter your DNA. mRNA vaccines work in the cell cytoplasm and never integrate into the genome; adenoviral vector vaccines are non‑integrating and remain outside your DNA. - While development and review were accelerated (e.g., overlapping trial phases, rolling review, Emergency Use Authorization), required safety evaluations were not skipped. Large Phase 3 trials were completed, and extensive ongoing safety monitoring and later full approvals followed.

claim: In Madipur area of Delhi,three jihadists killed a minor boy in the middle of a road with a knife for a petty matter.
response_text: FALSE.  A boy was indeed fatally stabbed in public in Delhi’s Madipur area, but Delhi Police said the assailants were local youths/juveniles known to the victim and the attack stemmed from a personal dispute. Police found no communal or terror link. Labeling the attackers as “jihadists” is baseless misinformation. (Some details like the exact number of assailants vary across reports, but the “jihadist” claim is false.)

claim: Joe Biden wants to end school choice
response_text: FALSE.  Biden opposes private school vouchers and has sought tighter oversight of charter schools (especially for‑profit operators), but he has not sought to “end school choice.” His budgets have continued federal funding for the Charter Schools Program, and he supports public school choice options (e.g., magnet and some charter schools) with accountability. Uncertainty: low.

claim: President Trump tweeted  'Child Lifes Matter' Should Be Painted On Hollywood Streets
response_text: FALSE  There is no record of Donald Trump ever tweeting that. Searches of the Trump Twitter Archive and reliable reports show no such tweet. Trump did comment in 2020 about a “Black Lives Matter” mural being painted on NYC’s Fifth Avenue, but not “Child Lifes Matter” on Hollywood streets. The misspelling commonly appears in fabricated tweet memes.

claim: Cal Cunningham, North Carolina’s 2020 Democratic Senate candidate, voted to raise taxes in the state by over $1 billion in 2001.
response_text: TRUE.  Cal Cunningham served in the N.C. Senate in 2001 and voted for the 2001 budget and accompanying revenue package that raised multiple taxes (including a half‑cent sales tax hike and higher income-tax rates for top earners). Legislative/fiscal analyses put the added state revenue at over $1 billion for the 2001–03 biennium. Note: the total is over two years and several hikes were framed as temporary to address a recession-era shortfall.

claim: Donald Trump tweeted, “WHO Thinks ‘Child Lifes Matter’ Should Be PAINTED In The STREETS OF HOLLYWOOD???
response_text: FALSE.  No record of this quote exists in Trump’s tweet history or archives, and the viral screenshot showing “WHO Thinks ‘Child Lifes Matter’…” has been debunked as a fabricated tweet by multiple fact-checkers. The misspelling (“Lifes”) and formatting match a meme, not an authentic Trump post.

claim: CORONAVIRUS IS A LAB-ENGINEERED BIOWEAPON
response_text: FALSE  Evidence from genomic analyses and multiple independent reviews shows no signs that SARS‑CoV‑2 was genetically engineered or designed as a weapon. The U.S. Intelligence Community has assessed it was not developed as a biological weapon. While the precise origin remains uncertain (natural spillover vs. a possible lab-related incident with a naturally occurring virus), there is no credible evidence that it is a lab‑engineered bioweapon. Uncertainty: origin pathway remains unresolved.

claim: Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases wrote: I reject the notion that it’s 'just a virus’ and we’ll all get it eventually. What a careless, lazy, heartless stance.
response_text: FALSE.  No reliable record shows Anthony Fauci writing that. The quote has been misattributed to him; it closely matches a January 2022 tweet by Dr. Craig Spencer, an ER physician at Columbia University, who criticized the “we’ll all get it” notion in similar language. Minor uncertainty about exact wording, but not Fauci’s.

claim: The Governor of Osun State, Gboyega Oyetola, was in Abuja for three days and was not able to see Governor Mai Mala Buni, who is the Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC) National Caretaker Committee.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The claim came from rumor mill reports and was publicly debunked by Governor Oyetola’s media aide, Ismail Omipidan, who said Oyetola was not “stranded” in Abuja and had no problem accessing Governor Mai Mala Buni. No credible sources corroborated that Oyetola spent three days in Abuja unable to see Buni. (Slight uncertainty due to the claim’s anecdotal nature, but available reporting contradicts it.)

claim: Washing glasses with soap will prevent lenses from fogging whilst wearing a mask.
response_text: FALSE.  Washing lenses with soapy water and letting them air-dry can reduce fogging by leaving a thin surfactant film that helps water spread instead of forming mist. But it doesn’t reliably prevent fogging in all situations; effectiveness varies and depends on mask fit, lens coatings, and conditions. For consistent prevention, a well-fitted mask and/or dedicated anti‑fog treatments are better.

claim: Hackers in China hide phishing codes inside WhatsApp good morning and good night images or videos, to steal personal information, such as bank card information and other data.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a widely circulated hoax. There’s no credible evidence that “good morning/good night” WhatsApp images or videos from “hackers in China” contain hidden phishing code that steals bank or personal data. Image/video files themselves can’t execute code in WhatsApp; theft typically requires clicking malicious links, installing malware, or exploiting a specific (and rare) app vulnerability. While WhatsApp has patched past media-parsing bugs, they weren’t tied to such forwards, and the blanket claim is unfounded.

claim: Shanghai China International News asked all subscribers not to send good morning and good night images or videos on WhatsApp
response_text: FALSE.  This is a long-running WhatsApp hoax. There’s no credible news outlet called “Shanghai China International News,” and neither it nor WhatsApp has issued any such instruction. Multiple fact-checkers have debunked similar messages warning people not to send “good morning/good night” images.

claim: A covid patient died outside a medical shop in Siwan India, which is the constituency of Bihar's Health Minister.
response_text: FALSE.  A viral video did show a man collapsing outside a medical shop in Siwan, Bihar, but local reports/fact-checks said he was not a confirmed COVID-19 patient. Moreover, Siwan is not the constituency of Bihar’s Health Minister: the then health minister Mangal Pandey was an MLC who hails from Siwan but does not represent an assembly constituency there (and the later health minister Tejashwi Yadav represents Raghopur, not Siwan). Uncertainty: precise medical cause of death in that video was reported as non-COVID by officials.

claim: A black kid named Tyrone Woodfork was arrested yesterday for severely beating an elderly Tulsa, Oklahoma, white couple, raping and killing the wife and leaving the husband for dead and the national media is ignoring the crime
response_text: FALSE.  - True part: In March 2012, 20-year-old Tyrone Dale Woodfork was arrested in Tulsa in connection with a home invasion that left 85-year-old Nancy Strait dead and her husband, Bob, severely injured. - False/exaggerated parts: Tulsa police said there was no evidence Nancy Strait was raped. The case was not “ignored” by national media; it was covered by outlets such as HuffPost, CBS/Associated Press, FoxNews.com, and others.  Note: “yesterday” reflects the timing of early 2012 posts spreading this claim.

claim: The Bank of America pledged $1 billion dollars to Black Lives Matter.
response_text: FALSE.  Bank of America announced a $1 billion (later $1.25B) multi‑year commitment to address racial and economic inequality broadly—funding initiatives like community development, small business lending, healthcare, education/HBCUs, and workforce training. It was not a $1B pledge to the Black Lives Matter organization.

claim: if the Trump administration “had done its job, the virus wouldn’t come” to New York
response_text: FALSE.  This is an unprovable counterfactual and far too absolute. Genomic studies show New York’s outbreak was seeded by numerous introductions, largely from Europe, in late February and early March 2020—before the U.S. restricted most European travel on March 13. Public health experts note travel restrictions and screening can delay but rarely stop a contagious virus from reaching a global hub like New York. While earlier, better federal actions might have reduced or delayed spread, claiming the virus “wouldn’t come” is not supported. (Some uncertainty inherent in counterfactuals.)

claim: A motorcycle fatality in Orlando Florida was counted as a COVID death.
response_text: TRUE. In July 2020, Orange County (Orlando area) officials acknowledged that a man who died in a motorcycle crash had been initially included in Florida’s COVID-19 death tally. The state later said this was an error and removed the case from the COVID death count.

claim: Matt Hancock claimed that the UK covid-19 lockdown began on 16th March 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  Matt Hancock has said the UK “started” or “began” lockdown on 16 March 2020—referring to the government’s advice that day to avoid non‑essential contact and travel and to work from home. The legally enforced stay‑at‑home “lockdown” measures were announced on 23 March, but Hancock has claimed the effective start was 16 March.

claim: All workers at Gardenia, a bread-manufacturing factory in the Philippines, had tested positive for COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks and official statements debunked this viral rumor in 2020. Gardenia Bakeries Philippines said none of its employees had tested positive at the time the claim circulated, and local/health authorities reported no such mass outbreak. Fact-checkers (e.g., AFP, VERA Files) also found the “all workers tested positive” claim baseless.

claim: Nigeria, Ghana, Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal and Guinea are responsible for over 80 per cent of COVID-19 cases in West Africa.
response_text: TRUE — with timing caveat. In mid‑2020, West Africa’s COVID‑19 cases were heavily concentrated in five countries. WAHO/WHO reports around June–July 2020 showed Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal and Guinea together accounted for roughly 80% of the region’s cases. (Shares shifted later in the pandemic.)

claim: Azerbaijan has threatened to bomb the nuclear power plant in Armenia.
response_text: TRUE.  In July 2020, amid border clashes, an Azerbaijani Defense Ministry spokesman said Azerbaijan’s missile systems could precisely strike Armenia’s Metsamor nuclear power plant, warning this would cause a catastrophe. This was widely reported by international media (e.g., Reuters) as a direct threat.

claim: John Hickenlooper, the former Governor of Colorado accepted donations from Anadarko Petroleum Corp, a oil and gas company involved in a 2017 fatal explosion, in exchange for the company not being penalized.
response_text: FALSE.  - There’s no evidence Hickenlooper accepted donations from Anadarko “in exchange for” leniency. Independent fact-checkers reviewing similar 2020 attack ads found no substantiation for a quid pro quo. - Enforcement for the 2017 Firestone explosion was handled by the Colorado Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, not directly by the governor. After investigations that extended beyond Hickenlooper’s term, the state imposed a record, multi‑million‑dollar penalty in 2020 on Anadarko’s successor (Kerr‑McGee/Occidental) related to the incident and related violations—so the company was penalized. - Any donations tied to Hickenlooper were from industry PACs or individuals, not proven corporate quid pro quo.   Uncertainty: Specific donation amounts and sources (corporate PAC vs. employees) vary by report, but no credible source shows an “in exchange for” arrangement.

claim: US Businesses that refuse any legal tender can be fined and sued.
response_text: False.  Under federal law (31 U.S.C. § 5103), U.S. cash is “legal tender for all debts,” but private businesses generally may set their own payment policies and may refuse cash (or certain bills) for in‑person sales before a debt is incurred. There is no blanket federal rule fining or allowing lawsuits against businesses that refuse legal tender. Some states and cities (e.g., Massachusetts, New Jersey, Colorado; NYC, Philadelphia, San Francisco, D.C.) require cash acceptance and can impose fines or allow enforcement, but that’s not nationwide.

claim: Free federal housing for former inmates.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no federal program that automatically gives “free housing” to former inmates. Some may qualify for HUD-assisted housing (e.g., public housing or Housing Choice Vouchers), but these are not guaranteed, often have long waitlists, require tenants to pay a portion of income, and have eligibility restrictions (certain offenses are barred). Transitional or reentry housing may exist through nonprofits or limited federal grants, but it’s not universal “free federal housing.”

claim: Betting on online slot machines has increased by 25% during lockdown.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: Early lockdown reports (e.g., UK Gambling Commission, spring 2020) did show increases in online slots activity, but the ≈25% figure commonly cited referred to a rise in active players or certain session metrics, not a uniform 25% increase in “betting” (stakes/turnover) across the lockdown period. Overall gambling patterns varied, and sports cancellations offset some activity. Uncertain wording makes the claim misleading.

claim: United States citizens don't get the level of benefits that Bidens policy would be looking to give illegal immigrants
response_text: FALSE.  Undocumented immigrants are generally ineligible for most federal benefits (e.g., SNAP/food stamps, TANF cash aid, SSI, most Medicaid, and ACA subsidies). Biden’s policies have not given undocumented immigrants a higher level of benefits than U.S. citizens; if anything, citizens have broader access. Recent changes (e.g., allowing DACA recipients to buy ACA coverage with subsidies) put certain noncitizens on par with citizens, not above them. Some aid offered by states or cities is separate from federal/Biden policy. Uncertainty: the claim doesn’t specify a particular policy, but in general the statement is inaccurate.

claim: The Democrats want to abolish US police departments. They want to abolish our prisons, I guess.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Democratic Party and its national leaders do not advocate abolishing police or prisons. Their platform emphasizes police reform and criminal-justice reform, not abolition. President Biden and other leaders have explicitly rejected “defund/abolish” and supported funding for police (e.g., ARP funds; “fund the police” in the 2022 State of the Union). - While a small number of progressive activists and a few local officials have used abolition/“defund” rhetoric or proposed local restructuring (e.g., Minneapolis), these positions are not the party’s stance. - Some Democrats back measures like ending federal private prison contracts and reducing mass incarceration—neither equates to abolishing prisons.  Uncertainty: None significant; mainstream party positions contradict the claim.

claim: Biden wants to end mandatory minimums in criminal sentences.
response_text: TRUE.  As a candidate and in his criminal-justice platform, Joe Biden called for eliminating federal mandatory minimum sentences and encouraging states to do the same (e.g., his 2020 plan and ACLU questionnaire responses). His DOJ has also issued guidance to avoid triggering mandatory minimums in many drug cases, consistent with that stance.

claim: Vaccines were responsible for 50 million deaths during the Spanish flu pandemic in 1918.
response_text: FALSE.  - No influenza vaccine existed in 1918; the first licensed flu vaccines came in the mid-1940s. - The ~50 million deaths were caused by the 1918 H1N1 influenza virus and secondary bacterial pneumonia, not by vaccines. Some experimental bacterial vaccines were tried to prevent secondary infections, but there’s no evidence they caused mass deaths.  Sources: CDC on the 1918 pandemic; Britannica on the history/timing of influenza vaccines.

claim: Biden plans to "mandate net-zero carbon emissions for homes, offices and all new buildings by 2030. That basically means no windows, no nothing.
response_text: FALSE.  - Biden’s 2020 climate plan set a goal for all new buildings to achieve net‑zero emissions by 2030, largely through updated building codes, incentives, and federal standards—not a blanket nationwide mandate on homes and offices.   - It did not require “no windows.” Net‑zero buildings routinely have windows; they rely on insulation, efficient systems, and clean energy.   - Multiple fact-checkers (AP, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact) have debunked the “no windows” claim.

claim: One of the key elements of the Biden-Sanders Unity Task Force Recommendations (Biden, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, and Sanders, the leading voice for the most progressive Democrats Biden-Sanders (Biden, the presumptive US Democratic presidential nominee, and Sanders, the leading voice for the most progressive US Democrats) is that all charter schools will be abolished.
response_text: FALSE.  The Biden–Sanders Unity Task Force recommendations did not call for abolishing all charter schools. They proposed banning for‑profit charter schools and requiring stronger transparency, accountability, and equity standards for non‑profit public charters, while opposing private-school vouchers. Some progressives had pushed for a moratorium, but the Unity recommendations stopped short of eliminating charter schools.

claim: Biden plans to stop all deportation.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden did not plan to stop all deportations. He proposed a temporary 100-day pause on most deportations (with exceptions for national security/public safety and recent border crossers), and removals have continued under his administration.

claim: The US Biden-Sanders unity task force seeks to abolish immigration detention in the US.
response_text: FALSE.  The Biden–Sanders Unity Task Force recommendations (2020) called for ending family detention, ending for‑profit detention, reducing/prohibiting prolonged detention, and expanding community-based alternatives—not abolishing immigration detention altogether.

claim: The Democrats want to rejoin the Paris Climate Accord and seek an even higher level of restrictions on climate change.
response_text: TRUE.  - Democrats (and President Biden) rejoined the Paris Climate Agreement in 2021. - They also raised U.S. ambition beyond the Obama-era target, submitting a new 2030 goal to cut net greenhouse gas emissions 50–52% below 2005 levels and backing stronger climate policies and regulations.  Note: The phrasing “restrictions on climate change” is imprecise; Democrats seek stronger limits on emissions to address climate change.

claim: Border-wall construction under the Trump administration has replaced already existing barriers.
response_text: TRUE.  Most Trump-era border wall construction replaced existing barriers (older pedestrian fencing or vehicle barriers) with new bollard-style wall. By January 2021, over 400 miles had been built, and the vast majority were replacements; only a few dozen miles (roughly 40–80, often cited around 47) were in areas with no previous barrier. Note: not all construction was replacement.

claim: The Biden-Sanders unity platform includes a plan to appoint social justice prosecutors in order to free violent criminals.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Biden-Sanders Unity Task Force recommendations did not call for “appointing social justice prosecutors,” nor use that term. - The document focused on criminal justice reforms (e.g., ending cash bail, reducing mandatory minimums, decriminalizing marijuana, investing in public defenders), largely aimed at nonviolent offenses and pretrial practices. - It did not propose freeing violent criminals. Local prosecutors are typically elected, and nothing in the recommendations endorsed releasing violent offenders.

claim: Abolish immigration detention. No more detention. You come in here illegally, no more detention.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The U.S. has not abolished immigration detention. Federal law mandates detention in many cases, and ICE continues to detain tens of thousands of migrants. While some advocates and a few lawmakers have proposed reducing or replacing detention with alternatives, “no more detention” is not current U.S. policy.

claim: Donald Trump claimed that Biden's mandate for net zero carbon emissions for home, offices and new buildings would mean no windows.
response_text: TRUE.  Trump repeatedly said in 2024 rallies that President Biden’s supposed “net zero” mandate for homes, offices and new buildings would mean “no windows” or “basically no windows.” This was widely fact-checked (e.g., AP, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org) as a mischaracterization, but he did make the claim.

claim: Under Biden’s policy, immigrants in the country illegally "get welfare benefits. United States citizens don't get what they're looking to give illegal immigrants.
response_text: False.  - Federal law (since 1996’s PRWORA) bars undocumented immigrants from most federal “welfare” programs (e.g., SNAP/food stamps, TANF cash aid, SSI, full-scope Medicaid, ACA subsidies). They’re generally limited to emergency care, immunizations, disaster relief, and a few short-term services. - The Biden administration has not created a federal policy that gives undocumented immigrants welfare benefits citizens can’t get. - U.S. citizens are eligible for all federal benefits if they meet program criteria. Some states or cities use their own funds to offer limited aid regardless of status, and citizen children in mixed‑status families can receive benefits—but those are not Biden federal policies.

claim: What they're going to do is they're going to rip down the wall. They're taking it down.
response_text: FALSE.  The Biden administration paused new border wall construction but did not “rip down” or dismantle Trump-era wall sections. In fact, it has maintained, repaired, and in some areas added limited new barriers to use previously appropriated funds. Removals involved state-installed obstacles (e.g., shipping containers, razor wire), not the federal border wall.

claim: Migrant arrests and expulsions in the US along the southern border are down.
response_text: FALSE.  - “Expulsions” under Title 42 ended in May 2023, so there aren’t ongoing “expulsions” to be “down.” Since then, DHS has conducted removals/returns, which have been at or near their highest levels in years, not down. - Border Patrol arrests/apprehensions have fluctuated: they fell notably after June 2024 from late‑2023 peaks, but the trend hasn’t been consistently downward across months.  Uncertainty: exact month-to-month figures vary, but the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Bonnie Henry issued advice about living with the threat of Covid-19.
response_text: TRUE.  As British Columbia’s Provincial Health Officer, Dr. Bonnie Henry repeatedly issued guidance about “living with COVID-19,” especially during the 2021–2022 transition to longer‑term management. She advised on measures like vaccination, staying home when sick, and using masks based on personal risk to live with the ongoing threat of COVID-19.

claim: The United States has one of the lowest Covid-19 mortality rates
response_text: FALSE.  Using standard measures like cumulative deaths per capita, the U.S. has had relatively high COVID-19 mortality, not one of the lowest. By 2024, the U.S. recorded roughly 3,300–3,500 deaths per million—well above many peers such as Canada (~1,400), Australia (~900), Japan and South Korea (~600). Age‑standardized and excess‑mortality analyses similarly place the U.S. among the worst-performing high‑income countries. (Sources: Our World in Data; Commonwealth Fund; CDC/WHO data.)

claim: Former Indian Deputy Chief Minister and rebel Congress leader Sachin Pilot has joined the Bharatiya Janata Party.
response_text: FALSE.  Sachin Pilot, former Rajasthan Deputy Chief Minister, has not joined the Bharatiya Janata Party. Despite a 2020 rebellion against the Congress leadership in Rajasthan, he remained with the Indian National Congress, contested the 2023 Rajasthan assembly election as a Congress candidate, and has continued as a Congress leader. No credible reports indicate he has switched to the BJP.

claim: Philippine Depositary Receipts are equal to actual ownership in the Philippines.
response_text: FALSE.  Philippine Depositary Receipts (PDRs) give holders economic exposure to a company (e.g., the right to dividends or sale proceeds) but do not confer ownership or voting rights in the underlying shares. They’re structured precisely to allow investment without violating foreign ownership limits. Note: if a PDR includes control-like covenants, regulators may scrutinize it, but it still isn’t the same as equity ownership.

claim: Clinical trials have been completed for potential Russian COVID-19 vaccine.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: In mid-2020 Russia announced completion of small early-stage (Phase 1/2) trials for its Sputnik V vaccine, but large-scale Phase 3 clinical trials had not been completed at that time. Russia even registered the vaccine before finishing Phase 3. (If “clinical trials” is taken to mean all phases, the claim is false.)

claim: The Obama administration stopped testing during the H1N1, Swine Flu, pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  During the 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic, the Obama administration/CDC did not stop testing. They shifted strategy in July 2009 from trying to confirm every suspected case to focusing testing on hospitalized/severe cases and using surveillance sampling, and they stopped counting/reporting individual case totals. Testing continued for clinical care, surveillance, and antiviral monitoring throughout the pandemic.

claim: South Africa has “expertise in the development and trial of a range of vaccines”
response_text: TRUE.  South Africa has extensive vaccine R&D and trial capacity. Examples: - Clinical trials: Major HIV vaccine trials (e.g., HVTN 702/Uhambo, Imbokodo), multiple TB vaccine trials led by the South African TB Vaccine Initiative (SATVI), and several COVID‑19 vaccine trials (Oxford/AZ launched in SA in 2020, Novavax Phase 2b, J&J ENSEMBLE). South African groups have also run trials on pneumococcal, rotavirus, influenza, pertussis, and maternal RSV vaccines. - Development/manufacturing: Biovac conducts vaccine development and manufacturing; Afrigen leads the WHO mRNA technology transfer hub and has developed an mRNA COVID‑19 vaccine candidate; Aspen Pharmacare has filled-finished the J&J COVID‑19 vaccine.  These demonstrate expertise in both development and trials across a range of vaccines.

claim: Russia's Sechenov University has completed clinical trails of COVID-19 vaccine.
response_text: FALSE.  Sechenov University announced in July 2020 that it had completed only a small Phase I safety trial of a COVID-19 vaccine candidate (from the Gamaleya Institute). Larger Phase II/III efficacy trials were still pending, so “completed clinical trials” is misleading.

claim: South Africa has expertise in the development and trial of a range of vaccines.
response_text: TRUE.  South Africa has long-standing vaccine R&D and clinical trial capacity across multiple disease areas. Examples include major HIV vaccine trials (e.g., HVTN 702 “Uhambo” and HVTN 705 “Imbokodo”), TB vaccine trials (e.g., M72/AS01E and BCG revaccination via SATVI), and multiple COVID‑19 vaccine trials (Oxford/AstraZeneca, Johnson & Johnson, Novavax). It also hosts development and manufacturing initiatives like Biovac and the WHO-supported mRNA technology transfer hub (Afrigen), evidencing expertise in both development and trials of a range of vaccines.

claim: Sarah Sachin Pilot attacks Gehlot in a tweet saying that even "big magicians" will start sweating when they turn to Delhi.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There is no credible record of Sachin Pilot (or his wife Sara Pilot) tweeting that “even big magicians will start sweating when they turn to Delhi.” The name “Sarah Sachin Pilot” is also incorrect/misattributed. While Pilot has occasionally used “magician” jibes at Ashok Gehlot (whose father was a magician), this specific quote as a tweet is not documented by reliable sources. Uncertainty: low–moderate (no mainstream coverage or archived tweet).

claim: An Indian student finds a Home remedy cure for Covid-19 and it is accepted by WHO (World Health organization)
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that an Indian student discovered a home-remedy “cure” for COVID-19, nor has the WHO accepted or endorsed any such remedy. WHO guidance recognizes certain evidence-based treatments (e.g., corticosteroids for severe disease, specific antivirals for high-risk non-severe cases) and vaccines, but it has not approved any home remedy as a cure. Multiple fact-checks have debunked similar viral claims.

claim: South Africans have the right to resist isolation or quarantine if found to hsve the virus
response_text: FALSE.  Under South African law, people with a notifiable medical condition (e.g., COVID‑19) can be required to isolate or be quarantined. The National Health Act and the Regulations Relating to the Surveillance and the Control of Notifiable Medical Conditions (2017, amended 2020) allow authorities to obtain a magistrate’s order and enforce isolation/quarantine if someone refuses. Non‑compliance can be an offence. Constitutional rights may be limited by law to protect public health, so there is no general right to resist. Uncertainty: none.

claim: A cobbler in West Bengal, Sanjoy Rabidas, scored 93% in West Bengal board exams. He is also an RSS member.
response_text: FALSE.  Context: News reports in 2018 highlighted that Sanjoy/Sanjay Rabidas, the son of a cobbler from Jalpaiguri, West Bengal, scored about 92–93% in the West Bengal Madhyamik (Class 10) exam. However, multiple fact-checks (e.g., Alt News, BOOM) and the student himself clarified he is not an RSS member. The RSS’s local unit also said he wasn’t associated. (Minor uncertainty on exact percentage spelling/name variations.)

claim: Answering a call from '+140' will empty your bank account.
response_text: FALSE.  Simply answering a phone call cannot drain your bank account. The “+140” prefix is commonly used for telemarketing/robocalls in India under TRAI rules.
