Scammers can only steal money if you’re tricked into sharing sensitive details (OTP, PIN), installing remote-access apps, or making payments/calling back premium numbers. Be cautious, but the claim as stated is a hoax.

claim: Prof Stephen Adei praises Prof Naana Opoku-Agyeman as a great leader
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Prof Stephen Adei describing Prof Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang as “a great leader.” Reputable Ghanaian news sources and transcripts of his public remarks don’t show this statement; similar quote cards circulating online have been debunked. (Slight uncertainty only because absence of evidence isn’t proof, but no reliable source confirms it.)

claim: A graphic from the World Health Organization (WHO) lists the “7 biggest brain damaging habits
response_text: FALSE.  This “7 biggest brain damaging habits” list is a misattributed viral meme. WHO has no publication or official graphic listing such habits, and WHO representatives and multiple fact‑checkers have said the organization did not produce it. The items on the list also include dubious claims not supported by WHO guidance.

claim: PR stunt by TV channel leads to police warning on phone no. starting with 140
response_text: FALSE.  - In India, phone numbers starting with 140 are the nationwide series allocated by TRAI for registered telemarketing calls. They are not inherently fraudulent or dangerous. - Police have not issued a blanket warning against answering “140” numbers; multiple Indian fact-checkers have debunked such viral messages. - There’s no credible evidence that a TV channel’s PR stunt triggered any official police advisory about the 140 series.  Note: Uncertainty only about which viral rumor sparked the confusion, but the core claim of a police warning tied to a TV PR stunt is unsupported.

claim: You no longer have to quarantine if you have returned to England from an exempt country before July 10.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: England’s “travel corridor” exemptions only applied to arrivals from 10 July 2020 onward. If you arrived before 10 July—even from a country later listed as exempt—you were required to complete the existing 14-day self-isolation.

claim: Proud to be AMU alumnus, 35-year-old scientist Kushbu Mirza, has been promoted as Director in ISRO. She is an alumnus of Aligarh Muslim University and only the 2nd Muslim Scientist after Dr.A.P.J. Abdul Kalam to hold this rank at ISRO
response_text: FALSE.  - Khushboo (Khushbu/Khushboo) Mirza, an AMU alumna involved in Chandrayaan missions, was promoted to Scientist/Engineer–SF (Grade F) at ISRO—not appointed as a Director of an ISRO centre. Multiple fact-checks and AMU’s note confirm this. - The “second Muslim scientist after A.P.J. Abdul Kalam to hold this rank” claim is baseless; many Muslim scientists have served at ISRO in various ranks, and Kalam himself was not an ISRO “Director” of a centre. - The stated age (35) is also inconsistent with public profiles.

claim: The CDC may have to stop calling COVID-19 an ‘epidemic’ due to a remarkably low death rate.
response_text: FALSE.  The CDC never said it would stop calling COVID-19 an “epidemic” because of a low death rate. Labels like epidemic or pandemic are based on the extent of spread and cases above expected levels, not mortality alone. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic in 2020 and, while emergency declarations ended in 2023, that change wasn’t due to a “remarkably low” death rate; COVID-19 has continued to cause substantial mortality.

claim: A letter from a consultant at a hospital in Surrey claims that hospitals are empty and that there is no pandemic.
response_text: FALSE  A viral “letter” claiming to be from a Surrey hospital consultant saying hospitals were empty and there was no pandemic was debunked. Local NHS trusts said it was not from their consultants, and hospital data at the time showed high Covid-19 admissions and pressure on services. (See fact-checks such as Full Fact and NHS England data from winter 2020–21.)

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) is advertising home-based jobs to "fight coronavirus" and says no experience is necessary.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim traces to widely circulated scam/phishing posts during COVID-19. WHO said it was not recruiting “work-from-home” staff with “no experience” to fight coronavirus. Official WHO vacancies are listed on its career site and require relevant qualifications; they don’t recruit via WhatsApp/viral links promising no experience.

claim: Deaths from COVID-19 are nearing zero in the U.S. in early July 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  In early July 2020, the U.S. was still recording hundreds of COVID-19 deaths per day. The 7-day average was roughly 400–600 daily deaths (after weekend/holiday dips and rebounds), far from “nearing zero.” National cumulative deaths had surpassed 130,000 by mid-July 2020. Sources such as CDC, Johns Hopkins, and the COVID Tracking Project show this pattern. Uncertainty: exact daily counts vary by reporting delays, but all credible series show substantial, not near-zero, deaths.

claim: People are developing fungal lung infections due to wearing face masks.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that wearing face masks causes fungal lung infections. Fungal lung diseases (e.g., aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, mucormycosis) arise from inhaling spores in the environment and are mainly a risk for people with specific exposures or weakened immunity. Masks act as a barrier and, if anything, reduce exposure to spores. Reports of “black fungus” during COVID-19 were linked to the illness and steroid use, not to mask-wearing. Regularly washing or replacing masks is still good hygiene.

claim: The founder of Ghana's Progressive People’s Party (PPP), Dr Paa Kwasi Nduom tweeted that Prof. Jane Opoku Agyeman was far better than Ghana's current Vice-President Mahamudu Bawumia.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The tweet attributed to Dr. Papa Kwesi Nduom (PPP founder) praising Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang as “far better” than Vice-President Mahamudu Bawumia was a fabricated post that circulated in July 2020. Nduom/PPP representatives stated he did not make the comment and that he is not active on Twitter. Ghanaian fact-checkers (e.g., GhanaFact, DUBAWA) debunked the claim. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Herbal drink made of snake grass can cure cancer by killing cancer cells in 24 hours.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible clinical evidence that “snake grass” (often marketed as Sabah snake grass/Clinacanthus nutans) cures cancer, let alone kills all cancer cells in 24 hours. Claims stem from lab (in vitro) studies where concentrated extracts can harm cancer cell lines, but such results do not translate to safe, effective cures in humans. No reputable oncology guidelines or regulatory bodies recognize any snake grass drink as a cancer cure. Relying on it in place of proven treatments can be dangerous.

claim: International students contributed over $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2018-19.
response_text: TRUE.  NAFSA’s 2019 analysis (based on IIE Open Doors data) estimated that international students contributed about $41.0 billion to the U.S. economy in the 2018–2019 academic year, supporting over 458,000 jobs—i.e., over $40 billion.

claim: Over 1 million international students studied at American universities in the 2018-19 school year.
response_text: TRUE.  The IIE/Open Doors 2019 report counted about 1,095,299 international students in U.S. colleges and universities in the 2018–2019 academic year—i.e., over one million.

claim: Ghana’s Health Minister, Kwaku Agyeman-Manu claims that President Akufo-Addo is tired of the coronavirus fight due to citizens reluctance to adhere to the preventive protocols.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record or verified report of Health Minister Kwaku Agyeman-Manu saying President Akufo-Addo is “tired of the coronavirus fight” because of citizens’ non-compliance. Ghanaian fact-checkers have debunked this claim; the minister has publicly expressed the President’s concern and urged adherence to protocols, not that he was “tired.” (Slight uncertainty due to the volume of social media misquotes, but no reliable source corroborates the quote.)

claim: President Donald Trump claimed that Nascar's decision to ban confederate flags at NASCAR events, has caused the lowest ratings ever.
NOT ONE POLITICIAN DIED, LOST THEIR JOB OR WORN MASKS DURING THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC
response_text: FALSE.  - Many politicians died of COVID-19, e.g., U.S. Rep. Ron Wright (Feb 2021) and U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Letlow (Dec 2020). Several Iranian MPs also died early in the pandemic. - Some lost their jobs or resigned over pandemic-related issues, e.g., UK Health Secretary Matt Hancock (June 2021) and New Zealand Health Minister David Clark (July 2020). - Politicians widely wore masks in public, including Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi, Mitch McConnell, and even Donald Trump (e.g., at Walter Reed in July 2020).

claim: An image in New Zealand shows that a rural New Zealand town is set to remove a trout statue
response_text: FALSE  Multiple local reports and council statements say there is no plan to remove any town’s iconic trout statue. A viral image claiming a rural NZ town (often cited as Tūrangi) would remove its trout statue was fabricated/misleading; the council denied it and confirmed no removal is planned.

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has seen conspiracy theories emerge with claims 5G vendors have used the lockdown in Australia – and elsewhere – to roll out 5G networks without public knowledge. Accompanying those are claims that the expanded network may cause negative health effects in people.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread 5G-related conspiracy theories emerged globally, including in Australia. These included claims that telecoms used lockdowns to install or expand 5G “in secret,” and assertions that 5G causes harmful health effects or was linked to COVID-19. Australian authorities and fact-checkers (e.g., ARPANSA, AFP/ABC) debunked these claims, and media reported incidents of tower vandalism tied to such conspiracies.

claim: Muslims failing to understand government messaging were responsible for Leicester’s local outbreak.
response_text: FALSE.  - Official analyses (e.g., Public Health England’s review of the Leicester spike in July 2020) found no single cause and did not blame any religious group. Factors included workplace transmission (notably in garment/textile settings), household density, and broader community transmission. - Local authorities had multilingual guidance in place, and Leicester’s mosques were closed with Muslim community leaders promoting restrictions. - No evidence supports the claim that Muslims’ failure to understand government messaging was responsible for the outbreak.

claim: Ghislaine Maxwell, the recently arrested associate of Jeffrey Epstein, has tested positive for COVID-19 in jail.
response_text: FALSE.  There were online rumors in July 2020 that Ghislaine Maxwell had COVID-19 after her arrest, but no credible outlets confirmed this. Reuters and other fact-checkers found no evidence she tested positive, and authorities did not report a positive test.

claim: American rapper Kanye West is running for President of the United States in the 2020 elections.
response_text: TRUE.  Kanye West announced on July 4, 2020 that he was running for U.S. president, filed with the FEC, and appeared on the ballot in multiple states as an independent (the “Birthday Party”) during the 2020 election.

claim: Obasanjo said there will be a second war in Nigeria
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Olusegun Obasanjo saying “there will be a second war in Nigeria.” Instead, he has repeatedly warned against conflict and urged steps to prevent any “second civil war,” stressing dialogue and reforms. Reports and speeches attributed to him emphasize avoiding war, not predicting it. (Slight uncertainty due to the volume of online misquotes.)

claim: Muslims can’t use alcohol-based hand sanitiser as it is against their religion.
response_text: FALSE.  Islam forbids consuming intoxicants, not using alcohol externally for hygiene or medicine. Major Islamic juristic bodies and fatwa councils have ruled alcohol‑based hand sanitisers permissible (and even recommended) for disinfection, especially for public health. Some individuals may prefer alcohol‑free options, but there is no blanket religious prohibition on their use.

claim: Zara closed 1,200 stores due to effects the covid19 pandemic had on the  economy
response_text: TRUE – with nuance. In June 2020, Zara’s parent company Inditex announced it would close 1,000–1,200 stores worldwide, mainly smaller shops, as the COVID-19 pandemic hit sales and accelerated a shift to online. Not all closures were Zara-branded stores, and the figure was “up to 1,200,” not exactly 1,200.

claim: The founder of AirBnb said that because of this pandemic, 12 years of efforts were destroyed in 6 -8 weeks due to effects the covid19 pandemic had on the  economy
response_text: TRUE.  Airbnb cofounder/CEO Brian Chesky said in mid-2020 that “We spent 12 years building Airbnb’s business, and within about six weeks, we lost almost everything,” referring to the impact of COVID‑19. While he didn’t use the exact word “destroyed” and often said “about six weeks” (sometimes “4–6 weeks”), the claim’s substance—12 years of work wiped out in roughly 6–8 weeks due to the pandemic’s economic effects—is accurate.

claim: Tata Motors has come up with a new electric car called EVision, which can run up to 1,000 kms on being charged once and the battery has a 10-year warranty.
response_text: FALSE.  Tata EVision is a 2018 concept sedan shown at the Geneva Motor Show, not a launched production car. Tata Motors has not announced a 1,000 km-per-charge range or a 10‑year battery warranty for it; Tata’s current EVs typically claim far lower ranges and offer about an 8‑year/160,000 km battery warranty.

claim: Rolex discontinued production due to effects the covid19 pandemic had on the  economy
response_text: FALSE.  Rolex did not discontinue production. It temporarily suspended manufacturing in March 2020 due to COVID‑19 health precautions and lockdowns, then gradually resumed operations a few weeks later. The pause was not a permanent shutdown, nor primarily an “economic” decision.

claim: Shanghai-based clothing company La Chapelle Closed 4391 stores due to effects the covid19 pandemic had on the  economy
response_text: FALSE.  La Chapelle did close about 4,391 stores, but that reduction occurred in 2019 (per its 2019 annual report), before COVID-19’s economic impact. The closures were driven by ongoing losses and restructuring; the pandemic later worsened its situation but did not cause that specific 4,391 figure.

claim: Viral video shows Pakistani and Chinese soldiers celebrating after 20 Indian soldiers were killed in action at Galwan Valley.
response_text: FALSE.  The circulated clip is older footage from a Pakistan–China joint military exercise where troops danced/celebrated during the drills. Fact-checks traced it to pre-2020 events, not to the June 2020 Galwan clash. It was miscaptioned as a celebration after the death of 20 Indian soldiers.

claim: Dr VK Srinivas, Vice President of Bharat Biotech photographed having the first COVID-19 vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The widely shared photo does not show “Dr VK Srinivas, Vice President of Bharat Biotech,” getting the first Covaxin shot. Bharat Biotech and trial-site officials clarified that the person in the image was a trial volunteer (and not a company VP), and the identity of volunteers is confidential. There is no evidence that a Bharat Biotech VP named “Dr VK Srinivas” was photographed receiving the first dose.

claim: One in four NI adults are now at risk of hunger and malnutrition.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Recent surveys in Northern Ireland show roughly 20–25% of households report food insecurity at times, which is not the same as “adults at risk of hunger and malnutrition.” Community prevalence of malnutrition risk is much lower; high rates (20–30%) are seen in hospital/care settings, not across all NI adults. So the claim overstates the situation. Uncertainty: figures vary by survey period and definition of food insecurity.

claim: A cartoon showing piglets with given names of Indian national media outlets feeding on a pig with the face of Indian Prime Minister Nerendra Modi is drawn by American cartoonist Ben Garrison.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “Modi-as-pig with media piglets” cartoon has been misattributed to Ben Garrison. It does not appear on Garrison’s official outlets (GrrrGraphics) and he has publicly listed such India-themed images as fake attributions to his name. Indian fact-checkers have also debunked the claim and found no evidence it was drawn by Garrison.

claim: People are starting to enter ERs with fungal lung infections from wearing masks.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible evidence of an ER uptick in fungal lung infections caused by wearing masks. Fungal pneumonias (e.g., aspergillosis, histoplasmosis) come from inhaling environmental spores and are seen mainly in people with specific exposures or weakened immunity. Masks actually reduce inhalation of particles, including spores. Health agencies report masks are safe; the “black fungus” surge in India was linked to COVID, steroids, and diabetes—not masks. Poor mask hygiene can cause skin irritation, not deep fungal lung infections. (Cannot rule out isolated anecdotes, but no documented trend.)

claim: Donald Trump tweeted that he told the South Dakota governor that “everyone is fine without a mask. They just need to close there (sic) border with California.”
response_text: FALSE.  No such tweet appears in Trump’s archived tweets, and fact-checkers have identified the screenshot/quote as fabricated. The line also makes little sense geographically—South Dakota doesn’t border California—reinforcing that it’s a hoax. (Trump and Gov. Kristi Noem did oppose mask mandates, but this specific tweet didn’t happen.)

claim: Budweiser admits several employees have been pissing in its beer tanks for years.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated on fake/satire sites and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Budweiser/AB InBev has made no such admission, and there’s no credible evidence of employees urinating in its beer tanks. A viral video about a worker urinating involved Tsingtao in China, not Budweiser.

claim: Photos showing sewer, sacks and trash-filled beaches in Boracay were taken during the past administration of former president Benigno Aquino III.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact checks (e.g., Rappler, Vera Files, AFP in April 2018) found the viral collage mixed photos from different years. At least two of the images (including the “sewer”/outfall and the sandbags along the shore) were taken in 2017–2018 under President Duterte, while the trash-strewn beach photo was from May 2015 after the LaBoracay party under President Aquino. So it’s incorrect to say the photos were taken during the Aquino administration. Uncertainty: exact photographers/dates vary by image, but the mixed timeline is well established.

claim: A Budweiser employee has been urinating in a beer tank for 12 years.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a satirical/fake-news story and has been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers. There are no credible reports or evidence that a Budweiser employee urinated in beer tanks for years. (A separate 2023 video of a worker at China’s Tsingtao Brewery sparked confusion but was unrelated to Budweiser.)

claim: Wearing of a face mask while carrying a gun is a class 4 felony.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There is no general law making this a Class 4 felony. The widely cited example is Arizona, where wearing a mask or disguise to conceal one’s identity while carrying a deadly weapon is a Class 6 felony under A.R.S. § 13-3102—not Class 4. In many states, wearing a mask while armed is not independently illegal unless tied to other criminal intent, and penalties vary by jurisdiction. (Some states also created health-related exceptions during COVID-19.) Uncertainty: Laws differ by state, but the “Class 4 felony” claim is not generally accurate.

claim: "Now Even The COMMON COLD Is Being Counted As A Positive COVID-19 Result.
response_text: FALSE.  PCR and antigen tests used to diagnose COVID‑19 are designed to specifically detect SARS‑CoV‑2 and are validated not to cross‑react with common cold viruses (like rhinoviruses or seasonal coronaviruses 229E, NL63, OC43, HKU1). While rare false positives can occur (e.g., contamination, clerical error), a typical “common cold” does not trigger a positive COVID result. Antibody (serology) tests can occasionally cross‑react, but they aren’t used to count acute COVID cases. Overlapping symptoms mean a person with “a cold” could actually have COVID, but that’s because they’re infected with SARS‑CoV‑2, not because cold viruses are being counted as COVID. Uncertainty: low.

claim: New Zealand’s national debt has risen to more than $NZ120 billion.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: On standard “gross” measures (e.g., government bonds and bills outstanding/GSID reported by NZ Debt Management), New Zealand’s government debt has been well above NZ$120 billion since the COVID‑19 period and is around the NZ$180–200b range recently. Note: on “net core Crown debt” measures the figure is lower (roughly ~NZ$90–110b in recent years), so the claim depends on the definition, but gross “national debt” clearly exceeds NZ$120b.

claim: Kapil Sibal, an Indian lawyer and politician, is going to challenge India's government’s decision to ban 59 Chinese apps, including TikTok, in India's Supreme Court.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports or court filings show Kapil Sibal planned to challenge the June 2020 ban of 59 Chinese apps (including TikTok) in India’s Supreme Court. Fact-checkers (e.g., Alt News/BOOM) debunked the viral claim at the time. The confusion likely stems from Sibal having represented TikTok in an unrelated 2019 Madras High Court matter.

claim: Everyone including essential workers will be compensated $1,000 by FEMA.
response_text: FALSE.  FEMA does not issue universal cash payments. Its assistance is limited to eligible disaster survivors who apply after a declared disaster, and amounts/eligibility vary. There is no FEMA program that pays everyone—or all essential workers—$1,000.

claim: Taylor Swift Says We Should Remove The Statue of Liberty
response_text: FALSE  There’s no credible record—no interviews, posts, or reputable news reports—of Taylor Swift calling for the Statue of Liberty to be removed. This claim appears to stem from fabricated/satirical online posts, not from anything she has said.

claim: A Muslim woman who ordered a drink from a Target Starbucks was given a cup with “ISIS” written on the cup instead of her name.
response_text: TRUE.  Widely reported in July 2020: A Muslim woman in hijab at a Starbucks kiosk inside a Target in St. Paul, Minnesota received a cup labeled “ISIS” instead of her name (“Aishah”). CAIR filed a discrimination complaint; Target apologized and said it was an error. The incident is documented, though intent was disputed.

claim: Dr. Kary B. Mullis, Nobel Laureate and inventor of the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test used to detect coronavirus said it couldn't be used for virus detection.
response_text: FALSE.  Kary Mullis did not say PCR can’t detect viruses. He often cautioned that PCR amplifies genetic material and doesn’t by itself prove disease or infectiousness, but he acknowledged it detects specific sequences. He died in August 2019, before COVID-19, so he never commented on PCR tests for coronavirus. The claim misrepresents his remarks.

claim: Whole Foods stores do not accept cash payments.
response_text: FALSE. Whole Foods Market accepts cash at checkout (along with cards, mobile pay, and often EBT). While some Amazon-affiliated store formats experimented with cashless models, Whole Foods itself is not cashless, and many locations are in cities that legally require cash acceptance.

claim: Leicester has gone back into lockdown soon after 5G coveage was rolled out there.
response_text: FALSE.  Leicester’s local Covid-19 lockdown was imposed at the end of June 2020. Parts of Leicester already had 5G service from major UK networks months earlier (in late 2019/early 2020). There’s no evidence of a new 5G rollout there just before the lockdown. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Covid 19 symptoms and 5G are related.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: COVID‑19 is caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus and cannot be created or spread by radio waves. 5G uses non‑ionizing radiofrequency energy that does not damage DNA or impair the immune system at exposure levels used in networks. The pandemic spread widely in places without 5G, and WHO/CDC and other health authorities report no link between 5G and COVID‑19 symptoms.

claim: The national security law will only target an extremely small minority of people who have breached the law, while the life and property, basic rights and freedoms of the overwhelming majority of Hong Kong residents will be protected.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Since its enactment in 2020, Hong Kong’s National Security Law has been enforced with broad, vague definitions that have curtailed freedoms well beyond an “extremely small minority.” Authorities have arrested hundreds, including opposition politicians, activists, journalists, and organizers (e.g., the “47 democrats” case; closures of Apple Daily and Stand News), and protests, vigils, books, and civil-society groups have been suppressed. Human-rights bodies and press-freedom indexes report a marked, system‑wide chilling effect on expression, assembly, and media—impacting the wider population, not just proven law‑breakers.  Note: Arrest totals remain a small share of Hong Kong’s population, but the law’s deterrent and restrictive effects are broad.

claim: US Congresswoman Maxine Waters of California introduced a bill, H.R. 2020, the Erasing Confederate History Act of 2020, to rename the 11 US states that originally made up the Confederacy.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no congressional record of a bill titled “Erasing Confederate History Act of 2020,” and Rep. Maxine Waters did not introduce any bill to rename former Confederate states. H.R. 2020 in the 116th Congress was an unrelated measure and not sponsored by Waters. The claim traces to a satirical/hoax post. Additionally, Congress does not unilaterally rename U.S. states.

claim: An image purported to show a political billboard from the young arm of New Zealand National Party shows a culturally insensitive slogan towards Māoris.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The circulating image is a doctored/meme edit, not a real Young Nats billboard. There’s no credible record or news coverage of such a billboard, and party sources denied it. Visual cues (e.g., missing required promoter statements) and reverse-image traces point to an edited National Party-style poster. Slight uncertainty only because viral posts varied, but the billboard itself wasn’t genuine.

claim: Charles Krauthammer wrote that former President Barack Obama’s non profit Organizing for Action, is the “shadow government organization aimed at resisting and tearing down the Constitutional Republic we know as America”.
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is from a viral, misattributed post; Charles Krauthammer did not write it. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) found no such column by Krauthammer, and the language mirrors other 2017 commentaries (notably Paul Sperry in the New York Post) about OFA as a “shadow government.” Krauthammer’s authorship was denied and there’s no record of him using that phrasing.

claim: Michelle Obama had to Surrender her Law License because she committed  'Insurance Fraud'
response_text: FALSE.  Michelle Obama did not surrender her law license for insurance fraud. Illinois bar records show she placed her license on voluntary inactive status in the early 1990s when she was no longer practicing law. There is no disciplinary history or evidence of any insurance-fraud case against her. Going inactive is common and does not imply misconduct.

claim: “Oklahoma 100% positive coronavirus test rate after Trump Tulsa rally.”
response_text: FALSE.  Oklahoma’s test positivity after the June 20, 2020 Tulsa rally was nowhere near 100%. State health data at the time showed single‑digit positivity (roughly 4–8% in late June/early July). While cases rose in Tulsa County after the rally, there was no statewide 100% positive test rate. This appears to be a misinterpretation; reports of 100% positivity involved some Florida labs later found to be reporting errors, not Oklahoma.

claim: Surface air temperatures at the bottom of the world have risen three times faster than the global average since the 1990s.
response_text: TRUE (with a caveat). Studies show the South Pole (the “bottom of the world”) warmed about 0.6°C per decade from 1989–2018—roughly three times the global average (~0.2°C/decade) over the same period. However, that rapid rate applies to the South Pole region, not the entire Antarctic continent, which shows more mixed trends.

claim: Democrat-controlled states suffered the harshest restriction in the US during the coronavirus pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple policy trackers and studies found that, on average, Democratic-led states adopted earlier, more stringent, and longer-lasting COVID-19 restrictions (stay-at-home orders, business and school closures, mask mandates) than Republican-led states. Rankings that scored state “strictness” (e.g., WalletHub and state-level stringency analyses) consistently placed states like California, Hawaii, New York, New Jersey, and New Mexico—largely Democrat-controlled—among the most restrictive for extended periods, while many Republican-led states (e.g., Florida, South Dakota, Oklahoma) had fewer or shorter restrictions.   Note: “Harshest” depends on the metric and time frame, and there were exceptions (some GOP governors imposed strict early measures), but the overall pattern supports the claim.

claim: Black Lives Matter was funded and designed by the US Democrats to be a social weapon.
response_text: FALSE.  Black Lives Matter began in 2013 as a decentralized movement founded by activists Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi, not by the Democratic Party. Its funding has come largely from individual donations and grants via fiscal sponsors (e.g., Thousand Currents, later Tides), with ActBlue serving only as a payment processor—not a DNC funnel. While many Democrats expressed support and a separate BLM PAC later endorsed candidates, there is no credible evidence that the Democratic Party designed or funded BLM as a “social weapon.”

claim: The US Democratic Party has a owned and controlled corporate media monopoly.
response_text: FALSE.  U.S. news media are owned by multiple private companies (e.g., Disney/ABC, Comcast/NBC, Fox Corp, Paramount/CBS, Warner Bros. Discovery, plus many independents and public broadcasters). None are owned or controlled by the Democratic Party. The media landscape is pluralistic with clearly Republican-leaning outlets (e.g., Fox News, Newsmax, talk radio, Sinclair) alongside centrist or liberal-leaning ones. While there is corporate concentration, there is no single “corporate media monopoly,” and it is not party-owned.

claim: The next major advantage of the pandemic for the Deep State was the case made to the public for mail-in voting, a highly insecure practice proven to be rampant with fraud.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that a “Deep State” engineered pandemic-related voting changes. More importantly, the assertion that mail-in voting is “highly insecure” and “proven to be rampant with fraud” is contradicted by extensive evidence: states that have long used mail voting (e.g., Oregon, Washington, Colorado, Utah) show extremely low fraud rates; 2020 audits, recounts, and court cases found no widespread mail-ballot fraud; and federal and state election officials—including Trump’s DOJ and bipartisan state authorities—reported no evidence of fraud on a scale that could affect results. Isolated cases occur, but “rampant” fraud has not been demonstrated.

claim: President Geingob of Namibia fined all those who attended the party he hosted to mark his political party Swapo’s (South West Africa People’s Organisation) 60th birthday during the coronavirus lockdown when gatherings were banned.
response_text: FALSE.  No such party took place. SWAPO’s 60th anniversary in April 2020 was marked without public gatherings due to Namibia’s Covid-19 restrictions, and the Namibian presidency denied any party was hosted. Also, the president has no authority to “fine” attendees—penalties for lockdown breaches are imposed by law enforcement/courts under the state of emergency regulations. Fact-checkers (e.g., Africa Check/AFP) debunked this claim as fabricated.

claim: US Democratic nominee for US President Joe Biden avoided interviews and debates during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns.
response_text: FALSE.  During the pandemic, Joe Biden continued doing numerous interviews remotely from Delaware (e.g., CNN, MSNBC, ABC, CBS, local media, and radio such as The Breakfast Club). He also participated in debates: the March 15, 2020 Democratic primary debate with Bernie Sanders (held without an audience), and two general-election debates with Donald Trump (Sept 29 and Oct 22, 2020). The second planned general-election debate was canceled after Trump refused a virtual format, but Biden held a town hall instead. He limited in-person events but did not avoid interviews or debates.

claim: They [Democrats and the Deep State] flooded US streets with deadly drugs to manufacture a devastating epidemic of addiction and mass incarceration.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Democrats or a “Deep State” intentionally flooded U.S. streets with drugs to engineer addiction and mass incarceration. The modern opioid crisis was largely driven by pharmaceutical companies’ aggressive marketing and overprescribing of legal opioids, later supplanted by illicit heroin and fentanyl trafficking. Earlier, while some individuals linked to the Contra war were involved in drug trafficking, official investigations (CIA and DOJ inspectors general) found no evidence of a government plot to flood communities with crack. The rise in mass incarceration resulted primarily from bipartisan policy choices (e.g., War on Drugs, mandatory minimums, the 1994 crime bill), not from deliberate government distribution of drugs.

claim: US President Barack Obama was directed by the Deep State to authorize millions in funding for the Wuhan Institute of Virology  to finance a global biological attack timed to release within an  election year.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no evidence of any “Deep State” directing Obama, nor of a plan to time a “global biological attack” to an election year. - The NIH/NIAID awarded a 2014 grant to EcoHealth Alliance for coronavirus research; a portion (roughly $600,000 over several years) was sub-awarded to the Wuhan Institute of Virology—not “millions” directly to WIV. Such grants are peer-reviewed agency awards, not presidential directives. - U.S. intelligence assessments and scientific reviews have found no evidence that COVID-19 was engineered as a bioweapon or intentionally released.

claim: COVID-19 (Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests are ‘scientifically meaningless’
response_text: FALSE.  PCR tests for COVID-19 are scientifically valid and widely validated tools for detecting SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA. They show high analytical sensitivity and specificity and are considered the diagnostic gold standard by public health agencies (e.g., WHO, CDC). While they have limitations—such as detecting viral RNA even when a person may no longer be infectious, and requiring careful interpretation of cycle threshold values and timing relative to symptom onset—they are far from “meaningless” and are essential for diagnosis and surveillance.

claim: COVID-19 Removal Cards kill Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  So-called “COVID-19 removal/anti-virus cards” (often chlorine dioxide–releasing badges) have no credible evidence that they kill coronavirus or protect wearers. Multiple regulators (e.g., Japan’s Consumer Affairs Agency, Australia’s TGA, Philippines FDA) have warned against or penalized such claims. At concentrations safe for people, chlorine dioxide from these cards is ineffective; at levels that could inactivate viruses, it would be unsafe to inhale.

claim: Drinking water will protect you from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Drinking water does not prevent or “flush out” COVID-19. Hydration is good for general health but doesn’t stop infection. Proven protections include vaccination, well-fitted masks, good ventilation, hand hygiene, and staying home when sick.

claim: Keir Starmer stopped Jimmy Savile being charged in 2009.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2009 the decision not to charge Jimmy Savile was made by local CPS prosecutors (Surrey/Sussex) based on the police file, not by Keir Starmer. An independent review by Alison Levitt QC (2013), commissioned while Starmer was Director of Public Prosecutions, found Starmer had no involvement in that decision. Starmer later apologised on behalf of the CPS for the failures identified.

claim: The Ministry of AYUSH, Government of India Has Approved Patanjali's 'Coronil'.
response_text: FALSE.  The Ministry of AYUSH did not approve Coronil as a treatment or cure for COVID‑19. After Patanjali’s 2020 launch claims, AYUSH directed them to stop advertising it as a COVID cure and later clarified (2021) that Coronil only had a state-issued license as an Ayurvedic medicine and could be marketed, at most, as a supportive/immunity product—not as a prevention or treatment for COVID‑19. WHO also said it had not certified Coronil.

claim: Seven people were shot in the neighbourhood of Newark in June 2018.
response_text: TRUE  Local reports (e.g., NJ.com/RLS Media) documented multiple shootings in Newark, New Jersey, in June 2018 with a total of seven people wounded in separate incidents. Slight uncertainty only about the exact phrasing “neighbourhood of Newark,” but the event count and timing align.

claim: Jay Inslee claims he's the first governor to implement a public option health insurance plan.
response_text: TRUE.  Washington, under Gov. Jay Inslee, enacted the nation’s first state “public option” (Cascade Care) in 2019, with plans launching in 2021. It was the first such program implemented; Colorado and Nevada followed later. Note: Washington’s model is state-designed but delivered by private insurers with capped provider rates.

claim: Most Americans support Roe v. Wade.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple polls over many years showed a majority of Americans supported Roe v. Wade or opposed overturning it—typically around 55–70%. For example, in 2022 major polls (Pew, NBC/WSJ, Quinnipiac, NPR/Marist) found about 60–65% opposed overturning Roe, and post-Dobbs surveys (Pew, KFF) show majorities disapproved of the decision to overturn it. Note: exact percentages vary with question wording and public familiarity with Roe.

claim: Idli is the healthiest breakfast item in the whole world as certified by UNESCO.
response_text: FALSE.  UNESCO does not certify or rank foods for healthiness. It designates World Heritage Sites and lists elements of Intangible Cultural Heritage, but there is no UNESCO recognition of idli (or any food) as the “healthiest breakfast.” This claim is a social media hoax, though idli can be a healthy option.

claim: Beto O'Rourke said that he does not want to repeal Section 1325.
response_text: TRUE.  In the June 26, 2019 Democratic primary debate, when Julián Castro pressed him on repealing 8 U.S.C. §1325 (criminalizing improper border entry), Beto O’Rourke said he would not repeal it, arguing repeal wasn’t necessary to address family separations. This was reported in the debate transcript and contemporaneous coverage (e.g., NBC, PolitiFact).

claim: South Africa is number one in the killing of women internationally.
response_text: FALSE.  South Africa has very high levels of femicide, but global datasets (e.g., UNODC’s Global Study on Homicide and WHO/IHME estimates) show several countries with higher female homicide/femicide rates—often in Latin America (such as El Salvador, Honduras, Jamaica) and sometimes Lesotho in Africa. South Africa is among the worst-affected and has very high intimate partner femicide rates, but it is not “number one” internationally. (Minor uncertainty stems from differences in definitions and years, but rankings consistently place other countries above South Africa.)

claim: The average family in America forks over more of their hard-earned income to their local hospital than to the IRS.
response_text: FALSE.  - IRS vs. hospitals: The IRS collects thousands of dollars per household on average each year (individual income taxes plus payroll taxes total roughly $3.8 trillion annually; spread over ~130 million households, that’s many thousands per household on average). - Hospital payments: Households’ direct out-of-pocket payments to hospitals are only a small slice of hospital funding—on the order of a few dozen billions total per year. That averages just a few hundred dollars per household (CMS National Health Expenditure data).  Even if some families owe little or no federal income tax, most still pay payroll taxes, and average IRS payments far exceed direct payments to hospitals. Uncertainty low.

claim: The United States Annual Arms Control Compliance Report does not address the U.S. withdrawal from the Arms Trade Treaty (ATT).
response_text: FALSE. The State Department’s Annual Arms Control, Nonproliferation, and Disarmament Compliance Report has noted the United States’ 2019 decision not to become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty (i.e., the “un-signing”) and that the U.S. therefore has no obligations under it. This acknowledgement addresses the U.S. withdrawal decision, even if no compliance assessment is provided for a treaty the U.S. is not party to. (Minor uncertainty about which edition a reader consults, but post-2019 reports include this point.)

claim: Covid-19 surcharges are being applied in the USA.
response_text: TRUE.  Many U.S. businesses implemented COVID-19 surcharges, especially in 2020–2021, to cover PPE, cleaning, and other pandemic-related costs (e.g., restaurants, dental offices, salons). Some employers also added health-plan surcharges for unvaccinated employees. These fees were not universal and often temporary, but they were applied in the USA. Uncertainty: prevalence has declined since.

claim: The US Annual Arms Control Compliance Report  Mulling resumption of nuclear tests.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The U.S. State Department’s Annual Arms Control Compliance Report is an assessment of countries’ adherence to arms control obligations; it does not set policy and does not “mull” resuming U.S. nuclear tests. The United States has observed a moratorium on nuclear explosive testing since 1992 and, under current policy, states it has no plans to resume testing. Media reports of internal discussions in 2020 did not stem from the Compliance Report.

claim: The US Annual Arms Control Compliance Report  Blocking negotiation of the  Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) verification protocol.
response_text: FALSE.  The Annual Arms Control Compliance Report is a U.S. assessment document; it does not itself block negotiations. Negotiations on a BWC verification protocol collapsed in 2001 when the U.S. government rejected the draft protocol and opposed continuing the Ad Hoc Group— a policy decision, not an action of the report (later reports have simply reiterated U.S. skepticism about BWC verifiability).

claim: The Honor Guard soldiers that march at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington Cemetery carry live ammunition
response_text: FALSE.  The Sentinels’ M14 rifles used in the ceremonial guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier are not loaded, and the guards do not routinely carry live ammunition on their person. However, ammunition and armed security are readily available nearby in case of an emergency. (Source: Society of the Honor Guard/Arlington Cemetery public information; slight uncertainty due to security procedures not publicly detailed.)

claim: In the Indian marketplace, Livfavir, manufactured by Livealth Biopharma, is cheaper than Glenmark's Fabiflu.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Glenmark cut FabiFlu’s price to about ₹49 per 200 mg tablet in 2020 (widely reported by Indian business media). Available trade listings for Livealth Biopharma’s Livfavir typically show higher MRPs per tablet (often ~₹65–₹75 for 200 mg). I find no reliable evidence that Livfavir is priced below FabiFlu. Uncertainty: prices can vary by time and channel, but prevailing data do not support the claim.

claim: In 1977, U.S. President Joe Biden said integrating black students would turn schools into "a jungle… a racial jungle."
response_text: TRUE.  Context: In a 1977 Senate hearing on court-ordered busing to integrate schools, then–Sen. Joe Biden said, “Unless we do something… my children are going to grow up in a jungle, the jungle being a racial jungle.” He was arguing against busing; the wording is accurate, though he framed it as a concern about racial conflict rather than calling Black students a “jungle.”

claim: There were issues with polling places in Kentucky
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Kentucky has had documented polling-place problems, notably in the June 2020 primary when the state drastically consolidated sites (e.g., just one in Louisville and one in Lexington), leading to long lines and confusion; a judge briefly extended voting after some voters were locked out at closing time. Isolated site glitches and delays have also occurred in other elections. (If a specific election was intended, details may vary.)

claim: Gargling with a salt water concoction, or drinking water with salt or vinegar will “kill” the virus causing COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that gargling salt water or drinking water with salt or vinegar kills SARS‑CoV‑2 in the body. These solutions may soothe a sore throat but do not prevent or cure COVID‑19; the virus replicates inside cells where such rinses can’t reach. Health authorities (e.g., WHO/CDC) specifically list this as a myth.

claim: No country currently has a functioning Covid-19 track and trace app.
response_text: TRUE.  By 2023–2024, most countries retired their COVID-19 contact-tracing apps (e.g., UK’s NHS COVID-19, Germany’s Corona-Warn-App, Singapore’s TraceTogether, Japan’s COCOA, Switzerland’s SwissCovid). Apple and Google also deprecated the Exposure Notifications framework, effectively ending support. Remaining apps were repurposed (e.g., health records) and no longer perform exposure notifications. Minor uncertainty only for any niche/local deployments, but no known countrywide systems remain functional.

claim: British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, speaking in the British Parliament, stated that no country currently has a functioning track and trace app for countering Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Boris Johnson did say this in Parliament (June 2020), but the statement was incorrect: several countries already had operational COVID-19 contact-tracing apps, including Germany (Corona-Warn-App), Italy (Immuni), Singapore (TraceTogether), and India (Aarogya Setu), among others.

claim: Transactions by Google Pay are not protected by the Reserve Bank of India nor by Indian law.
response_text: FALSE.  UPI payments made via Google Pay are processed by regulated partner banks and the NPCI, which operates UPI under the Reserve Bank of India’s oversight and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Google Pay is a third‑party app provider, not a payment system operator, but it must follow NPCI/RBI rules. Consumer disputes are handled through the customer’s bank/NPCI and RBI’s ombudsman mechanisms, so such transactions are protected under Indian law. (The confusion arose from a 2020 RBI filing noting GPay isn’t a PSO, not that UPI transactions via GPay lack protection.)

claim: Unused COVID-19 tests that already showed positive results were found in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence or news reports support that unused COVID-19 tests “already showing positive” were found in Tuscaloosa. Fact-checkers have debunked similar social media claims: rapid tests display a control line by design, and a positive result only appears after a sample is applied. Authorities in Alabama reported no such verified incident.

claim: A video showing emergency services helping COVID-19 patients in the streets of the Pune's Deccan Corner area in June 2020 is real
response_text: FALSE.  The footage is from a COVID-19 preparedness mock drill conducted by Pune authorities (PMC/Police/Fire Brigade) near the Deccan area in early June 2020. Officials and local media clarified that the people seen were role-players, not actual COVID-19 patients being treated on the street.

claim: U.S. coronavirus cases are increasing because more people are being tested for the virus.
response_text: FALSE. More testing can uncover more existing infections, but it doesn’t create them. In U.S. surges, test positivity rates and hospitalizations also rose—patterns that wouldn’t occur if increases were due only to more testing—indicating real growth in transmission.

claim: Glenmark Pharmaceuticals received approvals from Drug Controller General of India to manufacture and market Favipiravir, an anti-viral drug, to treat COVID-19 patients.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In June 2020, Glenmark Pharmaceuticals received DCGI approval for the manufacture and marketing of favipiravir (brand FabiFlu) for the treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19 in India, under restricted/emergency use.

claim: In June 2020, 46 US states had gyms/fitness centers open, while North Carolina was one of four states that did not.
response_text: TRUE.  As of late June 2020, most states had allowed gyms to reopen (often with capacity limits). North Carolina was among the few that still kept indoor gyms closed, along with New York, New Jersey, and Massachusetts. Note: counts varied slightly by date/definitions, and some states (e.g., parts of Michigan) had only partial regional reopenings.

claim: In June 2020, Nigerian debt servicing obligations stood at N943.12 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The N943.12 billion figure is widely reported as Nigeria’s federal government debt service for Q1 2020 (January–March), not “in June 2020.” By end-June (H1 2020), total debt service was higher (around N1.2 trillion per official budget performance/MTEF reports). So attributing N943.12 billion to June 2020 is inaccurate. Uncertainty: exact H1 total varies slightly by source, but 943.12bn is not a June or H1 figure.

claim: President Trump said coronavirus testing makes the U.S. look bad, "so I said to my people, ‘Slow the testing down.’"
response_text: TRUE.  At a June 20, 2020 rally in Tulsa, President Trump said that more testing finds more cases, which makes the U.S. “look bad,” and added: “So I said to my people, ‘Slow the testing down, please.’” (Aides later said he was joking, but he did make the remark.)

claim: Former US president Barack Obama  Declared He And His Family Will Leave the U.S. For Canada If Donald j. Trump Wins Re-Election in the U.S.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence or record of Barack Obama saying he and his family would move to Canada if Donald Trump won re-election. The claim has circulated on satire/misinformation sites and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Obama has made no such announcement and continues to reside in the United States.

claim: In June 2020, 99% of Nigerian revenue was being committed to debt servicing alone.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Nigeria’s finance ministry reported mid‑2020 that, over January–May 2020, federal government debt service (about ₦1.58 trillion) nearly equaled total federal revenue (about ₦1.62 trillion), a debt‑service‑to‑revenue ratio of roughly 98–99%. This was widely cited around June/July 2020. Note: the figure refers to the federal government and to the Jan–May period, not necessarily the single month of June.

claim: Masks violate the US Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s 19.5% minimum oxygen level respiratory protection standard.
response_text: FALSE.  OSHA’s 19.5% oxygen threshold applies to the ambient workplace atmosphere and to selecting respirators for oxygen‑deficient environments. It does not refer to the air inside a face mask. Cloth and surgical masks are not respirators, and N95s are used only in normal-oxygen settings. Evidence and OSHA/CDC guidance show masks do not reduce inhaled oxygen to unsafe levels or create oxygen‑deficient conditions.

claim: Alex Jones claimed on the InfoWars website that Covid-19 is only killing older people.
response_text: FALSE — Uncertain. Jones has repeatedly downplayed COVID-19’s risk to younger people, often saying it mainly affects the elderly and those with underlying conditions, but I find no reliable evidence that he stated on the InfoWars website that it is only killing older people. (And the “only older people” claim is factually wrong; COVID-19 has killed younger people too.)

claim: President Trump tweeted "Anyone who ordered a ticket to my (Tulsa) rally and didn't attend should be arrested and face very powerful charges."
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is from a fabricated tweet. There’s no record of Trump posting it in his Twitter timeline or archives, and multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Snopes) debunked the circulating image claiming he did.

claim: The Government of India has issued a memorandum and directed Google and Apple to restrict several Chinese applications from the respective stores with immediate effect.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: On multiple occasions (e.g., June 2020 and February 2022), India’s Ministry of Electronics and IT invoked Section 69A of the IT Act to block dozens of Chinese-linked apps and directed Google and Apple to remove/restrict them from their app stores with immediate effect. While official documents are typically “orders” under Section 69A (news reports sometimes called them memoranda), the substance of the claim is accurate.

claim: Alex Jones claimed on the InfoWars website that hospitals received $52,000 for every Covid-19 patient and knowingly misdiagnosed patients during the pandemic
response_text: TRUE — On his InfoWars platform in 2020, Alex Jones promoted the false talking point that hospitals were getting roughly $52,000 per COVID-19 patient (a misinterpretation combining $13,000 for a COVID admission and $39,000 for ventilator use) and alleged doctors/hospitals were intentionally misdiagnosing patients to inflate counts. Multiple fact-checks later debunked those figures and the accusation. Minor uncertainty: the exact $52,000 phrasing appears in various InfoWars posts/segments; whether every instance was Jones personally or staff is less clear.

claim: Cloth masks trap carbon dioxide which is a risk to health.
response_text: FALSE.  Cloth masks are porous and allow gases like carbon dioxide and oxygen to pass through. Studies measuring oxygen saturation and CO2 in mask wearers (including with cloth and surgical masks) show no harmful CO2 buildup or impaired gas exchange in healthy adults or children. Major health agencies (CDC/WHO) state masks are safe. While some people with severe lung disease may feel discomfort and should consult a clinician, cloth masks do not trap CO2 at levels that pose a health risk.

claim: Cloth masks do not filter anything.
response_text: FALSE.  Cloth masks do provide filtration. Their efficiency varies by material, weave, number of layers, and fit, but they typically capture a meaningful fraction of respiratory droplets and some aerosols. Studies show common fabrics can block around 10–60% of submicron particles and much higher percentages for larger droplets; multilayer or hybrid fabrics can exceed 80–90% under good fit. They are less effective than surgical masks or respirators but not “zero.”

claim: Alex Jones claimed on the InfoWars website that The United Nations said the economic crisis caused by the Covid-19 pandemic was ‘a good thing'.
response_text: TRUE.  An article/headline on Alex Jones’s InfoWars site claimed the United Nations said the COVID-19-driven economic crisis was “a good thing.” Fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact) noted this misrepresented a UN News piece; the UN did not say the crisis was good. Minor uncertainty: the article appears to have been by an InfoWars writer rather than Jones personally.

claim: Alex Jones claimed on the InfoWars website that Democratic-led areas told people to ‘never’ remove their masks during the pandemic.
response_text: TRUE — Alex Jones used InfoWars to claim that Democratic-run areas were telling people to “never” take off their masks during the pandemic, a hyperbolic framing he used in posts and videos criticizing mask guidance. Mild uncertainty on the exact wording, but the substance of the claim matches his InfoWars commentary.

claim: CERT-In issues a warning of possible phishing attacks.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) routinely issues advisories warning about potential phishing campaigns, and multiple such warnings have been publicly reported over the years. Without a date, I can’t confirm a specific advisory, but the claim aligns with their regular alerts.

claim: A phishing attack that seemed like an official communique on the COVID-19 pandemic was expected to be launched from June 21 2020 onwards in major metropolitan cities of India.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: On 19 June 2020, India’s CERT-In issued an advisory warning of a large-scale phishing campaign expected to start on 21 June 2020. Attackers would impersonate government communications (e.g., using ncov2019@gov.in) and offer “Free COVID-19 testing,” targeting residents of major metropolitan cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Chennai, and Ahmedabad. The advisory cautioned users to avoid clicking links in such emails.

claim: Surgical masks were designed and approved for sterile environments. Every time a person puts on their (surgical) mask they are breathing in the germs from everywhere they went. They should be changed or thrown out every 20-30 minutes in a non sterile environment.
response_text: FALSE.  - Surgical masks are medical devices for source control and splash protection in healthcare, not items “approved only for sterile environments.” Many are non‑sterile and are used widely outside operating rooms. - Wearing a mask does not make you “breathe in the germs from everywhere you went.” The mask filters inhaled air; contamination risks mainly come from touching the mask or reusing one whose inner surface has been contaminated. - No guideline supports changing a surgical mask every 20–30 minutes in non‑sterile settings. WHO/CDC advise replacing single‑use medical masks when damp, soiled, damaged, or hard to breathe through; in practice this is often several hours, not minutes.

claim: Alex Jones claimed on the InfoWars website that there were no patients for US hospital ships during the pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  InfoWars and Alex Jones pushed the “empty hospitals” narrative in early April 2020 and ran segments/posts asserting that the Navy’s hospital ships (USNS Comfort in New York and USNS Mercy in Los Angeles) had no patients. In reality, both ships did treat patients during their deployments (roughly 182 on Comfort and about 77 on Mercy). Slight uncertainty: exact headline phrasing on the site, but the “no patients” claim was made.

claim: Vijaya Hospital founder's son died of Covid-19
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: Vijaya Hospital in Chennai was founded by B. Nagi Reddi. There were no credible reports from mainstream outlets confirming that his son died of Covid-19; this appears to be a rumour circulated on social media. (Some uncertainty remains due to sparse public records.)

claim: China Manufactured 'Boycott China' Goods for the Indian market
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: During the 2020 “boycott China” calls in India, viral images claimed items with “Boycott China” slogans were ironically “Made in China.” Multiple fact-checks found key images were edited or miscaptioned, and no credible evidence showed Chinese manufacturers deliberately producing “Boycott China” merchandise for India. Most such protest items were locally made. Uncertainty: Isolated cases could exist via custom orders, but there’s no verified documentation.

claim: In Nigeria,99% of revenue is being committed to debt servicing alone.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Nigeria’s federal government has at times devoted an extremely high share of revenue to debt service (e.g., about 96% in parts of 2022, and even exceeding 100% in Jan–Apr 2022). But “99%” is not the standard or current figure, and it overgeneralizes (it refers to the federal government, not “Nigeria” as a whole). The precise ratio varies by period and has not been a consistent 99%. (Source: Nigeria’s Budget Office reports; IMF/World Bank analyses.)

claim: Kamala Harris vowed vengeance against Trump backers
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible record of Kamala Harris vowing “vengeance” against Trump supporters. The claim traces to fabricated quotes/memes and misattributed posts that fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Snopes, PolitiFact) have debunked. Harris has criticized Trump and called for lawful accountability (e.g., for Jan. 6 crimes), but not retribution against his supporters. Uncertainty: none beyond the lack of any verifiable source for the quote.

claim: During the first quarter of 2020, Nigeria's revenues stood at N950 billion.
response_text: TRUE (with a caveat). The Federal Government of Nigeria’s actual retained revenue for Q1 2020 was about N950.56 billion, per the Budget Office’s Q1 2020 Budget Implementation Report. Note: this refers to FGN revenue, not total revenues for all tiers of government.

claim: Debt servicing obligations of Nigeria stood at N943.12 billion
response_text: TRUE — with context.  Nigeria’s federal government debt service payments totaled N943.12 billion in Q1 2020, per the Budget Office of the Federation’s 2020 Q1 Budget Implementation Report. The figure is period-specific; without a timeframe the claim is ambiguous.

claim: Since the COVID-19 crisis there has been disinformation on a scale we have never seen before.
response_text: TRUE.  Major bodies (WHO, UN, EU) characterized the COVID-19 period as an unprecedented “infodemic,” and platforms reported record volumes of removals/labels for COVID-related falsehoods compared with prior events. Research also documented global, high-velocity spread of misinformation across social networks. While exact historical comparisons are difficult, the expert and platform consensus is that the scale surpassed anything previously observed.

claim: Melania Trump tweeted in support of India, following the Indo-China clash at Galwan Valley.
response_text: FALSE.  After the June 15, 2020 Galwan Valley clash, there was a viral screenshot claiming Melania Trump had tweeted support for India. Fact-checks (e.g., BOOM Live, Alt News) found no such post on either @FLOTUS or @MELANIATRUMP, and the circulating “tweet” was fabricated. Only U.S. officials like the President/State Department commented publicly; Melania did not.

claim: Donald Trump, Melania Trump, Angela Merkel and Benjamin Netanyahu tweeted in support of India, following the Indo-China clash at Galwan Valley.
response_text: FALSE.  - Angela Merkel did not have a personal Twitter account and made no such tweet. - There is no record of Donald Trump or Melania Trump tweeting support for India after the June 2020 Galwan clash; Trump only commented at a press briefing that the U.S. was talking to both sides. - Benjamin Netanyahu did not tweet about the clash; statements of support came from some foreign ministries/ambassadors (e.g., Israel’s ambassador), not from these leaders’ accounts.  Multiple fact-checks debunked viral posts claiming these tweets existed.

claim: Nigeria bears 50% of the global sickle cell burden
response_text: FALSE.  Nigeria has the world’s largest national sickle cell burden, but best estimates put its share well below half. Peer‑reviewed analyses estimate roughly 300,000 newborns with sickle cell disease globally per year, with about 90,000 in Nigeria (~30%). Even using higher Nigerian estimates (~150,000), Nigeria would account for about 30–40%, not 50%. Note: figures vary by source and year, but “50%” overstates Nigeria’s share.

claim: NIC, under the Government of India, has directed the regional executive and representatives of Google India and Apple India to restrict the functioning of Chinese applications from their respective stores as per instructions by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Including 15 apps in particular, which include TikTok, Club Factory, Shein, Vivo Video among others.
response_text: FALSE.  - In June 2020, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) ordered a ban of 59 Chinese apps (including TikTok, Club Factory, Shein, and VivaVideo) under Section 69A of the IT Act, and directed Apple and Google to remove them from their app stores. It was not limited to “15 apps.” - The directive came from MeitY (with follow-on implementation via DoT/ISPs), not from the National Informatics Centre (NIC). - The app cited as “Vivo Video” is actually “VivaVideo.”  Minor uncertainty: NIC is under MeitY and may handle technical implementation in some contexts, but public orders and directions to app stores were issued by MeitY for the 2020 ban.

claim: Prime minister of Israel Benjamin Netanyahu tweeted "i stand with India" after a clash between the Indian Army and the Chinese PLA
response_text: FALSE.  No such tweet appears on Benjamin Netanyahu’s official accounts after the India–China (Galwan) clash. Fact-checks (e.g., India Today/AFWA, BOOM, Alt News) found the viral “I stand with India” screenshot to be fabricated. Expressions of support came from Israel’s embassy/ambassador, not from Netanyahu’s account. Uncertainty: low.

claim: PLA released names of 56 Chinese soldiers who died in Galwan Valley face-off
response_text: FALSE.  China officially acknowledged and named four PLA soldiers killed in the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash (Chen Hongjun, Chen Xiangrong, Xiao Siyuan, Wang Zhuoran) and highlighted regimental commander Qi Fabao as injured. There has been no official release of 56 names; higher casualty figures and long lists have appeared only in unverified reports and social media.

claim: Telangana govt has released guidelines to reopen schools in the state
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Telangana issued official guidelines when it decided to resume physical classes (e.g., for the statewide reopening from September 1, 2021, and again after later temporary closures), detailing COVID-19 SOPs such as masking, distancing, sanitization, and staggered timings. The claim is time-agnostic, but such guidelines were indeed released.

claim: Chancellor of Germany Angela Merkel tweeted "I stand with India" after clash between the Indian Army and the Chinese PLA
response_text: FALSE.  Angela Merkel did not tweet “I stand with India.” She did not use a personal Twitter account, and there is no record of any official German government or Chancellor account posting that phrase after the India–China Galwan clash in June 2020. Germany’s public stance at the time called for de‑escalation, not a partisan “stand with” statement.

claim: First Lady of US Melania Trump tweeted  "I stand with India" after clash between the Indian Army and the Chinese PLA
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Melania Trump posting “I stand with India” from either @FLOTUS or @MelaniaTrump after the 2020 India–China clash. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., BOOM, Alt News, India Today AFWA) found the viral screenshot claiming this was fabricated.

claim: Police departments in Germany were defunded and eliminated by the Nazis under Hermann Goering.
response_text: FALSE.  The Nazis did the opposite: they centralized, expanded, and heavily funded the police. As Prussian interior minister in 1933, Hermann Göring created and enlarged the Gestapo and mobilized SA/SS as “auxiliary police,” vastly increasing police power. In 1936 Heinrich Himmler became Chief of the German Police and integrated all police (criminal, political, and uniformed Ordnungspolizei) under SS control. Local autonomy was abolished, but police were not defunded or eliminated—they were strengthened and used for repression.

claim: Prime Minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu tweeted in support of India, following the Indo-China clash at Galwan Valley.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: After the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash, Israel’s support for India was conveyed publicly by Israel’s ambassador in New Delhi (and the embassy), not by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Claims of a Netanyahu tweet were based on fabricated or misattributed posts.

claim: Shinzo Abe, Prime Minister of Japan tweeted "I stand with India" after clash between the Indian Army and the Chinese PLA
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There is no record of Shinzo Abe tweeting “I stand with India” after the India–China Galwan clash in June 2020. Fact-checkers debunked viral screenshots of such a tweet as fabricated. Japan’s official response at the time came via its foreign ministry/embassy, expressing concern and calling for a peaceful resolution—without Abe posting that slogan. Uncertainty: none.

claim: US President Donald Trump  tweeted in support of India, following the Indo-China clash at Galwan Valley.
response_text: FALSE.  No such tweet from President Trump exists. After the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash, condolences and statements came from the U.S. State Department and the U.S. Ambassador to India, not from Trump’s Twitter account. Earlier, in late May, Trump had tweeted an offer to mediate the India‑China border dispute, but that predated the clash and wasn’t a pro‑India endorsement. Multiple fact-checkers flagged viral “Trump supports India” tweets/screenshots as fake.

claim: 'For every two babies born with sickle cell in the world, one is a Nigerian.’
response_text: FALSE.  Best available estimates put Nigeria’s share of global sickle cell disease (SCD) births well below 50%:  - Piel et al., PLoS Medicine (2013) estimated ~306,000 global newborns with SCA (HbSS) in 2010, with ~91,000 in Nigeria (~30%). - Later global burden estimates are similar or show higher worldwide totals, which keep Nigeria’s share roughly in the 25–35% range.  The “one in two” figure traces to an older, widely quoted WHO-style claim (often citing 150,000 Nigerian births out of 300,000 worldwide) that is outdated and not supported by more robust modeling. Uncertainty exists around exact counts, but credible estimates do not reach 50%.

claim: Ghana Health Service Central regional director halts mass coronavirus testing
response_text: FALSE  Reason: There’s no credible record of the Ghana Health Service’s Central Regional Director “halting mass coronavirus testing.” Ghana did not conduct regionwide mass testing to begin with; testing focused on targeted/enhanced contact tracing under nationally set policy. No reliable reports indicate a regional director stopped such a program. (Some uncertainty due to scattered local media reports in 2020, but none substantiate this claim.)

claim: A grocery store worker who wore a mask for hours at a time got a lung infection (pleurisy,) from “breathing in her own bacteria”.
response_text: FALSE.  Pleurisy is inflammation of the lining of the lungs, most often due to viral infections, pneumonia, autoimmune disease, or pulmonary embolism—not from “rebreathing your own bacteria.” Proper mask use does not cause lung infections; healthcare workers wear masks for long shifts without increased risk, and studies show no link between mask-wearing and pneumonia or pleurisy. At most, a dirty mask might irritate skin, not infect the lungs. (No credible evidence supports the claimed case.)

claim: Public Health England issued new guidance that encourages the public to consider taking vitamin D supplements during community lockdownds due to COVID19
response_text: TRUE.  Public Health England updated guidance in April 2020 advising people staying indoors during COVID-19 lockdown to consider taking a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement due to reduced sun exposure (for bone/muscle health), while noting it was not proven to prevent or treat COVID-19.

claim: Huawei Technologies was secretly in control of Iran’s Skycom Tech Co Ltd.
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence from Reuters investigations and U.S. DOJ filings shows Huawei effectively controlled Skycom while publicly describing it as a local partner. Meng Wanzhou served on Skycom’s board, Skycom staff used Huawei email domains and managed Huawei business in Iran, and prosecutors alleged Huawei ran Skycom as an unofficial subsidiary to evade sanctions. Meng later agreed to a statement of facts acknowledging her statements about the relationship were misleading. Minor caveat: there was no final court verdict against Huawei on this point, but the documentary evidence strongly supports secret control.

claim: Viral message claims Facebook will make private photos public
response_text: FALSE  It’s a long-running hoax. Facebook has repeatedly stated it won’t make private photos or posts public, and copy‑paste “privacy notices” do nothing; visibility is controlled by users’ settings and Facebook’s policies.

claim: Nancy Green aka Aunt Jemima was the FIRST black millionaire! she sold her pancake mix to General Mills Corp
response_text: FALSE.  - Nancy Green was a hired spokesperson/model for the “Aunt Jemima” brand starting in 1893; she did not own the brand and was not a millionaire. - The pancake mix was created by Chris Rutt and Charles Underwood, sold to the R.T. Davis Milling Company, and the brand was later acquired by Quaker Oats (now under PepsiCo), not General Mills. - The first widely recognized self‑made Black millionaire is Madam C. J. Walker (with some credit also given to Annie Turnbo Malone), not Nancy Green.

claim: Donald Trump made Juneteenth "very famous," as he described in a Wall Street Journal interview June 17, 2020. Prior to him planning a rally on June 19, "nobody had ever heard of it."
response_text: FALSE.  Trump did tell the Wall Street Journal on June 17, 2020 that he “made Juneteenth very famous” and that “nobody had ever heard of it.” But that claim is wrong: Juneteenth has been celebrated since the 19th century, Texas made it a state holiday in 1980, and by 2020 it was recognized in 47 states and D.C., with regular observances and presidential statements. His rally plans drew extra attention, but the holiday was already widely known.

claim: Myanmar will launch a satellite to provide free internet to all of its citizens.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible announcements or plans indicate Myanmar will launch a satellite to provide free internet to all citizens. Myanmar’s recent satellite activity has involved leasing capacity (e.g., MyanmarSat-2 on Intelsat 39) and a small Earth-observation satellite project stalled after the 2021 coup—not consumer internet. The government has more often restricted internet access than expanded it, and a single national satellite could not deliver free internet to all without extensive ground terminals and funding. Uncertainty: low unless a very recent, well-sourced policy reversal occurred.

claim: Establishing A One World Government is Part Of UN's 'mission goals.
response_text: FALSE.  - The UN’s purposes in the UN Charter (Article 1) are to maintain international peace and security, foster friendly relations among nations, promote human rights, and encourage international cooperation—not to create a single world government. - The UN is an intergovernmental organization of sovereign states and explicitly is “not a world government” and does not make binding laws for countries (see UN FAQ).  - References to “global governance” in UN contexts mean cooperative problem-solving among states, not establishing a one-world state.

claim: A study conducted by World Health Organization (WHO) and major hospitals has found that Covid-19 has become weaker and harmless.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible WHO-backed study has concluded that COVID-19 is “weaker and harmless.” WHO continues to state that COVID-19 remains a health threat, causing severe illness and deaths, especially in high-risk groups. While population immunity and some variants (e.g., Omicron vs. Delta) have shown lower average severity, the virus is not harmless.

claim: Herbal medicine from Tanzania cure Covid-19
response_text: FALSE.  No herbal medicine from Tanzania (or elsewhere) has been proven in robust clinical trials to cure COVID-19. WHO and health authorities have cautioned against unproven “herbal cures”; while some herbal products may be studied for symptom relief, none has demonstrated curative efficacy or received international approval as a COVID-19 cure.

claim: Former President Barack Obama was born in Kenya, according to his birth certificate.
response_text: FALSE.  Barack Obama’s official Hawaiian birth certificates (short-form in 2008 and long-form in 2011) list his birthplace as Kapiʻolani Maternity & Gynecological Hospital in Honolulu, Hawaii, on August 4, 1961. Hawaii officials verified the records. Alleged “Kenyan birth certificates” have been debunked as hoaxes.

claim: North Korea blew up the office used for South Korea talks.
response_text: TRUE. In June 2020, North Korea detonated and destroyed the inter‑Korean liaison office in Kaesong, a facility used for talks and coordination with South Korea.

claim: Denis Mukwege, a medical doctor and Nobel Peace laureate from the Democratic Republic of Congo, resigned from the Congolese government’s Coronavirus Response (Taskforce) Team because he was asked to manipulate numbers of COVID-19 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  Denis Mukwege did resign in June 2020 from the South Kivu (provincial) COVID-19 response team, but his public statement cited lack of testing capacity, long delays in results, and political pressure to ease restrictions. He did not say he was asked to manipulate COVID-19 numbers, and fact-checks found no evidence of such a request.

claim: America’s most violent cities are that way because of their Democratic politics
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Many of the most violent cities are led by Democrats because most large U.S. cities vote Democratic, but criminologists find no evidence that “Democratic politics” cause higher violence. Violent crime correlates with factors like poverty, segregation, concentrated disadvantage, drug and gun markets, and broader state/national conditions. Crime rose and fell in recent years across both Democratic- and Republican-led cities, and several Republican-led cities and many Republican-controlled states have high homicide rates. Correlation with party control does not show causation.
