Guidelines generally do not recommend routine use, and in the U.S. FDA authorization is restricted to immunocompromised patients.

claim: Keep the room temperature at 30-40 degrees Celsius to prevent COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 spreads in all climates; keeping a room at 30–40°C does not prevent infection and may cause heat-related illness. Virus inactivation requires much higher, sustained temperatures, not safe for occupied rooms. Effective prevention includes vaccination, good ventilation, masks when appropriate, and hand hygiene.

claim: If the patient has energy then s/he should run half an hour twice a day. This will burn the cough inside.
response_text: FALSE.  Running does not “burn” a cough. A cough is a symptom (often from infection, irritation, asthma, etc.), and vigorous exercise can worsen cough, dehydration, and airway irritation—especially with chest symptoms or fever. Light activity may be okay once symptoms are mild, but prescribing 30 minutes of running twice daily to treat a cough is not evidence-based.

claim: Drinking milk three times a day with Shilajit, and Licorice (Mulethi) for five days can help beat the virus.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no clinical evidence that drinking milk with shilajit and licorice for five days treats or “beats” viral infections (including COVID-19). Licorice’s antiviral effects are limited to lab studies and it can cause harmful side effects (high blood pressure, low potassium, heart rhythm problems). Shilajit’s efficacy is unproven and contamination risks exist. Use evidence‑based prevention and treatments instead.

claim: Drinking milk with honey on an empty stomach is the antidote to COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no scientific evidence that milk with honey cures or prevents COVID-19, and “antidote” is not applicable to viral infections. Honey may soothe a sore throat, but it does not treat the virus. Proven measures include vaccination and, for eligible patients, authorized antivirals (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, remdesivir) and supportive care. Note: never give honey to infants under 1 year due to botulism risk.

claim: President Buhari of Nigeria has decided to resign but some Nigerians are against it.
response_text: FALSE.  Buhari never announced a decision to resign. He served out both terms (2015–2023) and left office at the end of his tenure. While there were rumors and calls for him to resign during periods of ill health and unrest, he did not decide to resign, and no credible reports showed Nigerians opposing such a decision.

claim: Drinking ash of Phyllostachys nigra (black bamboo) mixed with honey and cow’s milk is a potent treatment for COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no clinical evidence that ash of Phyllostachys nigra—alone or mixed with honey and cow’s milk—treats or cures COVID-19. WHO/CDC do not recommend such remedies; approved prevention/treatments include vaccination and authorized antivirals (e.g., nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) for eligible patients. Ingesting ash may also be unsafe due to potential contaminants.

claim: China halted exports of face masks to US during the coronavirus pandemic
response_text: FALSE.  China did not halt mask exports to the U.S. During 2020, U.S. imports of masks from China surged to massive volumes. China did tighten export quality controls in spring 2020, which caused some delays and confusion, but there was no blanket halt or ban on exporting face masks to the United States.

claim: Former President Olusegun Obasanjo donated 5000 naira each to Nigerians.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible announcement or reporting that Obasanjo or his foundation gave N5,000 to all Nigerians. Viral posts advertising such “Obasanjo N5,000 grants” are scams; neither he nor his foundation has launched a nationwide cash giveaway. Such a program would also cost about a trillion naira and would be widely covered if real.

claim: Prior to Nigeria’s former Chief of Staff Abba Kyari's death, Kyari was flown to the United Kingdom for medical treatment and his body was later cremated.
response_text: FALSE.  Abba Kyari received COVID-19 treatment in Nigeria (he announced he was moving to Lagos for care), not the UK. He died on April 17, 2020, and was buried the next day at Gudu Cemetery in Abuja according to Islamic rites—not cremated. The presidency publicly denied reports that he was flown abroad.

claim: Barcodes tell consumers where a product was manufactured.
response_text: FALSE.  Standard retail barcodes (UPC/EAN) do not encode the place of manufacture. The first digits (GS1 prefix) indicate where the brand owner registered its barcode, not where the product was made. A product can be made anywhere regardless of the barcode prefix. Country of origin must be shown separately (e.g., “Made in …”) if required.

claim: Chief of Staff to the President of Nigeria, Mallam Abba Kyari, died of ulcer and not coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Official statements from the Nigerian Presidency in April 2020 confirmed that Abba Kyari died from complications of COVID-19 after testing positive. He was buried under COVID-19 protocols. There’s no credible evidence he died of an ulcer.

claim: The seasonal flu killed 80,000 people in the United States in 2018-2019
response_text: FALSE.  CDC estimates about 34,000 U.S. deaths from influenza in the 2018–2019 season. The widely cited “80,000 deaths” figure referred to the prior 2017–2018 season (and was later revised to about 61,000).

claim: All vaccines contain MRC-5 cells, which are aborted fetal cells.
response_text: FALSE.  Only a few vaccines are grown in historic human cell lines such as MRC-5 or WI‑38 (e.g., some hepatitis A, varicella, rubella-containing, and rabies vaccines). Many others are made using eggs, yeast, bacteria, insect cells, or mRNA platforms and do not use MRC‑5. Even when a human cell line is used to grow the virus, the final vaccine is purified and contains no intact “aborted fetal cells” — at most, tiny residual DNA/protein fragments may remain. MRC‑5 is a decades-old cell line derived from fetal tissue in 1966; no ongoing abortions are involved.

claim: Chinese products can be identified by the first three digits of a barcode
response_text: FALSE.  The first three digits of an EAN/UPC barcode are a GS1 prefix identifying the GS1 member organization that issued the company’s barcode (e.g., 690–699 are allocated to GS1 China). They do not indicate where the product was made. A product manufactured in China can have a non-China prefix, and a company registered in China can make goods elsewhere. So you can’t reliably identify “Chinese products” by those digits.

claim: There is always the possibility of an iatrogenic reaction to a vaccine.
response_text: TRUE.  “Iatrogenic” means caused by a medical intervention. Vaccination is a medical intervention, and there is always a nonzero risk of adverse effects, from common mild reactions (soreness, fever) to rare serious events (e.g., anaphylaxis on the order of about 1–5 per million doses). The risk is very low and benefits far outweigh risks, but the possibility exists.

claim: Boko Haram leader, Shekau says he’s ready to surrender
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence shows Abubakar Shekau ever said he was ready to surrender. He repeatedly vowed not to surrender, and numerous past “Shekau to surrender” reports were unfounded. He ultimately died in May 2021 after a clash with ISWAP, reportedly killing himself to avoid capture.

claim: Autopsy reports suggest Jeffrey Epstein most likely died from COVID-19 not suicide in August 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Jeffrey Epstein died on August 10, 2019, and the New York City Chief Medical Examiner ruled the cause as suicide by hanging. While an outside pathologist hired by his brother questioned that ruling, no autopsy report suggested COVID-19. COVID-19 was not identified until later in 2019 and was not a known factor in August 2019.

claim: Immunization is compulsory in Canada
response_text: FALSE.  Canada has no nationwide compulsory vaccination. Immunization is voluntary; provinces/territories set policies. Some (e.g., Ontario, New Brunswick) require proof of certain vaccines for school attendance, but exemptions (medical and often religious/conscientious) exist, and no one is forcibly vaccinated. Unvaccinated students may be excluded during outbreaks.

claim: 26 members of one family in Jahangirpuri, Delhi, tested positive for coronavirus on April 17 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Around April 17–18, 2020, roughly two dozen people from Delhi’s Jahangirpuri area tested positive, prompting containment measures. However, officials clarified they were from multiple households in the locality—not 26 members of a single family. This was a misreported viral claim. (Some uncertainty on exact split across households, but not one family.)

claim: Immunization is mandatory in the United States
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The U.S. has no universal federal vaccine mandate. Vaccine requirements are set mainly by states and institutions, typically for school/childcare entry or certain jobs (e.g., healthcare, military), and most states allow exemptions (medical in all, religious in most, philosophical in some). There is no blanket requirement that all residents be immunized.

claim: There are 360,000 deaths a year in the US from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that.
response_text: FALSE.  CDC data show about 4,000 unintentional drowning deaths per year in the U.S. across all settings (pools, natural water, bathtubs, etc.), and pool drownings are only a subset of that total. The “~360,000” figure aligns with older WHO estimates for global drowning deaths worldwide, not U.S. swimming pool deaths. Sources: CDC Drowning Facts; WHO Global Report on Drowning.

claim: Donald Trump tweeted in 2009 that "Obama’s handling of this whole [H1N1] pandemic has been terrible! As President, ALL responsibility becomes yours during a crisis like this, whether or not you’re entirely to blame. John McCain, and myself for that matter myself, would never let thousands of Americans die from a pandemic while in office"
response_text: FALSE.  No such 2009 tweet exists in Trump’s archived tweets. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) have identified this as a fabricated quote; there’s no record of Trump tweeting about H1N1 like this in 2009. The phrasing and bracketed “[H1N1]” are also inconsistent with his tweet style at the time.

claim: Jay Leno Dead at 71
response_text: FALSE — Jay Leno is alive. Born April 28, 1950, he would be 75 in 2025. Recent reports in 2024–2025 (including coverage of his wife’s conservatorship and ongoing appearances) confirm he has not died.

claim: Africans living in China are being forced to sleep outside in the cold as Chinese nationals blame them for the rising number of new coronavirus cases in the country.
response_text: TRUE.  In April 2020, credible reports (BBC, CNN, Reuters, AP) and a U.S. consulate alert documented that in Guangzhou, China, some Africans were evicted, denied entry to hotels and businesses, and some ended up sleeping on the streets amid a backlash that blamed foreigners—particularly Africans—for imported COVID-19 cases. While this was localized (mainly Guangzhou) and “cold” is subjective, the described situation did occur.

claim: video showing policemen picking up currency notes lying on the road in Indore is being shared with the claim that they were thrown on purpose to spread Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The video is genuine, but Indore Police clarified the scattered notes were not thrown to spread coronavirus. The cash had accidentally fallen onto the road (reportedly from someone transporting money), and officers collected and sanitized it as a precaution. Fact-checks by multiple outlets found no link to any deliberate attempt to spread COVID-19. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Lady Michelle Obama  slam Country music industry, saying the the genre was for morons.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Michelle Obama said country music is “for morons.” The claim traces to fabricated/satirical posts that were reshared without context. In reality, the Obama White House hosted country music events, and there’s no verified statement of her disparaging the genre.

claim: COVID-19 is sparing essential workers, so it's not so deadly.
response_text: FALSE.  Essential workers were not “spared.” Early and throughout the pandemic, many essential occupations (healthcare, food/agriculture, transit, meatpacking, care work) had higher exposure, infection, and mortality than non–essential workers. Multiple analyses from the CDC, UK’s Office for National Statistics, and U.S. state studies (e.g., California) found elevated COVID-19 death rates in these groups. The claim that this means COVID-19 is “not so deadly” is incorrect; the virus has caused millions of deaths globally.

claim: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lied about the number of deaths caused by COVID-19 by combining the count with pneumonia and influenza fatalities.
response_text: FALSE.  CDC did not “combine” unrelated pneumonia and influenza deaths into the COVID-19 death tally. CDC reports COVID-19 deaths from death certificates where COVID-19 is listed as the underlying or a contributing cause. Separately, for respiratory surveillance, CDC also reports a combined “pneumonia, influenza, or COVID-19” (PIC) category, but that metric is distinct and clearly labeled. COVID-only death counts are published separately and are not inflated by adding flu- or pneumonia-only deaths.

claim: The drug Diamox, often used as treatment for high-altitude sickness, can cure the Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Diamox (acetazolamide) is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for altitude sickness, glaucoma, and some seizure disorders. It has no proven antiviral activity against SARS‑CoV‑2 and is not recommended or approved by WHO/CDC/NIH for treating COVID‑19. There’s no evidence it “cures” coronavirus; standard COVID-19 treatments involve evidence-based antivirals and anti-inflammatories, not acetazolamide.

claim: Other countries that reopened saw an increase in coronavirus infections.
response_text: TRUE.  Many countries saw cases rise after easing restrictions. Examples include South Korea (nightlife cluster after reopening in May 2020), Germany (R rose above 1 with local outbreaks after easing), Israel and Iran (surges following reopenings), and Spain/France (increases after summer reopening). Not universal or immediate in every case (e.g., Denmark, New Zealand initially), but the general pattern occurred in multiple countries.

claim: Alcohol plays a major role in killing the coronavirus because it is a “throat sanitizer”.
response_text: FALSE.  - Drinking alcohol does not “sanitize” the throat or prevent/treat COVID-19. WHO and CDC have warned this is a myth. - Alcohol-based hand rubs (≥60% ethanol) can inactivate SARS‑CoV‑2 on hands/surfaces, but ingesting alcohol does not kill the virus in the respiratory tract and can increase health risks. - Mouthwashes may transiently reduce oral viral load in lab settings, but they do not prevent infection or play a “major role” in killing the virus in people.

claim: An employee at a funeral home in New York City was accidentally cremated while taking a nap during the 2020 COVID-19 crisis
response_text: FALSE. This story originated on a satire website (World News Daily Report) during the 2020 pandemic and has no support from credible news sources or official records. Fact-checkers, including Snopes, debunked it as a hoax.

claim: 150 health workers quarantined at Max Hospital Saket.
response_text: TRUE  Several April 2020 news reports (e.g., Indian Express/Times of India) stated that around 150 healthcare workers at Max Hospital, Saket in Delhi were placed under quarantine after exposure to patients who later tested positive for COVID-19. Minor uncertainty arises from varying exact counts reported, but coverage consistently cited about 150.

claim: "The 1st Amendment comes before the 13th and 14th, and the Bible clearly approves of owning slaves" stated David Green on Fox News this morning.
response_text: FALSE  No credible reports, transcripts, or clips indicate that David Green said this on Fox News this morning. A remark that provocative would be widely covered, and there’s no reliable evidence of it. Note: constitutional amendments don’t have a hierarchy by number. Uncertain only because real-time verification isn’t possible here.

claim: Trump Claims ‘Ultimate Authority’ to Override States’ Virus Measures
response_text: TRUE.  On April 13, 2020, during a White House coronavirus briefing (and in tweets), Donald Trump said he had “total” and “ultimate” authority to decide when states reopen, implying he could override governors’ COVID-19 restrictions.

claim: The US media minimized the risk of the new coronavirus from the start,
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: “U.S. media” isn’t monolithic. While some outlets and commentators did downplay the threat in February–early March 2020 (e.g., comparisons to seasonal flu, some cable-news segments), many major outlets warned early and extensively covered the risk from January onward—reporting the WHO emergency, CDC briefings, and publishing stark analyses (e.g., The Atlantic’s Feb. 24 “You’re Likely to Get the Coronavirus,” STAT’s early alarms, major papers’ front-page coverage). The claim that the U.S. media minimized the risk “from the start” overgeneralizes. Uncertainty: mixed coverage, with some notable minimization in parts of the media.

claim: The Squad' Want's The Bible Deemed Hate Speech
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of any member of “the Squad” proposing that the Bible be deemed hate speech. No bills, official statements, or verified comments support this. Similar viral claims (e.g., about AOC or Ilhan Omar) have been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: Some 150 foreigners attended spiritual leader Jaggi Vasudev aka Sadhguru's event in March 2020, which has led to over 1,000 corona cases in Tamil Nadu. The foreigners are quarantined at Isha Yoga Center.
response_text: FALSE.  - Isha Yoga Center did not host a public event in March 2020; its large Mahashivratri event was on Feb 21–22, before India’s major COVID surge. The center said it closed to visitors from mid‑March and halted events. - Coimbatore district authorities and Isha clarified that no group of “150 foreigners” was quarantined at the ashram. - Tamil Nadu’s early case spike (over 1,000 by early April 2020) was largely linked by officials to the Nizamuddin Tablighi Jamaat cluster, not to Isha.  Multiple fact-checks (e.g., BOOM, Alt News, The Quint) debunked this rumor.

claim: In June 2017, Conservative MPs voted against a pay rise for nurses.
response_text: TRUE.  - On 28 June 2017, Conservative MPs voted against a Labour amendment to the Queen’s Speech that called for ending the 1% public‑sector pay cap. The cap covered NHS staff, including nurses, so opposing the amendment was a vote against a measure that would have enabled pay rises for nurses. - Note: It wasn’t a specific, binding vote on a nurses‑only pay award; it was a broader, non‑binding amendment about the public sector pay cap.

claim: Some states, like Montana and Nebraska, are getting more than $300,000 in federal stimulus money per reported COVID-19 case. New York is the hardest-hit state and yet we are getting only about $12,000 per case.
response_text: FALSE.  - The CARES Act’s Coronavirus Relief Fund was allocated mostly by population with a $1.25 billion minimum per state, not by COVID-19 case counts. Dividing allocations by cases is a misleading after-the-fact metric. - At the time of the claim, New York’s total allocation (state plus direct local aid like NYC and counties) was far higher than implied—roughly $7–8 billion—yielding well over $12,000 per case (often around $20,000–30,000 depending on the date/case count). The $12,000 figure counts only the state government’s share. - The “>$300,000 per case” for Montana/Nebraska depends entirely on choosing moments when those states had very few cases; it wasn’t how aid was determined and wasn’t consistently true.  Overall, the comparison is misleading and the New York figure is understated.

claim: NY: EXHAUSTED FUNERAL HOME EMPLOYEE CREMATED BY MISTAKE WHILE TAKING A NAP
response_text: FALSE.  This headline is a recurring hoax from the satirical site World News Daily Report, which has run the same made-up story with different locations (including New York). Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) have debunked it, and there are no credible news or official reports of such an incident. Cremation requires multiple ID checks and permits, making this scenario implausible.

claim: The coronavirus originated outside China.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The earliest known outbreak and ancestral viral lineages of SARS‑CoV‑2 are traced to Wuhan, China (late 2019). Epidemiological and genomic evidence places the initial emergence there, and there’s no verified evidence of circulation outside China before the Wuhan outbreak. While the exact origin mechanism (zoonotic spillover vs. lab-related) remains unresolved, all leading hypotheses place the origin in China, not outside it. Uncertainty: precise source within China is still debated.

claim: Ratan Tata has said “Experts are predicting huge downfall of Economy due to the Corona. I do not know much about these experts. But I know for sure that they do not know anything about the value of human motivation and determined efforts.”
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Ratan Tata saying this. The quote circulated virally in 2020 but does not appear in his verified statements or social media. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., BOOM, Alt News, AFP) debunked it, and Tata himself has cautioned against fake quotes being attributed to him.

claim: In November 2019 the Pirbirght Institute, funded by Bill Gates, was granted European patent number EP 317-2319B1 for a coronavirus vaccine that may be used to treat humans.
response_text: FALSE.  - EP 3172319 B1 is a Pirbright Institute patent for a live, attenuated avian coronavirus (infectious bronchitis virus) vaccine intended for poultry, not for humans. - It was unrelated to SARS‑CoV‑2; the application predates COVID‑19 and targets animal disease. - Pirbright is primarily UK government–funded; while it has received some grants from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation for livestock research, the claim implies a human-use vaccine and Gates-backed COVID link that isn’t supported.

claim: In the United States, the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) admitted in federal court that it does not have studies to support the claim that vaccines do not cause autism.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim misrepresents a FOIA lawsuit by the anti-vaccine group ICAN. In that case, the CDC did not “admit” in court that it lacks studies; FOIA proceedings only address whether records responsive to a narrowly worded request exist and were produced. The CDC provided numerous studies on autism and vaccines, and the court did not rule on vaccine safety. Extensive research finds no link between vaccines and autism (e.g., Hviid et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2019; Jain et al., JAMA, 2015; Taylor et al., Vaccine, 2014; DeStefano et al., Journal of Pediatrics, 2013). The CDC continues to state that vaccines do not cause autism and cites these studies.

claim: In October 2019, Bill Gates sponsored Event 201, a simulation that estimated 65 million people would be killed by coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE.  Event 201 was held in October 2019 by Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security with the World Economic Forum and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (i.e., Gates’ foundation helped sponsor it). The tabletop exercise used a hypothetical novel coronavirus scenario that resulted in about 65 million deaths over 18 months—this was a scenario for planning, not a prediction about COVID‑19.

claim: Former President Barack Obama gave $3.8 million to a lab in Wuhan, China.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Obama administration did not give $3.8 million directly to the Wuhan Institute of Virology. In 2014, NIH (NIAID) awarded about $3.7 million to the U.S. nonprofit EcoHealth Alliance to study bat coronaviruses; roughly $600,000 of that was subawarded to the Wuhan lab. The grant was later renewed in 2019 under the Trump administration. Separately, a USAID program sent additional subawards to the lab (about $1.1 million over many years), but the Wuhan lab did not receive $3.8 million, and it was not a personal grant from Obama.

claim: The U.S. government is planning to force Americans to take vaccinations during the coronavirus pandemic with the help of Bill Gates.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no U.S. government plan to forcibly vaccinate Americans, nor any program “with the help of Bill Gates.” During COVID-19, vaccines were offered voluntarily; some mandates existed for certain workplaces or sectors, but not forced injections. Bill Gates, through his philanthropy, funded vaccine research and global distribution efforts, but had no authority or role in U.S. government enforcement of vaccination.

claim: Kalonji or black cumin seeds contain 100% Hydroxychloroquine which can cure Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  - Kalonji (Nigella sativa, black cumin/black seed) does not contain hydroxychloroquine. Its main compounds include thymoquinone and related phytochemicals; hydroxychloroquine is a synthetic 4‑aminoquinoline drug, not a natural constituent of these seeds. - Hydroxychloroquine has not been shown to cure COVID-19. Large randomized trials and major health agencies (e.g., WHO/NIH) found no clinical benefit for treatment or prevention and recommend against its use for COVID-19.

claim: Bill Gates owns the patent and vaccine for coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Bill Gates does not own a patent on SARS‑CoV‑2, nor does he own COVID‑19 vaccines. A UK lab (The Pirbright Institute) holds an older patent on an attenuated avian coronavirus used in poultry research—not SARS‑CoV‑2—and while it has received some Gates Foundation funding, that funding was unrelated to that patent. COVID‑19 vaccines are developed and owned by companies and universities (e.g., Pfizer/BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca/Oxford), not by Gates.

claim: Bill Gates is a partner in the lab in Wuhan, China.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that Bill Gates or the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation is a partner or owner of any lab in Wuhan, including the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Major fact-checkers (AP, Reuters, Snopes) have debunked this claim. While the foundation funds global health projects worldwide, there’s no record of a partnership with the Wuhan lab; rumors often stem from confusion with unrelated institutions like the UK’s Pirbright Institute.

claim: 5G radiation is harmful to human health
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - 5G uses non-ionizing radiofrequency (RF) waves. At the exposure levels from networks and devices that comply with international limits (ICNIRP, FCC/FDA), there is no credible evidence of adverse health effects. - The only well-established effect of RF is tissue heating at high intensities; safety limits are set far below those thresholds. - Major health bodies (WHO, ICNIRP, FDA) report no established health risks from typical 5G exposures. Research continues, but current evidence does not support harm.

claim: North Carolina is "in the small minority of states that requires an absentee ballot to be signed by two witnesses or a notary public."
response_text: FALSE.  Why: North Carolina currently requires only one witness signature on an absentee ballot return envelope (see N.C. Gen. Stat. §163-231 and NC State Board of Elections guidance). While it’s true that only a minority of states require any witness or notary for mail ballots, North Carolina does not require “two witnesses or a notary.” It used to require two witnesses years ago, but that is no longer the rule.

claim: An image shared on Facebook purportedly shows former Vice President Joe Biden biting a young girl on the cheek.
response_text: FALSE. The viral photo was digitally altered. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Snopes) traced it to an original image from a public event where Biden was close to a girl, but he was not biting her; the “biting” mouth was added in post-production.

claim: Dr. Vandana Tiwari has died in the attacks of Muslims in UP when she went to screen them for COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks in April 2020 (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today AFWA) found no record of any Dr. “Vandana Tiwari” dying in Uttar Pradesh due to a mob attack during COVID-19 screening. While there were incidents where health workers were attacked (e.g., Moradabad, Indore), no doctor was killed in those events. Images circulated with the claim were misattributed.

claim: The Nigerian Finance Minister claims that Nigeria lost N700 billion Naira COVID-19 Relief Funds due to a fire.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: After a fire at Nigeria’s Treasury House (Office of the Accountant-General) in April 2020, rumors spread that N700 billion in COVID-19 funds had been lost. The Finance Ministry and the Accountant-General publicly denied any loss of funds or records, saying systems and data were intact. Fact-checkers (e.g., Africa Check, AFP, Dubawa) found no evidence that the Finance Minister made such a claim or that N700 billion was lost due to the fire.

claim: The U.S. “resisted” blacklisting ISIS.
response_text: FALSE.  The U.S. did not resist blacklisting ISIS. The group’s predecessor, al‑Qaida in Iraq (AQI), was designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the U.S. in 2004. As the group rebranded (Islamic State of Iraq, then ISIL/ISIS), the State Department treated it as the same entity and formally updated the designation to include the ISIL/ISIS aliases in 2014. The U.S. also supported UN sanctions against ISIL and led a military coalition against it. Any claim of “resistance” confuses name changes or refers to a different case (e.g., early debates over Boko Haram), not ISIS.

claim: N13 billion was devoted to the State House clinic in the last five years.
response_text: FALSE.  Public budget records show the State House Medical Centre received well below N13 billion over any recent five-year span prior to 2021—typically in the range of roughly N5–9 billion, depending on the years counted. The N13 billion figure over five years is an overstatement. (Note: excluding the later separate N21bn “Presidential Wing” project approved in 2021.)

claim: LA County sheriff’s deputies arrested a surfer for violating the state’s stay-at-home order
response_text: TRUE.  In early April 2020 near Malibu, Los Angeles County sheriff’s deputies arrested a lone man on the water (widely described as a paddleboarder/surfer) after he ignored lifeguards’ orders to leave amid COVID-19 beach closures. He was cited for violating the public health/stay-at-home orders and released. Minor nuance: many reports called him a paddleboarder, but the event matches the claim.

claim: The flu vaccine doesn’t work because the flu has not been eliminated.
response_text: FALSE.  A vaccine doesn’t need to eradicate a disease to work. Flu vaccines are imperfect because influenza viruses evolve, but they consistently reduce the risk of illness and, importantly, lower hospitalizations and deaths. The flu’s continued circulation reflects viral change and incomplete coverage, not vaccine ineffectiveness.

claim: U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders has not yet endorsed Joe Biden for President.
response_text: FALSE.  Bernie Sanders endorsed Joe Biden after suspending his own campaign in April 2020, and he again endorsed Biden’s 2024 reelection bid in April 2023.

claim: The price of oil was lower when president Obasanjo and Abubakar assumed office on 29 May 1999 than it is today ...
response_text: TRUE.  - On 29 May 1999, global crude prices were in the mid-to-high teens per barrel (Brent and WTI were roughly $16–18/bbl after the 1998 crash and early‑1999 OPEC cuts). - Today, benchmark crude prices are many times higher (recent years ~ $70–90/bbl).  Thus, oil was indeed cheaper on 29 May 1999 than it is today. (Minor ambiguity on benchmark, but both Brent and WTI fit this.)

claim: The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa is projecting that Africa’s growth will drop to 1.8%, and perhaps lower because of the COVID-19 pandemic
response_text: TRUE  In March 2020, the UN Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) warned that COVID-19 could cut Africa’s 2020 GDP growth from about 3.2% to 1.8%, and possibly lower depending on how the pandemic evolved. This was reported in UNECA statements and UN/Reuters coverage at the time.

claim: The price of oil was lower when president Obasanjo and Abubakar assumed office on 29 May 1999 than it was on 08/04/2020
response_text: TRUE.  - On 29 May 1999, crude prices were very low after the 1998 crash—Brent was roughly in the mid‑teens to high‑teens USD per barrel (about $15–18), and WTI around $16–18. - On 08/04/2020 (whether interpreted as 8 April 2020 or 4 August 2020), prices were higher: around $24–26 (WTI) and ~$30–33 (Brent) on 8 April 2020; and roughly $41–44 (WTI/Brent) on 4 August 2020.  So oil was cheaper on 29 May 1999 than on 08/04/2020. Note: Abdulsalami Abubakar did not assume office on 29 May 1999; he left office that day.

claim: There's a lot of fraudulent voting in the US elections.
response_text: FALSE.  Isolated cases of voter fraud occur, but multiple studies, audits, and court rulings have found it to be extremely rare and not widespread. Examples: a study of 1 billion ballots (2000–2014) found 31 credible voter-impersonation cases; Brennan Center analyses estimate incident rates near 0.0003–0.0025%; and in 2020, state audits, DOJ statements, and over 60 court decisions found no evidence of widespread fraud. The claim of “a lot” is unsupported.

claim: Sanders Has Ended His Fight for Democratic Nomination
response_text: TRUE. On April 8, 2020, Sen. Bernie Sanders suspended his presidential campaign, effectively ending his bid for the Democratic nomination (he later endorsed Joe Biden). He likewise conceded in 2016 after endorsing Hillary Clinton.

claim: The World Health Organisation states that there are up to 650,000 deaths per year associated with respiratory illnesses linked to seasonal flu.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO estimates that seasonal influenza is associated with about 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths globally each year, often summarized as “up to 650,000” deaths from respiratory illnesses linked to seasonal flu.

claim: Before the novel coronavirus pandemic hit the globe, Nigeria spent 42% of its earnings on debt servicing.
response_text: FALSE.  Before COVID-19 (i.e., in 2019), Nigeria’s federal government spent roughly 58–60% of its revenue on debt service, not 42%, according to the World Bank/IMF and Nigeria’s Budget Office. Earlier years were lower (about 45% in 2016), but the pre‑pandemic figure was well above 42%.

claim: N13 billion was devoted to the State House clinic in the last five years.
response_text: FALSE.  Appropriation records for the State House Medical Centre (Aso Rock clinic) over five years typically cited (2015–2019) add up to about N10–12 billion, not N13 billion. For example, reported appropriations were roughly: 2015 (~N3.9bn), 2016 (~N3.2bn), 2017 (~N0.33bn), 2018 (~N1.03bn), 2019 (~N0.82bn)—totalling well under N13bn. Actual releases were even lower. Minor uncertainty stems from whether one uses proposed vs. passed budgets, but none reach N13bn.

claim: All restaurants and hotels in India would be closed till October 15, 2020, due to Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: While restaurants and hotels were closed during the initial nationwide lockdown, the Government of India allowed them to reopen (with restrictions and outside containment zones) from June 8, 2020 under “Unlock 1.0.” There was no nationwide order keeping all restaurants and hotels closed until October 15; that date applied to certain venues like cinemas under later unlock guidelines.

claim: The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa is projecting that Africa’s growth will drop to 1.8%, and perhaps lower.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In March 2020, the UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) warned that COVID-19 could cut Africa’s GDP growth from about 3.2% to around 1.8% in 2020, and cautioned it could drop further under worse scenarios.

claim: Nigeria spent 1 billion naira on COVID-19 text messages
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: During early 2020, Nigerian telecom operators sent COVID-19 awareness SMS as a free public service (corporate social responsibility). The NCDC and telecom industry representatives stated the government did not pay for these messages, and there’s no credible evidence of a N1 billion spend on SMS.

claim: The state of California admitted in a court settlement that a million people voted improperly in the US elections in 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  In January 2019, California and Los Angeles County settled a lawsuit (brought by Judicial Watch) about complying with the National Voter Registration Act’s requirements to remove long‑inactive registrations. The settlement dealt with cleaning up voter rolls (including about 1.5 million inactive registrations in L.A. County); it did not admit that people voted improperly, nor did it show that a million improper votes were cast. State officials explicitly said it was about list maintenance, not evidence of fraud.

claim: British Prime Minister Boris Johnson is down with Covid-19 and admitted to hospital and has subsequently died.
response_text: FALSE.  Boris Johnson did contract COVID-19 and was hospitalized (including time in ICU) in April 2020, but he recovered, was discharged on April 12, 2020, returned to work, and did not die.

claim: Two nurses who were in intensive therapy units (ITUs) in Swansea, Wales have died and three more ventilated.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a WhatsApp/social media rumour during early 2020 that Swansea Bay University Health Board and Welsh authorities explicitly denied. They reported no nurse deaths and no such cluster of ventilated nurses in Swansea ITUs at the time.

claim: It’s illegal to hold an absentee-only election or mail ballots to every registered voter.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: U.S. election law is set largely by states, and several states legally conduct all-mail elections or mail ballots to all registered (typically active) voters. Examples include Oregon, Washington, Colorado, Utah, and Hawaii (all-mail elections), and states/jurisdictions like California, Nevada, Vermont, and D.C. that mail ballots to all active registered voters. While some states don’t allow universal mail balloting, there is no blanket illegality against absentee-only elections or mailing ballots to all registered voters.

claim: Consuming ewedu will cure COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no clinical evidence that ewedu (jute leaves) cures COVID-19. While it’s a nutritious food, no herb or food has been proven to eradicate the virus. Effective COVID-19 management relies on vaccination and evidence-based treatments (e.g., authorized antivirals), not herbal remedies.

claim: British author David Icke claimed that the Covid-19 pandemic was orchestrated by supernatural forces attempting to “dismantle” the world economic system and “control” the population using new technologies like 5G.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: In 2020 interviews and writings, David Icke argued that COVID-19 was a planned operation by a “global cult” to crash/dismantle the economy and impose a technocratic control system, repeatedly linking it to technologies like 5G. In his broader framework (e.g., “The Answer”), he says this cult is ultimately directed by non-human, interdimensional entities (often called Archons/reptilians)—i.e., essentially supernatural forces. Minor uncertainty only in the paraphrase “supernatural forces,” which is not his usual wording, but it accurately reflects his stated non-human/other-dimensional controllers.

claim: The RT-PCR test does not detect Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  RT‑PCR tests are designed to detect genetic material (RNA) from SARS‑CoV‑2, the virus that causes COVID‑19, and are the gold‑standard diagnostic test for infection. While no test is perfect (timing and sample quality can cause false negatives), RT‑PCR does detect COVID‑19 infection by identifying viral RNA specific to SARS‑CoV‑2.

claim: Cadbury gave away 500 Free baskets of Cadbury Chocolate to celebrate its 196th Anniversary.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a widely shared Facebook scam in 2020 claiming Cadbury was giving away free chocolate baskets for its 196th anniversary. Cadbury publicly stated it was not running such a promotion, and fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact, Snopes, Reuters) debunked the posts as from imposter pages designed to harvest engagement or data.

claim: British author David Icke claimed that Microscope images of exosomes and of the virus that causes Covid-19 are “exactly the same
response_text: TRUE.  David Icke echoed Andrew Kaufman’s claim in early 2020 videos/interviews, asserting that electron microscope images of exosomes and SARS‑CoV‑2 are “exactly the same.” This was documented by fact‑checkers (e.g., Reuters, Full Fact) and cited as part of the misinformation that led to his content’s removal from platforms.

claim: India's government is going to cut the pension of employees by 30 per cent and terminate it for those above the age of 80 in order to divert funds towards managing health services and tackle the adverse effects of the coronavirus pandemic in the country.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Government of India issued no order to cut pensions by 30% or to terminate pensions for those above 80. During the COVID-19 period, the Centre froze future increases in Dearness Allowance/Dearness Relief temporarily, but it did not reduce existing pensions. The Press Information Bureau’s Fact Check and the Department of Pension & Pensioners’ Welfare explicitly denied this rumor in 2020. In fact, central government pensions include additional pension increments starting at age 80, not termination.

claim: 5G antennas on fire in La Spezia, Italy.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A widely shared video claiming “5G antennas on fire in La Spezia” actually showed a brush/vegetation fire near existing radio/TV transmitters above the city. Local authorities and fact-checkers reported there were no 5G antennas involved and no towers were set on fire. (Minor uncertainty on the exact date, but multiple checks confirm the claim is wrong.)

claim: The Supreme Court of the United States issued an order to remove Rep. Ilhan Omar from Congress
response_text: FALSE.  The Supreme Court has neither issued such an order nor has the authority to do so. Under the U.S. Constitution (Article I, Section 5), only the House of Representatives can expel a member, by a two‑thirds vote. No credible record or court docket shows any Supreme Court order removing Rep. Ilhan Omar. Several fact-checkers have debunked this claim.

claim: There is a link between the launch of 5G and the Covid-19 outbreak in 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no scientific evidence linking 5G to Covid-19. Viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks, and Covid-19 spread widely in countries without any 5G service. Health authorities (e.g., WHO) state that 5G’s non-ionizing radio frequencies cannot cause viral infections or Covid-19.

claim: Doctors, scientist and political figures did not say we need to cancel Mardi Gras
response_text: TRUE.  Context: Mardi Gras 2020 concluded Feb. 25, before U.S. authorities began advising against large gatherings. At the time, CDC and federal guidance did not recommend canceling mass events (those advisories came in March). Louisiana state and New Orleans officials publicly said there was no guidance to cancel, and local health officials described the risk as low. While a few experts warned generally about COVID-19’s potential spread, there were no prominent or official calls from doctors, scientists, or political figures to cancel Mardi Gras beforehand. Minor uncertainty: isolated individuals may have voiced concern, but not in an official or widely publicized way.

claim: Dr Charles Lieber of Harvard University was arrested for manufacturing the novel coronavirus in collusion with China.
response_text: FALSE.  - Charles Lieber, a Harvard nanotechnology researcher, was arrested in January 2020 for allegedly making false statements to U.S. authorities about his ties to China’s Thousand Talents Program and Wuhan University of Technology, and was later convicted of tax offenses and lying to investigators. - He was not accused of, charged with, or linked to manufacturing the coronavirus; his work is in nanoscience, not virology. - No credible evidence connects him to creating SARS‑CoV‑2.

claim: People with lupus who take hydroxychloroquine have protection against COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence from lupus cohorts shows chronic hydroxychloroquine use does not lower the risk of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection or severe COVID-19. Randomized trials in the general population (post‑exposure and pre‑exposure) also found hydroxychloroquine does not prevent COVID‑19. Major guidelines (NIH/WHO/ACR) therefore do not recommend it for COVID‑19 prevention.

claim: Barack Obama told Africans to reject coronavirus vaccines in March 2020
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Barack Obama telling Africans to reject COVID-19 vaccines in March 2020. In March 2020 there were no authorized COVID-19 vaccines yet. Fact-checkers traced such claims to fabricated posts circulating on social media. Obama has consistently supported vaccination and later publicly encouraged people to get COVID-19 vaccines.

claim: Data from a Philippine General Hospital claims that there is a correlation between grocery shopping and COVID-19
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The Philippine General Hospital (UP-PGH) publicly denied releasing any study or data linking grocery shopping to COVID-19 cases. Fact-checkers in the Philippines (e.g., AFP, Rappler) debunked viral posts that misattributed such a claim to PGH; no official PGH data established this correlation.

claim: Lighting a Diya or candle, can kill Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  A diya/candle does not disinfect air or surfaces. The heat is too localized to inactivate SARS‑CoV‑2 in a room, and there’s no scientific evidence that burning lamps or candles kills the virus. Effective methods include vaccination, masks, ventilation, handwashing, and approved disinfectants (e.g., 70% alcohol, bleach).

claim: The United States had done more testing for COVID-19 infections in eight days than South Korea had done in eight weeks
response_text: FALSE.  - When President Trump made this claim (March 24, 2020), South Korea had conducted roughly 270,000–300,000 tests over its first eight weeks (late Jan to mid‑March), according to KCDC reports. - In the eight days prior to March 24, the U.S. conducted about 240,000–250,000 tests (COVID Tracking Project data), which is fewer than South Korea’s eight‑week total. - Estimates vary slightly by source and whether counting people or specimens, but none support the claim.

claim: A majority of 6,200 doctors said hydroxychloroquine is the most effective coronavirus treatment.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A widely cited Sermo survey of about 6,200 physicians (April 2020) found that 37% of doctors who had treated COVID‑19 patients rated hydroxychloroquine as the “most effective” among listed options. That is a plurality, not a majority, and it was not 37% of all 6,200 doctors. The claim overstates the survey’s findings.

claim: The WHO published a 4step lockdown procedure that countries need to follow to control Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO did not publish a mandatory “4-step lockdown procedure.” During COVID-19, WHO issued non-binding guidance on public health and social measures (e.g., testing, tracing, masking) and outlined criteria for adjusting restrictions (often six criteria for lifting measures), but no official four-step lockdown plan that countries “need to follow.” Claims of a WHO 4-step lockdown have been debunked as misattributions.

claim: COVID-19 testing kits imported by Britain supplied by China are contaminated with coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The widely shared claim misrepresented reports from early 2020. A European supplier (Eurofins) told UK labs that some test kit components had traces of synthetic positive-control material used for quality checks—not live virus—and said the affected items were not sourced from China. Separately, the UK later paused some Randox swab kits over possible sterility issues, but not because they were contaminated with coronavirus.

claim: Bill Withers left $2 Million estate to trump Re-election Campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a satire site (America’s Last Line of Defense/Potatriot Post) and has no basis in fact. No credible reports or FEC records show Bill Withers or his estate donating to Trump’s campaign. Moreover, U.S. law caps individual contributions to a candidate’s campaign (in 2020, $2,800 per election), making a $2 million bequest to a campaign legally impossible.

claim: VIRAL VIDEO SHOWS THE FBI SEIZING CORONAVIRUS-INFECTED FACE MASKS SENT FROM CHINA
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The clip was miscaptioned. There are no credible reports of the FBI seizing “coronavirus‑infected” masks from China. Authorities did seize counterfeit or price‑gouged PPE in 2020, but not because masks were contaminated. Health agencies also noted the risk of catching COVID‑19 from shipped packages is negligible.

claim: Video shows a Hindu priest being pinned down by a policeman.
response_text: FALSE  Briefly: The widely shared clip is miscaptioned. Fact-checks found it’s an older video from India showing police restraining a man dressed in saffron clothes during an arrest; he was not a Hindu priest. Exact location/date vary across reposts, but the “Hindu priest” claim is incorrect.

claim: WHO ranked Sri Lanka as the fifth best country for COVID-19 pandemic response.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO did not publish any global ranking of countries’ COVID-19 responses, and there is no WHO list placing Sri Lanka fifth. Claims of high rankings for Sri Lanka likely stem from third-party indices (e.g., Lowy Institute’s 2021 index), not WHO.

claim: The U.S. military rescued over 35,000 malnourished, caged children out of U.S. tunnels.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a baseless QAnon-style conspiracy claim. There are no credible reports, official statements, or evidence from the U.S. military, law enforcement, hospitals, or child-welfare agencies of any such mass rescue. Major fact-checkers (AP, Reuters, Snopes, USA Today) have repeatedly debunked similar “children in tunnels” stories. An operation of that scale would produce extensive public records and media coverage, which do not exist. Uncertainty: very low.

claim: Prince Charles was cured of Covid by Ayurveda medicine.
response_text: FALSE.  Prince Charles had mild COVID-19 in March 2020 and recovered after self-isolating per NHS guidance. Clarence House and the British High Commission in India explicitly denied claims he was treated or “cured” by Ayurveda; multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, BBC) debunked the Ayurveda/homeopathy cure stories.

claim: Morel Mushrooms are the source of Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Coronaviruses (including SARS‑CoV‑2) are viruses of mammals and birds; the closest known relatives are found in bats, with possible intermediate animal hosts. There is no evidence linking morel mushrooms (Morchella spp.), which are fungi, to the origin of coronavirus. Fungi are not recognized reservoirs or sources of coronaviruses.

claim: U.S. Democratic Presidential candidate Joe Biden called the coronavirus a "hoax"
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Joe Biden calling the coronavirus a “hoax.” Multiple fact-checkers (AP, PolitiFact, Snopes) found this claim false. The “hoax” remark is commonly associated with Donald Trump, who said Democrats’ criticism of his COVID-19 response was a “hoax” at a Feb. 28, 2020 rally—not that the virus itself was a hoax.

claim: Covid virus is now "gone" in South Korea because residents stayed at home for three weeks.
response_text: FALSE.  South Korea never eliminated COVID-19, and it did not implement a strict nationwide “stay-at-home for three weeks” lockdown. While early, aggressive testing, tracing, masking, and targeted distancing reduced cases, the virus continued to circulate and the country experienced multiple subsequent waves (e.g., late 2020 and the large Omicron wave in 2022).

claim: Alcohol weakens the immune system, making it difficult for the body to fight infections such as Covid-19.
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence shows alcohol—especially heavy or binge drinking—impairs both innate and adaptive immune responses, disrupts gut and respiratory defenses, and increases susceptibility to infections like pneumonia and ARDS. Public health bodies (e.g., WHO, CDC) and clinical studies link alcohol misuse to higher risk and worse outcomes from respiratory infections, including COVID-19. Note: the effect is dose-dependent; heavy use has the clearest impact, while light occasional drinking has smaller effects.

claim: All viruses are really common colds gone bad and can be defeated with fruits, vegetables and a strong immune system.
response_text: FALSE.  Viruses are a vast, diverse group of pathogens, not “common colds gone bad.” The common cold is just one mild syndrome caused by certain viruses (e.g., rhinoviruses, some coronaviruses). Many viruses cause severe or chronic diseases (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B/C, measles, rabies, Ebola) and some infect plants or bacteria. Good nutrition supports immune function but does not “defeat” all viral infections; effective control often requires vaccines, antivirals, and medical care, and some viruses can be lethal even in healthy people.

claim: Coronavirus is part of a conspiracy designed to introduce a "new world order.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 was orchestrated to impose a “new world order.” The “New World Order” narrative is a longstanding conspiracy theory. Genetic, epidemiological, and independent investigations indicate SARS‑CoV‑2 is a real virus that spread naturally (with debate over zoonotic spillover vs. possible lab-related accident), not a coordinated plot. Pandemic responses varied across countries and were subject to public scrutiny and legal oversight, inconsistent with a single global conspiracy.

claim: Barack Obama has urged Africans to reject  Covid-19 vaccines.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checkers (Reuters, AFP, Africa Check) found no record of Barack Obama urging Africans to reject COVID-19 vaccines; the quote circulating online was fabricated. In reality, Obama publicly supported COVID-19 vaccination, promoted it in PSAs, and was vaccinated himself.

claim: 52 group admins from WhatsApp are now at Dadar cyber crime police station for having misleading fowards in the group.
response_text: FALSE.  - There are no credible news reports or official statements about “52 WhatsApp group admins” being held in Mumbai for misleading forwards. - Mumbai Police have previously debunked similar viral messages; also, Mumbai’s dedicated Cyber Police Station is at BKC, not “Dadar cyber crime police station.” - Such mass detentions would likely be widely reported if true.  Minor uncertainty always exists with fast-moving events, but available evidence indicates this is a hoax.

claim: The radiation from cell phones and 5G towers are what is currently killing people, not coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  - COVID-19 is caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus; its genome is isolated, detected by PCR, cultured, and linked to characteristic disease and autopsy findings. Outbreaks track person-to-person respiratory transmission, and mortality falls with vaccination and antivirals—patterns incompatible with RF exposure. - Many severe outbreaks occurred where 5G was absent or minimal (e.g., early Iran, cruise ships), and there’s no credible correlation between 5G rollout and COVID-19 deaths. - Cell phone/5G signals are non-ionizing radiofrequency radiation at low power levels. According to WHO, ICNIRP, and national regulators, exposures within guidelines have not been shown to cause harm, let alone pandemic-scale fatalities.  Uncertainty: none.

claim: Air India is evacuating Indians stranded in UK
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During the COVID-19 pandemic, especially from May 2020 under the Vande Bharat Mission, Air India operated special repatriation flights from the UK (e.g., London, Birmingham) to India to bring back Indians stranded there. Similar limited evacuation/repatriation services also ran around Dec 2020–Jan 2021 after the UK-variant travel suspension. If referring to another period, the status could differ.

claim: India trying to prevent people from posting COVID-19 updates.
response_text: TRUE.  During the 2021 second wave, the Indian government asked platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram to remove or geo-block numerous COVID-19 posts—some critical of the government or reporting shortages—citing misinformation and panic. Twitter confirmed it withheld tweets in India following legal requests. This wasn’t a blanket ban on all updates, but it did involve restricting some COVID-19 posts.

claim: The president of Nigeria has dismissed his Chief of Staff because of his wellbeing challenge on the coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Nigeria’s Chief of Staff Abba Kyari contracted COVID-19 in March 2020 and died on April 17, 2020. He was not dismissed by the president; he remained in office until his death. No credible reports show a Nigerian president firing a Chief of Staff due to coronavirus-related health issues.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says “the government planned” it.
response_text: TRUE.  In September 2023, tests reported by the Washington Post (and echoed by outlets like The Verge and Rolling Stone) found that Alexa, when asked about the origin of COVID-19, responded that “the government planned it,” citing dubious sources. Amazon said it was a mistake and moved to fix the responses. Note: Alexa’s answers can change over time.

claim: Jio is giving Indian users a free recharge of ₹498.
response_text: FALSE.  This “free ₹498 Jio recharge” claim has repeatedly circulated as a phishing/hoax message. There’s no official Jio announcement offering a blanket free ₹498 recharge. Always verify offers only via the MyJio app, jio.com, or Jio’s verified social accounts.

claim: The anti-tuberculosis vaccine protects against coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The anti-tuberculosis (BCG) vaccine does not protect against COVID-19. Early ecological hints were confounded, and multiple randomized trials (e.g., BRACE and others) found no significant reduction in SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 illness with BCG. WHO and other health agencies do not recommend BCG for coronavirus prevention. (Minor uncertainty remains about nonspecific immune effects, but no proven protective benefit against COVID-19.)

claim: In Serbia, the stricter Covid19 curfew measures prevented dog walking for up to 14 hours at a time.
response_text: FALSE.  Serbia’s nightly COVID-19 curfew in spring 2020 generally ran from 5 pm to 5 am (12 hours). A brief pet-walking exemption during curfew was quickly scrapped, so dog walking was banned during those 12 hours. On some weekends, lockdowns were much longer (40–80+ hours), not 14. I find no evidence of a standard 14-hour curfew. (Slight uncertainty due to shifting rules, but reported hours were 12 nightly or much longer on weekends.)

claim: COVID-19 is transmitted through fruits and vegetables in Hong Kong
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 spreads mainly via respiratory droplets and aerosols, not through eating fruits or vegetables. Health authorities (including WHO/CDC and Hong Kong’s Centre for Food Safety) report no evidence that people contract COVID-19 from food or fresh produce. Normal hygiene—washing produce and hands—is sufficient. Uncertainty: none beyond general caution about surface contamination, which has not been shown to cause infections via produce.

claim: In India the 21-day lockdown due to COVID-19 is to be extended.
response_text: TRUE.  India’s initial 21-day nationwide COVID-19 lockdown (March 25–April 14, 2020) was officially extended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on April 14, 2020, to May 3, 2020.

claim: Depending on the poll, between 58% and 81% of Americans were supportive of keeping current restrictions in place or even expanding them to the nation as a whole.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple early-2020 COVID-19 polls showed broad support for maintaining or even expanding restrictions: - Quinnipiac (Apr 2020) found 81% supported a national stay-at-home order. - Fox News (Apr 2020) reported about 80% supported stay-at-home requirements. - Economist/YouGov (around Apr 2020) showed support for a nationwide lockdown in the high-50s to low-60s. - Other polls (CBS/YouGov, Pew) found roughly two-thirds favored keeping or tightening restrictions.  These results fit the cited 58%–81% range. Minor uncertainty on the exact lowest figure, but the range is supported.

claim: A Chinese doctor who went to help Italians found out that the main reason why COVID-19 spreads quickly in Italy is because Italians like to use the same shoes that they wear outside into the house, for some people even into the bedroom.”
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible source reports a Chinese doctor concluded Italy’s surge was mainly due to wearing outdoor shoes indoors. The Chinese Red Cross team in Italy (e.g., Sun Shuopeng) urged stricter lockdowns and masking, not shoe policies. - COVID-19’s primary transmission is via respiratory droplets and aerosols. Fomite transmission (including via shoes) is possible but not a major driver. Studies that found viral RNA on shoe soles were in hospital settings and did not show shoes were a significant community transmission route. - Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, AFP) have debunked this claim.

claim: Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chauhan said that from 01/04/2020 people who violate lockdown would be shot down immediately.
response_text: FALSE.  No such order or statement was issued. The “shoot-at-sight for lockdown violators from 01/04/2020” claim about MP CM Shivraj Singh Chouhan was a viral fake message in early 2020, debunked by multiple fact-checkers, and denied by official sources. There was no shoot-on-sight directive in Madhya Pradesh for lockdown violations.

claim: Democratic nominee for president Joe Biden has received campaign donations from Antifa.
response_text: FALSE.  - “Antifa” is not a formal organization capable of making campaign contributions. - FEC records showing donors with “ANTIFA” listed are from the donor’s self-reported employer/occupation fields, which are unverified and do not indicate an organization donated. - No evidence shows Joe Biden’s campaign received donations from an Antifa organization.  Sources: Reuters (Aug. 31, 2020); PolitiFact (Sept. 3, 2020); USA Today (Sept. 2, 2020).

claim: Illinois banned the sale of alcohol on March 30 2020
response_text: FALSE.  Illinois did not ban alcohol sales on March 30, 2020. During COVID-19, Illinois closed bars and restaurants to on-premise consumption starting March 16, and the March 20 stay-at-home order allowed liquor stores and packaged alcohol sales to continue as essential retail. Some local limits (e.g., Chicago’s late-night liquor sales curfew) came later, around April 2, but there was no statewide ban on that date.

claim: It has been confirmed and tested that 2 spoonfuls of palm oil every morning can stop the spread of Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that ingesting palm oil prevents COVID‑19 infection or transmission. Major health authorities (WHO, CDC) state that no food or supplement can stop COVID‑19; proven measures are vaccination, masks, ventilation, testing, and staying home when sick. Relying on palm oil is ineffective and could delay proper prevention or care. Uncertainty: none.

claim: A Sri Lankan military hospital, Kotelawala Defence University Hospital, has been reserved exclusively for the use of "VIPs" who test positive for COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Health and Kotelawala Defence University (KDU) Hospital publicly denied this rumor during the pandemic, stating the hospital was not reserved exclusively for “VIP” COVID-19 patients. COVID-19 treatment was provided through designated hospitals like the National Institute of Infectious Diseases (IDH), Homagama, Neville Fernando, etc. Independent fact-checkers (e.g., AFP Fact Check, FactCheck.lk) also debunked the claim. No credible evidence showed KDU Hospital was set aside solely for VIP COVID cases.

claim: Nigella Sativa contains 100% hydroxychloroquine.
response_text: FALSE.  Nigella sativa (black seed) does not contain hydroxychloroquine. Hydroxychloroquine is a synthetic 4‑aminoquinoline drug, whereas Nigella sativa’s constituents include compounds like thymoquinone, thymohydroquinone, nigellone, and various alkaloids and fatty acids. No credible evidence shows natural hydroxychloroquine in Nigella sativa, and a plant cannot be “100%” a single compound.

claim: It took Obama ‘millions infected and over 1,000 deaths’ to declare the H1N1 flu a health emergency.
response_text: FALSE.  HHS declared a federal public health emergency for H1N1 on April 26, 2009, when the U.S. had about 20 confirmed cases and no deaths. President Obama later declared a separate national emergency on Oct. 24, 2009, by which time there were over 1,000 U.S. deaths and widespread infections. The claim conflates the later national emergency with the earlier health emergency.

claim: Coronavirus caused the serious birth defect of a stillborn baby in Rajasthan, India.
response_text: FALSE.  Briefly: A viral rumour from Rajasthan in 2020 claimed a stillborn baby’s severe deformity was caused by coronavirus. Doctors identified the condition as a congenital anomaly (e.g., anencephaly), not related to COVID-19, and the mother was not COVID-positive. There is no evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 causes such birth defects.

claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are planning, in the next 10 days, to change guidance and advise Americans to wear masks in everyday life.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: When this claim circulated, the CDC said it was reviewing mask guidance but had not decided or announced any plan or timeline. No evidence showed a CDC plan to change guidance “in the next 10 days.” The CDC later (Apr. 3, 2020) recommended cloth face coverings in certain public settings, but that was not a preannounced 10‑day plan, nor a blanket “everyday life” mandate.

claim: PM Narendra Modi has given the contract for Coronavirus testing kits to a Gujurati company selling them for Rs4,500.
response_text: FALSE.  - Rs 4,500 was the early ICMR-capped maximum charge that private labs could bill patients for a COVID‑19 RT‑PCR test (screening + confirmatory), not the price the government paid for a “kit.” - Procurement of testing kits was handled by ICMR and various agencies from multiple suppliers (including imports and Indian firms like Pune-based Mylab), not via a personal contract “given” by the Prime Minister to a Gujarati company. - No credible evidence shows a sole contract awarded by PM Modi to a Gujarati company at Rs 4,500 per kit.

claim: Drinking water or other liquids will wash the coronovirus through the oesophasgus where they will be killed by the stomach acid.
response_text: FALSE.  Drinking water does not “wash” SARS‑CoV‑2 from the throat to be killed in the stomach. The virus infects cells in the nose, mouth, and airways by binding to receptors; once attached, drinking fluids won’t remove it. Stomach acid is not a reliable protection, and SARS‑CoV‑2 can also affect the gastrointestinal tract. Public health agencies (WHO/CDC) have debunked this myth.

claim: The coloured part of a surgical mask is to be worn inwards to the face to help  prevent of the spread of coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  On typical 3‑ply surgical masks, the colored side is fluid‑repellent and should face outward; the white side is absorbent and should face inward toward your face. Wearing the colored side inward reduces the mask’s intended effectiveness. (Always follow the specific manufacturer’s instructions, as not all masks are color‑coded.)

claim: A man in Pakistan threw a party consisting of 100 people after recovering from Coronavirus and after attending the party, multiple people present there were infected with the virus.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports document a man in Pakistan throwing a “recovery party” with 100 attendees that then led to multiple infections. This story circulated on social media in early 2020 but was not substantiated by reliable news or official sources. Known early clusters in Pakistan were linked to events like the Raiwind congregation and a returnee in Mardan, not a post-recovery celebration. (Slight uncertainty only because private events can go underreported, but this specific claim was widely shared and debunked.)

claim: The installation of 5G in the United Kingdom a cover-up for a secret weapon deployment
response_text: FALSE.  5G in the UK is standard telecommunications infrastructure, not a weapon. Its rollout is public: spectrum is auctioned by Ofcom, equipment and standards are openly specified by 3GPP/ITU, and deployments are widely documented and regulated. UK health and safety bodies (e.g., UKHSA, following ICNIRP guidelines) state that 5G’s non-ionizing RF emissions are safe within established limits. No credible evidence supports claims of a “secret weapon” cover-up; such allegations originated from debunked conspiracy theories (often tied to COVID-19) and conflict with extensive transparent oversight and independent testing. Uncertainty: none beyond the impossibility of proving negatives.

claim: 70% of Coronavirus cases are found in Muslims.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - COVID-19 case data are not tracked by religion, and no credible source reports such a distribution. - Muslims comprise about a quarter of the world’s population, while major COVID-19 case counts were spread across many non–Muslim-majority countries (e.g., the US, Brazil, much of Europe). There is no evidence that 70% of cases were among Muslims.

claim: Tea can cure COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  Tea does not cure COVID-19. While warm fluids can soothe symptoms and compounds in tea have shown limited lab activity against viruses, no clinical evidence shows tea can eliminate SARS-CoV-2. Effective treatments include authorized antivirals (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, remdesivir) and supportive care; vaccines reduce risk of severe disease.

claim: China and Japan are free of SARS-COV-2.
response_text: FALSE.  SARS‑CoV‑2 has not been eradicated and remains endemic worldwide. Both China and Japan continue to report COVID‑19 cases and circulating variants (including through 2024–2025). “Free of SARS‑CoV‑2” would imply no circulation, which is not the case.

claim: No Democrats voted for the coronavirus stimulus measures.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple COVID-19 relief bills had broad Democratic support. Examples: - Families First Coronavirus Response Act (March 2020): passed 363–40 in the House and 90–8 in the Senate. - CARES Act (March 2020): passed 96–0 in the Senate; House approved by voice vote. - Paycheck Protection Program/Health Care Enhancement (April 2020): passed by voice vote in the Senate and 388–5 in the House. - December 2020 relief package: passed 359–53 in the House and 92–6 in the Senate.  In 2021, the American Rescue Plan passed with only Democratic votes, showing Democrats supported stimulus, not opposed it.

claim: Extinction Rebellion issued a flyer that reads: “Corona is the cure, humans are the disease” .
response_text: FALSE.  A poster with the Extinction Rebellion logo saying “Corona is the cure, humans are the disease” circulated in 2020, but XR denied producing it and condemned the message. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Full Fact, Snopes) found it was not an official XR flyer; it appears to have been a hoax/unauthorized use of the logo.

claim: As prosecutor, Jill Karofsky Karofsky gave no jail time to a sexual predator who assaulted a 5-year-old girl.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Prosecutors don’t “give” jail time—judges do. In the child-assault case cited in ads against Jill Karofsky, she was not the local prosecutor who negotiated the plea or handled sentencing; she later worked at the Wisconsin Department of Justice on an appeal on behalf of the state. Fact-checks (e.g., PolitiFact Wisconsin and the Associated Press) found the claim misrepresents her role. Uncertainty: exact custody details in that case vary by report, but Karofsky did not control the sentence.

claim: Dr. Deborah Birx claimed that 40% of the USA had less than 200 cases combined of covid 19 on 26th of march 2020
response_text: FALSE.  At the March 26, 2020 White House briefing, Dr. Deborah Birx said roughly “40% of the country has fewer than 200 cases,” referring to states/areas individually. She did not claim that 40% of the USA combined had fewer than 200 cases. The word “combined” misstates her remark.

claim: Newborn baby advises people to eat boiled eggs during pandemic.
response_text: FALSE. Newborns cannot speak or give advice, and there are no credible reports of such an event. This was a social media hoax during COVID-19; moreover, eating boiled eggs does not prevent or cure COVID-19 according to health authorities.

claim: Free Netflix Account for All
response_text: FALSE. Netflix is a paid subscription service and does not offer free accounts for everyone. Any past free trials or limited regional tests (e.g., Kenya’s now-ended free mobile plan) were not universal and have been discontinued. Offers claiming “free Netflix for all” are typically scams.

claim: Lemon and baking powder can cure coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that lemon or baking powder can treat or cure COVID-19. Health authorities (e.g., WHO/CDC) confirm no foods or home remedies cure coronavirus; proven measures include vaccination and, for eligible patients, antivirals like nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir. Ingesting baking powder/soda in quantity can be harmful.

claim: Italy has apparently discovered that the microorganism which causes COVID-19 is a bacteria and not a Virus. This bacteria is responsible for blood clotting and hindering the transport of oxygen throughout the body.
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 is caused by SARS‑CoV‑2, a coronavirus (a virus), not a bacterium. Italian and international health authorities never “discovered” otherwise. While COVID-19 can cause abnormal blood clotting and low oxygen levels, these are complications of the viral infection and the body’s inflammatory response. Bacterial co-infections can occur in some patients, but they are not the cause of COVID-19.

claim: CNN published the news that Tea can cure Covid-19 patients as suggested by by China’s whistleblower doctor Li Wenliang.
response_text: FALSE.  No CNN report said tea cures COVID-19, and Dr. Li Wenliang never suggested that. The claim traces to fabricated screenshots/WhatsApp hoaxes misusing CNN’s branding. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, AFP, Snopes) have debunked it. No beverage cures COVID-19.

claim: Italy went against the WHO instruction of not performing autopsies on COVID-19 casualties.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO did not issue a blanket instruction to avoid autopsies. Its March 2020 guidance on managing bodies of people who died from COVID‑19 allowed autopsies provided appropriate precautions and PPE were used (it discouraged practices like embalming). Italy initially discouraged routine autopsies on COVID‑19 cases for safety/logistical reasons, and any autopsies conducted were not in defiance of a WHO ban, because no such ban existed.

claim: Dr Li Wenliang China's whistleblower doctor suggested tea can cure Covid-19 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a misattributed hoax. There is no credible record of Dr. Li Wenliang ever recommending tea as a cure for COVID-19; multiple fact-checks (e.g., AFP, Reuters, Snopes) debunked viral messages claiming he did. Dr. Li died in early February 2020, and tea is not a cure for COVID-19. Uncertainty: low.

claim: There are 2 million illegal immigrants in the UK.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no official count, and the best independent estimates put the UK’s irregular/undocumented population at roughly 0.8–1.2 million (e.g., Pew Research Center 2017; Oxford’s Migration Observatory). No credible source supports a figure as high as 2 million. Some uncertainty exists because these populations are hard to measure, but available evidence doesn’t reach 2 million.

claim: Vaccines to cure Covid-19 are ready
response_text: FALSE.  Vaccines prevent COVID‑19 or reduce its severity; they do not cure an existing infection. COVID‑19 vaccines have been available for years, but treatments like antivirals are used to treat active cases.

claim: Under Trump, “coronavirus was declared a health emergency and public safety measures were in place before a single U.S. death occurred.
response_text: TRUE.  - HHS declared a U.S. public health emergency on Jan. 31, 2020, and the administration imposed measures such as airport screening (from Jan. 17), quarantines for Wuhan evacuees, and travel restrictions on most travelers from China (effective Feb. 2). - The earliest confirmed U.S. COVID-19 death is now known to have occurred on Feb. 6, 2020 (Santa Clara County), with the first publicly reported death on Feb. 29.  Thus, the emergency declaration and key public-safety measures preceded any known U.S. death.

claim: People with pre-existing respiratory conditions such as COPD or Asthma will be given a “rescue pack” of medication from their general practitioners during the novel coronavirus pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no policy to universally give “rescue packs” during COVID-19. Some COPD patients already have rescue packs (usually steroids and antibiotics) as part of an individual flare-up plan, but they are not for treating coronavirus itself and were not to be issued broadly or for stockpiling. For asthma, rescue packs are not routinely prescribed; guidance from NHS/Asthma UK/BLF specifically advised against issuing them just because of the pandemic.

claim: A zoology book authored by Dr Ramesh Gupta speaks of COVID-19 and the treatment for the disease has already been found.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The viral claim comes from an edited image of a “R. Gupta’s” zoology/exam-prep book. The original text discussed coronaviruses in general (e.g., SARS), not COVID‑19 specifically, and did not say a treatment had been found. COVID‑19 was named only in 2020, so earlier editions couldn’t mention it. The publisher also clarified that “R. Gupta” is a house imprint, not a “Dr Ramesh Gupta,” and that the circulated page was doctored.
