claim: French astrologer Nostradamus had predicted the outbreak of coronavirus in his book “Les Prophéties”.
response_text: FALSE.  No passage in Nostradamus’s Les Prophéties mentions coronavirus, COVID-19, or a 2020 pandemic. The viral lines about a “twin year (2020)” and a “queen (corona) from the east” are fabricated and do not appear in his text. His quatrains are vague and have been retrofitted to events, but reputable fact-checks (e.g., Reuters, Snopes) found no specific COVID-19 prediction.

claim: Everyone is required to wear a mask everywhere at all times because of COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE. Mask requirements vary by location, setting, and time. There has never been a universal rule requiring everyone to wear a mask everywhere at all times; mandates (when in place) were limited to specific settings and have largely been lifted in many areas.

claim: Neem leaves can cure the novel coronavirus and relieve its symptoms.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no reliable clinical evidence that neem leaves cure COVID-19 or specifically relieve its symptoms. Health authorities (e.g., WHO, CDC) have stated no herbal remedy has been proven to cure COVID-19. Some lab studies suggest neem compounds may have antiviral activity, but this has not translated into effective, approved treatment in humans. Rely on vaccination and authorized therapies; using neem as a “cure” could delay proper care.

claim: Tom Hanks passes away after confessing his admiration for President Trump
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports that Tom Hanks has died; this is a recurring hoax. Moreover, Hanks has not professed admiration for Donald Trump—he has publicly supported Democrats (including Joe Biden) and has criticized Trump in past interviews.

claim: A zoology book authored by Dr Ramesh Gupta speaks of COVID-19 and Coronavirus can be cured with aspirin, antihistamines and nasal spray.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The page from Dr. Ramesh Gupta’s zoology book that circulated online discusses the common cold, noting that some colds are caused by coronaviruses, and lists symptomatic treatments (aspirin, antihistamines, nasal sprays). It was written before the COVID-19 pandemic and does not claim that COVID-19 can be cured with these drugs. Multiple fact-checks and the author’s clarification confirm this.

claim: A zoology book authored by Dr Ramesh Gupta speaks of COVID-19 and The novel coronavirus (nCoV) or COVID-19 is not a new disease.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Dr. Ramesh Gupta’s zoology book did include a section on COVID-19, but only in a post-2020 updated/reprinted edition after the outbreak. Older editions did not mention COVID-19. The text explains that coronaviruses have been known for decades; it does not assert that COVID-19 itself is “not a new disease.” The claim misstates the book’s wording and context. Uncertainty: low.

claim: From 23 March until the foreseeable future, Microsoft and Sony will shut down their gaming servers during UK school hours.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - In March 2020, Sony and Microsoft announced bandwidth-reduction measures (e.g., slowing game downloads) in parts of Europe to ease internet congestion, not shutting servers. - Multiplayer services remained online; there were no official plans to shut gaming servers during UK school hours. - The “school-hours shutdown” claim was a social media rumor that was publicly denied and debunked.

claim: Presidential candidate Joe Biden referred to the novel Coronavirus pandemic as a time when "people are dying that have never died before."
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Joe Biden saying that about COVID-19. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, FactCheck.org) found no evidence he made the remark; the line is an old quip often misattributed to figures like Mark Twain or Will Rogers and circulated as a meme during the pandemic.

claim: People Clapping together at 5pm during Janta Curfew will kill coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Clapping or making noise has no effect on viruses. SARS‑CoV‑2 can be inactivated by soap, alcohol-based disinfectants, bleach, heat, or UV—not by sound or vibrations. Clapping was meant as a show of support for workers, not a way to kill the virus, and gathering closely to clap could even increase transmission risk.

claim: Kenny Rogers' Wife plans to Donate part of his estate to Trumps Re-election campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible news or records support this. The claim traces to fake/satirical sites and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Moreover, U.S. campaign finance law wouldn’t allow donating a large “part of an estate” to a candidate’s campaign—only limited individual contributions are permitted.

claim: Cases of coronavirus in the United States are linked to the rollout of 5G, the fifth-generation wireless technology.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no scientific evidence linking 5G to COVID-19. Viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks; SARS‑CoV‑2 spreads via respiratory droplets/aerosols from infected people. COVID-19 outbreaks occurred widely in places without any 5G service, and 5G uses non-ionizing radio frequency energy that cannot create or transmit a virus or impair immunity at environmental levels. Organizations like WHO and CDC have explicitly debunked this myth.

claim: Kenny Rogers' wife donate half of the singer's estate to Trump's re-election
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated on a satirical/hoax site (part of the “America’s Last Line of Defense” network) after Kenny Rogers died in March 2020. There are no credible reports or FEC records showing such a donation, and U.S. campaign finance law wouldn’t allow an individual to give “half an estate” to a candidate’s campaign.

claim: American automakers, including Ford and General Motors, are manufacturing much needed medical ventilators “right now.”
response_text: FALSE.  Context: When this claim was made in late March 2020, Ford and GM were not yet producing ventilators. They were retooling and arranging partnerships (GM with Ventec; Ford with GE). GM’s ventilator production in Kokomo, IN began in mid-April 2020 under a federal contract, and Ford’s started around April 20, 2020. So “right now” was inaccurate at the time.

claim: LeBron James has said Duterte is "better" than Trump in handling the COVID-19 crisis.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible record of LeBron James saying Duterte is “better” than Trump in handling COVID-19. The quote originated from social media graphics/posts and has been debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., AFP Philippines). James has criticized Trump publicly, but there’s no verified statement from him comparing Trump to Duterte on COVID-19.

claim: President Donald Trump said, “Nobody knew there’d be a pandemic or an epidemic of this proportion.” at a White House briefing on March 19 2020
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During the White House Coronavirus Task Force press briefing on March 19, 2020, President Trump said, “Nobody knew there’d be a pandemic or an epidemic of this proportion.” This wording appears in the official White House transcript and was reported by multiple outlets.

claim: MPs in the UK have awarded themselves a £10,000 bonus to cover ‘expenses’ during the Covid-19 crisis.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: MPs did not “award themselves” a £10,000 bonus. The independent expenses watchdog (IPSA) temporarily allowed an increase of up to £10,000 in MPs’ office costs budgets during Covid-19 to cover things like IT and home‑working equipment for MPs’ offices. It was not an automatic personal payment, not a bonus, and claims had to be itemised and justified.

claim: Chloroquine, a Covid-19 drug, would be made available 'almost immediately.'
response_text: FALSE.  At the time this was said (March 2020), chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine were not approved COVID-19 treatments, and the FDA had not authorized immediate availability. A limited emergency use authorization came more than a week later (March 28, 2020) for hospitalized patients and was revoked in June 2020 after evidence showed no benefit—so it was neither a proven “COVID-19 drug” nor made available “almost immediately.”

claim: Several First Nations communities in Canada have closed their borders to avoid COVID-19
response_text: TRUE.  Several First Nations in Canada imposed entry restrictions, road checkpoints, and closures to non-residents during COVID-19 to protect their communities. Examples include Mohawk communities like Kahnawake and Kanesatake (Quebec), Tla-o-qui-aht and Ahousaht (B.C.), Six Nations of the Grand River (Ontario), and Peguis First Nation (Manitoba), among others. These measures were widely reported in 2020 as efforts to keep the virus out of vulnerable communities.

claim: Historic flu and other outbreaks are accurately named based on the country where they originated
response_text: FALSE.  Many disease names with places are misnomers or reflect where they were first reported, not where they originated. Examples: the 1918 “Spanish flu” likely didn’t start in Spain (Spain just reported it openly during WWI); “German measles” (rubella) didn’t originate in Germany; the 1968 “Hong Kong flu” was first detected there but likely emerged in mainland China. WHO now advises against using geographic names because they’re often inaccurate and stigmatizing.

claim: Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte approved the release of P20,000 (USD $400) to all recipients of the Philippines’ Social Security System (SSS) to help them through the novel coronavirus pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no Duterte-approved P20,000 cash grant to all SSS recipients during the COVID‑19 pandemic. What existed were: - DSWD’s Social Amelioration Program (5,000–8,000 pesos per month for two months) for low‑income families, not tied to SSS. - SSS programs like the Calamity Loan (up to 20,000 pesos, but a loan, not a grant) and unemployment benefits for eligible members—not a universal payout to all SSS pensioners/recipients.  SSS and government agencies also publicly denied viral posts claiming a P20,000 SSS cash release.

claim: Clapping hands  Kills Corona virus
response_text: FALSE.  Clapping your hands does not kill SARS‑CoV‑2. Inactivating the virus requires effective measures like washing with soap (which disrupts the virus’s lipid envelope), using alcohol-based hand sanitizer (≥60% alcohol), disinfectants like bleach, UV-C light, or sufficient heat—not the brief friction or air movement from clapping. Clapping could even spread germs if hands are contaminated.

claim: Italy did not close its borders from travellers from China during the coronavirus pandemic
response_text: FALSE.  Italy suspended all flights to and from China on 31 January 2020, and from mid‑March 2020 the EU’s external border closure to non‑essential travel (implemented by Italy) effectively barred most travelers from China. Note: Italy did not impose a permanent, China‑specific entry ban, and early on travelers could still arrive via third countries.

claim: temples ring bells “not only to bring the disciples into prayer mode but also to kill viruses and bacteria surrounding the temple.
response_text: FALSE.  While bells are traditionally used to call worshippers and mark ritual moments, there is no scientific evidence that ringing temple bells kills viruses or bacteria in the surrounding air. Audible bell sound (hundreds–thousands of Hz at typical sound levels) lacks the intensity and mechanisms needed to disinfect. Pathogen inactivation by sound generally requires high‑intensity ultrasound in liquids (via cavitation), not audible ringing in open air. Effective disinfection methods include UV light, heat, chemical disinfectants, and filtration—not bell ringing. Uncertainty: none.

claim: Chloroquine, a Covid-19 drug was almost ready to be used on March 19 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  On March 19, 2020, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine were not approved for COVID-19; the FDA said they were being studied, despite public claims to the contrary. An Emergency Use Authorization to allow limited hospital use from the U.S. stockpile wasn’t issued until March 28, 2020, and it was later revoked on June 15, 2020 after evidence showed no benefit and potential harms. Off‑label prescribing by some doctors did not make it an approved or “almost ready” COVID-19 drug.

claim: F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote a letter in the 1920 Spanish Influenza pandemic, in which he wrote to someone named “Rosemary” in which he wrote: “Even the bars, as I told Hemingway, but to that he punched me in the stomach, to which I asked if he had washed his hands,” the alleged letter says. “He hadn’t. He is much the denier, that one. Why, he considers the virus to be just influenza.”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - The passage comes from a 2020 satire/parody piece (widely circulated from McSweeney’s), not an authentic Fitzgerald letter. - It mentions Hemingway in 1920; Fitzgerald didn’t meet Hemingway until 1925. - “Rosemary” is a fictional character (Rosemary Hoyt) from Fitzgerald’s 1934 novel Tender Is the Night, not someone he’d be writing to in 1920. - No credible archival source contains this “letter.”

claim: US President Donald Trump referred to the novel Coronavirus pandemic as a time when "people are dying that have never died before."
response_text: FALSE.  No credible transcript or video shows Trump saying this. Fact-checkers have traced the line “People are dying who have never died before” to much earlier, often as a humorous tautology variously misattributed to figures like James Michael Curley or Will Rogers. It was circulated as a meme during COVID but not actually said by Trump.

claim: Passport of the passengers arriving at the T3 Of Delhi airport was taken away and kept till COVID-19 tests were completed, resulting in chaos at the airport on 18th March, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Official clarifications from Delhi Airport/MoCA/PIB around March 18–19, 2020 stated that passports were not being seized or held until COVID-19 tests were completed. At that time universal on‑arrival testing was not in place; passengers underwent immigration, health screening and formality checks, which caused crowding. Passports were handled for routine immigration and returned, not kept pending test results.

claim: Novel coronavirus could live up to 3 days, depending on the surface.
response_text: TRUE.  Lab studies (e.g., NEJM 2020) found viable SARS‑CoV‑2 detectable for up to about 72 hours (3 days) on plastic and stainless steel, shorter on cardboard (~24 hours) and copper (~4 hours). Real‑world survival and transmission from surfaces are typically lower; viability declines over time and depends on conditions.

claim: Gargling with warm salt water or warm vinegar water will cure you from Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that gargling with salt water or vinegar cures COVID-19. Gargling may temporarily soothe a sore throat, but it does not eliminate the virus or prevent disease progression. Health authorities (e.g., WHO, CDC) have debunked this myth. Effective measures include vaccination, masking/ventilation, and, if ill and eligible, evidence-based treatments such as authorized antivirals under medical guidance.

claim: Chennai municipal corporation has shut all vegetable and fruit markets in the city due to coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: During COVID-19, the Greater Chennai Corporation did not shut all fruit and vegetable markets citywide. It closed specific high‑risk markets (notably the Koyambedu wholesale complex) and relocated/regulated operations, while allowing retail sales and temporary/mobile markets with restrictions. The blanket claim that all such markets were shut is inaccurate.

claim: The Australian state of Western Australia has recently passed a “COVID-19 Emergency Powers Act” that authorises forcible medical examination and vaccination in schools.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no Western Australian law called the “COVID-19 Emergency Powers Act.”   - WA’s coercive public‑health powers come mainly from the Public Health Act 2016 and the Emergency Management Act 2005, both pre‑COVID.   - A 2022 amendment created temporary COVID-19 declaration powers but did not newly authorise forced vaccination, nor did it target schools.   - While the 2016 Public Health Act allows, in a declared public health emergency, orders for medical examination/treatment (and enforcement in limited circumstances), this is not a recent COVID‑specific law and is not school‑specific.  Note: Some confusion stems from misreading the pre‑existing Public Health Act as a new, school-focused COVID law.

claim: Covid-19 is very similar to the seasonal flu with U.S mortality rates just above 0.1 percent and students are being punished and academies easily incapacitated by the common cold.
response_text: FALSE.  - COVID-19 has been far deadlier than seasonal flu in the U.S. Over 1.1 million COVID deaths vs tens of thousands in a typical flu season. Early-pandemic infection fatality rates were around 0.5–1% (much higher than 0.1%), and even with vaccines/Omicron the per-infection risk and hospitalizations have generally remained above influenza, especially for older adults. - COVID-19 is not “the common cold”; it’s caused by SARS‑CoV‑2 and has caused widespread severe illness. School disruptions were due to COVID-19 mitigation, not incapacitation by ordinary colds.

claim: US President Donald Trump failed to make timely use of his powers under the Defense Production Act to compel companies to manufacture medical supplies that were expected to be needed to treat those infected with the novel coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: While Trump invoked the Defense Production Act on March 18, 2020, he initially said he would not use it to compel production, calling it a “backup.” The first order actually compelling a company was not issued until March 27 (to General Motors for ventilators), with additional orders (e.g., to 3M for N95 masks) in early April. This came after weeks of mounting shortages and pleas from states and hospitals, so the use of DPA authority to compel production was delayed. Note: “Timely” is somewhat subjective, but the timeline supports the claim.

claim: The World Health Organization's director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, overstated the COVID-19 fatality rate.
response_text: FALSE.  Tedros cited about 3.4% as the share of reported (confirmed) COVID‑19 cases that had died in early March 2020—a case fatality ratio that matched the data at the time. He was not claiming an infection fatality rate across all infections (including undetected mild/asymptomatic cases), which was later estimated to be lower. Data evolved, but his statement was accurate in context, not an overstatement.

claim: A recent survey found that Filipinos have rated President Rodrigo Duterte as the most loving, caring, solid and decisive among the five highest government officials in the Philippines.
response_text: FALSE.  No reputable pollster (SWS, Pulse Asia, OCTA, or Publicus Asia) has published a survey ranking the “five highest government officials” by traits like “loving, caring, solid, and decisive.” These firms track approval, trust, and satisfaction—not such adjectives. Similar graphics/posts attributing those trait rankings to SWS have been debunked; there’s no record of such a survey.

claim: There are people going door to door in Colorado Spring who are stating they are testing for Covid-19 so they can rob people
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: In March 2020, Colorado Springs/El Paso County law enforcement and local media addressed this rumor and said they had no reports of people going door to door claiming to do COVID-19 tests in order to rob residents. It circulated on social media but lacked credible evidence in Colorado Springs. (Uncertainty: similar scams were reported or warned about elsewhere, but not confirmed in Colorado Springs.)

claim: No city in the state can quarantine itself without state approval.
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: In states like Georgia, quarantine and isolation powers are reserved to the state (e.g., the Department of Public Health under O.C.G.A. § 31-12-4). Cities cannot unilaterally “quarantine themselves” without state authorization. Note: Authority can vary by state, but the claim matches Georgia law.

claim: Exposing ourselves to the sun or to high temperatures kills the Covid-19 virus
response_text: FALSE.  Sunlight or hot weather does not kill the virus inside your body or prevent COVID-19. WHO and CDC state that you can catch COVID-19 in sunny or hot climates, and hot baths/saunas don’t cure it. While high heat or UV can inactivate the virus on surfaces under controlled conditions, normal sun exposure or ambient heat isn’t sufficient to protect you.

claim: Japan has produced a cure for coronavirus disease (COVID-19).
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: As of 2025, no country, including Japan, has produced a definitive “cure” for COVID-19. Japan-based companies developed treatments such as favipiravir (Avigan) and ensitrelvir (Xocova), which can reduce viral load and symptoms when taken early, but these are treatments—not cures—and do not eradicate COVID-19 universally. Health authorities do not recognize any cure.

claim: The United Stated had 27 deaths from covid19 between January 22nd 2020 and march 17 2020
response_text: FALSE.  By March 17, 2020, the U.S. had well over 27 reported COVID-19 deaths—variously tallied at around 110–120 by trackers (e.g., Johns Hopkins/NYT). In fact, the U.S. surpassed 27 deaths by about March 9. Counts vary slightly by source and time of day, but all are far above 27.

claim: A 103-year-old Chinese grandmother has made a full recovery from Covid-19 after being treated for 6 days in Wuhan, China
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reports in March 2020 (e.g., Chinese state media and international outlets) stated that a 103-year-old woman in Wuhan, named Zhang Guangfen, tested negative and was discharged after six days of treatment for Covid-19. “Full recovery” reflects how outlets described her discharge and negative tests.

claim: Donald Trump tweeted that the US Treasury will check a recipients social media accounts for any anti President Trump comments before being considered for a covid19 stimulus cheque.
response_text: FALSE.  No such tweet exists. Images of a “Trump tweet” about checking recipients’ social media were fabricated. Eligibility for COVID-19 stimulus payments was determined by IRS tax data and statutory criteria, not by reviewing people’s social media or political views. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Snopes, PolitiFact) found no record of the tweet or any such policy.

claim: President Donald Trump always knew that the Coronavirus was a pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump did not consistently treat or describe COVID-19 as a pandemic. Through Jan–Feb 2020 he repeatedly downplayed it—e.g., “We have it totally under control” (Jan 22), “the 15 cases… will be close to zero” (Feb 26), “It’s going to disappear” (Feb 27), and comparisons to the flu (Mar 9). He only called it a pandemic after the WHO’s March 11 declaration, later saying on March 17, “I felt it was a pandemic long before it was called one,” which is contradicted by his earlier public statements.

claim: Marriott International effectively denied employees unemployment and health benefits by saying the company had not laid them off, instead putting them on a zero-hour schedule?
response_text: FALSE.  - In March 2020 Marriott furloughed tens of thousands of workers and publicly said furloughed (zero-hours) employees could apply for unemployment benefits; in most U.S. states, zero hours qualifies for unemployment. - Marriott also announced it would continue health benefits for enrolled furloughed employees for a period (e.g., through early summer 2020), rather than cutting them off immediately. - While some workers at specific properties reported issues, the broad claim that Marriott “denied” unemployment and health benefits by using zero-hour schedules is not supported by the company’s stated policies and widespread reporting.

claim: Doctors in India have been successful in treating Coronavirus using combination of drugs used: Lopinavir, Retonovir, Oseltamivir along with Chlorphenamine. They are going to suggest same medicine, globally
response_text: FALSE.  Rationale: Early in 2020, some Indian clinicians tried lopinavir/ritonavir experimentally in isolated cases, but authorities (ICMR/PIB Fact Check) explicitly said there was no proven cure and no such combination was being recommended. Oseltamivir (a flu drug) and chlorpheniramine (an antihistamine) are not effective treatments for COVID‑19. Large trials later showed lopinavir/ritonavir does not improve outcomes, and no global body recommended this combination.

claim: Cleveland Clinic developed a Covid-19 test that gives results in hours, not days.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In March 2020, Cleveland Clinic announced it had developed and validated an in-house PCR test for SARS‑CoV‑2 that could return results within hours (about eight hours), compared with multi‑day turnarounds from external labs at the time.

claim: China has closed down its last makeshift coronavirus hospital in Wuhan as there is not enough new cases to support them.
response_text: TRUE.  In March 2020, Wuhan closed the last of its 16 makeshift “Fangcang” coronavirus hospitals after discharging the remaining patients, as new infections and active caseloads had dropped sharply. This was widely reported by outlets such as Reuters, BBC, and China’s Xinhua.

claim: stated on March 17, 2020 in a Facebook post: All US citizens are entitled to $700 per week to stay at home to avoid the spread of COVID-19 novel coronavirus, starting from March 17 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  No U.S. program in March 2020 entitled all citizens to $700 per week to stay home. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act (signed March 18) required certain employers to provide limited paid sick leave, not a universal stipend. The CARES Act (March 27) later provided a one-time stimulus payment and a $600/week unemployment supplement for eligible jobless workers—not $700/week for all citizens. The claim predates these laws and misstates their provisions.

claim: The United States has had 4700 deaths from Flu between January 22nd 2020 and march 17 2020
response_text: FALSE  Reason: CDC’s preliminary burden estimates for the 2019–2020 U.S. flu season indicated roughly 22,000 influenza deaths by early March 2020 (cumulative since Oct 1). The period Jan 22–Mar 17 spans peak flu weeks and would account for many thousands of deaths—well above 4,700. Also, CDC reports seasonal estimates, not exact counts for that specific date window. Uncertainty: CDC figures are estimates, but they clearly exceed 4,700 for that timeframe.

claim: A charitable hospital in Pakistan charged patients for novel coronavirus tests
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In early 2020, Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital & Research Centre in Lahore—a charitable, not‑for‑profit hospital—offered COVID‑19 PCR testing and charged patients around PKR 8,000–9,000 per test to cover costs, while providing financial assistance/free testing for those unable to pay. This was acknowledged by the hospital and reported in Pakistani media.

claim: An Illinois News Station Air ‘Pre-Rigged Election Results’ The Day Before The Primary.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A Chicago TV station (Fox 32) accidentally aired test election graphics the day before the 2018 Illinois primary while preparing its systems. The station explained they were routine placeholders from a vendor/AP feed, not real results. The figures didn’t match the actual election outcomes. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) confirmed it was a testing error, not “pre‑rigged” results.

claim: All U.S. Citizens were entitled to $700 per week to stay at home to avoid the spread of Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no universal $700/week payment for all U.S. citizens to stay home. During COVID-19, eligible unemployed workers received a federal supplement to unemployment insurance—$600/week (Mar–Jul 2020), later $300/week for certain periods—not $700, and not for everyone. Separate stimulus checks were one-time payments, not weekly.

claim: Now, as it stands, The US health care system has adequate ventilators, ICU beds, medical professionals
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: While the U.S. has ample ventilators since the COVID-19 ramp-up, adequacy of ICU beds is often limited by staffing rather than physical beds, and there are widespread, ongoing shortages of medical professionals (especially nurses, behavioral health, and primary care physicians). Capacity and staffing vary by region, and many systems report persistent workforce shortfalls, making the blanket claim of adequacy incorrect. (Some uncertainty due to regional differences and changing conditions.)

claim: Disposable masks should be worn white-side-out to keep COVID-19 out
response_text: FALSE.  Disposable surgical masks are designed with the colored side (often blue/green) facing out and the white side facing in. The outer layer is fluid-repellent to block droplets; the inner white layer is absorbent to capture moisture from your breath. Wearing it white-side-out is incorrect and can reduce effectiveness. If a mask has no color, follow the manufacturer’s markings and ensure the nose clip is on top.

claim: United Emirates have completed mass arrests of their Royal Family and affiliates.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports from reputable international or Emirati sources of mass arrests of the UAE’s ruling families or their affiliates. This appears to conflate with Saudi Arabia’s 2017 anti-corruption roundup of princes; nothing comparable has occurred in the United Arab Emirates. The phrasing “United Emirates” is also incorrect, suggesting a dubious source. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Bernie sanders has nine super PACs.
response_text: FALSE.  Candidates do not “have” super PACs—by law super PACs are independent and cannot be controlled or coordinated by a candidate. Bernie Sanders has long campaigned against super PACs and did not run with one. While a few outside groups made independent expenditures supporting him, there is no evidence of anything like “nine super PACs” belonging to or run by Sanders. (Uncertainty: exact count of outside groups varies by cycle, but the claim’s premise and number are inaccurate.)

claim: "I went out and campaigned for (raising the minimum wage) … $15 an hour in New York City. Go talk to the governor."
response_text: FALSE.  She publicly supported a $15 minimum wage in high-cost places like New York City, but fact-checkers found little evidence she “went out and campaigned” for it. Her documented actions were statements, tweets, and general support while advocating a $12 federal minimum, with $15 left to states/cities. New York’s $15 push was led by Gov. Cuomo and unions; claims that she actively campaigned for it are overstated. (Some uncertainty: she occasionally appeared at related events and voiced support.)

claim: The lab-created coronavirus was a cover-up for the mass mandatory vaccination agenda.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no credible evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 was engineered in a lab. Genetic analyses found no signatures of manipulation, and U.S. and international assessments have not concluded it was lab‑created; the leading scientific view remains a natural (zoonotic) origin, with a lab‑related accident considered a separate, unproven possibility. - There is also no evidence of a global “mandatory vaccination agenda.” COVID‑19 vaccines were developed in response to a deadly pandemic. Some jurisdictions implemented limited mandates (e.g., for certain workplaces), but there was no worldwide, preplanned compulsory program being “covered up.”  Uncertainty: The precise origin of the virus remains unresolved, but nothing supports the claim’s engineered‑virus and cover‑up narrative.

claim: Italy's airports have been completely shut down.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence of a nationwide, total shutdown of all Italian airports. Italy occasionally sees localized closures or major disruptions (e.g., strikes, weather, volcanic ash affecting specific airports), but major hubs like Rome Fiumicino and Milan Malpensa remain operational. If this refers to a specific incident, it appears overstated.

claim: "You have been on the floor of the Senate time and time again talking about the need to cut Social Security, Medicare and veterans' programs."
The US has a lack of medical personnel and hospitals may not have the capacity to deal with hundreds of thousands of people at the peak of the coronavirus pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence from multiple surges (2020–2022) shows widespread staffing shortages and capacity strain. U.S. COVID-19 hospitalizations peaked at roughly 137,000 (Jan 2021) and about 159,000 (Jan 2022), filling ICUs in many regions. States declared crisis standards of care (e.g., Idaho, Alaska), elective surgeries were canceled, field hospitals opened (e.g., NYC Javits Center), and FEMA/National Guard staff were deployed. This demonstrates both a shortage of medical personnel and that hospitals often lacked capacity to handle the surge volumes.

claim: Cristiano Ronaldo is turning his CR7 hotels into hospitals for people with coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a widely shared March 2020 rumor, but Ronaldo’s management and the Pestana CR7 hotel group denied it. No hotels were converted to hospitals; outlets like Reuters and Snopes debunked the claim.

claim: Tom Hanks was arrested for paedophilia on 13/03/2020   in Australia, where he is  being kept in a hotel room, refusing to fly back to USA.
response_text: FALSE.  Tom Hanks was not arrested in Australia. He and Rita Wilson tested positive for COVID-19 in Queensland in March 2020 while he was filming, were isolated (first in hospital, then in quarantine), and later returned to the U.S. Australian authorities reported no arrest, and reputable outlets (e.g., Reuters/AP/Snopes) debunked the pedophilia-arrest rumor.

claim: Canadian prime minster Justin Trudeau was served a criminal indictment by the U.S. for corporate and financial crimes.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record on U.S. Department of Justice announcements or federal court dockets of any indictment of Justin Trudeau. Viral claims about the U.S. “indicting” or “arresting” Trudeau have been repeatedly debunked and trace to disinformation sites (e.g., Real Raw News). Moreover, indicting a sitting foreign head of government in the U.S. would face serious jurisdiction and immunity barriers and would be major, widely reported news—none of which exists.

claim: "I have been consistent (on the Hyde Amendment). I have always believed in that."
response_text: FALSE.  Joe Biden long supported the Hyde Amendment in the Senate and as vice president, then in June 2019 reversed and said he opposes it and favors repealing it. That shift means he has not been consistent or “always” believed in it. (If the quote refers to another Democrat like Tim Kaine, he also shifted positions in 2016.) Uncertainty: the speaker isn’t specified, but the claim is still false for prominent figures who have made it.

claim: Australia's Prime Minister Scott Morrison was served a criminal indictment by the US for corporate & financial crimes.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record or credible reporting that Scott Morrison was ever indicted by the U.S. for corporate or financial crimes. Such an action would be publicly documented by the U.S. Department of Justice and widely covered by major media; none exists. The claim traces to debunked conspiracy rumors.

claim: Every household in the United States receiving $500 in emergency food stamps and a $1,000 stimulus check
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no nationwide program giving every household $500 in emergency SNAP. SNAP emergency allotments during COVID-19 increased benefits to the maximum for household size (not a flat $500) and ended in most states by March 2023; SNAP is only for eligible low‑income households.  - Federal “stimulus checks” were the 2020–2021 Economic Impact Payments of $1,200, $600, and $1,400, subject to income/eligibility rules—not a universal $1,000 to every household.

claim: Novel coronavirus can be eliminated by drinking lots of water and gargling with warm water mixed with salt or vinegar.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that drinking lots of water or gargling with warm salt water or vinegar eliminates or prevents COVID-19. Hydration is healthy, and saline gargles can soothe a sore throat, but they don’t kill the virus or stop infection in the respiratory tract. Health agencies (WHO/CDC) have debunked this myth; proven measures include vaccination, masking in high-risk settings, hand hygiene, and good ventilation.

claim: An Italian company threatened to sue two men for 3D printing valves for a respiratory device.
response_text: FALSE.  Early reports in March 2020 claimed a manufacturer threatened legal action against Italian volunteers who 3D‑printed Venturi valves for hospital respiratory devices. However, both the volunteers (Isinnova) and the manufacturer (Intersurgical) said no lawsuit or threat was made. The company declined to share design files due to regulatory/safety reasons, not to threaten litigation. Multiple fact-checks (e.g., BBC, PolitiFact, Snopes) found no evidence of a legal threat.

claim: Harvard University admitted that the degrees held by former first lady Michelle Obama are fakes
response_text: FALSE.  Michelle Obama earned a J.D. from Harvard Law School (1988) and a B.A. from Princeton University (1985). There is no record or credible report of Harvard University stating her degrees are fake. This claim appears to be a hoax circulated by misinformation/satire sites.

claim: A story published by Tomas Pueyo about the grave threat posed by the new coronavirus overstated the threat.
response_text: FALSE.  Pueyo’s viral 2020 Medium pieces (“Coronavirus: Why You Must Act Now,” “The Hammer and the Dance”) warned of rapid spread and hospital overload without swift measures. Subsequent events—global surges, overwhelmed health systems in multiple regions, and millions of deaths—broadly validated the gravity he described. Fact-checkers at the time challenged misstatements about his credentials, not that he had overstated the threat. Uncertainty: “overstated” is subjective, but outcomes showed the threat was at least as severe as he warned.

claim: Gargling warm water with salt or vinegar can eliminate the novel coronavirus, COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Gargling with warm salt water or vinegar does not eliminate or cure COVID-19. It may temporarily soothe a sore throat, but it doesn’t reach or stop the virus replicating in the respiratory tract. WHO and CDC have stated there’s no evidence that saline or vinegar gargles prevent or treat COVID-19; effective measures include vaccination, masks, ventilation, and approved treatments.

claim: The Tokyo Olympics logo has been redesigned in the wake of the coronavirus outbreak.
response_text: FALSE.  The Tokyo 2020 emblem was redesigned in 2015 after plagiarism allegations, not because of COVID-19. Despite the pandemic and the Games’ postponement to 2021, organizers kept the existing “Tokyo 2020” logo unchanged.

claim: A Dallas student celebrating Spring Break on South Padre Island collapsed from symptoms resembling coronavirus in March 2020
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There’s no credible news or official report from March 2020 confirming that a Dallas student on South Padre Island collapsed with coronavirus-like symptoms. Contemporary coverage of SPI spring break incidents did not document such a case; similar claims circulated as rumors without verification. Uncertainty: possible confusion with other spring break COVID stories (e.g., Miami or UT Austin Cabo trip).

claim: Donald Trump cut funding to the CDC.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump repeatedly proposed cuts to CDC budgets in his annual requests, but Congress did not enact them. In practice, CDC’s appropriated funding stayed roughly level or increased during his term, and it rose substantially with COVID-19 emergency supplements. (Some specific programs faced proposed reductions or expired funds, but overall CDC funding was not cut.)

claim: The H1N1 response "was one of the worst on record. Our response is one of the best, with fast action of border closings & a 78% Approval Rating, the highest on record. His was lowest!"
response_text: FALSE.  - H1N1 response: Public health emergency was declared early (April 2009); while vaccine supply lagged, experts generally did not deem the federal response “one of the worst.” Polls at the time showed majority approval of Obama’s handling. - COVID response: The U.S. did not “close the borders”; it imposed partial travel restrictions (e.g., on non‑citizens from China) after community spread had begun. Overall U.S. outcomes (very high deaths among wealthy nations) and widespread critiques undercut “one of the best.” - Approval ratings: No reputable poll showed a 78% approval for Trump’s handling of COVID. Early 2020 polls typically put it around the mid‑40s to mid‑50s. Obama’s H1N1 handling was not the “lowest”; polls showed majority approval.

claim: "Biden was in charge of the H1N1 Swine Flu epidemic which killed thousands of people."
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: H1N1 (2009–2010) did kill thousands (CDC estimates about 12,000 deaths in the U.S.), but Joe Biden was not “in charge” of the response. As Vice President he wasn’t appointed to lead it; the response was led by HHS (Secretary Kathleen Sebelius) and the CDC, with DHS (Secretary Janet Napolitano) coordinating early on.

claim: COVID-19 came to the United States in 2019.
response_text: Mostly TRUE (with some uncertainty).  - The first confirmed U.S. case was identified in January 2020. - However, CDC testing of archived Red Cross blood donations found SARS‑CoV‑2 antibodies in samples collected in mid‑December 2019, suggesting the virus was already present in the U.S. by late 2019.  - While not definitive, the evidence indicates COVID‑19 likely arrived in the U.S. in 2019.

claim: Hand-washing with an ordinary soap protects against COVID-19.
response_text: TRUE.  Ordinary soap effectively inactivates SARS‑CoV‑2 by disrupting its lipid envelope and helps remove it from hands. Washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds reduces the risk of COVID‑19 transmission. It’s protective but not sufficient alone; other measures (e.g., vaccination, masks, ventilation) also matter.

claim: There is no vaccine for tuberculosis.
response_text: FALSE. The Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccine has existed for over a century and is used in many countries. It protects well against severe forms of TB in children, though its effectiveness against adult pulmonary TB is variable.

claim: In South Florida “all children and adults must remain in their homes” due to coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  South Florida counties issued “safer at home”/stay‑at‑home orders during COVID-19, but these allowed exceptions (e.g., essential work, groceries, medical care, exercise). It was not a total order requiring all children and adults to remain at home at all times.

claim: Donald Trump called the COVID-19 outbreak a hoax by the democrats.
response_text: FALSE.  At a Feb. 28, 2020 rally in South Carolina, Trump said Democrats were “politicizing the coronavirus” and called that “their new hoax.” Fact-checkers widely concluded he was labeling Democrats’ criticism/politicization as a hoax, not the COVID-19 outbreak itself. He later clarified this point.

claim: Prime Minister Narendra Modi tweet that his endless joy turned into endless grief after Devendra Fadnavis resigned as chief minister of Maharashtra on Tuesday
response_text: FALSE.  After Devendra Fadnavis resigned on Tuesday, 26 November 2019, PM Narendra Modi’s public tweets praised Fadnavis’s tenure and hard work; he did not tweet that his “endless joy turned into endless grief.” No credible record of such a quote exists in his official accounts or reputable coverage.

claim: President Donald Trump refused World Health Organization (WHO) tests.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The WHO did not offer COVID-19 test kits to the United States; the CDC developed its own test, which is standard practice for countries with their own public health capacity. There’s no evidence the Trump administration “refused” an offered WHO test, though the U.S. did not adopt the WHO/German protocol. (Multiple fact-checks: AP, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org.)

claim: Pandemics are cyclical and occur every 100 years
response_text: FALSE.  Pandemics do not follow a fixed 100-year cycle. Historical records show irregular timing: e.g., 1889–90 “Russian flu,” 1918 influenza, 1957–58 Asian flu, 1968 Hong Kong flu, HIV/AIDS (from the 1980s), 2009 H1N1, and COVID-19 (2019–20). Earlier pandemics (e.g., the Black Death in the 14th century, the Plague of Justinian in the 6th) also don’t align to 100-year intervals. The “every 100 years” idea is a myth based on selective examples.

claim: Ancient medical herb drink Ayurvedic treats Covid-19
response_text: FALSE.  No credible clinical evidence shows that Ayurvedic “herb drinks” treat or cure COVID‑19. Major health authorities (WHO, CDC, FDA) have not approved any Ayurvedic remedies for COVID‑19; effective treatments are evidenced antivirals and supportive care, and vaccines reduce severe disease risk. Some small or low‑quality studies exist but are not sufficient to claim efficacy. Uncertainty: the claim is vague about the specific drink, but broadly it’s unsupported.

claim: Australian Gold Coast hospital staff roll in a Wilson volleyball to keep actor Tom Hanks company in quarantine.
response_text: TRUE.  In March 2020, after Tom Hanks tested positive for COVID-19 and was isolated at Gold Coast University Hospital, Australian media reported that hospital staff delivered (reportedly “rolled”) a Wilson-branded volleyball to his room as a Cast Away reference to keep him company. Multiple reputable outlets covered the gesture.

claim: Some states are only getting 50 COVID-19 tests per day, and the Utah Jazz got 58.
response_text: TRUE.  - In mid-March 2020, Oklahoma health officials confirmed they tested 58 members of the Utah Jazz traveling party after Rudy Gobert’s positive test. - At the same time, due to shortages, many state public health labs could only process tens of tests per day; contemporaneous reports and APHL guidance noted capacities around 40–60 tests/day in some states.  Note: This reflected the rapidly evolving testing capacity in early March 2020.

claim: The places worst affected by Coronavirus cases are along the same Latitude 40° from left: France, Italy, Iran, Wuhan, South Korea, Japan, Seattle, Washington, New York.
response_text: FALSE.  Many of the cited locations are far from 40°N: - Wuhan ≈ 30.6°N - South Korea (Seoul/Daegu) ≈ 36–37°N - Iran’s main outbreaks (Qom/Tehran) ≈ 34–36°N - Seattle ≈ 47.6°N - Italy’s Lombardy ≈ 45°N; France (Paris) ≈ 49°N - Japan (Tokyo) ≈ 35.7°N  Only New York (~40.7°N) lies near 40°N. COVID-19 also spread widely at many other latitudes, so the claim is incorrect.

claim: Tom Hanks has a Wilson volleyball to keep him company while he’s quarantined.
response_text: TRUE. During his COVID-19 quarantine in Australia in March 2020, Tom Hanks shared a photo showing a “Wilson” volleyball (a nod to Cast Away) that had been given to him to keep him company. This was reported widely after his Instagram post.

claim: Republican Florida Rep. Ted Yoho said that black Americans should only get three-fifths of a vote.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2013 Rep. Ted Yoho discussed the historical Three-Fifths Compromise at a town hall, saying it limited slave states’ power. He did not say or advocate that modern Black Americans should have only three-fifths of a vote. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact) rated claims to that effect as false.

claim: Tom Hanks has passed away at 63
response_text: FALSE. Tom Hanks (born July 9, 1956) is alive. He is well past 63; there are no credible reports of his death.

claim: The first case of coronavirus in Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, had been declared as of March 11, 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: On March 11, 2020, the North Shore Health Department announced the first confirmed COVID-19 case in a Milwaukee County resident, marking the county’s first reported case by that date.

claim: The public thinks disruption caused by protests is “completely unacceptable” by a ratio of five to one.
response_text: TRUE.  UK polling (e.g., YouGov 2022–2023) on protest tactics finds roughly 55–65% say causing disruption to the public is “completely unacceptable,” while about 10–12% say it’s “completely acceptable” — about a 5:1 ratio. Exact figures vary by wording and tactic, but the claim matches the general polling pattern.

claim: University of Johannesburg student Phindile hacked the system and gave herself distinctions.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a satirical/fake-news post that went viral on South African social media. No credible reports or university statements substantiate that a University of Johannesburg student named Phindile hacked the system to award herself distinctions, and fact-checkers have debunked the story.

claim: Drinking water regularly will kill COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Drinking water helps you stay hydrated but does not kill SARS‑CoV‑2 or prevent COVID‑19. The virus infects cells in the respiratory tract; water cannot “wash it away” or sterilize the body. Proven protections include vaccination, masks, ventilation, and hand hygiene.

claim: Whole of Italy goes into quarantine, In Italy, people must stay home except for work or emergencies
response_text: TRUE. In March 2020 (effective March 10), Italy imposed a nationwide COVID-19 lockdown: residents were required to stay home and could leave only for work, health/emergencies, or essential needs, with self-certification for travel.

claim: A study published in the journal Antiviral Research claims that coronavirus was "genetically engineered for efficient spread in humans"
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - The often-cited Antiviral Research paper (Coutard et al., 2020) noted a furin-like cleavage site in the SARS‑CoV‑2 spike protein and discussed possible implications for infectivity, but it did not claim the virus was genetically engineered or designed for efficient human spread. - A separate preprint (not in Antiviral Research) early in 2020 speculated about unusual insertions and was later withdrawn; some media misreporting conflated these. Mainstream peer‑reviewed analyses (e.g., Nature Medicine, 2020) found no evidence of genetic engineering.

claim: Pennsylvania Governor Tom Wolf mandated closures for schools and workplaces to curb the spread of coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In March 2020, Gov. Tom Wolf ordered all Pennsylvania K–12 schools to close statewide and mandated that “non-life-sustaining” businesses shut their physical locations, actions taken explicitly to slow the spread of COVID-19.

claim: Harry Potter actor Daniel Radcliffe has tested positive for the novel coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  This rumor began with a fake BBC Breaking News Twitter account in March 2020 and was quickly debunked. Daniel Radcliffe’s representatives confirmed he had not tested positive, and multiple outlets reported it was a hoax.

claim: It took Barack Obama until October of 2009 to declare Swine Flu a National Health Emergency. It began in April of ’09 but Obama waited until 20,000 people in the US had been hospitalized & 1,000+ had died
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. declared a public health emergency for H1N1 on April 26, 2009 (by HHS, days after first cases).  - President Obama later declared a national emergency on October 24, 2009 to enable regulatory waivers for hospitals—this was a separate step, not the first emergency action. - CDC figures around late October did cite roughly 20,000 hospitalizations and 1,000+ deaths, but saying Obama “waited until then” to declare an emergency ignores the April public health emergency.

claim: Joe Biden mistook Idaho for Iowa in visit to Boise fundraiser.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports or transcripts show Biden mistaking Idaho for Iowa during his Boise visit. In September 2021 he was in Boise for a wildfire briefing (not a fundraiser) and correctly referred to Idaho. Fact-checkers have debunked viral posts claiming otherwise. (He has mixed up states on other occasions, e.g., Vermont/New Hampshire in 2019, which may fuel the rumor.)

claim: Congressional Democrats in the U.S. are planning to halt Social Security payments in 2024.
response_text: FALSE.  - Social Security benefits are mandatory spending paid from trust funds and continue automatically; they don’t rely on annual appropriations.   - No credible proposal from congressional Democrats in 2024 seeks to halt payments; Democratic leaders consistently pledge to protect/expand benefits.   - Payments would only be at risk in scenarios like a U.S. default or far-future trust fund depletion (projected in the 2030s), not due to a Democratic plan in 2024.

claim: Trade agreements like NAFTA and permanent normal trade relations with China, which forced American workers to compete against people making pennies an hour, has resulted in the loss of 160,000 jobs in Michigan.
response_text: FALSE  - Best-cited estimates (e.g., Economic Policy Institute) put Michigan’s job displacement from NAFTA at roughly 40,000–45,000 and from the China trade deficit since PNTR at about 80,000–110,000 (depending on the end year), totaling around 120,000–150,000—short of 160,000. - These figures are “jobs displaced,” not net job losses, and attributing them solely to the trade agreements is debated; other factors (technology, recessions, productivity) also played major roles.  Uncertainty: Different study windows and methodologies can nudge the total up or down, but solid sources don’t clearly support 160,000.

claim: 700,000 people died homeless on streets of England and Wales last year
response_text: FALSE.  ONS estimates show hundreds of deaths of homeless people in England and Wales each year (roughly 700–800 in recent years), not 700,000. Indeed, total deaths from all causes in England and Wales are around 600,000–700,000 annually, so 700,000 homeless deaths would be impossible. Note: figures vary by method/source, but they’re in the hundreds (or low thousands by some charities), not hundreds of thousands.

claim: The novel coronavirus has been found in crawfish in Mobile, Alabama.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports or public health confirmations that SARS‑CoV‑2 was found in crawfish in Mobile, Alabama. This rumor traces to hoax/satirical posts from early in the pandemic. Health agencies (CDC/FDA) have said there’s no evidence the virus infects or is transmitted via seafood or food products, and crustaceans are not known hosts for this respiratory virus.

claim: In Massachusetts, Biden’s vote exceeded exit polling by 15%. That’s statistically a huge red flag that fraud occurred
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible source shows a 15‑percentage‑point gap between Massachusetts’ certified 2020 results and the final state exit poll. Edison Research’s final, weighted exit polls are designed to align closely with official results; a miss that large would have been widely reported (it wasn’t). - Using raw/early exit-poll numbers to allege fraud is methodologically wrong. Exit polls have sampling and nonresponse biases and are reweighted as data come in; discrepancies are not evidence of fraud. Large exit‑poll vs. result gaps have occurred in past elections without fraud findings.

claim: Drinking water with lemon can prevent COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that drinking lemon water prevents COVID-19. While lemon provides vitamin C and hydration, these do not stop infection by SARS‑CoV‑2. Health authorities (WHO/CDC) recommend vaccination, well-fitting masks, ventilation, and hand hygiene for prevention. Lemon water can be part of a healthy diet but it won’t prevent COVID-19.

claim: Mexico does not have any cases of the novel coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Mexico confirmed its first COVID-19 cases on February 28, 2020, and has had many cases since. Without a specific early-2020 date, the claim is not accurate.

claim: COLLOIDAL SILVER KILLS CORONAVIRUS
response_text: FALSE. There’s no credible evidence that colloidal silver prevents or treats COVID-19 or “kills coronavirus” in people. FDA/FTC and CDC have warned against such claims; products are unproven and can cause harm (e.g., argyria, kidney/neurologic toxicity). Lab studies on certain silver nanoparticles don’t translate to safe, effective human treatment.

claim: Extensive research by Saint Luke’s Hospital of Kansas City in the U.S revealed that consuming alcoholic beverages may help reduce the risk of COVID-19 infection, and that vodka is most recommended for drinking, cleaning and sanitizing.
response_text: FALSE.  No such research or recommendation exists. Saint Luke’s Hospital of Kansas City publicly denied issuing this advice. Health authorities (WHO/CDC) state that drinking alcohol does not prevent COVID-19 and can be harmful. For sanitizing, solutions need about 60–70% alcohol; typical vodka is ~40% and is not recommended as a disinfectant.

claim: Tweets circulated from a twitter handle @dilawarshaik (with a Jazeera Correspondent profile Twitter account), giving an Anti-Hindu remark & screenshots of a tweet calling for "butchering Hindus" is not associated with Al Jazeera or The Wire
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple fact-checks found that the Twitter handle @dilawarshaik, which styled itself as an “Al Jazeera correspondent” (and was also linked online to The Wire), was an impersonator account. Neither Al Jazeera nor The Wire has (or had) a journalist by that name; both organizations publicly denied any association. The inflammatory “butchering Hindus” tweet screenshots circulated were from this fake account, which was later suspended/deleted. Uncertainty: low, based on consistent denials and lack of any bylines or staff records.

claim: Anybody that needs a COVID-19 test can have a test. They are all set. They have them out there.
response_text: FALSE.  When this claim was made (early March 2020), COVID-19 testing in the U.S. was severely limited. Labs lacked enough kits, swabs, and reagents; strict criteria restricted testing to high-risk or symptomatic patients; many people seeking tests were turned away. The claim overstated availability.

claim: As of 6th March 2020 there is no coronavirus testing kit shortage in the United States, nor has there ever been prior to this date.
response_text: FALSE.  By early March 2020 the U.S. faced significant shortages and constraints in COVID-19 testing. CDC’s initial test kits sent to state labs in February were faulty, forcing most testing to be centralized and severely limiting capacity. As of March 6, many states and hospitals were still rationing tests due to limited kits and reagents, and federal officials acknowledged there were not enough tests to meet demand.

claim: There have been no deaths from the novel coronavirus in South Africa (as of March 12, 2020)
response_text: TRUE.  As of March 12, 2020, South Africa had reported confirmed COVID-19 cases but no deaths. The country’s first COVID-19 death was reported later, on March 27, 2020.

claim: Bernard Sanders, United States senator is a communist.
response_text: FALSE.  Bernie (Bernard) Sanders identifies as a democratic socialist, not a communist. He supports a mixed, regulated market economy and liberal democratic institutions, and is not a member of any communist party.

claim: Kim Jong Un, Supreme Leader of North Korea, rejected calls from the Obama administration
response_text: TRUE.  During Obama’s presidency (2009–2017), after Kim Jong Un took power in 2011, North Korea repeatedly rejected U.S. calls to halt nuclear and missile activities, return to denuclearization talks, and release American detainees. Examples include public statements refusing denuclearization demands (e.g., after 2016 tests) and rebuffing or rescinding U.S. envoys in 2013–2014. Note: “calls” here refers to diplomatic appeals, not literal phone calls.

claim: Hunter Biden was unemployed when he joined the board of Burisma Holdings in 2014.
response_text: FALSE.  When Hunter Biden joined Burisma’s board in April 2014, he was not unemployed. He was a co-founder and managing partner at the investment firm Rosemont Seneca Partners and served as counsel at the law firm Boies Schiller Flexner LLP. This was noted in Burisma’s own announcement and contemporary reporting (e.g., New York Times).

claim: Hunter Biden left  China with a $1.5 billion for a fund.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence Hunter Biden “left China with $1.5 billion.” The $1.5 billion figure refers to an aspirational fundraising target for BHR Partners, a private equity firm formed in 2013 with Chinese and other partners. Hunter Biden did not receive $1.5 billion, and he did not hold an equity stake until 2017, when he acquired about 10%. Multiple fact-checks (Washington Post, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org) found no evidence China gave him or his fund $1.5 billion as a result of the 2013 trip.

claim: US illegal immigration numbers have been down for the past nine or 10 months.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The closest official proxy for “illegal immigration numbers” is CBP migrant encounters at the southwest border. Those did not fall for nine or 10 consecutive months. After a record high in Dec. 2023, encounters dropped in Jan. 2024, ticked up in Feb. and Mar., fell in late spring/early summer, and then rose again later in 2024. So there was no nine- or ten-month continuous decline. (If the claim meant “lower than the December peak,” several months were lower, but not in an unbroken nine- or ten-month streak.)

claim: The restrictions that Donald Trump placed on travel to and from China, saved a lot of lives, probably hundreds of thousands by early April 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Jan. 31, 2020 restrictions barred most non‑U.S. travelers recently in China but allowed many exemptions; tens of thousands still arrived from China afterward. - Genetic and epidemiologic studies show much of the U.S. outbreak—especially in New York—was seeded from Europe, which wasn’t restricted until mid‑March. - Modeling suggests such travel limits can delay spread by days to a couple of weeks, not avert it entirely. There’s no evidence they “saved hundreds of thousands” of lives by early April 2020; total U.S. COVID deaths by then were far below that figure.  Note: Exact counterfactual death estimates are uncertain, but available evidence does not support the claim.

claim: Trump closed the borders to China and other badly affected areas and closed them down very early against the advice of most people.
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. did not “close the borders” to China; on Jan. 31, 2020 it restricted entry of foreign nationals who had recently been in China, while allowing U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and others to continue entering with screening. Tens of thousands still arrived after the policy took effect. - Similar restrictions on other hard‑hit areas (e.g., Europe’s Schengen Area, UK/Ireland) were not imposed “very early” but in mid‑March, after substantial outbreaks; Iran was added Feb. 29 and Brazil in late May. - The China restrictions were not taken “against the advice of most people”; senior U.S. health officials (Azar, Redfield, Fauci) supported or recommended them, though WHO generally advised against travel bans.

claim: Children can’t get COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE. Children of all ages can be infected with SARS‑CoV‑2. They often have milder illness than adults but can still get sick, transmit the virus, and in some cases develop severe complications such as MIS-C or long COVID.

claim: We’ve gotten the highest poll numbers of anybody for handling a coronavirus outbreak.
response_text: FALSE.  Polling in March 2020 put approval of Trump’s COVID-19 handling around 50–60% (e.g., Gallup found 60%). That was below ratings for others’ handling of the outbreak—state governors (often 70–80%+), the CDC (~80%), and figures like Anthony Fauci (high 70s–80s). Some prior outbreak responses also polled higher than Trump’s. So it was not the “highest … of anybody.”

claim: HHS has designated the coronavirus test as an essential health benefit. That means, by definition, it's covered in the private health insurance of every American, as well as covered by Medicare and Medicaid.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: HHS/CMS guidance said COVID‑19 diagnostic testing falls within existing Essential Health Benefit categories for ACA‑compliant individual and small‑group plans. But EHB requirements do not apply to all private coverage (e.g., large‑group, self‑insured, grandfathered, and short‑term plans), so it was not “by definition” covered in the private insurance of every American. Medicare and Medicaid did cover COVID‑19 tests, but under their own program rules and later federal laws (FFCRA/CARES), not because of an EHB designation. Uncertainty: none significant.

claim: An employee of the Bojangles' fast food chicken restaurant placed a sign on a door banning customers who wear pro-Trump hats or shirts
response_text: FALSE.  A viral photo in 2016 showed a Bojangles’ door sign allegedly banning customers with pro‑Trump hats or shirts, but Bojangles’ corporate said no such policy existed and no employee or manager posted it. There’s no verified location or evidence beyond the circulated image, indicating it was a hoax or prank.

claim: Slowed Coronavirus testing was due to Obama-era regulations.
response_text: FALSE.  Delays stemmed mainly from a faulty CDC test kit and the FDA’s initial Emergency Use Authorization process, which required labs to seek authorization before widespread testing. That EUA framework dates to 2004 (Project BioShield), not the Obama era. A stricter Obama-era policy on lab-developed tests was only proposed and never implemented. Multiple fact-checks (FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, Washington Post) found no Obama regulation that caused the slowdown.

claim: Viral posts claim President Donald Trump received more votes in the California primary than the top two Democratic candidates combined.
response_text: FALSE.  Official California 2024 presidential primary results show Donald Trump received roughly 2.4 million votes, while the top two Democrats (Joe Biden plus the next-highest, e.g., Marianne Williamson) combined for well over 3.5 million. Even in 2020, the top two Democrats (Bernie Sanders and Joe Biden) together far outpaced Trump by millions. Some early, partial returns may have briefly suggested otherwise, likely fueling the viral claim, but final totals do not support it.

claim: Trump claims that the Obama administration “didn’t do anything” about the 2009 pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  The Obama administration took multiple actions during the 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic: declaring a public health emergency in April 2009, activating CDC’s emergency operations, releasing antivirals from the Strategic National Stockpile, developing and distributing vaccines (available by fall 2009), issuing school/healthcare guidance, and declaring a national emergency in October 2009. So it’s incorrect to say they “didn’t do anything.”

claim: The 3.4% mortality rate for Covid-19 as reported by WHO is false.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO’s 3.4% figure (March 3, 2020) referred to the global case-fatality ratio among reported cases at that time (“about 3.4% of reported COVID-19 cases have died”). That was a snapshot of detected cases, not the infection fatality rate across all infections, which was lower. So the number could be misleading if taken as overall mortality risk, but it wasn’t “false” for what WHO stated.

claim: The Obama administration made a decision on testing and that turned out to be very detrimental to what we’re doing, and we undid that decision a few days ago.
response_text: FALSE.  There was no Obama-era “decision on testing” that impeded COVID-19 testing. The FDA’s emergency use authorization framework predates Obama (created in 2004), and Obama’s proposed tighter oversight of lab-developed tests was never implemented. The late-February 2020 change that allowed more labs to develop and use tests before EUA was an FDA policy shift under the Trump administration, not an undoing of an Obama rule. Even HHS officials said they weren’t aware of any such Obama-era rule.

claim: Gargling with bleach is a cure for coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Bleach is a toxic, corrosive chemical that should never be ingested or used for gargling. It does not cure COVID-19 and can cause serious injury (burns, poisoning, lung damage). Health authorities (WHO/CDC) warn against using disinfectants inside the body; they are only for cleaning surfaces.

claim: Coronavirus has been discovered in rice bags.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence shows SARS‑CoV‑2 being discovered in rice or rice bags. Health agencies (WHO, FDA, EFSA) have stated there’s no evidence COVID‑19 spreads via food or typical food packaging, and fact-checkers have debunked social media rumors about “virus in rice bags.” Reports of detections on some frozen food packaging don’t apply to dry goods like rice and didn’t show infectious virus.

claim: In the US, it costs almost $4,000 to get tested for COVID-19 without insurance.
response_text: FALSE.  Typical out-of-pocket prices for a standalone COVID-19 test in the U.S. have been in the tens to low hundreds of dollars (roughly $20–$200 for PCR; often under $50 for antigen), and many public sites offered free testing, especially earlier in the pandemic. The “almost $4,000” figures came from rare outlier bills tied to emergency room visits and additional services, not the test itself. Costs vary, but $4,000 is not the normal price for getting tested without insurance. Uncertainty: individual cases can be higher if bundled with ER/facility fees.

claim: The World Health Organisation (WHO) have advised people to use contactless payments instead of cash to reduce the risk of Covid-19 transmission.
response_text: FALSE.  Early media reports misattributed this to WHO. The organization did not advise people to switch to contactless payments; it clarified that it had issued no such guidance. WHO’s advice was to practice hand hygiene—e.g., wash hands after handling money—rather than to avoid cash or prefer contactless payments.

claim: Seven things that can kill COVID-19: UV Temperatures higher than 56 degrees celsius Ventilated air   Chlorine disinfectants Alcohol 75% Frequently washed hands Strong human’s immunity system
response_text: FALSE.  - Ventilated air does not “kill” the virus; it dilutes and removes infectious aerosols, reducing exposure. - “Strong immunity” is not a disinfectant and “kills COVID‑19” is imprecise (COVID‑19 is the disease; the immune system can clear SARS‑CoV‑2 infection but this isn’t a method to kill the virus in the environment).  Notes: - SARS‑CoV‑2 can be inactivated by UV‑C (not ordinary UV exposure), sufficient heat (e.g., ~56°C for ~30 minutes), chlorine bleach, 70–75% alcohol, and soap/handwashing (which removes and disrupts the virus). However, including ventilation and “strong immunity” as “things that kill” makes the claim incorrect.

claim: The United States is right now ranked by far No. 1 in the world for preparedness.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The leading global benchmark (the Global Health Security Index by JHU/NTI) did rank the U.S. No. 1 in pandemic preparedness (e.g., 2019 and again in 2021), but only by a modest margin over the next countries—not “by far.” For example, in 2019 the U.S. scored 83.5 vs. the UK’s 77.9 on a 0–100 scale.

claim: The Treasury expects the UK economy to shrink by 4.9% under a Canada-style deal with the EU.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In the UK government’s 2018 long‑term analysis (coordinated by HM Treasury), an “average” Canada-style free trade agreement was projected to leave UK GDP about 4.9% lower after 15 years compared with remaining in the EU (assuming no change to migration). Under stricter migration assumptions the estimate was about 6.7% lower. It’s a relative estimate (smaller than otherwise), not a forecast of an absolute contraction.

claim: The United States is “actually screening fewer people (for the coronavirus than other countries) because we don't have appropriate testing."
response_text: TRUE.  In early March 2020, the U.S. had tested far fewer people—both in total and per capita—than countries like South Korea and Italy. For example, while South Korea had tested well over 100,000 people by early March, U.S. totals were only in the low thousands. The shortfall was largely due to problems with the initial CDC test kits and restrictive testing criteria/regulatory limits that delayed widespread testing, leading to fewer people being screened.

claim: Coronavirus symptoms emerge only after the virus has entered a person’s bloodstream.
response_text: FALSE.  Coronavirus (including SARS‑CoV‑2) typically infects and replicates in the respiratory tract mucosa. Many symptoms (fever, sore throat, cough, loss of smell) arise from local infection and immune responses, often before and even without detectable virus in the bloodstream. Viremia can occur, especially in severe cases, but it isn’t required for symptoms.

claim: US President Donald Trump hasn't allowed scientists to speak about the coronvirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Scientists did speak publicly about COVID-19 throughout 2020—e.g., Dr. Anthony Fauci, Dr. Deborah Birx, and CDC/NIH officials appeared at White House task force briefings and in numerous media interviews. While the White House at times centralized and constrained messaging (e.g., routing requests through the Vice President’s office and occasionally blocking specific interviews), it did not impose a blanket ban preventing scientists from speaking.

claim: As of March 1st 2020 the U.S. Trump administration hadn't even prepared a Coronavirus test kit.
response_text: FALSE.  The CDC (under HHS) had developed a RT‑PCR test and received FDA Emergency Use Authorization on Feb. 4, 2020, with kits shipped to public health labs in early February. Many early kits were flawed and capacity was very limited, but a test kit had been prepared before March 1.

claim: Shands Hospital of Gainesville Florida confirmed its first case of coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  UF Health Shands in Gainesville did not “confirm its first case.” Early 2020 rumors claiming Shands had a confirmed coronavirus case were explicitly denied by the hospital, and confirmations in Florida were issued by the Florida Department of Health. Alachua County’s first confirmed case was announced later by the state health department, not by Shands. (Slight uncertainty if the claim refers to a different time, but contemporaneous reports indicate it was a false rumor.)

claim: Pope Francis and two aides have tested positive for Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In early 2020 rumors claimed Pope Francis had COVID-19, but the Vatican stated he had a cold and later confirmed he tested negative. While some Vatican residents and Swiss Guards did test positive at various times, there’s no record that Pope Francis—or “two aides” alongside him—ever tested positive. This claim was debunked by multiple outlets and Vatican statements.

claim: The Canadian Army was deployed in Montreal to keep the peace during the Covid-19 pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: During COVID-19, the Canadian Armed Forces were deployed in Quebec (including the Montreal area) under Operation LASER to assist overwhelmed long-term care homes and provide logistical/medical support. They were not sent to “keep the peace” or police the public; public order was handled by municipal and provincial police. The army’s peacekeeping-style deployment in Montreal was during the 1970 October Crisis, not the pandemic.

claim: Florida Man Arrested For Robbery Using Cough As A Weapon
response_text: FALSE.  This headline originated from a satirical site (World News Daily Report) and has no corroboration from credible news sources. Fact-checkers have debunked it; the accompanying mugshot used in posts was from an unrelated case. While some people were arrested during COVID-19 for coughing on others, there’s no verified Florida robbery case matching this claim.

claim: US President Donald Trump called COVID-19 a hoax.
response_text: FALSE.  At a Feb. 28, 2020 rally, Trump said Democrats were “politicizing the coronavirus” and called that “their new hoax.” He did not call the virus itself a hoax, and later clarified he was referring to Democrats’ criticism of his administration’s response.

claim: John Mahama presided over a decline in Ghana's economic growth for his four years in office, while Nana Akufo-Addo presided over higher economic growth in his first three years in office before the COVID-19 pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  - Under John Mahama (2013–2016), real GDP growth fell sharply from 2013 to 2015 but rebounded in 2016 (approx. 2013: ~7.3%, 2014: ~2.9%, 2015: ~2.2%, 2016: ~3.4%). So it was not a continuous decline across all four years. - Under Nana Akufo-Addo (pre‑COVID, 2017–2019), growth was higher (approx. 2017: ~8.1%, 2018: ~6.3%, 2019: ~6.5%).  Figures vary slightly by source, but the pattern is consistent.

claim: Drinking water every 15 minutes prevents being infected by the novel coronavirus, COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that drinking water every 15 minutes prevents COVID-19. SARS‑CoV‑2 infects the respiratory tract; drinking water cannot “flush” the virus away or stop infection. Health agencies (WHO, CDC) have debunked this myth; hydration is good for general health but not a preventive measure against COVID-19.

claim: The first case of Covid19 reported in Australia  was from the New South Wales town of Dubbo
response_text: FALSE.  The first confirmed COVID-19 case in Australia was reported on 25 January 2020 in Victoria (Melbourne), involving a man who had returned from Wuhan. New South Wales reported its first cases the same day in Sydney—not in Dubbo.

claim: The coronavirus outbreak is US Democrats new hoax.
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 was a real, globally documented pandemic, not a hoax. The “Democrats’ new hoax” line stems from a Trump rally where he said Democrats’ criticism/politicization of his response was a “hoax,” not that the coronavirus outbreak itself was fake.

claim: 38 Percent of Americans are avoiding Corona Beer because of the Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  The “38%” figure came from a small PR firm’s online poll of 737 beer drinkers that asked if they would buy Corona “under any circumstances right now.” It did not establish that refusals were because of the coronavirus and it wasn’t a representative sample of all Americans. Subsequent data and surveys showed little to no coronavirus-related hit to Corona sales, with the brand reporting stable or growing sales at the time.

claim: Japan issued a health advisory listing drinking water as a prevention method for COVID-19.
