response_text: FALSE.  This was a widely shared hoax early in the pandemic. Posts falsely claimed “Japanese doctors” or Japan’s health ministry advised drinking water every 15 minutes to prevent COVID‑19. Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare did not issue such guidance, and WHO/health authorities have stated that drinking water does not prevent COVID‑19. Official Japanese advice focused on masks, hand hygiene, and avoiding the “3 Cs” (closed spaces, crowded places, close-contact settings).

claim: Mike Pence moved decisively when confronted with a disturbing HIV outbreak in a rural Indiana county in 2014-15 when he was governor of the state.
response_text: FALSE.  Pence initially resisted key public‑health measures, notably syringe exchange, despite a rapidly growing HIV outbreak in Scott County in late 2014–early 2015. He waited months to declare a public health emergency (March 26, 2015) and only then authorized a limited, temporary needle-exchange program after publicly saying he would “pray on it.” By that time, cases had already surged. This record is widely characterized as delayed rather than decisive.

claim: Jaffrabad Shooter In Red T-Shirt Is Mumbai's Actor Anurag Mishra
response_text: FALSE.  The red‑T‑shirt gunman at Jaffrabad during the 2020 Delhi riots was identified and arrested by Delhi Police as Shahrukh Pathan (also reported as Mohammad Shahrukh), not Mumbai actor Anurag Mishra. Fact‑checks showed the “Anurag Mishra” photos were from an unrelated acting shoot and do not match the Jaffrabad shooter.

claim: Holding your breathe for 10 seconds, without any discomfort or coughing, proves there is no infection in the lungs from COVID19
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: This “10‑second breath-hold test” is a debunked myth. Many people with COVID‑19 (including asymptomatic or mild cases) can hold their breath without coughing, and many without COVID‑19 may struggle due to asthma, anxiety, smoking, or other lung/heart issues. It does not diagnose or rule out COVID‑19. Only approved diagnostic tests (PCR or rapid antigen) and medical evaluation can assess infection.

claim: Russian Academy of Sciences Takes Aim at Musk’s SpaceX Satellites
response_text: TRUE  Russian Academy of Sciences bodies have publicly criticized SpaceX’s Starlink megaconstellation, warning about light pollution, radio interference, and orbital congestion, and urging regulatory action. Russian media framed this stance as the Academy “taking aim” at Musk’s satellites. (Minor uncertainty about the exact headline wording, but the substance is accurate.)

claim: 3,500 tonnes of gold was discovered in a field in the north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In Feb 2020, media reports claimed about 3,350–3,500 tonnes of gold were found in Sonbhadra, Uttar Pradesh. The Geological Survey of India quickly refuted this, clarifying the estimate was about 52,806 tonnes of ore with an average gold grade of ~3 g/tonne—equivalent to roughly 160 kg of gold, not thousands of tonnes.

claim: the Canadian government will welcome three million immigrants in 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Canada’s annual permanent resident admissions are in the hundreds of thousands, not millions. The 2020 target was about 341,000, and due to COVID-19 Canada actually admitted roughly 184,000 permanent residents that year (IRCC data). Three million in 2020 was never an announced target and is far beyond actual levels.

claim: Dettol products can kill Coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE.  Many Dettol disinfectant products are proven to inactivate/kills coronaviruses (including SARS‑CoV‑2) on hard, non‑porous surfaces when used as directed and with the stated contact time. This does not apply to internal use, and effectiveness varies by product—check the label for virucidal claims (e.g., EN 14476/SARS‑CoV‑2).

claim: The NHS has warned people should not shake hands to prevent the spread of the Wuhan coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  Early NHS/Public Health England guidance focused on frequent handwashing and hygiene; they did not tell people to stop shaking hands. In early March 2020 the UK’s Chief Medical Officer even said there was no strong advice against handshakes. Later, broad social‑distancing guidance advised avoiding close contact, but the NHS did not issue a standalone “do not shake hands” warning as claimed.

claim: The CDC recommends men shave their beards to protect against coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A 2017 NIOSH (part of CDC) chart about respirator fit resurfaced during COVID-19, showing which facial hair styles can interfere with tight‑sealing respirators like N95s. It was not a CDC recommendation for men to shave beards to protect against coronavirus, nor guidance for the general public. It applied specifically to workers who must wear tight‑fitting respirators; facial hair at the seal can reduce effectiveness.

claim: Sen. Lindsey Graham said "President Donald Trump probably knows more about medicine and specifically viruses than the so called scientists at the NIH and CDC".
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (speeches, interviews, congressional transcript, or verified social media) of Lindsey Graham saying this. The quote appears to originate from a satirical/fake-news meme, and fact-checkers have debunked it. Graham has at times publicly supported NIH/CDC guidance during COVID, making such a statement unlikely.

claim: Thailand’s Ministry of Health has raised the country’s alert on the novel coronavirus to the highest level.
response_text: FALSE  Thailand’s Ministry of Public Health did raise its COVID-19 alert/response level at various points (e.g., early 2020 and again in Jan 2022), but not to the maximum category. In 2022 it moved to Alert Level 4, which was below the top level, and earlier escalations were heightened surveillance/EOC activation rather than a “highest” national alert. (Some media phrased increases as “highest,” but official levels were not at the maximum.) Uncertainty: wording varies across reports.

claim: COVID-19 cases are going very substantially down, not up.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: When this claim was made (late June 2020 in the U.S.), reported COVID-19 cases were rising rapidly. The 7-day average climbed from roughly 20,000/day in early June to over 40,000/day by late June and continued upward into July. (If a different time/place was intended, context is needed, but generally cases were not “very substantially down” then.)

claim: Russian Cops Don’t Beat People For No Reason.
response_text: FALSE.  There is extensive, well-documented evidence of Russian police beating people without lawful justification. Human rights groups (e.g., Human Rights Watch, Amnesty, OVD-Info) and court rulings have recorded numerous cases of excessive force against peaceful protesters (2019 Moscow election protests, 2021 pro-Navalny rallies, 2022–2023 anti-war protests) and ill‑treatment in custody. Notable incidents include the 2012 Kazan case where a detainee died after police torture, and multiple videos showing officers striking nonviolent demonstrators (even people holding blank signs). One counterexample suffices to refute the absolute claim.

claim: US President Trump called for reduced funding for the Centre for Disease Control and Prevention.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Several Trump administration budget proposals asked Congress to reduce CDC funding (e.g., the FY2018 proposal sought about a $1.2 billion—roughly 17%—cut, and later budgets also proposed reductions). Congress largely rejected these cuts, but he did call for reduced CDC funding.

claim: Congress files charges against speaker of the U.S House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi, for tearing up her copy of the State of the Union speech.
response_text: FALSE.  Congress does not file criminal charges, and no charges were filed against Nancy Pelosi for tearing her copy of President Trump’s 2020 State of the Union speech. Some Republican members filed or proposed ethics complaints and censure resolutions, but no legal charges resulted. Legal experts and fact-checkers noted her copy was not an official record requiring preservation, and the speech is archived elsewhere.

claim: Kunal Kamra said, The RDX laden car which caused the blast in Pulwama, RTO has not been able to access its papers stating under whose name it was registered, till date. The government wants more than 70 year old papers in the NRC.
response_text: FALSE  - No credible record (tweet, interview, video) shows Kunal Kamra saying this; multiple fact-checks flagged the quote as a fabricated social-media graphic attributed to him. - The statement itself is factually wrong: NIA publicly said in March 2019 that the Maruti Eeco used in the Pulwama attack was traced and identified as having been bought by Sajjad Ahmad Bhat of Anantnag, J&K. So the idea that “RTO has not been able to access its papers till date” is incorrect.  Uncertainty: None significant; both the attribution and the content have been debunked.

claim: The majority of hunters and the majority of Trump voters now want universal background checks on gun buyers.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple recent polls show strong majority support for universal background checks, including among Republicans and gun owners. For example, Fox News (Apr. 2024) found 87% of voters favor requiring background checks for all gun buyers, including 77% of Republicans—implying a majority of Trump voters. Johns Hopkins’ National Survey of Gun Policy has repeatedly found large majorities of gun owners and Republicans support universal checks. Surveys that specifically sample hunters/sportsmen have likewise found big majorities (often ~80%+). Minor caveat: hunter-specific polling is less frequent, but available data consistently show majority support.

claim: Mayor Bloomberg blamed African Americans & Latinos for the housing crash of 2008.
response_text: FALSE.  Bloomberg (in 2008 remarks resurfaced in 2020) blamed the push to end “redlining” and political pressure on banks to lend to poor/underserved borrowers for contributing to the crisis—not African Americans and Latinos explicitly. His comments linked the crisis to lending in previously redlined (often minority) neighborhoods, which critics said implied blame, but he did not say African Americans and Latinos caused the crash. He later said those remarks were wrong and that banks and Wall Street bore the blame.

claim: Amy Klobuchar’s health plan is just two paragraphs long.
response_text: FALSE.  Briefly: Early in her 2019 campaign, Klobuchar’s website had a short health care blurb that some critics described as just a couple of paragraphs. But she later released a detailed health plan (public option, drug-price reforms, mental health, etc.). So saying her health plan “is just two paragraphs long” is outdated/misleading. Uncertainty: true only for a brief early snapshot of her website.

claim: Car thefts are increasing in 8 of the 10 most populous Wisconsin, US counties
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The claim lacks a timeframe. Using recent year-over-year data (e.g., 2023 vs. 2022), vehicle thefts fell in Milwaukee and several other large counties, so it’s not true that 8 of the 10 most populous Wisconsin counties are currently seeing increases. While thefts spiked widely in 2021–2022 (notably due to Kia/Hyundai vulnerabilities), more recent trends show declines in multiple top counties. Uncertainty: exact counts vary by the period chosen.

claim: Former mayor of New York, US, Mike Bloomberg owns more wealth than the bottom 125 million Americans.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Mike Bloomberg’s net worth is roughly on the order of $100–120 billion. Federal Reserve data show the bottom 50% of U.S. households hold about 2% of total household wealth; with total U.S. household wealth around $140–150 trillion, that’s several trillion dollars. The bottom ~125 million Americans (roughly the bottom 35–40% by population) would therefore have combined wealth far above Bloomberg’s. Only under nonstandard definitions (e.g., counting individuals including children with zero assigned wealth) could the comparison look closer, but standard household/adult measures make the claim false.

claim: Under the government’s new immigration rules anyone earning less than £25,600 is regarded as an unskilled worker.
response_text: FALSE.  Under the UK’s points-based immigration system, “skilled” is defined by the job’s skill level (RQF3/A‑level or above), not just salary. While £25,600 was a general salary threshold for the Skilled Worker route, applicants could still qualify below that (e.g., shortage occupations, new entrants, relevant PhDs, Health and Care roles), in some cases down to about £20,480. So earning under £25,600 does not mean being regarded as “unskilled.”

claim: While he was mayor of NYC, Bloomberg cut stop-and-frisk by 95% because they were doing too many.
response_text: FALSE.  As mayor (2002–2013), Bloomberg oversaw a sharp increase in stop‑and‑frisk, which peaked at about 685,000 stops in 2011. Stops then fell to about 192,000 in 2013—roughly a 70–72% drop from the peak, not 95%. The ~95%+ decline occurred after he left office. Moreover, Bloomberg long defended the practice and appealed a 2013 court ruling against it, so it wasn’t reduced because he thought “they were doing too many.”

claim: VIRAL IMAGE SHOWS SENATOR JAMES INHOFE NOW SERVES AS THE EPA’S CHIEF OF STAFF
response_text: FALSE.  James (Jim) Inhofe was a U.S. senator from Oklahoma (1994–2023) and never served as the EPA’s chief of staff. The EPA chief of staff during the Trump era was Ryan Jackson, who had been Inhofe’s Senate chief of staff, followed by Mandy Gunasekara; under Biden, Dan Utech has served in that role. A miscaptioned image likely confused Inhofe with his former aide. Additionally, Inhofe died in 2024, making the “now serves” claim impossible.

claim: Biden was arrested in 1977 in South Africa when trying to meet Nelson Mandela.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks found no record that Biden was arrested in South Africa, and Andrew Young—whom Biden said was with him—denied it. Biden later clarified he was not arrested but “stopped” and briefly separated by apartheid-era authorities. He also was not actually trying to meet Mandela (who was imprisoned then). Uncertainty: low.

claim: $150 million had been collected by the Australian Red Cross as of 16/02/2020.
response_text: FALSE.  As of mid-February 2020, Australian Red Cross reported having raised roughly $115–$138 million for bushfire relief; reports around 12–17 Feb cited ~$115m and ~$138m respectively. $150 million had not been reached by 16/02/2020. (Slight uncertainty on exact daily totals, but contemporaneous reports fall below $150m.)

claim: The High court in India,  passed a mandatory order that says Bank of Baroda’s license must be revoked.
response_text: FALSE.  - In India, only the Reserve Bank of India can revoke a bank’s license under the Banking Regulation Act. Courts do not order revocation of a bank’s license. - There have been no credible reports of any Indian High Court mandating that Bank of Baroda’s license be revoked. The notable recent action was RBI’s temporary restriction (2023) on onboarding new customers to BoB World, not a license issue. - Given the bank’s size and public ownership, such an order would be major news; none exists.

claim: Of the $150 million, only $7 million in $10,000 lots had been given out to bushfire victims by the Australian Red Cross as of the 16/02/2020.
response_text: FALSE.  As of mid-February 2020, the Australian Red Cross said it had raised about $115 million (not $150 million) for the bushfires and had disbursed roughly $7 million, mainly as $5,000 emergency grants to people who lost homes. The payments were not generally in $10,000 lots. Tens of millions more had been committed but were still being processed at that time.

claim: Rashtriya Sikhshit Berojgar Yojna launched a scheme to pay Rs 50,000 to educated unemployed citizens in India.
response_text: FALSE.  This “Rashtriya Shikshit Berojgar Yojna/Yojana” offer of Rs 50,000 has been repeatedly debunked by PIB Fact Check and independent fact-checkers. There is no Government of India scheme by this name, and the viral websites/posts using it are fraudulent (often not on a .gov.in domain).

claim: A U.S. federal judge released Benghazi evidence that puts former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in deep trouble.
response_text: FALSE.  No U.S. federal judge has “released Benghazi evidence” that newly implicates Hillary Clinton. Courts handling FOIA lawsuits (e.g., orders by Judges Amit Mehta in 2017 and Royce Lamberth in 2019) required additional searches or allowed limited discovery about State Department records and Clinton’s emails, but they did not unveil damning Benghazi evidence. Multiple investigations, including the House Select Committee and the State Department’s review, found no criminal wrongdoing by Clinton regarding Benghazi.

claim: FBI Ignored Evidence That Hillary Clinton Put A Hit Out On Brett Kavanaugh.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton ordered a hit on Brett Kavanaugh, nor that the FBI ignored such evidence. The only known assassination plot involved an individual (Nicholas Roske) arrested in 2022 who acted alone; DOJ charged him with attempted murder of a Supreme Court justice. No ties to Clinton were reported, and authorities did not “ignore” the case. This claim appears to be baseless misinformation.

claim: Very close to 160 million people are now working in the United States.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent BLS household-survey data put the number of employed people around 161–163 million, which is indeed very close to 160 million. (Exact figures vary month to month.)

claim: A doctor's office in New South Wales was visited by people who had been exposed to the coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE  NSW Health repeatedly listed GP clinics/doctor’s offices as exposure sites during COVID-19. Early in the pandemic (e.g., January–March 2020), close contacts and some confirmed cases attended Sydney GP clinics, prompting public health alerts and isolation advice. Exact clinics varied, but the event described did occur.

claim: Bernie Sanders returns a donation from Mike Bloomberg in the amount of $18.53
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated as a satirical headline (e.g., from The Babylon Bee) playing on Sanders’ reported average donation of $18.53 during the 2020 race. There’s no credible reporting or FEC record of Mike Bloomberg donating $18.53 to Bernie Sanders or Sanders returning such a donation.

claim: BJP leaders did not say that Shaheen Bagh protestors will enter homes and rape women and daughters.
response_text: FALSE.  BJP leader Parvesh Verma (MP, West Delhi) said at a January 2020 campaign event that people from Shaheen Bagh would “enter your homes” and “pick up your sisters and daughters… rape them, kill them.” The Election Commission censured him and imposed a campaign ban.

claim: Donald Trump cut scheduled federal worker pay raises in early 2020
response_text: FALSE.  In early 2020, federal civilian employees received a pay raise averaging 3.1% (2.6% across-the-board plus about 0.5% locality), which President Trump implemented via executive order after Congress approved it in late 2019. While he had previously attempted to freeze 2019 raises and later proposed limiting future increases in his FY2021 budget, he did not cut scheduled raises in early 2020.

claim: At the level of gender, at senior management level in South Africa, males remain dominant at 67.6% and females at 32.4%
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Commission for Employment Equity (CEE) annual reports consistently show that men hold about two‑thirds of senior management posts in South Africa. In recent years one CEE report listed senior management at roughly 67.6% male and 32.4% female. Percentages vary slightly by year, but the split around 2:1 male-to-female is accurate. (Minor uncertainty on the exact year the 67.6/32.4 figure refers to.)

claim: US Senator Amy Klobuchar vows to resettle no refugees in her neighbourhood.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Sen. Amy Klobuchar vowing to keep refugees out of her neighborhood. On the contrary, she has consistently supported refugee resettlement and higher national refugee admissions. The “won’t take refugees in her neighborhood” line appears to be an unsubstantiated accusation/meme rather than a documented statement.

claim: Turkey is responsible for the escalating tensions between Turkey and Russia in northwest Syria.
response_text: FALSE.  Tensions in northwest Syria have been driven by actions from both sides. Russia (backing the Syrian government) has repeatedly escalated through offensives and airstrikes in Idlib, while Turkey has expanded its military presence and conducted strikes in response. Responsibility is shared and context-dependent, not solely Turkey’s.

claim: Donald Trump cited 'serious economic conditions' as the reason for reducing federal worker pay raises in early 2020
response_text: FALSE.  - Federal civilian employees received about a 3.1% pay raise for 2020 (2.6% across-the-board + 0.5% locality), effective January 2020, set by Congress and implemented by Trump via executive order. - Trump did use the statutory phrase “national emergency or serious economic conditions” in alternative pay plan letters (e.g., Aug. 2019 for 2020 and Aug. 2020 for 2021) to limit proposed adjustments, but not to reduce raises in early 2020.  Minor uncertainty: He invoked that language in other years, but not to cut an already-implemented 2020 raise in early 2020.

claim: There has been no load shedding since August last 2015
response_text: FALSE.  Assuming the common South African context, Eskom still implemented load shedding in mid‑September 2015 (e.g., 14 September). Moreover, load shedding returned from 2018 onward. So it’s not correct to say there has been none since August 2015. (Slight uncertainty if a different country was meant.)

claim: To curb water wastage, the Department of Water and Sanitation has begun its programme of training 15,000 young people as artisans.
response_text: TRUE.  South Africa’s Department of Water and Sanitation launched the “War on Leaks” programme in 2015 to curb water losses, with a target of training 15,000 young people. Training began in phases (starting with a few thousand) and covered plumbers, water agents and artisans. Note: the programme was not limited to artisans only, and it later faced implementation challenges.

claim: BJP, the Bharatiya Janata Party lost a total of 8 seats by a margin of fewer than 100 votes, 19 seats by less than 1000 votes and 9 seats by less than 2000 votes, in India.
response_text: FALSE.  The claim doesn’t match official Election Commission of India data for recent national elections. In the 2024 Lok Sabha results, margins under 2,000 votes were only a handful nationwide, and there were not eight BJP losses by under 100 votes (such razor-thin margins are extremely rare in Lok Sabha contests). Similar figures also don’t appear for 2019. The numbers (8 under 100, 19 under 1,000, 9 under 2,000) come from a viral but debunked claim.   Note: If a specific state assembly election was intended, that’s not stated; no verified source matches these exact counts for BJP.

claim: Hollywood actor Mel Gibson says, "The only reason liberals hate Trump is they hate God"
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (interviews, video, reputable news coverage, or transcripts) of Mel Gibson saying “The only reason liberals hate Trump is they hate God.” The quote appears only in memes/social posts and resembles other fabricated statements frequently misattributed to Gibson.

claim: A bowl of “freshly” boiled garlic water cures ‘Wuhan’s coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that garlic—or “freshly boiled garlic water”—prevents or cures COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2). WHO and other health authorities have debunked this myth. Garlic may have some antimicrobial properties but it doesn’t treat viral infections like COVID-19. Use evidence-based measures (vaccination, approved antivirals, medical care).

claim: Sri Lanka's Ehelepola Walawwa Mansion school will be converted into a Muslim school.
response_text: FALSE.  Briefly: Ehelepola Walawwa is a protected heritage site in Kandy and the school operating there is not being converted. Local education authorities and Sri Lankan fact‑checkers have denied any plan to turn it into a Muslim school; the rumor appears to misinterpret separate discussions about facilities for a different nearby school. (Slight uncertainty due to evolving local administration, but no official decision supports the claim.)

claim: Thailand cured a COVID-19 patient within 48 hours using a cocktail of an anti-HIV drug and an antiviral drug used for treating influenza.
response_text: FALSE.  - In early Feb 2020, Thai doctors reported a 71-year-old patient’s symptoms improved and a test turned negative about 48 hours after giving lopinavir/ritonavir (HIV drugs) plus oseltamivir (flu drug).   - They cautioned it was a single case and not proof of a cure.   - Subsequent studies found no clear benefit of lopinavir/ritonavir for COVID-19.    So saying Thailand “cured” COVID-19 in 48 hours is misleading and not supported by evidence.

claim: The salaries of MPs in the UK have grown faster than the starting salaries of nurses, teachers and police officers between 2010 and 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  - MPs’ basic salary rose from about £65,700 in 2010 to about £81,900 in 2020 (≈+25%). - Nurses (Band 5 start, England) rose from about £21,200 (2010) to £24,900 (2020) (≈+18%). - Teachers (starting salary outside London) rose from about £21,600 (2010) to £25,700 (2020) (≈+19%). - Police constables’ starting pay was about £23,300 (2010) and in 2020 ranged roughly £21,400–£24,800 depending on entry route (≈−8% to +7%).  Across these benchmarks, MPs’ pay grew faster. Note: exact figures vary by UK nation and entry route, but the conclusion holds.

claim: Presidential candidate Bernie Sanders said supporting abortion up to birth is an "essential part of being a Democrat."
response_text: FALSE.  Sanders said during the 2020 primary that being “pro‑choice” is an essential part of being a Democrat. He did not say “abortion up to birth.” His stated position is to uphold/codify Roe v. Wade, which allows restrictions on late‑term abortions except for the life or health of the mother. The “up to birth” phrasing misrepresents what he said.

claim: As of February 10th 2020, the United States only had 11 cases of Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  CDC’s situation update on Feb 10, 2020 reported 12 confirmed COVID-19 cases in the United States (including two from person-to-person transmission). Counts could fluctuate during the day, but the official total by that date was 12, not 11.

claim: People were pursued with Fulani Knives after an attack on Peter Obi's Convoy in Abuja Market.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports show Peter Obi’s convoy was attacked in an Abuja market, nor that people were chased with “Fulani knives” afterward. Viral clips used to push this claim have been traced to unrelated violence in Abuja’s Dei-Dei market in May 2022 (and other older incidents), not to any attack on Obi’s convoy.

claim: Seven Cars in Peter Obi's Convoy were burnt by Hausa Men during an attack at Abuja Market
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports show Peter Obi’s convoy was attacked in an Abuja market or that seven of his cars were burnt. Fact-checks traced the circulating images/videos to unrelated incidents (notably the May 2022 Dei-Dei market riot in Abuja), and Obi’s camp denied any such attack. The claim appears to be repurposed, inflammatory misinformation.

claim: President Trump said he removed Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman from the White House's National security Council because his superior publicly stated that 'Vindman had problems with judgment, adhering to the chain of command, and leaking information'
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In a Feb. 8, 2020 tweet, President Trump justified removing Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman by saying Vindman’s superior had publicly stated he had “problems with judgment, adhering to the chain of command, and leaking information.” Note: That superior, Tim Morrison, did express concerns about judgment and chain-of-command, but he testified he did not think Vindman leaked information.

claim: Cocaine kills the Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Cocaine does not kill coronaviruses or prevent/treat COVID-19. It’s a harmful stimulant with no antiviral or disinfectant properties. Protection comes from vaccines, masks, hand hygiene, and approved disinfectants (e.g., 60–70% alcohol or bleach) on surfaces—not cocaine.

claim: Over 700,000 children accessed early childhood education in South Africa in 2018
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Department of Basic Education figures show Grade R enrolment alone exceeded 800,000 in 2018, and broader pre‑primary/ECD participation (including pre‑Grade R) was well over 1 million according to national and UNESCO statistics. So “over 700,000” is certainly met, though it understates the scale. (Exact totals vary by definition of ECE.)

claim: China sought court approval to kill over 20,000 patients who were infected by the deadly novel Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a hoax/fake-news post circulating on social media in early 2020. No credible evidence or official reports support it, and major fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, Snopes) debunked it. Chinese authorities imposed lockdowns and medical quarantines, not executions, and such an action would be illegal and inconsistent with documented public health measures.

claim: William Barr tweeted, “ IN A COMPLETELY UNRELATED STORY Senator Mitt Romney is also the only Republican Senator who has a son who sits on the board of a Ukrainian Energy Company.”
response_text: FALSE.  - There’s no record of William (Bill) Barr having posted such a tweet; he did not maintain a public personal Twitter account as AG, and fact-checks found the quote misattributed. - The content is also wrong: none of Mitt Romney’s sons served on the board of a Ukrainian energy company. The confusion likely stems from H. Cofer Black, a former Romney adviser, joining Burisma’s board—not a Romney son.

claim: China is seeking the court's permission to kill over 20,000 coronavirus patients in order to prevent the virus from spreading further.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a hoax/fake-news site and has been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers. There is no credible evidence that China sought court approval to kill COVID-19 patients; euthanasia is illegal in China, and authorities focused on quarantine, treatment, and building hospitals, not killing patients.

claim: William Barr tweeted, “BREAKING NEWS Senator Mitt Romney is the only Republican Senator who voted to remove President Trump from office
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of William (Bill) Barr posting that tweet. Barr did not maintain a public, verified Twitter account as Attorney General, and archived/verified tweets show no such post from him. The statement about Romney being the only Republican to vote to convict (on one article) is accurate, but it was misattributed to Barr.

claim: A ‘HUGE PERCENTAGE’ OF DEPORTED SALVADORANS KILLED OR HARMED UPON RETURN TO EL SALVADOR
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence shows serious risks but not a “huge percentage.” A 2020 Human Rights Watch report documented at least 138 Salvadorans killed after U.S. deportation since 2013 and dozens more raped, tortured, or otherwise harmed—hundreds of cases in total—out of tens to hundreds of thousands of deportations in that period. That’s a small fraction of 1%, not a large percentage. Exact rates are uncertain due to underreporting, but available data don’t support “huge percentage.”

claim: Sen. Chuck Schumer deleted a tweet criticizing President Donald Trump’s decision to ban some forms of travel to and from China.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact‑checks (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) found no evidence that Schumer ever posted—let alone deleted—a tweet criticizing Trump’s China travel restrictions. No such tweet appears in archives or the Wayback Machine, and Schumer’s office said it never existed. Viral screenshots purporting to show it were fabricated.

claim: President Donald Trump will protect patients with pre-existing conditions.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is what protects people with pre-existing conditions (guaranteed issue and community rating). - As president, Trump backed repeal bills (e.g., the AHCA) that would have weakened or rolled back those protections and supported a lawsuit to overturn the ACA entirely, including its pre-existing condition rules. - His 2020 executive order declaring a policy to protect pre-existing conditions created no enforceable protections. - He also expanded short-term plans that can deny or exclude coverage for pre-existing conditions.  Net effect: his actions threatened, rather than protected, these protections.

claim: In America, we are spending twice as much on health care as the people of Canada or any other major countries
response_text: FALSE.  - It’s roughly true for Canada: US health spending per person is about double Canada’s (e.g., 2022 OECD: US ~$12.6k vs Canada ~$6.3k). - But it’s not true for “any other major countries.” The US does not spend twice as much as high spenders like Switzerland, Norway, or Germany (US is ~1.4–1.7× those countries, not 2×). - As a share of GDP, the US (~17–18%) is also not double other rich countries (~10–12%).

claim: Two racist black thugs in Brunswick, Georgia, shot a white baby in the face for fun.
response_text: FALSE.  In 2013 in Brunswick, Georgia, a 13‑month‑old white baby was fatally shot in the face by a black teenager, De’Marquise Elkins, during an attempted robbery; his accomplice, Dominique Lang, was present but did not fire the shot. There is no evidence the crime was racially motivated or done “for fun.” Elkins was convicted of murder; prosecutors described it as a robbery that escalated, not a hate crime.

claim: Cannabis Boosts immunity against Novel Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no reliable clinical evidence that cannabis boosts immunity or protects against COVID‑19. Some cannabinoids have shown effects in lab studies, but these haven’t translated into proven benefits in humans. Cannabis can also be immunosuppressive, and smoking it can harm the lungs. Health authorities do not recommend cannabis for preventing or treating COVID‑19; vaccination and standard public health measures remain the proven protections.

claim: Three people have more wealth than the bottom half of American society
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: That line traces to a 2017 report claiming the three richest Americans then (Gates, Bezos, Buffett) had more wealth than the bottom 50%, based on specific data choices that were criticized. Using current, comprehensive Federal Reserve data, the bottom half of U.S. households now hold trillions of dollars in net worth (roughly 2–3% of total household wealth), far more than the combined wealth of the top three individuals (hundreds of billions). So it’s not true today, and the original claim was methodologically contested.

claim: In eight years under the President Barack Obama administration, over 300,000 working-age people dropped out of the workforce.
response_text: TRUE.  BLS data show the number of people “not in the labor force” (working-age 16+ who are neither employed nor looking for work) rose from about 80.5 million in Jan 2009 to about 95.4 million in Jan 2017—an increase of roughly 15 million. So “over 300,000” is correct, though it greatly understates the actual increase.

claim: Traditionally, the Speaker says: ‘Members of Congress, I have the high privilege and distinct honor of presenting to you the President of the United States.’ (Tonight) Speaker Pelosi said, ‘Members of Congress, the President of the United States.’
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The customary introduction used by many Speakers (e.g., Ryan, Boehner, Hastert—and Pelosi herself in 2007) is “Members of Congress, I have the high privilege and distinct honor of presenting to you the President of the United States.” In both 2019 and 2020, Speaker Pelosi instead said, “Members of Congress, the President of the United States.” The exact wording isn’t required by rule, but her omission of the traditional phrasing is accurate.

claim: Over 130 legislators in the USA have endorsed legislation that would bankrupt our nation by providing free taxpayer-funded health care to millions of illegal aliens, forcing taxpayers to subsidize free care for anyone in the world who unlawfully crosses our borders.
response_text: FALSE.  - Kernel of truth: 130+ members of Congress have co‑sponsored “Medicare for All” bills that aim to cover “all U.S. residents,” which likely includes undocumented residents. - But the claim overreaches: The bills do not grant coverage to “anyone in the world who unlawfully crosses our borders”; eligibility is tied to U.S. residency (to be defined by regulation), not mere entry. - “Would bankrupt our nation” is speculative rhetoric. Independent analyses project large increases in federal spending but do not show certain “bankruptcy,” and some estimates find potential overall national health spending could fall.  Uncertainty: exact co‑sponsor counts vary by year and “resident” is defined by rulemaking, but the sweeping bankruptcy/“anyone who crosses” assertions are misleading.

claim: Nigeria is one of the Freest Countries for the Press and Media
response_text: FALSE.  Nigeria is not among the freest media environments. In RSF’s 2024 World Press Freedom Index, Nigeria ranks around the middle-to-lower tier (112th of 180), reflecting a “problematic/difficult” environment with harassment and arrests of journalists and regulatory pressures. Freedom House also rates Nigeria “Partly Free,” noting significant constraints on media.

claim: Sex traffickers are leaving $100 bills, laced with a debilitating substance attached to the handles of parked cars at Northgate Mall in Revere, Massachusetts.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a recurring viral hoax. No credible evidence or verified police reports show sex traffickers leaving drug‑laced $100 bills on car handles—at Northgate in Revere or elsewhere. Fact‑checkers and law enforcement have repeatedly debunked similar claims, and experts note that incidental skin contact with substances like fentanyl would not rapidly incapacitate someone as these posts suggest. (If a specific incident were alleged, authorities would typically issue confirmations or warnings, which have not materialized.)

claim: The UK has taken in 41,000 unaccompanied children since 2010.
response_text: TRUE  Home Office data show roughly low–to–mid 40,000 asylum applications from unaccompanied children since 2010. Depending on the cut‑off date, the cumulative total is about 41,000–45,000. Note: this counts applications, not necessarily unique children, and some were later found to be adults.

claim: Sri Lanka is the first country in the world to completely eradicate the coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE. COVID-19 has not been eradicated anywhere globally; eradication means permanent worldwide zero cases. Sri Lanka experienced multiple COVID-19 waves and was not the first to eliminate community transmission either. Uncertainty: none.

claim: As of 2019, unemployment in the US, is at a 49-year low, under the Trump-led administration
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: BLS data show the U.S. unemployment rate fell to 3.6% in April 2019—the lowest since December 1969 (about 49 years). It later reached 3.5% in September/October 2019, tying a 50-year low—all under the Trump administration.

claim: American workers are seeing the “best wage growth in a decade,” under the Trump administration
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: By 2018–2019, nominal average hourly earnings were rising about 3.2–3.4% year over year—the fastest pace since around 2009, per BLS data—so “best in a decade” is accurate on a nominal basis. However, after inflation the gains were more modest and not clearly decade-leading, and the acceleration began before Trump. Uncertainty: depends on whether you mean nominal or inflation-adjusted wages.

claim: Under a COVID-19 financial relief scheme called Rashtriya Shikshit Berojgar Yojana, the Government of India will provide financial aid of Rs 50,000 to ration cardholders.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Government of India has not announced any COVID-19 relief scheme called “Rashtriya Shikshit Berojgar Yojana” offering Rs 50,000 to ration cardholders. PIB Fact Check and multiple fact-check outlets have debunked this as a fake/ phishing claim. Official COVID-19 relief included schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package, not this.

claim: Dr. Charles Lieber, chair of Harvard University’s Dept of Chemistry and Chemical Biology and two Chinese students were arrested for creating the COVID-19 virus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In January 2020, Harvard chemist Charles Lieber was arrested for making false statements about his ties to China’s Thousand Talents Program and Wuhan University of Technology, and later faced tax-related charges. Two Chinese nationals were separately charged the same day: one for visa fraud/acting as a foreign agent (Yanqing Ye) and another for attempting to smuggle research samples (Zaosong Zheng). None were accused of creating COVID-19, and no evidence supports that claim.

claim: NZ cricket captain said " I request to NZ government please cancel KL Rahul's visa immediately."
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible record of any New Zealand cricket captain publicly asking the NZ government to cancel KL Rahul’s visa. The quote appears to be a fabricated social-media meme; no reputable news outlet or official source reports such a statement.

claim: World Health Organisation reports 340,000 people infected with Coronavirus in China.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO situation reports around March 2020 listed about 81,000–82,000 confirmed cases in China. The ~340,000 figure referred to global cases at that time, not cases in China.

claim: World Health Organisation reports 75,000 people have been killed by the 2019 Novel Coronavirus in China.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO did not report 75,000 deaths in China from the 2019 novel coronavirus. Early 2020 WHO situation reports listed deaths in the hundreds to low thousands. The ~75,000 figure circulating then referred to an estimate of infections in Wuhan from a Lancet/University of Hong Kong model, not deaths. (Later in the pandemic China’s reported deaths rose, but WHO never issued such an early “75,000 killed” report.)

claim: World Health Organisation labels Coronavirus a plague.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO declared COVID‑19 a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (Jan 2020) and later characterized it as a pandemic (Mar 2020). “Plague” is a specific disease caused by Yersinia pestis; WHO did not label coronavirus/COVID‑19 as a plague.

claim: The EU did not help Britain during the Falklands War, and instead sent weapons to Argentina.
response_text: FALSE.  In 1982 the European Community (predecessor of the EU) supported the UK: it unanimously imposed economic sanctions and an arms embargo on Argentina (e.g., EC import ban Regulation 877/82) and halted ongoing arms deliveries. France, for example, suspended further delivery/support for Super Étendard aircraft and Exocet missiles and assisted Britain with counter‑measures. Some Argentine weapons of European origin had been sold before the war, but EC states did not “send weapons to Argentina” during the conflict.

claim: Weapons seized from a West Bengal madrassa.
response_text: FALSE  Multiple fact-checks have shown that viral photos/videos claiming “weapons seized from a West Bengal madrassa” were miscaptioned; the footage was from outside West Bengal (reported to be from Bangladesh), not a madrassa in West Bengal. No credible local reports match the claim. (Slight uncertainty about the exact original location, but it was not West Bengal.)

claim: The fatality rate stood at 17.40% for H1N1 compared to 2% for the ongoing coronavirus outbreak.
response_text: FALSE.  The 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic did not have a 17.4% fatality rate. Estimates from WHO/CDC suggest an infection fatality rate on the order of 0.01–0.08% (hundreds of thousands of deaths out of hundreds of millions of infections), far below 1%. While early crude case-fatality estimates for COVID-19 were around 2–3% in some places, the H1N1 figure cited is wildly inaccurate.

claim: A Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs.
response_text: FALSE.  Briefly: Viral posts mischaracterized optional cultural activities where students could try on a headscarf if they wished. Colorado school districts stated participation was voluntary; no school forced students to wear hijabs, and doing so would violate constitutional protections. (Low uncertainty)

claim: World Health Organization officially declares the Coronavirus as a plague.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO declared COVID-19 a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (Jan 2020) and later characterized it as a pandemic (Mar 2020). WHO does not classify COVID-19 as a “plague”; “plague” refers to disease caused by Yersinia pestis, not coronaviruses.

claim: Under three years of Donald Trumps administration, net farm income has already gone up nearly 50%.
response_text: FALSE.  USDA data show net farm income was about $61–62 billion in 2016 and about $92–93 billion in 2019 (nominal), which is roughly a 50% increase—but that compares to the pre‑Trump 2016 low. Counting “under three years of his administration” (i.e., from 2017 to 2019), the increase is only around 20–25% nominal (smaller after inflation), and much of the 2019 level came from unusually large federal payments. Uncertainty: exact figures vary slightly by revision, but the pattern is consistent.

claim: The Delhi Police in India is being slammed for their apparent inaction when a man was shot at Jamia Millia Islamia University
response_text: TRUE.  On January 30, 2020, a teenager brandished a pistol and shot a student (Shadab Farooq) during an anti-CAA protest near Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi. Videos showed the gunman walking toward protesters with police standing nearby, prompting widespread criticism of the Delhi Police for apparent inaction before the shot was fired. Police arrested the shooter afterward, but were widely slammed on social media and by opposition leaders for not intervening sooner.

claim: CHUCK SCHUMER SAY ‘IT’S RACIST TO ONLY ALLOW CITIZENS TO VOTE’
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Chuck Schumer saying “it’s racist to only allow citizens to vote.” He has publicly stated that only U.S. citizens should vote, while opposing certain GOP proposals (like added proof‑of‑citizenship requirements) on the grounds they’re unnecessary and could block eligible voters. The quote appears to be a fabricated social media meme.

claim: President Donald Trump claimed that the new trade agreement with China “will boost American agriculture by $50 billion every year.”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Phase One U.S.–China trade deal did not promise a $50 billion annual boost to U.S. agriculture. The agreement’s text set agricultural purchase targets roughly at $36.5 billion in 2020 and $43.5 billion in 2021 (about $12.5b and $19.5b above the 2017 baseline), not a $50b yearly increase. In practice, China also fell short of those targets, so a $50b annual boost never materialized.

claim: Trump signed a bill "to clean millions of tons of garbage from world’s oceans.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2018 (and again in 2020), Trump signed the Save Our Seas Acts, which reauthorized and expanded NOAA’s Marine Debris Program and other measures focused on research, prevention, coordination, and limited cleanup. The laws did not mandate or fund the removal of “millions of tons” of ocean garbage; funding levels were relatively modest (e.g., about $10 million/year for the NOAA program) and not tied to such a scale of cleanup. Uncertainty: He did sign bills addressing marine debris, but the “millions of tons” claim is an exaggeration.

claim: Germ scientists have confirmed that the ‘five-second rule’ for eating food off the floor is fairly accurate.
response_text: FALSE.  Studies show bacteria can transfer to food almost instantly. A 2016 Rutgers University study found contamination can occur in less than one second; while longer contact time can increase transfer, surface type and moisture are bigger factors. Media reports of a 2014 Aston University project suggesting the rule “works” were overstated. Scientists have not confirmed the five‑second rule as accurate.

claim: Kobe Bryant's business ventures in China, posed a threat to the NBA's success.
response_text: FALSE.  Kobe Bryant’s activities in China—endorsements, annual tours, and partnerships (e.g., with Nike and a 2015 Alibaba deal to distribute content and sell merchandise)—boosted his and the NBA’s popularity there. There’s no credible evidence that his China ventures threatened the NBA’s success; if anything, they helped expand the league’s fan base. The major NBA-China tensions (e.g., 2019 Morey tweet) were unrelated to Bryant.

claim: Clorox and Lysol Already Knew About New Coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Disinfectant labels from brands like Clorox and Lysol listed “Human Coronavirus” long before COVID-19 because coronaviruses have been known since the 1960s (e.g., 229E, OC43, SARS, MERS). Those claims reflected efficacy against existing coronaviruses, not advance knowledge of the novel SARS‑CoV‑2 that emerged in late 2019.

claim: Kobe Bryant was assassinated by the NBA
response_text: FALSE.  Kobe Bryant died in an accidental helicopter crash on January 26, 2020. The NTSB concluded the probable cause was the pilot’s decision to continue flight into poor weather, leading to spatial disorientation and loss of control. There is no credible evidence of foul play or any involvement by the NBA.

claim: Viral newspaper clipping shows Arvind Kejriwal Was Accused Of Rape In College
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple Indian fact‑checkers (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today AFWA) have shown the “newspaper clipping” is a morphed/fabricated image. It uses anachronistic design elements and a much later photo of Arvind Kejriwal, and there is no credible archival or police record of him being accused of rape in college.

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) infographic advises people to avoid unprotected sex with animals to reduce their risk of contracting coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO’s guidance said to “avoid unprotected contact with live wild or farm animals” (i.e., handling animals without protective gear), not “unprotected sex.” The viral “sex with animals” version was a misinterpretation/edited meme of the original advice.

claim: The novel coronavirus has been found in Ethiopia.
response_text: TRUE. Ethiopia confirmed its first COVID-19 (novel coronavirus) case on March 13, 2020, and subsequently reported many cases (per Ethiopia’s Ministry of Health and WHO).

claim: In India, the health ministry warns people not to keep their throats dry and to avoid spicy and fried foods.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Messages claiming India’s Health Ministry advised “keep your throat moist (don’t let it dry)” and to avoid spicy/fried foods were widely circulated during COVID-19 but were debunked by official PIB Fact Check—no such general advisory was issued by MoHFW. Note: Some heatwave or AYUSH guidelines do suggest staying hydrated and avoiding oily/spicy foods, but that’s different from the specific “don’t keep your throat dry” warning attributed to the Health Ministry. Uncertainty: wording varies across different advisories.

claim: Punjab province in Pakistan issued a warning against eating goat meat for 60 days following a coronavirus outbreak in the livestock.
response_text: FALSE.  Punjab did not issue a 60‑day warning against eating goat meat due to a “coronavirus outbreak” in livestock. A fake notice with that claim circulated online during the COVID-19 pandemic and was publicly refuted by Punjab authorities; there was no official advisory and no evidence of SARS‑CoV‑2 spreading via goat meat.

claim: A Kenyan showing flu-like symptoms has been quarantined at the Kenyatta National Hospital
response_text: TRUE.  In late January 2020, a Kenyan student who had traveled from China and showed flu-like symptoms was isolated at Kenyatta National Hospital as a precaution during the early COVID-19 outbreak. Authorities confirmed the quarantine; subsequent tests were negative.

claim: People in Australia are warned not to consume certain foods made or held in neighbouring areas close to Wuhan China and to not visit certain locations in Sydney Australia to avoid the risk of becoming infected with coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Australian authorities did not issue advice to avoid foods made near Wuhan or to stay away from particular Sydney locations. NSW Health publicly stated that circulating messages listing Sydney suburbs to avoid were fake, and health agencies (including WHO/Australian authorities) said COVID‑19 was not spread via food or imported goods.

claim: American Muslim woman, Dr. Debbie Almontaser, made history by reciting the Koran during the inauguration ceremony of US President Joe Biden.
response_text: FALSE.  No Quran was recited at Joe Biden’s official inauguration ceremony, and Dr. Debbie Almontaser did not participate. The next day’s National Prayer Service included a Muslim prayer by Imam Azhar Subedar, not Almontaser. Some viral posts miscaption clips from other interfaith events as the inauguration.

claim: Namibian social media posts claim that Coronavirus is a hoax
response_text: TRUE.  There were indeed social media posts from Namibia claiming that Covid-19 was a hoax; local media and fact-checkers documented such misinformation. (The hoax claim itself is false—Covid-19 is real.)

claim: U.S. President Joe Biden has lowered the age of consent.
response_text: FALSE.  Age of consent laws are set by individual U.S. states, not by the President. There has been no federal law or executive action by President Biden lowering any age of consent, and federal statutes still treat anyone under 18 as a minor in sexual exploitation laws.

claim: Comedian, Samuel Whitcomb Hyde is behind the spread of Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Samuel Whitcomb “Sam” Hyde is an internet comedian frequently named in hoax memes falsely blaming him for various tragedies. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus and spread via human-to-human transmission; there is no evidence linking Hyde to its origin or spread. This claim is a meme-driven falsehood.

claim: American TV series 'The Simpsons' predicted the outbreak of Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  The Simpsons did not predict COVID-19. A 1993 episode (“Marge in Chains”) shows a fictional “Osaka Flu” from Japan spreading in Springfield; it’s not a coronavirus and has no link to COVID-19. Images claiming the show mentioned “coronavirus” are edited, and the “murder hornets” gag is a separate, coincidental joke.

claim: Nobody had ever even heard of Ebola before 2014
response_text: FALSE.  Ebola virus disease was first identified in 1976 (Sudan and Zaire/DRC) and caused several well-documented outbreaks before 2014 (e.g., 1995 Kikwit, 2000 Uganda). It was widely discussed in public and media too, including the 1994 bestseller “The Hot Zone,” so many people had heard of Ebola long before 2014.

claim: The Chinese Communist Party "will finally admit that the real source of the coronavirus is from ‘a lab in Wuhan’ linked to its covert biological weapon programs.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: There has been no admission by the Chinese government that COVID-19 came from a Wuhan lab, nor credible evidence that it was linked to a covert biological weapons program. U.S. intelligence assessments (ODNI, 2023–2024) state the virus was not developed as a biological weapon; agencies remain split, with low confidence, between natural spillover and a possible lab-related incident. WHO has likewise said the origin remains uncertain, with no evidence of a bioweapon. Uncertainty: the precise origin is still unresolved.

claim: A spray known as Miracle Mineral Solution can offer protection against coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  Miracle Mineral Solution (MMS) is essentially chlorine dioxide (a bleach). Health authorities including the FDA and WHO have warned it has no proven benefit against COVID-19 and can cause serious harm (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, low blood pressure, respiratory irritation). It does not protect against coronavirus.

claim: Doctors have expressed fears that the entire population of the Chinese city of Wuhan will die following the global outbreak of the 2019 Novel Coronavirus (2019-nCoV).
response_text: FALSE.  No credible source reported doctors saying Wuhan’s entire population would die. Fact-checkers debunked this rumor in early 2020. While Wuhan suffered thousands of deaths, it was nowhere near its ~11 million population.

claim: The coronavirus recently discovered in China was lab created and patented in 2015 by the CDC, the leading US public health agency.
response_text: FALSE.  - SARS‑CoV‑2 was first identified in 2019; there is no CDC patent from 2015 on it.  - The often-cited patents are either CDC/HHS patents from the mid‑2000s related to the original 2003 SARS virus (for sequencing/diagnostics) or a 2018 Pirbright Institute patent on avian coronavirus—neither involves SARS‑CoV‑2 or its “creation.” - Genetic analyses found no evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 was engineered.   Minor note: Some agencies have differing views on a possible lab leak origin, but that is not the same as lab creation or a 2015 CDC patent.

claim: Trump's lawyer Jay Sekulow says Trump’s hold on Ukraine aid is like Obama with Egypt in 2013
response_text: TRUE.  During Trump’s first impeachment defense in January 2020, Jay Sekulow cited President Obama’s 2013 suspension of some aid to Egypt as a comparison to Trump’s pause on Ukraine aid. (Fact-checkers later noted key differences between the two situations, but Sekulow did make the comparison.)

claim: Correct way” to wear a disposable blue and white face mask, coloured side out,(If you are sick & dont want to spread the germs around and white side out when you are not sick & want to keep germs from getting in.
response_text: FALSE.  Surgical/disposable masks are not reversible. They are designed to be worn with the colored side facing out and the white side in, regardless of whether you’re sick or trying to avoid getting sick. The outer colored layer is fluid‑repellent; the inner white layer is absorbent for your breath. Flipping it reduces effectiveness and is incorrect. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions (nose strip on top; pleats facing down).

claim: The average Wisconsin resident’s tax burden is at its lowest level in nearly 50 years, while incomes continue to grow.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Wisconsin Policy Forum analyses show the state-local tax burden (taxes as a share of personal income) has fallen to its lowest level since at least the 1970s—i.e., roughly a 50‑year low. Over the same period, personal incomes in Wisconsin have generally continued to grow (at least in nominal terms). Minor caveat: “average resident’s tax burden” is shorthand for this statewide measure, not an individual-by-individual calculation.

claim: iPhone belonging to Amazon CEO and Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos was hacked via a WhatsApp account used by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: It’s an allegation, not a proven fact. A consultant’s report for Bezos and UN rapporteurs said there was “credible” or “medium-to-high” confidence that data exfiltration began after Bezos received a WhatsApp message from a number used by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia denied it, independent experts criticized the forensics as inconclusive, and no official investigation has publicly confirmed the hack. Therefore the claim remains unproven.

claim: Google threatened to shut down search in Australia if they pass a digital news code.
response_text: TRUE.  In January 2021, during an Australian Senate hearing on the proposed News Media Bargaining Code, Google Australia’s managing director said that if the code became law as drafted, Google would have “no real choice but to stop making Google Search available in Australia.” Google later struck deals after amendments, so search remained, but the threat was made.

claim: Presidential candidate Joe Biden fought for decades to cut social security in the US.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden has at times backed deficit-reduction measures that touched Social Security (e.g., voting for the 1983 reforms that gradually raised the retirement age, and proposing/endorsing short-term spending freezes that would have included Social Security COLAs). He also supported bipartisan commissions that contemplated benefit changes. But he did not wage a sustained, decades-long campaign to cut Social Security; he opposed privatization under George W. Bush and, in recent years, has run on protecting and expanding benefits. Overall, the claim overstates and mischaracterizes his record.

claim: In 2018, US presidential candidate Joe Biden lauded Paul Ryan for proposing cuts to Social Security and Medicare
response_text: FALSE.  In a 2018 speech, Biden said “Paul Ryan was correct” in the sense that Republicans would use the deficit from their tax cuts as a pretext to target Social Security and Medicare. He was criticizing that strategy, not praising cuts. He also wasn’t a declared presidential candidate in 2018. Fact-checks by PolitiFact and Snopes reached the same conclusion.

claim: Man accused of sexual Harassment of minor girls is a muslim.
response_text: FALSE — Unsubstantiated. The claim gives no case details or reliable sources to verify the person’s religion. Without specific, credible reporting confirming this, asserting the accused is Muslim is not supported.

claim: In the Senate trial, not even House Intelligence Chairman Adam Schiff’s Republican colleagues were allowed into the SCIF during the House impeachment investigation.
response_text: FALSE.  Republican members of the committees conducting the depositions (Intelligence, Oversight, and Foreign Affairs) were allowed into the SCIF and participated in questioning. Only non-committee Republicans were barred, which is standard practice for closed depositions. Several GOP committee members (e.g., Devin Nunes, Elise Stefanik, John Ratcliffe, Mark Meadows) attended; the “storming” incident involved Republicans who were not on those committees.

claim: Gold fringe on a U.S. flag signifies maritime and martial law is in effect.
response_text: FALSE.  Gold fringe on a U.S. flag is purely decorative for indoor and ceremonial use and has no legal significance. The U.S. Army’s regulations and the Institute of Heraldry describe fringe as an “honorable enrichment,” not part of the flag itself. Courts have repeatedly rejected claims that fringe signals admiralty/maritime or martial law; jurisdiction is determined by law and subject matter, not by flag adornments.

claim: Biden Is The First President to Denounce White Supremacy in His Inaugural Address?
response_text: TRUE.  Biden’s 2021 inaugural is the first known to explicitly denounce “white supremacy” by name (“a rise of political extremism, white supremacy…”). Earlier presidents condemned racism or defended civil rights in inaugurals (e.g., Grant, Truman, LBJ, Obama), but available transcripts don’t show them using or directly denouncing the term “white supremacy.” Minor uncertainty if “denounce” is taken to include broader, non-explicit language.

claim: Witnesses have been part of "every other impeachment trial the US Senate has ever had.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In every completed Senate impeachment trial before Donald Trump’s, the Senate heard witness testimony—either live before the full Senate or via Rule XI trial committees and depositions (e.g., Andrew Johnson 1868, Belknap 1876, numerous judicial impeachments, and Bill Clinton 1999 with videotaped depositions). Proceedings that lacked witnesses were typically dismissals or ended due to resignation, not full trials. Trump’s 2020 (and 2021) trials were the first without witnesses.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria gained independence on 1 Oct 1960, and UN demographic estimates put its 1960 population at about 45 million (~45.1m). While censuses around that period were contested, “about 45 million” is a widely accepted estimate.

claim: 52% of Nigeria’s current population lives in urban areas
response_text: TRUE  Recent estimates from sources like the UN and World Bank put Nigeria’s urban population share at roughly 52–53% in 2022–2023, trending upward. So 52% is a reasonable rounded figure, though the latest value may be slightly higher.

claim: Barack Obama had $3 million before running for president and $40 million after.
response_text: FALSE.  - Before running (2006–2007), Obama’s Senate/ethics disclosures put his assets roughly in the low millions at most (about $1–2.5 million, not a documented $3 million). - Upon leaving office, his final presidential financial disclosure (2015) showed assets in broad ranges that translate to roughly $2–8 million net—far short of $40 million. - The $40 million figure comes from speculative celebrity net-worth estimates. While post‑presidency book, speaking, and media deals likely boosted the Obamas’ combined wealth substantially, there’s no official evidence that Barack Obama personally had $40 million “after.”  Note: Net-worth figures are imprecise because disclosures report ranges, not exact amounts.

claim: Nigeria’s urban population at independence was approximately 7 million
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: At independence in 1960, Nigeria’s total population was about 45 million. UN/World Bank estimates put the urban share around 15–16% then, implying roughly 6.8–7.3 million urban residents. So “approximately 7 million” is consistent. (Exact figures vary by source.)

claim: Nigeria has a population exceeding 200 million.
response_text: TRUE.  Most recent estimates (e.g., UN and World Bank) place Nigeria’s population around 220–225 million, clearly above 200 million.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of 60 years of existence as a nation, Nigeria has been under military rule.
response_text: TRUE.  - Military rule periods:   - Jan 15, 1966 – Oct 1, 1979 ≈ 13.7 years   - Dec 31, 1983 – Aug 26, 1993 ≈ 9.7 years   - Nov 17, 1993 – May 29, 1999 ≈ 5.5 years - Total ≈ 28.9 years, i.e., about 29 years out of Nigeria’s first 60 years (1960–2020).

claim: There was a 40% drop in oil prices
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The claim lacks a timeframe and benchmark (WTI or Brent). In recent years there hasn’t been a 40% drop; swings since 2022 have been smaller. While oil did fall by ~40% or more during specific past episodes (e.g., 2014–15, early 2020), the statement as given is too vague and not supported for the current period. Uncertainty: true only in certain historical contexts.

claim: All data relating to Qwikloan have been lost and cannot be restored
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There are no credible or widely reported sources indicating that all Qwikloan data were irretrievably lost. Such a total, permanent data loss would likely prompt prominent public statements and coverage. Absent specific, verifiable evidence, this absolute claim is unsubstantiated. (Some uncertainty remains without a cited incident/date.)

claim: Colloidal silver is effective for any infection when applied topically and taken orally and can be used to fight infections and heal wounds, support the immune system, and eliminate nasty germs
response_text: FALSE  - No credible clinical evidence shows oral colloidal silver treats infections, boosts immunity, or “eliminates germs.” The FDA has ruled OTC colloidal silver products are not safe or effective for any disease, and NCCIH states there’s no proven health benefit. - Oral use can cause serious harms (e.g., argyria/skin discoloration, kidney and neurologic problems) and drug interactions. - While some silver-containing topical dressings have limited, specific uses to reduce bioburden in certain wounds, they are not colloidal silver and do not justify the claim of effectiveness for “any infection” or general immune support.

claim: The NHS operate on the wrong part of someone’s body four times a day.
response_text: FALSE.  NHS England’s “never events” data show wrong‑site surgery happens on the order of a few hundred times per year—roughly 4–6 times a week—not four times a day (~1,400/year). The “four times a day” figure has sometimes referred to all never events combined, not specifically operating on the wrong body part. Numbers vary by year, but are nowhere near 4/day for wrong‑site surgery. (Slight uncertainty due to year‑to‑year variation.)

claim: A casting call for crisis actors coincided with a pro-gun rally in Virginia on 16th January 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Virginia gun-rights rally in Richmond was on January 20, 2020, not January 16. - Viral posts claiming a “crisis actors” casting call were based on misrepresented or unrelated listings (some older, some not in Virginia). Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) found no credible evidence of a casting call tied to the rally.

claim: Elizabeth Warren is the only person out of the six candidates for the US presidency on stage at the January 2020 debate in Iowa, who has beaten an incumbent Republican in the past 30 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Elizabeth Warren did defeat an incumbent Republican (Sen. Scott Brown in 2012), but Bernie Sanders also defeated an incumbent Republican within the past 30 years—Rep. Peter P. Smith in Vermont’s at-large U.S. House race in 1990. Therefore, Warren was not the only candidate on that stage to have done so.

claim: The remaining male candidates for the US presidency in January 2020 (Pete Buttigieg, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders, Tom Steyer) have collectively lost 10 elections.
response_text: TRUE.  Breakdown (using common counts of “elections lost,” including party elections and unsuccessful presidential bids): - Bernie Sanders: 6 losses (VT: 1972 U.S. Senate special; 1972 Governor; 1974 U.S. Senate; 1976 Governor; 1988 U.S. House; 2016 Democratic presidential primary). - Joe Biden: 2 (unsuccessful presidential runs in 1988 and 2008). - Pete Buttigieg: 2 (2010 Indiana state treasurer; 2017 DNC chair). - Tom Steyer: 0.  Total = 10. Note: If one counts only public, voted elections, excluding Biden’s 1988 run (dropped before voting) and Buttigieg’s DNC chair bid (withdrew before voting), the total would be lower (about 8).

claim: Emeka Ihedioha won just 9 LGAs and lost in 18 during the 2020 elections.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There was no “2020” Imo governorship election. Emeka Ihedioha was elected in the March 2019 Imo governorship poll. In that election he topped the vote and won more than 9 of the state’s 27 LGAs (commonly reported as about 11–12 LGAs), not just 9. The claim misstates both the year and the LGA count. (Minor uncertainty exists over exact LGA breakdown across sources, but it is clearly above 9.)

claim: Former U.S President Barack Obama said "He's low risk" in reference to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi before he was released from U.S custody.
response_text: FALSE.  Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi was detained by U.S. forces at Camp Bucca in 2004 and released that same year under the George W. Bush administration, not Obama. There is no credible record of Barack Obama saying “he’s low risk” about Baghdadi or being involved in his release. (Some reports once cited a 2009 release, but the Pentagon later clarified the 2004 date.)

claim: Senator Bernie Saunders told a Democratic presidential primary debate that the healthcare industry makes $100 billion a year.
response_text: TRUE.  Bernie Sanders (not “Saunders”) said during the Feb. 7, 2020 New Hampshire Democratic primary debate that the health care industry makes about $100 billion a year in profits. He framed it as “the function of a rational health care system is not to make $100 billion in profits,” referring to combined profits across sectors like drug and insurance companies.

claim: Patrick Mahomes thinks George Zimmerman is innocent.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Patrick Mahomes saying George Zimmerman is “innocent.” Old, widely shared posts misrepresented 2013 tweets in which Mahomes referenced the trial verdict (not guilty) without endorsing Zimmerman’s innocence. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) found no evidence he expressed that view.

claim: The remaining female candidates for the US presidency in January 2020, Elizabeth Warren and Amy Klobuchar, have won every election they have been in.
response_text: FALSE.  - In January 2020, Tulsi Gabbard was also still a female presidential candidate, so it wasn’t just Warren and Klobuchar. - It is true that both Warren and Klobuchar had never lost an election up to that point, but the claim’s premise about the “remaining female candidates” is incorrect.

claim: Nigeria’s cancer cases are about 15% of all cases in West Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  Best available estimates (IARC/WHO GLOBOCAN) put Nigeria at roughly 120–130k new cancer cases annually, while West Africa as a whole has around 220–240k. That means Nigeria accounts for about 50–55% of West Africa’s cancer cases, not ~15%. Uncertainty: low.

claim: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa has ordered an investigation into the whereabouts of state-owned goods, including a bus and “other priceless, high technological equipment”.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The order to investigate missing state-owned property — “including a bus and other priceless, high technological equipment” — came from Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe’s office in July 2022 after protesters occupied official residences. It was not ordered by President Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who had fled the country and soon resigned at that time.

claim: Indian Oil is now owned by the Adani group.
response_text: FALSE.  Indian Oil Corporation is a government-owned public sector undertaking under India’s Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. The Government of India holds the controlling stake (over 51%). It has not been acquired by the Adani Group.

claim: Iain Duncan Smith has been awarded a knighthood for services to the country.
response_text: TRUE.  Iain Duncan Smith was knighted in the 2020 New Year Honours. The official citation was for “political and public service,” commonly described as services to the country.

claim: 6 months ago the DWP promised a review of Universal Credit for the terminally ill.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In July 2019 the UK government/DWP announced a review of the “special rules for terminal illness” (the six‑month rule) across benefits, including Universal Credit. So a claim made six months later that the DWP had promised such a review is accurate. (Exact accuracy depends on when the claim was made.)

claim: Jussie Smollett Charges Reinstated
response_text: TRUE.  After the initial 2019 charges were dropped, a special prosecutor secured a new indictment in February 2020 on six counts related to filing false police reports—effectively “reinstating” charges (though technically they were new counts rather than the exact original ones). He was later convicted on most counts in 2021.

claim: Each month 22 NHS patients with glaucoma unnecessarily lose their sight due to NHS treatment delays.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: The widely quoted “22 per month” figure comes from Royal College of Ophthalmologists/NHS patient-safety reports estimating at least 22 patients a month suffer severe sight loss due to hospital-initiated delays in ophthalmology follow‑up across all eye conditions. It is not specific to glaucoma, and the category is “severe sight loss (including blindness),” not all losing all sight. So the claim overstates and misattributes the statistic.  Uncertainty: The estimate is from past analyses; current rates may differ.

claim: Rep. Ilhan Omar said, “There is no way to overstate how ASHAMED I am to be called an ‘American.’ We need every world leader to rise and demand that someone stops Trump from starting a catastrophic war with Iran. THE TIME FOR VIOLENCE IS NOW!
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is fabricated. No credible record (news, transcripts, tweets) shows Rep. Ilhan Omar saying she was “ashamed to be called an American” or that “the time for violence is now.” Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) have debunked this meme, which traces to satirical/misleading pages. In reality, Omar’s public statements about Iran in early 2020 called for de-escalation and congressional oversight, not violence.

claim: Nancy Pelosi defended Qassem Soleimani, Iran's top military commander.
response_text: FALSE.  Pelosi did not defend Qassem Soleimani. After the U.S. strike in January 2020, she criticized the Trump administration for acting without congressional authorization and questioned the claimed “imminent” threat. But she characterized Soleimani as a terrorist and a killer responsible for deaths; her objections were about process and escalation risk, not a defense of him.

claim: Volcanoes Melting West Antarctic Glaciers, Not Global Warming. Three new research studies confirm that geothermal heat flow, not man-made global warming, is the dominant cause of West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) melting.
response_text: FALSE.  Geothermal heat and subglacial volcanism do exist beneath parts of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet and can cause localized basal melting, but they are not the dominant driver of the recent, rapid ice loss. Observations and modeling show that most WAIS thinning and grounding-line retreat are driven by warm ocean water (Circumpolar Deep Water) melting ice shelves from below—processes linked to anthropogenic climate change altering winds and ocean circulation. Typical geothermal fluxes produce melt rates orders of magnitude smaller than ocean-driven melt and cannot explain the rapid, widespread changes seen in recent decades. Major assessments (e.g., IPCC AR6) and peer‑reviewed studies do not conclude that volcanoes are the main cause.

claim: Olive Garden Revoke 'Never Ending Pasta Pass' For Sean Hannity And Capitol Insurrectionists
response_text: FALSE.  This originated as a satirical/viral post during January 2021. There’s no evidence Olive Garden revoked “Never Ending Pasta Passes” for Sean Hannity or Capitol rioters, and the company publicly denied doing so. Fact-checkers also debunked the claim.

claim: Iran’s hostilities substantially increased after the foolish Iran nuclear deal was signed in 2013 and they were given $150 billion, not to mention $1.8 billion in cash
response_text: FALSE.  - The Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) was concluded in July 2015 and implemented in January 2016, not 2013 (2013 saw only an interim accord). - The U.S. did not “give” Iran $150 billion; sanctions relief unfroze Iran’s own overseas assets.
