U.S. Treasury estimates put Iran’s accessible funds at roughly $50 billion, far below $150 billion. - The “$1.8 billion in cash” refers to a legal settlement over a pre-1979 arms deal; the amount was about $1.7 billion, much of it paid in cash due to sanctions. - Claims that Iran’s “hostilities substantially increased” because of the deal are not well supported; Iran’s regional activities predated the JCPOA, some indicators rose and others fell, and major escalations came after the U.S. left the deal in 2018.  Overall, the statement misstates the timing, exaggerates/mischaracterizes the money, and makes an unsupported claim about hostilities.

claim: By the way, in terms of the money, it got there two or three weeks ahead of schedule, long before it was supposed to be there
response_text: FALSE.  Context: This line refers to 2019 U.S. security assistance to Ukraine. The White House, via OMB, withheld the aid from late July until Sept. 11, 2019. It was released only weeks before the Sept. 30 fiscal-year deadline—after a delay, not “ahead of schedule.” The GAO later found the withholding violated the Impoundment Control Act, and about $35 million required a late extension to be obligated.

claim: Trump-Owned Property In Agrabah Burned To The Ground By Terrorists
response_text: FALSE.  Agrabah is a fictional city from Disney’s Aladdin. No Trump-owned property exists there; the headline is a satirical joke, not a real event.

claim: Ratan Tata has stated that Tata Group will not recruit students from Jawaharlal Nehru University.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Ratan Tata making such a statement. In early 2020, a viral post claimed he said Tata Group would not hire from JNU, but Tata Group/Ratan Tata’s office publicly denied it as fake. Multiple Indian fact-checkers also debunked the claim.

claim: Nancy Pelosi assured Iran that Trump will "pay for his crimes."
response_text: FALSE.  This claim traces to a fabricated/satirical article and there is no credible evidence Pelosi told Iran that Trump would “pay for his crimes.” Pelosi’s public statements after the Soleimani strike criticized the administration’s actions and called for congressional oversight, but she did not make such an assurance to Iran. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes/PolitiFact) have debunked the claim.

claim: There are only DUP members (who are/were members of a Northern Ireland political party) in the House of Lords.
response_text: FALSE.  There are peers in the House of Lords from other Northern Ireland parties besides the DUP. Examples: - Lord Alderdice (John Alderdice), former leader of the Alliance Party. - Lord Empey (Reg Empey), former leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP). - Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick (Margaret Ritchie), former leader of the SDLP.  These show that not only DUP members (past or present) from Northern Ireland parties sit in the Lords.

claim: Saudi's rent the entire 45th floor of Trump Tower, And pay him in cash.
response_text: FALSE.  Reports show the Saudi government purchased (owned) multiple units comprising much of the 45th floor of Trump World Tower (845 United Nations Plaza) around 2001— a different building from Trump Tower on Fifth Avenue. That’s ownership, not renting, and there’s no credible reporting that they “pay him in cash.”

claim: Nancy Pelosi Said Trump Must Apologize To Iran "Or Else".
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Pelosi saying Trump must “apologize to Iran.” The quote originated in a satirical/hoax article from the America’s Last Line of Defense network and was spread as if real. Pelosi criticized Trump’s actions around Iran but did not issue such an ultimatum.

claim: New York is trying to pass a bill that would place non mask wearers and unvaccinated people in concentration camps for forced vaccination.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This rumor misrepresents a New York proposal (A416). That bill would have allowed health officials, during a declared public health emergency, to order isolation/quarantine of people who were cases/contacts/carriers of a dangerous disease, with due process. It did not target “non-mask wearers” or “the unvaccinated,” did not create “concentration camps,” and did not become law (it was withdrawn).

claim: Amy Klobuchar has won Michele Bachmann's district every one of her 3 U.S Senate campaigns.
response_text: FALSE.  Amy Klobuchar did not carry Minnesota’s 6th Congressional District in her first Senate race in 2006; Republican Mark Kennedy, the then-incumbent MN‑6 U.S. Representative, won his home district in that contest. Klobuchar did carry MN‑6 in her 2012 and 2018 landslide reelections. (Note: district lines changed after 2010, but either way she didn’t win MN‑6 in all three campaigns.)

claim: Iihan Omar tweeted "There is no way to overstate how ASHAMED I am to be called an 'American'. We need every world leader to rise up and demand that someone stops Trump from starting a catastrophic war with Iran." THE TIME FOR VIOLENCE IS NOW! #NoWarWithIran
response_text: FALSE.  - No record of this tweet exists in Rep. Ilhan Omar’s timeline or archives. - Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, AFP) debunked circulating images of this supposed tweet as fabricated, noting telltale spoof details (look‑alike handle and formatting inconsistencies). - Omar publicly called for de-escalation and diplomacy during the Iran tensions; she did not advocate violence or say she was “ashamed to be called an American.”

claim: Donald Trump was given $413 million from his dad over the course of his career.
response_text: TRUE  A 2018 New York Times investigation, based on extensive tax records, found that Donald Trump received at least $413 million (in 2018 dollars) from his father Fred Trump over decades through gifts, loans, bailouts, and inheritance. The figure is inflation-adjusted and an estimate; Trump has disputed it, but the reporting is widely cited and won a Pulitzer.

claim: Trump had not brought pharmaceutical costs down, as he claimed he would, in May 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: By May 2019 there was no broad, durable decline in prescription drug costs attributable to Trump’s policies. Brand-name list prices were still rising (albeit more slowly), and overall prescription drug prices remained above their level when he took office. A brief year-over-year dip in the CPI for prescription drugs in early 2019 was small and not clearly linked to his actions. (Minor uncertainty stems from that short-term CPI dip.)

claim: A biodiesel plant in Crawfordsville, Iowa, closed, "partly due to the trade war but mostly due to the waivers that Trump secretly gave to the oil companies"
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: The W2 Fuel biodiesel plant in Crawfordsville, Iowa, idled/closed in 2019. Company statements and industry groups cited the surge in EPA small refinery exemptions (SREs) under the Trump administration—which reduced biofuel blending demand—as a key reason, along with the lapse of the $1/gal biodiesel tax credit; the trade war compounded market pressures. At the time, EPA did not publicly name the refineries receiving SREs, so critics labeled them “secret” waivers. Note: apportioning “mostly” is somewhat subjective since the expired tax credit was also a major factor.

claim: There are 64 mental health beds in the state of Iowa.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “64” figure typically refers to the limited number of state-operated adult acute psychiatric beds at Iowa’s two Mental Health Institutes. Statewide, including beds in private and general hospitals, Iowa has several hundred psychiatric/mental health beds—far more than 64. The claim, as stated, is misleading without that context.

claim: A non-profit, public health care option was Barack Obama's plan from the beginning of his presidency.
response_text: TRUE.  Obama’s 2008 campaign plan included a public insurance option, and early in his presidency he voiced support for giving Americans the choice of a public plan (e.g., his June 2009 letter to Congress). He later signaled it wasn’t a dealbreaker, and the final ACA did not include a public option, but it was part of his initial plan.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Americans do not need a licence to drive automobiles on public roads
response_text: FALSE.  The Supreme Court has never ruled that Americans can drive on public roads without a license. To the contrary, it has repeatedly upheld states’ authority to require driver licensing and vehicle registration as valid safety regulations, e.g., Hendrick v. Maryland (1915), Kane v. New Jersey (1916), and Reitz v. Mealey (1941). The constitutional “right to travel” does not eliminate licensing requirements for operating motor vehicles.

claim: Mayor Bloomberg helped lower the number of people without health insurance in New York, by 40 percent.
response_text: FALSE.  During Bloomberg’s tenure (2002–2013), the uninsured rate in New York fell, but not by 40%. The roughly 40% drop in the number/rate of uninsured occurred after 2013 with the Affordable Care Act’s coverage expansions. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by survey and subgroup, but no reliable series shows a 40% overall decline attributable to Bloomberg’s years.

claim: NASA had 58% Indian employees
response_text: FALSE.  - NASA civil-service jobs require U.S. citizenship, so Indian citizens generally cannot be NASA employees.   - NASA’s official workforce data show Asians (all Asian origins combined) are about 8–9% of NASA’s civil-servant workforce, with “Indian” not a separate category; the share of employees of Indian origin would be a subset of that, nowhere near 58%.   - This widely circulated claim is a long-debunked myth.

claim: CO-2 is not a greenhouse gas.
response_text: FALSE.  Assuming “CO-2” means CO2 (carbon dioxide): CO2 is a greenhouse gas. It absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation (notably around 15 micrometers), trapping heat in the atmosphere; this is confirmed by laboratory spectra, atmospheric measurements, and satellite observations. If “CO-2” was a typo for CO (carbon monoxide), CO is not a strong greenhouse gas itself but has indirect warming effects by influencing methane and ozone.

claim: Former secretary of state Hillary Clinton let four Americans die in Benghazi.
response_text: FALSE.  Four Americans were killed in the 2012 Benghazi attacks, but multiple investigations—including the State Department’s independent Accountability Review Board (2012), the Republican‑led House Select Committee on Benghazi (2016), and the Senate Intelligence Committee—found no evidence that Hillary Clinton knowingly withheld help, ordered a stand‑down, or otherwise “let” them die. Findings cited systemic security failures within the State Department below the secretary’s level and concluded available military assets could not have arrived in time to prevent the deaths.

claim: Trump rushed in reinforcements.
response_text: FALSE  Assuming this refers to the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack: evidence and official timelines show Trump did not quickly order reinforcements; the National Guard was activated by Pentagon and DC officials after delays, with key calls made by others (e.g., the Vice President). If a different event was meant, more context would be needed.

claim: Trump Threatened to destroy Iran.
response_text: TRUE.  In May 2019, Trump tweeted: “If Iran wants to fight, that will be the official end of Iran. Never threaten the United States again!” He also said a war would mean “obliteration like you’ve never seen before” for Iran (June 2019). While he didn’t use the exact words “destroy Iran,” these statements clearly threatened Iran’s annihilation.

claim: Hot temperatures in a car can cause hand sanitiser to catch fire without a spark.
response_text: FALSE.  Hand sanitizers (typically 60–70% ethanol or isopropanol) are flammable, but they do not spontaneously ignite from hot car temperatures. Their autoignition temperatures are roughly 365–400°C (689–752°F), far higher than the 50–90°C (122–194°F) a hot car might reach. Heat can increase vapor buildup, so vapors can ignite if exposed to a spark or flame, but heat alone won’t make them catch fire.

claim: California is refusing to cooperate with the “Federal Election Integrity Program.”
response_text: TRUE  Context: In 2017, California refused to provide voter data to the Trump administration’s Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity (often referred to as a federal “election integrity” effort). California’s Secretary of State Alex Padilla publicly declined to cooperate. Note: that commission was disbanded in January 2018, so there is no ongoing federal program by that name today.

claim: There have been 317 criminal indictments under three recent Republican presidents and only three indictments under three recent Democratic presidents.
response_text: FALSE.  Those numbers come from a viral meme and don’t hold up under any consistent definition. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, AP) have shown: - Republican administrations of Reagan, George H.W. Bush, and George W. Bush saw several dozen indictments of officials (Iran‑Contra, HUD, etc.), not hundreds. - Democratic administrations of Carter, Clinton, and Obama had more than three indictments (e.g., Mike Espy, Henry Cisneros, Web Hubbell, and others during the Clinton years alone).  Totals vary with what you count, but no credible tally supports “317 vs. 3.”

claim: Nigeria owed its foreign creditors $81.274 billion in 2019, despite being “debt free” in 2007 after all its external loans were “paid off”.
response_text: FALSE.  - The $81.274 billion figure in 2019 refers to Nigeria’s total public debt (domestic + external), not what it owed “foreign creditors.” Nigeria’s external (foreign) public debt in 2019 was about $27.7 billion (DMO data). - Nigeria was not “debt free” in 2007. After the 2005–06 Paris Club deal, it cleared Paris Club debts but still had several billion dollars in external obligations (e.g., multilateral loans).

claim: A 13-year-old boy attacked at a northern California skate park by Hispanic youths because he was white and a supporter of President Trump.
response_text: FALSE.  This story circulated on partisan/hoax sites after the 2016 election and used misattributed photos. Local police in Northern California reported no evidence of a politically motivated assault at a skate park matching this description, and fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) debunked the claim. Uncertainty: none beyond typical limits of archived reports.

claim: Aysha Renna tweeted a comment celebrating the Pulwama attack in India.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks (Alt News, BOOM, India Today AFWA, Factly, The Quint) found the “Pulwama celebration” tweet attributed to Aysha Renna was a fabricated screenshot. Her verified account was created months after the February 2019 attack, making such a tweet impossible, and no credible record shows she posted anything celebrating the attack.

claim: An irrational House Speaker Nancy Pelosi was handcuffed by federal agents as they raided her office.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence or news reporting that federal agents raided Nancy Pelosi’s office or handcuffed her. The claim originated from a satirical/hoax website and has been debunked by fact-checkers. An event of that magnitude would have been widely covered by reliable media; it wasn’t.

claim: There is a phone scam in which "these guys only ring once and hang up," and if you call back, they can copy your contact list in three seconds as well as your bank or credit details.
response_text: FALSE.  There is a real “one ring” (Wangiri) scam where scammers let the phone ring once to prompt a callback to a premium-rate or international number, leading to hefty charges. But calling back does not let them automatically copy your contacts or bank/credit details—phone calls don’t grant that kind of access. Data theft would require you to install malware or voluntarily share information.

claim: Pervez Musharraf led a Pakistani commando unit to flush out rebels occupying the Grand Mosque in Mecca, Saudi Arabia in 1979.
response_text: FALSE.  - Saudi forces led the 1979 Grand Mosque retaking, with limited foreign assistance (e.g., French GIGN advisors and reportedly some Pakistani SSG help). - There is no credible record that Pervez Musharraf led any unit in the operation. His service record shows he left the SSG years earlier (he served in SSG in the late 1960s–early 1970s) and was a lieutenant colonel in artillery/staff roles in 1979. - Online claims to the contrary are not supported by reliable sources.

claim: Actress Parineeti Chopra's role as brand ambassador for the 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' campaign was cut short after she tweeted condemning the violence against the anti- Citizen Amendment Act protestors.
response_text: FALSE.  Context: Reports in Dec 2019 claimed Haryana “dropped” Parineeti Chopra as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao brand ambassador after her tweet against violence on anti-CAA protesters. However, the Haryana Women and Child Development Department clarified her state-level BBBP contract had already ended months earlier (well before the CAA protests) and was not terminated because of the tweet.

claim: Hong Kong uses AI technology using facial recognition to identify protesters if they so much as do anything on the street, so they can follow up with them and detain them later.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Hong Kong authorities use extensive surveillance (CCTV, phone/computer searches, online monitoring, Octopus/transport records, ANPR, tips) and have arrested people later using reviewed footage. But there’s no public evidence of a citywide, automated facial-recognition system identifying protesters on the street in real time. Officials and the privacy regulator have said police did not deploy facial recognition for crowd control; “smart lampposts” were audited as not using FR. Some limited or trial use of facial-recognition tools for investigative, post-event matching has been reported, but the blanket claim of ubiquitous AI FR tracking anyone “doing anything on the street” is unsubstantiated. Uncertainty: specific investigative uses may occur but are not the pervasive system described.

claim: The sixth Democratic presidential debate of the 2020 campaign, hosted by PBS and Politico, had seven candidates, lasted more than 2½ hours — and did not have many statements that merited fact-checking. Here are six claims that caught our attention, some of which may seem familiar from previous debates. Our practice is not to award Pinocchios in debate roundups.
response_text: FALSE.  - Correct: The sixth 2020 Democratic debate (Dec. 19, 2019) was hosted by PBS and Politico and had seven candidates. The Washington Post Fact Checker typically says it doesn’t award Pinocchios in debate roundups and highlighted six claims. - Incorrect: The debate did not last more than 2½ hours; it ran about two hours (roughly a bit over two hours at most), not exceeding 2:30.   Minor uncertainty: exact end time reports vary by a few minutes, but not beyond 2½ hours.

claim: 50 Journalists who were in Mangaluru to cover anti-Citizenship Amendment Act protests were fake journalists that had come from Kerala and have been arrested.
response_text: FALSE.  Mangaluru Police denied arresting “50 fake journalists.” Fact-checks and police statements from December 2019 said no such arrests took place. Around 30 people were briefly detained for verification in the city and about 58 people from Kerala were turned back at the border during curfew, but they were not journalists and were not arrested. Some journalists were stopped and asked for IDs, but there was no mass arrest of “fake journalists.”

claim: Hong Kong has banned protesters from wearing face masks.
response_text: TRUE.  In October 2019, Hong Kong invoked emergency powers to prohibit face coverings at public assemblies. Courts later upheld the ban for unauthorized/illegal assemblies (while striking it down for approved ones), with exemptions (e.g., health, work, religion). So protesters at unauthorized gatherings can be barred from wearing masks.

claim: Before he was mayor, Pete Buttigieg ran statewide in Indiana and lost by 20 points.
response_text: TRUE — with a caveat. Before becoming South Bend’s mayor, Buttigieg ran statewide in 2010 for Indiana state treasurer and lost to Republican Richard Mourdock. The margin was closer to 24–25 points (about 62.5% to 37.5%), not exactly 20.

claim: Donald Trump is rated international public opinion polls below Xi Jinping.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple Pew Research Center global surveys during Trump’s presidency found lower median “confidence in” ratings for Donald Trump than for Xi Jinping. For example: - 2017 (37 countries): Trump 22% vs. Xi 28%. - 2020 (13 advanced economies): Trump 16% vs. Xi 19%.  Note: Results vary by year and sample; in some surveys the gap was small or occasionally reversed, but overall Trump was often rated below Xi.

claim: Real wages went up last year 1.1%
response_text: TRUE  BLS data show real wages rose by about 1% over the most recent year, with year‑over‑year gains ranging roughly 0.8% (all employees) to about 1.1% (production/nonsupervisory), depending on the measure and exact period. Slight uncertainty stems from which series and timeframe (“last year”) is used.

claim: Heavy Artillery in Donbas comes from sympathetic governments and not Russia.
response_text: FALSE.  Extensive independent evidence shows Russia supplied and operated heavy weapons in Donbas. OSCE monitors, NATO/US satellite imagery (2014), and investigations (e.g., JIT on MH17, Bellingcat) documented Russian-origin systems and cross‑border artillery fire, including equipment not in Ukraine’s inventory (e.g., T‑72B3 tanks, Pantsir-S1, modern EW systems; the MH17 Buk traced to Russia’s 53rd Brigade). While some arms were captured from Ukrainian stocks, there’s no credible record of “sympathetic governments” other than Russia providing heavy artillery to the separatists, and from 2022 Russia’s regular forces openly used heavy artillery in Donbas.

claim: Former European Commission president, Jean-Claude Juncker said that "the world's most foolish voters are from India"
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Jean‑Claude Juncker ever said this. Searches of his speeches and interviews and multiple fact-checks (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today AFWA) found no such remark, and the EU’s representation in India publicly denied the quote as fake when it went viral. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Pete Buttigieg won voting with 80% in Indiana.
response_text: FALSE.  He never won 80% of the vote statewide in Indiana. The “80%” figure refers to his 2015 re-election as mayor of South Bend, where he won about 80% of the vote in the city—not statewide.

claim: Elizabeth Warren proposed tax for the wealthy is two percent for millionaires and billionaires
response_text: FALSE.  Warren’s “Ultra-Millionaire Tax” proposed a 2% annual tax on net worth above $50 million, with a higher rate for billionaires (3% originally, later proposed to rise to 6%). It did not levy 2% on billionaires, nor did it apply to ordinary millionaires below $50 million.

claim: Donald Trump did not support the people in Hong Kong standing up for democracy.
Failed Senate Impeachment Conviction Means Trump Can Run Two More Times
response_text: FALSE.  The 22nd Amendment limits a person to being elected president no more than twice. Impeachment acquittal does not reset or expand that limit. While a Senate conviction could have allowed a separate vote to disqualify him from future office, failing to convict only leaves him eligible under the normal two-term cap—meaning, after being elected once in 2016, he could be elected at most one more time, not two.

claim: China produces ninety percent of global carbon emissions.
response_text: FALSE.  China is the largest emitter, but it produces about 30% of annual global CO2 emissions, not 90%. For example, recent estimates (Global Carbon Project/IEA) put China around 30–31%, the U.S. ~14%, the EU ~7%, and India ~7%. No single country comes close to 90% of global emissions.

claim: RBI has said that ₹2000 notes are banned and ₹1000 notes have been introduced
response_text: FALSE.  - RBI has not “banned” ₹2000 notes. In May 2023 it announced their withdrawal from circulation under the Clean Note Policy, but they remain legal tender and can be exchanged at RBI Issue Offices. - RBI has not introduced new ₹1000 notes since the 2016 demonetization; reports of reintroduction have been officially denied.  Source: RBI press release “Withdrawal of ₹2000 banknotes” (May 19, 2023) and subsequent RBI updates.

claim: RBI said you can exchange ₹2000 notes only up to the amount of ₹50,000
response_text: FALSE.  RBI’s guideline for exchanging ₹2000 notes over the counter was ₹20,000 “at a time,” not ₹50,000. Depositing ₹2000 notes into bank accounts was allowed without a specific monetary cap (subject to KYC/AML rules). After Oct 8, 2023, exchanges continued at RBI Issue Offices with the same ₹20,000-at-a-time cap. No RBI rule set a ₹50,000 exchange limit.

claim: The Reserve Bank of India said from 1st January 2020, they are going to implement new ₹1000 note
response_text: FALSE.  RBI never announced a new ₹1000 note for 1 January 2020. After the 2016 demonetization, ₹1000 notes were withdrawn and have not been reintroduced. Viral images and posts in late 2019 claiming a new ₹1000 note were debunked by official fact-checks; RBI issued no such notification.

claim: Koalas are functionally extinct because bushfires have continued to destroy their habitat
response_text: FALSE.  Koalas suffered major declines and habitat loss—especially in the 2019–20 bushfires—and are listed as Endangered in parts of eastern Australia. But they are not “functionally extinct” overall: tens of thousands remain, they are reproducing, and still play ecological roles. Some local populations may be severely reduced or locally extinct, but the species as a whole is not functionally extinct.

claim: A TMZ news alert claimed 4 people died and 12 were injured after singer Melissa Jefferson aka Lizzo, performed a stage dive at a New York concert in 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  A viral image of a “TMZ news alert” claiming 4 dead and 12 injured after Lizzo stage-dived in New York was fabricated. TMZ never issued such an alert, and no credible reports of such an incident exist. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) debunked it.

claim: During Michael Bloomberg's mayoral tenure of New York City between 2005 and 2013, the city's carbon footprint was reduced twice as much as the rest of the US.
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence: - New York City’s official greenhouse gas inventory shows citywide emissions fell about 19% from 2005 to 2013. - U.S. emissions over the same period fell roughly 9–10% (EPA/EIA data on total GHG or energy-related CO2). That makes NYC’s reduction about twice the national decline. Minor caveat: exact percentages vary slightly by dataset and whether you compare total GHGs vs CO2 only.

claim: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said 'women should be raped'.
response_text: FALSE.  Rahul Gandhi did not say “women should be raped.” The line has been falsely attributed to him via misleading/edited clips. In December 2019 he said “Rape in India” while criticizing rising sexual violence and the BJP’s handling of cases; he did not advocate or endorse rape. Multiple Indian fact-checkers reported the attribution as fake.

claim: Trump Mocks Global Warming, Lowballs Sea Level Rise
response_text: TRUE.  - Trump has repeatedly mocked global warming (e.g., his 2012 tweet calling it a “hoax” and frequent jokes during cold snaps like “we need global warming”).   - He has also lowballed sea-level rise, claiming at rallies that oceans would rise only about 1/8 inch over 200–300 years—far below scientific estimates and the observed rate (~3.3 mm/yr, about 1/8 inch per year, with projections of roughly 0.7–2+ feet by 2100 depending on emissions).

claim: 104 US House Democrats voted for impeachment of US President Donald Trump before the Ukraine call in which Trump asked  Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to  look into activities in Ukraine by Democratic presidential contender Joe Biden’s son Hunter.
response_text: TRUE.  Before Trump’s July 25, 2019 call with President Zelensky, the House had already held multiple votes on impeachment resolutions offered by Rep. Al Green. On Dec. 6, 2017 (58 Democrats) and Jan. 19, 2018 (66 Democrats), and again on July 17, 2019 (95 Democrats), Democrats voted in favor of proceeding with impeachment (in votes to not table Green’s resolutions). Counting unique members across those votes, 104 different House Democrats had cast at least one pro-impeachment vote before the Ukraine call. These were procedural/impeachment-resolution votes that were ultimately tabled.

claim: Bernie Sanders lost third place spot in Nevada primary polls to Pete Buttigieg
response_text: FALSE  Nevada Democratic primary/caucus polling in 2019–2020 consistently had Bernie Sanders ahead of Pete Buttigieg (often 1st or 2nd), and the RealClearPolitics Nevada average never showed Buttigieg overtaking Sanders. Sanders ultimately won the Nevada caucus by a wide margin. (Possible outlier single polls aside, there was no sustained “loss of third place” to Buttigieg.)

claim: Over the past two years, climate and weather disaster damage has cost the U.S. over $400 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  NOAA’s Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters data put recent two-year totals well below $400B. For example: 2022 ≈ $165B and 2023 ≈ $93B (about $258B combined). Even with 2024’s preliminary totals, the most recent two-year sum doesn’t approach $400B. Only certain older pairs (e.g., 2017–2018) exceed $400B, so saying “over the past two years” is misleading. Uncertainty: exact totals vary with updates and inflation adjustments, but not enough to reach $400B for the latest two years.

claim: Finkenauer voted to extend the ExIm bank.
response_text: TRUE.  Abby Finkenauer (then a U.S. Representative from Iowa) voted yes on the House bill to reauthorize the Export–Import Bank (H.R. 4863) on Nov. 15, 2019, and also voted for the FY2020 NDAA in December 2019, which ultimately enacted a multi‑year EXIM reauthorization.

claim: The Export-Import Bank “costs taxpayers billions in corporate welfare subsidies.
response_text: FALSE.  By standard federal accounting (FCRA), the Export-Import Bank has historically generated a surplus and sent money to the U.S. Treasury, not cost taxpayers. The Congressional Budget Office found that under FCRA, Ex-Im would reduce deficits, while under an alternative “fair‑value” method it could impose a modest cost—about $2 billion over 10 years in one estimate. That’s not an ongoing burden of “billions” in subsidies; the claim overstates the cost. Uncertainty: depends on accounting method, but even under fair‑value the estimated cost is small.

claim: The ExIm Bank provided taxpayer-backed handouts to foreign companies such as Air China and Saudi Aramco.”
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The U.S. Export-Import Bank provides government-backed loans and guarantees to foreign buyers of U.S. exports. Critics label these “taxpayer‑backed handouts,” though they are loans/guarantees, not grants. EXIM has supported: - Saudi Aramco–related projects, notably multi‑billion‑dollar financing for the Sadara chemical complex (a JV majority-owned by Saudi Aramco) and other Aramco-affiliated ventures. - Foreign airlines buying U.S. aircraft/engines, including Chinese carriers; Air China has received EXIM-backed financing in past aircraft/engine deals.  Note: “Handouts” is a value judgment, but the underlying taxpayer-backed support to entities like Saudi Aramco and Air China is documented. (Minor uncertainty on the specific Air China deals’ details, but EXIM has financed Chinese carriers’ Boeing/engine purchases.)

claim: After the election debate on ITV between Boris Johnson and Jeremy Corbyn, ITV and the BBC quoted the only poll which didn’t find Jeremy Corbyn to be the winner.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple snap polls followed the 19 Nov 2019 ITV head‑to‑head. YouGov’s widely cited poll had Boris Johnson narrowly ahead (about 51–49). Other instant polls (e.g., Savanta ComRes) had Jeremy Corbyn ahead, and at least one (e.g., Survation) reported a draw. So it isn’t true that ITV and the BBC quoted “the only poll” not showing Corbyn as winner—there wasn’t a unanimous set of polls putting Corbyn ahead. (Exact margins vary by poll; some uncertainty on specific figures.)

claim: Thai politician Thanathorn Juanroongruangkit faked his military service documents.
response_text: FALSE.  Opponents accused Thanathorn Juangroongruangkit in 2019 of draft-dodging and forging his conscription papers, but the Thai army/recruitment authorities reviewed the paperwork and said it was genuine. No charges or official findings of forgery were made. (Name is often misspelled; correct: Juangroongruangkit.)

claim: It's against the law for Medicare to negotiate lower drug prices.
response_text: FALSE.  Historically, the 2003 Medicare Part D law barred the HHS Secretary from negotiating drug prices directly (“non‑interference” clause). But the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 now authorizes Medicare to negotiate prices for a limited set of high‑spend Part D and Part B drugs, with the first negotiated prices scheduled to take effect in 2026. So it is no longer against the law for Medicare to negotiate some drug prices. (Part D plans have also long negotiated rebates with manufacturers.)

claim: Zurab Khangoshvili was one of the organizers of explosions in the Moscow metro.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence links Khangoshvili to organizing Moscow metro attacks. The 2010 bombings were attributed to militants of the Caucasus Emirate, with organizers named such as Magomedali Vagabov; earlier metro attacks (2004) were also linked to other groups. After Khangoshvili’s 2019 killing in Berlin, pro-Kremlin outlets spread unsubstantiated claims portraying him as a terrorist, but official investigations do not name him.

claim: A female army sergeant who became a hero for her war-time actions is the first woman to earn a Silver Star since WWII.
response_text: TRUE. In 2005, Sgt. Leigh Ann Hester (Army National Guard) received the Silver Star for valor in Iraq, becoming the first woman to earn the medal since World War II (when a few Army nurses received it). Another woman, Spc. Monica Lin Brown, was awarded it later in 2007.

claim: Facebook meme suggests that the measles vaccine caused 2019 Samoa measles outbreak
response_text: FALSE.  The meme’s suggestion is wrong. Samoa’s 2019 measles outbreak was driven by very low vaccination coverage after a 2018 medical error (incorrectly prepared MMR shots that led to two infant deaths) caused the immunization program to be suspended and trust to collapse. When measles was imported, many people—especially children—were unvaccinated, and most cases and deaths occurred in the unvaccinated. The MMR vaccine does not cause measles outbreaks.

claim: China responsible for 90 percent of the world's carbon emissions.
response_text: FALSE.  China is the largest annual emitter, but it accounts for roughly 30% of global CO2 emissions—not anywhere near 90%. Other major contributors include the U.S., India, the EU, and many others; collectively, the rest of the world emits well over half. Sources: Global Carbon Project; IEA; Our World in Data.

claim: Telangana Police started a service for women safety with a helpline number ‘9969777888’ for tracking the vehicle in which they are travelling through GPRS.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a long-running hoax circulated on WhatsApp. Telangana/Hyderabad Police have publicly denied launching any GPRS vehicle-tracking service via the number 9969777888, and that number does not belong to the police. For women’s safety in Telangana, use official channels like 100/112, the SHE Teams, 181 (women’s helpline), or the Hawk Eye app.

claim: Donald Trump got $130 billion increase  from Nato.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “$130 billion” refers to the cumulative increase in European allies’ and Canada’s own defense budgets compared with 2016, projected by NATO for the end of 2020. It was not money paid to Trump, the U.S., or “from NATO” as an organization. Allies had already pledged in 2014 (pre‑Trump) to raise spending toward 2% of GDP, though Trump’s pressure may have contributed.

claim: Over 95% of people living in South Belfast own their own home.
response_text: FALSE.  Owner-occupation in Belfast (including South Belfast) is well below 95%. Northern Ireland Census 2021 data show fewer than half of Belfast households are owner-occupied, with South Belfast having a large private-rented/student sector. Exact figures vary by boundary and whether measuring households vs people, but they are nowhere near 95%.

claim: A study showed one in four people have had a package stolen from their residence in the U.S.
response_text: TRUE  Several consumer surveys have reported roughly one-quarter (or more) of Americans have had a package stolen from their residence. For example, polling by firms like YouGov and C+R Research’s package theft studies have found figures in the ~25–36% range. Exact percentages vary by year and methodology, but “one in four” is consistent with published findings.

claim: Police have launched a free ride scheme in LUDHIANA where any women who is alone & not able to find vehicle to get home between 10pm-6am can call helpline numbers (1091 & 7837018555) 24×7. PCR vehicle will drop her home Free of Cost.
response_text: TRUE  Ludhiana Police have publicized a night-time “free drop” facility for women who are alone and unable to find transport, with PCR vehicles dropping them home between 10 pm and 6 am. The women’s helpline 1091 and the Ludhiana Police helpline 7837018555 have been listed for this service. Note: policies and numbers can change; in emergencies, 112 also works.

claim: Northern Ireland remains the only UK jurisdiction without funded childcare provision.
response_text: FALSE.  Northern Ireland does have government-funded provision: a funded pre‑school education place for most children in the year before primary (typically about 12.5 hours per week in term time), plus Sure Start in targeted areas and UK‑wide schemes (e.g., Tax‑Free Childcare, Universal Credit childcare support). What NI lacks—unlike England, Scotland and Wales—is a broad “30 hours”-style funded childcare entitlement for working parents. So it isn’t without funded provision, but its offer is much more limited. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Male birth control testing has been halted in India after 30 test subjects’ testicles exploded during sexual intercourse.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a satirical/hoax website (e.g., World News Daily Report) and has been debunked by fact-checkers. India’s male contraceptive research (e.g., RISUG) reported only mild, temporary side effects in trials and was not halted due to “exploding testicles.” No credible medical reports or regulatory notices support such an event.

claim: Donald Trump is waging a trade war against Wisconsin farmers forcing 1600 dairy farms to close.
response_text: FALSE.  About 1,600 Wisconsin dairy farms did close over several years during Trump’s term, but economists point to long‑running factors—chronic low milk prices, oversupply, consolidation, and tight margins—that predate Trump. The 2018–2019 tariff fights hurt dairy exports and likely worsened conditions, but it’s not accurate to say Trump was “waging a trade war against Wisconsin farmers” or that his trade policies “forced” all 1,600 closures. (Some uncertainty on the exact count/timeframe, but the causal claim is overstated.)

claim: Video shows police distributing tasbeehs as a part of Shiv Senas secularism campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  The clip doing the rounds is not from Maharashtra or any Shiv Sena “secularism campaign.” Fact-checks traced it to Pakistan, where local police were filmed distributing tasbeehs during Ramadan. The uniforms, Urdu markings, and police vehicles in the video match Pakistani police, not Indian/Maharashtra Police.

claim: Former Ukraine President Poroshenko actively worked on behalf of US Secretary Hillary Clinton.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible evidence that Petro Poroshenko “actively worked on behalf of” Hillary Clinton. U.S. intelligence and bipartisan Senate investigations concluded Russia—not Ukraine—undertook a government-backed effort in 2016. A 2017 Politico report noted some Ukrainian individuals criticized Trump and shared information about Paul Manafort, but it did not show Poroshenko directing such actions or working for Clinton. Also, Clinton left the State Department in 2013, before Poroshenko became president (2014). Any claim of an agency-like role “on behalf of” Clinton is unsupported.

claim: As of December 2019 the Narendra Modi govt had enacted a new law on self-defence, to combat crimes against women in India.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: By December 2019, the Modi government had not enacted any new “self-defence” law. India’s self-defence provisions already exist in the Indian Penal Code (Sections 96–106) since 1860. In 2018–2019 the Centre passed amendments increasing punishments for sexual offences (e.g., Criminal Law Amendment 2018; POCSO Amendment 2019) and set up fast-track courts, but no new law on self-defence was enacted. A much-discussed “Disha” law in December 2019 was a state law in Andhra Pradesh, not a central law by the Modi government. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Zip ties on windshield wipers linked to human trafficking
response_text: FALSE.  This is a recurring urban myth. Law enforcement agencies and anti-trafficking experts report no credible evidence that zip ties on cars or windshield wipers are used by human traffickers. Trafficking typically involves coercion by acquaintances or networks, not random abductions in parking lots. Some items on cars may be pranks or attempted theft distractions, but they are not linked to human trafficking.

claim: US governments speaker of the  House Nancy Pelosi Spent $106K of tax payer Money on a party With Hollywood Elitists
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible news or official records show Nancy Pelosi used $106,000 in taxpayer funds for a “party with Hollywood elites.” - Fundraisers Pelosi attends in Hollywood are paid for by campaigns/party committees (e.g., the DCCC), not taxpayers; House rules bar using official funds for such events. - The dollar figure resembles past, debunked claims that misread documents about in‑flight expenses for congressional travel, not a Pelosi “party.”

claim: As mayor, Cory Booker, US Democratic presidential candidate and US New Jersey Senator,  passed criminal justice reform in a US Republican Senate.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Cory Booker was mayor of Newark from 2006–2013. The U.S. Senate did not have a Republican majority until 2015. The major federal criminal justice reform (the First Step Act) passed in 2018 under a Republican-controlled Senate, when Booker was a U.S. Senator—not mayor.

claim: A screenshot shows a tweet from UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn saying the London Bridge attacker was "murdered by British Police”.
response_text: FALSE.  The “screenshot” is a fabricated tweet. There is no record of Jeremy Corbyn ever posting this, and fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact, Reuters) found no trace in his timeline or archives. In reality, Corbyn said police were right to use lethal force in the London Bridge incident.

claim: Soros and Clinton paid women to accuse Trump of sexual attacks.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence shows George Soros or Hillary Clinton paid women to accuse Donald Trump. Fact-checks have repeatedly debunked this rumor. A 2017 report did show attorney Lisa Bloom sought donor money (from some Democratic-aligned donors) to cover security/relocation costs for women considering coming forward, but there’s no evidence Soros or Clinton funded this, nor that anyone was paid to fabricate accusations.

claim: Democratic presidential candidate and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker was a Rhodes scholar.
response_text: TRUE. Cory Booker won a Rhodes Scholarship and studied at The Queen’s College, Oxford, earning a degree in 1994 before later attending Yale Law School.

claim: Adam Schiff used tax dollars to settle sexual harassment lawsuit witha 19 year old man.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated on fringe websites in 2018 and has been debunked by multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact). There is no record or evidence that Rep. Adam Schiff faced such a lawsuit or used taxpayer funds for any settlement, and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights (formerly the Office of Compliance) shows no such payout. Schiff’s office has also denied it.

claim: Nigeria was exposed to less than $7 billion of debt in 2015.
response_text: FALSE.  By end-2015, Nigeria’s total public debt was around $60–65 billion (per Nigeria’s Debt Management Office), and even its external debt alone was about $10–11 billion—both well above $7 billion. Uncertainty: figures vary slightly by source and exchange rate, but all are far higher than $7 billion.

claim: Michelle Obama slammed First Lady Melania Trump, saying, "She's a terrible role model for America's women."
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Michelle Obama saying this. The quote originated on a satire/fake-news site and was later recycled by clickbait posts. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) have debunked it, and Michelle Obama has generally avoided direct personal attacks on Melania Trump.

claim: Only 3 out of 12 regions are net contributors to the UK Treasury
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The UK has 12 NUTS1 regions (9 English regions plus Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland). ONS “Country and regional public sector finances” consistently show that only London, the South East, and the East of England raise more in taxes than they receive in public spending; the other nine regions are net recipients. This can vary slightly year to year (the East of England can be close to balance), but the broad picture matches the claim. Uncertainty: exact counts can shift in unusual years.

claim: Raising teachers' starting salaries to £30,000 by 2022/2023 would make it among the most competitive in the graduate labour market in England.
response_text: FALSE.  £30,000 would be above the overall median graduate starting salary and competitive with many public‑sector roles, but data around 2022 show typical starting pay at large graduate recruiters around £31–33k (and much higher in sectors like law, banking and consultancy). That puts £30k around the middle-to-upper part of the distribution, not “among the most competitive.” (Wording is vague, so there’s some ambiguity.)

claim: House Speaker Nancy Pelosi approved $4.8 million in impeachment-related consulting fees to the Clinton Foundation.
response_text: FALSE.  This originated from a satirical/fake-news post. There is no record in House disbursements or credible reporting of any impeachment-related payment to the Clinton Foundation, and the Speaker cannot unilaterally approve such expenditures. The Clinton Foundation’s filings also show no such income.

claim: Xavier Becerra the California Attorney General says there are now ten million illegal aliens in the state.
response_text: FALSE.  Becerra did not say there are 10 million “illegal aliens” in California. He spoke about roughly 10 million immigrants (foreign-born residents) in the state, not undocumented immigrants. Credible estimates put California’s undocumented population around 2 million, far below 10 million. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) have debunked this misquote.

claim: Xavier Becerra the California Attorney General says California will receive thirteen extra seats in congress by including ten million illegal aliens in the 2020 census.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Xavier Becerra ever saying that. The numbers are wrong, too: California does not have “10 million illegal aliens” (estimates are around 2–2.5 million), and no reputable analysis shows California gaining anything like 13 House seats from counting undocumented residents. In fact, after the 2020 Census, California lost one seat. This quote appears to be a fabricated meme misattributing claims to Becerra.

claim: Dominic Raab posted and then deleted a tweet describing Scotland as a region of England.
response_text: FALSE.  Fact-checkers found no evidence that Dominic Raab ever tweeted this. The screenshot circulating online is a fabricated image; there is no record of such a tweet on his timeline or in archives, and outlets like Full Fact have debunked the claim.

claim: European countries aren't giving financial support to Ukraine.
response_text: FALSE.  European countries and the EU have provided substantial financial support to Ukraine. Examples: - EU: €18 billion in macro‑financial assistance in 2023 and a €50 billion Ukraine Facility for 2024–2027, with billions already disbursed for budget and recovery support, plus humanitarian aid. - Individual European states (e.g., Germany, France, Netherlands, Nordic countries) and Norway’s multi‑year Nansen Support Programme (about €6+ billion) have given grants, loans, guarantees, and humanitarian funding. - European institutions like the EIB and EBRD have extended financing backed by EU guarantees.  So the claim that European countries aren’t giving financial support is incorrect.

claim: Putin publicly approved Wagner’s activities numerous times.
response_text: TRUE.  Examples: - 2018: Asked about Wagner/PMCs, Putin said private military firms have the right to work abroad if they don’t violate Russian law—an implicit approval of such activity. - May 21, 2023: The Kremlin said Putin congratulated Wagner assault units (and the army) for the capture of Bakhmut/Artyomovsk. - Late June 2023 (after the mutiny): Putin repeatedly called most Wagner fighters “patriots,” said they “fought honorably,” and even publicly acknowledged the state had financed Wagner.  These are multiple, public endorsements of Wagner’s activities.

claim: The National Committee of the USA's Democratic party gave their computer server to the Ukrainian company CrowdStrike
response_text: FALSE.  - CrowdStrike is a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm, not Ukrainian. - The DNC hired CrowdStrike in 2016 to investigate a breach. CrowdStrike analyzed the network on-site and made forensic images; there was no single physical “server” handed over. - The FBI received forensic copies and logs rather than seizing hardware, which is common practice.

claim: CNN admitted the Entire Russian Collusion Theory Was A Hoax
response_text: FALSE.  - CNN has not “admitted” that the entire Russia–Trump collusion matter was a hoax. The network reported the Mueller findings: Russia interfered “in sweeping and systematic fashion,” Mueller did not establish a criminal conspiracy with the Trump campaign, and there were numerous contacts.  - CNN also covered the bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee report reaching similar conclusions. - Corrections (e.g., a retracted 2017 story) and coverage of the Durham report’s criticism of the FBI are not an admission that the whole issue was a hoax.

claim: Nigel Farage stated Nearly two-thirds of British businesses do not make a profit of over £10,000 but are subjected to corporation tax.
response_text: FALSE  - Corporation tax applies only to companies. Nearly two‑thirds of UK “businesses” are sole traders or partnerships, which are not subject to corporation tax. - HMRC data have shown that around 60% of companies with a corporation tax liability had profits under £10,000, but that’s a subset of companies, not “British businesses” overall, and many such firms pay little or no CT after allowances.  So the statement conflates all businesses with companies and overstates who is “subjected to” corporation tax. (Some uncertainty if he meant “companies with taxable profits,” but that isn’t what he said.)

claim: Northern Ireland has the highest femicide rate in Western Europe
response_text: FALSE  Reason: There’s no robust evidence that Northern Ireland has the highest femicide rate in Western Europe. Comparable, consistent “femicide” statistics aren’t published across Western Europe at a sub‑national level, and female homicide rates vary year to year—especially in small populations like Northern Ireland—so a single year’s spike can be misleading. Over multi‑year periods, available data do not place Northern Ireland above Western European countries such as Luxembourg or Iceland in female homicide rates. Fact-checkers have also found this claim unsupported. (Some uncertainty stems from differing definitions of “Western Europe” and “femicide.”)

claim: Saving A Quarter A Day For A Year Will Get You $9100.25.
response_text: FALSE.  A “quarter” is $0.25. Saving $0.25 per day for 365 days totals 0.25 × 365 = $91.25 (or $91.50 in a leap year), not $9,100.25. The claim is off by about a factor of 100.

claim: Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Marie Yovanovitch’s net worth is as high as $23 million.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Public federal financial disclosure forms for Marie Yovanovitch show assets in the low-to-mid single-digit millions (approximately around $1–4 million range), not anywhere near $23 million. The $23 million figure traces to unreliable “net worth” websites and lacks credible documentation. (Some uncertainty on the exact range due to disclosure categories, but it’s far below $23M.)

claim: In the 266 days since we sent this bill, about 25,000 people have died from gun violence in our country, 47 percent of them teenagers or children younger than that.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Recent CDC/Gun Violence Archive data show about 44,000–49,000 U.S. firearm deaths per year (~120–135 per day), so 266 days would yield closer to 30,000–35,000 deaths, not “about 25,000.” More importantly, children and teenagers (typically defined as ages 0–19) account for about 10% of firearm deaths (e.g., ~4,600 of ~48,200 in 2022), not 47%. Even with differing definitions of “gun violence,” the share of victims who are children/teens is nowhere near half.

claim: Bay leaves eliminate the need for a pharmacy as the plant cures or alleviates everything from digestive disorders to kidney stones.
response_text: FALSE.  Bay leaves (Laurus nobilis) are a culinary herb with limited, mostly preliminary evidence for mild effects such as aiding digestion or modestly affecting blood sugar. There’s no clinical evidence they “eliminate the need for a pharmacy” or that they cure or alleviate “everything,” including kidney stones. Such sweeping claims are unsupported and misleading.

claim: 13 Uber drivers were arrested for alleged sex trafficking in Atlanta, Georgia.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports show 13 Uber drivers arrested for sex trafficking in Atlanta. The often-cited incident with “13 Uber/Lyft drivers” occurred in Polk County, Florida, during a prostitution/human‑trafficking sting, and those arrests were largely for solicitation—not sex trafficking—and not in Atlanta. (Some uncertainty due to multiple stings, but none match this claim in Atlanta.)

claim: The U.S. Constitution sets up the  election redistricting process to be partisan.
response_text: FALSE.  The Constitution does not mandate a partisan redistricting process. Article I, Section 4 leaves the “Times, Places and Manner” of congressional elections to state legislatures, subject to Congress’s oversight. It neither requires nor endorses partisan control. States may (and many do) use independent or bipartisan commissions (upheld in Arizona State Legislature v. AIRC, 2015). While partisan gerrymandering isn’t barred by the federal Constitution (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019), the Constitution does not set the process up to be partisan.

claim: No other city in America did what (New York) did. We reduced murders by 50%, reduced police shootings to historic lows, reduced the number of people incarcerated by nearly 40% during Bloomberg's tenure
response_text: FALSE.  - Murders: NYC homicides fell roughly 50% from 2001 to 2013, so that part is basically right. - Police shootings: NYPD reported historic lows around 2012–2013, also broadly right. - Incarceration: The drop during Bloomberg’s tenure was smaller than “nearly 40%” if you look at the city jail population (closer to ~20–25%). You only approach ~40% with broader/longer measures (e.g., combining state prison plus city jail or extending beyond his term).  Most importantly, the “No other city in America did what New York did” overstates uniqueness. Other large cities (e.g., Los Angeles) also cut murders by more than 50% in that period and reported record-low police shootings, while reducing incarceration. So the exclusivity claim is not supported. (Some uncertainty hinges on how “incarcerated” is defined.)

claim: Ron Kind is the only member of Congress that voted for inquiries into Bill Clinton and Donald Trump
response_text: TRUE.  - 1998: The House voted 258–176 to authorize an impeachment inquiry into President Bill Clinton; 31 Democrats voted yes, including Rep. Ron Kind. - 2019: The House voted 232–196 to formalize the impeachment inquiry into President Donald Trump; all Republicans voted no, two Democrats voted no, and Ron Kind voted yes.  Among members who served in both eras, Ron Kind was the only one to vote yes on both inquiry authorizations. (For example, Collin Peterson voted yes in 1998 but no in 2019.)

claim: Under the current system, people on a work, study or family visa in the UK incur average NHS costs of £625 per year.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The £625 figure reflects the old Immigration Health Surcharge level (£624) that the government once said broadly matched average NHS usage by surcharge payers. Since 6 February 2024, the surcharge is £1,035 per adult per year (£776 for students/under‑18s). There is no current official estimate that average NHS costs for people on work, study or family visas are £625; that number is outdated. Uncertainty: the government has not recently published a precise average-cost figure, but the “£625” is no longer aligned with the current system.

claim: Dwayne Johnson 'The Rock' Johnson dies at 47
response_text: FALSE.  Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson (born May 2, 1972) did not die at 47. He has remained active publicly well after 2019–2020 (age 47), with roles in Black Adam (2022), Fast X (2023), WWE appearances in 2024, and other recent projects. Death claims around that time were hoaxes.

claim: The Chinese government spent the same amount -- Rs 3,000 crore -- to construct a bridge that the Indian government spent to build the Statue of Unity in Gujarat.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Statue of Unity cost about Rs 2,989 crore (≈ Rs 3,000 crore). - The Chinese bridge often cited in such comparisons—the 55-km Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge—cost around 127 billion yuan (about US$18–20 billion), i.e., roughly Rs 1.2–1.4 lakh crore, not Rs 3,000 crore. Even other major Chinese sea bridges (e.g., Jiaozhou Bay Bridge) cost well above Rs 3,000 crore.

claim: Tirupati Balaji Temple Will Donate Rs. 100 Crores For Ram Mandir.
response_text: FALSE.  Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), which administers the Tirupati Balaji Temple, publicly denied reports that it would donate Rs 100 crore to the Ayodhya Ram Mandir. TTD officials said they have made no such decision and, under their rules, TTD funds are to be used for its own temples and related charitable activities—not for donations to external trusts. Several fact-checks and news reports in early 2024 flagged the Rs 100-crore claim as fake.

claim: In 2019 there have been over fifty reports of attacks and harassment on Nigerian journalists.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple watchdogs recorded well over 50 incidents in 2019. For example, the Coalition for Whistleblower Protection and Press Freedom’s Press Attack Tracker documented around 70–74 press freedom violations (including assaults, arrests, and harassment) in Nigeria in 2019, and CPJ reported over 30 incidents around the 2019 elections alone. Counts vary by source but consistently exceed 50.

claim: Political Scientist Alexey Martynov said ‘Transnistria is an Independent State.’
response_text: TRUE.  Russian political scientist Alexey Martynov (director of the International Institute of Newly Established States) has been quoted in Russian/Transnistrian media saying “Приднестровье — независимое государство” (“Transnistria is an independent state”), in interviews and commentaries around Transnistria’s status. Note: he frames it as de facto independence; Transnistria lacks broad international recognition.

claim: The US is  winning World Trade Organization cases for the first time.
response_text: FALSE.  The United States has been winning WTO disputes since the system began in 1995 and historically has one of the highest success rates when it brings cases. Analyses of completed disputes show the U.S. has prevailed on most issues in 80–90% of the cases it initiated—well before recent years—so it is not “winning for the first time.” (As with most members, the U.S. tends to lose more often when it is the respondent.) Uncertainty: low.

claim: Ivanka Trump has created 14 million jobs.
response_text: FALSE.  The 14 million figure refers to “training and skill-building opportunities” pledged by companies under Ivanka Trump’s Pledge to America’s Workers initiative—not actual jobs created. Those were voluntary commitments (often including training for existing employees), not verified new jobs, and they were not created by Ivanka. For context, total U.S. job growth during the Trump administration never approached 14 million.

claim: Every UK taxpayer  will have an additional bill of £2,400 per year under a Labour  Government.
response_text: FALSE.  - The widely cited Conservative costing was about £2,094 per working household over four years (roughly £525 per year on average), not £2,400 per year, and not “every taxpayer.”  - Those figures relied on contested assumptions about Labour’s plans and were criticised by the UK Statistics Authority and independent analysts (e.g., IFS) as not a reliable forecast of tax rises.  - Labour has pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, NI or VAT; while future fiscal choices are uncertain, no independent evidence supports an added £2,400 per year for every taxpayer.

claim: South African public utility Eskom generates approximately 45% of the electricity used in Africa
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The oft-quoted “45%” figure is outdated. In recent years Eskom has generated roughly 170–210 TWh annually, while Africa’s total electricity generation is on the order of 900–1,100 TWh. That puts Eskom’s share closer to 15–25%, not ~45%. Figures vary by year, but it’s nowhere near 45% today.

claim: Sri Lanka's Election Commissions announced a three-day social media ban around the country November 16 2019 election.
response_text: FALSE.  Sri Lanka’s Election Commission did not announce a three-day social media ban for the Nov. 16, 2019 presidential election. Officials publicly denied such rumors, noting only the standard pre‑election “silence period” on campaigning (including online propaganda), not a nationwide social media shutdown. Social media blocks in Sri Lanka occurred earlier in 2018 and after the April 2019 attacks, not for the 2019 election.

claim: South African public utility Eskom generates approximately 95% of the electricity used in South Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: That “95%” figure was historically true, but in recent years independent power producers and private generation have grown. Current reporting typically puts Eskom’s share closer to about 90% (or slightly less) of South Africa’s electricity generation, not ~95%. (So the claim is outdated.)

claim: US manufacturing jobs have increased by over 600,000
response_text: TRUE  BLS data show U.S. manufacturing employment rose from roughly 12.1 million in Jan 2021 to around 12.9–13.0 million by 2024–2025—an increase of about 800,000, i.e., over 600,000. Note: versus the pre‑pandemic peak (Feb 2020 ~12.8 million), the net gain is much smaller, so the timeframe matters.

claim: About 2% of pregnancy terminations are between 20 and 24 weeks in Great Britain in 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Official stats show around 1% of abortions occurred at 20 weeks and over in 2018, not ~2%. In England and Wales (DHSC, Abortion statistics 2018), 20+ weeks accounted for about 1% of terminations; Scotland’s figures are similar. Since almost all ≥20-week procedures are 20–24 weeks, the share for 20–24 weeks is likewise about 1%. Note: Small uncertainty arises from aggregating England/Wales and Scotland, but the combined proportion remains near 1%, not 2%.

claim: Scotland’s youth unemployment rate fell by 0.3 percentage points over 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Based on the Annual Population Survey (APS) for Scotland, the youth (16–24) unemployment rate was about 9.1% in 2019, down from roughly 9.4% in 2018—a fall of 0.3 percentage points. (Slight uncertainty stems from differing sources/periods, but APS annual figures support the 0.3 pp decrease.)

claim: More people are coming home from Iraq with brain cancer than any other war.
response_text: False.  - There’s no solid evidence or comprehensive data showing Iraq War (2003–2011) veterans have the highest numbers or rates of brain cancer compared with veterans of other wars. - Large reviews (Institute of Medicine/National Academies; VA) have found insufficient evidence that burn‑pit or similar Iraq‑era exposures increase brain cancer risk, and studies of post‑9/11 cohorts have not shown a clear elevation versus non‑deployed peers. - Conversely, some VA/DoD studies of the 1990–91 Gulf War found elevated brain cancer mortality among troops potentially exposed to the Khamisiyah nerve‑agent plume. - Wars with much larger cohorts (e.g., Vietnam, WWII) would also be expected to yield more absolute brain cancer cases.  Note: Cancer latency and incomplete surveillance add uncertainty, but the superlative claim is not supported.

claim: In 2018, South African police service officers were accused of 217 cases of torture and 3,661 cases of assault
response_text: TRUE.  The Independent Police Investigative Directorate (IPID) 2018/19 annual report recorded 217 complaints of torture and 3,661 complaints of assault against South African Police Service members. Note: these figures are for the 2018/19 financial year and reflect allegations/complaints, not necessarily proven cases.

claim: 558 people were killed by the police in 2018, while 201 people died in police custody
response_text: FALSE.  - The claim lacks a country, but it doesn’t match major datasets. In the U.S., around 1,000+ people were killed by police in 2018 (e.g., ~992 shot and killed per Washington Post; ~1,143 total per Mapping Police Violence), and deaths in police custody number in the thousands, not 201.  - In India, NCRB reported far fewer police-custody deaths (on the order of dozens in 2018) and not 558 killed by police. - In South Africa (IPID 2018/19), figures were roughly ~393 deaths due to police action and ~214 in custody, not 558/201.  Uncertainty: exact source unspecified, but no standard national dataset aligns with 558 killed and 201 custody deaths for 2018.

claim: Confederate veterans were conferred with many of the same benefits of other United States military veterans by Acts of Congress back in 1929 and 1957
response_text: FALSE.  Confederate veterans were never made U.S. veterans and did not receive “many of the same benefits” as United States military veterans. Federal actions involving Confederates were narrowly limited to memorialization—e.g., authority (from 1906 onward, with later appropriations such as in the 1920s) to mark and maintain Confederate graves and cemeteries. Pensions and most benefits for Confederate veterans came from state governments, not the federal government. Claims about a 1957 (often misstated as 1958) act conferring U.S. veteran status or broad VA benefits are incorrect; at most, mid‑20th‑century measures addressed grave markers or one‑off recognition, not general veteran benefits.

claim: Since 2002, South Africa’s police force has grown by 50%
response_text: FALSE.  SAPS headcount did rise sharply after 2002, but not by 50%. SAPS annual reports show total personnel increasing from roughly 145,000–150,000 in 2002/03 to a peak of about 195,000–200,000 around 2011/12—about 35–40% growth. Numbers have since slipped slightly, keeping the increase below 50%. (Small uncertainty depends on whether you count only sworn officers or total staff, but either way the rise is under 50%.)

claim: The South African Police Service kills three times more people per capita than the United States police force
response_text: FALSE.  Using comparable measures, South Africa’s “deaths as a result of police action” are typically about 350–450 per year in a population ~60 million (roughly 6–8 per million). The U.S. records about 1,000–1,200 police killings annually in a population ~330 million (about 3–4 per million). That’s roughly double, not triple. Note: figures vary by year and definitions; including in-custody deaths would raise South Africa’s rate but isn’t directly comparable to most U.S. counts.

claim: Nancy Pelosi said Dems will 'shut it all down' if they don't get their way on impeachment.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Nancy Pelosi saying this. The quote originated on a satirical/fake news site and was later shared as if real. No credible transcripts, news reports, or official statements show Pelosi threatening to “shut it all down” over impeachment.

claim: Total university enrolment for university in South Africa, 1994 was around 300,000.
response_text: FALSE.  Most historical sources place South African university headcount enrolment in 1993/1994 in the mid-to-high 300,000s (roughly 350,000–380,000, including UNISA), with total higher education (universities + technikons) around 500,000. So “around 300,000” understates the university total by a sizable margin. (Exact figures vary by source and coverage, but not as low as 300,000.)

claim: Access to antiretroviral therapy in the South African public health sector was given to 45,500 patients in 2004.
response_text: TRUE  Multiple contemporaneous sources (DoH progress updates and WHO/UNAIDS “3 by 5” reporting) put the number of people receiving ART in South Africa’s public sector by the end of 2004 at roughly 45–47 thousand. The figure 45,500 is consistent with those estimates. (Minor uncertainty due to reporting/rounding differences.)

claim: The size of the South African economy over the past 25 years has doubled.
response_text: FALSE.  In real (inflation-adjusted) terms, South Africa’s GDP has increased by roughly 50–70% over the past 25 years—well short of doubling. Average real growth has been around 1–2% a year, far below the ~2.8% needed to double in 25 years. Only in nominal terms (affected by inflation and exchange rates) has GDP more than doubled, which doesn’t reflect real economic size.

claim: 84% of all households in South Africa have electricity.
response_text: FALSE.  Best recent estimates put household electricity access in South Africa closer to about 88–90% (e.g., Stats SA General Household Survey and World Bank data around 2021–2023). The 84% figure reflects older levels and understates current access. (Uncertainty: depends on year and whether measuring mains connection vs. electricity used for lighting.)

claim: In 2017, South Africa recorded an inflow of foreign direct investment amounting to R17 billion.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: UNCTAD’s World Investment Report put South Africa’s 2017 FDI inflows at about US$1.3 billion, which converts to roughly R17 billion at the average 2017 exchange rate. This is the figure widely cited by the SA government. Note: South African Reserve Bank figures can differ due to methodology and timing.

claim: Over the past five years the South African government has invested in electrifying more than a million homes.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Through the Integrated National Electrification Programme (INEP) and Eskom/municipal projects, South Africa has been adding roughly 180,000–220,000 household connections per year in recent years. Over about five years (roughly 2019/20–2023/24) this totals just over 1 million homes connected or funded for connection. Figures vary by source and whether off‑grid systems are included, but the cumulative total exceeds one million. (Minor uncertainty stems from year-by-year reporting differences.)

claim: Since introducing the Safe initiative, 699 schools in SA have been provided with safe and appropriate sanitation facilities and projects and a further 1,150 schools are either in planning, design or construction stages.
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: In his February 2019 State of the Nation Address, President Ramaphosa said that since launching the SAFE (Sanitation Appropriate for Education) initiative in August 2018, 699 schools had been provided with safe sanitation and a further 1,150 were in planning, design or construction. Department of Basic Education updates at the time reflected these figures. Note: many of these projects were delivered through broader DBE/provincial programmes alongside SAFE, but the numbers are accurate for that period.

claim: Donald Trump and the Republicans have spent the past four years trying to dismantle the Affordable Care Act. They are doing everything they can — without a plan to replace it
response_text: TRUE.  - During Trump’s term, Republicans repeatedly tried to roll back the ACA: a 2017 repeal/replace push (AHCA passed the House but failed in the Senate), zeroing out the individual mandate penalty, cutting outreach, expanding short‑term plans, ending cost‑sharing reduction payments, and supporting a lawsuit (California v. Texas) to strike down the entire law. - When urging the courts to invalidate the ACA, the administration did not have a detailed, consensus replacement ready; Trump’s touted “plan” never materialized beyond broad principles and a symbolic 2020 executive order. - Caveat: Republicans did propose replacement ideas (e.g., AHCA, Graham‑Cassidy), but none were enacted or stood as a concrete, ready alternative if the ACA were dismantled.

claim: Over the past five years the SA government has built two new universities.
response_text: FALSE.  Assuming “SA” refers to South Africa: the government established two new public universities—University of Mpumalanga and Sol Plaatje University—in 2013, with first student intakes in 2014. That is more than five years ago. In the past five years no additional two universities have been built (plans for new institutions, such as in Ekurhuleni and a policing/crime-detection university, have not materialised).

claim: The SA government launched the Safe initiative in August 2018.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In August 2018, the South African government (President Cyril Ramaphosa) launched the SAFE initiative—Sanitation Appropriate for Education—to eradicate unsafe school pit latrines. Note: This refers to South Africa (SA), not South Australia.

claim: Over the past five years the SA government has  invested in building hundreds of thousands of new homes.
response_text: FALSE.  - The claim is ambiguous (“SA” could mean South Africa or South Australia), but under either reading it overstates reality. - South Australia: Government-backed new builds are in the low thousands over five years; the entire state only completes around 10–15k dwellings per year across all sectors, so “hundreds of thousands” is impossible. - South Africa: Recent five-year delivery of completed government houses is well under 200,000; totals only reach “hundreds of thousands” if one includes serviced sites or “housing opportunities,” not new homes. Uncertainty: exact recent annual totals vary, but they don’t support the claim as stated.

claim: The SA government  launched the Youth Employment Service, which is placing unemployed youth in paid internships in companies across the country.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Youth Employment Service (YES) was launched in 2018 by the South African Presidency in partnership with business and labour. It is a business‑led initiative that places unemployed youth in paid, year‑long work experience placements at companies across the country (often akin to internships). Minor nuance: it’s not solely a government program, but government‑backed.

claim: Over the past 5 years the SA government has invested more than R1.3 trillion in the country's infrastructure.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: - National Treasury’s public‑sector infrastructure expenditure data for the most recent five completed fiscal years totals roughly R1.0–R1.2 trillion, not “more than R1.3 trillion.” If you count only “government” (national, provincial and local) rather than the whole public sector (including SOEs like Eskom and Transnet), the total is even lower. - The R1.3 trillion figure is often cited in government statements as a pipeline/plan or projected over future periods, not actual past spend.  Note: Exact totals vary with the 5‑year window and definition used, but available Treasury data does not support “more than R1.3 trillion actually invested” in the past five years.

claim: Every month 17.5 million social grants are provided to South Africans.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: SASSA’s monthly permanent social grants have grown to roughly 18–19 million in recent years (2023–2025), and if you include the SRD grant, total monthly grant payments are about 27–28 million. The 17.5 million figure was roughly accurate several years ago but is outdated. Uncertainty: exact month-to-month counts fluctuate slightly.

claim: If Donald Trump is successful in dismantling the Affordable Care Act, there is no guarantee for people who have pre-existing conditions.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: The ACA created nationwide, federal protections requiring insurers to cover people regardless of pre-existing conditions and to charge them the same rates (guaranteed issue and community rating). If the ACA were dismantled without a replacement law, those federal guarantees would disappear. Some states might maintain protections, but there would be no nationwide guarantee for people with pre-existing conditions.

claim: There is a possibility that this poisonous gas could have been released by any neighboring country which is afraid of us
response_text: FALSE. The claim is speculative and offers no evidence linking a neighboring country to the gas release. Without verifiable information, asserting even “a possibility” is unsupported. (Uncertain due to lack of context, but no credible reports substantiate this.)

claim: The UK will send Trump £500 million a week in a trade deal that will fund US drug firms instead of NHS.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There is no UK–US trade deal that requires the UK to pay £500 million a week to the US or to “Trump,” nor any official proposal to do so. Trade agreements do not involve weekly tribute payments to a foreign leader. While drug pricing was a discussion point in past UK–US talks, no deal was reached that would force UK funds away from the NHS to US drug firms, and the £500m/week figure has no credible source.
