claim: Americans in swing states do not want to hear about the impeachment of Donald Trump in 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: 2019 polling in key battleground states showed mixed views—many voters opposed removing Trump and preferred Congress focus on other issues (e.g., NYT/Siena, USA Today/Suffolk, Marquette in WI). But substantial shares supported the inquiry and followed it closely. So it’s an overgeneralization to claim swing‑state Americans “do not want to hear” about impeachment. (Some did; opinions varied by state.)

claim: Indian social activist Mahatma Gandhi once said, “First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win.”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The line is widely misattributed to Mahatma Gandhi and does not appear in his collected works. A closely related passage comes from union leader Nicholas Klein in a 1918 speech to the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America: “First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. Then they attack you… And then they build monuments to you.” The “then they fight you, then you win” version became popular much later.

claim: Over 200,000 NHS nurses have resigned since 2010.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely quoted “200,000” comes from counting all nurse job leavers from NHS hospital and community services in England over multiple years (since 2010), regardless of reason, with people counted each time they leave a post. It includes retirements, transfers to other NHS employers, and those who later rejoined—so it’s not a count of unique nurses “resigning.” Using “resigned” overstates what the data shows. (Uncertainty: figures depend on definitions and England-only data, but there isn’t solid evidence that 200,000+ uniquely resigned from the NHS.)

claim: The Information and Communication Technology sector contributes more to Nigeria’s Gross Domestic Product than the Oil and Gas sector.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) GDP reports show that Information and Communication (the ICT-related sector: telecoms, broadcasting, publishing, etc.) typically contributes about 15–18% of Nigeria’s real GDP, while the Oil and Gas (crude petroleum and natural gas) share has fallen to around 5–7%. So ICT’s GDP contribution is larger. Note: Oil still dominates export earnings and government revenue, but not GDP share.

claim: This is the first health-care plan in the U.S. proposed by anyone in this presidential primary that lays out the full cost and how to pay for it.
response_text: TRUE.  At the time this was said (early 2007, during the Democratic presidential primary), John Edwards had released a detailed universal health-care plan with a full cost estimate and specified funding sources, while other candidates had not yet provided complete costs and pay-fors. Note: This assessment depends on that timeframe; in later cycles multiple candidates provided detailed costs and financing.

claim: 35 million votes were counted in the October 21, 2019 Canadian federal elections although Canada only has 27.4 million eligible voters.
response_text: FALSE.  Elections Canada reported about 27.4 million registered electors and roughly 18.3 million ballots cast (around 67% turnout) in the Oct. 21, 2019 federal election. The claim of 35 million votes counted is far above both the number of eligible voters and the actual ballots cast.

claim: BBC producer Rob Burley hired his son to pose as a Brexit & Boris Johnson supporter on Question Time.
response_text: FALSE.  - Question Time is produced by Mentorn Media, not by Rob Burley or his BBC team. - Rob Burley did not work on Question Time and said he had no role in its audience selection. - The audience member in question is not his son. Fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact) debunked this rumor.

claim: Drinking Cold Water After Meals Can Cause Cancer
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no scientific evidence that drinking cold water after meals causes cancer, and no cancer agency lists it as a risk factor. In contrast, very hot beverages (above ~65°C/149°F) are linked to higher esophageal cancer risk due to thermal injury (IARC 2016). Cold water may cause transient discomfort (e.g., esophageal spasm or migraine in sensitive people), but it doesn’t cause cancer.

claim: United States Republican Matt Gaetz has had numerous DUIs and his dad, a Florida State senator, got him off each time,
response_text: FALSE.  - Public records show Matt Gaetz had one DUI arrest (2008) that prosecutors declined to pursue for insufficient evidence; there are no verified records of “numerous” DUIs. - He did have many traffic citations over the years, which may have fueled the rumor. - His father, Don Gaetz, was a Florida state senator at the time, but there’s no evidence he intervened to get charges dropped. Prosecutors have said the case was dismissed on evidentiary grounds.

claim: Democrats in the USA have issued more subpoenas than they’ve passed bills.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The premise flips the scale. Congressional Democrats have passed far more bills than they have issued subpoenas. For example, in the 116th Congress (2019–2021) the House passed hundreds of bills and Congress enacted hundreds into law, while Democratic committee chairs issued only a few dozen subpoenas at most. Similar fact-checks in 2019 found the “more subpoenas than bills” talking point to be incorrect. (Slight uncertainty because no timeframe is specified, but on any reasonable period the claim doesn’t hold.)

claim: The World Health Organization is still pushing this [MMR vaccine] depopulation agenda throughout Africa
response_text: FALSE  There is no credible evidence that the WHO is using the MMR (or MR) vaccine for a “depopulation agenda.” WHO supports measles and rubella vaccination to prevent illness and death; vaccination has averted millions of child deaths globally. Extensive studies show MMR does not cause infertility or population reduction. Past “depopulation” rumors (e.g., around tetanus vaccines) have been investigated and found baseless.

claim: US President Donald Trump's administration built the greatest economy in history.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: - Pre‑pandemic, the U.S. economy was strong (unemployment hit 3.5%, poverty fell, stock market highs), but on core metrics it was not the best on record. - Real GDP growth under Trump (2017–2019 average ~2–3%) trailed periods like the late 1990s and 1960s. Job creation was slower than some prior expansions (e.g., Obama’s later years, the 1990s). The unemployment rate, while very low, was not the lowest in U.S. history (it was lower in the early 1950s). - In 2020 the economy suffered the sharpest downturn since the Great Depression, with unemployment spiking to 14.7%.  Sources: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (GDP), Bureau of Labor Statistics (unemployment, payroll jobs), U.S. Census Bureau (poverty, incomes).  Note: “Greatest economy in history” is subjective, but standard indicators do not support it.

claim: The Conservatives plan to take on 6,000 more police officers in 12 months at a cost of £750 million.
response_text: TRUE.  In the 2019 Spending Round, the Conservative government allocated about £750 million for 2020–21 to fund the first tranche of its 20,000-officer recruitment pledge, targeting 6,000 additional officers within that 12-month period. (Note: later Home Office details referred to £700m ring‑fenced within that package, but the plan was framed as £750m for the first 6,000.)

claim: More than 500 scientists and professionals in climate and related fields have sent a "European Climate Declaration" to the Secretary-General of the United Nations.
response_text: TRUE.  In September 2019 the Dutch group CLINTEL organized a letter titled the “European Climate Declaration” (“There is no climate emergency”), claiming over 500 signatories. It was sent to UN Secretary‑General António Guterres (and EU leaders). Note: many signatories were not climate scientists, but a mix of scientists and other professionals.

claim: EUPATORIUM PERFOIAM 200 can cure dengue in 48 hours.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible clinical evidence that Eupatorium perfoliatum (often sold as a homeopathic “200C/200” remedy) cures dengue, let alone within 48 hours. Dengue has no specific antiviral cure; standard care is supportive (fluids, monitoring, managing complications). Major health agencies (e.g., WHO/CDC) do not recommend homeopathy for dengue. Claims of rapid “cure” are unsubstantiated and potentially dangerous if they delay proper medical care.

claim: Texas, US school district mandate teaches kids how to have anal sex.
response_text: FALSE.  - Texas has no mandate requiring schools to teach students “how to have anal sex.” State standards emphasize abstinence and risk avoidance (Texas Education Code §28.004), and parents must opt in for sex-ed. - Some districts (e.g., Austin ISD) have considered or adopted curricula that mention anal sex in the context of STI risk and prevention for older students, but not “how-to” instruction. - Viral claims framing this as a mandate to teach “how to have anal sex” are mischaracterizations.

claim: Viral Photos show new coins minted for a paperless currency in the Philippines
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The viral photos show the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ New Generation Currency coins released in 2018. They were not minted for a “paperless” or coin‑only currency, and the BSP explicitly said there was no plan to eliminate banknotes. Banknotes (including later polymer notes) continued to circulate alongside the new coins.

claim: Islamic State (IS) “doesn’t exist anymore,
response_text: FALSE.  IS lost its territorial “caliphate” in Iraq and Syria by 2019, but the organization persists as an insurgent/terrorist network. Its core and affiliates (e.g., ISIS-K in Afghanistan, IS in Syria/Iraq, ISWAP in West Africa, IS in the Sahel/Mozambique/DRC) have continued to carry out attacks through 2023–2025. The group still exists, even if it no longer holds significant territory.

claim: Obama tweeted on Al Baghdad "he was a great man, an innocent man and my friend".
response_text: FALSE.  Barack Obama never tweeted praise for Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. No such tweet exists on his accounts, and fact-checkers have debunked circulated fake screenshots claiming he did. Obama consistently condemned ISIS during his presidency; al-Baghdadi was killed in 2019, after Obama left office.

claim: Kenyan revenue has been under-performing for the last 10 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya has frequently missed its revenue (tax) collection targets over much of the past decade, but not in every single year. For example, KRA reported meeting or surpassing targets in at least one recent year (notably around FY 2021/22, depending on whether original or revised targets are used). So the blanket claim that revenue has been under-performing “for the last 10 years” is an overstatement. Note: exact assessments can vary with whether one uses original vs. revised targets.

claim: Cambridge University Student Union (CUSU) banned Remembrance Day celebrations remembering British war veterans.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Cambridge’s student union did not “ban” Remembrance Day. On past occasions it declined to run or endorse an official SU-led Remembrance campaign, but it also stated it had no power to stop commemorations. Colleges and the university continued to hold Remembrance services as normal. Reports of a “ban” were mischaracterisations.

claim: Kathy Griffin, Tom Arnold, Robert DeNiro and Barbara Streisand have had U.S federal warrants issued for threats against President Donald Trump.
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible reports or law-enforcement records show federal arrest warrants for any of them. - Kathy Griffin was investigated by the Secret Service over her 2017 photo but was not arrested or charged. - Tom Arnold, Robert De Niro, and Barbra (not “Barbara”) Streisand made critical remarks but faced no federal warrants. - Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) have debunked viral posts claiming such warrants.

claim: 90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: HUD’s 2023 point-in-time count estimates about 181,000 people experiencing homelessness in California, with roughly 68% unsheltered—around 123,000 people—well above 90,000. (PIT counts are estimates but consistently place the unsheltered number over 90k.)

claim: A majority of UK voters say violence against MPs is “worth it” to get their way in Brexit.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A widely cited 2019 “Future of England”/YouGov study found that around half of Leave voters in England (and a substantial minority of Remain voters) said violence toward MPs would be a “price worth paying” to achieve their preferred Brexit outcome. That is not a majority of UK voters overall, and the key figures often reported were for English Leave voters specifically. No credible poll shows a majority of UK voters endorsing violence against MPs over Brexit.

claim: Actress Shaina Magdayao, Died at the Age of 30 Because of Hypothyroid Disease
response_text: FALSE.  Shaina Magdayao (born 1989) is alive. There are no credible reports from reputable Philippine media or her official channels of her death, and she has remained publicly active in recent years. The claim that she died at age 30 from hypothyroid disease is a baseless hoax.

claim: Lakshmi Vilas Bank shuts down 569 branches and 1046 ATMs
response_text: FALSE.  Those numbers (about 569 branches and 1,046 ATMs) were the rough size of Lakshmi Vilas Bank’s network, not units being shut. In November 2020, LVB was placed under moratorium and then amalgamated with DBS Bank India; RBI stated all LVB branches/ATMs would continue as DBS Bank India outlets, not be closed.

claim: US Red flag laws allow gun seizure without a judge's ok.
response_text: FALSE.  In nearly all states with red‑flag laws, firearms can be removed only after a court (a judge or magistrate) issues an Extreme Risk Protection Order—often first as a temporary ex parte order, which is still judge‑approved. A narrow exception exists (e.g., Indiana) where police may temporarily seize without a prior order in an emergency, but a judge must review it promptly (typically within 48 hours). So the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Four U.S Republicans, Will Hurd of Texas, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Fred Upton of Michigan and Susan Brooks of Indiana voted to have President Donald Trump impeached.
response_text: FALSE.  - In the 2019 House votes to impeach Trump, no Republicans voted for either article; Will Hurd, Brian Fitzpatrick, Fred Upton, and Susan Brooks all voted no. - In the 2021 impeachment after January 6, only Fred Upton (of the four) voted to impeach. Will Hurd and Susan Brooks were no longer in Congress, and Brian Fitzpatrick voted against.

claim: The WHO said that the Polio vaccine is responsible for the return of Polio in the Philippines.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO reported that the 2019 polio outbreak in the Philippines involved “vaccine-derived poliovirus,” which can occur when oral polio vaccine strains circulate and mutate in under-immunized communities. WHO emphasized that the root cause is low immunization coverage and poor sanitation—not the vaccine itself—and urged intensified vaccination to stop transmission.

claim: Cream Of Tartar Mixed With Orange Juice Will Help You Quit Smoking.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible clinical evidence that cream of tartar (potassium bitartrate) mixed with orange juice helps people quit smoking. Health agencies and guidelines do not list it as a cessation aid. Claims that it “flushes nicotine” or reduces cravings lack scientific support. Meanwhile, cream of tartar is high in potassium and can pose risks (e.g., hyperkalemia) for some people. Evidence-based methods include nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline or bupropion, and behavioral support.

claim: Thomas Jefferson said, “When the people fear the government, there is tyranny. When the government fears the people, there is liberty.”
response_text: FALSE.  No reliable source places this line in Jefferson’s writings. Monticello (the Thomas Jefferson Foundation) lists it as a spurious quotation; the earliest known version is from 1914, attributed to John Basil Barnhill.

claim: Mombasa is Kenya’s oldest town.
response_text: TRUE.  Mombasa is widely regarded as Kenya’s oldest city, with settlement evidence from around the 10th century and mentions by 12th‑century writers like al‑Idrisi. Other historic Kenyan towns such as Lamu date mainly from the 14th century (though Lamu is noted as the oldest well-preserved Swahili town). Slight uncertainty stems from differing definitions of “oldest,” but by conventional historical dating, Mombasa is oldest.

claim: Life expectancy in Kenya has increased to 67 years currently.
response_text: TRUE.  Recent estimates place Kenya’s life expectancy at about 66–67 years. For example, World Bank/UN figures for 2021–2023 are around 66.5–67 years, so saying “67 years currently” is a reasonable rounded value. (Small uncertainty due to source and year differences.)

claim: Mombasa is Kenya’s oldest town.
response_text: FALSE.  Lamu (Lamu Old Town) is widely recognized as Kenya’s oldest continually inhabited town and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Mombasa is very old and is often called Kenya’s oldest city, but not the oldest town.

claim: The Kenyatta administration has more than doubled the volume of cleared cargo passing through Kilindini, Mombasa's main port, annually.”
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya Ports Authority/KNBS data show the Port of Mombasa (Kilindini) increased total cargo from roughly 22–23 million tonnes in 2012/13 to about 35–37 million tonnes by 2019–2021, and container traffic from ~0.9 million to ~1.4 million TEUs—substantial growth but not a doubling. Moreover, under Kenyatta some cargo clearance shifted inland to ICDs (Nairobi/Naivasha), making a doubling of “cleared” cargo at the port even less likely.

claim: Kenyan President Kenyatta in national day speech stated Our life expectancy [has increased] from 35 years at independence
response_text: TRUE.  In a national day address (Jamhuri Day), President Uhuru Kenyatta said Kenya’s life expectancy had risen “from 35 years at independence to about 61 years.” Note: the 35-year figure is inaccurate; estimates for 1963 were closer to around 50 years.

claim: US White House did not withhold security aid to Ukraine, in part, because the administration wanted Ukraine to investigate Democrats and the 2016 election.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence from the 2019 impeachment inquiry shows the White House put roughly $391 million in Ukraine security assistance on hold in July 2019 and linked its release (and a White House meeting) to Ukraine announcing investigations into the Bidens/Burisma and the 2016 election. Multiple officials (e.g., Gordon Sondland, William Taylor, Fiona Hill) testified to this linkage, and Acting Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney publicly said the hold was partly about 2016 before attempting to walk it back. The GAO also found the hold violated the Impoundment Control Act (though it didn’t assess motive). While the administration denied a quid pro quo, the preponderance of evidence indicates the aid was withheld in part to prompt such investigations. Uncertainty: the White House disputed intent, but the record strongly contradicts the claim.

claim: Kenyan President Kenyatta in national day speech stated Our life expectancy [has increased to 67 years currently.
response_text: TRUE — In a national day address during his tenure (e.g., 2021), President Uhuru Kenyatta said Kenya’s life expectancy had risen to about 67 years. Official estimates at the time were around 66–67 years, so his rounded figure aligns with the data. (Minor uncertainty on the exact occasion/wording.)

claim: Over the last six years, the counties of Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, Taita Taveta and Tana River, have cumulatively received close to KSh190 billion from the Kenyan national treasury.
response_text: TRUE  Reason: Controller of Budget/CRA allocation schedules show that over six recent fiscal years (e.g., FY2013/14–2018/19), the six Coast counties’ cumulative equitable share from the National Treasury sums to roughly KSh195–200 billion. Even counting only the equitable share (excluding conditional grants), the total is around KSh190 billion, and including conditional grants pushes it higher. So “close to KSh190 billion” is accurate.   Note: Exact totals vary slightly with the six-year window chosen and whether conditional grants are included.

claim: Over the last six years, the Kenyan counties of Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, Taita Taveta and Tana River, have cumulatively received close to KSh190 billion from the national treasury.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Using the County Allocation of Revenue (equitable share) over the most recent six fiscal years, these six coastal counties together average roughly 40–45 billion shillings per year, implying a cumulative total around 230–250 billion—well above KSh190 billion. Even before adding conditional grants, the six-year sum comfortably exceeds KSh190b. Exact totals vary by fiscal years and whether “received” includes conditional grants, but the figure is clearly higher than 190b.

claim: Kenyan life expectancy at independence in 1963 was 35 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Best estimates (e.g., UN World Population Prospects, World Bank) put Kenya’s life expectancy at birth in the early 1960s around 49–51 years. A figure of 35 years would be more typical of earlier decades or lower-income African averages, not Kenya in 1963.

claim: Mombasa is Kenya’s oldest town.
response_text: FALSE.  Mombasa is often described as Kenya’s oldest city, but the country’s oldest town is generally considered to be Lamu (Lamu Old Town), a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the oldest continuously inhabited Swahili town in East Africa. Some sources still call Mombasa the oldest city, which causes the confusion.

claim: Over the last six years, the counties of Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, Taita Taveta and Tana River, have cumulatively received close to KSh190 billion from the national treasury.
response_text: TRUE.  Controller of Budget/National Treasury data for the first six years of devolution (roughly FY2013/14–FY2018/19) show the six Coast counties together received about KSh 195–205 billion in exchequer releases (equitable share plus conditional grants). Describing this cumulative amount as “close to KSh190 billion” is reasonable. Minor uncertainty depends on the exact six-year window and whether conditional grants are included.

claim: Kenyan President Kenyatta in national day speech stated Under this administration … at Kilindini we have more than doubled the volume of cleared cargo passing [through] the port annually.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya Ports Authority data show Mombasa/Kilindini’s throughput rose, but not by “more than double,” under Kenyatta. Total cargo increased from roughly 22–23 million tonnes in 2012 to about 30–36 million tonnes by 2018–2019 (≈35–60% up), and container traffic from ~0.9 million TEUs to ~1.3–1.4 million TEUs—not a doubling. (Slight uncertainty on exact year referenced, but no period under his administration shows a doubling.)

claim: Trump has sent 14,000 troops to Middle East since May.
response_text: TRUE.  Pentagon officials said in early December 2019 that roughly 14,000 additional U.S. forces had been deployed to the Middle East since May 2019 amid tensions with Iran. This approximate figure included units such as a carrier strike group, bomber task force, and air/missile defense assets (some at sea).

claim: Life expectancy in Kenya was 35 years in 1963 - the year Kenya became independent from Britain.
response_text: FALSE.  Best-available estimates (World Bank/UN/Our World in Data) put Kenya’s life expectancy at birth around 49–51 years in the early 1960s (e.g., ~49 in 1960 and ~52 in 1965), not 35. A figure as low as 35 would reflect much earlier decades, not 1963. Uncertainty: exact year-to-year estimates vary slightly by source, but none are near 35.

claim: Mombasa is Kenya’s oldest town.
response_text: TRUE.  Mombasa is widely regarded as Kenya’s oldest city, with documented references from at least the 12th–14th centuries and occupation dating to around the 10th century. Note: some sources call Lamu Old Town the oldest and best-preserved Swahili town (in terms of intact urban fabric), which can cause confusion, but Mombasa’s settlement predates Lamu’s.

claim: Kenyan President Kenyatta in national day speech stated Over the last six years, the counties of Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, Taita Taveta and Tana River, have cumulatively received close to KSh190 billion from the national treasury.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In his Mashujaa Day address in Mombasa on 20 October 2019, President Uhuru Kenyatta stated that over the previous six years the Coast Region counties—Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, Taita Taveta and Tana River—had cumulatively received “close to KSh190 billion” from the National Treasury. This phrasing appears in reports and the official speech transcript.

claim: “Under this administration … at Kilindini we have more than doubled the volume of cleared cargo passing [through] the port annually
response_text: FALSE.  Why: Kenya Ports Authority data show only modest growth at Kilindini/Mombasa since the current administration took office (e.g., total cargo throughput rose from about 33.9m tonnes in 2022 to about 36.0m in 2023, and container traffic increased from roughly 1.45m TEUs in 2022 to around 1.6m+ TEUs in 2023). That is growth, but nowhere near a doubling. If “cleared cargo” refers specifically to the share cleared at Mombasa rather than inland depots, that share likely rose after policy changes, but total volume “passing through the port annually” did not double. Uncertainty: the phrase “cleared cargo” is ambiguous, but on any standard volume metric the claim is not supported.

claim: German TV said there were 2.2 million people at the People’s Vote march on Saturday 19 October.
response_text: FALSE.  German broadcasters (e.g., ZDF and ARD) did not report 2.2 million attendees for the 19 October 2019 People’s Vote march; their coverage referred to “hundreds of thousands.” The 2.2 million figure circulated via social media but is not supported by any German TV report.

claim: President Donald Trump has endorsed a supposed “Congressional Reform Act of 2017''.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no real “Congressional Reform Act of 2017.” It’s a long-running viral hoax/chain post that lists sweeping changes to congressional pay, benefits, and term limits. Trump did advocate term limits for Congress during his campaign, but there’s no record of him endorsing (or Congress introducing) a bill by that name. Fact-checkers have debunked the claim.

claim: In 2008 the US Congress gave Wall Street trillions of dollars of zero interest loans.
response_text: FALSE.  - In 2008 Congress created TARP, authorizing up to $700 billion (not “trillions”) mainly as capital injections and loans that carried dividends/interest and warrants—not zero‑interest loans. - The multi‑trillion emergency lending during the crisis was done by the Federal Reserve, not Congress, and those facilities charged interest (often low) and were repaid.

claim: Pricking a needle on the fingertips of a stroke victim can save their life as they will gain consciousness in some time.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no medical evidence that pricking a stroke victim’s fingertips helps, restores consciousness, or “saves their life.” Major authorities (American Heart Association/American Stroke Association, CDC, Red Cross) specifically advise against this myth. It can delay urgent, proven treatments (thrombolysis or thrombectomy) and may cause harm (infection, bleeding). The correct action is to call emergency services immediately, note the time symptoms began, keep the person safe and upright if possible, and do not give food or drink.

claim: Once a stroke victim's mouth is crooked, you should pull their the ears until they are red and prick them until they bleed. This technique will stop capillaries in the victim’s brain from bursting.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no medical evidence that pulling or pricking the ears (or fingers) helps a stroke. This “needle/ear” technique is a widely debunked myth. Strokes are typically caused by a blocked artery (ischemic) or, less commonly, a ruptured brain vessel (hemorrhagic); neither is treated by releasing blood from the ears or skin, and doing so can cause harm and, critically, delay lifesaving care.  What to do instead: recognize FAST (Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services), call EMS immediately, note symptom onset, keep the person safe and monitor breathing.

claim: Tote bags made from cotton harm the environment
response_text: TRUE — but with nuance.  Cotton totes have real environmental impacts. Cotton cultivation and fabric production are resource- and pollution‑intensive (high water use, land, energy; pesticides/fertilizers for conventional cotton; impacts from dyeing). Life‑cycle assessments (e.g., UK Environment Agency 2011; Danish EPA 2018) show cotton totes must be reused many times (often dozens to 100+ times for climate impacts, and far more for some other impact categories) to outperform lightweight plastic bags. If used only a few times or treated as disposable fashion items, cotton totes can have higher overall impacts.

claim: Asaduddin Owaisi, president of All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) danced at an election rally to celebrate the murder of Hindu Samaj leader, Kamlesh Tiwari.
response_text: FALSE.  A viral clip of Asaduddin Owaisi dancing was from an election rally held days before Kamlesh Tiwari was killed on October 18, 2019, and was unrelated to the murder. Multiple fact-checkers (Alt News, BOOM, India Today, Factly) verified the video predated the killing and that Owaisi had condemned Tiwari’s murder.

claim: Donald Trump stated "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
response_text: FALSE  Trump has often said variants like “They’re not after me, they’re after you. I’m just in the way,” and he frequently talks about guns, religious liberty/Christian values, and freedom. But there’s no reliable record of him stating this exact merged line with “Make no mistake … your guns, your Christian values, your freedom” as quoted; it appears to be a paraphrase/meme that embellishes his usual phrasing. Uncertainty: high only about exact wording, not about the general sentiment.

claim: Late US advice columnist Ann Landers was the originator of the quote: "At age 20, we worry about what others think of us. At age 40, we don’t care what they think. At age 60, we discover that they have not been thinking of us at all."
response_text: FALSE.  The line is widely attributed to Ann Landers, but researchers (e.g., Quote Investigator) have found earlier versions in print decades before her column. A closely related aphorism appears in the 1930s (credited to Olin Miller), and the 20–40–60 formulation is documented in print by the 1940s/50s—well before Landers popularized it. She did not originate it.

claim: You need a toll receipt during any medical emergency, flat tyre, or in need of fuel, where you can call the phone number given on the other side of the toll receipt for assistance.
response_text: FALSE  - On Indian national highways, you don’t need a toll receipt to get help; you can dial the unified NHAI helpline 1033 for accidents, medical aid, breakdowns, or fuel assistance. Emergency numbers are also posted on highway signboards. - Not all toll receipts consistently print such numbers, and many trips now use FASTag without a printed receipt. - The claim is framed as a general rule, which isn’t true universally or even consistently within India.

claim: Eric Trump claims that the Trumps' no longer profit from foreign deals
response_text: FALSE.  Eric Trump pledged no new foreign deals while his father was president and said they’d donate “profits” from foreign government patronage at Trump properties. In reality, the Trump Organization continued earning money from existing overseas ventures and foreign government spending during the presidency, and has since pursued new projects abroad (e.g., in Indonesia and the Gulf). House Oversight Democrats reported millions in payments from foreign governments to Trump businesses during his term. So it’s not accurate that the Trumps no longer profit from foreign deals.

claim: Americans prefer giving people under 65 an option to join Medicare as opposed to requiring them to give up their current coverage.
response_text: TRUE.  Polling consistently shows Americans favor an optional Medicare buy‑in/public option over plans that would replace existing private coverage. KFF polls (2019–2021) found roughly 65–75% support for allowing people under 65 to buy into Medicare or a public option, while support drops markedly when a plan would eliminate private insurance. Similar patterns appear in Pew, Quinnipiac, and Morning Consult surveys.

claim: A twitter account @Polytikle changed their account name to Abhikit Banerjee in an attempt to parody the real Abhikit Banerjee, Nobel Prize Winner.
response_text: FALSE  - The Nobel laureate’s name is Abhijit Banerjee, not “Abhikit” Banerjee. - There is no reliable, widely reported evidence (as of 2024) that the handle @Polytikle changed its display name to impersonate/parody Abhijit Banerjee.   Note: If the claim intended “Abhijit,” it still lacks corroboration; uncertainty remains due to limited verifiable records.

claim: Union Jack flags in London have replaced EU flags outside parliament ahead of the opening of parliament by the Queen.
response_text: FALSE. EU flags outside Parliament were protestors’ flags, not official installations, so there were no EU flags to “replace.” Union Jacks were put up on nearby routes as routine ceremonial decorations for the State Opening (and other events), not as replacements for EU flags. Protest EU flags continued to be displayed by demonstrators.

claim: $53 million a week is coming across the Mexico/US border in drugs
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The figure comes from rough averages of what CBP has seized and (sometimes) valued in past years, not from a measured total of drugs “coming across.” Agencies don’t know the total inflow; they only know seizures, which vary widely by year, drug, valuation method, and often include ports of entry and sometimes borders beyond Mexico. So stating “$53 million a week is coming across” is unsupported and misleading. (Uncertainty: exact totals are unknowable; only seizures are measured.)

claim: There has been a reduction in Right to Information (RTI) applications filed in the last few years leading upto 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  CIC annual reports show RTI applications to central public authorities rose year-on-year up to 2018–19 (e.g., roughly 9.8 lakh in 2015–16 to about 13.7 lakh in 2018–19). While some departments or states may have seen dips, the overall trend leading up to 2019 was an increase, not a reduction. (A decline appears in 2019–20, which is after 2019.) Uncertainty: exact figures vary by source, but the upward trend is consistent.

claim: Rapper Kurtis Blow is In Critical Condition After Emergency Heart Surgery
response_text: FALSE.  Kurtis Blow did undergo emergency heart surgery in 2019 and later had a successful heart transplant in 2020, but credible reports at those times said he was stable and recovering, not in critical condition. No reliable sources substantiate that he was “in critical condition” after those procedures.

claim: AOC Said Children Should Be Raised By The State.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record (speech, interview, tweet, or transcript) of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying children should be “raised by the state.” Fact-checkers have traced this to fabricated/misattributed memes. Her positions advocate expanded childcare, education, and family support—not replacing parents with the state.

claim: Every week, at least 12 doctors leave Nigeria to seek employment in the UK.
response_text: FALSE.  Best available data come from the UK General Medical Council, which tracks Nigerian-trained doctors joining the UK medical register. In the mid-to-late 2010s, annual joiners from Nigeria were typically in the low hundreds (roughly 150–300 per year), i.e., about 3–6 per week—well below 12. While migration has risen in more recent years and some years may now exceed 12 per week on average, the blanket claim “every week, at least 12” is not consistently supported. Uncertainty: recent spikes could meet or exceed that rate, but not across the period when the claim became popular.

claim: There are only eight neuropsychiatric hospitals in Nigeria.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Nigeria has eight federally run specialist Neuropsychiatric Hospitals (e.g., Aro/Abeokuta, Yaba/Lagos, Enugu, Benin/Uselu, Kaduna, Maiduguri, Calabar, Kware/Sokoto). But there are additional state-owned and private psychiatric hospitals and many psychiatric units in teaching/general hospitals, so the total number of neuropsychiatric facilities is more than eight. (If one means only the federal specialty hospitals, then the number is eight.)

claim: 134ft Anaconda snake found in the Amazon has killed 257 human beings and 2325 animals.
response_text: FALSE.  - No snake approaches 134 ft (41 m). The longest scientifically measured snakes are under 10 m; green anacondas typically max out around 6–7 m (20–23 ft).   - There is no credible record of any snake killing hundreds of humans; anaconda attacks on people are extremely rare.   - This claim has circulated for years as a viral hoax, often with miscaptioned or edited photos.  Confidence: high.

claim: There are less than 150 psychiatrists in this country of 200 million.
response_text: FALSE.  Likely referring to Nigeria (≈200+ million people), most recent estimates report around 250–300 psychiatrists, not under 150. Other ~200 million countries (e.g., Pakistan, Brazil) also have far more than 150 psychiatrists. Note: older Nigeria figures sometimes cited <150, but current numbers are higher.

claim: Nigeria has an estimated physician-patient ratio of one doctor to every 4,000 to 5,000 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  Best available official data (WHO/World Bank) put Nigeria’s physician density at about 0.38–0.40 per 1,000 people (roughly 3.8–4.0 per 10,000), which is about one doctor per 2,500–2,600 people—better than 1:4,000–5,000. The higher ratio is often cited by local bodies based on counts of actively practicing/public-sector doctors and uneven distribution, but it isn’t supported by the national physician-density series. Some uncertainty remains due to data lags and emigration.

claim: Nigeria has Africa's highest rate of depression.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: WHO/GBD estimates indicate Nigeria has the largest number of people living with depression in Africa (because of its large population), not the highest prevalence rate. Several African countries—such as Tunisia, Lesotho, Libya, South Africa and others—have higher estimated depression rates than Nigeria. (Exact rankings vary by dataset/year.)

claim: Nigeria ranks fifth in the world in the frequency of suicide.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO data do not place Nigeria 5th by suicide rate or by total suicides. Nigeria’s age‑standardized suicide rate is roughly 6–7 per 100,000 (2019 WHO estimates), far below the highest‑rate countries (e.g., Lesotho, Guyana, Lithuania, South Korea, Russia). By absolute numbers, countries like India, China, the U.S., Russia, Indonesia/Japan are higher. While underreporting in Nigeria is likely, no credible ranking supports 5th.

claim: By 2018, Nigeria had allocated just 3.95% of its budget to funding its ministry of health.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria’s 2018 federal budget allocated about N340.5 billion to the health sector out of a proposed total N8.612 trillion—roughly 3.95% (and about 3.9% of the final N9.12 trillion budget). This is widely cited as far below the 15% Abuja Declaration target.

claim: Nigeria ranks fifth in the world in the frequency of suicide.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO and other global estimates show Nigeria is not among the top five countries by suicide rate (per 100,000). Nigeria’s age‑standardized rate is mid-to-low globally and below or around the global average, while the highest rates are in countries such as Lesotho, Guyana, Eswatini, Lithuania, and others—not Nigeria. Even by absolute numbers, Nigeria is not fifth. (There is underreporting, but not enough to place it near top five.)

claim: There are less than 150 psychiatrists in this country of 200 million.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: For countries around 200 million people (e.g., Nigeria, Pakistan, Brazil), available estimates show far more than 150 psychiatrists—Nigeria roughly 250–300, Pakistan several hundred, and Brazil many thousands. Without a specific country/year, the claim is most likely incorrect. (Some older Nigeria estimates were lower, but current figures exceed 150.)

claim: Nigeria has Africa's highest rate of depression.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: WHO estimates indicated Nigeria had the largest number of people with depression in Africa (due to its large population), not the highest prevalence rate. Several African countries have equal or higher depression prevalence than Nigeria. (Uncertainty: exact rankings vary by dataset/year, but the consensus does not place Nigeria highest in rate.)

claim: Congressional benefits include 67 paid holidays, three weeks paid vacation, unlimited paid sick days.
response_text: FALSE.  - Members of Congress are salaried elected officials, not federal “employees,” and do not accrue federal leave. There is no formal allotment of “paid holidays,” “paid vacation,” or “paid sick days” for members. - The “67 paid holidays” figure misrepresents days when chambers are not in session or on recess/district work periods; it’s not a list of official paid holidays (there are about 11 federal holidays). - While Congress has recesses, these are not codified as paid vacation, and there is no policy of unlimited paid sick leave for members.

claim: WHO estimates that fewer than 10% of mentally ill Nigerians have access to the care they need.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: WHO reporting on Nigeria’s mental health system (e.g., WHO-AIMS/Mental Health Atlas) and national surveys cited by WHO indicate a treatment gap of about 90%—meaning fewer than 10% of people with mental disorders receive the care they need. Figures vary by disorder and source, but the “<10% receive care” estimate aligns with WHO’s assessments. (Minor uncertainty over wording of “access” vs “receive,” but the magnitude is consistent.)

claim: The Amazon river is in Africa
response_text: FALSE. The Amazon River is in South America (mainly Brazil, Peru, and Colombia), not Africa.

claim: Nigeria ranks fifth in the world in the frequency of suicide.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO/Global Health Estimates do not place Nigeria in the top five for suicide rates; Nigeria’s rate is roughly 6–7 per 100,000, far below countries like Lesotho, Guyana, Eswatini, and Lithuania. Even by absolute numbers, the largest totals are in India, China, the United States, Russia, and Japan—not Nigeria. There may be underreporting in Nigeria, but no credible data rank it fifth.

claim: Nigeria has Africa's highest rate of depression.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO’s 2017 estimates show Nigeria has the largest number of people with depression in Africa (due to its large population), not the highest rate (prevalence). Several African countries have higher estimated prevalence than Nigeria.

claim: Nigeria ranks fifth in the world in the frequency of suicide
response_text: FALSE.  Why: WHO’s most recent global estimates (2019) put Nigeria’s age‑standardized suicide rate around 6–7 per 100,000—nowhere near the top. Countries with the highest rates include Lesotho, Guyana, Eswatini, Kiribati, Lithuania, Russia, South Korea, etc. Nigeria is not in the top 5 (or even top 20) by rate. Even by absolute number of suicides, larger-population countries like India, China, the United States, Indonesia, and Russia report higher totals. While underreporting exists in Nigeria, no credible data rank it fifth globally.

claim: Nigeria has an estimated physician-patient ratio of one doctor to every 4,000 to 5,000 patients.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple Nigerian official and professional sources (e.g., the Federal Ministry of Health and the Nigerian Medical Association) frequently cite an estimated doctor-to-patient ratio of about 1:4,000–1:5,000. Note: some international datasets (e.g., World Bank physician density) imply a less severe ratio (~1:2,500), but those figures are older and may overcount non-practicing or emigrated doctors; rural areas can be worse.

claim: Congressional benefits include retirement package.
response_text: TRUE.  Members of Congress receive retirement benefits as part of federal employment. They participate in Social Security, the Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) with a pension based on age and years of service, and the Thrift Savings Plan (TSP).

claim: WHO estimates that fewer than 10% of mentally ill Nigerians have access to the care they need.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO reporting (e.g., Mental Health Atlas and country briefs) has long indicated an enormous “treatment gap” in Nigeria—around 80–90% of people with mental disorders receive no care—implying fewer than 10% get the treatment they need. Minor variability exists across sources, but the claim aligns with WHO estimates.

claim: The snake found in the Amazon is 134 feet long and 2067 kgs
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record supports a 134‑foot (≈41 m), 2,067‑kg snake from the Amazon. The largest living snakes (reticulated pythons and green anacondas) reliably reach roughly 6–10 m (20–33 ft) and well under ~250 kg. Even the largest known extinct snake, Titanoboa, is estimated at about 13–14 m (42–47 ft) and ~1,100 kg—far smaller and lighter than the claim. This viral claim has been repeatedly debunked.

claim: There are less than 150 psychiatrists in Nigeria who has a population of 200 million.
response_text: FALSE.  Most recent estimates put Nigeria’s psychiatrist workforce well above 150—roughly 200–300. For example, WHO’s Mental Health Atlas (2020) reports about 0.12–0.13 psychiatrists per 100,000 population, which translates to roughly 240–270 for a 200+ million population. Nigerian professional bodies and media reports in 2021–2023 commonly cite about 250 psychiatrists. Figures below 150 appear in older/outdated statements.

claim: There are only eight neuropsychiatric hospitals in Nigeria.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Nigeria has eight federally owned neuropsychiatric hospitals (e.g., Aro Abeokuta; Yaba Lagos; Enugu; Calabar; Uselu Benin; Kaduna; Maiduguri; Kware Sokoto). But there are additional neuropsychiatric/psychiatric hospitals outside the federal network—such as the state-run Neuro Psychiatric Hospital, Rumuigbo (Port Harcourt)—and various private facilities. So the total number is more than eight. (If one meant only federal neuropsychiatric hospitals, then eight is correct.)

claim: In Nigeria, the physician-patient ratio is six times smaller (one physician to every 600 doctors) than what is recommended by WHO.
response_text: FALSE.  - The parenthetical “one physician to every 600 doctors” is nonsensical. - WHO does not have an official global “recommended” doctor‑to‑patient ratio (1:1,000 is often used as a rough benchmark, not a formal standard). - Nigeria’s physician density is roughly 0.3–0.4 per 1,000 people (about 1 doctor per 2,500–3,500 people; some estimates are nearer 1:5,000+), which is several times worse than 1:1,000—but the claim’s figures and “six times smaller” characterization are incorrect.  Uncertainty: exact ratios vary by source and year, but the claim as stated is still wrong.

claim: Congressional benefits include free health care.
response_text: FALSE.  Members of Congress do not get free health care. To receive the government’s employer contribution, they must buy insurance through the DC exchange under the Affordable Care Act, and they still pay premiums, deductibles, and copays. They can use the Office of the Attending Physician at the Capitol for basic care, but that requires an annual fee and is subsidized—not free.

claim: By 2018, Nigeria had allocated just 3.95% of its budget to funding its ministry of health.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria’s 2018 federal budget allocated roughly N340–356 billion to the health sector out of a total N8.6–9.1 trillion, amounting to about 3.9–4.0%. The 3.95% figure matches the 2018 proposed budget; the approved budget still left health at about 3.9%. Minor variation by source, but the claim is essentially accurate.

claim: WHO estimates that fewer than 10% of mentally ill Nigerians have access to the care they need.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO assessments (e.g., WHO-AIMS and Mental Health Atlas data cited in WHO/AFRO materials) describe a mental health “treatment gap” in Nigeria of around 90%—meaning fewer than 10% of people with mental disorders receive the care they need. Figures vary by year and condition, but WHO consistently reports a very large (>80–90%) gap, supporting the claim.

claim: Nigeria has Africa's highest rate of depression.
response_text: FALSE. WHO/GBD estimates show Nigeria has the largest number of people with depression in Africa (due to its large population), not the highest prevalence rate; several other African countries have higher depression prevalence than Nigeria.

claim: Nigeria has an estimated physician-patient ratio of one doctor to every 4,000 to 5,000 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  Recent estimates from the Nigerian Medical Association (2022–2024) put Nigeria’s doctor‑to‑patient ratio around 1:10,000–1:12,000, reflecting significant emigration of physicians. Older or registry-based figures sometimes cited 1:4,000–1:5,000, but these are outdated or count non-practicing doctors. Uncertainty: estimates vary by source and method, but current credible figures are worse than 1:5,000.

claim: Joe Biden wants to abolish the "stepped up basis" that currently reduces inheritance taxes.
response_text: FALSE.  Why: - Biden has proposed ending the step‑up in basis at death for large unrealized gains (generally above $1M per person, with carve‑outs), but step‑up affects capital gains taxes on inherited assets, not inheritance/estate taxes. - The U.S. federal “inheritance tax” doesn’t exist; a federal estate tax does, and step‑up doesn’t reduce it. It reduces heirs’ capital gains taxes when they sell the asset.  Note: His proposals have not been enacted by Congress.

claim: CNN reported Philip Andrei Gancia Became a Porn Star
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record in CNN’s archives or other credible outlets of CNN reporting this. The claim appears unsubstantiated and likely fabricated. (Low uncertainty)

claim: Viral Video states that Filipino National ID's can now be obtained.
response_text: TRUE  Filipinos can obtain a National ID under the Philippine Identification System (PhilSys). The ePhilID (digital/printed version) has been available and valid, and physical PhilID cards are being issued gradually. Note: IDs aren’t instantly downloadable; you must register and claim via official PSA channels.

claim: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will introduce a new ₹1000 banknote post January 1, 2020
response_text: FALSE.  RBI has not reintroduced a ₹1000 banknote since the 2016 demonetisation. Ahead of and after January 1, 2020, official channels (including PIB Fact Check and RBI statements) denied such rumors, and no ₹1000 note has been issued. As of today, the Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series includes ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, and previously ₹2000 (now withdrawn from circulation), but no ₹1000.

claim: In the US the impeachment process has always gone through the House Judiciary Committee, because it is the committee of jurisdiction over the Constitution and over impeachment, not the Intelligence Committee.
response_text: FALSE.  - The House Judiciary Committee has general jurisdiction over impeachment under House rules, but the House can delegate work to other committees or select committees. - Historical exceptions:   - Early impeachments (e.g., Justice Samuel Chase in 1804) predated the Judiciary Committee and were handled by select committees.   - Andrew Johnson’s 1868 impeachment was driven by the Committee on Reconstruction, with articles drafted by a select committee—not Judiciary.   - In 2019, the House Intelligence Committee led the impeachment inquiry and public hearings under H.Res. 660 before transmitting findings to Judiciary. Thus, it has not “always” gone through Judiciary, and Intelligence has played a leading role at least once.

claim: The Trump family was disallowed from operating any charity in the State of New York because they stole from a kids cancer charity.
response_text: FALSE.  - New York forced the Donald J. Trump Foundation to dissolve and a judge ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million for misusing the foundation (self‑dealing and political use). The court imposed training for his children and some restrictions/oversight on future charitable roles, but not a blanket, permanent ban on the “Trump family” operating any charity in New York. - The action was not “because they stole from a kids’ cancer charity.” That phrasing refers to media reports about the Eric Trump Foundation’s St. Jude fundraising, not a court finding of theft, and it was not the basis of the New York case. (Minor uncertainty on the exact duration/terms of restrictions, but no blanket family ban or kids‑cancer‑theft finding.)

claim: US food standards allow for insect fragments in peanut butter.
response_text: TRUE.  The FDA’s Defect Levels Handbook sets “defect action levels” for unavoidable contaminants. For peanut butter, enforcement begins at an average of 30 or more insect fragments per 100 grams—meaning smaller amounts are tolerated under U.S. standards.

claim: Minneapolis "city government preemptively informed the Target Center that it would be responsible for $530,000 in security and other costs" related to a Trump rally, "more than 26 times the estimated security costs for a 2009 Target Center health care rally held by President Barack Obama.
response_text: TRUE.  - In Oct. 2019, Minneapolis told the Target Center’s operator (AEG Facilities) in advance that it would be responsible for about $530,000 in security and related public safety costs tied to a Trump rally. - Records and contemporaneous reporting put the city’s estimated costs for Obama’s 2009 Target Center health‑care event at roughly $20,000, making $530,000 “more than 26 times” that figure.  Note: The comparison is imperfect—Obama’s 2009 figure did not include broad police overtime and was an official presidential visit with federal involvement—so the numbers aren’t strictly apples to apples.

claim: US food standards allow for maggots in orange juice.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The FDA’s Defect Levels Handbook does set allowable limits for unavoidable defects in foods, but for citrus/orange juice the standard is based on mold count (Howard mold count), not fly eggs or maggots. Maggot/fly egg tolerances apply to some other products (e.g., tomato products, canned mushrooms), not orange juice. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Thomas Jefferson said, “The government will one day be corrupt and filled with liars, and the people will flock to the one that tells the truth."
response_text: FALSE.  No such quotation appears in Jefferson’s writings. Monticello’s Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia lists this as a spurious quote, and researchers have found no contemporaneous source; it seems to be a modern internet fabrication.

claim: One in four women in Africa suffer from depression.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO estimates put point prevalence of depression around 4–5% globally and roughly 4% in the African Region, with women having somewhat higher rates (about 5–6%), not 25%. The “1 in 4” figure is often a misquote referring to the lifetime risk of any mental disorder, not current depression, and not specific to African women. Uncertainty: data in some subgroups (e.g., perinatal, HIV) can be higher, but not population-wide.

claim: "New Starbucks CEO" Rosalind Brewer admits she doesn't like white people?
response_text: FALSE.  - Rosalind “Roz” Brewer was Starbucks’ COO (2017–2021), not its CEO. She later became CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance. - She never said she “doesn’t like white people.” The rumor misrepresents a 2015 interview where she advocated for supplier and leadership diversity; she did not express dislike for white people. Fact-checkers have debunked this claim.

claim: Cancer is a fungus called myotoxin, not a disease.
response_text: FALSE.  Cancer is a group of diseases caused by uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal human cells, not a fungus. “Myotoxin” refers to toxins (often from snake venom) that damage muscle; “mycotoxins” are toxins made by fungi. Neither is a fungus that “is” cancer, and antifungal treatments do not cure cancer.

claim: Theoretical physicist Albert Einstein once stated, “The difference between stupidity and genius is that genius has its limits.”
response_text: FALSE.  No reliable source ties this line to Einstein. Quote references (e.g., The Ultimate Quotable Einstein and Quote Investigator) list it as apocryphal. A close precursor exists from Elbert Hubbard: “Genius may have its limitations, but stupidity is not thus handicapped” (early 1900s).

claim: Trump TV Ad Misleads on Biden and Ukraine
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Trump campaign ad claimed Joe Biden forced Ukraine to fire its prosecutor to protect his son. Fact-checks found this misleading: Biden’s pressure to oust Prosecutor General Viktor Shokin reflected broad U.S., EU, and IMF policy over corruption concerns; there’s no evidence Biden acted to help Hunter. Shokin was not actively investigating Burisma at the time, and multiple independent reviews found no proof of a Biden-directed effort to shield his son.

claim: Democrats are draining Americans’ health care to finance open borders.
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. does not have “open borders.” Border enforcement continues (millions of CBP encounters, removals, and recent asylum restrictions), and Democrats have supported additional border resources and reforms. - There is no evidence Democrats are “draining” Americans’ health care to fund immigration. Health care funding has generally increased (e.g., ACA subsidy expansions, Medicare drug reforms). While HHS has at times reprogrammed limited funds to care for unaccompanied children—something done under both parties—these are small, legal shifts within HHS and do not meaningfully cut Americans’ health care to “finance open borders.”

claim: Donald Trump and the Republicans are committed to protecting people who have preexisting medical conditions.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump and congressional Republicans repeatedly backed measures that would have weakened or eliminated ACA protections for preexisting conditions: the 2017 repeal bills (AHCA, BCRA, Graham‑Cassidy) allowed state waivers and higher premiums for sick people; the Trump DOJ asked courts to strike the ACA’s guaranteed‑issue and community‑rating rules; and the administration expanded short‑term/association plans that can exclude or surcharge people with preexisting conditions. Public statements aside, their actions did not reflect a commitment to preserving those protections.

claim: In Nigeria, the physician to patient ratio is one doctor to every 4,000 to 5,000 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  Most reliable national estimates (WHO/World Bank) put Nigeria’s physician density around 0.3–0.4 per 1,000 people (3–4 per 10,000), which is roughly 1 doctor per 2,500–3,300 people. The often-quoted 1:4,000–5,000 figure reflects shortages in some regions or counts of only actively practicing public‑sector doctors, but it overstates the national average. (Some uncertainty exists because active-in-country numbers vary and distribution is highly uneven.)

claim: The physician to patient ratio in Nigeria of one doctor to every 4,000 to 5,000 patients is six times smaller than the World Health Organisation's recommendation of one physician to every 600 patients.
response_text: FALSE.  - WHO does not have a formal global recommendation of 1 physician per 600 people; that figure is a common misquote. WHO uses broader health‑worker density thresholds (e.g., combined doctors/nurses/midwives), not a physician-only 1:600 target. - Even arithmetically, a ratio of 1:4,000–5,000 vs 1:600 would be about 6.7–8.3 times worse, not “six times.”  - Nigeria’s exact ratio is debated, but the claim’s comparison to a non-existent WHO standard makes it incorrect. Uncertainty: estimates for Nigeria range widely (often cited as 1:4,000–5,000; World Bank data suggest ~1:2,500).

claim: Nigeria is fifth in the world rankings for the frequency of suicides.
response_text: FALSE.  By global suicide rates (per 100,000 people), Nigeria is nowhere near the top five. WHO/Global Health Estimates place Nigeria around 6–7 per 100,000—far below countries with the highest rates (many above 20–30 per 100,000, e.g., Lesotho, Guyana, Eswatini, Lithuania, etc.). Even by absolute numbers of suicides, Nigeria is not fifth globally. Uncertainty: exact rank varies by year/source, but it is not close to 5th.

claim: The World Health Organisation estimates that fewer than 10% of Nigerians suffering from mental health disorders have access to the care that they need.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO reporting (e.g., WHO-AIMS and subsequent WHO materials) places Nigeria’s mental health treatment gap at about 90%, meaning fewer than 1 in 10 people with mental health disorders receive the care they need. Figures vary by condition and study, but the WHO-cited estimate supports the claim.

claim: By 2018 only 3.95% of Nigeria's budget for funding the country's ministry of health had been allocated.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In Nigeria’s 2018 federal budget proposal (N8.612 trillion), about N340.45 billion was allocated to the health sector/Federal Ministry of Health—about 3.95% of the total. After passage the total budget rose to N9.12 trillion, making the share roughly 3.7%, but the often-cited 3.95% figure refers to the proposed 2018 budget. Uncertainty: wording could conflate proposed vs approved budget.

claim: Donald Trump  put a stop to  Millionaires being eligible for the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP), commonly known as food stamps in the US.
response_text: FALSE.  - SNAP already has strict income limits; “millionaires” (by assets) were only theoretically eligible in some states that waived asset tests via “broad-based categorical eligibility” (BBCE), and such cases were exceedingly rare. - The Trump USDA proposed in 2019 to restrict BBCE (a change that would have reintroduced asset tests and addressed that theoretical loophole), but the rule never took effect and was later withdrawn under the Biden administration.

claim: Nigeria has the highest rate of depression within the continent of Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO/Global Burden of Disease estimates show Nigeria has the largest number of people with depression in Africa (due to its large population), not the highest rate (prevalence). Several countries—particularly in southern and some North African states (e.g., Lesotho, South Africa, Tunisia)—have higher estimated prevalence than Nigeria. Rankings can vary by dataset/year, but none reliably place Nigeria as the highest rate.

claim: Nigeria has a population of 200 million and there are less than 150 psychiatrists in the country.
response_text: FALSE.  - Nigeria’s population is now over 220 million (UN estimates), not 200 million. - Most reliable estimates put the number of psychiatrists in Nigeria around 200–300 (often cited ≈250), not fewer than 150, though figures vary by source and over time.

claim: Every week in Nigeria, twelve doctors leave to seek employment in the United Kingdom.
response_text: FALSE.  UK General Medical Council data show far more Nigeria‑trained doctors join the UK register than 12 per week in recent years—for example: 852 in 2018 (~16/week), 1,347 in 2019 (~26/week), and 1,769 in 2022 (~34/week). The “12 per week” figure is outdated and understates the current flow. Note: GMC registrations are a proxy for migration.

claim: The government should distribute multivitamins, vitamin c and zinc tablets to the common people as it will cure people of coronavirus and to those people who don't have the disease, they will get immune to the disease.
response_text: FALSE.  Vitamins and zinc do not cure COVID-19, nor do they make people immune to it. High-quality studies and major health guidelines (e.g., WHO, NIH) have found no proven benefit of vitamin C, zinc, or multivitamins for treating or preventing COVID-19 beyond correcting a deficiency. Specific immunity comes from vaccination or prior infection, not from these supplements. Overuse can also cause side effects.

claim: Donald Trump says his impeachment is a coup.
response_text: TRUE. In September 2019, during the first impeachment inquiry, Donald Trump tweeted that what was taking place was “not an impeachment, it is a COUP,” and he repeated that characterization in remarks and tweets around that time.

claim: The South African government has successfully increased the contribution of clean energy from 0% in 2010 to over 4.5% within five years.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: In 2010 South Africa already had “clean” generation from nuclear (~5%) and hydropower, so the share was not 0%. It is true that utility‑scale wind and solar grew from near zero around 2010–2011 to roughly 4–5% of electricity by 2015 under the REIPPPP, but the claim as worded (“clean energy” from 0% in 2010) is misleading.

claim: Rules for whistle-blowers recently changed.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: In multiple jurisdictions, whistleblower rules have been updated in the last few years. Examples include the EU Whistleblower Directive (2019) being implemented by member states during 2021–2023, adding new internal reporting-channel and protection requirements; and the U.S. SEC amending its whistleblower program rules in 2022, with the U.S. DOJ announcing a new whistleblower rewards pilot program in 2024. Uncertainty: the claim is vague about jurisdiction and timing, but broadly it is accurate.

claim: YES Bank may shut down
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: YES Bank is operating normally. After its 2020 crisis and RBI-imposed moratorium, it was reconstructed with capital led by SBI, has since returned to profitability, reduced bad loans, and strengthened its balance sheet. There have been no official indications from the bank or the RBI of any plan to shut down; in India, regulators typically pursue resolution, not closure, for systemically important banks.

claim: Pretty Little Thing products may contain chemicals that can cause cancer, birth defects or other reproductive harm.
response_text: TRUE.  PrettyLittleThing includes a California Proposition 65 notice stating that some products can expose consumers to chemicals known to the State of California to cause cancer, birth defects, or other reproductive harm. This means certain items may contain such chemicals. Note: Prop 65 warnings are precautionary and don’t necessarily indicate dangerous levels in a given product.

claim: Donald Trump asked Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky to "make up dirt" on Biden.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump’s July 25, 2019 call with Zelensky (per the White House call memo) shows he asked Ukraine to “look into” the Bidens/Burisma and to coordinate with Giuliani and the U.S. attorney general. It does not show him asking Zelensky to fabricate or “make up” dirt. Critics argued he sought a politically helpful announcement of investigations, but “make up dirt” overstates what the record shows.

claim: Trump said Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky to not call back until he'd satisfied Donald Trump's demands.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence Trump told Zelensky “not to call back” until demands were met. The July 25, 2019 call record shows Trump pressing for “a favor” (investigations) but not giving an instruction about calling back. Testimony indicated intermediaries (Giuliani, Sondland) conditioned a White House meeting and, informally, leverage over aid on Ukraine announcing investigations, but not that Trump himself told Zelensky not to call back.

claim: During his telephone call with Ukrainian President Zelensky on 25th July 2019 Donald Trump said the United States had been good to Ukraine.
response_text: TRUE.  In the White House memorandum of the July 25, 2019 call, Trump told Zelensky that “the United States has been very very good to Ukraine” and that the U.S. does “a lot for Ukraine.”

claim: Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison has given himself a pay rise.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Australian Prime Minister cannot set his own pay. MP and ministerial salaries are determined by the independent Remuneration Tribunal and apply across the board. While Scott Morrison’s salary did rise during standard tribunal increases, he did not “give himself” a pay rise.

claim: Luxembourg benefits the most from being in the EU, getting back 3,304% of what it pays in.
response_text: FALSE.  EU budget data don’t show Luxembourg getting back 3,304% (33×) of what it pays. That figure appears to be a decimal error; a commonly cited ratio for a past year is about 330% (roughly 3.3×), largely because EU administrative spending is located in Luxembourg. Depending on method (net balances, excluding admin spend, per capita, etc.), Luxembourg is not the biggest beneficiary; several Eastern EU countries receive more relative to contributions. (Exact ratios vary by year and methodology.)

claim: Hunter Biden, son of then Vice President Joe Biden  had a payoff of $1.5 billion from China, after accompanying his father, on a 2013 diplomatic trip to Beijing.
response_text: FALSE.  - Hunter Biden did accompany then–Vice President Joe Biden to Beijing in 2013, and later joined the board of a new private equity firm, BHR Partners. - The oft-cited $1.5 billion was a fundraising target for BHR’s fund, not a “payoff” to Hunter Biden, and there’s no evidence he personally received $1.5 billion or that such funds were provided because of the trip. - At the time, Hunter Biden was an unpaid board member; he did not acquire a 10% equity stake until 2017, after his father left office.  This has been repeatedly debunked by independent fact-checkers (e.g., Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact).

claim: Donald Trump released a summary of his call with the Ukrainian President, Zelensky because Adam Schiff gave a false rendition of the call.
response_text: FALSE.  The White House released the memo of the Trump–Zelensky call on Sept. 25, 2019, amid mounting pressure and the newly announced impeachment inquiry. Adam Schiff’s widely criticized “parody” reading of the call happened the next day, Sept. 26, during a congressional hearing. The release therefore did not occur “because” of Schiff’s rendition; it preceded it.

claim: US Democratic senators  threatened Donald Trump with votes and no money coming into Ukraine.
response_text: FALSE.  - There’s no credible record of Democratic senators threatening Donald Trump with “votes” and “no money coming into Ukraine.” Throughout 2023–2024, Senate Democrats largely supported Ukraine aid and criticized Republicans aligned with Trump for blocking it. - A commonly cited item is a 2018 letter from three Democratic senators to Ukraine’s prosecutor general urging cooperation with the Mueller investigation and noting that U.S. aid enjoyed bipartisan support—this was addressed to Ukrainian officials, not to Trump, and is often mischaracterized as a threat.  - In 2019, it was Trump who withheld Ukraine aid, which led to his first impeachment.

claim: Hunter Biden made millions of dollars from a deal made in China. The deal put $1.5 billion into a fund after one quick meeting in China which he flew into on Air Force Two.
response_text: FALSE.  - Hunter Biden did fly to China on Air Force Two in 2013 and briefly met a Chinese financier, but there’s no evidence a “quick meeting” led China to put $1.5 billion into a fund. - The $1.5 billion figure was a fundraising target for the private equity firm BHR, not a verified investment resulting from that trip. Public records show modest registered capital, and how much was ultimately raised is unclear. - Hunter joined BHR’s board (his lawyer says unpaid) and later bought a 10% stake around 2017; there’s no verified evidence he personally “made millions” from that BHR deal.  Note: Hunter did have other China-linked business dealings years later, but they are separate from the Air Force Two trip and do not substantiate this claim.

claim: Indian equity stock index markets, Sensex and Nifty have their biggest single day gains in the last ten years on 20th September 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  On 20 September 2019, after a surprise cut in corporate tax rates, the Sensex jumped about 1,921 points (~5.3%) and the Nifty about 569 points (~5.3%). These were the biggest single-day gains for both indices in the preceding decade; larger surges (e.g., May 2009 election rally) occurred more than 10 years earlier.

claim: The Trump family took seats reserved for disabled guests at the 74th session of the UN General Assembly.
response_text: FALSE.  Fact-checks (e.g., Reuters, Snopes) and UN officials said Ivanka Trump and other Trump family members sat in seats allocated to the U.S. delegation during the 74th UN General Assembly in 2019. The wheelchair symbol seen in viral photos indicated an accessible area, not seats reserved exclusively for disabled guests, and they did not displace disabled attendees.

claim: President Muhammadu Buhari of Nigeria told the United Nations Climate Action Summit in New York last month that the Lake Chad basin has shrunk significantly due to climate change, depriving many people of their livelihood in the region.
response_text: TRUE. At the UN Climate Action Summit in New York in September 2019, President Muhammadu Buhari said Lake Chad had shrunk dramatically due to climate change and that this shrinkage had deprived millions in the Lake Chad basin of their livelihoods (e.g., fishing, farming, herding).

claim: ERNEST HEMINGWAY SAID, WE ARE ALL BROKEN — THAT’S HOW THE LIGHT GETS IN
response_text: FALSE.  The “that’s how the light gets in” line comes from Leonard Cohen’s song “Anthem” (1992): “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” Hemingway did write, “The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places” (A Farewell to Arms), but he did not write the quoted line.

claim: Russian Energy Narrative Targets Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic States
response_text: TRUE.  Russia has long used energy as a tool of influence and information operations, frequently targeting Poland, Ukraine, and the Baltic states. Narratives have included claims that Ukraine “steals gas,” that Poland and the Baltics’ “Russophobia” causes high energy prices, and that EU sanctions harm those countries more than Russia. This messaging has accompanied concrete leverage like gas disputes with Ukraine (2006, 2009), the 2022 gas cutoff to Poland and the Baltics over ruble payments, and broader disinformation documented by EUvsDisinfo and others.

claim: A Muslim man in India was killed by a mob after being accused of cow slaughter.
response_text: TRUE.  Documented cases exist. For example, in September 2015 in Dadri, Uttar Pradesh, 52-year-old Mohammad Akhlaq, a Muslim man, was lynched by a mob after rumors that he had slaughtered a calf and stored beef at home. Similar cow-related mob killings (e.g., Pehlu Khan in Rajasthan in 2017) have also been reported.

claim: Banks in India will be closed from September 26 to October 2 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A viral rumor claimed a week-long shutdown, but banks were not closed nationwide from Sep 26 to Oct 2, 2019. Only Sep 28 (fourth Saturday), Sep 29 (Sunday), and Oct 2 (Gandhi Jayanti) were holidays across India. Sep 30 and Oct 1 were normal working days. The proposed Sep 26–27 strike was partial and/or withdrawn by major unions, so there was no continuous nationwide closure. (PIB Fact Check and multiple news outlets debunked the claim.)

claim: Congress party claims regarding shortfall in Government earnings
response_text: FALSE  Reason: Without a specific statement to assess, the broad claim of a “shortfall in Government earnings” is not supported by recent official data. India’s gross tax revenues and non-tax revenues have generally risen year-on-year, and the RBI’s surplus transfer reached record levels in FY24—contradicting the notion of a broad earnings shortfall. Uncertainty: the exact Congress statement and time frame aren’t specified.

claim: About universal basic income, Thomas Paine was for it at our founding ... Martin Luther King, champion in the ‘60s, called it a guaranteed minimum income for all Americans… It passed the U.S. House of Representatives twice in 1971
response_text: FALSE.  - Thomas Paine did advocate an early “citizen’s dividend”/basic pension funded by a land tax (Agrarian Justice, 1797), which is UBI-like, though not exactly a modern UBI and not literally part of the U.S. founding framework. - Martin Luther King Jr. did call for a guaranteed income in the 1960s. - The measure that advanced in Congress was Nixon’s Family Assistance Plan (a means‑tested guaranteed minimum income for families with children, with work requirements—not a universal basic income). It passed the House once in 1970 and again in 1971; it did not pass the House “twice in 1971,” and it was not “for all Americans.”

claim: Congresswoman Tulsi Gabbard is of Indian-origin.
response_text: FALSE.  Tulsi Gabbard was born in American Samoa and raised in Hawaii. Her father is of Samoan/European ancestry and her mother is of European-American ancestry. She is Hindu but has no Indian ancestry, so she is not of Indian origin.

claim: AN 11-YEAR-OLD GIRL KILL TWO ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS DURING AN ATTEMPTED HOME INVASION
response_text: FALSE.  This story is a long-circulating hoax from fake-news/satire sites. No credible police reports or news coverage support an 11-year-old girl killing two “illegal immigrants” in a home invasion, and fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) have debunked it. Unrelated photos were used to lend it false credibility.

claim: On average, one person dies by suicide every 22 hours in West Virginia, United States.
response_text: TRUE  Reason: “Every 22 hours” implies about 398 deaths per year (8,760 hours ÷ 22). Recent CDC/state data show West Virginia has roughly 350–430 suicide deaths annually, which aligns with an average near one death about every 22 hours. (Exact figures vary by year, so there’s minor uncertainty.)

claim: French philosopher Voltaire said “To learn who rules over you, simply find out who you are not allowed to criticize.”
