response_text: FALSE.  No reliable source places this line in Voltaire’s writings or correspondence. The earliest known phrasing is by Kevin Alfred Strom, an American white supremacist, in 1993. The quote has been widely misattributed to Voltaire (and sometimes Orwell), but it is not found in Voltaire’s works. Sources: Quote Investigator; Snopes.

claim: Your reaction to an optical illusion is an indication of your state of mind.
response_text: FALSE.  Briefly: Visual illusions mainly probe how the visual system processes information. Although attention, expectations, mood, and traits can subtly bias perception (and some lab tasks show small group-level correlations), a person’s reaction to a typical optical illusion is not a reliable or validated indicator of their “state of mind.” Any effects are variable and not diagnostic. (Minor nuance: transient states can influence perception slightly, but not in a way that lets an illusion read your mental state.)

claim: Indian banks are to be closed continuously from 26th September 2019 to 30th September 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Bank unions had called a two-day strike for 26–27 September 2019, and banks were anyway closed on 28–29 September (fourth Saturday and Sunday). However, 30 September 2019 was a normal working day, and private banks were not universally shut during the strike. So there was no continuous nationwide bank closure from 26th to 30th.

claim: Science fiction and popular science writer Isaac Asimov said your assumptions are your windows on the world.Scrub them off every once in a while, or the light won’t come in.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This quote is widely attributed to Alan Alda, not Isaac Asimov. It appears in Alda’s writings (e.g., “Things I Overheard While Talking to Myself,” 2007). No reliable source ties it to Asimov.

claim: Cherie Blair is representing Shamima Begum.
response_text: FALSE.  Shamima Begum has been represented by solicitor Gareth Peirce (Birnberg Peirce) and barristers including Samantha Knights KC and Dan Squires KC in her appeals. There is no credible evidence that Cherie Blair (Cherie Booth KC) represents her; claims suggesting this have been debunked.

claim: In the U.S fifty million people a year lose their private insurance when they quit a job, are made unemployed or employers change insurance policies.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Fifty million a year is far too high. At the height of the Great Recession, estimates of people losing employer-sponsored insurance due to job loss were on the order of a few million per year (e.g., “14,000 a day” ≈ 5 million annually), not 50 million. While many Americans experience coverage “churn” or switch plans when employers change carriers, that is not the same as losing insurance; only a minority change plans in any given year. No credible data show 50 million people annually losing private coverage for the reasons cited. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by year and definition, but they are nowhere near 50 million.

claim: In Congress, Elizabeth Warren introduced 110 bills. 2 passed. Cory Booker introduced 120 bills. 0 passed," the Sept. 12 post reads. "Kamala Harris introduced 54 bills. 0 passed. Bernie Sanders never held a job until age 53. He lived off of welfare and four different women
response_text: FALSE.  Why: - The bill tallies are inaccurate/misleading. Counts vary by date and method, but public trackers (Congress.gov, GovTrack) show Elizabeth Warren sponsored more than the post claims and had more than two measures enacted; Cory Booker and Kamala Harris were not at “zero” — each had sponsored measures signed into law or had sponsored provisions folded into laws. The meme cherry-picks and understates their records. - The Bernie Sanders claims are plainly false. Sanders worked long before age 53 (odd jobs, writer/filmmaker, teacher, nonprofit work) and was elected mayor of Burlington at 39; there’s no evidence he “lived off welfare and four different women,” and he has been married twice.  Note: Exact bill counts depend on timeframe and whether you count only standalone bills versus provisions folded into larger laws, but the post’s bottom-line assertions are wrong.

claim: Actress Jane Fonda was denied service at Sir Scott’s Oasis Steakhouse in Montana which is run by a Vietnam War veteran.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a long-circulating viral rumor. Fact-checkers contacted Sir Scott’s Oasis Steakhouse in Manhattan, Montana, and the restaurant said the incident never happened; there’s no evidence Fonda was refused service there. The story has been debunked by multiple outlets (e.g., Snopes). Uncertainty: none.

claim: Kamala Harris say criminals and illegals are better than U.S. servicemen.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible record—speech, interview, tweet, or transcript—of Kamala Harris saying criminals or undocumented immigrants are “better than” U.S. servicemembers. Fact-checkers have debunked similar viral memes as fabricated or misattributed. Harris has repeatedly publicly praised U.S. service members.

claim: Americans lost wealth and income under Barack Obama's presidency.
response_text: FALSE  Incomes and wealth fell early in Obama’s term because of the Great Recession he inherited, but they rebounded strongly later. By 2016, real median household income had risen back to about its pre‑recession level and was higher than in 2009 (Census). Aggregate household net worth hit record highs by 2016 (Federal Reserve). Median wealth was still below 2007 but climbed in Obama’s second term. So Americans did not, on net, lose both wealth and income under his presidency.

claim: New numbers from the US Census Bureau show an uptick in the number of Americans who have no health insurance.
response_text: TRUE. The Census Bureau’s latest annual health insurance data show a small increase in the uninsured in 2023 versus 2022, as states began unwinding pandemic-era Medicaid continuous coverage. Note: the uptick is modest and can vary by Census measure (ACS point-in-time vs. CPS full-year), but the new ACS numbers indicate an increase.

claim: The Conservatives are levelling up per pupil funding in schools in the UK.
response_text: FALSE.  - Education funding is devolved, so the UK Conservative government only controls school funding in England, not across the UK. - In England, they introduced minimum per‑pupil funding levels that raised the floor for some lower‑funded schools, but this is not a UK‑wide policy and does not “level up” per‑pupil funding overall (large differences persist and real‑terms funding only recently returned to around 2010 levels).

claim: Thousands of companies are leaving China because they can’t pay the tariffs.
response_text: FALSE.  - Tariffs on Chinese goods are imposed by importing countries (e.g., the U.S.) and are typically paid by the importer; suppliers may share costs, but it’s not that companies in China “can’t pay” them. - While some firms have diversified or shifted portions of production (the “China+1” strategy), credible surveys (e.g., AmCham, EU Chamber) show most foreign companies remain in China, with only a minority relocating, and for multiple reasons (costs, regulation, geopolitics), not tariffs alone. - There’s no evidence of “thousands” leaving China because of tariffs. At most, reports have documented dozens to some hundreds adjusting supply chains.   Uncertainty: Exact counts are hard to verify, but available data do not support the claim.

claim: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been and are coming into our country in the form of tariffs, and China’s eating the cost.
response_text: FALSE.  - Tariffs are paid to U.S. Customs by U.S. importers, not by China. Economic studies (Fed, IMF, NBER) find the costs were largely passed on to U.S. firms and consumers through higher prices, with only limited price cuts by Chinese exporters. - Tariff revenue rose to tens of billions of dollars per year (roughly $70–90 billion at peak), not “hundreds of billions” annually. Even if cumulative collections over several years exceed $100 billion, describing it as money “from China” is misleading since the payments come from U.S. buyers. (Some uncertainty if the speaker meant multi‑year totals.)

claim: China lost 3 million jobs as a result of the US-China trade war.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There’s no reliable evidence that China definitively “lost 3 million jobs” due solely to the US‑China trade war. Estimates vary widely and are uncertain; many analyses put potential or realized job losses in the low millions at most (often around 1–2 million or “at risk”), and China still recorded net urban job gains during those years. The specific 3 million figure is not established. Uncertainty: attribution and counts vary by method and timeframe.

claim: Zaira Wasim who quit acting in June citing religion is making a comeback to Bollywood.
response_text: FALSE.  Zaira Wasim announced in June 2019 that she was quitting acting for religious reasons. Since then, there has been no credible announcement of her returning to Bollywood, and she has not signed any new films. Reports of a “comeback” have been unsubstantiated. Uncertainty: none beyond the lack of any verified return announcement.

claim: Several well-known charities such as Goodwill and American Red Cross overpay their CEOs and spend a small percentage on helping people
response_text: FALSE.  - The “small percentage” claim is a long‑running viral myth. Independent watchdogs and the charities’ filings show the American Red Cross typically spends about 88–90% of expenses on programs/services (not a “small” share). Goodwill affiliates generally report a majority—often around 85–90%—going to mission-related programs, though figures vary by local affiliate and year. - CEO pay is sometimes portrayed with exaggerated numbers online. In reality, recent reported compensation has been roughly in the mid–six figures for the Red Cross CEO and roughly high six to low seven figures for Goodwill’s national CEO, with local Goodwill CEOs lower. Whether that is “overpaid” is subjective, but it is broadly in line with compensation at very large nonprofits.  Note: Exact percentages and salaries vary by year and affiliate, but the core claim that these charities spend only a small fraction on helping people is not supported.

claim: Some women have no choice but to take epidural injections during childbirth.
response_text: FALSE. Epidurals are not mandatory. They’re an elective form of pain relief in labor, and even for cesarean delivery there are alternatives (spinal or general anesthesia). In fact, some women can’t receive epidurals due to contraindications (e.g., bleeding risks, infection), underscoring that they’re not required.

claim: Epidural injections given during childbirth are one of the worst and dangerous injections in the world resulting in chronic back pain.
response_text: FALSE.  Epidural analgesia for childbirth is widely used and generally very safe when performed by trained clinicians. Serious complications (e.g., epidural hematoma, infection, permanent nerve injury) are extremely rare—on the order of roughly 1 in tens to hundreds of thousands. While temporary side effects (e.g., drop in blood pressure, itching, fever, postpartum “spinal headache,” or local back soreness at the insertion site) can occur, high‑quality studies and reviews show no credible link between labor epidurals and chronic back pain. Postpartum back pain is common regardless of epidural use due to pregnancy-related changes and strain.

claim: VA hospitals were removing Bibles and banning Christmas carols under Obama administration
response_text: False.  - There was no Obama/VA-wide policy to remove Bibles or ban Christmas carols. Patients could have Bibles and receive religious items, and religious carols were allowed when consistent with patients’ wishes. - A few isolated, local incidents occurred: e.g., a VA hospital in Augusta, GA asked student carolers to choose secular songs, then apologized and reversed; some facilities removed Bibles from common-area POW/MIA displays after complaints about government endorsement of religion. These were not national bans. - A widely cited “Bible ban” memo was at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center (a Defense Department facility, not VA) and was rescinded quickly.  The claim misrepresents isolated/local actions as a broad Obama-era VA policy.

claim: Sinn Féin MPs do not receive parliamentary salaries.
response_text: FALSE.  Sinn Féin MPs follow an abstentionist policy and do not take their seats at Westminster, but they are still entitled to, and do receive, UK MP salaries and can claim expenses. They are not eligible for “Short Money” (opposition party funding) and historically have said they take only an “average industrial wage,” but the parliamentary salary is still paid to them. (See House of Commons Library briefings and BBC/Full Fact reality checks.)

claim: The presidents of Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Malawi boycotted the 2019 World Economic Forum (WEF) summit in Cape Town in protest against xenophobic attacks in South Africa.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reputable outlets (e.g., BBC, Reuters, Bloomberg) reported that after xenophobic attacks in South Africa in early September 2019, the presidents of Rwanda (Paul Kagame), the Democratic Republic of Congo (Félix Tshisekedi) and Malawi (Peter Mutharika) withdrew from/declined to attend the WEF Africa summit in Cape Town, widely described as a boycott in protest. (Nigeria’s vice president also pulled out.) Minor uncertainty exists because some official statements were terse, but coverage consistently framed their withdrawals as protest-related.

claim: Lewis Carroll once wrote, “You know what the issue is with this world? Everyone wants a magical solution to their problems, and everyone refuses to believe in magic.”
response_text: FALSE.  This line is widely misattributed to Lewis Carroll. It comes from the TV series Once Upon a Time (Season 1, “Hat Trick”), spoken by the character Jefferson (the Mad Hatter), not from Carroll’s writings. There’s no known source for it in Carroll’s works.

claim: U.S.A. now leads the world in energy production.
response_text: False.  - The U.S. is the world leader in oil and natural gas production and set record total output recently, but in overall primary energy production China is larger (driven by its massive coal output).  - Recent IEA/BP/EIA data (2022–2023) show China’s total primary energy production exceeds the U.S.’s.   Note: If “energy” were meant to mean only oil and gas, the statement would be true, but for total energy it is not.

claim: US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tweeted, "I see people are rushing out to fill up their cars for this hurricane at the gas station. This wouldn’t be an issue if they had electric cars. If the power is out for a week how are they going to get gas? We need to start planning ahead and moving forward."
response_text: FALSE. There is no record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever tweeting this. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, Reuters) have traced the quote to fabricated meme screenshots; it does not appear in her tweet history or archives.

claim: Donald Trump threatened economic sanctions over recent xenophobic violence in South Africa with a posted tweet stating “This barbaric attacks by South African is very disappointing, its time we put South Africa under strong economic sanctions, first it was the minority White people now its African. Either Cyril get his people in line or we pull out all our investments and they learn.”
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is from a fabricated tweet. Fact-checkers (e.g., Africa Check and AFP Fact Check, Sept 2019) found no record of Donald Trump posting it, and it does not appear in his archived tweets. Trump did tweet in 2018 about South African land expropriation, but he did not threaten economic sanctions over xenophobic violence.

claim: No Americans are exposed to air pollution above the World Health Organization’s suggested level.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO’s 2021 Air Quality Guidelines set very strict levels (e.g., PM2.5 annual average 5 µg/m3; 24‑hour 15 µg/m3). Large parts of the U.S. exceed these, especially during wildfire events, and most Americans live in areas with annual PM2.5 above 5 µg/m3. The U.S. EPA’s own annual PM2.5 standard (recently tightened to 9 µg/m3) is still less strict than WHO’s, underscoring that many Americans are above the WHO guideline.

claim: The USA now has, under Trump, got crystal clean water.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: U.S. water was not universally “crystal clean” under Trump. EPA data show tens of millions of Americans are served each year by community water systems with health‑based violations of the Safe Drinking Water Act. High‑profile problems like lead contamination in places such as Flint, MI and Newark, NJ persisted, and PFAS “forever chemicals” were found in water supplies across dozens of states. The Trump administration also rolled back the 2015 Clean Water Rule, reducing protections for some streams and wetlands, which does not support the claim of cleaner water. Uncertainty: none.

claim: 91% of the world’s population is exposed to air pollution above the World Health Organization’s suggested level.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO estimated in 2018 that about 91% of the world’s population lived in places where air quality exceeded its guideline limits. Note: with the stricter 2021 guidelines and 2022 data, WHO now reports roughly 99%, so 91% is an older (understated) figure.

claim: America has the cleanest and safest air and water
response_text: FALSE.  The United States performs fairly well but does not have the cleanest or safest air and water by global measures. Many countries (e.g., Finland, Iceland, New Zealand, Australia) report lower fine-particulate (PM2.5) levels than the U.S., and the U.S. average exceeds the WHO guideline. While U.S. drinking water access is high, it is not uniquely safest; violations and contamination issues (e.g., lead, PFAS) persist. Composite rankings like Yale’s Environmental Performance Index place the U.S. well below the top tier.

claim: Thomas Jefferson Said "Freedom is lost gradually from an uninterested, uninformed and unresponsive people.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Thomas Jefferson writing or saying “Freedom is lost gradually from an uninterested, uninformed and unresponsive people.” The Monticello/Thomas Jefferson Foundation lists this as a spurious attribution. A genuine Jefferson sentiment on the topic is: “If a nation expects to be ignorant and free... it expects what never was and never will be.”

claim: The last time people created a Hollywood blacklist, people ended up killing themselves. They were accused, and they lost their right to work.
response_text: True.  During the McCarthy-era Hollywood blacklist (late 1940s–1950s), many accused of Communist ties were denied employment for years (the Hollywood Ten, and hundreds named in HUAC hearings or Red Channels). At least one high-profile blacklist victim, actor Philip Loeb of The Goldbergs, died by suicide in 1955 after losing his job due to the accusations. While not everyone met this fate, the claim’s substance—that accusations led to loss of work and some suicides—matches the historical record. Uncertainty: “people” is general, but documented cases exist.

claim: Democrats in the United States are calling for the Second Amendment to be repealed.
response_text: FALSE.  The Democratic Party and its leaders do not call for repealing the Second Amendment. Their platforms and public statements support gun‑safety measures (e.g., background checks, assault‑weapons bans) while acknowledging Second Amendment rights. A few individual commentators have floated repeal (e.g., retired Justice John Paul Stevens), but this is not a mainstream or official Democratic position. Uncertainty: none beyond isolated individual opinions.

claim: A new EU withdrawal bill allows the EU to choose the length of a further Brexit extension and the UK has no say in it.
response_text: FALSE.  Under the European Union (Withdrawal) (No. 2) Act 2019 (the “Benn Act”), the Prime Minister had to request an extension to 31 January 2020. If the EU proposed a different date, the Prime Minister could only accept it if the House of Commons approved. So the EU could not unilaterally choose the length with the UK having “no say.” (UK MPs had a veto over any alternative date.)

claim: Dan McCready, a Democratic candidate standing in the special election for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District, is a socialist.
response_text: FALSE.  Dan McCready ran as a centrist Democrat, Marine veteran, and businessman. He rejected the “socialist” label, was not affiliated with democratic socialist groups, and opposed policies like Medicare for All and the Green New Deal, positioning himself as a moderate. Uncertainty: none.

claim: Author Theodor Seuss Geisel once said, “Be who you are and say what you feel, because those who mind don’t matter and those who matter don’t mind.”
response_text: FALSE.  The line is widely misattributed to Dr. Seuss. Researchers (e.g., Quote Investigator, Snopes) find no source for it in Seuss’s works. A core form of the saying—“Those who mind don’t matter and those who matter don’t mind”—is most often linked to Bernard M. Baruch, with print evidence from the 1940s; the “Be who you are and say what you feel” preface appears to be a later embellishment.

claim: Life expectancy in the UK is falling
response_text: FALSE.  Life expectancy in the UK fell sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021), but recent data show it has since stabilized or ticked up slightly. It remains below its pre‑pandemic peak, so the long-term improvement has stalled, but it is not currently continuing to fall. (Source: UK ONS life expectancy releases.) Uncertainty: exact figures vary by year/sex and whether single-year or 3‑year averages are used.

claim: America has more governors who’ve worn blackface than black governors
response_text: FALSE.  - Black governors in U.S. history: at least five — P.B.S. Pinchback (LA, acting), L. Douglas Wilder (VA), Deval Patrick (MA), David Paterson (NY), and Wes Moore (MD). - Governors documented wearing blackface: chiefly Ralph Northam (VA) and Kay Ivey (AL).  Even allowing for disputed historical cases, the blackface total does not exceed the number of Black governors. Note: A 2019 meme seemed “true” if limited to then-sitting governors (2 with blackface scandals, 0 Black), but as a general claim it’s false.

claim: Getting up too quickly in the middle of the night can cause sudden death.
response_text: FALSE.  Standing up quickly (especially at night) can cause orthostatic hypotension, leading to dizziness or fainting (e.g., micturition syncope). In healthy people this is not a direct cause of sudden death. Rarely, in those with serious heart rhythm disorders, severe autonomic failure, major blood loss/dehydration, or in the frail elderly, abrupt standing could precipitate fainting with injury or trigger an arrhythmia—but that’s uncommon. Overall, the claim is misleadingly alarmist.

claim: contraceptive pills destroys the fertility system within 72 hours
response_text: FALSE.  Oral contraceptives (including emergency contraception taken within 72 hours) work mainly by delaying ovulation and thickening cervical mucus. They do not “destroy” the reproductive system or cause permanent infertility. Fertility typically returns quickly after stopping regular birth control pills (often within weeks to a few months), and emergency contraception has no lasting effect on fertility.

claim: I-Pill contains arsenic.
response_text: FALSE.  I-Pill (an emergency contraceptive by Cipla) contains levonorgestrel (1.5 mg) as the active ingredient plus common tablet excipients. Arsenic is not an ingredient, and there’s no credible evidence of arsenic contamination. Pharmaceutical products must meet strict limits for elemental impurities.

claim: Former top cop Mumbai Police Commissioner Ahmed Javed a 1980-batch IPS officer had only taken Rs 1 salary throughout his 36 years tenure.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no credible report or official record that Ahmed Javed drew a Re 1 salary. An extraordinary claim like this would have been widely reported. - IPS officers are paid according to government pay scales under service rules; they cannot legally opt to be paid Re 1 for their entire tenure (they could donate salary, but it would still be paid as per the scale). - Fact-checks have debunked similar social media forwards about this claim.

claim: Arsenic is present in the unwanted 72 contraceptive pill.
response_text: FALSE.  Unwanted 72 is an emergency contraceptive containing levonorgestrel (1.5 mg) as the active ingredient. Its listed excipients are common tablet additives (e.g., starches, cellulose/povidone, magnesium stearate), and arsenic is not an ingredient. Pharmaceuticals are also subject to strict heavy‑metal limits; any trace arsenic, if present at all, would be at negligible levels and not an intentional component.

claim: Crimea was taken away from President Obama.
response_text: FALSE.  Crimea was annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014. It was not U.S. territory and wasn’t “taken from President Obama,” though it occurred during his presidency. The U.S. condemned the annexation and imposed sanctions on Russia.

claim: Canada’s Liberal Finance Minister Bill Morneau is related to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) High Commissioner Brenda Lucki
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Brenda Lucki is the RCMP Commissioner (not “High Commissioner”) and is married to Dave Lucki. Bill Morneau is married to Nancy McCain of the McCain family. Public records and multiple fact-checks (e.g., Reuters/AFP) found no familial connection between Lucki and Morneau, and the rumor has been debunked.

claim: Florida’s red flag gun law has been used about five times a day.
response_text: TRUE.  Since Florida enacted its red flag (risk protection order) law in 2018, state court data show thousands of petitions—on the order of 8,000–10,000+ within the first 4–5 years—averaging roughly 5–6 uses per day statewide. Exact rates vary by year and county, but “about five times a day” is a fair characterization.

claim: Former U.S. President Barack Obama wanted Russia to be out of the G-8.
response_text: TRUE.  After Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, President Obama joined other G7 leaders in suspending Russia from the G8, canceling the Sochi summit and proceeding as the G7. Obama said Russia was “no longer in the G8” while it continued its actions in Ukraine. Note: this was framed as a suspension rather than a permanent expulsion.

claim: Obama's motivation for wanting Russia out of the G8 was the Russian annexation of Crimea.
response_text: TRUE.  In March 2014, after Russia annexed Crimea, President Obama and other G7 leaders suspended Russia from the G8, explicitly citing the annexation and Russia’s violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty/international law as the reason for exclusion.

claim: The rupee is now lower than even the Bangladeshi taka
response_text: FALSE.  As of now, 1 Indian rupee is worth more than 1 Bangladeshi taka (roughly 1 INR ≈ 1.3–1.4 BDT; USD ≈ 83–86 INR vs ≈ 115–120 BDT). So the rupee is not “lower” than the taka. Note: If “rupee” meant the Pakistani rupee, the claim would be true, but for the Indian rupee it’s false.

claim: As the main importer of Chinese goods, India should stop all trade ties with Beijing.
response_text: FALSE.  - India is not the main importer of Chinese goods; the United States, the European Union, and ASEAN countries import significantly more from China. - The “should stop all trade ties” part is a value judgment, not a factual claim.

claim: Japan has refused to import even a needle from US as a mark of patriotism as Americans had nuked Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
response_text: FALSE.  Japan has no such boycott. It imports tens of billions of dollars’ worth of U.S. goods and services annually, including beef, corn, wheat, aircraft, medical devices, software, and consumer electronics brands (e.g., iPhones widely sold in Japan). The U.S. and Japan are close economic and security partners; there has never been a national policy to refuse U.S. imports because of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

claim: PLATO SAID, ‘YOU CAN DISCOVER MORE ABOUT A PERSON IN AN HOUR OF PLAY THAN IN A YEAR OF CONVERSATION’?
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This line is widely attributed to Plato but no source exists in his works, and scholars have not found it in the Greek texts. Reputable references (e.g., Wikiquote/Quote Investigator) list it as apocryphal; the wording appears only in modern sources. Plato does discuss play in education (e.g., Laws), but he does not say this.

claim: Proscribed indigenous leader of Biafra, Nnamdi Kanu ordered members of the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) to arrest the Nigerian president and hand him over to the Japanese authorities.
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2019, ahead of President Muhammadu Buhari’s trip to Japan for the TICAD summit, Nnamdi Kanu (IPOB leader) publicly instructed IPOB members in Japan to carry out a “citizen’s arrest” of Buhari and hand him over to Japanese authorities for alleged crimes. This directive was reported in IPOB statements and widely covered by Nigerian media at the time.

claim: An old Nokia 3310 phone found in a drawer after 20 years with 70% battery remaining
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The Nokia 3310 used NiMH or early Li‑ion removable batteries. NiMH self-discharges ~20–30% per month; Li‑ion ~1–3% per month plus substantial calendar aging. Over 20 years, either chemistry would be fully drained long ago and heavily degraded (often to the point of not powering on). A 3310 showing ~70% after two decades in a drawer would require the battery to have been replaced or recharged, or the image/story to be staged.

claim: President Donald Trump can force US firms out of China.
response_text: FALSE.  A U.S. president cannot simply order American companies to leave a foreign country. While the president can, after declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), restrict or prohibit certain transactions with China—pressure that could indirectly push firms to exit—this is not a blanket power to “force” firms out and would be legally bounded and contestable. (Some uncertainty because broad sanctions could have similar practical effects.)

claim: 40% of NI Unionists are happy about a potential trade border in the Irish Sea.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Polls have consistently shown most Northern Ireland unionists oppose an Irish Sea trade border. While a minority have said they would accept a sea border as the least-worst option compared with a hard land border (in some forced-choice polls roughly a third to around 40%), that is not the same as being “happy” about it. Overall unionist support/approval has been very low. Uncertainty: figures vary by poll and wording, but “happy” at 40% overstates unionist approval.

claim: West Virginia highways move up twenty places in the U.S national highway system to place sixteenth, and affirms all the hard work we do on our states roads.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason Foundation’s 26th Annual Highway Report (2021) ranked West Virginia’s state highway system 16th overall, up 20 places from 36th the prior year. Note: this refers to a think-tank ranking of state highway systems, not the federal “National Highway System.” The “affirms hard work” part is opinion.

claim: The 5G radiation is bad for humans.
response_text: FALSE.  5G uses non-ionizing radiofrequency radiation (similar to earlier mobile networks). At the exposure levels from phones and base stations that comply with international safety limits (ICNIRP/WHO/FDA), there’s no credible evidence of adverse health effects. The only well-established risk is tissue heating at much higher intensities than public exposures. Millimeter-wave 5G mostly penetrates only the outer skin. Research continues, but current evidence does not support the claim that 5G radiation is bad for humans.

claim: Donald Trump's fuel efficiency plan would reduce the cost of cars “by more than $3000” and make them “substantially safer.”
response_text: FALSE.  - The Trump administration’s own final analysis of the 2020 SAFE Rule projected roughly a $1,000 reduction in average new-vehicle sticker price compared with the prior standards—not “more than $3,000.” Independent analyses also found that higher fuel costs would erase any up-front savings, raising total ownership costs. - The rule did not show cars becoming “substantially safer.” The final modeling found only small, uncertain changes in fatalities (some scenarios showed increases due to more driving), and outside experts criticized the safety claims.  So neither the $3,000 savings nor a clear, substantial safety improvement is supported by the evidence.

claim: A 5G test in the Netherlands resulted in the death of 297 birds.
response_text: FALSE.  Dutch authorities and fact-checkers found no 5G testing took place in The Hague when ~300 starlings were found dead in 2018. Necropsies indicated blunt-force trauma consistent with birds panicking and colliding (e.g., fleeing a predator), with no evidence of poisoning or radiation. Sources: Dutch telecom regulator statements; Dutch Wildlife Health Centre/Wageningen investigations; Snopes/Reuters fact-checks.

claim: President Trump wanted the USA to buy Greenland from Denmark.
response_text: TRUE.  In 2019, while president, Donald Trump publicly confirmed he had asked advisors about purchasing Greenland (an autonomous Danish territory) and said the U.S. was “looking at” the idea. Denmark and Greenland rejected it, and Trump canceled a planned visit to Denmark after the Danish prime minister called the idea “absurd.”

claim: In the US, medical bills drive half a million people into bankruptcy every year.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely quoted “530,000 a year” comes from a 2019 survey-based study that counted any mention of medical bills or illness as a factor, a method many economists say overstates causation. More rigorous analyses using administrative data (e.g., Dobkin/Finkelstein/Kluender/Notowidigdo, 2018) find medical issues account for only a small share of bankruptcies (roughly a few percent). Also, total U.S. consumer bankruptcies were about 400–450k in 2022–2023—so 500k “medical” bankruptcies per year is impossible in recent years. Uncertainty: estimates vary by method, but credible evidence does not support the 500k figure.

claim: The UK has lost its measles free status just three years after the virus was eliminated.
response_text: TRUE.  WHO verified the UK had eliminated endemic measles transmission based on 2016 data (announced in 2017). In August 2019, WHO said the UK had lost its measles-free status after sustained transmission returned. That’s roughly three years after elimination was achieved.

claim: Trump has challenged Nevada’s new state election law - that requires mail-in ballots to be sent to all active voters amid the coronavirus pandemic - in court. Nevada’s Republican Secretary of State has asked the judge to dismiss the Trump lawsuit.
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2020, the Trump campaign sued Nevada over AB4, the new election law that directed mailing ballots to all active registered voters during the pandemic. Nevada’s Republican Secretary of State, Barbara Cegavske, filed a motion asking the federal court to dismiss the lawsuit.

claim: Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said, 'Courage is what it takes to stand up and speak; courage is also what it takes to sit down and listen'.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Although widely attributed to Winston Churchill, no reliable source or citation in his speeches or writings supports this quote. The International Churchill Society and quote researchers (e.g., Quote Investigator) classify it as apocryphal/misattributed.

claim: Andrew Jackson said “One man with courage makes a majority.”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The line “One man with courage makes a majority” is widely attributed to Andrew Jackson, but researchers have found no evidence he said or wrote it. The phrase appears in print decades after Jackson’s death and is considered a spurious attribution (also often misattributed to Thomas Jefferson). Uncertain origin, but not reliably Jackson.

claim: Pennsylvania just opened up a $10 billion plant, during the presidency of Donald Trump, this would never normally have happened because they wouldn't have allowed them to frack.
response_text: FALSE.  - The “$10 billion plant” is Shell’s ethane cracker in Beaver County, PA (Shell Polymers Monaca). It began operations in November 2022, under President Biden—not during Trump’s presidency. The final investment decision was made in June 2016 under President Obama, after Pennsylvania approved major tax incentives in 2012. - Fracking was legal and widespread in Pennsylvania under Obama, Trump, and Biden. Neither Obama nor Biden banned fracking, and Pennsylvania continued to allow it under both Democratic and Republican state leaders.  Sources: Shell press release (Nov. 15, 2022); PolitiFact/FactCheck.org reporting on the plant’s timeline and approvals.

claim: TRUMP SAID Earlier this month, the U.S. government officially labeled China for the first time ever a currency manipulator — another promise kept.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: While the U.S. Treasury did label China a currency manipulator in August 2019, it was not the first time ever. Treasury previously designated China a currency manipulator in 1992 and again in 1994 under the 1988 law.

claim: TRUMP said If he was a great president (barack Obama), how come he left me 138 judges to appoint when everybody said that’s the single most important thing a president of the United States has to do?
response_text: TRUE.  Trump repeatedly made this claim at rallies and interviews, sometimes giving the number as 138 (and other times 128, 140, 142, etc.), and saying judicial appointments are the most important thing a president does. Note: the figure is exaggerated—there were about 105 judicial vacancies when he took office, per federal judiciary data, many due to Senate inaction.

claim: "wealthy people in Canada donate to hospitals" to get better health care treatment.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In Canada’s publicly funded health system, hospitals are legally required to provide care based on medical need, not ability to pay or donate. Hospital foundations do solicit “grateful patient” donations and may offer non-clinical perks (recognition, a liaison, help with scheduling, private rooms if available), but policies prohibit donors from receiving faster or better medical treatment. While there have been occasional controversies about “VIP/concierge” amenities, preferential clinical care for donors is not permitted and is not standard practice.

claim: Robert Sweet, a federal judge who was overseeing a civil case against Jeffrey Epstein was killed.
response_text: FALSE.  Robert W. Sweet, a senior federal judge in the Southern District of New York who handled parts of Virginia Giuffre’s civil defamation case against Ghislaine Maxwell (linked to Jeffrey Epstein), died on March 24, 2019 at age 96 of natural causes. Obituaries (e.g., New York Times, AP) report no foul play. He was not killed.

claim: The push by Assembly Democrats seeking Americans with Disabilities Act accommodations for a lawmaker were timed to make Vos look bad.
response_text: FALSE.  Available records and reporting show Democrats had been pressing for ADA accommodations for Rep. Jimmy Anderson for years and requested accommodations ahead of the relevant floor session. There’s no evidence the request was orchestrated or timed to embarrass Speaker Vos; the claim is an unsubstantiated assertion of motive. Uncertainty: motive is inherently hard to prove, but documentation contradicts the “timed” allegation.

claim: Professor HC Verma still drives an old scooter.
response_text: Answer: TRUE (with some uncertainty)  Explanation: H. C. Verma, the IIT Kanpur physicist and author of “Concepts of Physics,” has long been noted in news features and widely shared photos for commuting around the IIT Kanpur campus on an old scooter, a habit reported even after his 2017 retirement. While this reputation persists, there’s no recent authoritative confirmation that he still does so today, hence minor uncertainty.

claim: Eminent Physics professor HC Verma donates Rs 1 crore to PM relief fund and for charity.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This was a viral rumor during 2020. Prof. H.C. Verma publicly denied it, saying he had not donated Rs 1 crore to the PM relief fund or to charity, and asked people to stop sharing the claim. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., India Today, Alt News, BOOM) verified it was false.

claim: Professor HC Verma,  gets Rs 1 cr as royalty per year for his book "'Concepts of Physics'
response_text: FALSE.  Professor H. C. Verma has publicly denied the viral claim that he earns Rs 1 crore per year in royalties from “Concepts of Physics.” Fact-checks (e.g., Alt News/BOOM) reported his clarification that the figure is exaggerated; while he donates his book royalties to educational causes like Shiksha Sopan, the actual amount is not disclosed and is not Rs 1 crore annually. Slight uncertainty remains because exact figures aren’t public, but his own denial makes the claim false.

claim: CNN's Chris Cuomo exploded at a man who called him fredo.
response_text: TRUE.  In 2019, a viral video showed CNN host Chris Cuomo angrily confronting a man who called him “Fredo,” comparing the slur to the N-word and threatening the man. He later acknowledged the incident and CNN backed his defense of not tolerating slurs, though he was off-air at the time.

claim: Would Florida assault weapon law amendment proposal ban virtually all guns?
response_text: FALSE.  The proposed Florida amendment targeted only certain semiautomatic rifles and shotguns (those with magazines or feeding devices over 10 rounds). It did not cover handguns and would not ban non‑semiautomatic firearms (e.g., revolvers, bolt‑action rifles, pump shotguns). So it would restrict many long guns but not “virtually all guns.”

claim: Britons have spent £4bn stockpiling goods in case of no-deal Brexit.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The £4bn figure comes from a single 2019 survey by Premium Credit that extrapolated from a small online sample to the whole UK. The question referred to “Brexit” rather than specifically “no-deal,” and the estimate relied on averaging self-reported spending, which is prone to skew and large uncertainty. Fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact) judged the methodology too weak to support a firm claim that Britons “have spent £4bn” stockpiling. Uncertain but not reliably evidenced.

claim: U.S. Attorney General William Barr made a secret visit to the Manhattan jail where Jeffrey Epstein was being held just two weeks before the accused sex trafficker was found dead in his cell
response_text: FALSE.  Attorney General William Barr did make an unannounced (not “secret”) visit to the Manhattan federal jail (MCC) — but it was after Jeffrey Epstein was found dead, not two weeks before. Multiple outlets reported Barr’s visit on August 12, 2019, two days after Epstein’s August 10 death. There’s no credible reporting that Barr visited the jail two weeks prior.

claim: Attorney General William Barr visited the prison where accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein was being held.
response_text: TRUE.  Attorney General William Barr made an unannounced visit to the Metropolitan Correctional Center in Manhattan—the jail where Jeffrey Epstein had been held—after Epstein’s death in 2019, as reported by outlets such as Reuters and the Associated Press.

claim: In the weeks following El Paso and Dayton, evidence of an impending mass shooting spread on Snapchat and iMessage.
response_text: FALSE  In the immediate weeks after the El Paso (Aug 3, 2019) and Dayton (Aug 4, 2019) shootings, the major subsequent mass shooting was Midland–Odessa (Aug 31, 2019), which had no widely reported advance warnings circulating on Snapchat or iMessage. High-profile cases where threats or “evidence” spread via Snapchat/iMessage (e.g., Oxford High School, 2021) occurred much later. Uncertainty: there were scattered hoax/threat arrests post–El Paso/Dayton, but not a documented impending mass shooting broadly spreading on Snapchat and iMessage as claimed.

claim: Jean Monnet said a European superstate should be created without the understanding of European people.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely circulated line about Monnet wanting a “European superstate” created “without the people understanding” has no credible source. It does not appear in his Memoirs or archived correspondence, and fact‑checkers and the Jean Monnet Foundation have said they can’t find any record of it. Monnet did advocate gradual integration, but there’s no evidence he called for deceiving the public, nor did he promote a “superstate” in those terms.

claim: Donald Trump said that he 'did criminal justice reform, which President Obama could not get approved...'
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump has repeatedly said he passed criminal justice reform (the First Step Act) and that President Obama couldn’t get it approved. For example, at campaign events and in the Oct. 22, 2020 presidential debate, he boasted that he “did criminal justice reform” and that Obama/Biden “didn’t” or “couldn’t” get it done.

claim: Democratic Republicans  Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar have vowed to take benefits like Social Security and Medicare away from senior citizens.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence either Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Ilhan Omar has vowed to take Social Security or Medicare away from seniors. In fact, both have consistently supported expanding these programs (e.g., backing Medicare for All and proposals to increase Social Security benefits) and have opposed cuts. Fact-checkers have debunked similar viral claims.

claim: Olive Garden restaurant chain  are funding trumps 2020 campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  - Olive Garden (owned by Darden Restaurants) publicly stated in 2019 that they do not donate to presidential candidates. - FEC records show no contributions from Olive Garden/Darden or its PAC to Donald Trump’s 2020 campaign committees. - While individual employees may donate personally, that is not the company funding a campaign.

claim: Abortion is never medically necessary.
response_text: FALSE.  Medical consensus holds that abortion is sometimes necessary to save a pregnant person’s life or prevent serious harm. Examples include ectopic pregnancy, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, sepsis after previable membrane rupture, uncontrollable hemorrhage, molar pregnancy, and situations where urgent cancer treatment is required. Major medical bodies (e.g., ACOG, WHO) recognize abortion as essential medical care in such cases.

claim: The Nigerian Embassy in The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has been ejected from its premises.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Viral posts in 2024 claimed Nigeria’s mission in Kinshasa was “ejected,” but Nigeria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs clarified that the chancery (embassy) was not expelled. A dispute involved a separate leased/ancillary property (reported as staff quarters/annex), not the main embassy premises. The embassy has continued operations in DRC. Minor uncertainty remains about the exact property affected, but it was not the embassy itself.

claim: Social Security beneficiaries count on the US post office to get their checks.
response_text: FALSE.  Since March 1, 2013, nearly all Social Security benefits are paid electronically (direct deposit or Direct Express debit card) under U.S. Treasury rules. Only rare hardship exceptions still receive paper checks by mail, so most beneficiaries do not rely on the U.S. Postal Service for their payments.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg has suffered a massive stroke.
response_text: FALSE.  There were no credible reports that Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg suffered a massive stroke. She had various health issues (cancers, a 2014 heart stent, 2018 rib fractures, 2019 radiation) and died in 2020 from complications of metastatic pancreatic cancer. Rumors about a stroke were hoaxes; a different justice, John Paul Stevens, died after a stroke in 2019. Uncertainty: none from reliable sources.

claim: White supremacy is a hoax and "not a real problem in America."
response_text: FALSE.  White supremacist extremism is documented as a real and significant problem in the U.S. DHS and the FBI have repeatedly assessed since 2019–2024 that racially/ethnically motivated violent extremists—particularly those advocating white supremacy—pose the most persistent and lethal domestic terror threat. Recent deadly attacks tied to white supremacist ideology include Charleston (2015), Pittsburgh synagogue (2018), El Paso (2019), Buffalo (2022), and Jacksonville (2023). Hate-crime data and watchdog reports also show ongoing activity and violence linked to white supremacist groups.

claim: Plane crashes resumed after FFK’s tenure as Minister of Aviation.
response_text: TRUE.  - Femi Fani-Kayode served as Nigeria’s Minister of Aviation from Nov 2006 to May 2007. The major crashes just before his tenure were Bellview (Oct 2005), Sosoliso (Dec 2005), and ADC (Oct 2006). - After his tenure, fatal airline crashes occurred again, notably Dana Air Flight 992 in Lagos (June 3, 2012) and Associated Airlines Flight 361 (Oct 3, 2013).  Note: There was a multi-year lull that extended beyond his tenure; smaller incidents may have occurred, but major fatal commercial crashes did resume after he left office.

claim: Five plane crashes with a death toll of 453 were recorded the year before Femi Fani Kayode became Nigeria’s Minister of Aviation.
response_text: FALSE.  - Femi Fani-Kayode became Minister of Aviation in November 2006. - In the preceding calendar year (2005), Nigeria had two major commercial crashes: Bellview Flight 210 (22 Oct 2005, 117 dead) and Sosoliso Flight 1145 (10 Dec 2005, 108 dead) — total about 225 deaths. - Even if you include crashes before his appointment in 2006 (Nigerian Air Force Dornier crash in Sept 2006 ~13 dead; ADC Flight 53 on 29 Oct 2006 ~96 dead), the total is still roughly 4 crashes and about 334 deaths, not five crashes and not 453 deaths.  So the claim overstates both the number of crashes and the death toll.

claim: Just like Omoyele Sowore, a Nigerian human rights activist, President Muhammadu Buhari called for a revolution in 2011.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Muhammadu Buhari calling for a street or “Egypt‑style” revolution in 2011. The quotes often circulated to claim this are misattributed (several came from his 2011 running mate, Tunde Bakare, and other activists), or refer to a “revolution at the ballot box,” not an extra‑constitutional uprising. Fact‑checks (e.g., Dubawa/Africa Check) have found the claim unsupported. Slight uncertainty only if one counts metaphorical “ballot” language as a “revolution.”

claim: Mental illness is main driver of mass shootings says Donald trump when talking about the shootings in Texas and Ohio that killed 31 people.
Donald Trump said, "Last year - 2018, we prosecuted a record number of firearms offenses."
response_text: FALSE  Reason: DOJ reported that FY2018 saw the highest number of defendants charged with federal firearms offenses in over a decade, not an all‑time record. Some datasets (and the “charged” vs. “prosecuted” distinction) show mid‑2000s levels comparable or higher, so calling 2018 a “record” overstates it. (Small uncertainty due to differing data series/definitions.)

claim: Republicans voted to allow people with pre-existing mental illness to buy firearms.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2017, the GOP-led Congress repealed an Obama-era Social Security rule that would have automatically reported certain disability beneficiaries with mental impairments who need a representative payee to the federal background check system. Repeal kept the status quo; it did not legalize gun purchases for “people with mental illness” broadly. Federal law still bars those adjudicated mentally defective or involuntarily committed from buying guns. The rule targeted a narrow subset and hadn’t fully taken effect, so saying Republicans “voted to allow people with pre-existing mental illness to buy firearms” is misleading. Uncertainty: a subset who would have been reported under the rule were not automatically flagged after repeal.

claim: The common theme with mass shooters is that the assailants were on psychotropic drugs.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no reliable evidence that most mass shooters were on psychotropic medications. Government and academic reviews and shooter databases (e.g., U.S. Secret Service NTAC reports, The Violence Project, major media databases) do not find psychiatric drug use as a common or defining factor; in many cases medication status is unknown, and among those with known toxicology many had no such drugs in their system. A few attackers had been prescribed meds, but this is not a consistent or predominant pattern.

claim: AG William Barr Tweets Odds Of Mass Shootings In Hometowns Of 2 Democrat Presidential Candidates Are 250 Billion To 1
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of William Barr tweeting such a claim, and the “250 billion to 1” line traces to satire (e.g., Babylon Bee-style content). No credible sources or official accounts show Barr making this statement, and the odds figure is baseless.

claim: Police stopped a mass shooting in Omaha, NE, in early August 2019
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There were multiple arrests across the U.S. in mid‑August 2019 for alleged mass‑shooting plans (e.g., in Youngstown, OH; Long Beach, CA; Volusia County, FL; Springfield, MO), but no credible contemporaneous reports that Omaha police stopped a mass shooting in early August 2019. Fact‑checks of viral lists that included “Omaha” found no substantiating local news or police reports for such an incident. Slight uncertainty due to the breadth of August 2019 reports, but available evidence does not support this claim.

claim: Police stopped a mass shooting in Des Moines, IA, in early August 2019
response_text: FALSE  I can find no credible reports or police statements that Des Moines, Iowa police “stopped a mass shooting” in early August 2019. Around that time there were widespread threat arrests nationwide and unfounded rumors (including about the Iowa State Fair), but no verified incident in Des Moines matching this claim. (Some social media posts appear to conflate locations or unrelated arrests.) Uncertain only to the extent of possible conflation with another city.

claim: President Buhari approves the creation of state police.
response_text: FALSE.  Muhammadu Buhari consistently opposed creating state police while president (2015–2023), favoring “community policing” under the federal Nigeria Police. Establishing state police would require constitutional amendments, which did not occur during his tenure, and no state police were created. (Moves toward state police only gained traction under President Tinubu in 2024.)

claim: "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
response_text: TRUE  Context is El Paso after the Aug. 3, 2019 Walmart shooting. Before the attack, El Paso had recorded 5 homicides in 2019; over the prior decade the city averaged about 18 homicides per year, and the 22 killed that day exceeded that average. Minor caveat: saying “the entire year” was imprecise—those 5 were year-to-date at the time.

claim: Social media videos claim that Clearblue pregnancy tests contain a type of morning-after pill called Plan B.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Clearblue pregnancy tests do not contain Plan B (levonorgestrel). The small tablet seen inside some test casings is a moisture-absorbing desiccant used to keep the test accurate, not a medication. Clearblue and multiple fact-checks have confirmed this; the desiccant should not be ingested.

claim: George Washington said “It will be found an unjust and unwise jealousy to deprive a man of his natural liberty upon the supposition he may abuse it.”
response_text: FALSE.  The line is from John Milton’s Areopagitica (1644), not George Washington. It does not appear in Washington’s writings; quote references trace it to Milton’s argument against prior restraint on publication.

claim: Zomato's Sales Have  Dropped By 60% In 10 Hours
response_text: FALSE.  - There’s no credible report or official disclosure from Zomato (a listed company) of a 60% sales drop “in 10 hours.” Companies don’t report intra-day “sales” like this, and any material collapse would trigger an exchange filing and wide media coverage.   - The claim appears to be a social‑media rumor (often confusing “sales” with stock price). Zomato’s stock has not seen a 60% intraday crash.  Uncertainty: No company publishes 10‑hour sales data; conclusion based on absence of reliable sources and standard disclosure practices.

claim: News report claims that Ghana has been named the second most corrupt country in Africa by Transparency International (TI).
response_text: FALSE.  Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index does not rank Ghana as the second most corrupt country in Africa. In recent CPI editions (e.g., 2023), Ghana scored around 43/100 and ranked about 70th of 180 globally—well above many African countries with much lower scores (e.g., Somalia, South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Sudan, DRC, Burundi). TI has not labeled Ghana the “second most corrupt” in Africa.

claim: Telecommunications company Airtel Nigeria is giving away 500,000 iPhones.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible announcement from Airtel Nigeria or major news outlets supports such a massive giveaway, and Airtel has previously warned about fake “free iPhone” promos circulating online. The scale (500,000 iPhones) is implausible and typical of phishing/scam schemes.

claim: Leaves of sweet potatoes can kill cancer.
response_text: FALSE.  Sweet potato leaves contain antioxidants and some extracts have shown anti‑proliferative or cytotoxic effects on cancer cells in test tubes/animals. But there’s no clinical evidence that eating the leaves “kills cancer” or cures cancer in humans. They should not be considered a cancer treatment.

claim: Joe Biden, whilst vice president, said the Obama administration had passed the criminal justice reform bill.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The phrase “the criminal justice reform bill” typically refers to the First Step Act, which passed in 2018 under President Trump. Biden later (in 2019, after serving as vice president) wrongly suggested “we passed the criminal justice reform bill,” a claim fact‑checkers flagged. While vice president, the Obama administration did pass the Fair Sentencing Act (2010), but Biden did not—and could not—have claimed the administration had passed the 2018 reform bill during his vice presidency. Uncertainty: none significant.

claim: In an op-ed, then-sen. Joe Biden wrote that he believed that women working outside the home would, quote, "create the deterioration of family." He also said that women who were working outside the home were, quote, "avoiding responsibility."
response_text: FALSE.  Those phrases come from a 1981 op-ed in which then‑Sen. Joe Biden criticized a proposed expansive federal child‑care program. He argued such a program could “create the deterioration of family” and allow “people/parents” to “avoid responsibility” for child‑rearing. He did not write that women working outside the home were causing family deterioration or “avoiding responsibility.” The claim misattributes his critique of a policy to working women. (Minor uncertainty on the exact newspaper/date wording, but multiple fact‑checks confirm the context.)

claim: Rodrigo Duterte changed his position again on opening in-person classes amid the coronavirus 2019 pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  Duterte repeatedly shifted on face-to-face classes. In 2020 he said he wouldn’t allow in-person classes until vaccines were available, then in Dec 2020 approved a January 2021 pilot, only to suspend it days later over new variants. In Sept 2021 he again approved limited pilots in low-risk areas, which proceeded in late 2021 and expanded in 2022.

claim: The City of New York could not proceed with the case of murder of Eric Garner because the Justice Department was pursuing its prosecution.
response_text: FALSE.  - New York City does not prosecute crimes; local district attorneys do. The Staten Island DA took the case to a grand jury in 2014, which declined to indict. - The Justice Department was conducting a federal civil-rights investigation (not a “murder” prosecution) and ultimately brought no charges (2019). That federal probe did not legally prevent state/local prosecution, nor did it bar the City from administrative discipline; the City chose to wait on discipline during the federal review.

claim: Companies like Amazon that made billions in profits did not pay one nickel in federal income tax
response_text: FALSE.  Context matters. Amazon did pay $0 in federal corporate income tax in some years despite billions in profits (notably 2018, and reportedly 2017) due to credits and deductions. But it has paid federal corporate income taxes in other years (e.g., 2019 and after). So the blanket claim that companies like Amazon “did not pay one nickel” is misleading unless tied to specific years. (Exact amounts vary by year.)

claim: As governor of Colorado, John Hickenlooper created the No. 1 economy in the country.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Colorado’s economy performed very well while Hickenlooper was governor—often top tier in job growth and low unemployment, and it was ranked No. 1 in the “economy” category by U.S. News in some years. But it was not consistently the nation’s No. 1 by core metrics (e.g., GDP growth) across sources, and saying he “created” that economy overstates causation. So the blanket claim is misleading. (Some nuance: certain rankings did place Colorado No. 1 in specific years.)

claim: 500,000 Americans are sleeping out on the street
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: On a single night in January 2023, HUD estimated about 653,000 people experiencing homelessness in the U.S., of whom roughly 40% were unsheltered (around 250,000–260,000). “Sleeping out on the street” refers to unsheltered homelessness, which is far below 500,000. (Estimates vary by year and methodology, but unsheltered counts have not approached 500,000.)

claim: In 1988 Bernie Sanders lost an election because he called for the ban of the sale and distribution of assault weapons.
response_text: FALSE.  Sanders did call in 1988 for a ban on the sale and distribution of semiautomatic “assault” weapons, but there’s no evidence that this is why he lost. He lost a three-way race for Vermont’s at‑large U.S. House seat to Republican Peter Smith while a Democrat also ran, splitting the left‑leaning vote. Analyses of that race attribute his loss mainly to the three‑way split, not specifically to his gun stance. (In fact, guns became a bigger factor in 1990, when Smith backed an assault‑weapons ban, lost NRA support, and Sanders then won.) Uncertainty: exact causal attribution is inherently hard, but the claim overstates the case.

claim: Pinning Down Prescription Drug Prices
response_text: FALSE — This is a phrase/title, not a verifiable factual assertion, so it cannot be evaluated for truth.

claim: 87 million Americans are uninsured or underinsured
response_text: TRUE — with caveats.  The widely cited “87 million” comes from Commonwealth Fund surveys (e.g., 2018; similar magnitude in 2022) estimating about 43% of working‑age adults (19–64) were inadequately insured—meaning uninsured, underinsured, or had a gap in coverage during the year—roughly 85–90 million people.  Caveats: - It refers to working‑age adults, not all Americans. - The figure includes those who had a coverage gap; if you count only people who are currently uninsured or underinsured at a point in time, the number is lower (roughly 60–70 million).

claim: Albert Einstein once said, “Art is standing with one hand extended into the universe and one hand extended into the world, and letting ourselves be a conduit for passing energy.”
response_text: FALSE.  This line is widely misattributed to Albert Einstein. It originates with artist Alex Grey, who wrote essentially this phrasing in The Mission of Art (1998). No reliable Einstein source or publication contains this quote.

claim: The health-care industry made $100 billion in profits last year
response_text: TRUE  Reason: Analyses (e.g., Axios, cited by fact-checkers) found that the combined net profits of major U.S. health-care companies—insurers, drugmakers, device makers, hospitals, PBMs—were roughly $100 billion in 2018 (and similar magnitude in adjacent years). Caveat: “health-care industry” and “last year” are vague, and totals depend on which firms are included and whether global profits are counted.

claim: Pro-Kremlin Pundit Blames Demonstrators for Police Crackdown on Moscow Protest
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: During Moscow’s opposition protests (e.g., summer 2019 over city council elections), prominent pro-Kremlin TV figures such as Dmitry Kiselyov and Vladimir Solovyov publicly argued that demonstrators provoked police and were responsible for the ensuing crackdown. This framing was reported by independent outlets like The Moscow Times and RFE/RL. Slight uncertainty on the exact pundit the headline refers to, but the characterization is accurate.

claim: Ancient Roman politician Marcus Tullius Cicero once said, “The Budget should be balanced, the Treasury should be refilled, public debt should be reduced.”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This wording is part of a modern, widely circulated misattribution. No passage in Cicero’s extant works matches it, and there is no Latin source. The quote first surfaces in the 20th century (notably in the 1960s, often via Taylor Caldwell’s novel A Pillar of Iron and later compilations). Reputable sources (e.g., Quote Investigator, Wikiquote, Yale Book of Quotations) mark it as spurious.

claim: Hitesh Mulchandani was burnt to death.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: There are no credible, widely reported sources as of 2024 indicating that a person named Hitesh Mulchandani was burnt to death. This appears unsubstantiated; if it refers to a very local incident, it isn’t verifiable from reliable public records. Uncertainty: moderate.

claim: More than half of death row prisoners are people of color
response_text: TRUE.  In the U.S., people of color (Black, Latino, and other non-White groups) make up a majority of death row. Recent tallies from sources like the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Death Penalty Information Center show roughly 41–42% White, about 41% Black, around 13–15% Latino, and a few percent other—i.e., well over 50% are people of color. Minor year-to-year variation, but consistently a majority.

claim: Robert S Mueller's investigation into Russia’s interference in the 2016 presidential election took over 2 years and cost over £25 million.
response_text: FALSE.  - Duration: Mueller was appointed May 17, 2017, and delivered his report March 22, 2019—about 22 months, not over two years (though he formally closed the office May 29, 2019). - Cost: The final cost was about $32 million in total, which is roughly £25 million; whether it’s “over £25m” depends on the exchange rate, but the “over two years” part is inaccurate.

claim: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau took two billion dollars from Canada’s retirement fund in order to give it to housing projects in India.
response_text: FALSE.  Canada’s pension assets are managed by the independent Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), not by the prime minister. CPPIB makes global, profit-seeking investments—including in India—at arm’s length from government. The “$2 billion” figure circulating online refers to CPPIB investments over time in Indian real estate platforms, not money “taken” by Justin Trudeau or a government gift to India.

claim: Robert S Mueller can't provide evidence that his investigation into  Russia’s interference in the 2016 presidential election reached a conclusion.
response_text: FALSE.  Mueller’s Special Counsel investigation formally concluded. He delivered his final report to the Attorney General on March 22, 2019; a redacted version was released April 18, 2019; and on May 29, 2019 he announced the closure of the Special Counsel’s Office. The report states its conclusions, including that Russia interfered “in sweeping and systematic fashion,” that evidence did not establish a criminal conspiracy with the Trump campaign, and that the report did not exonerate the President on obstruction.

claim: The European Union asked for a 100 billion euro settlement for the UK to leave the EU.
response_text: FALSE.  The EU never officially demanded a €100 billion “divorce bill.” It set a methodology to settle mutual obligations without naming a figure. Some media reports in 2017 estimated a gross liability of up to €100bn, but that was not an official ask. The eventual settlement, based on the agreed methodology, has been widely estimated at about €35–45bn (roughly €40–50bn), far below €100bn.

claim: An exercise being done in a video can cure heart blockage and back pain in 7 days
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible evidence that a single exercise (or any exercise routine) can “cure” coronary artery blockage within 7 days. Coronary blockages are due to atherosclerotic plaque and/or clots; management involves medications, risk-factor control, and sometimes procedures like angioplasty or bypass—improvements occur over months to years, not a week. While some uncomplicated back pain can improve quickly with movement and exercises, no one exercise reliably cures all back pain in 7 days. Claims like this are medically implausible and potentially dangerous if they delay proper care.

claim: President Trump fully co-operated with the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S presidential campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Mueller Report notes that President Trump refused an in-person interview; he provided written answers limited to Russia-related questions that investigators deemed inadequate, and he declined to answer obstruction questions.   - The report also documents multiple efforts by Trump to curtail or end the investigation (e.g., attempting to have Mueller removed, directing efforts to limit the probe’s scope, and urging aides to create false records), which are inconsistent with “full cooperation.”  Sources: Special Counsel Robert Mueller, Report on the Investigation into Russian Interference in the 2016 Presidential Election (2019), especially Vol. II (Obstruction).

claim: Robert Mueller applied and was interviewed for the job of FBI director the day before he was appointed Special Counsel.
response_text: FALSE.  Mueller did meet with President Trump at the White House on May 16, 2017, the day before he was appointed special counsel. But Mueller did not apply for, nor interview as a candidate for, the FBI director job. He testified in 2019 that he was not seeking the position and did not interview for it; the meeting was to discuss the state of the FBI. He also had already served the maximum term as director absent special congressional action.

claim: The Trump campaign welcomed and made full use of Russian intervention  in the 2016 U.S presidential election.
response_text: TRUE.  - Mueller Report: Russia interfered via social-media operations and hacking/“dumping” of Democratic emails. The investigation “established that the Campaign expected it would benefit electorally from information stolen and released through Russian efforts” and that the campaign “showed interest in and welcomed” WikiLeaks’ releases. Trump and senior aides sought information about forthcoming releases and Trump repeatedly promoted them (“I love WikiLeaks”).   - Senate Intelligence Committee (bipartisan) likewise found the campaign sought advance information on WikiLeaks releases and that Manafort shared internal polling with a Russian intelligence associate.  Note: Mueller did not establish a criminal conspiracy between the campaign and the Russian government, but the campaign did welcome and actively exploit the Russian-enabled disclosures.

claim: A dossier by former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele containing contacts between Russian officials and members of the Trump campaign started the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  The FBI’s Russia investigation (Crossfire Hurricane) began on July 31, 2016, after a tip from an Australian diplomat about Trump adviser George Papadopoulos claiming Russia had damaging emails on Clinton. The Steele dossier was received later and did not trigger the opening of the investigation, though parts of it were later used in FISA applications. This is documented by the DOJ Inspector General’s 2019 report and the Mueller report.

claim: The Baltnews.lv news website is an “independent and not controlled by the state media.”
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence from investigations and Latvian authorities shows Baltnews.lv is a project of Russia’s state-owned media group Rossiya Segodnya (which runs Sputnik), financed and managed via intermediaries. Latvian security services have even pursued cases for violating EU sanctions related to cooperation with Rossiya Segodnya through Baltnews. Thus, it is not independent of state control.

claim: London has no go areas.
response_text: FALSE.  Authorities (Metropolitan Police, Mayor’s Office) consistently state there are no “no‑go zones” in London; police and emergency services operate across all neighborhoods. Some areas have higher crime or gang activity, but none are off-limits to law enforcement. (If the claim meant the opposite—“London has no-go areas”—it’s still false.)

claim: London has a Muslim mayor.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The elected Mayor of London is Sadiq Khan, who is a practicing Muslim (in office since 2016, re-elected, including in 2024). Note: This refers to the Mayor of London (Greater London), not the ceremonial Lord Mayor of the City of London.

claim: London is now one of the world’s most violent capital cities.
response_text: FALSE.  By standard measures of violence (especially homicides per 100,000 people), London ranks low among world capitals. London’s homicide rate in recent years has been around 1–2 per 100,000—well below many capitals in the Americas and Africa, and below the global average. Capitals such as Washington, D.C., Mexico City, Bogotá, Kingston, Port-au-Prince, and others have rates many times higher. While London has issues like knife crime, it is not among the world’s most violent capitals by commonly used metrics. Note: “most violent” is vague, but on recognized indicators this claim doesn’t hold.

claim: Police in Gujarat seized weapons from a mosque.
response_text: FALSE  Briefly: No credible reports confirm Gujarat police seizing weapons from a mosque. Viral posts making this claim have been debunked by Indian fact-checkers as misattributed or unrelated, and there are no official police reports of such a seizure. (Some uncertainty remains because the claim is vague about time/place.)

claim: Some government buildings in London are operating under sharia law.
response_text: FALSE.  UK government buildings are governed by UK law. While there are private Sharia councils/tribunals in the UK that offer religious guidance or voluntary arbitration in limited civil matters, they have no state legal authority, cannot override UK law, and are not government-run or housed as official operations in government buildings. No credible evidence shows any London government building “operating under sharia law.”

claim: More than 450 mosques have opened in London.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The oft-repeated claim (e.g., “423 new mosques in London”) comes from unreliable counts that mix purpose-built mosques with prayer rooms and proposals. Fact-checkers (e.g., Full Fact, Snopes) found no authoritative evidence that hundreds of new mosques—let alone more than 450—have “opened” in London. Total numbers of Muslim prayer spaces in London may be in the hundreds, but the specific claim about 450+ openings is unsupported. Uncertain exact totals, but the stated claim overreaches.

claim: 19th century writer and feminist Margaret Fuller said: Today a reader, tomorrow a leader.
response_text: FALSE.  The line is widely attributed to Margaret Fuller, but no reliable source places it in her 19th‑century writings. Earliest known uses appear much later as 20th‑century reading-promotion slogans, making the Fuller attribution doubtful. (Don’t confuse it with Truman’s documented line: “Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers.”)

claim: Rep. Ilhan Omar "voted yes" to "provide further funding for the 9/11 First Responders Victims Fund
response_text: TRUE.  Rep. Ilhan Omar voted “Yea” on H.R. 1327, the “Never Forget the Heroes” act, which permanently authorized and provided additional funding for the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. The House passed it on July 12, 2019.

claim: Abraham Lincoln said "America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we lose our freedoms it will be because we have destroyed ourselves from within."
response_text: FALSE.  It’s a popular paraphrase, not a verbatim Lincoln quote. In his 1838 Lyceum Address, he said: “If it ever reach us, it must spring up amongst us; it cannot come from abroad… If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher.” The exact wording in the claim does not appear in his writings or speeches.

claim: Sen. Rand Paul "voted no." to provide further funding for the 9/11 first responders Victims Fund.
response_text: TRUE.  In July 2019, the Senate passed the “Never Forget the Heroes” Act to permanently authorize and fund the 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund, 97–2. The two “no” votes were Sens. Rand Paul and Mike Lee. Paul had also earlier objected to unanimous consent, citing cost concerns.

claim: Is Donna Shalala correct in saying that Children at Homestead migrant facility "get 30 minutes over a month to talk to family members. If they were in a prison — a federal prison — they would get 300 minutes."
response_text: FALSE.  Why: ORR policy — and statements from the Homestead influx facility in 2019 — said children were allowed at least two 10‑minute phone calls per week, i.e., about 80 minutes per month, not 30. The federal prison figure (300 minutes per month) is roughly correct, but Shalala’s claim understates the children’s phone access, making the comparison inaccurate. Note: Some children faced practical hurdles reaching family, but the policy was still far above 30 minutes.

claim: President Donald Trump’s 2020 campaign is selling plastic straws with the president’s name on them.
