response_text: FALSE.  - There is no credible evidence of Sri Lankan Muslims “demolishing mosques” or converting en masse to Hinduism.   - In recent years, mosques in Sri Lanka have more often been targets of anti-Muslim violence (e.g., 2014 Aluthgama, 2018 Kandy riots), not demolished by Muslims themselves.   - While isolated intra-Muslim disputes (e.g., Sufi–Salafi tensions) and rare individual conversions exist, they do not amount to a broader trend of Muslims converting to Hinduism.

claim: About 14.4 million Nigerians are currently on drugs
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The widely cited figure comes from the 2018 National Drug Use Survey (UNODC/NBS), which estimated about 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15–64 had used psychoactive drugs (excluding alcohol/tobacco) at least once in the previous year—about 14.4% prevalence. That is not the same as “currently on drugs” or addiction. No official, newer survey confirms that 14.4 million Nigerians are presently using drugs. (Some uncertainty remains because the latest comprehensive data are from 2018.)

claim: “Excise revenue has declined from approximately 3% of GDP in 2003/04 to about 2% in 2017/18.”
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: For Kenya, World Bank/KRA data show excise revenue fell from about 3% of GDP in FY2003/04 to roughly 2% of GDP by FY2017/18. If the claim refers to Kenya, it is accurate. (If a different country was intended, the trend may differ.)

claim: Over 2013-2018, the Russian economy has grown by only 3%, i.e. less than 1% per year
response_text: TRUE.  Using real GDP data (Rosstat/World Bank), annual growth rates were roughly: 2014 +0.7%, 2015 −2.0% to −2.5%, 2016 +0.3%, 2017 +1.8%, 2018 +2.3%–2.5%. Compounded, 2018 real GDP is only about 2.8–3.4% higher than 2013—well under 1% per year on average. Minor variation depends on the exact series/revisions.

claim: During the tenure of Nigerian President Jonathan, the inflationary pressure was kept at single digit.
response_text: FALSE.  Goodluck Jonathan’s tenure (2010–2015) saw double‑digit inflation for several years. Nigeria’s CPI inflation was mostly above 10% in 2010–2012 (around 13–14% in 2010, ~11% in 2011, ~12% in 2012), and only fell to single digits in 2013–2015 (about 8–9%). Sources: National Bureau of Statistics/CBN inflation series.

claim: The growth of the Russian economy in the decade from 1999 to 2008 averaged 6.9%
response_text: TRUE.  Using standard real GDP growth rates (World Bank/IMF) for Russia: 1999: 6.4; 2000: 10.0; 2001: 5.1; 2002: 4.7; 2003: 7.3; 2004: 7.2; 2005: 6.4; 2006: 8.2; 2007: 8.5; 2008: 5.2. These sum to 69.0; divided by 10 years gives an average of 6.9%. (Minor dataset/rounding differences may vary by ±0.1.)

claim: Nigeria was the number one destination for foreign direct investment during the tenure of President Jonathon.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Nigeria was never the world’s number one FDI destination under President Goodluck Jonathan. In Africa, Nigeria did top FDI inflows in some years (e.g., around 2011–2012 per UNCTAD), but it did not hold the top spot throughout his tenure (South Africa, Mozambique, and Egypt led in other years). So the blanket claim is inaccurate. Uncertainty: if the speaker meant “in Africa” and only for specific years, that narrower claim would be partly true.

claim: Nigeria has made solid progress in fighting corruption in the past four years
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Independent indicators show little to no improvement. Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index has kept Nigeria around 24–25/100 over the last four years, with rankings roughly in the 145–154/180 range—stagnant or slightly worse than 2019. World Bank governance indicators likewise show no clear gains. Despite some reforms (e.g., beneficial ownership register), persistent scandals and weak enforcement outcomes undercut claims of “solid progress.” Uncertainty: “solid” is subjective, but available data do not support it.

claim: Nigeria has made solid progress in the area of economic growth and agriculture and industrial output have recovered since the recession
response_text: FALSE  Reason: While Nigeria exited recession, overall growth since has been modest (around 2–3% y/y), below population growth, so per‑capita incomes remain below pre‑recession levels. Industrial output has been weak and volatile—industry contracted in 2022 amid oil production problems, and manufacturing has struggled with FX shortages and high costs. Agricultural growth has been subdued and disrupted by insecurity and flooding, with food inflation at record highs. The claim of “solid progress” and a broad recovery in agriculture and industry overstates the post‑recession performance. (Timeframe is unclear, but this holds after both the 2016 and 2020 recessions.)

claim: In 2014 in McDowell County, West Virginia, life expectancy for men was 64 years.
response_text: TRUE.  Briefly: IHME’s county-level life expectancy estimates for 2014 put male life expectancy in McDowell County, West Virginia at about 63.9 years—commonly rounded to 64. (These are modeled estimates, but the figure aligns with widely cited reports.)

claim: The U.S. women’s soccer team bring in more revenue but get paid less than the men
response_text: FALSE.  - Revenue: The USWNT exceeded the men in ticket (gate) revenue in some years (e.g., 2016–2018), but not consistently or across all revenue streams (TV, sponsorship, etc.). So “bring in more revenue” is only true for certain slices/years, not as a blanket statement. - Pay: Before 2022, women had lower per-game/bonus rates but received guaranteed salaries and benefits; in aggregate 2015–2019 they actually earned slightly more from U.S. Soccer, according to court filings. Since 2022, new CBAs guarantee equal pay structures (including pooling World Cup prize money), so they are not paid less now.  Note: The claim reflects a common but time- and metric-dependent talking point; taken broadly, it’s inaccurate.

claim: Mexican drug cartels make £500 billion a year.
response_text: FALSE.  Credible estimates put Mexican cartels’ annual revenues in the tens of billions of dollars, not hundreds. U.S. government and research estimates commonly range roughly $6–$39 billion per year from U.S. drug sales, with other criminal income adding more but still far below £500 billion. Moreover, UNODC estimates for the entire global illicit drug market are on the order of a few hundred billion dollars, making £500 billion for Mexican cartels alone implausible.

claim: India's Bharatiya Janata Party workers were killed in West Bengal by 11 Bajrang Dal members.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports of BJP workers in West Bengal being killed by “11 Bajrang Dal members.” Killings of BJP workers in the state, where reported, are typically linked to clashes with rival parties (often the TMC). Bajrang Dal is ideologically aligned with the BJP, and no verified incident matching this specific claim has been reported. Uncertain only to the extent that absence of evidence can’t prove impossibility, but the claim lacks any reliable sourcing.

claim: 1.5 lakh sub centers and primary health centers being transformed as health and wellness centers (HWCs) to provide comprehensive primary healthcare services.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Under the Ayushman Bharat program announced in 2018, the Government of India set a target to transform 1.5 lakh (150,000) Sub-Health Centres and Primary Health Centres into Health and Wellness Centres to deliver comprehensive primary healthcare. By 2024, over 1.6 lakh HWCs had been operationalized, aligning with this plan.

claim: Ayushman Bharat provides comprehensive health coverage up to Rs. 5 lakh per family per year to around 50 crore people.
response_text: TRUE.  Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) offers health insurance cover of up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization, targeting about 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families (~50 crore people). Note: the Rs 5 lakh cover is for hospitalization, not all health services, so “comprehensive” is slightly overstated.

claim: Former Vice President Joe Biden leaked the names of US Navy SEAL Team 6 families to Al Qaeda.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence that Joe Biden leaked the names of any SEAL Team 6 members or their families to Al Qaeda. After the bin Laden raid, Biden publicly credited U.S. Navy SEALs for the operation, but he did not disclose names. Multiple fact-checkers have debunked claims that he exposed identities or caused later casualties (e.g., the Extortion 17 shootdown), and no official source or investigation supports the allegation.

claim: Standing next to a mobile phone antenna or staying too long in its vicinity is a radiation risk.
response_text: FALSE.  For the general public, RF exposure from mobile/cell antennas in accessible areas is typically hundreds to thousands of times below international safety limits (ICNIRP/FCC/WHO). The main beam is directed away from the ground, and RF is non‑ionizing; no health risk has been established at these low levels, regardless of time spent nearby.  Caveat: Exposure can exceed limits only if you are very close and directly in front of an active antenna (e.g., on a rooftop/maintenance situation). Those areas are restricted for that reason.

claim: Prolonged exposure to radiofrequency radiation from a mobile phone antenna may exceed the recommended guidelines.
response_text: FALSE.  Exposure limits (ICNIRP/FCC) are time-averaged and set to be safe even for continuous use. Certified mobile phones and publicly accessible areas near base-station antennas are required to remain below these limits under worst-case operation. Prolonged duration doesn’t make compliant exposures exceed the guidelines. Exceedances would be rare and typically involve non-compliant devices or occupational, very close proximity to transmit antennas.

claim: Three men were hung on a crane and shot for the rape and murder of a 10-year-old boy in Yemen in August 2018
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple outlets (e.g., Reuters, AFP) reported that Houthi-run authorities in Sana’a, Yemen, publicly executed three men in August 2018 after convicting them of raping and murdering a 10-year-old boy. The men were shot (in the heart) and their bodies were then hung from cranes in a public square.

claim: Indian Prime Minister Modi launched an initiative for improving women's safety by setting up a helpline number that helps in keeping GPRS track of the vehicle that women are travelling in.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There’s no record of Prime Minister Narendra Modi launching a helpline that “keeps GPRS track of the vehicle” women are traveling in. Women’s helplines like 181 and 1091 predate his tenure or are run by states/police; GPS/GPRS tracking features have typically been part of state police apps (e.g., Delhi Police’s Himmat) or transport mandates (GPS devices in public transport) issued by ministries, not a PM-launched helpline. The claim mixes elements from different programs. Uncertainty: Some state initiatives combine helplines with GPS-enabled response, but not as a PM-launched national helpline tracking a woman’s vehicle.

claim: Former Minnesota Senator Franken was accused credibly by eight women of groping and forceable kissing, all of which were corroborated in real time.
response_text: FALSE.  About eight women did accuse Al Franken in 2017 of inappropriate touching (often during photo ops) and, in two cases, attempted/forced kissing. Some allegations had contemporaneous corroboration (e.g., Tweeden’s 2006 photo; a 2010 Facebook message; friends/family told at the time), but not all did. Several accounts were anonymous or lacked independent “real‑time” corroboration. Therefore the claim that all eight were credibly accused with real-time corroboration is overstated.

claim: Taylor Swift says most Democrats, independents, Republicans back nondiscrimination for LGBTQ people.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple national polls (especially PRRI’s American Values Atlas, across years) show majorities of Democrats, independents, and Republicans support laws that prohibit discrimination against LGBTQ people in jobs, housing, and public accommodations. Typical findings: about 80–85% of Democrats, around 70–75% of independents, and a slim-to-solid majority (roughly mid‑50s to low‑60s) of Republicans support such protections. Minor uncertainty comes from wording/year variations, but the cross‑party majority pattern holds.

claim: Virginia Beach USA mass shooting a "false flag" ordered by the "Deep State" to distract attention away from the investigation of "SPYgate"
response_text: FALSE.  This is an unsubstantiated conspiracy theory. Official investigations into the 2019 Virginia Beach Municipal Center shooting identified a lone perpetrator (a city employee) and found no evidence of government orchestration, “false flag” activity, or any link to “Spygate.”

claim: Being vegan for a year saves 3,320kg of CO2.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The size of the savings depends on the baseline diet and country, and food emissions are usually measured as CO2e (including methane and nitrous oxide), not just CO2. Peer‑reviewed studies generally find that switching from an average meat‑eating diet to vegan saves about 1,000–1,600 kg CO2e per year in the UK, and up to roughly 2,000–2,800 kg CO2e when compared to very high meat consumption. A blanket figure of 3,320 kg CO2 (and not CO2e) is higher than typical estimates and lacks context. Uncertainty: exact savings vary by individual diet and methodology.

claim: Michael Jordan Said  'I Won't Release Another Shoe Until Black People Unite'
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Michael Jordan saying this. The quote circulated as a viral meme/hoax and has been debunked by fact‑checkers. Jordan and Jordan Brand continued regular shoe releases throughout the years such claims appeared; while he issued statements supporting racial justice and pledged major donations, he never tied shoe releases to “Black people uniting.”

claim: In Kenya, over one in 20 children die before their fifth birthday.
response_text: FALSE.  Recent estimates put Kenya’s under‑5 mortality at about 41–42 deaths per 1,000 live births (~4%), roughly 1 in 24–25 children—below “over 1 in 20.” Sources: UNICEF/IGME 2023; World Bank; Kenya DHS 2022.

claim: Bhajan kirtans being organised in Srinagar for the first time in 40 years
response_text: FALSE.  Bhajan–kirtans have been held in Srinagar many times in recent decades, including at active temples like Shankaracharya, Durga Nag, Ganpatyar and Shitalnath, and even public bhajan events reported at Lal Chowk in the early 2020s. So it is not the “first time in 40 years.” (If the claim refers to a very specific venue/event not stated, that could change the assessment, but as stated it’s inaccurate.)

claim: Abortion is more dangerous now than ever before
response_text: FALSE.  Modern abortions using approved methods (medication with mifepristone/misoprostol or vacuum aspiration in clinical settings) are among the safest medical procedures. In the U.S., the death rate from legal abortion is around 0.4 per 100,000 procedures, far lower than childbirth, and far safer than in earlier eras—especially before legalization and antibiotics—when unsafe abortions caused large numbers of injuries and deaths. While recent restrictions can increase delays or push some toward unsafe methods in certain places, abortion is not “more dangerous than ever before” historically.

claim: Trump insisted that the special counsel was totally conflicted
response_text: TRUE.  Trump repeatedly claimed Special Counsel Robert Mueller had conflicts of interest, including tweeting on July 26, 2018 that “Bob Mueller is totally conflicted,” and making similar statements on other occasions.

claim: Trump said Bill Clinton was found guilty
response_text: FALSE  I can’t find a reliable record of Trump saying “Bill Clinton was found guilty.” Trump has often said Clinton was impeached, lied under oath, lost his law license, or paid a fine, but Bill Clinton was not convicted in a criminal trial—he was impeached by the House and acquitted by the Senate, and later held in civil contempt. (Some uncertainty due to the vast volume of Trump remarks.)

claim: “America is like a healthy body and its resistance is threefold: its patriotism, its morality and its spiritual life. If we can undermine these three areas, America will collapse from within.
response_text: FALSE.  This line is widely attributed to Joseph Stalin, but no reliable record of him (or any Soviet leader) saying it exists. Fact-checkers have found no source in Stalin’s writings or speeches, and the quote only appears in late-20th-century American publications. It’s considered apocryphal.

claim: Literal manure is coming out of taps in some US counties with CAFOs.
response_text: TRUE.  In several rural, CAFO‑dense counties (notably Kewaunee County, Wisconsin), private household wells have intermittently delivered brown, foul‑smelling tap water after manure spreading and rain, and testing has detected bovine fecal markers and pathogens—i.e., manure‑derived contamination—in the water. State agencies have documented “manure‑to‑well” incidents, and peer‑reviewed studies (e.g., in Kewaunee’s karst geology) link tap‑water contamination to cattle manure. Note: this refers to private wells in rural areas, not municipal systems, and events are episodic. Uncertainty: “literal manure” is a colloquial overstatement, but the underlying claim—manure‑contaminated water coming out of taps—has been documented.

claim: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said the U.S. doesn’t have to worry about Chinese missile attacks because of the difference in time zones between the two countries
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is a fabricated meme. There’s no record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever saying it, and fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes/PolitiFact) have debunked it. It appears to be a satirical/viral hoax, not a real statement.

claim: Javed Akhtar said "If Narendra Modi becomes the prime minister of India again, then  he and his wife Shabana Azmi and I will leave the country"
response_text: FALSE.  This quote is a fabricated claim that has circulated before. In 2019, when similar posts alleged Javed Akhtar said he (and Shabana Azmi) would leave India if Narendra Modi returned as PM, Akhtar publicly denied it, stating he never made such a remark and that he would not leave the country. Multiple Indian fact-check outlets documented his denial.

claim: Robert E. Lee opposed slavery and secession and has come to symbolize both slavery and secession.
response_text: FALSE.  Lee did write that slavery was a “moral and political evil” and initially opposed secession, but in practice he owned and managed enslaved people, opposed immediate abolition, and chose to lead the Confederate army when Virginia seceded—fighting for a republic founded to preserve slavery. He has indeed come to symbolize the Confederacy, and thus slavery and secession. The first part is misleading enough to make the overall claim false. (Some nuance: he expressed personal misgivings about both but acted in support of the slaveholding, secessionist cause.)

claim: Most research shows that (UW salaries) are a little behind, and (in) some areas we're behind more than others.
response_text: TRUE (with minor uncertainty about which “UW”)  Multiple compensation benchmarking studies (e.g., CUPA-HR, AAUP, and internal market studies) have found that UW salaries generally trail peer medians overall, with variation by unit/discipline—some areas lag more than others while a few are closer to market. This pattern has been reported for UW in recent years and used to justify targeted and across‑the‑board raises.

claim: Drug Abuse Resistance Education has removed cannabis from its list of gateway drugs.
response_text: TRUE.  D.A.R.E. revised its materials in the mid‑2010s (with the “keepin’ it REAL” curriculum) and removed marijuana/cannabis from its website’s “gateway drugs” list, moving away from the “gateway” framing. They still discourage youth cannabis use and oppose legalization, but they no longer label it a gateway drug. Slight caveat: wording can vary across older or local materials.

claim: At least 15 men die every day from prostate cancer in Nigeria.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: WHO/IARC GLOBOCAN estimates for Nigeria indicate several thousand prostate cancer deaths annually—on the order of roughly 8,000–10,000+ per year (e.g., about 8,500 in 2020), which equates to roughly 23–27 deaths per day. That comfortably exceeds “at least 15 per day.” (Exact figures vary by year/source, but all recent estimates are well above 5,475 per year.)

claim: $16 billion in US farmer aid will come from China.
response_text: FALSE.  The $16 billion in farm aid (2019 Market Facilitation Program) was funded through the USDA’s Commodity Credit Corporation, i.e., U.S. Treasury funds. While the administration pointed to tariff revenue from imports of Chinese goods as an offset, tariffs are paid by U.S. importers (often passed to U.S. consumers), not directly by China, and tariff receipts aren’t earmarked to this program. At most, some economic burden may fall on Chinese exporters via lower prices, but the aid money does not “come from China.”

claim: Video shows House Speaker Nancy Pelosi slurred and slowed during a speech, showing that she is drunk.
response_text: FALSE.  A viral 2019 clip of Nancy Pelosi was digitally altered—slowed down (with pitch adjusted) to make her voice sound slurred and her cadence sluggish. Fact-checkers and audio/video analyses confirmed the manipulation, and the original footage shows normal speech. There’s no evidence she was drunk.

claim: Journalist Arfa Khanum Sherwani tweet mentioning the Arabic name for the prophet Moses shows sympathy with the slain terrorist Hizbul commander Zakir Musa in Pakistan.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: - “Musa” is the Arabic name for the prophet Moses. Arfa Khanum Sherwani’s tweet referenced the prophet, not the militant Zakir Musa; fact-checks (e.g., Alt News, BOOM) have debunked the claim that she expressed sympathy for Zakir Musa. - Additionally, Zakir Musa—a former Hizbul commander who later led Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind—was killed in Tral, Jammu & Kashmir, India, not in Pakistan.  Uncertainty: Low.

claim: Kenyan health minister Sicily Kariuki claimed the Kenyan government  increased the health sector budget by more than 30% between 2017 and 2019.
response_text: FALSE  Official budget data show the overall health sector allocation (combining national and county health budgets) rose by less than 30% between FY2017/18 and FY2019/20—roughly in the 20–25% range, depending on which approved/actual figures are used. So “more than 30%” over that period is overstated. (Some uncertainty arises from different classification/baseline choices, but none push the combined sector increase above 30%.)

claim: Chris Jacobs is a "Never-Trumper", i.e. someone who does not support Donald Trump
response_text: FALSE.  Rep. Chris Jacobs (R–NY) was endorsed by Donald Trump in his 2020 special election, generally aligned with Trump in Congress, and voted against Trump’s second impeachment. While he later broke with many Republicans on gun-control measures in 2022, that does not make him a “Never-Trumper.”

claim: None of Kinya's ministers asked to step aside in 2015 has made it to court because the allegations that were made against them did not have any basis.
response_text: FALSE.  At least two of the cabinet secretaries who were asked to step aside in 2015 were charged and appeared in court: Transport CS Michael Kamau (arraigned in June 2015 on abuse-of-office/procurement charges) and Lands CS Charity Ngilu (charged in June 2015 with obstructing EACC investigations over the Karen land case). Some cases were later dropped or quashed on procedural grounds, but they did make it to court, so “none” is incorrect.

claim: Wisconsin's prison population expanded and vacancy rates for correctional officers went from 2.9% to 15.2%" over the last eight years.
response_text: TRUE.  - Wisconsin’s adult prison population did rise modestly over the Walker years (roughly 2011–2018), from about 22,000–23,000 to roughly 23,000+. - State Department of Corrections figures show correctional officer vacancy rates increased from about 2.9% in 2011 to around 15% (about 15.2%) by 2018.  Minor uncertainty: exact percentages vary by month/report, but the trend and approximate figures align with DOC/Legislative Fiscal Bureau data.

claim: Kenyan law says if you are allocated a piece of land, you must develop it within two years. If you do not develop it within two years, it is supposed to revert to government.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - Kenyan law does not impose a universal “develop within two years or it reverts to government” rule. - The two‑year development requirement often appears as a condition in specific government grants/leases or letters of allotment for public land. It is a term of that particular allocation, not a blanket statute. - If such a condition exists and is breached, the government may move to cancel/forfeit the grant or lease, but reversion is not automatic; due process is required under the current legal framework (Land Act 2012/National Land Commission processes). - Freehold/private land has no such general two‑year development duty.

claim: The Jubilee party had pledged in its manifesto to build 57 mega dams to provide more food and water to Kenyans.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In its 2017 manifesto, Kenya’s Jubilee Party pledged to construct 57 large (often reported as “mega”) dams across the country to boost irrigation, food security, and water supply. Media and government documents at the time echoed this 57-dam target. Minor caveat: the manifesto’s wording was “large dams,” not specifically “mega.”

claim: The phrase "high crimes and misdemeanors" is not defined in the American Constitution.
response_text: TRUE.  The U.S. Constitution uses the phrase “high Crimes and Misdemeanors” in Article II, Section 4 as grounds for impeachment but does not define it. Its meaning has been interpreted through historical context, English parliamentary usage, and congressional practice, not by a constitutional definition.

claim: £22 billion was taken out of welfare spending in England between 2010 and 2015.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The coalition’s benefit and tax credit changes from 2010 to 2015 reduced welfare spending by roughly £20–22 billion per year by 2015/16 across Great Britain (and typically excluding the state pension). Welfare policy wasn’t confined to England, so saying “in England” is inaccurate. Figures also vary with what’s counted, adding some uncertainty.

claim: Evil is the result of what happens when man does not have God’s love present in his heart.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: This is a theological opinion, not an empirically testable or universally accepted claim. Many moral frameworks explain “evil” without reference to God, and real-world evidence shows both believers committing harmful acts and nonbelievers acting morally. Uncertainty: depends on one’s religious/philosophical worldview.

claim: Joe Biden improperly used his influence as vice president to get Ukraine to sack its top prosecutor, Viktor Shokin, to benefit his son Hunter Biden in 2016
response_text: FALSE.  - Biden’s push to remove Prosecutor General Viktor Shokin reflected official U.S. policy, shared by the EU, IMF, and Ukrainian anti-corruption advocates, who viewed Shokin as failing to pursue corruption cases. - There is no credible evidence Biden acted to benefit Hunter Biden. At the time, Shokin was not actively investigating Burisma; his office had stalled related cases. Replacing him was expected to increase, not reduce, anti-corruption scrutiny. - Multiple diplomatic officials and contemporaneous records support that the loan-guarantee pressure was tied to broader reform demands, not personal gain.  Uncertainty: low.

claim: The Chinese government put millions of dollars into Biden's family business.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence the Chinese government directly put millions into any “Biden family business.” Some Biden relatives (not Joe Biden) did business with Chinese companies. In 2017, private Chinese firms such as CEFC and affiliates sent payments totaling millions to entities linked to Hunter and James Biden. And Hunter was involved with BHR, a fund that had Chinese state‑owned partners, but that is not the Chinese government paying the Bidens or investing in a “family business.” Claims that China invested $1.5 billion with Hunter have been debunked.

claim: There were 25% cuts to local government spending between 2010 and 2015.
response_text: TRUE (broadly). In England, councils’ overall “spending power” fell by about 26–27% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2015–16 (NAO/DCLG). IFS estimates suggest service spending fell roughly 20–25% over a similar period. The exact figure varies by measure and area, but “around 25%” is a fair summary.

claim: Poland has lowered its retirement age from 67 to 60.
response_text: FALSE.  Poland reversed a planned rise to 67 and, from October 2017, set the statutory retirement age to 60 for women and 65 for men. So it was not lowered to 60 for everyone—only for women (men’s age is 65).

claim: Tariffs are now being paid to the United States by China of 25% on 250 Billion Dollars worth of goods & products. These massive payments go directly to the Treasury of the U.S.
response_text: FALSE.  Tariffs are taxes on imports collected from the U.S. importer of record (often U.S. companies), not paid directly by China. While about $250 billion of Chinese goods were subject to a 25% tariff in 2019 and the revenue is remitted to the U.S. Treasury, the payments are made by U.S. importers (with costs often passed to U.S. consumers), not by China.

claim: The UK’s pension age is going up.
response_text: TRUE.  The UK State Pension age has been rising and is scheduled to keep rising: it reached 66 in 2020, is legislated to increase to 67 between 2026 and 2028, and is set to rise to 68 in the 2040s (no acceleration decided yet). Separately, the minimum private pension access age is also due to rise from 55 to 57 in 2028.

claim: Pakistani man sentenced to death for farting in mosque during Ramadan.
response_text: FALSE.  This story originated on a satirical/fake-news site (often attributed to World News Daily Report) and has no basis in credible reporting. While Pakistan has strict blasphemy laws, there is no record of anyone being sentenced to death for “farting in a mosque,” and fact-checkers have debunked the claim.

claim: You inherit your DNA, temperament, tastes, and emotions from your maternal grandmother
response_text: FALSE.  - You inherit about 50% of your nuclear DNA from each parent and, on average, ~25% from each grandparent—not specifically from the maternal grandmother. The egg that became you existed as a precursor in your mother before birth, but its final genetic makeup was formed later by recombination and is not a copy of your grandmother’s DNA. - The only DNA you reliably inherit strictly through the maternal line is mitochondrial DNA, which is tiny (~0.0005% of your total DNA). It does not determine complex traits like temperament, tastes, or emotions. - Traits such as temperament, preferences, and emotional tendencies are influenced by many genes from both sides of the family and by environment; there’s no evidence they come predominantly from the maternal grandmother. - Rare exceptions (e.g., X‑linked traits, epigenetic effects) can bias specific traits but do not support the blanket claim.

claim: It is illegal for mayors to even bring up gun reform for discussion in Florida, US.
response_text: FALSE.  Florida’s firearm preemption law (Fla. Stat. § 790.33) bars cities and counties from enacting or enforcing local gun regulations and allows fines and lawsuits against local officials who knowingly and willfully do so. But it does not make it illegal to discuss or propose gun reform ideas. The prohibition is on passing or enforcing local measures, not on bringing them up for discussion. (Penalties were upheld by the Florida Supreme Court in 2023.)

claim: US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said, “Waiting hours longer in the waiting room will allow you to make new friends.” This is regarding emergency care waits.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (speeches, interviews, transcripts, or news coverage) of Nancy Pelosi saying this. The line appears to be a fabricated/misattributed quote that has circulated in memes and satire; fact-checkers have found no evidence she ever made such a remark about ER waits.

claim: Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko is preparing for a third round of presidential elections.
response_text: FALSE.  Ukraine’s presidential elections use a two-round system. There is no provision for a third round. Poroshenko won outright in the first round in 2014, and in 2019 he lost to Volodymyr Zelensky in the second-round runoff.

claim: Many companies are leaving China so that they will be more competitive for USA buyers.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is a noticeable “China+1” trend: some firms add capacity in places like Vietnam or Mexico to reduce tariff exposure and lead times for U.S. customers. U.S. import share from China has fallen since 2018 as sourcing diversified. - But most multinationals are not “leaving” China entirely; surveys consistently show only a minority plan full relocations. China remains a core manufacturing base, with companies diversifying rather than exiting. - Motivations are mixed (tariffs, geopolitics, costs, supply‑chain risk), not solely “to be more competitive for USA buyers.”  Uncertainty: “many” and “leaving” are vague, but the broad claim overstates the scale and the single-cause rationale.

claim: King Mswati III, Africa's last absolute monarch who has 14 wives, has ordered men to have at least two marriages or face jail.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This claim originated from a 2019 viral hoax. Eswatini’s government publicly denied that King Mswati III ordered men to marry at least two wives or face jail, and no law or royal decree to that effect exists. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., AFP, BBC, Snopes) debunked the story. While polygamy is legal under customary law in Eswatini and the king is often described as Africa’s last absolute monarch, there was no such mandate.

claim: U.S Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says 'trucks are killing America'.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no reliable record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying “trucks are killing America.” She has criticized oversized vehicles and diesel truck pollution for safety and health impacts, but the specific quote appears to be a misattribution/paraphrase circulating in partisan memes. Uncertain only to the extent that offhand social media comments can be hard to exhaustively search.

claim: NASA spent more than $165 million over 10 years to develop a pen that writes in zero gravity, upside down and in extreme temperatures while the Russians used a pencil instead.
response_text: FALSE.  - The pressurized “space pen” was developed privately by Paul C. Fisher (Fisher Pen Co.), not by NASA. Fisher reportedly spent about $1 million of his own money. - NASA later bought the pens (in 1967) for a few dollars each (about $6 per pen), and the Soviets also adopted them. - Early on, both programs did use pencils, but they were problematic (flammable wood, graphite dust), which is why both switched to the Fisher pen. - NASA did not spend $165 million over 10 years developing a pen.

claim: A change in US federal policy under the Trump administration,was responsible for a newly operational natural gas export terminal.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: U.S. policy and federal approvals allowing liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports were established before Trump. The first lower‑48 LNG exports began at Cheniere’s Sabine Pass in February 2016 (Obama era). Terminals that became operational during Trump’s tenure (e.g., Cove Point in 2018, Corpus Christi and Cameron in 2018–2019) had their key DOE/FERC approvals and construction starts years earlier under Obama. No Trump-era policy change was required to make them operational.

claim: Liquefied natural gas exports in USA were in decline before Trump took office.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: U.S. lower‑48 LNG exports began in February 2016 (Sabine Pass) and ramped up through 2016, then expanded rapidly in 2017. EIA data show exports rising—not declining—immediately before Trump took office. Earlier declines were limited to the small, aging Alaska Kenai LNG exports earlier in the decade, which had largely ceased by 2015.

claim: More children in Scotland leave school without qualifications than 20 years ago.
response_text: FALSE.  Scottish Government “School Leaver Attainment and Destinations” statistics show the share of pupils leaving with no passes at SCQF Level 3 or better has fallen markedly over the last two decades—from roughly 5–7% in the mid‑2000s to around 1–2% in recent years. So fewer, not more, children leave school without qualifications now. (Exact figures vary by year and definition, but the long‑term trend is down.)

claim: Caitlyn Jenner was "pissed" none of her kids wished her a happy mothers day.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Caitlyn Jenner has said she was “pissed” that none of her kids reached out on Father’s Day, not Mother’s Day. She’s repeatedly noted she is still “Dad” to her children. Slight uncertainty on exact wording, but the holiday in the claim is wrong.

claim: There is no reason for the U.S. Consumer to pay the Tariffs, which take effect on China today. This has been proven recently when only 4 points were paid by the U.S., 21 points by China because China subsidizes product to such a large degree.
response_text: FALSE.  Tariffs are legally paid by U.S. importers at the border and are largely passed through to U.S. businesses and consumers via higher prices. Empirical studies of the 2018–2019 U.S. tariffs (e.g., Amiti–Redding–Weinstein; Fajgelbaum et al.) find near-full pass-through to U.S. prices, with only a small share offset by foreign price cuts or currency moves—nowhere close to “4 points by the U.S., 21 by China.”

claim: US president Joe biden said "This idea that the 1994 crime bill generated mass incarceration — it did not generate mass incarceration. If you go back and look, the black caucus supported the bill"
response_text: TRUE.  During the 2019–2020 campaign, Joe Biden repeatedly defended the 1994 crime bill by saying it did not generate mass incarceration and noting that the Congressional Black Caucus supported it. Fact-checks and coverage (e.g., Washington Post Fact Checker, PolitiFact, 2019) quote him saying, “This idea that the 1994 crime bill generated mass incarceration — it did not,” and pointing out that the Black Caucus backed the bill (a majority did, though not unanimously).

claim: Jailing parents was an unintended consequence of a 2010 state truancy law Kamala Harris sponsored.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The 2010 California truancy law (SB 1317), which Kamala Harris’s San Francisco District Attorney’s office sponsored, explicitly created a misdemeanor for parents of chronically truant K–8 students, punishable by fines and up to one year in county jail. While Harris later said jailing wasn’t her goal and San Francisco did not jail parents under it, some parents elsewhere were jailed (e.g., a Kings County mother received a jail sentence in 2011–2012). Because jail was an explicit penalty written into the law, it was not an “unintended consequence.”

claim: Barack Obama did not release his tax returns.
response_text: FALSE.  Barack Obama publicly released many years of his tax returns—starting with 2000–2006 during the 2008 campaign and then annually while in office (e.g., returns for 2009–2015). These were posted by his campaign and on the White House website and are archived publicly.

claim: Gombe state had a debt profile of N110 billion as at December 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  According to Nigeria’s Debt Management Office, Gombe’s debt stock at 31 December 2018 was far below N110bn: about N63–64bn in domestic debt plus roughly $36–38m in external debt (≈N11–13bn at the official rate then), totaling around N75–77bn. Claims near N110bn likely include other liabilities not in the DMO debt stock. Uncertainty: exact naira conversion for the external portion varies with the exchange rate used.

claim: Kirsten Gillibrand in 2005 ran on Medicare for all.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In her first run for Congress (announced in 2005 for the 2006 race), Gillibrand backed expanding coverage through measures like a Medicare buy‑in/public option, not a single‑payer system that replaces private insurance. When she entered the House in 2007, she did not co-sponsor the then “Medicare for All” single‑payer bill (HR 676). Some materials referenced broader access to Medicare, but not the single‑payer Medicare-for-all plan. (Slight uncertainty stems from wording in old campaign literature, but her policy position was not single‑payer.)

claim: The US have lost 500 Billion Dollars a year, for many years, on Crazy Trade with China.
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. goods trade deficit with China has never been $500 billion; it peaked around $419 billion in 2018 (U.S. Census Bureau). In recent years it has been lower. - Including services (where the U.S. runs a surplus) makes the overall deficit smaller, not larger. - Calling a trade deficit “lost” money is also misleading; it reflects the value of imports exceeding exports, not a net loss of dollars.  Sources: U.S. Census Bureau trade data; Bureau of Economic Analysis.

claim: The Covi-19 fatality rate in Scotland is 13.9%, the same as in Italy.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: “Fatality rate” depends on measure and date. Italy’s early-pandemic case fatality rate briefly hovered around ~13–14%, but Scotland’s was not identically 13.9% at that time, and over the pandemic both places’ cumulative fatality rates were far lower than 13.9%. Unless cherry‑picking a specific early snapshot, the claim is inaccurate. (Some uncertainty due to unspecified date/metric.)

claim: England is easing the lockdown.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: This is time-sensitive. As of now (2025), there is no national lockdown in England to “ease”; COVID-19 lockdown restrictions were lifted years ago. If the claim refers to 2020–2021, it was true at certain times then.

claim: Prakash Javadekar, Human Resource and Development Minister of India, said, "Cyclone Fani Was An Indicator Of A Modi Wave."
response_text: FALSE.  No credible report, video, or transcript shows Prakash Javadekar saying “Cyclone Fani was an indicator of a Modi wave.” The line originated from a morphed news graphic that was debunked by Indian fact-checkers at the time; Javadekar did not make such a statement.

claim: China hurts U.S. farmers by not buying their produce.
response_text: FALSE.  China is one of the largest buyers of U.S. farm products (especially soybeans, corn, pork), purchasing tens of billions of dollars’ worth in many years. While reductions in Chinese purchases during trade tensions (e.g., 2018–2019 tariffs) did hurt U.S. farmers, China does buy substantial volumes overall. The blanket claim that China hurts U.S. farmers by not buying their produce is an overgeneralization.

claim: Joe Biden tried to cut Social Security and Medicare for decades. … Now Biden’s promising your benefits to illegal immigrants.
response_text: FALSE.  - “Tried to cut Social Security and Medicare for decades” overstates Biden’s record. Over the years he backed some deficit‑reduction ideas (e.g., temporary spending freezes, and at one point considering a slower cost‑of‑living formula) during bipartisan talks, but he also opposed privatization, supported the 1983 rescue of Social Security, and as president has pushed to protect benefits and lower Medicare drug costs. Fact-checkers have rated the sweeping “decades of cuts” claim misleading.  - “Promising your benefits to illegal immigrants” is wrong. Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for Social Security or Medicare, and Biden has not proposed making them eligible. Recent moves involved allowing DACA recipients (a lawfully present group) to buy ACA marketplace coverage—not Social Security or Medicare.

claim: Ondo state’s monthly IGR has increased to over N1.5 billion.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Recent NBS/state revenue figures put Ondo’s annual IGR in the tens of billions of naira, implying a monthly average well above N1.5bn. Officials have also cited monthly IGR figures in the N2–3bn range in recent years. Thus “over N1.5bn” is a conservative but accurate description. (Exact current month-to-month figures may vary.)

claim: US Suicides have risen by 30% in 15 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: CDC data show U.S. suicide rates rose about 30% from 1999 to 2016 (a 17-year span). Over a 15‑year window, the increase in the age‑adjusted rate is typically closer to roughly 20–28%, depending on the exact years. (Raw counts rose by more than 30%, but public-health comparisons use rates.) Slight uncertainty stems from unspecified years.

claim: US President Donald Trump says four hundred miles of wall are getting built along the US-Mexico border.
response_text: TRUE — Trump repeatedly said roughly 400 miles of wall were being built. By late 2020, CBP reported around 400+ miles of border “wall system” completed (mostly replacing existing barriers rather than new stretches). Uncertainty: wording often mixed future/ongoing construction, but the figure was commonly used by him.

claim: Texas leads in the number of Confederate monuments removed from public land.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple tallies (e.g., Southern Poverty Law Center’s “Whose Heritage?” database) show Virginia—not Texas—has removed the most Confederate monuments from public property, especially after 2020 (Richmond’s Monument Avenue removals among them). Texas has removed several, but it does not lead.

claim: 7,182 students have been killed in U.S. schools since 2012
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The number 7,182 refers to children killed by guns nationwide since 2012, not “in U.S. schools.” Credible trackers of violence on school grounds (e.g., Washington Post, Everytown) show fatalities in the low hundreds since 2012—not thousands—even when counting all people (students and adults) killed on K–12 campuses. The claim conflates total child gun deaths with deaths occurring at schools. Uncertainty: exact tallies vary by dataset, but all are orders of magnitude below 7,182 for on-campus deaths.

claim: Puerto Rico has been given $91 billion by US congress for Hurricane Disaster Relief in March 2019
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In March 2019, Puerto Rico had not been “given $91 billion.” Congress had approved on the order of roughly $41 billion for Puerto Rico’s hurricane recovery by then, and only a fraction had actually been spent. The $91 billion figure cited at the time was a long‑term estimate of potential future federal disaster aid exposure, not money appropriated or delivered.

claim: 70% of Americans in poverty are white.
response_text: FALSE.  U.S. Census data show that non-Hispanic whites make up about 40% of Americans in poverty (e.g., ~15 million of ~38 million in 2022), not 70%. Even counting “white” regardless of Hispanic origin, the share is well below 70%.

claim: Ilhan Omar said If Israel Is So Innocent, Then Why Do They Insist On Being Jews?
response_text: FALSE.  This line is from a satirical article by The Babylon Bee (March 2019), not a real quote from Ilhan Omar. No credible record shows her saying this.

claim: The South African freedom fighter, Solomon Mahlangu, was killed by the man who started the Democratic Alliance (DA), the country's official opposition.
response_text: FALSE.  Solomon Mahlangu was executed by hanging on 6 April 1979 by the apartheid state after a controversial trial. His death warrant was approved under State President B.J. Vorster, with Justice Minister Jimmy Kruger then in office—neither had anything to do with the later Democratic Alliance.  The DA was formed in 2000, chiefly led by Tony Leon’s Democratic Party in alliance with the New National Party and Federal Alliance. None of the DA’s founders “killed” Mahlangu or were responsible for his execution.

claim: In 2010, U.S. Rep Maxine Waters steered $12 million in Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) funds to her husband’s private bank account. She was indicted but served no time
response_text: FALSE.  - OneUnited Bank (not her husband’s private account) received about $12 million in TARP funds in 2008. Rep. Waters had helped arrange a meeting between Treasury and minority-owned banks, including OneUnited, where her husband held stock. - She was not criminally indicted. She faced a House Ethics Committee case in 2010 and was cleared of the main charges in 2012; her chief of staff was reprimanded. No criminal charges or jail time.

claim: If the Congress Party comes to power in India, then it will waive off the entire bill of patients who die in any government or private hospital.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Neither the Congress party’s national manifesto nor official statements include any promise to “waive the entire bill” of patients who die in government or private hospitals. Related policies (e.g., Rajasthan’s Right to Health Act under a Congress-led government) mandate emergency treatment without advance payment and prohibit withholding bodies for non-payment, but they do not cancel hospital bills for deceased patients. Several fact-checks have debunked this viral claim. Uncertainty: none noted in credible official sources.

claim: Nelson Mandela said 'When a woman rejects a man of vision, and accept [sic] a man with television, she will end up watching the man of vision on her own husband's television,” it reads.   “Don't judge a man by his pocket but judge him by his vision. Because where a man is going in life is more important than his present condition.”
response_text: FALSE.  No reliable source or Mandela speech/writing contains this quote. It’s absent from the Nelson Mandela Foundation’s archives and reputable collections of his quotations. The phrasing is uncharacteristic of Mandela and appears to be a modern social‑media aphorism often misattributed (sometimes to figures like Robert Mugabe or Myles Munroe).

claim: US Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke ordered a special flag to be raised whenever he entered the building.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reports (e.g., Washington Post, CNN, The Hill, Oct. 2017) confirmed that under Ryan Zinke the Interior Department began raising the department’s secretarial flag over headquarters to signal he was in the building—a practice he instituted, citing Navy tradition. It does not appear to have been a routine practice under prior secretaries.

claim: Nigeria has the highest number of out-of-school children in sub-Saharan Africa.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple authoritative sources (UNESCO/UNICEF) consistently report that Nigeria has the largest number of out‑of‑school children—often cited as over 10 million for primary age and about 18.5 million for ages 5–14—more than any other country in sub‑Saharan Africa (and globally). Figures vary by age group and methodology, but the ranking is consistent.

claim: Boy died due to birthday bumps
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple verified news reports (e.g., in India) have documented boys/students dying after “birthday bumps” or birthday bashing by peers, typically from internal injuries such as a ruptured spleen. Exact incident not specified here, but the phenomenon has been reported. Uncertainty: no single case is identified in the claim.

claim: More than 10.2 million children are out of school in Nigeria.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple authoritative estimates put Nigeria’s out‑of‑school children well above 10.2 million. UNICEF has reported around 18.5 million (2022), and earlier figures from UNICEF/UNESCO and Nigeria’s UBEC commonly ranged from about 10.5 to 13.2 million, depending on definitions and year. Hence “more than 10.2 million” is supported. (Exact totals vary by source and methodology.)

claim: William Barr, the US Attorney General's testimony lacked context in investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential campaign.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Special Counsel Robert Mueller wrote to William Barr on March 27, 2019 that Barr’s March 24 summary “did not fully capture the context, nature, and substance” of the Mueller Report. Barr’s subsequent testimony defending that summary and his characterizations was widely criticized for omitting key context from the report’s findings. Slight uncertainty: Mueller’s explicit “lacked context” critique targeted Barr’s summary letter, not the testimony itself, though the criticism carried into evaluations of his testimony.

claim: A Facebook meme claims  five House Republicans voted with Democrats to create a “firearms registry.”
response_text: FALSE.  A handful of House Republicans did side with Democrats on a vote involving an ATF rule, but that vote did not create a firearm registry. It was about overturning an ATF rule clarifying who must conduct background checks; keeping the rule in place is not a registry. Federal law prohibits a federal gun registry, and the ATF does not maintain one. The meme mischaracterizes the vote’s effect.

claim: Salman Rushdie said that 99% of Muslims are terrorists by thought.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible source—speech, interview, book, or article—where Salman Rushdie said “99% of Muslims are terrorists by thought.” The line is a misattributed social‑media hoax that fact‑checkers have debunked. Rushdie has criticized Islamism and defended free expression, but he has not made such a sweeping claim about Muslims.

claim: Joe Biden was one of the first to introduce a climate change bill to the US Houses of Congress.
response_text: TRUE.  As a senator in 1986–1987, Joe Biden introduced the Global Climate Protection Act, an early bill focused explicitly on global warming; its provisions were enacted in 1987 as Title XI of Public Law 100-204. While not the first climate-related law (e.g., the 1978 National Climate Program Act predates it), Biden’s measure is widely cited as among the first climate change bills in Congress.

claim: Singapore's prime minister has one of the highest salaries of any world leader.
response_text: TRUE.  Singapore pegs ministers’ pay to top private-sector benchmarks. The prime minister’s annual package has been widely reported at around S$2.2 million (roughly US$1.6–1.8 million), varying with bonuses and periodic reviews. That is far above most counterparts (e.g., the U.S. president earns US$400,000), making it among the highest—often cited as the highest—of any head of government.

claim: US  Attorney General William P. Barr mischaracterized special counsel Robert Mueller's remarks about his office's decision not to reach a determination about  whether President Donald Trump had committed obstruction of justice. This issue referred to Russia's attempts to damage Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign.
response_text: TRUE.  - Barr said Mueller’s decision not to reach an obstruction conclusion was not based on the Office of Legal Counsel opinion that a sitting president cannot be indicted. Mueller’s report and his May 29, 2019 public statement made clear the OLC policy did factor in—“charging the President with a crime was not an option we could consider.” Thus Barr mischaracterized Mueller’s explanation. - The obstruction question arose from the investigation into Russian interference in 2016, which included efforts that harmed Hillary Clinton’s campaign (social media operations and hacking/leaks).

claim: Kenyans with old generation passports will still be issued with U.S visas.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The U.S. issues visas only in valid passports. Kenya has phased out the old-generation (non‑e) passports, making them invalid for international travel, so they are not acceptable for new U.S. visas. Note: Previously, while still valid, the U.S. accepted old passports; existing U.S. visas in an old passport remain usable if carried with a new e‑passport. (Slight uncertainty on Kenya’s final cutoff date, but old-generation passports are no longer valid.)

claim: A million Australians are doing two jobs.
response_text: TRUE.  ABS Labour Account data show the number of multiple job holders has hovered around one million in recent years, reaching roughly 0.95–1.05 million depending on the quarter (record highs around 2023–2024). The exact figure fluctuates, but “a million” is a reasonable approximation.

claim: The Mortality Rate for Road Accidents Drops in Russia.
response_text: TRUE.  Russian official stats and international datasets show a sustained decline in road-traffic mortality over the past decade, with deaths falling markedly from the 2000s through the 2010s and continuing to drop in recent years (reports indicate record lows around 2023). Minor uncertainty: exact rates vary by source and year, but the downward trend is consistent.

claim: A million Australians are underemployed.
response_text: TRUE.  ABS Labour Force data typically shows roughly 0.9–1.3 million Australians underemployed in recent years (spiking higher in 2020). So “a million” is a reasonable rounded figure, though the exact number varies month to month.

claim: US president claims that the $2 Trillion tax cut did not benefit most people as it all went to the folks at the top and corporations that pay no taxes.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (often rounded to ~$2 trillion over a decade) delivered tax reductions across the income distribution; analyses by the Tax Policy Center and Joint Committee on Taxation found that a clear majority of households received a tax cut in 2018 (with larger dollar gains skewed to higher earners). The benefits did not “all” go to the top. Likewise, while some profitable corporations paid zero federal income tax in certain years, many did pay taxes—the cut wasn’t limited to “corporations that pay no taxes.”

claim: IN 2017 61 PERCENT OF DRUG OVERDOSE DEATHS IN THE US STATE OF DELAWARE INVOLVE THE DRUG FENTANYL
response_text: TRUE.  Delaware health/forensic officials reported that in 2017 roughly 61% of the state’s drug overdose deaths involved fentanyl. This figure was cited in state reports and local news coverage summarizing 2017 overdose fatalities.

claim: Viral image quotes Joe Biden as saying the Germans Bombed Pearl Harbour.
response_text: FALSE.  A meme circulated with that quote, but it’s fabricated. There’s no record of Joe Biden saying “The Germans bombed Pearl Harbor.” Fact-checkers found the image misattributes a line from the film Animal House, and historically Pearl Harbor was attacked by Japan, not Germany.

claim: Photo shows Kanhaiya Kumar pulling out of election due to health reasons, appeals to vote for RJDs Tanvir Hasan
response_text: FALSE.  A doctored image/letter went viral during the 2019 Begusarai election claiming Kanhaiya Kumar had withdrawn due to health issues and urged votes for RJD’s Tanveer Hasan. Fact-checks showed it was fake; Kanhaiya Kumar denied it and continued contesting the election.

claim: Sadhvi Pragya said Manohar Parrikar died of cancer because he allowed the consumption of beef in Goa
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks (e.g., Alt News, BOOM) found no credible source—no video, speech, or news report—of Pragya Singh Thakur saying Manohar Parrikar died of cancer because he allowed beef in Goa. The quote circulated as a fabricated social media graphic. She made other controversial statements in 2019, but not this one.

claim: Fee-paying schools save the UK taxpayer £20 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  Best estimates put the annual “saving” at around £4–5 billion, not £20 billion. For example, Oxford Economics (for the Independent Schools Council) estimated c.£4.4bn a year based on the number of pupils in independent schools and average state per‑pupil funding. Net savings would be lower once tax breaks (e.g., business rates relief) are considered. The £20bn figure only arises if you (misleadingly) cumulate several years or conflate with broader GDP contributions, not as a yearly saving. Uncertainty: exact amounts vary with assumptions, but nowhere near £20bn per year.

claim: Drinking Tequila helps to loose weight.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There’s no good evidence that tequila promotes weight loss. The “agavins” from agave that showed weight-related benefits in animal studies don’t survive the distillation process, so they aren’t in tequila. Tequila is alcohol (≈7 kcal/g), which can add calories, reduce fat oxidation, increase appetite, and disrupt sleep—factors that tend to hinder weight loss. Any effect on body weight depends on overall energy balance, not a specific liquor. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Donald Trump said that there were very fine people on both sides of the violent protests in 2017, at Charlottesville.
response_text: TRUE.  In an Aug. 15, 2017 press conference about Charlottesville, Trump said, “you also had people that were very fine people on both sides.” He then added, “I’m not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists because they should be condemned totally.” The events were violent, and he asserted there were “very fine people” among both sides of the broader protest, while excluding white supremacists.

claim: A Facebook post claims that Joe Biden has run for President 3 times (1984, 1988, and 2008).
response_text: FALSE. Biden ran for president in 1988 and 2008 (and later in 2020), but he did not run in 1984. He reportedly considered a 1984 bid but never entered the race.

claim: A CIA survey, published by the BBC, has predicted the NDA's defeat in the ongoing Lok Sabha polls
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The CIA does not publish public election surveys, and there is no record of any CIA poll on India’s Lok Sabha elections. The BBC has not published such a survey. Multiple fact-checks have debunked viral posts claiming a “CIA survey” predicting the NDA’s defeat.

claim: The Russian government has no desire to create problems for the new Ukrainian government but to tolerate a situation in which people living in the territory of these Donetsk and Luhansk republics are generally deprived of any civil rights. This is already crossing the line from the point of view of human rights.
response_text: TRUE. Vladimir Putin said this in April 2019, shortly after Volodymyr Zelensky’s election, when defending Russia’s move to fast‑track Russian passports for residents of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk “people’s republics.” He stated Russia had no desire to create problems for the new Ukrainian government but could not tolerate residents there being deprived of civil rights, calling it a human-rights issue.

claim: There is more bacteria found in a mans beard than in a dogs fur.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The viral claim stems from a small 2019 Swiss study (18 bearded men vs. 30 dogs) that found higher average bacterial counts on those men’s beards than on those dogs’ fur. But the sample was small and non-representative, results depend on location, hygiene, and measurement, and most bacteria found aren’t harmful. There’s no robust evidence that men’s beards generally harbor more bacteria than dogs’ fur. At best, it’s an overgeneralization from a limited study.

claim: You've got millions of families paying 40, 50, 60% of their limited incomes to put a roof over their heads
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence: In the U.S., Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies reports that in 2022 about 22.4 million renter households were cost-burdened (paying >30% of income), including roughly 12.1 million severely burdened renters paying more than 50%. Many of these are low-income households, and a substantial subset pay 60% or more. Adding burdened homeowners increases the totals further.   Note: “Families” is colloquial here; figures are typically reported for “households,” but the claim’s substance holds.

claim: Donald Trump says In the ‘old days’ if you were president and you had a good economy, you were basically immune from criticism
response_text: TRUE  Trump has repeatedly argued that “in the old days” a president with a strong economy would face little or no criticism, often saying such a president would have very high approval ratings and be largely “immune” from attacks, especially from the media. Exact wording varies by appearance, but the sentiment matches his public remarks. (Minor uncertainty on the precise phrasing.)

claim: North Carolina has banned and criminalized Islamic Sharia Law
response_text: FALSE.  North Carolina did not ban or criminalize Sharia. In 2013 it passed a “foreign law” statute that prevents state courts from applying any foreign or religious law if it conflicts with federal or state constitutional rights (often aimed at family law). It doesn’t mention Sharia specifically, and it doesn’t make practicing Islamic religious norms a crime.

claim: The enumeration clause of the US Constitution speaks to the count of every individual and not just Americans, not just citizens. It’s everyone."
response_text: TRUE.  Article I, Section 2 and the 14th Amendment require apportionment based on the “whole number of persons,” not “citizens.” By law and longstanding practice, the census counts all usual residents regardless of citizenship or legal status (including noncitizens and undocumented people). Historically, “Indians not taxed” were excluded, a now‑moot exception. Note: the count is of usual residents, not temporary visitors.

claim: Ken Kercheval is not dead at 83
response_text: FALSE. Ken Kercheval, the actor best known for “Dallas,” died on April 21, 2019 at age 83.

claim: In my own state of Vermont, from the very first days of our state's history, what our Constitution says is that everybody can vote. That is true. So people in jail can vote."
response_text: TRUE  - Vermont is one of two states (with Maine) that have long allowed people to vote while incarcerated; today, Vermonters in jail or prison can vote, typically by absentee ballot. - The phrasing “everybody can vote” is overstated—historically Vermont limited voting to men and, like today, has age, citizenship, and residency requirements—but with respect to felony/incarceration, Vermont’s constitution has not disenfranchised prisoners since the state’s early days.

claim: 74% of the people in Texas are crammed into 4% of the land.
response_text: FALSE.  - The four largest Texas metros (DFW, Houston, San Antonio, Austin) together hold about two-thirds of Texans (~66–67%), not 74%, and their combined county land areas are well over 4% of the state. - If you use Census “urban areas,” the share of Texans living there is higher (about 80%+), but then the statement “74% in 4% of land” understates the population share.  So no common, consistent geographic definition supports “74% of Texans in 4% of the land.” Uncertainty: exact percentages vary by definition, but none align with 74%/4%.

claim: India's Congress President Rahul Gandhi has apologised to India's Supreme Court for saying Chowkidar Chor Hai  in relation to the Rafale aircraft deal.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2019, Rahul Gandhi filed an affidavit tendering an unconditional apology to India’s Supreme Court for wrongly attributing his “chowkidar chor hai” remark (made in the context of the Rafale deal) to the Court. The SC later closed the contempt proceedings after accepting his apology.

claim: Elizabeth Warren says she warned about the financial crisis before it happened
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Years before the 2008 crash, Warren publicly warned about dangerous mortgage lending and a looming housing/credit meltdown. Examples include her 2003 book The Two-Income Trap (warning of a housing bubble and rising foreclosures) and her 2007 writings and testimony advocating a financial product safety regulator amid growing risks. Independent fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact) have rated her claim as true. (She did not predict precise timing, but she clearly warned of the crisis conditions in advance.)

claim: Pragya Singh Thakur, better known as Sadhvi Pragya, (Indian politician and Member of Parliament), was 4 years old when the Babri Mosque was demolished.
response_text: FALSE.  Babri Masjid was demolished on 6 December 1992. Pragya Singh Thakur (Sadhvi Pragya) was born in 1970 (she reported being 48–49 in 2019), making her about 22 in 1992, not 4.

claim: An image shows litter left by Extinction Rebellion environmental protestors in Hyde Park.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely shared litter photos from Hyde Park were from the annual 4/20 cannabis event on 20 April 2019, not from Extinction Rebellion protests. The Royal Parks confirmed this and published matching images. XR’s main London sites were Marble Arch and nearby streets, and they organized clean‑ups at their protest areas.

claim: Ilhan Omar tweeted “they reap what they sow” in response to the fire at Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a fabricated screenshot that circulated after the 2019 Notre Dame fire. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) found no such tweet from Rep. Ilhan Omar; instead, she posted messages expressing sympathy for those affected by the fire.

claim: With repeated use of vaccines, cell-mediated immunity weakens, encouraging viral mutations, and future infections of the cells.
response_text: FALSE.  - Vaccines generally strengthen, not weaken, cell‑mediated immunity; boosters recall and maintain T‑cell memory. T‑cell “exhaustion” occurs with chronic ongoing antigen exposure (e.g., persistent infection), not the brief exposure from vaccination. - Viral mutations arise during viral replication. By reducing infections and viral load, vaccination decreases opportunities for mutations. While immune pressure can influence which variants spread, vaccines do not “encourage” mutations. - There’s no evidence vaccination increases future susceptibility to infection; it lowers risk (especially of severe disease). Any waning over time reflects declining antibody levels or viral evolution, not vaccine‑induced weakening of immunity.  Note: Rare pathogen‑specific exceptions in animals (e.g., Marek’s disease in chickens) are not generalizable to human vaccines.

claim: The South African Government have recently built 4 million houses.
response_text: FALSE.  Government data show roughly 3 to 3.5 million houses have been built since 1994. The oft-cited “over 4 million” refers to “housing opportunities” (houses plus serviced sites/subsidies), not houses alone, and it’s a cumulative figure over decades—not “recent.” (Exact totals vary by report, but houses built are well below 4 million.)

claim: Ramaphosa promised to build 1 million in Alexandra.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There’s no record of Ramaphosa promising to build 1 million houses in Alexandra. The “1 million” figure is from broader housing pledges (e.g., the ANC’s 1994 national pledge to build 1 million houses in five years, and later provincial targets for “housing opportunities” across Gauteng), not a promise specific to Alexandra. Plans for Alexandra’s renewal envisaged far smaller numbers (tens of thousands), not anything near 1 million. Uncertainty: none.

claim: There were Muslim ties to the Notre Dame fire.
response_text: FALSE.  Official investigations by French authorities found no evidence of arson or terrorism in the 2019 Notre-Dame fire. Prosecutors concluded it was an accidental blaze, most likely caused by an electrical fault or a discarded cigarette during renovation work. No credible link to Muslims or Islamist groups was established. Uncertainty: the exact ignition source wasn’t pinpointed, but the cause was ruled accidental.

claim: Bumblebee has officially been added to the ever-growing list of endangered species
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: “Bumblebee” isn’t a single species. While some bumblebee species have been officially listed as endangered (e.g., the rusty patched bumble bee in the U.S., and several species in California), bumblebees as a whole have not been added to an endangered species list.

claim: The War Powers Act has been invoked for the first time.
response_text: FALSE.  The War Powers Resolution (often called the War Powers Act) has been invoked many times since 1973—presidents have repeatedly filed reports “consistent with” it for military actions. While Congress’s 2019 Yemen measure was the first time both chambers passed a War Powers resolution to end U.S. involvement in a conflict, the law itself was not being invoked for the first time.

claim: The United States has "three families owning more wealth than the bottom half of the American society.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The bottom 50% of U.S. households hold on the order of trillions of dollars in net worth (per Federal Reserve distributional data), far exceeding the combined wealth of the three richest U.S. families (e.g., Walton, Koch, Mars), which is in the hundreds of billions. A frequently cited line about “three” referred to three individuals and relied on a narrower dataset (Credit Suisse) that has been criticized; even then, it did not apply to families. Uncertainty: figures vary by source and date, but no reputable estimates show three families exceeding the bottom half.

claim: The United States has three families owning more wealth than the bottom half of the American society.
response_text: FALSE.  - Today the bottom 50% of U.S. households collectively hold trillions of dollars in net worth (roughly $3–4+ trillion per Federal Reserve data in 2023–2024). - The combined wealth of the three richest U.S. dynastic families (commonly cited: Walton, Koch, Mars) is on the order of a few hundred billion dollars (roughly $450–600 billion by recent Forbes estimates), far below the bottom half’s total. - Note: A similar claim about “three individuals” briefly held using 2016–2017 data, but it does not hold now—and the “three families” wording misstates that earlier finding.

claim: Bernie Sanders' Medicare-for-all will save Americans money.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: Whether Medicare-for-All would “save Americans money” is uncertain and depends on assumptions about provider payment cuts, drug prices, utilization, and the tax financing used. Independent analyses reach different conclusions: Urban Institute estimates total national health spending would rise under a Sanders-style plan, while the Mercatus study finds slight savings only under optimistic assumptions its author deems unlikely. The CBO likewise says overall spending could be lower or higher depending on design. And while many households might pay less in premiums/out-of-pocket, others (especially higher earners) could pay more in taxes. So a blanket “will save Americans money” claim overstates what is not assured.

claim: Amazon, owned by the wealthiest person in this country, paid zero in federal taxes.
response_text: FALSE.  - Amazon is a publicly traded company, not “owned” by a single person (though Jeff Bezos was the largest shareholder and, at times, the wealthiest American). - While Amazon paid zero (and even received refunds) in U.S. federal corporate income tax in some years (notably 2017–2018), it did not pay “zero in federal taxes” overall; it pays payroll taxes, customs duties, etc., and has paid federal income tax in other years.  Note: If the claim meant “zero federal corporate income tax in a specific year (e.g., 2018),” that narrower statement would be accurate.

claim: Pat Robertson claimed that the Notre Dame cathedral fire on April 2019 was the result of "Hell bubbling over with burning homosexuals"
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (transcripts, video, or reputable reporting) of Pat Robertson saying Notre Dame burned because “Hell [was] bubbling over with burning homosexuals.” The quote appears to be a fabricated meme; fact-checkers have debunked similar attributions. Robertson made many controversial statements over the years, but not this one regarding the April 2019 Notre Dame fire.

claim: Unemployment in Germany is 3.1, percent, In Japan it's 2.8 percent, In the U.K., it's a hair higher than us.
response_text: TRUE  Using internationally comparable (ILO/OECD/Eurostat “harmonized”) unemployment rates in recent years: - Germany has been about 3.0–3.2% (≈3.1%). - Japan about 2.6–2.8% (≈2.8%). - The U.K. has generally been a bit above the U.S. (e.g., ~4.2–4.6% vs U.S. ~3.7–4.1%).  Note: Figures vary by month and definition; Germany’s national measure is higher, but on harmonized rates the statement is accurate.

claim: Unemployment in Germany is 3.1%. In Japan it's 2.8%. In the UK, it's a hair higher than the US.
response_text: TRUE  - Using OECD/ILO harmonized unemployment rates in 2023–2024, Germany was about 3.1% and Japan about 2.7–2.8%. - Over the same period, the UK’s unemployment rate (≈4.1–4.4%) was slightly higher than the U.S. (≈3.8–4.1%).  Note: Exact figures vary by month and by measurement method (national vs harmonized), so these are approximate.

claim: Barack Obama wrote "If the political winds should shift, I will side with the muslims" in his book titled "Audacity of Hope".
response_text: FALSE.  Obama did not write that. In The Audacity of Hope he wrote, referring to Arab and Pakistani Americans after 9/11: “I will stand with them should the political winds shift in an ugly direction.” The misquote replaces “them” (Arab and Pakistani Americans) with “the Muslims” and changes “stand with” to “side with,” altering both wording and context (civil liberties for U.S. minorities).

claim: Canadian Prime Minister begs Nigerian President for one million immigrants
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Canada’s prime minister asked Nigeria’s president for “one million” immigrants. Canada’s immigration plans set overall annual targets (roughly 465k–500k permanent residents in recent years) across all countries, not quotas from a single nation, and there’s no record of such a request to Nigeria. Similar viral claims have been repeatedly debunked.

claim: Republicans rushed to repeal law preventing the mentally ill from buying guns in 2017
response_text: FALSE.  In 2017, Republicans (with a few Democrats) used the Congressional Review Act to overturn an Obama-era Social Security Administration regulation—not a law—finalized in late 2016. That rule would have reported certain Social Security disability beneficiaries who required a representative payee due to mental impairments to the federal background-check system, barring them from gun purchases. Repealing it did not legalize gun purchases for all “mentally ill” people; the longstanding federal prohibition on those adjudicated as mentally defective or committed to mental institutions remained in place. The claim overstates both the scope and nature of what was repealed.

claim: Barkha Dutt, an Indian television journalist and author, called India's Bharatiya Janata Party anti-Muslim.
