response_text: FALSE  I can’t find a reliable, verifiable instance where Barkha Dutt explicitly called the Bharatiya Janata Party “anti-Muslim.” She has criticized majoritarian politics and policies she sees as targeting Muslims, but attributing that exact characterization to her lacks clear sourcing. Uncertain, but no definitive quote or citation found.

claim: Bill to expand access to college tuition for military families blocked by New York Democrats after they approved aid for illegal immigrants.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In April 2019, New York Senate Democrats voted to block (table as non-germane) a Republican amendment that would have expanded state college-tuition benefits for Gold Star/military families. Earlier that year they had passed the Jose Peralta DREAM Act, which opened state financial aid to undocumented students. Note: the blocked measure was an amendment rather than a standalone bill, and the DREAM Act provides access to aid rather than automatic “free college.”

claim: Kenya’s deputy president Ruto said ‘We put it in our manifesto, to construct 57 mega dams…”
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In February 2019, amid debate over the Arror and Kimwarer dam projects, then–Deputy President William Ruto publicly said the Jubilee administration had put in its manifesto a plan “to construct 57 mega dams.” Kenyan media reported the remark at the time as he defended advance payments for dam projects. (Wording may vary slightly by outlet, but the substance is the same.)

claim: “In health care, we have to deal with the fact that if you’re a black woman in America today — in New York City, you’re 12 times more likely to die in childbirth, four times more likely nationwide.
response_text: FALSE  - The disparity is real, but the numbers are off. Nationally, Black women are about 2.5–3 times (not 4 times) more likely than white women to die from pregnancy‑related causes, per recent CDC data. - In New York City, an often‑cited 12× figure comes from older data (early 2000s). More recent NYC health department reports show a large gap but closer to about 8–9×, not 12×. - Also, “die in childbirth” is shorthand; the standard measure is pregnancy‑related mortality (during pregnancy to up to one year postpartum).

claim: None of the ministers the Kenyan Government asked to step aside in 2015 went to court because the allegations that were made against them did not have any basis.
response_text: FALSE.  Several of the Cabinet Secretaries asked to step aside in 2015 went to court. For example, suspended Transport CS Michael Kamau filed a petition and obtained High Court orders staying his prosecution; the High Court later quashed the charges on the ground that the EACC lacked a lawful quorum when recommending them. Suspended CSs Charity Ngilu and Kazungu Kambi also filed court challenges over the EACC process and recommendations. Hence it is incorrect to say none went to court.

claim: 85% of Kenya is arid and semi-arid.
response_text: TRUE (approximately). Estimates from Kenyan government and UN sources commonly state that about 80–89% of Kenya’s land area is arid and semi‑arid; thus 85% falls within the cited range. Note: figures vary by definition and source.

claim: Special Trains from Hyderabad were provided to facilitate people going to Andhra Pradesh for the AP Elections, in 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple news reports in April 2019 said South Central Railway ran special trains from Hyderabad/Secunderabad to various Andhra Pradesh destinations (e.g., Vijayawada, Kakinada Town, Visakhapatnam, etc.) around April 10–12 to clear the extra rush of people traveling to vote in the April 11 AP Assembly/LS elections.

claim: BBC Poll Shows BJP Win Between 323 To 380 Seats In The 2019 General Elections
response_text: FALSE.  BBC did not conduct any opinion or exit poll for the 2019 Indian general elections. The “BBC poll” claims predicting 323–380 seats for BJP were viral fabrications; BBC publicly clarified it had run no such survey.

claim: The Kenyan Government put  the construction of 57 large scale dams in their 2017 manifesto.
response_text: FALSE.  The “57 dams” target is from the government’s post‑election National Water Harvesting and Storage Programme (2018–2022) and related announcements, not from the 2017 Jubilee Party manifesto. The manifesto pledged to expand water storage and build dams but did not specify the number 57. (Small uncertainty: different summaries circulate, but credible copies of the 2017 manifesto don’t list “57”).

claim: If you’re a black woman in America today — in New York City, you’re 12 times more likely to die in childbirth compared to a White woman and four times more likely nationwide.
response_text: FALSE.  - Nationwide: CDC data show Black women are about 2.5–3 times more likely than White women to die from pregnancy‑related causes in recent years (not 4x). - New York City: The “12 times” figure comes from older data (circa 2006–2010). More recent NYC analyses put the disparity closer to about 8–9 times.   So the claim overstates the national gap and uses an outdated NYC figure. (Some uncertainty due to differing time frames and definitions.)

claim: The Kenyan law states that if you are allocated a piece of land you must develop it within two years or it reverts to the government.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - There is no blanket Kenyan statute that automatically makes “allocated” land revert to the government if it is not developed within two years. - Many government leasehold grants (especially urban plots allocated by the state/county) include a special condition to develop within a set period—often 24 months—contained in the letter of allotment or lease. Breach can lead to forfeiture/re-entry, but only through due process (notice and enforcement under the Land Act), not automatic reversion. - Freehold or privately acquired land generally has no such statutory two-year development requirement.  Note: The 24‑month condition is common in specific leases/allocations, but it is not a universal rule in Kenyan law.

claim: None of the allegations made against Kenyan government ministers in 2015 made it to court.
response_text: FALSE.  Several 2015 allegations against Kenyan cabinet secretaries led to court cases. For example, Transport CS Michael Kamau was charged in June 2015 with abuse of office over a road tender, and Lands CS Charity Ngilu was charged the same month with obstructing EACC investigations (Karen land case). These matters were filed and heard in court, even if some were later quashed or did not result in convictions.

claim: Kenya’s deputy president, Ruto, asked six ministers in the last term to step aside.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2015 it was President Uhuru Kenyatta—not Deputy President William Ruto—who directed cabinet secretaries named in an anti-corruption report to step aside. Five CSs did so (Felix Koskei, Davis Chirchir, Michael Kamau, Charity Ngilu, Kazungu Kambi), not six. Ruto, as deputy president, had no authority to order ministers to step aside.

claim: Kenya’s deputy president Ruto said “None of [the dropped ministers] even made it to court because the allegations that were made [against them] did not have any basis.”
response_text: FALSE.  At least two of the cabinet secretaries who were “dropped” in the 2015 graft purge were arraigned in court: Charity Ngilu (then Lands CS) was charged in 2015 over the Karen land case, and Michael Kamau (then Transport CS) was charged with abuse of office in 2015 (his case was later quashed then revived in 2018). So it’s not true that “none … even made it to court.”

claim: Like every budget passed by the Senate since Dan Patrick has been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Texas’ constitutional spending limit (Article VIII, Section 22) caps growth in appropriations from state tax revenue not dedicated by the constitution. The Legislative Budget Board sets the growth rate each biennium. Since Dan Patrick became lieutenant governor (2015), the Senate’s general appropriations bills (SB 1 for 2016–17, 2018–19, 2020–21, 2022–23, and 2024–25) have been written to stay under that constitutional cap, and no record vote to exceed the cap was taken for these budgets. Some large spending items (e.g., separate property‑tax relief measures) have been handled outside the main budget or structured to avoid breaching the cap, but SB 1 itself has remained within the constitutional limit.

claim: Housing costs are crushing the middle class. Over 11 million Americans are spending more than half of their income on housing.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: The standard measure of “severely cost-burdened” is spending over 50% of income on housing. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies, using ACS data, reports about 12 million renter households were severely cost-burdened in 2022, and the total across renters and owners is even higher. That means well over 11 million people. Note: figures are typically reported for households, and “middle class” is subjective.

claim: Hyderabad Police seized Rs 8 crore cash withdrawn from BJP’s bank account.
response_text: FALSE.  Hyderabad police did seize around Rs 8 crore in cash during election-time checks, but they officially clarified that the money was not withdrawn from the BJP’s bank account and had no established link to any political party. The viral claim misattributed the source of the seized cash. (Some uncertainty on the exact date of the seizure, but police clarification denying a BJP account link is clear.)

claim: William Shakespeare wrote “I always feel happy, you know why? Because I don’t expect anything from anyone. Expectations always hurt. Life is short, so love your life, be happy. And keep smiling. Just live for yourself and before you speak, listen. Before you write, think. Before you spend, earn. Before you pray, forgive. Before you hurt, feel. Before you quit, try. Before you die, live.”
response_text: FALSE.  This passage is a modern inspirational quote, not found in Shakespeare’s works. Its language (“I always feel happy…,” “keep smiling,” “expectations always hurt”) is anachronistic for Early Modern English. The “Before you speak, listen… Before you die, live” sequence closely mirrors a well-known aphorism by 20th‑century writer William Arthur Ward, not Shakespeare.

claim: Russian President Vladimir Putin has said more than once that for settling the conflict in Donbass the most important thing is not dialogue with Moscow, because Moscow is not a party to this conflict. It is an intra-Ukrainian conflict and it is up to the Ukrainians to settle it, if they talk to each other."
response_text: TRUE.  Putin has repeatedly said Russia is not a party to the Donbass conflict and that Kyiv must negotiate directly with representatives of Donetsk and Luhansk, framing it as an “intra‑Ukrainian” issue. Examples include: - Paris Normandy-format press conference (Dec 10, 2019): He said Russia is not a party to the conflict and stressed the need for direct Kyiv–Donetsk/Luhansk dialogue (Kremlin.ru transcript). - Annual press conferences (e.g., Dec 19, 2019; earlier years as well): He reiterated that settlement requires Ukraine to talk with Donbass representatives and that Moscow is not the interlocutor (Kremlin.ru; widely reported by Reuters/TASS).

claim: The 2008 United States election was the first election in which voters of color comprised over 25 percent of the electorate, and that number is going up.
response_text: TRUE.  - Standard measures (non-Hispanic white vs. all others) show nonwhite voters were about 26% of the 2008 electorate—up from roughly 23% in 2004 and ~20% in 2000—making 2008 the first time above 25%. - The share has continued to rise: about 28% in 2012, ~29% in 2016, and roughly one-third by 2020 (estimates vary by source/exits vs. CPS).  Note: Exact percentages differ slightly by dataset, but all major sources show 2008 as the first year crossing 25% and an upward trend thereafter.

claim: African-American women inmates in Caifornia prisons are sterilized to cut welfare costs in California.
response_text: FALSE.  Investigations found that about 150 women in California prisons were sterilized (2005–2013), often without proper consent, but this was not an official policy to cut welfare costs nor targeted solely at African-American women. A prison doctor controversially cited “welfare” savings as a personal justification, but the state later banned sterilizations for birth control in prisons (SB 1135, 2014).

claim: NATO Caused the Crisis in Libya with terrorism, weapons smuggling and illegal immigration beginning after the 2011 NATO intervention.
response_text: FALSE.  - Terrorism, weapons smuggling, and irregular migration involving Libya did not begin after 2011. Examples: Libya’s state-sponsored terrorism (e.g., Lockerbie, 1988), the Libyan Islamic Fighting Group in the 1990s, Gaddafi-era arms smuggling (including to the IRA), and pre-2011 irregular migration routes (e.g., Italy–Libya migration deals in 2008–2009) all predate NATO’s intervention. - The 2011 UN-authorized NATO operation helped topple Gaddafi and was followed by state collapse, which intensified terrorism, arms proliferation, and smuggling via Libya. But attributing the crisis and these phenomena solely to NATO is an oversimplification; internal Libyan dynamics and regional actors were major drivers. - Thus, while the post-2011 instability worsened these problems, they did not start then, and NATO did not “cause” them in the asserted sense. Uncertainty: degree of causal contribution is debated, but the claim’s absolutes are inaccurate.

claim: Prime Minister Scott Morrison says an electric vehicle can't tow a boat or trailer.
response_text: TRUE.  In April 2019, during the federal election campaign, Prime Minister Scott Morrison criticised Labor’s EV policy and said of electric vehicles: “It’s not going to tow your boat. It’s not going to tow your trailer.”

claim: Kenya is outperforming the average global growth
response_text: TRUE.  Recent figures show Kenya’s real GDP growth above the global average: in 2023 Kenya grew around 5–5.6% (KNBS/IMF) versus ~3.2% globally (IMF). Projections for 2024–2025 also have Kenya near 5%+ against a roughly 3.2% global pace, so it is outperforming.

claim: In 2018, provisional estimates show the Kenyan economy grew by 6.1%
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya’s statistics office (KNBS) reported in its 2019 Economic Survey that provisional estimates showed real GDP growth of about 6.3% in 2018, not 6.1%. Some forecasts from other institutions varied slightly, but the official provisional figure was 6.3%.

claim: Kenya's broad-based economic growth averaged 5.6% over the last five years

claim: Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Attorneys don’t know much about the law as lawyers do and Ben Shapiro is just an attorney. So, yeah.”
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying this. The quote appears in memes but not in any credible transcript, interview, speech, or reputable news source, and fact-checkers have debunked it. It’s also nonsensical since “attorney” and “lawyer” are generally synonymous.

claim: Mission Indradhanush (ensuring full immunisation with all available vaccines for children up to two years of age and pregnant women), has completed four phases covering 528 districts in India.
response_text: TRUE.  Government of India (MoHFW/PIB) reports from 2017 state that Mission Indradhanush completed four phases (2015–2017) covering 528 districts, targeting full immunisation for children up to two years of age and pregnant women.

claim: US senators being consulted about circuit court judicial nominees in their home states was a long standing requirement.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There has never been a formal requirement that home‑state senators be consulted on circuit court nominees. The “blue slip” is a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition dating to 1917, not a rule, and its weight has varied by chairman and era. Especially for circuit court nominees, chairs have often proceeded without positive blue slips (e.g., under Chairs Hatch and Grassley), showing it was not a binding, long‑standing requirement.

claim: Since 1973 the income of the bottom 90% of Americans didn't budge.
response_text: FALSE.  While growth has been much slower for most than for the top, multiple official series show the bottom 90% did see real income gains since the 1970s.  - Census Bureau: Real median household income is higher than in 1973 (roughly 10–30% higher by the late 2010s, depending on the inflation index; it peaked in 2019 before slipping during/after the pandemic). - CBO: Since 1979, average after‑tax incomes rose substantially for lower and middle groups (about 40–80% across the bottom 80%), contradicting “no change.” - Even research using pre‑tax tax‑return data (e.g., Piketty/Saez) shows modest growth for the bottom 90%, not zero.  Notes: Results vary with definitions (pre‑ vs after‑tax, household size, CPI vs PCE), and male wages did stagnate, which fuels the perception—but the blanket claim that the bottom 90% “didn’t budge” is inaccurate.

claim: During Ukraine's presidential election in 2019, the current electoral process bypassed the Donbas side, and no presidential election will be held, polling stations are open only on the territory of Donetsk and Luhansk regions controlled by Kyiv.
response_text: TRUE.  In the 2019 Ukrainian presidential election, polling stations did not operate in Russia-occupied Crimea or in the parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts controlled by Russia-backed separatists. Voting was conducted only in government-controlled areas of those regions. Residents of the non‑government‑controlled areas could vote only by temporarily changing their polling location to territory controlled by Kyiv. This was noted by Ukraine’s Central Election Commission and international observers (e.g., OSCE/ODIHR).

claim: L.A Rapper YG Shot 4 Times In Drive By Shooting
response_text: FALSE.  Reliable reports say YG was shot three times in the hip in June 2015 at a Studio City recording studio after an altercation—not in a drive-by. There are no credible reports of him being shot four times. (Note: A 2019 drive-by involved a vehicle linked to him, but YG was not shot.)

claim: President Donald Trump wants to abolish the pre-existing conditions protections within the U.S Affordable Care Act (ACA).
response_text: TRUE.  While Trump often said he supported protecting people with pre‑existing conditions, his actions sought to eliminate the ACA—and thus its protections. He backed the 2017 ACA repeal bill (AHCA), which would have weakened pre‑existing condition safeguards, expanded short‑term plans that can exclude such conditions, and his Justice Department asked courts in the Texas v. United States/California case to strike down the ACA (at points specifically targeting its pre‑existing condition provisions). Small uncertainty stems from his contrary public statements.

claim: When Winston Churchill was asked to cut arts funding in favour of the war effort, he simply replied, ‘then what are we fighting for?
response_text: FALSE.  No reliable record shows Churchill said this. The International Churchill Society and Churchill Archives report no trace in his speeches, papers, or Parliament’s Hansard. The line seems to appear decades later as an anecdote. While Churchill praised the arts, the specific “then what are we fighting for?” reply to cutting arts funding is apocryphal. (Mild uncertainty only because absence of evidence isn’t absolute.)

claim: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called on Nigeria to "start teaching the Biafran anthem to your citizens now".
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record or credible report of UN Secretary‑General António Guterres saying this. The UN has not recognized Biafra and consistently affirms Nigeria’s territorial integrity. UN officials (through the Secretary‑General’s spokesperson) have dismissed similar viral quotes as fabricated, and fact‑checkers (e.g., AFP, Dubawa/Africa Check) have debunked this claim.

claim: The House of Commons has little more than 635 employees.
response_text: FALSE.  The UK House of Commons employs several thousand staff. Recent reports put the House of Commons Service at roughly 2,500–3,000 employees (and more if including the bicameral Parliamentary Digital Service), far above “little more than 635.”

claim: 19% of WVians rely on SNAP," or food stamps.
response_text: FALSE.  Best recent estimates put West Virginia’s SNAP participation at roughly 17–18% of residents (about 0.31–0.33 million people out of ~1.78 million). That’s a bit below 19%, though it may have briefly approached that level during the pandemic. Uncertainty: exact share varies by year and measure.

claim: This year alone, MPs have cost the British taxpayer £92,993,748 in expenses.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: IPSA’s figures show MPs’ total “business costs” (staff salaries, office, accommodation, travel, etc.) typically amount to around £130–£150 million for a full recent year—so £92,993,748 would at best be a partial, mid‑year running total. Moreover, that figure (often seen on IPSA’s live dashboard) includes staff pay and office costs, not just MPs’ personal “expenses,” so the claim misrepresents what the money is. Uncertainty: the claim gives no date, but on available data it’s not accurate as stated.

claim: The U.S. has created 5.5 million new jobs, including 600,000 brand new manufacturing jobs, since Donald Trump's election. Nobody would have believed that was possible.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - BLS data show total nonfarm jobs did rise by roughly 5–6 million in the first few years after the 2016 election (depending on the exact month used), so the 5.5 million figure is in the ballpark. - But the “600,000” new manufacturing jobs is overstated. From the 2016 election through the pre‑pandemic peak, manufacturing employment rose by roughly 500,000–520,000, not 600,000. Even measured from Trump’s inauguration, the gain was closer to 450,000–500,000.  Note: The “nobody would have believed” line is subjective and not fact-checkable.

claim: The US Trump administration passed massive tax cuts, the biggest in the history of the country
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Trump administration’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a large tax cut, but by standard metrics (inflation-adjusted dollars or as a share of GDP) it was not the largest in U.S. history. The 1981 Reagan tax cut was significantly bigger, and the 1964 Kennedy-Johnson cut also rivals it. Analyses by the Tax Policy Center and others rank the 2017 law well below the top spot.

claim: President Donald Trump will get full funding of $300 million for the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, which the program has been waiting 30 years for.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative began in 2010, not 30 years earlier, so it hadn’t been “waiting 30 years.” - It had already been funded at about $300 million annually for several years before Trump (after an initial $475 million in 2010). - Trump’s early budgets proposed deep cuts to the GLRI; Congress repeatedly restored funding to roughly $300 million (and later increased it).

claim: In the US, more manufacturing jobs were created in 2018 than any year in 21 years
response_text: TRUE.  BLS data show U.S. manufacturing employment rose by about 264,000 in 2018 (Dec–to–Dec), the largest annual gain since 1997. Note: using annual-average comparisons, earlier years (e.g., 1994) were larger, but the common Dec–to–Dec measure makes the claim accurate.

claim: President Donald Trump revitalizing automobile industries that were decimated before he took office.
response_text: FALSE.  The U.S. auto industry was “decimated” during the 2008–09 crisis, but it had largely recovered before Trump took office: vehicle sales were at/near record highs in 2015–2016 and industry employment had rebounded. Under Trump, sales were flat-to-down from the 2016 peak, several plants closed (e.g., GM Lordstown), and steel/aluminum tariffs raised costs; employment rose modestly in 2017–2018 but softened in 2019 and fell sharply in 2020 due to the pandemic. So it’s inaccurate to say he revitalized an industry that was decimated before he began. (Some subjectivity around “revitalizing,” but overall evidence contradicts the claim.)

claim: There is an agreement on real time information sharing between India and Switzerland.
response_text: FALSE.  India and Switzerland have an Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI) arrangement under the OECD Common Reporting Standard and other treaty mechanisms, but these provide annual (periodic) exchanges or exchanges upon request—not real-time sharing. The first AEOI exchange occurred in 2019 and continues yearly. No formal “real-time information sharing” agreement is in place. (Slight uncertainty only in wording people sometimes use informally to describe AEOI.)

claim: Bluegill fish are responsible for over 500 peoples deaths in the United States of America every summer.
response_text: FALSE.  Bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) are small, nonvenomous freshwater sunfish that at most cause minor puncture injuries from their spines. There is no credible record of bluegill causing human fatalities in the U.S., let alone 500 each summer. U.S. animal-related death statistics identify bees/wasps, dogs, and livestock as leading causes; fish are not a significant category for fatalities. This claim appears to be a hoax/meme.

claim: America's Fox News shows beat their average performance, as their CNN and MSNBC counterparts plunged on March 26 and 27, 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Nielsen ratings reports for March 26–27, 2019 show Fox News’s key shows (e.g., Hannity, Tucker Carlson, Ingraham) delivered audiences above their typical 2019 averages, while comparable CNN and MSNBC programs were notably below their averages after the Barr summary of the Mueller report. For example, Fox primetime climbed versus its early‑2019 norms, while MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow and CNN’s primetime hours dropped well below their usual levels on those two nights. (Source: Nielsen data as summarized by industry trades and Reuters at the time.)

claim: Founding father Thomas Jefferson said, “A government big enough to give you everything you want is strong enough to take everything you have.”
response_text: FALSE.  There is no evidence Jefferson ever said this; Monticello classifies it as spurious. The line is commonly credited to President Gerald R. Ford, who used a version of it in 1974, and it has also been misattributed to Daniel Webster.

claim: Since US President Trump's election in November 2016, 5.5 million new jobs have been created.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Using Bureau of Labor Statistics nonfarm payroll data, total employment rose by roughly 5.5 million between the November 2016 election and early 2019, which is the timeframe when this claim was commonly made. Note: counting from Trump’s inauguration (Jan 2017) yields a slightly smaller number, and by the end of his term the pandemic erased many of those gains.

claim: The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)  removed thousands of  gang members
response_text: TRUE.  ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations has reported removing several thousand known or suspected gang members in single fiscal years (e.g., roughly 5,400 in FY2017 and about 5,800 in FY2018). So the general claim that ICE removed “thousands of gang members” is accurate. Note: ICE counts are for “known or suspected” gang members, and figures vary by year.

claim: The US Great Lakes Initiative is to receive full funding of $300 million after a more than 30 years wait.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) was created in 2010 and has been funded at roughly $300 million per year since then, with recent increases and an additional $1 billion from the 2021 infrastructure law. It was not waiting “more than 30 years” for $300 million. - A different program—the Land and Water Conservation Fund—was “fully funded” after decades, but at $900 million, not $300 million.

claim: In 2018, US drug prices  declined for the first time in 46 years.
response_text: FALSE.  BLS data show the prescription drug CPI rose slightly in calendar year 2018 (about 0.2–0.3%). The first annual decline since the 1970s occurred in 2019. Some 12‑month windows ending in late 2018 (e.g., Dec 2018 vs. Dec 2017) did show a small drop, which likely sparked the “first time in 46 years” talking point, but 2018 as a whole did not decline.

claim: Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni said trees in Finland can take 120 years to mature.
response_text: TRUE. Museveni has made speeches comparing tree growth in cold Europe to tropical Africa, saying that in Finland trees can take about 120 years to mature, versus roughly 10–15 years in Uganda. (Note: actual Finnish rotation ages are often around 60–100 years, but he did use the 120-year figure.)

claim: “In 2017, there were more marijuana arrests in this country than all violent crime arrests combined.”
response_text: TRUE.  FBI Uniform Crime Reports show about 659,700 marijuana arrests in the U.S. in 2017 (roughly 88% for possession), compared with about 520,000 arrests for all violent crimes combined (murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault). So marijuana arrests exceeded violent-crime arrests that year.

claim: “Jokowi administration offers Bogor city to China."
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence or official record that the Jokowi administration “offered” or ceded Bogor city to China. Indonesian law prohibits transferring sovereignty over territory. The claim appears to be a hoax/misinterpretation of routine investment or cooperation outreach to Chinese investors, which does not equate to offering a city. Uncertainty: claim lacks date/context, but no reputable sources support it.

claim: In 2017, there were more marijuana arrests in this country than all violent crime arrests combined.
response_text: TRUE.  Assuming the United States: FBI Uniform Crime Report data for 2017 show roughly 659,700 marijuana arrests (possession plus sale/manufacture) versus about 518,000 arrests for all violent crimes combined (murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault). Thus marijuana arrests exceeded violent-crime arrests that year.

claim: Robert Soros (Son of George Soros) is married To Sister of Adam Schiff.
response_text: FALSE.  Robert Soros married Melissa Robin Schiff in 1992. Despite the shared last name, she is not related to Rep. Adam Schiff. New York Times wedding records list her parents as Marcia and Haskel Schiff of New York, and multiple fact-checks (e.g., Snopes, Reuters) have debunked any connection.

claim: In 2017, there were more marijuana arrests in the US, than all violent crime arrests combined.
response_text: TRUE.  FBI Uniform Crime Reports for 2017 show about 659,700 marijuana arrests (roughly 599,000 for possession only), while total arrests for all violent crimes combined were about 518,600. Thus, marijuana arrests exceeded violent-crime arrests in 2017.

claim: Police in Thailand can issue fines to anyone who does not wear a face mask in public during the novel coronavirus pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  During parts of the COVID-19 pandemic, Thai authorities (under the Communicable Disease Act and local orders) made mask-wearing in public compulsory, with fines of up to 20,000 baht for violations. Police, alongside local disease-control officials, enforced these rules—for example, Bangkok’s 2021 mandate, when even the prime minister was fined. Note: requirements and enforcement varied by province and time.

claim: President Trump immediately dropped American sanctions against Russia after his election,
response_text: FALSE.  Trump did not lift U.S. sanctions on Russia after the 2016 election or upon taking office. Existing sanctions stayed in place, and many were expanded—most notably under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA) signed in August 2017. While there were minor licensing adjustments, there was no immediate or wholesale dropping of sanctions.

claim: Prime Minister Narendra Modi tops the list of 50 most honest politicians that was released in the USA.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible U.S. organization or media has published a “50 most honest politicians” list, and multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, Factly, PIB Fact Check) have debunked this viral claim as a hoax. Transparency International also ranks countries by perceived corruption, not individual politicians.

claim: Nudist beach to open soon on Lake Texoma in Marshall County.
response_text: FALSE.  Local officials and news outlets debunked this as a hoax/satire. Oklahoma Tourism and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (which manages much of Lake Texoma shoreline) said no such plan exists, and public nudity is prohibited under state law and Corps regulations.

claim: South Africa’s official opposition party, the Democratic Alliance (DA), launched its election manifesto in Johannesburg on 23 February 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reports confirm the DA launched its 2019 election manifesto at Rand Stadium in Johannesburg on 23 February 2019, led by then party leader Mmusi Maimane.

claim: Eight Democratic candidates ‘boycott’ the AIPAC conference
response_text: FALSE.  Context: Progressive groups urged 2020 Democratic presidential hopefuls to skip AIPAC, and several said they wouldn’t attend. But calling it a “boycott” by “eight” candidates is overstated. Many framed their absence as scheduling, not a boycott, and at least one major Democratic candidate (Michael Bloomberg) addressed the 2020 AIPAC conference. So the blanket claim that eight Democratic candidates “boycotted” AIPAC is inaccurate. (Uncertainty: counts varied by outlet and year, but the “eight” boycott framing is not supported.)

claim: In summary of Robert Mueller's report Bill Barr concludes that Special Counsel Robert Mueller stated, "while this report does not conclude that the President committed a crime, it also does not exonerate him.”
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: In his March 24, 2019 summary letter to Congress, Attorney General Bill Barr explicitly quoted Mueller’s report on obstruction: “The Special Counsel states that ‘while this report does not conclude that the President committed a crime, it also does not exonerate him.’” This line comes from Mueller’s own report and was relayed verbatim by Barr.

claim: The Council on American-Islamic Relations was founded in response to 9/11.
response_text: FALSE.  CAIR was founded in 1994 in Washington, D.C., seven years before the 9/11 attacks. It gained greater prominence after 9/11, but it was not created in response to them.

claim: An estimated 1 million people marched for a People's vote on Saturday 23rd March.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The 1 million figure was the organisers’ claim for the 23 March 2019 People’s Vote march. There was no official police count, and independent assessments and media reports put the turnout at several hundred thousand (roughly 300k–400k), not 1 million. Uncertainty remains due to lack of an official count, but evidence suggests the organiser figure was overstated.

claim: CAIR was founded after 9/11, because they recognized that some people did something and that all of us were starting to lose access to our civil liberties
response_text: FALSE.  CAIR (the Council on American-Islamic Relations) was founded in 1994, seven years before the 9/11 attacks. While CAIR expanded its civil rights advocacy after 2001, it was not founded in response to 9/11.

claim: The 2019 DMK parliamentary Manifesto says that: ‘People occupying encroached Temple lands will be regularized and ownership transferred’, ‘Encroached Wakf properties will be reclaimed and handed over to wakf’
response_text: FALSE.  The quoted lines do not appear in DMK’s 2019 Lok Sabha manifesto. The manifesto states that encroachments on temple lands would be removed and temple lands reclaimed, and that encroached Waqf properties would be recovered and restored to the Waqf Board. The “regularize and transfer ownership” wording for temple lands is a fabricated/misattributed claim (often conflating separate promises about regularizing encroachments on certain government lands, not temple lands).

claim: America’s life expectancy has declined for the last three years in a row, the first time in a hundred years, because of surges in suicides and drug overdoses.
response_text: TRUE.  CDC data show U.S. life expectancy fell three years in a row (2015, 2016, 2017) — the first such multi‑year decline since the 1915–1918 period about a century earlier. The drop was driven largely by rising drug overdose deaths and suicides (with some contribution from alcohol-related liver disease). Note: 2016’s decline is small and can be obscured by rounding, but CDC characterizes it as a consecutive three‑year slide.

claim: The UK and US have exported no vaccines.
response_text: False.  Both countries did export COVID-19 vaccines. The United States shipped hundreds of millions of doses abroad from mid-2021 onward (including early loans of AstraZeneca doses to Mexico and Canada and large-scale Pfizer/Moderna donations via COVAX and bilaterally). The United Kingdom also exported vaccines, donating tens of millions of doses internationally in 2021–2022. Note: Early in 2021 both prioritized domestic use, which may have led to the impression of “no exports,” but it was not true overall.

claim: American middle schools caught forcing students to do Muslim prayers 5 times a day.
response_text: FALSE.  - There are no credible reports of U.S. middle schools forcing students to perform Muslim prayers. Similar viral claims have been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers. - Public schools are legally barred from compelling religious practice (e.g., Engel v. Vitale). They may teach about religions, and may accommodate voluntary student prayer. - Practically, five daily Islamic prayers don’t all occur during school hours (only midday/afternoon ones do), making the claim even less plausible.

claim: Women in Russia get paid less than men for the same work.
response_text: TRUE.  Russia has a large gender pay gap: Rosstat reports women’s average wages are roughly 70–75% of men’s. Studies that adjust for occupation, industry, education, and hours still find a persistent “unexplained” gap, indicating women are often paid less than men for comparable work, despite laws requiring equal pay. Magnitude varies by sector and employer, so the claim is generally true, though not universal.

claim: United States G.D.P is above 3 percent for the first time in fourteen years but the press took odd months and said it was 2.9.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: BEA’s official annual (year-over-year) real GDP growth for 2018 was 2.9%, not above 3%. The last calendar year above 3% was 2005. The 3%+ figure sometimes cited (~3.1%) is a different metric—fourth-quarter-to-fourth-quarter growth. The media used the standard annual measure; they didn’t “take odd months” (GDP isn’t reported monthly by BEA).

claim: For four years President Obama budgeted for zero upgrades to U.S tanks which affected U.S military readiness and slashed the work force by sixty percent at manufacturing plants in Lima, Ohio.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Obama administration (at the Army’s request) proposed pausing Abrams tank upgrades for about three fiscal years (FY2014–FY2016), not “four years,” and Congress repeatedly added money anyway. - Army leaders said the pause would not harm readiness because the service already had more tanks than it needed. - The Lima, Ohio tank plant’s workforce did drop roughly 60% during the drawdown, but attributing that solely to an Obama four‑year zero‑funding policy is misleading; reductions reflected lower post‑war demand and intermittent orders, not a confirmed four‑year budget of zero upgrades.

claim: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code has led to significant results in India.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: Since its 2016 enactment, India’s Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) has materially improved insolvency resolution outcomes. Creditor recoveries under IBC have generally exceeded those from earlier mechanisms (like DRTs/SARFAESI), several large cases (e.g., Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel) saw substantial recoveries, many cases have been settled or withdrawn due to the credible threat of admission, and India’s “resolving insolvency” standing in the World Bank Doing Business rankings improved sharply after IBC reforms. While delays, court backlogs, and high haircuts persist, the overall impact has been significant.

claim: The gross domestic product grew 3.1 percent in 2018, after adjusting for inflation.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: According to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, real (inflation‑adjusted) GDP grew 2.9% in 2018 on the standard annual basis (annual average vs. previous year). The oft-cited 3.1% refers to a different measure (Q4‑to‑Q4), which was later revised to about 3.0%.

claim: The Indian Government has approved Public Sector Banks to amalgamate through an alternative mechanism to facilitate consolidation
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2017, India’s Union Cabinet approved setting up an “Alternative Mechanism” (a ministerial panel) to facilitate consolidation of Public Sector Banks. Under this framework, PSB boards could propose amalgamations, which the Alternative Mechanism would consider and approve. This mechanism was used for subsequent mergers (e.g., BOB–Dena–Vijaya in 2018 and the 2019 mega-mergers).

claim: Illegal immigrants to the USA kill 4,000 people per year.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible data showing 4,000 people are killed each year by undocumented immigrants. That figure traces to a misreading of a 2011 GAO report that tallied arrests (not killings), over many years, of all non‑citizens in custody (legal and illegal), with possible double counting; some later divided that total to claim “~4,000 per year.” National homicide totals are about 17,000–24,000 annually; 4,000 would imply roughly 1 in 5 murders by undocumented immigrants, which is contradicted by available evidence. State-level data (e.g., Texas DPS) show undocumented immigrants are convicted of homicide at rates at or below native-born residents. Uncertainty: the U.S. lacks a complete national database by immigration status, but the best evidence does not support this claim.

claim: West Virgina has fewer science, technology, engineering and math graduates than any neighbouring state.
response_text: TRUE.  Reasoning: Using recent NCSES/IPEDS completions data for science and engineering (a standard proxy for STEM), West Virginia awards far fewer STEM/S&E degrees than each bordering state (Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky). WV’s totals are only a few thousand annually, while neighbors each award many times more (roughly 2–10x). This holds across recent years and common STEM definitions. Minor uncertainty depends on the exact STEM definition and year, but rankings remain the same.

claim: People who are vaccinated against chickenpox need to keep getting boosters.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The chickenpox (varicella) vaccine is a 2‑dose series. Once you’ve had both doses (in childhood or as an adult without immunity), no routine boosters are recommended for healthy people. Later-life shingles vaccination is separate and not a “chickenpox booster.”

claim: Fewer than 500 people a year in the USA are killed by rifles.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: FBI Uniform Crime Reports show rifles are used in fewer than 500 murders per year in recent years (e.g., 2019: 364; 2020: 455; 2021: ~447; 2022: ~480). Note: this refers to homicides; if one included suicides and other deaths involving rifles, the total would be much higher.

claim: Natural chickenpox infection in childhood will have 99.999 percent no long-term repercussions.
response_text: FALSE.  Varicella (chickenpox) establishes lifelong latent infection; about 1 in 3 people later develop shingles (herpes zoster), a clear long‑term consequence, and some develop postherpetic neuralgia or scarring. Serious neurologic or vascular sequelae are rare but occur. This is far from 99.999% having no long‑term repercussions.  Sources: CDC (Shingles: “About 1 in 3 people will develop shingles in their lifetime”); CDC (Chickenpox complications and VZV latency).

claim: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand has the most votes against Donald Trump cabinet nominees
response_text: TRUE.  During the 2017 confirmation period for Donald Trump’s initial Cabinet, multiple contemporaneous tallies (e.g., Politico/The Hill) showed Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand cast more “no” votes than any other senator. She opposed nearly all of Trump’s Cabinet picks and was the lone vote against James Mattis. Note: this assessment refers to the early Cabinet confirmations; totals could vary if counting later replacements, but reporting at the time supports the claim.

claim: 50% of Americans agree that Robert Mueller’s investigation is a Witch Hunt.
response_text: FALSE.  Most national polls in 2018–2019 found a minority of Americans agreed the Mueller probe was a “witch hunt,” while majorities called it legitimate. One USA Today/Suffolk poll in March 2019 did show about 50% agreement, but it was an outlier against consistent findings from Quinnipiac, Monmouth, and others. So as a general claim about Americans, it’s misleading. (Some uncertainty stems from that single poll.)

claim: Nigeria generates over 62 million tonnes of waste a year
response_text: FALSE.  Most credible estimates put Nigeria’s municipal solid waste at about 32–43 million tonnes per year (e.g., World Bank “What a Waste 2.0” and subsequent estimates based on ~0.5 kg/person/day), well below 62 million. Higher figures typically conflate other waste streams or lack solid sourcing. Uncertainty: depends on scope (including industrial/agricultural waste would raise totals).

claim: 50%of all school teachers in Texas (US) are working second or third jobs.
response_text: FALSE.  Best-available data show less than half of Texas teachers hold outside jobs during the school year. A long‑running Sam Houston State University/Texas teacher survey (“Texas Teachers, Moonlighting, and Morale”) has found roughly 35–40% work a second job during the school year (around 55% in summer). National NCES data are even lower (~18% with outside jobs in the school year). Only if one counts extra paid school assignments (coaching, stipends) do figures approach or exceed 50%, but that’s not typically what “second or third jobs” implies. Uncertainty: exact percentages vary by survey/year, but none credibly support 50% during the school year.

claim: Each person [in Nigeria] generates an average of 0.65 kg of waste per day
response_text: FALSE.  Most authoritative estimates put Nigeria’s average municipal solid waste generation closer to 0.5 kg per person per day. For example, the World Bank’s What a Waste 2.0 (2018) reports about 0.51 kg/capita/day for Nigeria (2016 data). Urban areas like Lagos can be higher (often 0.7–1.0 kg), but nationwide averages are typically below 0.65 kg. Note: figures vary by source and year, but 0.65 kg is above commonly cited national averages.

claim: POLITICS Nigeria HAS Won Over 700 Medals In The Last 3 year
response_text: FALSE.  Public, verifiable tallies of Nigeria’s recent medal hauls don’t approach 700 in three years. For example: 2022 Commonwealth Games (35 medals) and the 2023 African Games held in 2024 (about 121 medals) together are ~156. Even adding notable continental/para championships does not credibly total 700 without counting numerous minor or domestic events. No audited source supports “over 700 medals” in that span. Uncertainty: depends on what events are counted, but major international results fall far short.

claim: No one in Mid Ulster speaks Irish as their first language.
response_text: FALSE.  Northern Ireland census data show that some residents of Mid Ulster report Irish as their main/home language, and there are Irish‑speaking households in areas like Carntogher (a designated Irish Language Network area). This means at least some people in Mid Ulster have Irish as their first language.

claim: Wall Street got a trillion dollar bail out in 2008.
response_text: FALSE.  The 2008 congressional “bailout” (TARP) authorized $700 billion, not $1 trillion (later capped at $475 billion, much of it repaid). While the Federal Reserve’s emergency lending and guarantees during 2008–09 at times exceeded $1 trillion, that was a set of temporary liquidity programs rather than a single “trillion‑dollar bailout” passed in 2008.

claim: The Indian government has issued an order against sharing political posts online.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no blanket order by the Government of India prohibiting citizens from sharing political posts online. Such claims have been repeatedly debunked by PIB Fact Check. Restrictions do exist for government employees under service conduct rules, and the Election Commission enforces a 48‑hour “silence period” on campaigning/advertising near polling, but that isn’t a general ban on individuals sharing political opinions.

claim: Images of the new Indian e-passport.
response_text: FALSE — India has announced/started work on e‑passports, but viral “first look” pictures circulating online have repeatedly been debunked as mock-ups or illustrative images, not official photos. Without an official release from MEA/Passport Seva, such images shouldn’t be treated as genuine. (Some uncertainty without seeing the specific images.)

claim: Senator Thom Tillis changes position on President Trump's national emergency declaration for border wall funding
response_text: TRUE.  In February 2019, Sen. Thom Tillis wrote an op-ed saying he would vote to block President Trump’s national emergency declaration for border wall funding. When the Senate voted on March 14, 2019, he reversed course and voted against the resolution to terminate the emergency, effectively supporting Trump’s declaration.

claim: sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) can cure cancer.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible clinical evidence that sodium bicarbonate cures cancer. Reputable organizations (e.g., NCI, ACS) classify this as an unproven and discredited claim. Baking soda is used in supportive care (e.g., mouth rinses, urine alkalinization for certain chemotherapy), but it does not treat or cure tumors. Misuse can cause dangerous alkalosis and electrolyte disturbances.

claim: Joe biden said The Trump budget cuts $845 billion, almost a trillion dollar cut in Medicare.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: Trump’s FY2020 budget proposed about $845 billion in Medicare “savings” over 10 years relative to current-law projections, largely from lower payments to providers and anti-fraud efforts. Overall Medicare spending would still increase, and the proposal did not cut beneficiaries’ core benefits. Calling it “almost a trillion dollar cut in Medicare” is misleading. (Minor uncertainty stems from budget-speak, where reduced projected spending is sometimes termed a “cut.”)

claim: Democrats in the House of Representatives voted for the right of illegal immigrants to vote in the US.
response_text: FALSE.  - Federal law already makes it illegal for noncitizens (including undocumented immigrants) to vote in federal elections, and no House Democrats voted to change that. - The votes often cited are:    - A 2019 procedural motion Republicans offered to add symbolic language to H.R. 1; Democrats voted it down, but that did not legalize noncitizen voting.   - A 2023 GOP resolution to overturn Washington, D.C.’s local law allowing noncitizens to vote in DC local (not federal) elections; many Democrats opposed overturning the local law. That was not a vote to allow illegal immigrants to vote “in the US,” nor in federal elections.

claim: 52 counties in the state of New York have average taxes of above the SALT (state and local taxes) $10,000 cap
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: New York has 62 counties, and only a handful (mainly downstate suburbs like Westchester, Nassau, Rockland, Putnam, and sometimes Suffolk) have average property-tax bills above $10,000. Most upstate counties’ average property taxes are far below that. Even if one considers combined SALT (state income + local property), available IRS/Tax Foundation/ATTOM data do not support anything close to 52 counties averaging above $10,000. Uncertainty: the claim is vague about which “taxes” are averaged, but under any standard reading it’s not 52 counties.

claim: The Boeing 737 Max 8, the type of plane that crashed in Ethiopia, continues to fly in the United States, despite the FAA saying "software updates are likely coming."
response_text: TRUE.  After the Ethiopian Airlines 737 Max 8 crash on March 10, 2019, the FAA initially allowed the 737 Max 8 to continue flying in the United States while noting that a flight-control software update (to MCAS) was coming and would be mandated. The U.S. grounded the aircraft on March 13, 2019. (The quoted phrasing is a paraphrase, but the substance is accurate.)

claim: Thomas Jefferson third president of the United States said hemp is of first necessity to the wealth and protection of the country.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence Jefferson ever wrote or said this. Monticello (the Thomas Jefferson Foundation) lists “Hemp is of first necessity to the wealth and protection of the country” as a spurious quotation; it does not appear in Jefferson’s papers. Jefferson did grow hemp, but this specific line is a modern misattribution.

claim: The Catholic Church announced that it was introducing burkas for altar servers.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no official Catholic Church announcement introducing burkas for altar servers. Standard altar server vestments are cassock and surplice or an alb. The “burkas for altar servers” claim traces to satirical/fake-news posts, not real Church policy.

claim: Kenya has one of the worst maternal mortality rates in the world.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya’s maternal mortality ratio is high by global standards but not among the world’s worst. Recent UN/WHO estimates put Kenya around 300–400 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births (about 355 in 2020), which is below the sub‑Saharan Africa average (~545) and far lower than the highest-burden countries (often >800–1,000, e.g., South Sudan, Chad, Sierra Leone, Nigeria). Hence the claim overstates Kenya’s standing.

claim: Kenya has one of the worst maternal mortality rates in the world
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya’s maternal mortality ratio is high relative to the global average but is not among the highest in the world. Recent estimates put Kenya around a few hundred maternal deaths per 100,000 live births (e.g., ~300–400; KDHS 2022 reports ~362), which is below the sub‑Saharan Africa average and far lower than the worst-affected countries where rates exceed 700–1,000. Uncertainty: exact figures vary by source and method, but the ranking remains well short of the “worst” group.

claim: Poland has had no terror attacks.
response_text: FALSE.  Poland has experienced terrorist attacks. A clear example is the 1934 assassination of Interior Minister Bronisław Pieracki in Warsaw by the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, widely regarded as a terrorist act. More recently, there was a 2016 bomb explosion on a Wrocław city bus that injured a passenger.

claim: Poland has a no-migrants policy.
response_text: FALSE.  Poland does not have a blanket “no‑migrants” policy. It admits migrants and refugees, issues large numbers of work and residence permits (among the highest in the EU), and has hosted over a million Ukrainians under temporary protection since 2022. While recent governments have opposed EU relocation of irregular migrants and tightened the border with Belarus, that is not a total ban on migrants.

claim: HR 1 is going to take your hard-earned tax dollars and millions more and send them to (a political candidate’s) campaign so (they) can put ads on TV
response_text: FALSE.  - H.R. 1 (the For the People Act) proposed a voluntary small‑donor matching system for campaigns, but it specified that the match would be paid from a “Freedom From Influence Fund” financed by surcharges on certain criminal and civil fines/penalties—not from income tax revenues. - The bill also never became law. - Candidates opting in could use campaign funds for typical campaign expenses (including ads), but the “take your hard‑earned tax dollars” part is incorrect.  Note: Some critics still call it “taxpayer money” because it’s public revenue, but it is not funded by taxpayers’ income taxes as claimed.

claim: Four members of the Congress and Samajwadi Party assaulted two Kashmiri dry fruit sellers in Lucknow, India in March 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The assault on two Kashmiri dry fruit sellers in Lucknow in March 2019 did occur, but the attackers were members of a Hindutva fringe outfit (notably Vishwa Hindu Dal), not the Congress or Samajwadi Party. Uttar Pradesh Police arrested multiple suspects, including a Vishwa Hindu Dal member, and media/fact-checks (e.g., NDTV, Alt News, BOOM) found no link to Congress or SP.

claim: Russia has historically reaffirmed its role as a state  that is the guarantor of stability and security, and is a party that brings peace, not agression.
response_text: FALSE.  Russia’s historical record includes numerous aggressive actions that contradict the claim. Examples: the Soviet invasion of Poland (1939) and Finland (1939–40), annexation of the Baltic states (1940), crushing of uprisings in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968), invasion of Afghanistan (1979), and, under the Russian Federation, wars in Chechnya (1994–96; 1999–2009), the war with Georgia (2008), annexation of Crimea (2014), and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine (2022). While Russia has at times engaged in mediation or “peacekeeping,” its repeated use of force and territorial expansion undermine the claim that it “brings peace, not aggression.”

claim: The Nigerian Supreme Court nullified the results of the 2019 Nigerian Presidential Election.
response_text: FALSE.  The Supreme Court did not nullify the 2019 Nigerian presidential election. It dismissed the opposition’s appeal and affirmed Muhammadu Buhari’s victory (decision delivered in late October 2019, with reasons issued subsequently).

claim: MMR Vaccine does not causes autism in Children.
response_text: TRUE.  Extensive, well-designed studies show no causal link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A large Danish cohort study (2019) and a 2014 meta-analysis covering over a million children found no association. The 1998 paper that originally suggested a link was fraudulent and has been fully retracted. Public health agencies (CDC, WHO, National Academy of Medicine) concur.

claim: Nigeria’s central bank has banned textile imports
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In March 2019 the Central Bank of Nigeria barred textile importers from accessing foreign exchange through official windows to encourage local production, but it did not ban textile imports outright. Imports remained legal if funded from other sources. The CBN later lifted such FX restrictions on listed items in October 2023.

claim: Former U.S. President Barack Obama didn't turn over any documents to Congress.
response_text: FALSE.  The Obama administration turned over many documents to Congress during oversight investigations. For example, in the Fast and Furious inquiry, the Justice Department provided thousands of pages (about 7,600) before some additional materials were withheld under executive privilege. In the Benghazi investigations, the State Department produced tens of thousands of pages. While certain internal deliberative documents were withheld, it’s not true that no documents were turned over.

claim: Muslim Figure Said "We must have Pork-Free Menus Or We Will Leave U.S
response_text: FALSE.  This quote originated from a fake-news/satire story that circulated with different country names swapped in. It used a photo of French imam Hassen Chalghoumi (who never said it and isn’t a U.S. figure). No credible source shows any U.S. Muslim leader issuing such an ultimatum, and fact-checkers have debunked the claim.

claim: PAHAL, India's Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG consumer scheme, is the world’s largest cash transfer program.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: PAHAL (Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG) has been recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s largest cash transfer/benefit program (households), with tens of millions of LPG consumers receiving subsidy directly into bank accounts. Note: rankings can change over time, but it has held this recognition.

claim: When the Coalition came to power, it inherited a 755 million tonne emissions deficit needed to reach Australia's second Kyoto target because Labor hadn't done the hard work.
response_text: FALSE.  At the 2013 change of government, the official “abatement task” to meet Australia’s 2020 (Kyoto Protocol second commitment period) target was about 421 million tonnes CO2-e cumulatively to 2020, not 755 Mt. Under Kyoto rules Australia also had carry‑over units from the first commitment period that further reduced the task. The 755 Mt figure reflects an earlier or different calculation (e.g., pre‑policy estimates) and is not what the Coalition “inherited.” Labor had also legislated a carbon pricing scheme intended to deliver abatement toward the target.

claim: Vice President, Prof. Yemi Osinbajo has said that "the N10,000 loan given to traders under the Tradermoni scheme of the Federal Government has been stopped".
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Vice President Yemi Osinbajo saying the N10,000 TraderMoni loan “has been stopped.” In early 2020, after reports claimed TraderMoni was suspended, his office clarified the scheme was not stopped but being restructured to improve implementation. Later iterations (GEEP 2.0) adjusted amounts, but that’s not Osinbajo declaring the N10,000 loan stopped. Uncertainty: amounts and modalities changed over time, which may have fueled the misunderstanding.

claim: Obama's 2 terms were a crime spree.
response_text: FALSE.  “Crime spree” implies widespread criminal activity. Obama himself was never charged, and his White House had no senior officials indicted. While a few isolated cases occurred (e.g., CIA Director David Petraeus’s misdemeanor plea for mishandling classified information; a GSA official’s fraud case), multiple high-profile investigations (IRS targeting, Fast and Furious, Benghazi, Solyndra) resulted in no criminal charges against senior administration officials. Overall, the record doesn’t support a “crime spree.”

claim: Donald trump claims "Nobody shows up (for immigration hearings). Three percent of the people come back for a trial."
response_text: FALSE.  Government court data and independent analyses show the majority of migrants attend their immigration hearings, not 3%. EOIR/TRAC data over multiple years typically find roughly 70–90% appearance rates overall, and well over 90% for those with legal representation or seeking asylum. Rates vary by group and year, but nothing approaches “3%.”

claim: Donald Trump claims that Virginia’s Democratic governor said he would allow parents, "if they didn’t want the child, who is now outside of the womb — long outside of the womb — they will execute the baby after birth."
response_text: FALSE.  Ralph Northam did not say parents could “execute” a baby after birth. In a 2019 radio interview, he discussed rare cases of severe fetal anomalies or non-viable infants, saying the baby would be delivered, kept comfortable, and that decisions about resuscitation would be made with the family. He did not endorse killing newborns, and infanticide is illegal. Trump's characterization misstates Northam’s remarks.

claim: More people are working today in the United States than ever before in the history of our country.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: According to recent BLS data, both total nonfarm payroll employment and the household-survey count of employed people are at or near all-time highs (roughly 160M on payrolls and about 163M employed), surpassing pre‑pandemic peaks. Because the U.S. population grows, the absolute number working often reaches new records during expansions. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation releases; series CES0000000001 (total nonfarm payrolls) and LNS12000000 (Employment Level). Note: “Today” depends on the latest monthly report, but current readings are record-level.

claim: The Trump administration passed the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history.
response_text: FALSE.  The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was not the largest tax cut in U.S. history by standard measures. On a meaningful basis—share of the economy (GDP) or inflation‑adjusted revenue impact—earlier cuts were bigger, notably the 1981 Reagan tax cut (ERTA) and the 1945 and 1964 tax cuts. TCJA’s estimated cost was about $1.5 trillion over 10 years (roughly under 1% of GDP in the early years), which is smaller than those prior cuts.

claim: The visa lottery in the US, allows foreign governments to send criminals and people they don't want.
response_text: FALSE.  The U.S. Diversity Visa (DV) “lottery” is an individual application process run by the U.S. State Department. Entrants apply themselves; foreign governments do not select or “send” people. Winners are chosen randomly by a U.S. system and must still pass consular interviews, biometrics, background/security checks, medical exams, and provide police certificates. Applicants with disqualifying criminal or security grounds are inadmissible under U.S. law. While any system can have rare failures, the program does not allow foreign governments to send criminals or unwanted persons.

claim: Donald trump claims that 'We passed the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history'
response_text: False.  Independent analyses show the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was not the largest tax cut in U.S. history. By the standard measure—share of the economy—it was much smaller than the 1981 Reagan tax cut (about 2.9% of GDP) and other post‑WWII cuts; TCJA was roughly 0.8–1% of GDP. Fact-checkers (Tax Policy Center, CRFB, PolitiFact, Washington Post) have repeatedly found Trump’s “largest ever” claim incorrect.

claim: The BJP government published an infographic on the 48-months portal that makes four claims about the Jan Suraksha Yojana. This article is a fact check of those claims.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: During 2018, the government’s “48 Months” (MyGov) portal carried infographics summarizing achievements, including one on the Jan Suraksha (PMJJBY/PMSBY/APY) schemes with multiple bullet-point claims. Several fact-check pieces (e.g., by Factly) explicitly introduced their articles by noting that the 48-months portal infographic made four claims and then evaluated them. Minor uncertainty is only about the exact phrasing (“Jan Suraksha Yojana” vs “Jansuraksha” umbrella) and the count of claims, but such an article exists.

claim: More people are working today in the United States than ever before in the history of our country.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: BLS data show total U.S. employment (both nonfarm payroll jobs and the household-survey “employment level”) reached all‑time highs in 2023–2024, reflecting population growth and ongoing job gains. Note this refers to the absolute number of people working, not the employment rate, which is not at a record.

claim: The  Visa lottery — that’s where they put in the names; they put it in a lottery, and you pick, ‘Oh, here’s a wonderful person. Wonderful.’ You know, he killed four people. ‘Here’s — here’s another wonderful.’ … They send us the people they don’t want.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Diversity Visa (DV) program is run by the U.S. State Department. Individuals apply themselves online; foreign governments do not “put in names” or “send” people. - Winners are randomly selected from eligible entries, then must meet education/work requirements and pass extensive security, criminal, and medical vetting. Applicants with serious criminal records are inadmissible. - The cited notion that countries “send us the people they don’t want” misstates how the program works. (If referencing the NYC attacker, he entered via DV but was not “sent” by a country, and he killed eight, not four.)

claim: When the wind stops blowing, that’s the end of your electric (power).
response_text: FALSE.  Modern power grids don’t rely on a single source. When wind output drops, other resources—such as hydro, gas, nuclear, solar, imports, and increasingly battery storage—balance the system. Wind is also geographically diverse and forecasted, so operators plan reserves accordingly. You only “lose electricity” if a grid were dependent solely on wind with no backup or storage, which is not how real grids are run.

claim: For many, many decades veterans have been trying to get VA Choice. You couldn’t get it. ... Now these great veterans, if there’s a big wait, they go outside, they go to a local doctor. We pay the bills. They get better. Everybody is happy. And we actually save a lot of money, if you can believe it. And I got that approved after 44 years of being unable to get it approved.
response_text: FALSE.  - The Veterans Choice Program (allowing veterans to use non-VA doctors if wait times or distance were excessive) was created and signed into law in 2014 under President Obama, not by Trump. - In 2018, Trump signed the VA MISSION Act, which replaced and expanded Choice; he did not “get VA Choice approved,” nor was it “after 44 years.” - Claims that it “saves a lot of money” are contradicted by nonpartisan estimates (e.g., CBO) projecting the MISSION Act would increase federal spending by tens of billions, not save money.

claim: Not a single bulletproof jacket was procured in UPA rule from 2009 to 2014.
response_text: FALSE.  Parliamentary replies and audit records show the Army did procure bulletproof jackets during 2009–2014 (UPA). The CAG (2017) and MoD answers to Parliament note tens of thousands of jackets were bought via revenue/emergency procurements in that period (often cited in the ~50,000–60,000 range), even though the large capital contract for 1.86 lakh jackets was concluded later under the NDA. Hence, it’s incorrect to say “not a single” jacket was procured. (Minor uncertainty on the exact count, but it was clearly non-zero.)

claim: Donald trump claims When the wind stops blowing, that’s the end of your electric (power)
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump repeatedly mocked wind power with lines like “When the wind stops blowing, that’s the end of your electric.” For example, at a March 28, 2019 rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, he said, “When the wind stops blowing, that’s the end of your electric,” and made similar remarks at other events (e.g., CPAC 2019).

claim: We have created "5.3 million new jobs, including over, now, 600,000 beautiful, brand-new manufacturing jobs."
response_text: FALSE.  - The total jobs part is roughly in the ballpark for mid‑2019 (about 5.3 million nonfarm jobs added since Jan. 2017). - But the manufacturing part is overstated: BLS data show manufacturing employment increased by roughly 450,000–520,000 at its pre‑pandemic peak, not “over 600,000.”

claim: Donald trump made claims about the veterans choice program being something that people has failed to create for four decades.
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump repeatedly claimed he secured Veterans Choice after others had failed for “40–44 years,” saying things like “they’ve been trying to get Veterans Choice for 44 years, I got it.” In reality, the Veterans Choice program was created in 2014 under President Obama; Trump signed the 2018 VA MISSION Act, which replaced/expanded it. Sources: Washington Post Fact Checker (2020), FactCheck.org (2020), PolitiFact.

claim: Donald trump claims "One in three women is sexually assaulted on the dangerous journey north."
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump said this during his Jan. 8, 2019 Oval Office address on border security, stating “one in three women are sexually assaulted on the dangerous trek up through Mexico,” a figure he and others attributed to a Doctors Without Borders report.

claim: Donal d trump claims "The unemployment rate has reached the lowest in over 51 years. And African American, … Hispanic American, Asian American unemployment rates are at their all-time historic lows."
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Before the pandemic, the U.S. unemployment rate fell to 3.5% in 2019–early 2020, the lowest since 1969 (roughly 50+ years). BLS data also show record lows at that time for Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino, and Asian unemployment rates (within the history of those series—Black since 1972, Hispanic since 1973, Asian since 2000). Minor caveat: “over 51 years” is rounding, but the substance is accurate.

claim: Cancer is Candida or Fungus.
response_text: FALSE.  Cancer consists of abnormal human cells that acquire mutations and grow uncontrollably; it is not Candida or any fungus. While fungi (including Candida) can infect people with cancer or occasionally colonize tumors, they are not the cause or the tumor itself. Antifungal treatments do not cure cancer. Note: some fungal toxins (e.g., aflatoxin) can contribute to cancer risk, but that is toxin exposure, not cancer being a fungus.

claim: CORY AQUINO's Presidency of the Philippines is unconstitutional.
response_text: FALSE.  Cory Aquino initially assumed power via the 1986 People Power Revolution, an extra-constitutional (revolutionary) transfer. However, she then governed under the “Freedom Constitution” (Proclamation No. 3, March 25, 1986), and the 1987 Constitution was ratified by plebiscite, which legitimized her presidency. The Philippine Supreme Court recognized her government’s legitimacy (e.g., Lawyers League v. Aquino, 1986).

claim: In North Carolina, US absentee voters had no way to track whether their ballots were ever delivered in the November US 2018 congressional election.
response_text: FALSE.  North Carolina’s State Board of Elections provided an online Voter Search/absentee ballot lookup in 2018 that showed whether an absentee ballot was received and accepted by the county board. While there wasn’t package-style postal tracking then, voters could verify delivery/acceptance status online.

claim: Buncombe County Sheriff Quentin Miller says an ICE detainer request is not a valid warrant.
response_text: TRUE.  Sheriff Quentin Miller has repeatedly said his office will not hold people on ICE detainers without a judge-signed warrant, stating that an ICE detainer is a request, not a valid judicial warrant or court order. This has been his public policy since taking office in 2019.

claim: Blake Griffin, a forward for the Detroit Pistons basketball team, will pay $258,000 per month in child support to his ex Brynn Cameron.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely circulated $258,000-per-month figure came from a tabloid report in 2018 and was later disputed. Reputable outlets (e.g., People, TMZ) reported that the actual child-support amount was much lower (reported around $32,000/month), and there’s no court order confirming $258,000 per month.

claim: Trump promised during the campaign not to cut Social Security or Medicare, his proposed 2019 budget included cuts of $500 billion to Medicare and $72 billion to Social Security
response_text: TRUE.  - Trump repeatedly pledged in 2016 not to cut Social Security or Medicare. - His FY2019 budget proposal (released in 2018) called for large Medicare reductions over 10 years—commonly reported at about $554 billion (so “$500 billion” is a rounded figure)—largely via provider payment changes. - It also proposed about $72 billion in cuts to Social Security programs, chiefly Social Security Disability Insurance, not old‑age benefits.  Note: These were proposed “savings” in the budget and were not all enacted, but they were included in the proposal.

claim: In the United States right now, we have more income and wealth inequality than any other country on Earth.
response_text: FALSE.  By standard measures, the U.S. is highly unequal but not the most unequal globally. For income, World Bank/OECD Gini coefficients show countries like South Africa, Brazil, Colombia, and Namibia with substantially higher inequality than the U.S. For wealth, global reports (e.g., Credit Suisse/UBS) put the U.S. among the most unequal, but several countries (such as Russia and South Africa) have equal or higher wealth inequality. The U.S. ranks near the top among rich countries, but not above every country on Earth.

claim: Youth unemployment in South Africa is amongst the highest in the world.
response_text: TRUE.  Statistics South Africa reports youth (15–24) unemployment around 55–65% in recent years, and even the broader 15–34 group is about 40–50%. ILO/World Bank comparisons show this is among the highest rates globally, with only a few countries (e.g., Namibia, Eswatini, Palestine) in a similar range.

claim: There is no human-caused climate change
response_text: FALSE.  Extensive evidence shows humans are the dominant cause of recent climate change. The IPCC concludes it is “unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.” Key lines of evidence include: - CO2 rose from ~280 ppm preindustrial to over 420 ppm today, with isotopic fingerprints tying much of it to fossil fuels. - Climate models reproduce observed warming only when human greenhouse gases and aerosols are included; natural factors alone cannot. - Consistent “fingerprints” (e.g., stratospheric cooling with surface warming, nights warming faster than days, rising ocean heat content) match greenhouse-gas forcing.

claim: The BJP government aims to cover 28.5 lakh hectare area under irrigation
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2016–17, the BJP-led central government (under PMKSY/AIBP) set a target to bring about 2.85 million hectares (28.5 lakh ha) under irrigation as part of fast-tracking 99 priority irrigation projects intended to ultimately create roughly 7.6 million hectares of irrigation potential. Note: If the claim refers to a specific state or a different period, context could vary, but this central-government target matches the figure.

claim: French President Emmanuel Macron said the UK must take its share of migrants, 300,000 now immediately and up to 100,000 every year until the situation is resolved if it wants to remain in the EU.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of President Emmanuel Macron ever saying this. Fact‑checkers have debunked the quote. The EU’s 2015 refugee relocation plans involved far smaller numbers, and the UK had opt-outs from such schemes. Moreover, Macron became president in 2017, after the UK’s 2016 referendum, so the “if it wants to remain in the EU” framing doesn’t fit the timeline.

claim: In 1963 Bernie Sanders was arrested for throwing eggs at black civil rights protestors.
response_text: FALSE.  Bernie Sanders was arrested in 1963 in Chicago while protesting school segregation as a student activist with CORE. He was charged with resisting arrest after refusing to move during a civil rights demonstration. The “egg‑throwing at black protestors” claim is a debunked hoax that misattributes a different 1963 photo to Sanders.
