claim: The BJP government has uploaded an infographic on their 48-months portal that makes claims about the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY). one such claim is - Facilitating farmers for installing solar water pumps in field irrigation.
response_text: TRUE  Reason: The “48 Months” achievements portal showcased infographics on various schemes, including PMKSY, and one of the listed bullets mentioned facilitating farmers to install solar water pumps for irrigation. (Whether solar pumps properly fall under PMKSY is a separate issue; PM-KUSUM later became the main solar-pump scheme.) Minor uncertainty only about exact wording, but such a claim appeared on the portal’s PMKSY infographic.

claim: The BJP government has uploaded an infographic on their 48-months portal that makes claims about the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY). one such claim is - Dedicated micro irrigation fund of 5000 crore rupees.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In May 2018, the Union Cabinet approved a dedicated Micro Irrigation Fund (MIF) of Rs 5,000 crore with NABARD under PMKSY. The BJP’s “48 months” achievements portal featured an infographic on PMKSY that listed this as an achievement. (PIB release, 16 May 2018).

claim: French President Emmanuel Macron said the UK will only be allowed to stay in the EU if they fully adopt all EU rules and regulations including adopting the Euro within six months of stopping Brexit.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Macron saying this. Under the ECJ’s 2018 Wightman ruling, the UK could have unilaterally revoked Article 50 and remained an EU member on its existing terms, including its opt-outs (notably from the euro). Adopting the euro is not required to “stay,” and in any case cannot be forced or done within six months (it requires meeting convergence criteria and at least two years in ERM II).

claim: Sen. Kamala Harris is the aunt of “Empire” actor Jussie Smollett
response_text: FALSE.  Kamala Harris is not related to Jussie Smollett. Harris has one sibling, her sister Maya Harris. Smollett’s parents are Janet (née Harris) Smollett and Joel Smollett; Janet Harris is not related to Kamala Harris. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) have debunked this rumor.

claim: The Jobs Fund in South Africa is a vital component to private sector job creation. The fund has created well over 200,000 jobs since its inception.
response_text: TRUE  - The Jobs Fund (a National Treasury initiative launched in 2011) co‑finances private-sector–led projects and, in official reports and reviews, has claimed cumulative job creation well above 200,000 since inception (often distinguishing permanent and short‑term jobs, but totals exceed 200k). - The phrase “vital component” is subjective, but the quantitative part of the claim aligns with reported figures.  Note: Exact totals vary by whether permanent vs short‑term jobs are counted and are largely self‑reported by projects.

claim: The trade balance between the US and the EU is $151 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: “Trade balance” is ambiguous, but on the latest full-year data it isn’t $151B. In 2023 the U.S. ran about a $160B goods deficit with the EU (Census), and when including services the overall U.S.–EU trade deficit was roughly $80–100B (BEA). $151B aligns only with some older goods-only figures; it’s not the current balance. Uncertainty: exact numbers vary by year, EU definition (EU‑27), and whether services are included.

claim: The South African Jobs Fund has created well over 200,000 jobs since its inception.
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: The National Treasury’s Jobs Fund (launched in 2011) reports cumulative job opportunities well above 200,000 when combining permanent and short‑term jobs. Some official updates place the total in the 230k–260k range. If counting only permanent jobs, the figure is nearer to ~180k–200k, but the claim as stated (without specifying permanence) is broadly accurate. Uncertainty: depends on whether “jobs” is taken to mean permanent only.

claim: Jobs for 1.1 million young people are supported by the Employment Tax Incentive (ETI) scheme in South Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The 1.1 million figure was an older estimate (around 2017–2018). More recent National Treasury/SARS reports state that, since its 2014 inception, the ETI has supported well over that number (roughly 1.7–2.0 million young people by 2022–2023). So saying “1.1 million … are supported” is outdated and understates the scale. (Exact totals vary by whether figures are cumulative or average per period.)

claim: A meme that asks "When will liberals check out the Quran?" lists nine supposed quotes from the Muslim holy book.
response_text: TRUE.  A widely shared meme with the caption “When will liberals check out the Quran?” circulates online and lists nine supposed quotes/verses from the Quran. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact) have examined it and noted issues with context and translation.

claim: Man who cited religious reasons for not paying his income taxes “has won a historic lawsuit against the IRS.”
response_text: FALSE.  Courts have consistently rejected claims that religious beliefs allow someone to refuse to pay federal income tax. The Supreme Court held in United States v. Lee (1982) that neutral tax laws apply despite religious objections, and there is no religious exemption from income tax (limited exemptions exist only for certain Social Security/Medicare taxes under statute). Viral posts sometimes miscast procedural rulings in individual cases, but no court has granted a blanket religious right to not pay income taxes or a “historic” win against the IRS on that basis.

claim: Genetically modified yeast, animal, bacterial and viral DNA in vaccines can be incorporated into the recipient’s DNA causing unknown genetic mutations.
response_text: FALSE.  - Licensed vaccines do not alter your DNA. mRNA vaccines contain no DNA and do not enter the nucleus. Adenoviral‑vector vaccines deliver DNA that remains episomal (non‑integrating) and lacks enzymes needed for genome integration; integration has not been observed at meaningful rates in humans. - While tiny amounts of residual DNA from production cell lines can be present, regulations strictly limit it to trace, highly fragmented pieces that are rapidly degraded and lack the capacity to integrate or function. Decades of vaccine use and surveillance show no evidence of vaccine DNA incorporating into recipients’ genomes or causing mutations.  Uncertainty: In theory, random integration of small DNA fragments could occur at vanishingly low frequencies, but this has not been demonstrated to cause harm with vaccines and is mitigated by strict limits and fragmentation.

claim: Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez puts out a press release on Twitter saying that a Alabama mother who supports ISIS is a bigger hero than our U.S veterans and should be welcomed home.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez issuing any press release or tweet praising an ISIS-supporting Alabama woman or calling her a “bigger hero than our U.S. veterans.” This claim traces to fabricated/satirical posts; fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) have debunked it.

claim: Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez puts out a press release on Twitter demanding that President Trump should be blocked from stopping the return of a heroic mother from Alabama who supports ISIS.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim appears to be a fabricated/satirical story tied to the 2019 case of Hoda Muthana, the Alabama woman who joined ISIS. There is no record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez issuing a press release or tweeting that Trump should be blocked from preventing Muthana’s return, nor did she call Muthana “heroic.” Fact-checkers debunked similar viral posts at the time.

claim: Formaldehyde is in vaccines and causes cancer in humans among other issues and is banned from vaccines in most European countries
response_text: FALSE.  - Fact: Trace formaldehyde is used in some vaccines to inactivate viruses/toxins; tiny residual amounts may remain after purification. - Cancer context: Formaldehyde is classified as carcinogenic to humans based on high, chronic inhalation exposures (e.g., certain workplaces), not on the minute amounts in vaccines. There’s no evidence that vaccine trace levels cause cancer. - Regulation: It is not banned from vaccines in European countries. The EU/EMA permits its controlled use, with strict limits, and many EU-licensed vaccines list formaldehyde as an excipient.  So while formaldehyde can be present in vaccines, the cancer claim is misapplied to vaccine exposures, and the “banned in most European countries” part is false.

claim: Today’s minimum wage worker making $7.25 an hour has less buying power than a minimum wage worker in the 1960s."
response_text: TRUE.  By CPI inflation adjustments, the federal minimum wage peaked at $1.60 in 1968, worth roughly $13–$14 in 2024 dollars. Even early-1960s levels ($1.00–$1.25) equal about $10–$12+ today. That’s well above the current federal $7.25, so today’s $7.25 buys less than the 1960s minimum wage did. (Exact amounts vary slightly by inflation index/year.)

claim: Mercury (aka thimerosal or thiomersal) is in vaccines and can damage the brain, gut, liver, bone marrow, nervous system, and kidneys. It is linked to autoimmune disorders, including autism.
response_text: FALSE.  - Thimerosal (thiomersal) is an ethylmercury-containing preservative, not the same as elemental “mercury.” It has been removed from routine childhood vaccines in the U.S./EU since the early 2000s; only some multi‑dose influenza vials still use it. Many vaccines are thimerosal‑free. - Ethylmercury from thimerosal is cleared from the body quickly. Extensive studies and reviews by CDC, FDA, WHO, and the Institute of Medicine/National Academies find no credible evidence that thimerosal in vaccines causes brain, gut, liver, bone marrow, nervous system, or kidney damage at vaccine doses. - Large epidemiologic studies show no link between thimerosal-containing vaccines and autism or autoimmune disorders. Autism rates did not decrease after thimerosal was removed from most childhood vaccines. - While high doses of certain mercury compounds can be toxic, the amounts used in some vaccines have not been shown to cause harm.

claim: Farmers are declaring bankruptcy "in record numbers" and "the median income for U.S. farm households was -$1,548 in 2018."
response_text: FALSE.  - “Record numbers” of farmer bankruptcies is inaccurate. Chapter 12 farm bankruptcies did rise in 2018–2019, but were not at all-time records; they were the highest in several years (e.g., since around 2011), far below the 1980s farm crisis. - The -$1,548 figure refers to median farm income from farming operations, not total household income. In 2018, the median total income for farm households was positive (around the mid-$70,000s), while the median farm income component was slightly negative.

claim: Alexandreia Ocasio-Coretz posted in a tweet, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
response_text: FALSE.  No such tweet exists from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The claim originated from a fabricated meme circulating in 2019 about Hoda Muthana (the Alabama woman who joined ISIS). Fact-checkers, including Snopes and PolitiFact, found no record of this on her account or in archives. She did not call Muthana a hero or compare her to veterans.

claim: Farm credit target raised to 11 lakh crore rupees for 2018-19
response_text: TRUE.  In the Union Budget 2018–19, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley announced that the agricultural/farm credit target would be raised to Rs 11 lakh crore (up from Rs 10 lakh crore in 2017–18).

claim: Countries are putting bad people into the United States visa lottery program.
response_text: FALSE.  The U.S. Diversity Visa (DV) lottery is run by the U.S. Department of State. Individuals apply directly; foreign governments do not nominate or “put” people into the program. Winners are selected randomly and must pass U.S. security and background checks before receiving a visa. While fraud can occur, there’s no evidence that countries are inserting “bad people” into the lottery.

claim: China has a death penalty for drug dealers
response_text: TRUE.  China’s Criminal Law (e.g., Article 347) allows the death penalty for severe drug offenses such as smuggling, trafficking, transporting, or manufacturing narcotics in large quantities or with aggravating circumstances. It is not automatic for all “dealers,” but courts do impose and carry out death sentences in serious drug cases.

claim: Former President Barack Obama would have gone to war with North Korea.
response_text: FALSE.  This is a counterfactual claim with no evidence. Obama’s North Korea approach was “strategic patience”: sanctions, pressure, deterrence, and missile defense (e.g., THAAD), while saying “all options” were on the table. He did not initiate or prepare to initiate war, and his record shows caution rather than a move toward military conflict. Uncertainty: counterfactuals can’t be proven, but available evidence points against it.

claim: President Obama put more debt on the USA than any president in the history of our country combined.
response_text: FALSE.  By gross federal debt (the common measure), the debt was about $10.6 trillion when Obama took office (Jan 2009) and about $19.9 trillion when he left (Jan 2017)—an increase of roughly $9.3 trillion. All prior presidents combined had accumulated about $10.6 trillion, which is more than Obama’s added amount.  Note: Using a narrower metric (debt held by the public), Obama’s increase exceeded the prior total, but the claim as stated is a sweeping overstatement.

claim: The US Government may be using parts of one of the national emergencies that (President Barack Obama) signed having to do with cartels, criminal cartels
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2011, President Obama issued Executive Order 13581, declaring a national emergency under IEEPA against “significant transnational criminal organizations,” which includes criminal cartels. That emergency has been renewed by subsequent presidents and is used to authorize measures like sanctions and asset blocking. So it’s accurate that the U.S. government may be using parts of that Obama-era national emergency related to cartels.

claim: When countries put people into the diversity visa lottery program, they’re putting some very bad people in the lottery
response_text: FALSE.  Individuals apply themselves to the U.S. Diversity Visa lottery; foreign governments do not “put” people into it. Entries are randomly selected by the U.S. State Department, and selectees must pass eligibility requirements and extensive security/background checks before any visa is issued.

claim: A big majority of the big drugs, the big drug loads, don't go through ports of entry. They can't go through ports of entry.
response_text: FALSE.  CBP data consistently show that the majority of hard drugs (especially fentanyl, heroin, and methamphetamine) seized at the southern border are interdicted at official ports of entry, typically hidden in passenger cars and commercial trucks—often driven by U.S. citizens. While seizures aren’t a perfect proxy for total flows, the best available evidence contradicts the claim. Marijuana historically saw more between‑port smuggling, but that’s not the main “big drug” today. The assertion that big drug loads “can’t” go through ports is plainly incorrect.

claim: Sayfullo Saipov, the Uzbekistan-born suspect on trial for the 2017 truck attack in New York, US, is an example of chain migration, ie bringing many people into the US.
response_text: FALSE.  Saipov entered the U.S. in 2010 through the Diversity Immigrant Visa (“green card lottery”), not via family-based “chain migration.” There’s no public evidence he subsequently sponsored multiple relatives. While a principal immigrant can have a spouse/children as derivatives on the same case, that isn’t what “chain migration” typically refers to, and reports indicate his children were born in the U.S. Minor uncertainty remains about his wife’s pathway, but the claim that he is an example of “bringing many people” through chain migration is unsupported.

claim: Drug loads can't enter the US through US ports of entry.
response_text: FALSE.  Drugs are routinely smuggled through official U.S. ports of entry—land crossings, seaports, airports, and international mail/express facilities. CBP and DEA data show most fentanyl seized at the southwest border is intercepted at ports of entry, often hidden in cars, trucks, or cargo. The absolute claim that drug loads “can’t” enter via ports is incorrect.

claim: The U.S. may be using one of the national emergencies that (President Barack Obama) signed having to do with cartels, criminal cartels.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2011, President Obama declared a national emergency via Executive Order 13581 targeting “transnational criminal organizations” (including drug cartels), enabling sanctions and asset blocking under IEEPA. That emergency has been renewed and used for sanctions actions. Note: it concerns financial/legal measures against TCOs, not broad domestic measures like building a wall.

claim: In China, a drug dealer gets a thing called the death penalty. Our criminal list, a drug dealer gets a thing called, how about a fine?
response_text: FALSE.  - China does allow the death penalty for serious drug offenses (e.g., trafficking or manufacturing large quantities such as 50+ grams of heroin/meth), though it’s not automatic. - In most countries, including the U.S., drug dealing/trafficking is a serious felony punishable by substantial prison terms (often years to life) in addition to fines—not “a fine” alone.  Uncertainty: The claim’s “our” is unspecified, but virtually no modern jurisdiction punishes drug dealing only with a fine.

claim: US President Obama was ready to have gone to war with North Korea.
response_text: FALSE.  Obama’s North Korea policy was “strategic patience,” focused on sanctions, deterrence, and diplomacy. While the U.S. maintained defense commitments to South Korea and Japan, there’s no credible evidence Obama was prepared to initiate war with North Korea; his administration consistently warned of the catastrophic costs of such a conflict.

claim: The US has chain migration, where a family member can bring in 20+ people and that is what happened on the West Side highway. A young man killed eight people and brought in many people because of chain migration.
response_text: FALSE.  - The 2017 West Side Highway attacker, Sayfullo Saipov, entered the U.S. in 2010 via the Diversity Visa (green-card lottery), not through family-based “chain migration.” - Claims that he “brought in 20+ people” were debunked; DHS later clarified that a cited “23” figure referred to people for whom he appeared as a point of contact, not beneficiaries he sponsored. There’s no evidence he brought in many people. - U.S. family-based immigration lets citizens and green-card holders sponsor certain close relatives under strict categories and long backlogs; one person cannot simply bring in “20+” relatives.

claim: The U.S. will have a national emergency and will then be sued in the Ninth Circuit.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: It’s a prediction about future events with no timeframe, so it isn’t currently verifiable. While national emergencies and subsequent lawsuits in the Ninth Circuit have occurred in the past, the claim as stated cannot be confirmed as true now. Uncertainty: unverifiable prediction.

claim: Lawsuits challenging the emergency order to secure funding for a border wall shouldn't be heard in the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.
response_text: FALSE.  Challenges to a federal action can be filed where a plaintiff resides or where a substantial part of the events occurred (28 U.S.C. § 1391(e)). Several plaintiffs (e.g., California, Sierra Club) filed in the Northern District of California, making venue proper there; appeals from that district go to the Ninth Circuit (28 U.S.C. § 1294). Indeed, the Ninth Circuit heard Sierra Club v. Trump and related cases. There is no requirement that such cases be heard elsewhere (e.g., D.C. Circuit or Fifth Circuit).

claim: You have the lottery — It’s a horror show. Because when countries put people into the lottery, they’re not putting you in. They’re putting some very bad people in the lottery. It’s common sense.
response_text: FALSE.  - In the U.S. Diversity Visa (DV) lottery, foreign governments do not “put people into the lottery.” Individuals from eligible countries apply themselves; the U.S. State Department runs a random selection. - Applicants must meet education/work requirements and pass security, criminal, and medical checks before any visa is issued. - There’s no evidence that countries use the DV lottery to send “very bad people,” and analyses of DV immigrants show no elevated crime risk.  Sources: U.S. State Department DV program instructions; FactCheck.org and PolitiFact fact-checks of similar claims; Cato Institute analyses.

claim: In the US a drug dealer gets a fine.
response_text: FALSE.  In the U.S., drug dealing is a criminal offense typically punishable by incarceration, with possible fines and asset forfeiture. Penalties vary by drug, quantity, and prior record; under federal law (e.g., 21 U.S.C. § 841) distribution can carry years to life in prison, with fines often in addition—not just a fine.

claim: President Donald Trump will sign a national emergency which has been signed many times before. It's been signed by other presidents from 1977 or so, it gave the presidents the power. There's rarely been a problem.
response_text: TRUE.  - The National Emergencies Act was passed in 1976 and took effect in 1977, giving presidents a formal framework to declare national emergencies. - Presidents have declared many such emergencies since then (dozens; over 50 by 2019), most involving sanctions and drawing limited controversy. - Caveat: Using an emergency to reprogram funds for a border wall was unusual and did face significant legal and congressional pushback, so “rarely been a problem” is subjective.

claim: You have chain migration. Where a bad person comes in, brings 22 or 23 or 35 of his family members, because he has his mother, his grandmother, sister, cousin, uncle. They are all in. You know what happened on the west side highway? That young wise guy drove over and killed eight people... He had many people brought in because he was in the United States.
response_text: FALSE.  - U.S. family-based immigration doesn’t allow sponsoring cousins, uncles, or grandparents; only certain close relatives (spouses, minor children, parents of U.S. citizens, some adult children and siblings) can be petitioned, often after long waits. The idea that one person routinely brings “22, 23 or 35” relatives is unsupported; studies show far smaller averages. - The West Side Highway attacker, Sayfullo Saipov, entered via the Diversity Visa Lottery, not through “chain migration.” Government officials said there was no evidence he had brought in large numbers of relatives; claims he sponsored dozens were refuted. At most, he could have sponsored a spouse/children, not the broad list cited.  Uncertainty: He may have later brought or married a spouse, but not “many” relatives, and not cousins/uncles/grandparents.

claim: The U.S. may be using one of the national emergencies that President Barack Obama signed having to do with cartels, criminal cartels.
response_text: TRUE.  In 2011, President Obama declared a national emergency against transnational criminal organizations via Executive Order 13581, targeting groups including drug cartels (e.g., Los Zetas). That authority has been renewed and used by the U.S. government to sanction cartel-linked entities, so the claim is accurate.

claim: Beto O’Rourke said, "If I could throw two kinds of people in the garbage it would be the elderly and wounded veterans. When a tool breaks, you don’t fix it; you throw it in the damn trash."
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (speech, interview, video, transcript, or news report) of Beto O’Rourke saying this. The quote originated as a fabricated meme from satirical/hoax pages and has been debunked by fact‑checkers.

claim: Net migration to the UK could be 100,000 higher after Brexit under the government’s plans.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Official analysis of the government’s post‑Brexit immigration plans (Home Office White Paper/impact assessment and MAC advice) suggested EU migration would fall substantially and any rise in non‑EU skilled migration would be much smaller, yielding a flat or lower overall net migration—not an increase of 100,000. Claims of a +100,000 rise came from speculative external estimates, not supported by the government’s modelling. Uncertainty remains because flows depend on behaviour, but the best evidence didn’t back a +100k increase.

claim: Green New Deal would eliminate air travel
response_text: FALSE.  The 2019 Green New Deal resolution does not ban or eliminate air travel. It calls for reducing transportation emissions and investing in clean transit and high‑speed rail. A separate, quickly retracted FAQ from a sponsor’s office mentioned making air travel “less necessary,” but that language was not in the resolution and had no binding force.

claim: Mississippi passed the 5-71-226 Anti-Youth Subversion Act banning talking to minors about atheist Richard Dawkins.
response_text: FALSE.  - No Mississippi law exists titled “Anti-Youth Subversion Act,” nor is there a Mississippi statute numbered 5-71-226 (that numbering style matches Arkansas Code). - There is no record of any Mississippi law banning discussion of Richard Dawkins with minors. - A law singling out discussion of a specific person’s views would be an obvious First Amendment violation.

claim: Prior to 2019, South Korea was paying $500 million a year under a cost-sharing deal that helps fund American military forces in that country..
response_text: FALSE.  Under the 2014–2018 Special Measures Agreement, South Korea contributed roughly 920–960 billion won per year—about $800–900 million depending on exchange rates. In 2019 the figure rose to about 1.04 trillion won (roughly $920 million). The $500 million claim substantially understates what South Korea was already paying prior to 2019.

claim: The US trade deficit has decreased during US President Trump's term of office.
response_text: FALSE.  Using the overall U.S. trade balance in goods and services, the deficit rose during Trump’s term. It was about $500 billion in 2016 (pre-term), increased in 2017–2018, dipped slightly in 2019, then widened to roughly $679 billion in 2020—its highest since 2008. Net result: larger deficit at the end of his term than at the start. (Sources: U.S. BEA/Census trade data.)

claim: There were 1,200 murders in 2018 in Juarez, Mexico compared with 23 just across the border in El Paso, Texas, US, due to the construction of the border fence.
response_text: FALSE.  - The numbers are roughly right: Ciudad Juárez recorded about 1,200–1,250 homicides in 2018, and El Paso had about 23. - But attributing the difference to the border fence is not supported. El Paso has been one of the safest large U.S. cities since before the modern fence (built mostly post‑2006), and research doesn’t show the fence as the causal factor behind the homicide gap; disparities are driven by broader differences in institutions, policing, and cartel violence.

claim: Actor and legendary comedian Bill Murray has died.
response_text: FALSE. There are no credible reports from major news outlets that Bill Murray has died; he is widely reported to be alive. Death hoaxes about him circulate periodically.

claim: A terminally ill 17-year-old and HIV-positive, Jeffrey Jones, requests oral sex from a porn star as his final wish, hoping to get it fulfilled by the Make-A-Wish foundation.
response_text: FALSE.  This story originated on fake/satire sites and has no credible reporting. The Make-A-Wish Foundation does not grant sexual or illegal requests, and a 17-year-old’s sexual encounter with a porn performer would be unlawful. Fact-checkers have debunked this claim.

claim: A diet based on your blood type fights fatigue.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence does not support “blood type” diets. A 2013 systematic review found no credible studies showing benefits of eating by blood type, and a 2014 study showed no link between ABO blood type and response to “blood-type” diets on health markers. No trials show such diets reduce fatigue. Any energy improvements likely come from general healthier eating, not blood type matching.

claim: Vice-Presidential candidate of the Peoples’ Democratic Party (PDP), Peter Obi’s Convoy Was Attacked In Abuja Market, Nigeria.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports confirmed such an attack. Fact-checkers in 2018 debunked viral posts claiming Peter Obi’s convoy was attacked in an Abuja market while he was PDP vice‑presidential candidate; the circulating video was miscaptioned/older and unrelated. Campaign and local sources said no attack occurred. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Peter Obi was almost killed during an attack on his convoy in Abuja Market.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports from Nigerian mainstream media, Peter Obi’s team, or the FCT police of an attack on his convoy in an Abuja market, let alone that he was “almost killed.” The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated social‑media rumor. (Low uncertainty.)

claim: For 50 years, prior to 2019, only 2.3 million Kenyans were connected to electricity.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “2.3 million” figure refers to Kenya Power customer connections around 2013 (about 50 years after independence), and it counts customer accounts/households—not individual Kenyans. By 2019, Kenya had roughly 6.7–7 million grid customers, with many more people having access. So the claim misstates both the timeline and the unit. (Minor uncertainty on exact annual totals by source, but the order of magnitude is clear.)

claim: The Kenyan railway was planned by the government for 30 years.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The modern Standard Gauge Railway (Mombasa–Nairobi) was conceived in the late 2000s (feasibility around 2009), contracted in 2012–2013, and built 2013–2017—far short of 30 years of government planning. The colonial-era Uganda Railway (1890s) also was planned over just a few years before construction. Uncertainty: the claim is vague about which railway, but no major Kenyan railway fits a 30-year government planning timeline.

claim: The Kenyan government have connected 6.9 million people to electricity in the last five years.
response_text: FALSE (likely understated)  Reason: Kenya’s electrification expanded much faster than that. Kenya Power’s customer base grew by several million connections over recent five-year periods (e.g., roughly from about 6.7 million in 2018 to over 9 million by 2023). Using Kenya’s average household size (~3.7–4 people), that implies on the order of 9–12+ million people newly connected—well above 6.9 million. Exact totals vary by the precise five-year window and whether off‑grid is included, but available data indicate the true figure is significantly higher than 6.9 million.

claim: The diaspora is the largest contributor to Kenya's foreign exchange.
response_text: TRUE.  - Central Bank of Kenya data show diaspora remittances have been Kenya’s largest single source of foreign exchange for several years, surpassing tea, horticulture, and tourism. - In 2023 remittances were roughly USD 4+ billion, compared with tourism (~USD 2–3 billion) and tea/horticulture (each ~USD 1–2 billion).  - Note: This refers to the largest single source; aggregating whole sectors could change rankings.

claim: It is a constitutional requirement in Kenya, that when the president is away, the deputy president must be in the country.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya’s Constitution does not require the Deputy President to be physically in the country whenever the President is away. It provides that the Deputy President acts as President when the President is absent or otherwise unable to perform the functions of the office (Article 147(3)), with certain limits on powers during such temporary incumbency (Article 134). There is no clause mandating the DP’s presence in Kenya or prohibiting both from being abroad at the same time, though it can raise practical concerns.

claim: In Kenya it is a constitutional requirement that when the president is away, the deputy president must be in the country
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya’s 2010 Constitution does not require the deputy president to remain in the country when the president is away. It provides that the deputy president is the president’s principal assistant and acts as president when the president is absent or temporarily incapacitated (Articles 134 and 147), but it does not mandate the DP’s physical presence in Kenya or state that one of the two must always be in the country. Any such arrangement is practice, not a constitutional requirement. Uncertainty: none.

claim: For 50 years only 2.3 million Kenyans were connected to electricity.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The 2.3 million figure refers to Kenya Power customer connections around 2013 (about 50 years after independence)—i.e., meters/accounts—not individual Kenyans. Each connection typically serves a household or institution. In 2013, Kenya’s electricity access rate was roughly 20–25% of a ~43 million population (about 8–11 million people), far more than 2.3 million. Note: If the claim intended “connections/customers,” 2.3 million is roughly correct.

claim: The number of people on health insurance in Kenya has increased from 3 million to 7 million in a record five years.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: NHIF administrative data show active principal members in Kenya rose from about 2.7–3.0 million in 2012/13 to roughly 7–7.7 million by 2017/18—about a five‑year span. Note: if “people on health insurance” is taken to mean all beneficiaries (members plus dependents), the totals are much higher; the 3→7 million figure refers to principal members.

claim: The current Kenyan government has connected 6.9 million people to electricity in the last five years.
response_text: FALSE.  - The current administration (Ruto, since Sept 2022) hasn’t been in office for five years, so it can’t credibly claim five-year results. - Kenya Power data show about 2–3 million additional customer accounts over roughly the last five years, not 6.9 million. Converting to people (using average household size) would be roughly 8–10 million, and much of that predates the current government. - The “6.9 million” figure resembles older Jubilee-era talking points about total customer accounts, not people connected in the last five years.  Minor uncertainty stems from differing ways of counting “people” vs “households” and access definitions.

claim: The diaspora, money sent by a person abroad to their home country, is the largest contributor to Kenya's foreign exchange.
response_text: TRUE.  Diaspora remittances have been Kenya’s largest single source of foreign exchange in recent years, surpassing tea, horticulture, and tourism. The Central Bank of Kenya reported remittances of roughly USD 4+ billion in 2022–2023, higher than earnings from those other sectors. Note: “diaspora” refers to people abroad; the money is “diaspora remittances.”

claim: For 50 years only 2.3 million Kenyans were connected to electricity.
response_text: FALSE.  The 2.3 million figure refers to electricity customer connections/households around 2013 (about 50 years after independence), per Kenya Power data—not to individual Kenyans. Each connection serves multiple people, so the number of Kenyans with access was far higher than 2.3 million.

claim: The Kenyan government has connected 6.9 million people to electricity between 2013 and 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya Power’s customer base grew from about 2.3 million in 2013 to about 6.8–7.0 million in 2018—an increase of roughly 4.4 million new household connections, not 6.9 million “people.” In people terms, the gain was far larger: World Bank data show electricity access rose from ~29% (2013) to ~64% (2018), implying roughly 18–20 million additional people with access. The “6.9 million people” figure does not match the period or the correct unit (households vs people).

claim: Diaspora remittances contributed upwards of KSh290.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The figure lacks a unit. Kenya’s diaspora remittances are in the hundreds of billions of shillings annually (e.g., about KSh 670 billion in 2023 per the Central Bank of Kenya). Saying “KSh290” (290 shillings) is meaningless/misleading. If the intent was KSh 290 billion, that should be stated; as written, the claim is inaccurate. Uncertain only if “billion” was omitted.

claim: The Kenyan government connected 6.9 million people to electricity supply, in the period 2014 to 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Kenya Power’s customer base grew from about 2.3 million in 2013/14 to roughly 7.6 million in 2018/19—an increase of about 5.3 million new connections. This aligns with access rising from roughly 36% (2014) to about 75% (2019), implying tens of millions gained access. claim: Official international Red cross records reveal the actual Concentration camp total death during World War 2 toll was 271,301.

It excludes the vast majority of victims—especially those murdered on arrival who were never registered—and many records were destroyed.  Scholarly consensus, supported by the ICRC and institutions like the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, holds that about six million Jews were murdered, with total Nazi camp and genocide victims numbering in the millions, far beyond 271,301.

claim: The Safe initiative was launched during the Ramaphosa administration in August last year
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: President Cyril Ramaphosa launched the Sanitation Appropriate for Education (SAFE) initiative in August 2018 to eliminate unsafe school pit latrines. If “last year” refers to 2018 (relative to a 2019 statement), the claim is accurate.

claim: In 2018, 10 million tourists visited South Africa
response_text: TRUE — South Africa recorded about 10.5 million international tourist arrivals in 2018 (Stats SA/South African Tourism), so “10 million” is a reasonable rounded figure.

claim: Over the past five years… President Cyril's government has built two new universities in South Africa
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The only “new” public universities created since 1994 are Sol Plaatje University (Kimberley) and the University of Mpumalanga (Mbombela), established in 2013 and opened to students in 2014—under President Jacob Zuma, not during Cyril Ramaphosa’s past five years. Ramaphosa’s government has announced plans for two more (an Ekurhuleni University of Science and Innovation and a Crime Detection/Policing university in Hammanskraal), but as of the last five years they have not been built or opened.

claim: South Africa has launched the Youth Employment Service, which is placing unemployed youth in paid internships in companies across the country
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2018, South Africa (through the Presidency, with business partners) launched the Youth Employment Service (YES). It places unemployed young people (18–35) into paid, 12‑month work experience positions with companies nationwide. While YES typically describes these as “work experience” jobs rather than formal “internships,” the substance of the claim is accurate.

claim: Over the past five years, more than R1.3 trillion has been invested to build (infrastructure included) hundreds of thousands of new homes in South Africa.
response_text: FALSE.  Official data don’t support a figure anywhere near R1.3 trillion. South African Reserve Bank/Stats SA series show total gross fixed capital formation in residential buildings has averaged well under R150 billion per year in recent years—adding up to roughly R600–700 billion over five years. Government human settlements grants are on the order of R30–40 billion per year (about R150–200 billion over five years), not trillions. Even allowing for related bulk infrastructure, the total remains far below R1.3 trillion. “Hundreds of thousands” of homes may be plausible, but the investment value is overstated.

claim: In 2017, we recorded an inflow of foreign direct investment amounting to R17 billion
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: UNCTAD data put South Africa’s 2017 FDI inflows at about US$1.3 billion, which is roughly R17 billion at the 2017 average exchange rate. Note: South African Reserve Bank figures differ due to methodology, but the R17bn figure aligns with UNCTAD and is commonly cited.

claim: Over 2014-2018, two new universities were built in South Africa
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: South Africa created two new, purpose‑built universities in this period: Sol Plaatje University (Northern Cape) and the University of Mpumalanga (Mpumalanga). They were legally established in 2013, took their first students in 2014, and their campuses were constructed in phases largely during 2014–2018 (with some works continuing thereafter). Note: Sefako Makgatho Health Sciences University was also established in 2014 but on an existing campus, not a new build.

claim: “We have launched the Youth Employment Service, which is placing unemployed youth in paid internships in companies across the country.”
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: South Africa’s Youth Employment Service (YES) was launched in 2018 as a partnership between government, business and labor. It places unemployed youth in paid, 12‑month work experiences with companies nationwide (often described as internships), and has placed tens of thousands of youths since launch.

claim: South Africa launched the Safe (Sanitation Appropriate For Education) initiative in August 2018
response_text: TRUE.  President Cyril Ramaphosa launched the Sanitation Appropriate for Education (SAFE) initiative in August 2018 (on 14 August) to eradicate unsafe school sanitation, particularly pit latrines, through government–private sector partnerships.

claim: Over the past five years, we’ve made significant progress with the provision of infrastructure. More than R1.3 trillion has been invested
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There’s no credible evidence that more than R1.3 trillion was actually invested in infrastructure over the past five years. Government figures often cited at this scale (around R1.3–R1.5 trillion) refer to economy‑wide investment pledges from the SA Investment Conferences, not realised infrastructure spend. Treasury data show public‑sector infrastructure outlays of roughly R250–R300 billion per year and Infrastructure Fund approvals/works under construction in the low hundreds of billions, well below R1.3 trillion over five years. Uncertainty: depending on how “infrastructure” is defined and summed across spheres, totals could approach this order of magnitude, but no official source confirms >R1.3 trillion actually invested.

claim: Over the past five years, we’ve made significant progress with the provision of infrastructure. More than R1.3 trillion has been invested.” the president said about South Africa
response_text: FALSE (with some uncertainty)  I can’t find a reliable record of President Ramaphosa saying that exact line about infrastructure. In recent speeches he typically cited “over R1.5 trillion” in investment commitments raised since 2018 via the SA Investment Conference (not specifically infrastructure spend). Government infrastructure figures he’s quoted elsewhere (Infrastructure Fund and project pipelines) are different and generally lower than R1.3 trillion in actual investment.

claim: Over the past five years South Africa have built two new universities.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: South Africa’s two most recent new universities—Sol Plaatje University (Kimberley) and the University of Mpumalanga (Mbombela)—were established in 2013 and opened in 2014, more than five years ago. In the last five years there have only been plans (e.g., a proposed University of Science and Innovation in Ekurhuleni and a crime-detection university in Hammanskraal), not completed new builds.

claim: Over the past five years, from 2013 - 2018, more than R1.3 trillion has been invested to build [infrastructure including electrifying] more than a million homes
response_text: TRUE.  - National Treasury data show public‑sector infrastructure spending averaged roughly R250–R300 billion a year; over 2013/14–2017/18 this totals about R1.3 trillion+.  - Department of Energy/municipal electrification figures for the same period add up to just over 1 million new household electricity connections.  Minor uncertainty: totals depend on including SOE and municipal capital spend, which Treasury does in its public-sector infrastructure figures.

claim: Over 700,000 children in South Africa [accessed] early childhood education in the last financial year of 2018
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: The Department of Social Development’s 2017/18 annual reporting (the last completed financial year before 2018/19 closed) recorded roughly 770,000–780,000 children accessing early childhood development services in South Africa, which is comfortably over 700,000. Minor uncertainty stems from differing definitions of “accessed” (e.g., subsidised/registered centres), but available official figures support the claim.

claim: Since South Africa launched the initiative, 699 schools have been provided with safe and appropriate sanitation facilities and projects, and a further 1,150 schools are either in planning, design or construction stages.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The figures were cited by President Ramaphosa in 2019 after launching the SAFE (Sanitation Appropriate for Education) initiative, but they conflated older ASIDI sanitation projects and work initiated before SAFE. Independent checks found far fewer schools had received new facilities under SAFE itself by that point, making the “since we launched” 699 (and the 1,150 in pipeline) misleading rather than a true SAFE-only outcome. Uncertainty: exact SAFE-only counts at that date vary by source, but they were well below 699.

claim: Over the past five years South Africa has built two new universities.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: South Africa’s last new public universities—University of Mpumalanga and Sol Plaatje University—were established around 2013–2014 (with first intakes in 2014). Two additional universities (a science and innovation university in Ekurhuleni and a policing/crime detection university in Hammanskraal) have been proposed in recent years, but they have not been built or opened in the past five years.

claim: Every month 17.5 million social grants are provided to South Africans.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: 17.5 million was roughly correct several years ago, but recent official figures show about 18.8–19.2 million permanent social grants paid monthly (2023–2024), and even more if the SRD R350 grant is included. Thus 17.5 million is an outdated, low estimate. Uncertainty: totals fluctuate slightly month to month.

claim: Trump tweeted on February 6, 2019 that he was “extremely happy with the leadership of President Ramaphosa, he is a great deal! Business community is happy too! And don’t make mistakes by voting useless leadership on this coming election!!”
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of such a tweet on February 6, 2019 (or any other date) in Trump’s verified Twitter history. Archives of his tweets for that day show posts about the State of the Union, not about Cyril Ramaphosa. Fact-checkers (e.g., Africa Check) have identified the circulating image/text as a fabricated tweet.

claim: The 1939 Cancer Act makes researching cancer cures illegal.
response_text: FALSE.  The Cancer Act 1939 does not ban researching cancer cures. Its key provision (Section 4) prohibits advertising claims to treat or cure cancer, aimed at preventing misleading promotions. Scientific research and clinical trials are legal and regulated under other laws (e.g., MHRA regulations).

claim: In 2019 there were more women in the US workforce than ever before."
response_text: TRUE.  BLS data show the number of women in the U.S. labor force hit a record high in 2019 (about 76.9 million). While women’s participation rate peaked around 1999, the absolute number was highest in 2019 due to population growth. (Assumes “workforce” means labor force/headcount.)

claim: According to a 2017 Doctors Without Borders Report, more than 30 percent of women are sexually assaulted on the trek to the border.
response_text: TRUE.  Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) reported in 2017 that about 31% of women surveyed had experienced sexual violence during their transit through Mexico toward the U.S. border. This figure comes from MSF’s report on migrants from Central America and refers to the surveyed population, not all migrants, but it supports the “more than 30 percent” claim.

claim: More than 12.5 crore Soil Health Cards have been distributed in India.
response_text: TRUE.  Government of India data report over 20 crore Soil Health Cards distributed across the first two cycles of the scheme (2015–19), well above 12.5 crore.

claim: Maternal mortality rates show that mothers, especially black mothers, risk death to give birth in America.
response_text: TRUE.  U.S. maternal mortality is real and higher than in peer countries. In 2022, the U.S. maternal mortality rate was about 22 per 100,000 live births overall, and Black mothers faced roughly 2.5–3 times the risk of White mothers (about 49.5 vs 19 per 100,000). These data (CDC/NCHS) show that mothers—especially Black mothers—do face a nontrivial risk of death related to pregnancy and childbirth in America.

claim: China produces 50,000 jobs every 24 hours.
response_text: FALSE.  Official figures show China has created about 12–14 million new urban jobs per year in recent years (e.g., ~13.5 million in 2018–2019; ~12.4 million in 2023), which averages roughly 33,000–38,000 per day. Hitting 50,000 per day would imply ~18 million a year—well above reported levels. Note: broader “gross” job churn isn’t published, but standard measures don’t support 50,000/day.

claim: We have created 5.3 million new jobs and importantly added 600,000 new manufacturing jobs.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - The line comes from Trump’s 2019 State of the Union. BLS data show that from his inauguration (Jan 2017) to about the time of the speech, total nonfarm jobs rose by roughly 4.9 million, not 5.3 million. The 5.3 million figure counts from Election Day, which isn’t the standard baseline. - Manufacturing jobs increased by about 450,000–470,000 over that period, not 600,000. So both numbers are overstated.

claim: The United States is now the number one producer of oil and natural gas anywhere in the world.
response_text: TRUE.  The U.S. has been the world’s largest producer of natural gas since about 2009 and became the largest producer of crude oil in 2018. It has remained at or near the top since, setting record oil output in 2023 while also leading in natural gas production (EIA/IEA data).

claim: Wages struggle to keep pace with the actual cost of living in America.
response_text: TRUE.  - For typical workers, inflation-adjusted wages have grown slowly over decades, while key costs—housing, healthcare, childcare, and education—have risen much faster (EPI, KFF, Federal Reserve/Case-Shiller). - The 2021–2022 inflation surge caused real wages to fall; although real wages improved in 2023–2024 as inflation cooled, they only modestly regained ground and housing/rent affordability remains at multi-decade lows. - Conclusion: While there are short periods of catch-up, overall wages have struggled to keep pace with the actual cost of living, especially for essentials.  Note: Exact results vary by time frame, region, and which wage measure is used.

claim: In 2016-17, 62% of income received by farmers in Northern Ireland came from the European Union.
response_text: FALSE.  Best official figures show EU support made up a much larger share of Northern Ireland farm income in 2016/17. DAERA’s Farm Business Survey indicates around 85–90% (commonly cited as 87%) of Farm Business Income in NI came from EU payments that year. The roughly 60–62% figure applies to the UK average, not specifically to Northern Ireland. Note: exact percentages vary by definition and farm type, but NI’s reliance was clearly higher than 62%.

claim: Since the Republican tax cuts became law, manufacturing plants are closing, layoffs are looming, and wages struggle to keep pace with the actual cost of living.
response_text: FALSE.  - After the 2017 Republican tax law took effect, U.S. manufacturing employment increased by hundreds of thousands in 2018–2019, and unemployment hit 50‑year lows. While some high‑profile plants (e.g., GM facilities) did close, that was not a broad, sector‑wide trend.   - Layoffs were not “looming” in aggregate during that period; jobless claims were historically low.   - Wages generally kept pace with or modestly outpaced inflation pre‑pandemic (real wages rose slightly in 2018–2019 per BLS). Real wages did fall during the 2021–2022 inflation spike, but that was driven by the pandemic-era shock, not the tax law.  Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics employment and earnings data; unemployment and jobless claims reports (2018–2019). Uncertainty: wording is broad and time‑open, but overall trend claims are misleading.

claim: IN 2016-17 80% of income received by farmers in Northern Ireland came from the European Union
response_text: TRUE.  DAERA’s Farm Business Survey for 2016–17 shows that EU CAP direct payments accounted for about 87% of Northern Ireland farm business income on average. So saying “80%” came from the EU is a conservative, broadly accurate summary. Note: this refers to farm business income; total household income for farm families can include off‑farm earnings and would differ.

claim: Richer, older men in England more likely to drink to excess.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: UK/England surveys (e.g., Health Survey for England; ONS Adult Drinking Habits) consistently find that men are more likely than women to exceed low-risk guidelines, prevalence is highest in middle-to-older age groups (around 45–64/55–64), and rates of regularly exceeding the 14‑unit weekly guideline are higher among higher‑income and managerial/professional households. Note: binge drinking on a single day is more common among younger adults, but regular “excess” drinking skews to older, richer men.

claim: Alcohol deaths in England are at a record high after 6 per cent rise in a year.
response_text: TRUE.  ONS data show alcohol-specific deaths in England rose by about 6% from 2021 to 2022, reaching the highest number on record. Note: this refers to alcohol-specific deaths (the standard ONS measure), not all deaths where alcohol is a contributing factor.

claim: For the first time in 65 years America is a net exporter of energy
response_text: TRUE — The U.S. became a net exporter of total energy in 2019, the first time since 1952, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The “65 years” figure is slightly off (it was about 67 years).

claim: Americans pay vastly more than people in other countries for the exact same drugs, often made in the exact same place
response_text: TRUE.  - Multiple studies find U.S. prices for the same brand‑name prescription drugs are much higher than in peer countries. A RAND analysis estimated U.S. drug prices average about 2.5–3.5 times those in other OECD nations, with insulin around 4x higher. House Ways & Means and other analyses report similar multiples. - While U.S. generics can be cheaper than abroad, the big differentials for brand‑name drugs dominate overall comparisons. - Many brand‑name medicines are made in global manufacturing plants that supply multiple countries, so the price gap isn’t due to different production sites; the same products from the same manufacturers (often the same facilities) sell for far less abroad.  Note: “Often made in the exact same place” is generally true for many brand‑name drugs, though manufacturing footprints vary by product.

claim: African-American, Hispanic-American and Asian-American unemployment have all reached their lowest levels ever recorded
response_text: TRUE.  BLS data show each group has hit its lowest rate on record: Black/African American (as low as 4.7% in Apr 2023; series since 1972), Hispanic/Latino (3.9% in Sept 2019; since 1973), and Asian (about 2.0% in 2019/2023; since 2000). Note: “ever recorded” refers to the period these data have been collected.

claim: The border city of El Paso, Texas, used to have extremely high rates of violent crime — one of the highest in the country, and considered one of our nation's most dangerous cities. Now, immediately upon its building, with a powerful barrier in place, El Paso is one of the safest cities in our country.
response_text: FALSE.  El Paso has been one of the safest large U.S. cities for decades, long before any border fencing was built. FBI crime data show its violent crime rate was already low and had been declining since the 1990s. The main border fence segments by El Paso were completed around 2008–2009; there was no “immediate” drop tied to the barrier—violent crime actually ticked up around that time before resuming longer-term declines. The city was never among the nation’s most dangerous, so the before/after portrayal is incorrect.

claim: India produces 450 jobs every 24 hours.
response_text: FALSE.  Even the narrowest official indicators show far more jobs than 450 per day. EPFO payroll data (a proxy for formal job creation) typically adds around 0.8–1.5 million net subscribers per month—about 25,000–50,000 per day. Broader surveys like the PLFS indicate multi‑million annual increases in employment, i.e., tens of thousands per day. Measurement methods vary, but all credible figures are orders of magnitude above 450/day.

claim: Nearly 5 million Americans have been lifted off food stamps.
response_text: TRUE (with context)  USDA data show SNAP enrollment fell by roughly 4–5 million during 2017–2019 (e.g., from about 42 million in 2017 to around 36–38 million by 2019). So “nearly 5 million” is numerically reasonable, though the decline largely reflects an ongoing post‑recession trend rather than people being “lifted off” by specific policies. Timing/months chosen affect the exact figure.

claim: One in five people aged 16 and over are drinking more than recommended levels.
response_text: TRUE.  In the UK, the recommended limit is no more than 14 units of alcohol per week. National surveys typically find about 20% of adults aged 16+ exceed this. For example, the Health Survey for England has reported around 21% (with higher rates in men than women). Figures vary slightly by year and region, but “one in five” is a fair rounded summary.

claim: Wages are rising at the fastest pace in decades with President Donald Trump in 2019.
response_text: FALSE.  In 2019, nominal wages did accelerate to about 3–3.5% year-over-year (e.g., BLS average hourly earnings, ECI), the fastest in roughly a decade. But wage growth was higher in the late 1990s/2000s (often 4%+ on comparable measures, and higher on the Employment Cost Index around 2000–2001). Real wage gains were also not at decades-long highs. So it was not the fastest pace “in decades,” just the fastest in about a decade.

claim: Secretary of State Mike Pompeo refused to meet with Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate for the People's Democratic Party, when the Nigerian politician visited the US.
response_text: FALSE.  Atiku Abubakar did visit the U.S. in January 2019, but there’s no official record that Mike Pompeo “refused” to meet him. The State Department said no meeting was scheduled, and Pompeo later spoke by phone with both Buhari and Atiku about Nigeria’s elections. So it’s accurate that no in‑person meeting occurred, but “refused to meet” overstates what is documented. (Some uncertainty stems from media speculation at the time.)

claim: Kenya Ports Authority is looking to hire 140 people, aged 18 - 35, who have graduated from a well recognised university between 2012 and 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  Kenya Ports Authority disowned a viral advert with those exact details, warning it was fake. KPA said any vacancies are announced only via its official website and mainstream media, not through such posts. (Slight uncertainty if a similarly worded legitimate program ever existed, but this specific claim matches a debunked hoax.)

claim: South African footballer Ekstein resigns from Kaizer Chiefs after fight with manager Middendorp
response_text: FALSE  Ekstein did leave Kaizer Chiefs in April 2019 after requesting to terminate his contract, but there’s no confirmed “fight” with coach Ernst Middendorp. Official statements and reliable reports cited contract issues; rumours of a bust‑up were denied.

claim: Atiku Abubaka, Nigerian presidential candidate, claimed Nigeria had 21 million unemployed young men and women in 2018.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During his 2018/19 campaign, Atiku Abubakar repeatedly said about 21 million Nigerian youths were unemployed, echoing NBS’s Q3 2018 figure of 20.9 million unemployed persons. Note: the 20.9 million covered all unemployed adults, not just “youth,” so his phrasing as “young men and women” was imprecise.

claim: South Africa has one of the highest dropout rates
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: South Africa does experience substantial school dropout after Grade 9, and only about half of a cohort completes Grade 12, which is high relative to other upper‑middle‑income countries. However, UNESCO/Stats SA data show lower-secondary dropout/out‑of‑school rates are low, and even at upper‑secondary age (15–17) the out‑of‑school share is around a quarter to a third—well below many low‑income countries where upper‑secondary non‑attendance exceeds 50–70%. So it is high for its peer group, but not “one of the highest” globally. (Some uncertainty stems from differing definitions of “dropout.”)

claim: 80%of the population continues to occupy less than 10% of the South African Land
response_text: FALSE.  This appears to conflate apartheid-era figures with the present. Under apartheid, about 13% of land (the “homelands”) was reserved for the Black majority (≈80% of the population). Today, while land ownership remains highly unequal, population “occupancy” is different: roughly two-thirds of South Africans live in urban areas (which cover a small share of land), and about a third live in the former homelands (≈13% of land). There is no credible current evidence that 80% of the population “continues to occupy” less than 10% of South Africa’s land. Uncertainty: definitions of “occupy” vary, but available data do not support this claim.

claim: Close to 40% of South Africans who need jobs are unemployed, meaning that more than nine million South Africans who need jobs and are capable of working cannot find employment
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: Using South Africa’s expanded (broad) definition of unemployment—which counts people who want work, are able to work, and include discouraged jobseekers—the unemployment rate has been around 41% in 2024, i.e., “close to 40%.” The number of people who want a job but can’t find one (unemployed plus discouraged work-seekers) is roughly 11–12 million, which is indeed “more than nine million.” Note: under the narrower official measure, the rate is ~32–33% with about 8–8.5 million unemployed.

claim: The post-1994 governments have cumulatively bought less than 7% of the targeted 30% of land meant for redistribution over a period of 25 years.
response_text: TRUE.  - The 30% target refers to redistributing about 30% of South Africa’s commercial farmland. - By roughly 2018–2020 (about 25 years post‑1994), government had acquired on the order of 4.8–5.5 million hectares for redistribution, out of ~82 million hectares of commercial farmland—about 5–7%. - Including restitution increases the total transferred to around 8–10%, but the 30% target pertains to redistribution specifically.  Minor uncertainty arises from varying official totals, but they consistently place redistribution below 7% at that point.

claim: Nigeria has 90 million people living in extreme poverty as of 2019
response_text: TRUE  Multiple 2019 estimates (e.g., World Poverty Clock) put Nigeria’s population living in extreme poverty (under $1.90/day, 2011 PPP) around 90 million—often cited in the 86–94 million range. Note: Nigeria’s official 2018/19 survey reported 82.9 million poor under the national line (a different metric), but international extreme-poverty estimates for 2019 were roughly 90 million. Uncertainty: figures vary by source and method.

claim: Nigeria earned US$383 billion from oil revenues in the four years preceding the Buhari government but there were no savings.
response_text: FALSE.  - NEITI audits show Nigeria’s oil-and-gas revenues to the federation for 2011–2014 at roughly $240–270 billion, well below $383 billion. - “No savings” is incorrect: at the May 2015 handover there were balances in fiscal savings vehicles—about $2 billion in the Excess Crude Account and roughly $1–1.5 billion in the Sovereign Wealth Fund—and foreign reserves were near $30 billion.  Conclusion: The amount is overstated by standard official measures, and there were savings. (Minor uncertainty on exact totals, but not on the direction.)

claim: Nigerian vice presidential candidate Peter Obi claimed that Nigeria had 90 million people living in extreme poverty.
response_text: TRUE.  As the PDP vice-presidential candidate in 2018/2019, Peter Obi repeatedly stated that roughly 90 million Nigerians were living in extreme poverty, referencing Brookings/World Poverty Clock estimates (often cited as 87–90 million). Minor uncertainty: he sometimes used 87 million in specific appearances.

claim: Russia will not place short or intermediate range weapons in Europe or other regions.
response_text: FALSE.  Russia already deploys short‑range, nuclear‑capable missile systems (e.g., Iskander‑M) in Europe, including Kaliningrad and, since 2023, in Belarus. After the INF Treaty collapsed, Moscow floated a conditional moratorium on land‑based intermediate‑range missiles, but it was not an unconditional pledge and has not prevented deployment of short‑range systems in Europe.

claim: Obama declared Flint water crisis a National Emergency and never fixed it.
response_text: FALSE.  - Obama did not declare a “National Emergency.” On Jan. 16, 2016 he approved a federal emergency declaration for Flint under the Stafford Act and denied a “major disaster” request (lead contamination isn’t eligible as a natural disaster). - He also directed federal aid (FEMA, HHS, EPA) and later signed legislation that provided substantial funding. The crisis wasn’t “fixed” by Obama alone—it required years of state/local work—but Flint’s water returned to meeting federal standards and lead service-line replacements proceeded in subsequent years.

claim: In Tshwane, the Democratic Alliance (DA) inherited a deficit of over R1 billion from the African National Congress (ANC) and turned it into a surplus in a year.
response_text: FALSE.  Audited financial statements show Tshwane did not have a deficit in the year the DA took over (2015/16, under ANC control). The city recorded a surplus that year, and it also recorded a surplus in 2016/17. Fact-checks (e.g., by Africa Check) found the DA’s “inherited deficit” claim to be inaccurate—any cited “deficit” refers to selective or different measures, not the audited overall result.

claim: The German press launched a massive campaign to discredit Russian and Russian language media.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There is no evidence of a coordinated, press-wide campaign in Germany to discredit all Russian or Russian‑language media. German outlets have reported on Russian state disinformation (e.g., RT/Sputnik, the 2016 “Lisa case”) and regulatory/EU actions restricted specific state-controlled channels after rule violations and the 2022 invasion. Those are government/regulatory decisions and routine journalism, not a unified “massive campaign” by the German press. Uncertainty arises only from the vagueness of “massive campaign.”

claim: Expanding Medicaid would bring 40,000 jobs to North Carolina.
response_text: TRUE — with caveat. Multiple credible analyses project job gains in this range if North Carolina expands Medicaid. A 2019 George Washington University/Milken Institute study (for Cone Health Foundation and Kate B. Reynolds) estimated about 37,200 additional jobs, and later updates and similar models often land around the high-30,000s to low-40,000s. It’s an estimate (not a guarantee), but “about 40,000 jobs” is consistent with the research.

claim: Germany owes £3.7 trillion of WWII debt.
response_text: FALSE.  Germany does not have a recognized or enforceable £3.7 trillion liability from WWII. Postwar reparations and debts were largely settled or waived through agreements such as the 1953 London Debt Agreement and the 1990 Two Plus Four Treaty. Germany completed remaining agreed payments (mostly unrelated to WWII reparations) in 2010. While some countries have voiced new or additional reparations claims, these are disputed and not legally acknowledged as debts, and no credible source supports the £3.7 trillion figure.

claim: More than 9 million eligible voters aren’t registered for South Africa’s 2019 elections.
response_text: TRUE.  IEC figures for 2019 show about 26.74 million registered voters. Estimates of eligible voting‑age citizens were around 35.9 million, implying roughly 9.1–9.2 million eligible but unregistered—i.e., more than 9 million. (This relies on population estimates, so the exact number is approximate.)

claim: The biggest donor for Mitch McConnell is the Russian oligarch that the GOP controlled Congress just lifted sanctions on.
response_text: FALSE  - The sanctions in question: In Jan. 2019 the U.S. Treasury lifted sanctions on three companies linked to Oleg Deripaska after restructuring; Deripaska himself remained sanctioned. The GOP‑led Senate voted against a resolution to block Treasury’s action, but Congress did not “lift” the sanctions. - The “biggest donor” claim: There is no evidence Deripaska donated to Mitch McConnell (foreign nationals are barred from donating). The donor often cited is Len Blavatnik, a U.S.-U.K. citizen with past business ties in Russia, who gave to McConnell‑aligned super PACs—but he was not McConnell’s largest donor. Far larger contributions came from others (e.g., the Adelsons to the Senate Leadership Fund).

claim: Microwaves from cell phones can pop popcorn
response_text: FALSE.  Cell phones do emit radio waves in the microwave band, but their power output is far too low (milliwatts to about 1–2 watts, unfocused and not contained) to heat kernels enough to pop. Popping popcorn typically requires hundreds of watts inside a resonant cavity (like a microwave oven). The viral videos showing phones popping popcorn were staged/hoaxes.

claim: The world’s first human head transplant has been successfully achieved
response_text: FALSE. There is no verified, peer-reviewed evidence of a successful human head transplant. Reports to date involve cadaver experiments or animal studies; reconnecting a human spinal cord and achieving functional recovery in a living person has not been accomplished.

claim: PZ is pulling out of Nigeria after 120 years.
response_text: TRUE — with a caveat. PZ Cussons announced plans to exit/sell its Africa operations, including Nigeria, after more than a century in the country. It’s a planned divestment rather than an abrupt shutdown, and completion depends on executing the sale and approvals.

claim: US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said that owning guns was not a right.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Ocasio-Cortez saying “owning guns was not a right.” This line has circulated in fabricated memes/satire. While she supports stricter gun regulations, she has not denied the existence of the Second Amendment right. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Alien Enthusiasts Shot Dead At Area 51.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports show “alien enthusiasts” being shot dead at Area 51. During the 2019 “Storm Area 51” event, there were no fatalities and only a few minor arrests. Viral claims of people being shot stem from hoax/satire posts. A separate shooting occurred at the Nevada National Security Site (a different facility), not Area 51, and did not involve “alien enthusiasts.”

claim: The question of Almajiris’ lack of primary or basic education are all local government problems.
response_text: FALSE.  Primary/basic education in Nigeria is a shared responsibility. The federal government (via UBEC) sets policy and co-funds UBE, states (through SUBEB) run and fund primary schools and teachers, and local governments (via LGEAs) handle local administration. The Almajiri issue also involves state legislation (e.g., Child Rights Act domestication/enforcement), federal initiatives (e.g., Almajiri model schools), and socio-economic factors beyond LG control. So it is not “all” a local government problem.

claim: Every country in the world that wants to undergo serious development borrows money. Our debt-to-GDP ratio of about 20% is one of the lowest in the world.
response_text: FALSE.  - The universal claim “every country that wants serious development borrows” is too strong. Some countries have developed while relying mainly on resource revenues or surpluses with little or no borrowing (e.g., Brunei, Kuwait in many years; jurisdictions like Hong Kong/Macau). Borrowing is common, but not universal or strictly necessary. - A debt-to-GDP ratio “about 20%” would be low relative to the global average (around 90% per IMF), but it is not uniquely low—several countries are in single digits or the teens. Also, without knowing which country “our” refers to, this part can’t be verified.

claim: Nigeria earned US$383 billion from oil revenues in the four years preceding our government [but] there were no savings.
response_text: FALSE.  - While oil receipts in 2011–2014 were very large (variously estimated in the $350–$380 billion range depending on whether you count export value or government take), there were savings when the Buhari administration took office in May 2015. - Nigeria’s Excess Crude Account still held roughly $2.0–$2.1 billion, the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (sovereign wealth fund) had about $1.4–$1.6 billion, and foreign exchange reserves were around $28–29 billion (CBN data). - So the “no savings” assertion is incorrect, even if the revenue figure is in the right ballpark.

claim: Chelsea Clinton said Satanism is a religion that deserves respect.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In a 2018 Twitter exchange, Chelsea Clinton wished the Church of Satan a happy new year and later said people can be civil and respectful toward fellow Americans, even if they don’t share their beliefs. She did not say “Satanism is a religion that deserves respect.” Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact) debunked that quote as a misrepresentation.

claim: More than R2 trillion was invested in South Africa in infrastructure projects over 10 years (2008-2018) to build more schools, clinics, roads and the freight logistics network.
response_text: TRUE.  National Treasury data show public‑sector infrastructure spending totalled about R2.2 trillion (nominal) over 2008/09–2017/18. This includes general government and state‑owned companies (e.g., Eskom, Transnet) on energy, transport/logistics, roads, water, schools and clinics. Sources: National Treasury Budget Review (2018/2019) and Stats SA’s Capital expenditure by the public sector.

claim: South Africa has invested more than R2 trillion in infrastructure projects over the past 10 years to build more schools, clinics, roads and the freight logistics network.
response_text: TRUE.  National Treasury’s budget reviews show cumulative public‑sector infrastructure spending (national, provincial, municipal and state‑owned companies) over the past decade exceeds R2 trillion in nominal terms, covering social infrastructure such as schools and clinics, and economic infrastructure like roads and freight/logistics. Note: this is cumulative nominal spend; annual investment has declined in recent years.

claim: On 11th January 2019 Wisconsin  property taxes are lower than they were in 2010.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Using the standard statewide metric (the property tax on a median‑valued home), Wisconsin’s 2018 tax bill—paid around Dec 2018/Jan 2019—was slightly lower (by roughly $100) than the 2010 bill, according to the Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau and multiple fact-checks. Note: totals vary by community and property, and the overall levy rose, but the median homeowner’s bill was lower than in 2010.

claim: Nigerian PDP vice presidential candidate Peter Obi claimed that Nigeria 90 million people living in extreme poverty in 2018/2019.
response_text: TRUE.  During the 2018/2019 campaign, Peter Obi (then PDP vice‑presidential candidate) repeatedly cited World Poverty Clock figures, sometimes saying 87 million and at other times rounding to “about 90 million” Nigerians living in extreme poverty. Multiple interviews and campaign appearances from late 2018 to early 2019 quote him with the ~90 million figure. (Minor uncertainty comes from him also using the 87 million figure in the VP debate.)

claim: Nigeria had 21 million unemployed young men and women in 2018/2019.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The widely cited 20.9 million figure in Q3 2018 from Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics refers to all unemployed Nigerians, not specifically “young” people. Youth-only unemployment was lower. So saying 21 million “young men and women” were unemployed in 2018/2019 misstates the statistic. (Slight uncertainty stems from varying definitions of “youth,” but no official 2018/2019 youth-only count is ~21 million.)

claim: Nigeria earned US$383 billion from oil revenues in the four years preceding 2019 but that there were no savings.
response_text: FALSE.  - The $383 billion figure typically refers to oil earnings around 2010–2014, not the four years before 2019 (2015–2018), when receipts were much lower due to the price crash. - “No savings” is inaccurate: Nigeria still had balances in the Excess Crude Account and the Sovereign Wealth Fund (e.g., ECA had a few billion dollars around 2014 and about $600+ million late in 2018; the NSIA held over $1 billion), though these were modest and fell over time.  Minor uncertainty: exact totals vary by source and whether exports or government oil revenues are counted, but the “no savings” claim is still wrong.

claim: Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “The only reason Trump is keeping his campaign promises is to influence the outcome of the election.”
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows AOC said this. The quote originated on a satirical/fake-news site (America’s Last Line of Defense) and was later spread as a meme. Fact-checkers like PolitiFact and Snopes have debunked it as a fabricated quote.

claim: Vegans now claiming that stuffing a turkey is sexual assault
