claim: or the first time ever, an African passport is among the top five most powerful in the world. Revealing this on Monday on its website, the Henley Passport Index released its ranking for the year 2020 and Nigeria had a dramatic rise from being at the 95th spot to going up to the 5th most powerful knocking out both Spain and Denmark and tying with Luxembourg.
response_text: FALSE.  Henley Passport Index 2020 ranked the top five as Japan, Singapore, South Korea/Germany, Italy/Finland, and Spain/Luxembourg/Denmark. No African country was in the top five. Nigeria ranked around 95th, not 5th. The highest-ranked African passports then were Seychelles and Mauritius (around 29th–32nd).

claim: 5G can suppress the immune system, thus making people more susceptible to catching the Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  5G uses non-ionizing radiofrequency energy that lacks the energy to damage DNA or suppress the immune system at exposure levels used for telecommunications. International and national health bodies (WHO, ICNIRP, FDA) report no credible evidence that 5G harms immune function. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus and has spread widely in areas without 5G; viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks.

claim: There is pork in Covid-19 vaccines.
response_text: FALSE.  Ingredient lists for authorized COVID‑19 vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, Johnson & Johnson, AstraZeneca, Novavax, Sinovac, Sinopharm) do not include pork or porcine gelatin. Health agencies (e.g., WHO, EMA/FDA, UK NHS) have confirmed they contain no animal-derived pork products. Note: some non‑COVID vaccines use porcine gelatin, and some manufacturing steps may use animal-derived enzymes, but these are not present in the final COVID‑19 vaccine product.

claim: Nando's serve only chicken dishes made from halal chicken in their UK restaurants.
response_text: FALSE.  Nando’s UK states that only a small number of their restaurants serve halal chicken (clearly signposted). Most UK Nando’s do not serve halal chicken, so it’s not true that they serve only halal chicken across all UK restaurants. (Policy can vary by location and time.)

claim: Joe Biden then US former vice president in 2015 pressured the Ukrainian government to fire Viktor Shokin, the top Ukrainian prosecutor, because he was investigating Ukraine’s largest private gas company, Burisma, which had added Biden’s son, Hunter, to its board in 2014.
response_text: FALSE.  - In 2015–2016, Joe Biden was the sitting U.S. vice president (not “former”) and, in line with official U.S. policy and the positions of the EU, IMF, and anti‑corruption advocates, pressed Ukraine to remove Prosecutor General Viktor Shokin for failing to pursue corruption cases. - Multiple contemporaneous reports and Ukrainian anti‑corruption officials said Shokin was not actively investigating Burisma; cases related to its owner were dormant. U.S. Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt publicly criticized Shokin’s office for undermining, not pursuing, such cases. - There is no evidence Biden acted to protect his son; the push to oust Shokin was a broad, internationally supported anti‑corruption effort, and Shokin was removed in March 2016.  Note: Shokin later claimed he was investigating Burisma, but independent evidence contradicts that.

claim: Diane Abbott said that Chairman "Mao did more good than harm."
response_text: TRUE.  Diane Abbott said on BBC’s “This Week” in 2008 that, “on balance, Mao did more good than harm,” while discussing Mao’s record; she later faced criticism and sought to clarify the remark.

claim: An MP’s salary was £66,000 in 2010 and £77,000 in 2018.
response_text: TRUE (rounded)  - 2010: MPs’ basic salary was £65,738 (≈£66k). - 2018: From 1 April 2018 it was £77,379 (≈£77k).  Figures from IPSA/House of Commons sources; the claim uses rounded amounts.

claim: A recipe for a drink called Kashayam is the cure for the Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Kashayam is a traditional herbal decoction sometimes used for cold/flu symptoms, but there is no credible clinical evidence that it cures COVID-19. Health authorities (e.g., WHO, CDC) do not recognize any herbal drink as a cure; only evidence-based treatments (like antivirals) and vaccines reduce risk and severity. At best, such drinks may provide symptomatic relief, not a cure.

claim: Did Conservative MP, Mark Francois deny the existence of the gender pay gap?
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Mark Francois denying the existence of the gender pay gap. When he has discussed it publicly, he has tended to argue about its causes or measurement (e.g., differences in occupation and hours) rather than claim it doesn’t exist. Note: if a specific quote is being referenced, it does not appear in reliable reporting.

claim: Doctors in Israel and the medical company, Gomorra, have found a “100% cure for HIV.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no proven, general “100% cure” for HIV. A few individual patients have been cured after risky stem‑cell transplants, but this isn’t a scalable treatment. The Israeli story likely refers to Zion Medical’s drug “Gammora,” which made headline claims around 2018–2019 but lacked peer‑reviewed evidence, was criticized by experts, and has not been validated or approved. No major health authority (WHO, CDC, UNAIDS) recognizes any 100% cure.

claim: A series of photos showed the supposed interiors of Del Monte Land Transport Bus Company's (DLTB Co) new bus.
response_text: FALSE.  Those viral photos were miscaptioned. They show the interiors of Indonesian “suites/sleeper class” buses (e.g., Laksana Legacy SR2 Suites Class operated by firms like Harapan Jaya/Rosalia Indah), images that had circulated online years earlier. They are not DLTB Co’s new bus, and there was no corresponding DLTB announcement.

claim: A person does not need a West African Examination Council [WAEC] certificate to become the President of Nigeria.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: The Nigerian Constitution (1999, as amended) only requires a presidential candidate to be “educated up to at least School Certificate level or its equivalent” (Section 131(d)). “School Certificate or its equivalent” (Section 318) can be satisfied by various qualifications (e.g., NECO SSCE, GCE O’Level, Grade II Teachers’ Certificate, higher degrees) or by specified combinations of education, work experience, training, and English proficiency. A specific WAEC certificate is not mandatory.

claim: 24,641 die of heart disease every day.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Globally, ischemic heart disease (often called “heart disease”) causes about 9 million deaths per year, which is roughly 24,000–25,000 per day. Note that all cardiovascular diseases together cause about 17–18 million deaths per year (~49,000/day), and in the U.S. it’s around 1,900/day. Figures vary by year and definition, but the stated daily number aligns with global ischemic heart disease deaths.

claim: Trump's government delivered the largest tax cut and reform in the history of the USA
response_text: FALSE.  The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a major overhaul and included a large corporate rate cut, but it was not the largest tax cut in U.S. history. By standard measures (inflation-adjusted dollars or, more appropriately, as a share of GDP), it was smaller than the 1981 Reagan tax cut, the post–World War II tax reductions, and the combined 2001/2003 Bush tax cuts. JCT/CBO estimates put the TCJA at roughly 0.8–1% of GDP initially, versus about 2–3% for the largest past cuts.

claim: Ilocos Norte Governor Imee Marcos graduated cum laude from the University of the Philippines (UP) College of Law
response_text: FALSE. UP Diliman’s Office of the University Registrar and UP College of Law said Imee Marcos did not graduate from the UP College of Law and therefore could not have received Latin honors. (This was confirmed publicly in 2019; her name is not on UP’s list of law graduates or honor awardees.) Uncertainty: none.

claim: In 2010, a newly qualified teacher’s salary was £21,500 and in 2018 was £22,000.
response_text: FALSE.  - 2010: The NQT (M1) starting salary outside London was about £21,588 (STPCD). - 2018: The minimum NQT starting salary outside London was about £23,720 (higher in London), not £22,000.  So the 2018 figure is too low by roughly £1,700.

claim: 108 people died from Covid-19 in China on February 10th, one of the worst days so far.
response_text: TRUE.  Chinese authorities reported 108 new COVID-19 deaths on February 10, 2020, which at the time was the highest daily toll (i.e., one of the worst days so far).

claim: For a cumulative 29 years out of 60 years of existence as a nation, Nigeria has been under military rule.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria had military rule from Jan 1966 to Oct 1979 (~13 years 8 months) and from Dec 1983 to May 1999 (~15 years 5 months), totaling about 29 years. Out of 60 years since independence in 1960 (to 2020), that leaves roughly 31 years civilian and ~29 years military.

claim: Boris Johnson said in 2007 that Gordon Brown should not have become Prime Minister after Tony Blair with no public vote.
response_text: TRUE.  In 2007, after Tony Blair resigned and Gordon Brown became Prime Minister without a general election, Boris Johnson (then a Conservative MP) publicly argued Brown lacked a personal mandate and should call an immediate public vote. He criticized Brown’s “coronation” and said “no one voted for Gordon Brown,” urging a general election. Note: he framed it as a democratic/mandate issue rather than a constitutional impossibility.

claim: Covid-19 cases are way down from where they were two weeks ago, this weekend is one of the lowest the United States have had.
response_text: FALSE (uncertain due to missing date)  - The claim lacks a specific date. COVID-19 case levels vary seasonally and by reporting artifacts (weekends often look “low” due to delays). - “One of the lowest the United States has had” is a very strong, historical claim that is unlikely without clear evidence from a known trough. - Case counts have also become less reliable over time due to reduced testing and reporting changes, making such a sweeping statement hard to substantiate.

claim: Covid-19 tests detect any coronavirus, not just the one that causes Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Most COVID-19 diagnostic tests (PCR/NAAT and antigen) are designed to specifically detect SARS‑CoV‑2, using primers/probes or antibodies targeting unique parts of this virus. Validation studies show no cross‑reactivity with common seasonal coronaviruses (e.g., 229E, NL63, OC43, HKU1). Rarely, some assays can detect the closely related SARS‑CoV‑1, which isn’t circulating. Serology (antibody) tests can sometimes cross‑react, but they are not used to diagnose current infection.

claim: NASA has announced the possibility of the sun rising from the west
response_text: FALSE.  NASA has not announced any possibility that the Sun will rise from the west on Earth. That would require Earth’s rotation to reverse, which is not something expected or predicted. Magnetic pole reversals (often cited in such rumors) do not change Earth’s rotation or sunrise direction. The Sun does rise in the west on Venus due to its retrograde rotation, but that’s a property of Venus, not Earth.

claim: 26,383 people die of cancer each day.
response_text: TRUE (approximately)  Global estimates put cancer deaths at about 9.6–10 million per year, which is roughly 26,300–27,400 per day. The specific figure 26,383/day corresponds to ~9.63 million/year—within earlier WHO/IARC estimates—though current estimates are closer to 10 million (~27,400/day). The exact number varies by year and is not precise day-to-day.

claim: The former actor and Congress politician, Urmila Matondkar, said, "By abusing martyr Rajiv Gandhi, Modi has proved he is mentally ill."
response_text: TRUE.  In May 2019, after PM Narendra Modi called Rajiv Gandhi “corrupt no. 1,” Congress candidate Urmila Matondkar told reporters that by insulting (“abusing”) the “martyr” Rajiv Gandhi, Modi had shown he was “mentally ill/unstable.” Multiple Indian media outlets reported her remark at the time. (Wording varies slightly in translation, but the substance matches.)

claim: Israeli Prime minister Netanyahu confirmed Israel is responsible for the Beirut Explosion.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible source reports Netanyahu confirming Israeli responsibility. Israeli officials (including Netanyahu’s government) denied involvement and even offered aid after the 4 Aug 2020 Beirut port blast. Investigations have attributed the explosion to improperly stored ammonium nitrate ignited by a fire, not an Israeli attack.

claim: The Covid-19 spike protein which the Pfizer vaccine causes an immune response against also trains the body to attack syncytin-1, a protein in the placenta, which could lead to infertility in women.
response_text: FALSE.  - Spike and syncytin‑1 are different proteins with no meaningful sequence similarity; a tiny shared motif is far too short to cause antibody cross‑reactivity. - Experiments show antibodies from vaccinated or infected people do not bind syncytin‑1, and vaccination does not raise anti–syncytin‑1 antibodies. - Large studies and surveillance (including IVF and fecundability studies, and pregnancy outcome registries) show no reduction in female fertility or increase in miscarriage after mRNA COVID‑19 vaccination. - If spike induced anti‑syncytin‑1 immunity, natural COVID‑19 infection (which produces much more spike) would be expected to cause widespread fertility problems, which has not been observed.

claim: Blue trick or treat pumpkin buckets are not official symbols for the autistic community
response_text: TRUE.  Some families use blue Halloween buckets to signal a child is autistic, but this is not an officially recognized or standardized symbol by major autism organizations. Unlike the teal pumpkin (an official FARE initiative for food allergies), blue buckets have no formal endorsement and aren’t an official autism community symbol.

claim: Justice Clarence Thomas And His Wife Ginni Thomas Chartered Buses For January 6, 2021, Capitol Protesters
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence shows either Justice Clarence Thomas or Ginni Thomas chartered buses for Jan. 6 protesters. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., AP, PolitiFact, Snopes) debunked viral claims that Ginni Thomas funded or organized buses; her attorney and her Jan. 6 committee testimony indicated she did not organize or finance transportation for the rally. There is no evidence Justice Thomas had any involvement.

claim: Abortion has been legalised in Indonesia by President Joko Widodo
response_text: FALSE.  Abortion in Indonesia remains a criminal offense except in limited circumstances (such as medical emergencies or pregnancies resulting from rape, within set gestational limits and with counseling/medical conditions). These exceptions stem from laws and regulations dating back to the 2009 Health Law, later regulations (2014) and the 2022 criminal code/2023 health law updates, not a blanket legalization by President Joko Widodo.

claim: The material, Ankara, a fine cotton fabric is not indigenous to Nigeria or Africa.
response_text: TRUE.  Ankara (African wax print) originated from 19th‑century European industrial imitations of Indonesian batik, especially by Dutch manufacturers like Vlisco. It was later traded to and widely adopted in West Africa. While it’s now produced and culturally embedded in countries like Nigeria and Ghana, its origins are not indigenous to Nigeria or Africa.

claim: Scotland’s bill for the HS2 railway is £17 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: HS2 is funded from UK-wide taxation; there is no discrete “bill” charged to Scotland. The £17bn figure comes from attributing a population-share of some high-end HS2 cost estimates, which is not how funding works. In practice, Scotland has actually received extra money via Barnett consequentials from HS2 spending in England, so you can’t meaningfully say Scotland “owes” £17bn for HS2. (Exact totals are uncertain and have changed as the project scope and costs changed.)

claim: The index finger is the only finger approved for marking a ballot paper in the Nigerian General Elections
response_text: FALSE.  INEC has clarified that any finger can be used to mark the ballot paper, as long as the mark stays within the box for the chosen party/candidate. The index finger has been recommended in some voter-education materials for ease, but it’s not the only approved finger.

claim: 5G technology is spreading Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks. COVID-19 spreads via respiratory droplets/aerosols and close contact. Many places with major outbreaks had no 5G service. Health authorities (e.g., WHO) have debunked this myth; 5G uses non-ionizing radiation that cannot create or transmit a virus.

claim: A police officer’s starting salary was £24,000 in 2010 and £23,000 in 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  - In England & Wales, a new police constable’s starting salary in 2010 was about £23,259 (not £24,000). - By 2018, entry salaries varied by route; the lowest starting point was about £20,370, with a higher entry point around £23k. So saying it “was £23,000” in 2018 is incomplete/misleading.  Sources: Home Office/Police Remuneration Review Body pay scales. (Minor uncertainty from rounding and entry-route variation.)

claim: Well-behaved women rarely make history was said by Eleanor Roosevelt
response_text: FALSE.  The line “Well-behaved women rarely make history” was coined by historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich in 1976, not Eleanor Roosevelt. It was later widely popularized and frequently misattributed.

claim: Drinking a glass of water before taking a bath helps lower blood pressure.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no scientific evidence that drinking a glass of water before a bath lowers blood pressure. If anything, water ingestion can cause a small, transient rise in blood pressure in some people (the “osmopressor” response), and bath temperature—not pre-bath drinking—affects BP (warm baths may transiently lower it; cold raises it). Hydration is healthy, but it’s not a blood‑pressure–lowering intervention.

claim: Humans kill 1,300 fellow humans every day.
response_text: TRUE (approximately)  Recent UN estimates put global homicides at about 450,000–470,000 per year, which averages roughly 1,200–1,300 people killed by other people per day. The exact figure varies by year and would be higher if deaths in armed conflicts were included.

claim: There were no Covid-19 deaths in Ireland in August 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Ireland’s Department of Health daily updates recorded several Covid-19 deaths during August 2020. The cumulative death toll rose over the month (reported around 1,763 at the start of August and about 1,777 by 31 August), so it was not zero. Sources: Irish Dept of Health/RTE daily updates.

claim: 26% of NHS doctors are foreign-born.
response_text: FALSE.  It understates the share. Recent NHS/GMC data show about 29% of NHS doctors are non‑UK nationals and roughly 35–40% trained overseas; estimates of foreign‑born doctors are around a third, not 26%. The 26% figure aligns more with older “non‑UK nationality,” not birth. (Some uncertainty because “foreign‑born” isn’t directly reported, but available indicators point higher.)

claim: Vladimir Putin is the world's richest man, with an estimated fortune of $250 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no verified evidence that Vladimir Putin is the world’s richest man or that he has $250 billion. Estimates of his wealth are highly speculative; major outlets like Forbes do not list him due to lack of verifiable data, while publicly disclosed assets are modest. The title of richest person is typically held by figures like Elon Musk or Bernard Arnault based on transparent, auditable holdings. Uncertainty: Putin’s true wealth is opaque, but the $250B claim isn’t substantiated.

claim: Prime Minister Sanna Marin has announced that Finland is going to have a four-day working week and six-hour days.
response_text: FALSE.  Media reports in early 2020 misattributed this to Sanna Marin. She had floated the idea of shorter working hours in 2019 as a long‑term vision while serving as transport minister, but as prime minister she did not announce such a policy. Her office said it wasn’t on the government’s agenda, and Finland has not adopted a four‑day week or six‑hour day nationwide.

claim: BBC Radio 2 DJ gets paid over £1.3 million a year.
response_text: TRUE.  BBC salary disclosures show Radio 2 Breakfast Show hosts have been paid over £1.3m—e.g., Zoe Ball earned about £1.36m in 2019–20 (and Chris Evans earned over £2m before leaving). Note: Ball’s more recent pay has been lower.

claim: Covid-19’s infection fatality rate is 0.1%
response_text: FALSE.  Covid-19’s infection fatality rate is not a single fixed number and has varied sharply by age, setting, variant, and immunity. Pre-vaccine, meta-analyses and public health estimates placed the overall IFR around 0.5–1% in many populations, far above 0.1% (with a steep age gradient; much lower in young people, much higher in older adults). Later, with vaccines/Omicron, IFR fell in many places, but an across-the-board 0.1% is not accurate. Uncertainty: estimates differ by study and period, but the blanket 0.1% claim is misleading.

claim: The salary of a newly qualified nurse was £22,000 in 2010 and the same in 2018.
response_text: FALSE.  In England, the NHS starting salary for a newly qualified nurse (Band 5) was about £21,176 in 2010/11. By 2017/18 it was £22,128, and after the 2018 pay deal (from July 2018) it rose to £23,023. So it was not £22,000 in both years; it increased in cash terms. (Real-terms pay fell, but the claim gives nominal figures.)

claim: Grenfell Tower was built by a Labour Council under Labour government in 2007-2008, when Sadiq Khan was the Housing Minister.
response_text: FALSE.  - Grenfell Tower was built in the early 1970s (completed 1974), not in 2007–2008. - It was built by the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, a long‑time Conservative-run council, not a Labour council. - Sadiq Khan was never the Housing Minister; in 2007–2008 the Housing Minister role was held by Caroline Flint (then Margaret Beckett). The major refurbishment occurred in 2015–2016 under a Conservative council and government.

claim: Drinking a glass of water before going to bed helps prevent stroke and heart attacks
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no clinical evidence that drinking a glass of water before bed prevents heart attacks or strokes. The popular “thins the blood overnight” notion is a myth. Adequate hydration is generally healthy, but a bedtime glass doesn’t reduce cardiovascular events and may worsen sleep via nighttime urination; in some people (e.g., heart or kidney disease), extra fluids can be harmful. Proven prevention focuses on controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, not smoking, exercising, managing diabetes and atrial fibrillation, and using indicated medications.

claim: US President Joe Biden lied when he said he had never spoken to his son, Hunter Biden  about his son's overseas business dealings.
response_text: FALSE  Evidence shows Joe Biden occasionally interacted with Hunter Biden’s business associates (calls with pleasantries, dinners) and once left a 2018 voicemail referencing a news article about Hunter’s China dealings. But witnesses (e.g., Devon Archer) testified Joe Biden did not discuss business matters, and no verified record shows Joe Biden discussed or was involved in Hunter’s overseas business dealings. The blanket denial may be overly broad, but calling it a “lie” is not supported by current evidence. (Some uncertainty stems from how one interprets the voicemail and “about” the business.)

claim: While western countries have been busy fighting the new coronavirus, international terrorism has stopped
response_text: FALSE.  Terrorist activity did not stop during the COVID-19 pandemic. Attacks continued worldwide, and some groups even sought to exploit the crisis. Examples from 2020 alone include ISIS/IS-K attacks in Iraq and Afghanistan (e.g., Kabul gurdwara, March; Kabul hospital area, May), Boko Haram massacres in Nigeria, al‑Shabaab operations in Somalia/Kenya, and attacks in Europe such as the Reading stabbing (UK, June), the beheading of Samuel Paty and the Nice church attack (France, October), and the Vienna shootings (Austria, November).

claim: Moon and Mars will appear to be the same size in the night sky on August 27, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Mars never appears anywhere near the Moon’s size to the naked eye. Even at its closest in 2020 (early October, not August 27), Mars’s apparent diameter was about 22–23 arcseconds, while the Moon is about 1,800 arcseconds across—roughly 80 times larger. The August 27 “same size” claim is a long-running hoax originating from a misread 2003 email about viewing Mars through a telescope.

claim: Student nurses of the 2017 cohort were asked to join the NHS workforce early this year, due to Covid-19.
response_text: TRUE.  In March–April 2020, as part of the COVID-19 response, the NHS (via Health Education England) and the NMC invited final-year nursing students to opt into paid extended clinical placements/early deployment. Students who began in 2017 would have been in their final year in 2020, so they were among those asked to join the workforce early.

claim: Stanley Johnson, father of Prime Minister Boris Johnson, wrote a novel called ‘The Virus’ in 1982.
response_text: FALSE.  Stanley Johnson did write a pandemic thriller in 1982, but its original title was “The Marburg Virus.” It was later reissued under the shorter title “The Virus,” which likely caused the confusion.

claim: The Covid-19 vaccine will cause infertility in younger men.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple studies and reviews show COVID-19 vaccination does not impair male fertility or cause infertility. Semen parameters (count, motility, morphology) and reproductive hormones are unchanged after mRNA vaccination in controlled studies (e.g., JAMA 2021; other cohorts and meta-analyses up to 2023–2024). One study noted a transient dip in some semen measures after vaccination that resolved on follow‑up, not consistent with infertility. Major health bodies (CDC, WHO, ASRM) state there is no evidence vaccines harm fertility. In contrast, COVID-19 infection itself can temporarily worsen sperm parameters via fever/inflammation.

claim: The cladding used on Grenfell Tower has previously been banned in the USA.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Grenfell cladding was aluminum composite panels with a polyethylene (PE) core. In the US there is no blanket, nationwide ban on this material. Building codes (e.g., the International Building Code/NFPA 285) generally prohibit combustible PE-core ACM on high‑rise buildings unless part of a tested compliant assembly, but it can be used on some low‑rise buildings. So it’s heavily restricted for tall buildings, not outright “banned in the USA.”

claim: This photo shows women working for the Red Cross arriving at Normandy beach in 1944 to assist injured troops.
response_text: FALSE.  The widely shared photo actually shows U.S. Women’s Army Corps (WAC) personnel coming ashore in Normandy in July 1944, not Red Cross workers. They arrived weeks after D‑Day to perform administrative/communications duties, not to provide frontline medical aid to injured troops. Some Red Cross “Clubmobile” teams did reach Normandy later, but this image is miscaptioned.

claim: Jacob Rothschild owns a patent to coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  - No one “owns” SARS‑CoV‑2; patents can cover engineered strains or methods, not a naturally occurring virus. - The frequently cited patent (US 10,130,701) is held by the UK’s Pirbright Institute for an avian coronavirus vaccine, unrelated to COVID‑19; Pirbright is not owned by Jacob Rothschild. - Another rumor cites a 2020 application by Richard A. Rothschild for a COVID‑19 testing/data system—this is a different person, not Jacob Rothschild. - Major fact‑checkers (Reuters, AP, Snopes) have debunked the claim.

claim: A no deal Brexit means UK fishing waters are back in our control.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Outside the EU and its Common Fisheries Policy, the UK becomes an independent coastal state under UNCLOS, with the right to control access to and manage fisheries in its Exclusive Economic Zone (up to 200 nautical miles/median line). EU vessels would no longer have automatic access, and the UK can set licensing and quotas. Caveats: the UK must still cooperate on shared fish stocks and, if it cannot harvest the full allowable catch, may grant access to others by agreement; so control is not absolute.

claim: U.S., Germany and France have no educational requirement for the office of President.
response_text: TRUE.  - United States: The Constitution requires a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and 14 years’ residency; no education requirement. - Germany: The Basic Law requires a German eligible for the Bundestag and at least 40 years old; no education requirement. - France: Constitutional and electoral rules require being a French citizen, at least 18, with 500 sponsorships and other formalities; no education requirement.  So none of the three countries imposes a formal educational qualification for the presidency.

claim: A no deal Brexit means we wouldn’t have to make any more annual payments of £26 billion to £32 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  - The UK never made annual EU payments of £26–32 billion. Before Brexit, the UK’s gross contribution was about £18–20bn a year; after the rebate and EU spending in the UK, the net contribution was roughly £8–10bn (ONS/HM Treasury). - A “no deal” exit would not have automatically erased the UK’s existing financial obligations to the EU (the “divorce bill”); those commitments were still expected to be settled even without a deal.

claim: University of Zimbabwe will begin serving exotic game meat from wildlife parks due to rising prices of beef and chicken.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible announcement or policy exists. The claim traces to a viral social media post/fake memo; the University of Zimbabwe and the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority denied any plan to serve “exotic game meat.” No reliable news outlet or official notice corroborates it.

claim: To self diagnose for COVID-19, hold your breath for ten seconds without coughing, discomfort, stuffiness or tightness and this proves no fibrosis in the lungs and no infection.
response_text: FALSE.  Holding your breath for 10 seconds is not a valid test for COVID-19 or lung fibrosis. Many healthy people (e.g., older adults, those with asthma/anxiety) may struggle with this, while people with COVID-19 can still pass it. COVID-19 infection often occurs without lung fibrosis, and fibrosis is not an early marker. Diagnosis requires approved tests (PCR or rapid antigen) and clinical assessment, not breath-holding.

claim: In Britain, you’re allowed to wave terrorist flags
response_text: FALSE.  Under the UK Terrorism Act 2000 (s.13), it is an offense to display an article (e.g., a flag) in a way or in circumstances that arouse reasonable suspicion you are a member or supporter of a proscribed terrorist organization (e.g., ISIS, Hamas, Hezbollah). Police assess context, but waving a terrorist group’s flag will typically meet this threshold, so it’s generally not allowed. (Note: flags of non‑proscribed groups, like the Palestinian flag, are not banned.) Uncertainty only in edge cases of context/enforcement.

claim: Consuming certain plants will stop women from getting pregnant.
response_text: FALSE.  No plant eaten orally has been proven safe and reliably effective at preventing pregnancy in humans. While some herbs are traditionally claimed to have contraceptive or abortifacient effects, high‑quality clinical evidence is lacking, none are approved contraceptives, and some can be toxic. Reliable pregnancy prevention requires evidence‑based methods (e.g., condoms, pills, IUDs, implants).

claim: 122 Muslims acquitted by Gujarat court for alleged link with SIMI were in prison for 20 years.
response_text: FALSE.  A Gujarat (Surat) court did acquit 122 people in a 2001 case alleging links to SIMI, but they were not in prison for 20 years. Most were arrested in 2001 and released on bail long ago; the case dragged on for about two decades before acquittal in 2021. Reports (e.g., Indian Express, The Hindu) note prolonged trial, not continuous imprisonment.

claim: half of the GOP candidates don't live in the 9th congressional s district of north Carolina
response_text: FALSE  Reason: There’s no substantiated evidence that “half” of the Republican candidates for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District lived outside the district in recent cycles. In 2024, the GOP field for NC-9 was small, with incumbent Rep. Richard Hudson (who resides in-district, Southern Pines/Moore County) and limited opposition; available records do not show that half the field lived elsewhere. Note: House candidates must live in the state, not necessarily the district, but this specific “half don’t live there” claim isn’t supported. Uncertain on the exact cycle intended, but available data doesn’t back it.

claim: A picture shows a woman holding a protest sign saying “stop killing volcanoes to make lava lamps”, from the People’s Vote march.
response_text: FALSE  This image is a meme: the “stop killing volcanoes to make lava lamps” text was digitally added to a commonly used protest-sign photo template. It’s not from the UK People’s Vote march. (Uncertainty: exact original event for the base photo varies in reports, but it predates and is unrelated to the People’s Vote.)

claim: HS2 will cost £150 billion.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There is no official estimate that HS2 “will” cost £150bn. Before the 2023 truncation, the government’s own range for the full network was about £72–98bn in 2019 prices (roughly £100bn+ in today’s money). Some media reports speculated figures up to £150bn including inflation and risks, but that isn’t an official forecast. After the project was scaled back to London–Birmingham, expected costs are far lower. Uncertainty remains because costs are still evolving, but £150bn is not a supported figure.

claim: If you have been recently vaccinated you need to stay away from babies, young children, pregnant women, immunocompromised people, the elderly, and terminally ill people for at least two weeks minimum.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no blanket need to avoid others after vaccination. Most vaccines (e.g., mRNA, inactivated, protein, non-replicating viral vector) do not “shed” and pose no risk to contacts, including babies, pregnant women, the elderly, or immunocompromised people. - Limited exceptions apply to certain live vaccines:    - Intranasal live flu vaccine: avoid close contact with severely immunocompromised people in protected environments for 7 days.   - Rotavirus (given to infants): virus can be shed in stool—caregivers should use good hand hygiene, but routine contact is fine.   - Varicella/zoster: if the vaccinated person develops a rash, avoid susceptible immunocompromised contacts until it resolves.   - Smallpox (vaccinia, not routine): cover the site and avoid high‑risk contacts until the scab falls off. - There is no general “two weeks minimum” rule; vaccinating close contacts is usually recommended to protect vulnerable people.

claim: Posting on social media such as Instagram for Blackout Tuesday dilutes feeds and erases protesters’ posts burying the voices it's meant to amplify.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: During Blackout Tuesday (June 2, 2020), millions posted black squares on Instagram, many using hashtags like #BlackLivesMatter. This flooded those tags and algorithmic feeds with blank images, pushing down timely posts from organizers and protesters (e.g., safety updates, legal aid, protest info). Activists and BLM accounts publicly urged users not to tag black squares with #BLM for this reason. “Erases” is figurative, but the effect of burying/muting those voices was documented.

claim: A picture post has surfaced on the internet in which Union Minister Nitin Gadkari has been quoted praising interim Congress President Sonia Gandhi and former President Rahul Gandhi.
response_text: FALSE  A viral image did circulate, but the quote attributing praise of Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi to Nitin Gadkari is fabricated. No credible report or official record supports such remarks, and multiple fact-checks flagged the quote card as fake.

claim: Ewedu can cure cancer.
response_text: FALSE.  Ewedu (jute mallow, Corchorus olitorius) is nutritious and contains antioxidants, and some lab studies suggest potential anti-cancer activity in cells. However, there is no clinical evidence that it cures cancer in humans. It should not replace proven cancer treatments.

claim: As Mayor, Sadiq Khan produced a report to say that the Fire Services did not need further funding.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: There’s no evidence Sadiq Khan “produced a report” saying London’s fire service did not need further funding. Under his mayoralty, reviews affecting the London Fire Brigade (e.g., the London Safety Plan drawn up by the Brigade/Fire Authority, independent inspections, and later culture reviews) were not authored by Khan and did not assert that no extra funding would be needed. Khan has repeatedly called for greater fire-safety funding after Grenfell and has increased the LFB’s budget via the council tax precept. Some point to LFB’s own planning documents pre‑ and shortly after 2016–17 saying they could operate within then-current budgets, but those were produced by the Brigade/Fire Authority, not by Khan, and do not amount to him issuing a report that no further funding was needed.  Uncertainty: Wording of some budget/plan documents can be misconstrued, but none were a Khan-authored report making that claim.

claim: Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison stands alone during the 2019 G7 Leaders’ Summit in France
response_text: FALSE — The widely shared image claiming this actually shows Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at the 2019 G7 in Biarritz, not Australia’s Scott Morrison. Multiple fact-checks identified the man in the photo as Trudeau.

claim: Kenyans working at Mara North private wildlife park have been made to carry white tourists in sedan chairs depicting modern 'slavery'
response_text: FALSE.  This claim stems from miscaptioned posts. No credible reporting or evidence shows tourists being carried in sedan chairs at Mara North Conservancy. The viral images/videos used to allege this are from elsewhere (commonly Asian mountain “sedan chair” services), not Kenya. Mara North camps and the conservancy say such practices are not permitted. Slight uncertainty remains only because social posts circulated without verifiable source details.

claim: Suicide is the cause of death for around 3,000 people per day.
response_text: FALSE.  Global estimates from the WHO put suicide deaths at around 700,000–800,000 per year, which is roughly 1,900–2,200 per day. Saying 3,000 per day would imply about 1.1 million deaths annually, well above current estimates.

claim: Using the air conditioning (AC) in a vehicle consumes more fuel.
response_text: TRUE.  Using a car’s air conditioning engages a compressor that adds load to the engine, so it burns more fuel to produce the same power. Estimates from fuel-economy sources show AC can reduce fuel economy by roughly 3–20% (more in extreme heat or stop‑and‑go driving). Note: in EVs it doesn’t use fuel but still increases energy use; at high speeds, open windows may waste more fuel than AC due to aerodynamic drag.

claim: The BMA advises that without immigrants “many NHS services would struggle to provide effective care”.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The BMA has explicitly warned that without international (particularly EU/overseas) doctors, many NHS services would struggle to provide effective care. For example, BMA statements around 2017–2018 said “without EU doctors, many NHS services would struggle to provide effective care to their patients.” The claim paraphrases “immigrants” for overseas/EU doctors, but the substance matches.

claim: The Wuhan coronavirus is a more virulent version of the normal cold.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “common cold” is caused by many viruses (mostly rhinoviruses and some seasonal coronaviruses like OC43, 229E, NL63, HKU1). SARS‑CoV‑2, the virus first identified in Wuhan, is a distinct, novel coronavirus that can cause COVID‑19, ranging from mild cold‑like illness to severe pneumonia and systemic disease. It isn’t simply a “more virulent version” of the common cold; it’s a different virus with different biology and disease severity.

claim: In the UK in 2020 there were 48,000 illegal immigrants staying in 4/5 star hotels.
response_text: FALSE.  - In 2020 the Home Office used hotels to house asylum seekers during the pandemic, but the number in hotels was about 9,500–12,000, not 48,000.  - The c.48,000 figure refers to the total number of people on asylum support across all accommodation types, most in longer‑term dispersal housing.  - Calling them “illegal immigrants” is incorrect; people seeking asylum are lawfully accommodated while their claims are processed. - Hotels used were often budget/mid-range chains, not uniformly 4/5 star.

claim: 5G wrecks immune systems and that is why people in Wuhan are suffering with this illness.
response_text: FALSE.  - 5G uses non-ionizing radiofrequency waves that, at regulated exposure levels, do not damage DNA or suppress the immune system. No credible evidence links 5G to immune dysfunction. - The illness in Wuhan was COVID-19, caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus. Large outbreaks occurred in many places with no 5G service, and radio waves cannot cause or transmit viral infections. - WHO and other health agencies have stated 5G does not spread COVID-19 or harm the immune system.

claim: Bollywood star Shah Rukh Khan has slammed the Modi-government for not paying enough attention to Rohingya Muslims.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Shah Rukh Khan criticizing the Modi government over Rohingya Muslims. The claim has circulated via fabricated quotes and doctored screenshots, which fact-checkers (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today) have debunked. SRK has not publicly made such a statement.

claim: Drinking one glass of water before bed prevents heart attacks.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible evidence that drinking a glass of water before bed prevents heart attacks. Overall hydration is healthy, but the timing (bedtime) doesn’t confer proven cardiac protection. Heart attack prevention relies on managing risk factors (blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking), exercise, diet, and appropriate medications. For some people (e.g., heart/kidney failure, prostate issues), extra bedtime fluids can be counterproductive. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Mixing one tablespoon of 2% iodine and one cup of baby oil will create a substance that removes body hair.
response_text: FALSE.  Iodine (2%) is an antiseptic and baby oil is mineral oil; neither can dissolve or break the keratin bonds in hair. Effective chemical depilatories use thioglycolates to break disulfide bonds, or hair is removed mechanically (shaving, waxing, threading). This mixture won’t remove hair and may irritate or stain skin.

claim: In a letter to Steve Jobs, Sean Connery refused to appear in an apple commercial.
response_text: FALSE.  A scathing “letter” purportedly from Sean Connery to Steve Jobs refusing to do an Apple ad has circulated online, but fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes) have shown it’s a hoax. There’s no credible evidence Connery wrote such a letter. Apple did approach various celebrities for campaigns like “Think Different,” but the Connery letter itself is not authentic. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
response_text: FALSE.  Leaked HHS vetting documents for a planned Trump administration COVID ad campaign noted that Billie Eilish was “not a Trump supporter” and had said of Trump that “he is destroying our country and everything we care about.” The documents did not claim that Eilish herself was destroying the country.

claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence supports this. In late 2020, after Imran Khan criticized Emmanuel Macron, rumors claimed France had canceled 183 Pakistani visas and deported 118 Pakistanis. The French Embassy in Pakistan publicly denied any such mass cancellations or deportations, and no reputable French or Pakistani government source or major news outlet reported them. The figures circulated via false social media posts.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no record or announcement from UNESCO declaring the Nadar community “the most ancient race.” - UNESCO does not rank or certify “races” or communities; in fact, it has explicitly rejected racial classifications (UNESCO Statement on Race, 1950). - This claim matches a common pattern of false social media posts attributing superlatives to UNESCO.

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
response_text: FALSE.  - The $75 million settlement was paid by VITAS Healthcare/Chemed in 2018 to resolve federal allegations of Medicare billing fraud in hospice care. - Matt Gaetz was not part of VITAS; his father, Don Gaetz, co‑founded the company and sold it to Chemed in 2004, years before the settlement. There’s no evidence Matt had any role in the company. - The case concerned fraud against Medicare, not “stealing from dying people” directly.   (Notes: Some alleged conduct predated the 2004 sale, but it involved the company/founders—not Matt Gaetz.)

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Allegations of Chemical Weapons Convention violations reported in Western media have largely drawn on findings from independent bodies like the OPCW and UN mechanisms (e.g., OPCW confirmation of a Novichok-type agent in the Skripal and Navalny cases, and OPCW Investigation and Identification Team reports attributing multiple chemical attacks to the Syrian government). There is no credible evidence that the US and its allies have systematically used media to publish fabricated information on CWC non‑compliance. Some disputes (e.g., over the Douma 2018 reporting) exist, but the OPCW stands by its conclusions, and the broad claim of coordinated fabrication is unsupported.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
response_text: TRUE  - By late October 2020, U.S. COVID-19 deaths had surpassed 225,000 (e.g., Johns Hopkins data). - A Columbia University National Center for Disaster Preparedness report (Oct 2020) estimated 130,000–210,000 U.S. COVID deaths were avoidable with a more effective, earlier, coordinated response. “160,000 fewer” falls within that range.  Note: The avoidable-deaths figure is model-based and uncertain, but the claim aligns with published estimates.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
response_text: TRUE.  - The New York Times reported (and later congressional release of his returns confirmed) that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income tax in both 2016 and 2017. - In the 2016 presidential debate, when told he might not have paid federal income taxes, Trump replied, “That makes me smart,” and he has repeatedly said he uses the tax laws to his advantage. The phrase “I know how to game the system” is a paraphrase, but captures the substance of his comments.  Note: Trump has claimed he paid “millions” in other taxes, but the $750 figure for federal income tax for those years is documented.

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
response_text: FALSE.  - There was no evidence of widespread “phony ballots” in 2020; courts, state election officials of both parties, DOJ, and DHS found no systemic fraud. - Counting after Election Day is normal and set by state law. Many states legally count ballots received or processed in the days following Nov. 3 (some up to a couple of weeks), especially mail and military ballots. This is not evidence of cheating but routine procedure.

claim: New Zealand’s new Food Bill bans gardening
response_text: FALSE.  New Zealand’s Food Bill (which became the Food Act 2014) regulates food that is sold. It does not ban home gardening or growing food for personal use, nor does it stop people from sharing or giving away home-grown produce. Requirements mainly apply when food is sold (including some forms of barter) as part of a business.

claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Masks reduce the risk of transmitting and acquiring COVID-19—especially high-quality, well-fitted masks—but they do not completely stop spread on their own. Effectiveness depends on mask type, fit, and consistent use, and masks work best combined with other measures (ventilation, vaccination, testing).

claim: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) in Pakistan/India was removed from the United Nations (UN) list of “unresolved disputes”.
response_text: FALSE.  The UN has no official “list of unresolved disputes” from which Jammu & Kashmir could be removed. The UN’s position on J&K has not changed: relevant UN Security Council resolutions remain in place, and UN officials have clarified there’s been no alteration in its status. J&K has also never been on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence from lab, clinical, and epidemiologic studies shows masks—especially well‑fitted respirators (N95/FFP2)—substantially reduce both emission and inhalation of infectious aerosols. Laboratory work demonstrates high filtration of submicron particles; studies of exhaled breath show masks reduce viral aerosol shedding; and real‑world data (e.g., case‑control and healthcare cohort studies) find markedly lower SARS‑CoV‑2 infection risk with respirators, with smaller but still measurable benefits for surgical masks. Community RCTs are mixed largely due to adherence/implementation limits, but they do not show that masks “would not meaningfully help.”

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
response_text: FALSE.  Ballot receipt rules vary by state. Many states count mailed ballots that arrive after Election Day if they’re postmarked by Election Day and received within a set grace period (e.g., California about 7 days, Illinois about 14 days), and military/overseas ballots often have extended deadlines. Only some states require ballots to be received by Election Day.

claim: Video shows attack of French embassy in Sudan
response_text: FALSE  The circulating footage is miscaptioned. Fact-checks show the video comes from protests that targeted French diplomatic sites in West Africa (e.g., the French embassy/Institute in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, in Oct 2022, or Niamey, Niger, in July 2023), not from Sudan. There’s no verified video of the French embassy in Sudan being attacked matching that clip. (Slight uncertainty about which exact misattributed clip the claim refers to.)

claim: Viral video purportedly shows Pakistani opposition MPs chanted ‘Modi, Modi’ (India's PM)  inside the Pakistani Parliament
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The viral clip being shared is not from Pakistan’s Parliament. It shows India’s Lok Sabha, where BJP MPs chanted “Modi, Modi.” Visual cues (the Speaker’s chair and Ashoka emblem, layout) and fact-checks have confirmed the footage is from India, not Pakistan. No credible evidence shows Pakistani MPs chanting “Modi, Modi” inside their Parliament.

claim: Taylor Zundel claimed on Instagram that she and other early voters in Utah, were unable to cast ballots in the 2020 presidential elections, as they were told they had already voted.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In early November 2020, a Utah woman named Taylor Zundel posted on Instagram claiming that she and other early voters were told at polling places that they had already voted and couldn’t cast ballots. The post went viral; Utah election officials later said the claim was inaccurate and that voters in such situations could cast provisional ballots, with no evidence of a broader problem. Sources include contemporaneous reports by outlets such as the Salt Lake Tribune, USA Today, and PolitiFact.

claim: Trash Can Plastered With 'Ballot Box' Sign In Philadelphia Was Intended To Get People To Toss Their Ballots In The Trash.
response_text: FALSE.  The photo shows a prank/satirical sign put on a Philadelphia trash can by a local street artist (Kid Hazo), not an official drop box or an effort to trick voters. City election officials confirmed there were no ballot drop boxes on trash cans; at the time, ballots could be returned only at designated, staffed locations. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, Billy Penn/WHYY) debunked the claim.

claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
response_text: FALSE.  Biden has repeatedly said he does not support a nationwide ban on fracking. His position has been to restrict it by ending new oil and gas leasing (including fracking) on federal lands and tightening regulations, not to ban fracking outright.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
response_text: TRUE.  In early November 2020, after earlier warnings that the Thai king must not conduct politics from German soil, German Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said Germany had no evidence the king had violated German law or conducted state business while staying in Bavaria. He noted authorities would keep monitoring the situation. (Reported by outlets such as Reuters and Deutsche Welle.)

claim: McDonald’s Azerbaijan's official account was promoting the military taking of Nagorno-Karabakh.
response_text: TRUE.  In October 2020, during renewed fighting over Nagorno-Karabakh, McDonald’s Azerbaijan’s verified social media accounts posted pro-military graphics and slogans (e.g., praising the Azerbaijani army, maps showing territorial gains, “Karabakh is Azerbaijan”). After criticism, the posts were removed and McDonald’s corporate stated it does not take political positions. Sources at the time included Reuters, Eurasianet, and Insider.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
response_text: FALSE.  - Effectiveness: Both untreated nets (physical barrier) and insecticide-treated/long-lasting insecticidal nets (ITNs/LLINs) significantly reduce mosquito bites and malaria. Randomized trials and meta-analyses show ~40–50% fewer malaria episodes and ~17–20% lower all-cause child mortality in endemic areas. WHO strongly recommends ITNs/LLINs and credits them with millions of cases and deaths averted.  - Safety: The insecticides used (typically pyrethroids) have low toxicity to humans at the doses in nets. When used as directed, adverse effects are uncommon and usually mild and transient (e.g., slight skin or eye irritation); they are considered safe for children and pregnant women.  Note: Insecticide resistance can reduce efficacy but does not make nets harmful.

claim: Pogba Has Quit The French National Team Over Macron's Remarks on Islam.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a viral rumor from October 2020. Paul Pogba publicly denied quitting the French national team over President Macron’s remarks on Islam, calling the reports fake. No official retirement was announced, and Pogba continued to be selected for France afterward.

claim: The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker
response_text: False.  - “Racist” claim: The Wire ran criticism of specific Durga Puja themes/pandals that used blackface/“African” stereotypes, calling those depictions racist — not the festival of Durga Puja itself. - “Sex worker” claim: The Wire published coverage/photo-essays about Durga Puja organised by sex workers (e.g., in Sonagachi) or artistic reinterpretations, but did not call the goddess Durga a sex worker. The line is a misrepresentation of such coverage.  Note: Some viral posts conflate or distort headlines from context to suggest these claims.

claim: Paul Pogba, who plays for Manchester United and the French national team, retired from international football in response to French President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a widely circulated 2020 rumor that Paul Pogba had quit the French national team over President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism. Pogba publicly denied it as “fake news,” and he continued to play for France afterward (e.g., Euro 2020/2021, Nations League 2021). No official retirement occurred.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed as US Supreme Court Justice on October 26, 2020
response_text: TRUE. The U.S. Senate confirmed Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court on October 26, 2020 (52–48 vote). She took the constitutional oath that evening and the judicial oath the next day.

claim: The New York post Endorsed Donald trumps bid for re-election.
response_text: TRUE.  The New York Post’s editorial board endorsed Donald Trump for re-election in 2020 (e.g., an Oct. 26, 2020 editorial backing his second-term bid), though it later urged him to accept the election results.

claim: The United States, New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and the EU have not included the NDF in their official list of terrorist groups.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The U.S., U.K., Australia, New Zealand, and the EU list the Communist Party of the Philippines/New People’s Army (CPP-NPA) as a terrorist organization, but they do not list the National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDF/NDFP) as a designated terrorist group. Some individuals linked to these groups have been sanctioned separately, and the Philippines itself has designated the NDF, but these jurisdictions have not.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible evidence shows COVID-19 was pre-planned or that Bill Gates helped plan it.   - References often cited (e.g., Gates’s 2015 TED talk warning about pandemics, the 2019 Event 201 tabletop exercise) were public pandemic-preparedness efforts, not plans to cause a pandemic.   - Scientific and investigative findings indicate SARS‑CoV‑2 emerged in late 2019; debates over zoonotic vs. lab-related origins do not implicate Gates or pre-planning.  Uncertainty: None supported by reliable evidence.

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Robin Vos became Assembly speaker in 2013. In the 2014 and 2016 elections, Republicans did not lose any GOP‑held Assembly seats and grew to 64 seats. In 2018, Democrats flipped one Republican-held seat—the 14th Assembly District (previously held by Republican Dale Kooyenga, won by Democrat Robyn Vining)—reducing the GOP to 63 seats. This was the first loss of a Republican-held Assembly seat under Vos’s speakership.

claim: Breitbart News reports that the daughter of Delaware Democratic Senator Chris Coons and seven other underage girls were featured on Hunter Biden's laptop.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim stems from a fabricated Breitbart screenshot. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact/USA Today) found no such Breitbart article, and the image circulating was doctored. Breitbart did not report that Sen. Chris Coons’ daughter and seven other underage girls were “featured” on Hunter Biden’s laptop.

claim: Hunter Biden, son of US President Joe Biden has died.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There are no credible reports that Hunter Biden has died. As of my latest update (Oct 2024), he was alive; such a death would be widely reported by major outlets. Some rumors confuse him with his brother Beau Biden, who died in 2015. (If this changed very recently, I may not have the latest.)

claim: 5G causes COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 is caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus, not by wireless networks. 5G uses non‑ionizing radio waves that cannot create or transmit viruses or damage DNA. The disease spread widely in regions without 5G, and health authorities (e.g., WHO) have confirmed there is no link.

claim: Rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed for 12 people and 7 pumpkins at a campaign event for Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden in Pennsylvania.
response_text: FALSE.  A viral clip misrepresented the scene. Bon Jovi performed at an Oct. 24, 2020 drive-in Biden rally in Dallas, Pennsylvania, with hundreds of attendees in hundreds of cars. The “12 people and 7 pumpkins” line came from a tight shot near the stage that showed a few staff and fall decorations, not the full audience.

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.
response_text: FALSE.  Properly used masks don’t cause bacterial infections like staphylococcal infections. Studies and public health agencies report no increased risk of respiratory or systemic infection from mask use. Masks can cause skin irritation (“maskne”) and, if dirty, moist, or shared, could rarely contribute to a localized skin infection—but that’s due to poor hygiene or skin breakdown, not an inherent effect of wearing masks.

claim: An 'anti-Black Lives Matter' flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump during a Waukesha campaign rally.
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks found that video/images claiming an “anti–Black Lives Matter” flag was behind Trump at a Waukesha rally were digitally altered. Original footage and photos from the event show standard American flags as the backdrop; no such “anti‑BLM” flag replaced them.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
response_text: FALSE.  Deliberately infecting children with COVID-19 is unsafe and unethical. Children can develop serious complications (e.g., MIS-C) and long COVID, and they can transmit the virus to vulnerable people. Infection-induced immunity is variable and wanes, with reinfections common—especially with new variants—so it’s unreliable for achieving herd immunity. Public health authorities (WHO, CDC) explicitly discourage attempting “herd immunity” through natural infection; vaccination is the safe, effective route. Uncertainty: none.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
response_text: FALSE.  - Passive “natural” immunity (maternal IgG antibodies) is transferred across the placenta before birth, not after. Clamping the cord earlier or later does not meaningfully change antibody transfer. - Delayed cord clamping (about 30–60+ seconds) is recommended mainly to improve newborn blood volume and iron stores; studies show benefits for hemoglobin/iron and no evidence of immune harm. Some increase in jaundice treatment is noted. - There is no evidence that cord clamping practices are intended to justify vaccination. Vaccines are recommended because maternal antibodies wane and do not cover many diseases.  Sources: WHO and ACOG guidelines on delayed cord clamping; Cochrane reviews showing hematologic benefits without immune-related disadvantages.

claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence-based guidelines recommend delayed cord clamping for about 30–60 seconds (up to 1–3 minutes or until pulsations stop), which improves iron stores. Placental transfusion is essentially complete within a few minutes; waiting 1 hour offers no added benefit and is not recommended. Immediate clamping does not leave most newborns “without enough blood,” though delaying briefly is beneficial when feasible.

claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE — It’s an oversimplification. COVID-19 outcomes vary sharply by age, health status, vaccination, variant, and care access. Overall infection fatality has ranged roughly 0.2–1% across the pandemic, but for older or high‑risk people it’s several percent or higher—well above the “1% die” implied. Also, a notable minority have prolonged symptoms (long COVID), so “recover” isn’t guaranteed even among survivors.

claim: The US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration.
response_text: TRUE.  U.S. energy-related CO2 emissions fell sharply in 2020 (during Trump’s term) to their lowest level since 1983—i.e., more than 35 years. That drop was driven largely by the COVID-19 pandemic and longer-term shifts from coal to gas and renewables; 2019 alone did not meet the 35-year-low mark.

claim: People who do not vote for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 elections will not get the COVID vaccine free of cost.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In 2020 the BJP’s Bihar election manifesto promised free COVID-19 vaccination for all residents of Bihar if elected, not only BJP voters. Later, the Government of India made COVID-19 vaccines free for all adults nationwide (from June 21, 2021). Voting choices are secret and were never tied to vaccine eligibility.

claim: President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund.
response_text: FALSE.  The IMF and World Bank were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference by 44 Allied nations, with key architects John Maynard Keynes (UK) and Harry Dexter White (US). Dr. José Rizal died in 1896—decades before these institutions existed—and Ferdinand Marcos (Philippine president 1965–1986) played no role in their founding. The Philippines later became a member, but neither Marcos nor Rizal founded these institutions.

claim: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The FBI took custody of a MacBook Pro and an external hard drive from a Delaware repair shop in December 2019 under subpoena, identified as Hunter Biden’s laptop. DOJ/FBI filings and trial testimony in Hunter Biden’s 2023–2024 federal cases confirmed the FBI’s possession and use of data from that device.

claim: India’s imports from China increased by 27% in April-August 2020
response_text: FALSE.  Official DGCI&S/Commerce Ministry data show India’s imports from China fell year‑on‑year in Apr–Aug 2020 (roughly to about $21–22 billion from about $29–30 billion in Apr–Aug 2019), a decline of around 26–28%. The ~27% increase applies to Apr–Aug 2021 vs 2020, not to 2020 itself.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
response_text: FALSE. COVID-19 deaths have not been “pretty flat” overall; they have shown pronounced waves with large spikes (e.g., winter 2020–21, Delta in 2021, Omicron in 2022) and subsequent surges. Moreover, “flatten the curve” aims to reduce peak strain on healthcare systems, not to keep death counts flat over time.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible evidence that influenza vaccination increases susceptibility to COVID-19. Early “virus interference” speculation involved common cold coronaviruses and was misapplied; subsequent studies and public health authorities (e.g., CDC, WHO) found no increased risk of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection from flu shots. Linking President Trump’s COVID-19 infection to prior flu vaccination has no evidentiary basis; infection risk is driven by exposure and other factors, not flu vaccine history.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
response_text: FALSE  - Nate McMurray was Town Supervisor of Grand Island, New York (Erie County), not Grand Island, Nebraska. Grand Island, NE is a city with a mayor/city council, not a “town supervisor.” - Reporting from his tenure in Grand Island, NY indicates the town property tax rate was reduced in multiple budgets he oversaw, not raised. (While some fees can change year to year, the claim as stated—Nebraska and a vote to raise homeowner taxes—is incorrect.)

claim: The large image of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris logo projected onto a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee US indicates the motorcycle manufacturer's endorsement of the US Democratic presidential nominee.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Biden-Harris logo was projected onto the Harley-Davidson Museum in Milwaukee during the 2020 campaign/DNC period by outside organizers as a visual backdrop. Harley-Davidson stated it did not authorize the projection and was not endorsing any candidate. Fact-checks (e.g., Reuters, USA Today, Snopes) confirmed it was not an endorsement.

claim: Scientific American magazine warned that 5G technology is not safe.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: Scientific American did not issue an editorial warning about 5G safety. In 2019 it ran a guest blog/op‑ed by Joel M. Moskowitz titled “We Have No Reason to Believe 5G Is Safe,” which reflected the author’s opinion (with a standard disclaimer) rather than the magazine’s official stance. Scientific American has also published pieces arguing there’s no good evidence that 5G is harmful.

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
response_text: TRUE.  In October 2020, a City of Miami police officer, identified as Daniel Ubeda, was photographed in uniform wearing a “Trump 2020” mask inside a polling location (Miami’s Government Center) during early voting. The police chief and mayor said the conduct violated department policy on political activity and that the officer would face disciplinary action.

claim: Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump are banned from ever operating a charity again because they stole donations for children with cancer.
response_text: FALSE.  - New York’s civil case against the Donald J. Trump Foundation ended with the foundation’s dissolution, a $2 million payment by Donald Trump to charities, and mandatory fiduciary training for Donald Jr., Ivanka, and Eric. There was no lifetime ban on the children from operating charities. - The case involved misuse of the Trump Foundation’s funds (self-dealing and political use), not a court finding that they “stole donations for children with cancer.” Claims about Eric Trump’s fundraising for St. Jude were media investigations, not a court-imposed lifetime ban.

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
response_text: FALSE.  Under the ACA, the individual mandate penalty (2014–2018) was not a flat $10,000. It was the greater of a per-person amount (up to $695 per adult) or 2.5% of household income, capped at the national average bronze-plan premium. People for whom coverage was unaffordable (or with very low incomes) could claim an exemption and owe no penalty. Since 2019, the federal penalty is $0, though a few states have their own mandates.

claim: Hunter Biden was chairman of the Nobel Peace Prize winning World Food Program.
response_text: FALSE.  Hunter Biden was not chairman of the United Nations World Food Programme, which won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize. He served as board chair of World Food Program USA, a separate U.S. nonprofit that supports the UN agency. The Nobel was awarded to the UN WFP, not WFP USA.

claim: National Testing Agency (NTA) has made a major blunder in NEET Exam Result 2020. They stated that the all India topper had failed.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports or official records indicate that NTA declared the NEET 2020 all-India topper as “failed.” NEET 2020’s topper, Soyeb Aftab, was officially announced with a perfect 720/720, and Akanksha Singh also scored 720/720 (AIR 2 via tie-break rules). The “topper declared failed” claim appears to be a rumor; there was no such blunder reported by reputable sources.

claim: White House coronavirus adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote a 2008 paper that found most 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
response_text: FALSE.  Dr. Anthony Fauci coauthored a 2008 Journal of Infectious Diseases paper concluding that most deaths in the 1918–1919 pandemic were due to secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza infection. The paper does not attribute those bacterial infections to mask wearing and does not claim masks caused the deaths.

claim: Dr Anthony Fauci wrote a paper regarding the Spanish Flu and stated that the majority of deaths in 1918-1919 was because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
response_text: FALSE.  Anthony Fauci co-authored a 2008 paper (Journal of Infectious Diseases) concluding that many 1918–1919 influenza deaths were due to secondary bacterial pneumonia. The paper did not attribute those pneumonias to mask-wearing and did not claim masks caused the deaths. The “from wearing masks” part is a misrepresentation.

claim: India's imports from China increased by 27% during the period April-August 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Official Ministry of Commerce/DGCI&S data show India’s imports from China in April–August 2020 decreased year-on-year by roughly 27% compared to April–August 2019 (PIB also clarified this), not increased.

claim: The daughter of Muahammadu Buhari (the President of Nigeria) is a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).
response_text: FALSE.  No daughter of President Muhammadu Buhari has served on the NNPC board. Official lists of NNPC/NNPC Limited board members released during Buhari’s tenure (2016, 2019, 2021) include names such as Ibe Kachikwu, Maikanti Baru, Mele Kyari, Timipre Sylva, Margery Chuba-Okadigbo, Pius Akinyelure, Umar Ajiya, and Tajudeen Umar—none of whom are Buhari’s daughters (e.g., Zahra, Halima, Hanan). The claim appears to stem from misinformation.

claim: The Iowa Farm Bureau, US says that it would no longer be endorsing US Republican Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst for her re-election
response_text: FALSE.  Iowa Farm Bureau said it does not endorse candidates for federal office and had not endorsed Sen. Joni Ernst, so there was nothing to withdraw. A separate group, the American Farm Bureau Federation’s AgPAC, endorsed Ernst in 2020, and there was no report of that endorsement being rescinded.

claim: Joe and Jill Biden's income has increased recently.
response_text: TRUE.  According to their 2023 tax return released in April 2024, the Bidens reported about $619,976 in adjusted gross income, up from roughly $579,514 in 2022—an increase of about $40,000.

claim: A third of excess deaths in the United States between 1 March and  1 August 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic could not be directly attributed to the coronavirus
response_text: TRUE.  Evidence: A JAMA analysis of U.S. mortality data (Woolf et al., Oct 2020) found that from March 1 to August 1, 2020 there were about 225,530 excess deaths, of which 150,541 (67%) were attributed to COVID-19 on death certificates—leaving roughly 33% not directly attributed to the virus. This aligns with “about a third.”

claim: Prominent US Democrat party members including Hillary and Bill Clinton, were running a child sex-trafficking ring in the basement of a Washington, D.C., pizzeria.
response_text: FALSE. This “Pizzagate” claim is a debunked conspiracy theory: police and journalists found no evidence of any trafficking operation, and the pizzeria in question doesn’t even have a basement. The story led to a 2016 incident where an armed man entered the restaurant and confirmed nothing was there. Multiple fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, The New York Times, Washington Post) and law enforcement have refuted it.

claim: Anthony Weiner’s laptop contained proof Hillary Clinton & her associates are involved in child trafficking & paedophilia
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The FBI’s 2016 review of emails found on Anthony Weiner’s laptop did not uncover evidence of criminal activity by Hillary Clinton or her associates. James Comey stated the review did not change the FBI’s prior conclusion, and the DOJ Inspector General’s 2018 report found the laptop emails were largely duplicates and provided no new incriminating information. Claims about alleged “proof” (e.g., supposed videos or a “life insurance” file) have been denied by law enforcement and debunked by credible fact-checkers.

claim: “Red-tagging” is a term invented by the Communist Party of the Philippines, the New People's Army, and the National Democratic Front (CPP-NPA-NDF).
response_text: FALSE.  “Red-tagging” is a long-standing term used to describe the practice of labeling individuals or groups as communists or terrorist sympathizers, predating and existing independently of the CPP-NPA-NDF. It is used in international human rights reports (e.g., UN OHCHR’s 2020 report on the Philippines), Philippine media and academia, and has been recognized by Philippine courts. Independent fact-checkers (e.g., Rappler, Vera Files, AFP) have found no evidence that the CPP-NPA-NDF invented the term.

claim: Pennsylvania US rejects 372,000 mail-in ballots.
response_text: FALSE.  Pennsylvania has never rejected anything close to 372,000 mail-in ballots. In the 2020 general election, statewide mail-ballot rejections were on the order of roughly ten thousand (well under 1% of about 2.6–2.7 million returned). Even in the 2020 primary, rejections were in the tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands. The 372,000 figure stems from misreports about undeliverable mailings or applications, not actual rejected ballots. (High confidence)

claim: It's unclear how Joe Biden acquired his recent wealth since leaving office in 2017
response_text: FALSE  Public tax returns and federal financial disclosures detail Biden’s post-2017 income. After leaving the vice presidency, the Bidens earned roughly $15 million in 2017–2018, largely from book advances/royalties (Joe’s “Promise Me, Dad” and Jill’s “Where the Light Enters”) and paid speaking engagements, much of it routed through their S-corporations (CelticCapri and Giacoppa). These sources are documented and were released publicly.

claim: India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani installed Jinnah's portrait at AMU.
