response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The Jinnah portrait in AMU’s Students’ Union Hall has been there since 1938, when Muhammad Ali Jinnah was granted life membership of the Union. Maskoor Usmani, a former AMU Students’ Union president and later a Congress candidate, did not install it; he only defended not removing it during a 2018 controversy.

claim: Donald Trump Jr. said, “My father doesn’t need to rape women. It’s more likely a woman would rape him. That’s how popular he is.”
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record (video, transcript, reputable news) of Donald Trump Jr. saying this. The quote originated as a viral meme/fabricated story during the 2016 campaign and has been debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes).

claim: Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) is delivering 1kg bleaching powder, chlorine tablets to people’s doorsteps
response_text: FALSE.  HMWSSB has publicly clarified that viral messages claiming it will deliver 1 kg bleaching powder and chlorine tablets to households are fake. The board said there is no such doorstep distribution; its helpline is for water/sewerage complaints, not ordering bleaching powder or chlorine tablets.

claim: A man who received four ballot applications votes four times in the 2020 election.
response_text: FALSE.  A ballot application is just a request form, often sent by multiple groups. Election offices will issue only one ballot per registered voter and track it with voter rolls/barcodes. Submitting multiple applications does not yield multiple counted votes; duplicates are rejected or canceled. Voting multiple times is illegal and not enabled by receiving multiple applications.

claim: Most deaths in the 1918 influenza pandemic originated from bacterial pneumonia caused by face masks and that Dr Anthony Fauci, the US government’s top expert in the fight against Covid-19, knew about it.
response_text: FALSE.  - While many 1918 flu deaths were due to secondary bacterial pneumonia, there is no evidence it was caused by wearing face masks. The pneumonia resulted from influenza damaging the respiratory tract and subsequent bacterial invasion in an era without antibiotics, not from mask use. - Anthony Fauci coauthored a 2008 review concluding bacterial coinfections caused most deaths in 1918, but it did not link them to masks. The paper emphasized bacterial pathogens and the lack of antibiotics, not mask-related causes.

claim: BJP MP Kirron Kher Said "Rape Is A Part Of Indian Culture And It Can't Be Stopped"
response_text: FALSE.  No credible report shows Kirron Kher saying “Rape is a part of Indian culture and it can't be stopped.” The viral line is a misattribution. Kher did face criticism in 2017 for a victim‑blaming remark advising women to avoid getting into an auto with multiple men, but she did not describe rape as part of Indian culture. Similar outrageous quotes have been made by other politicians (e.g., Babulal Gaur’s 2014 “sometimes it’s right” remark), which likely fueled the false attribution.

claim: A message will be sent to your phone claiming to show that the Covid19 curve is flattening in India, But It will contain a malicious file
response_text: FALSE  This was a widely circulated WhatsApp-style hoax during 2020. Indian government fact-check (PIB) and outlets like Alt News/BOOM debunked warnings about a supposed “flattening the curve in India” video/file that would hack phones. No credible evidence shows such a mass malicious message existed. General caution with unknown links still applies.

claim: US Sen Kamala Harris failed the bar exam  (qualifying examination for lawyers)on her first attempt
response_text: TRUE.  Kamala Harris has written that she did not pass the California bar exam on her first try; she passed on her second attempt and was admitted to the California bar in 1990 (per her 2019 memoir “The Truths We Hold” and State Bar records).

claim: US Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class at Notre Dame Law School
response_text: TRUE.  Amy Coney Barrett graduated from Notre Dame Law School in 1997 summa cum laude, first in her class, and received the Hoynes Prize (the law school’s highest honor), which is awarded to the top graduate.

claim: Saved by the Bell actor, Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot.
response_text: FALSE. Dustin Diamond (Screech on Saved by the Bell) died on February 1, 2021 from small-cell lung cancer in a hospital, not in a prison riot.

claim: Controversial abortion methods are allowed under New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020).
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: New Zealand’s Abortion Legislation Act 2020 treats abortion as a health service, allows abortion on request up to 20 weeks and after 20 weeks if clinically appropriate, and does not ban or specify particular procedures. Method choice is left to clinical judgment and guidelines, so techniques some consider controversial (e.g., surgical D&E, later‑gestation methods) are legally permitted when deemed clinically appropriate. (Minor uncertainty stems from “controversial” being subjective.)

claim: Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairman Chito Gascon called a “surprise military attack” by the Philippine Army,  conducted on members of the New People’s Army (NPA) a “violation of human rights.”
response_text: FALSE.  This quote was fabricated and circulated via memes/satirical posts. There is no record of CHR Chair Chito Gascon calling a Philippine Army “surprise attack” on NPA members a human rights violation. The CHR publicly denied this claim, noting that legitimate military operations against armed combatants are governed by international humanitarian law and are not per se human rights violations. (Minor uncertainty only in exact origin of the meme, but the attributed statement is not authentic.)

claim: IMAGE CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP CURRENTLY FACES A COURT CASE FOR ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTING A 13-YEAR-OLD
response_text: FALSE.  A civil lawsuit filed in 2016 alleging Trump assaulted a 13-year-old at Jeffrey Epstein’s residence was voluntarily dismissed before the 2016 election and did not proceed; no criminal charges were filed. As of the latest available reporting (through 2024/early 2025), Trump does not currently face a court case over that allegation. (Minor uncertainty only if a new case was filed very recently.)

claim: The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter.
response_text: TRUE.  Apple announced in 2020 that all iPhone 12 models ship without EarPods and a power adapter, including only a USB‑C to Lightning cable. (There were limited regional exceptions initially, e.g., France required EarPods at the time.)

claim: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.
response_text: TRUE.  The Abortion Legislation Act 2020 does not include any clause requiring that a baby born alive after an abortion be given medical care; an amendment to add such a requirement was proposed and voted down. However, separate New Zealand laws and standards (e.g., Crimes Act 1961 duties and the Health and Disability Code) already require appropriate care for any baby born alive. Note: “appropriate care” may be active treatment or palliative care depending on clinical circumstances and viability.

claim: Kanye West was ahead of Biden and Trump in the Kentucky polls in October 2020
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: A viral screenshot in October 2020 showed Kanye West leading in Kentucky, but it came from a local TV station’s website (LEX 18) that briefly displayed placeholder/test data by mistake. The station corrected it and said it was not a real poll or result. No credible Kentucky polls had West ahead of Biden or Trump; Kentucky polling and the final vote showed Trump with a large lead.

claim: Former President Donald Trump who lost the popular vote by 3 million has nominated a full third of The United Supreme Court, as of 13th October 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  - Trump lost the 2016 popular vote by about 2.9 million (often rounded to 3 million). - By Oct 13, 2020, he had nominated three justices—Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett—i.e., one-third of the nine-seat Supreme Court. (Barrett was still in hearings then; she was confirmed on Oct 26, 2020.)

claim: Amy Coney Barrett's nomination to the Supreme Court would be confirmed in October 2020, by a Senate majority that represents 15 million fewer people than the minority party.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed by the Senate on October 26, 2020, in a 52–48 vote. At that time, the Republican Senate majority collectively represented fewer Americans than the Democratic minority—commonly estimated at about 15 million fewer, depending on population estimates and counting method—reflecting the Senate’s small-state bias. Minor variance in the exact figure exists, but analyses at the time consistently put the gap around 14–15 million.

claim: President Trump said Anthony Fauci said, “This is not a threat. This is not a problem. Don’t worry about it.” when talking about the pandemic
response_text: TRUE — At his Oct. 15, 2020 NBC town hall (and again around the Oct. 22 debate), President Trump claimed that Dr. Anthony Fauci had said, “This is not a threat. This is not a problem. Don’t worry about it.” (Trump’s attribution was misleading; Fauci hadn’t used those exact words.)

claim: Amy Coney Barrett, associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States,  said during her Supreme Court confirmation hearing that she was not using notes because she has seven kids and is used to stupid questions.
response_text: FALSE.  During her 2020 confirmation hearing, Amy Coney Barrett was asked what notes she was using and held up a blank notepad, saying it only had the Senate letterhead. She did not say she wasn’t using notes because she has seven kids or that she’s used to “stupid questions.” That line originated as a social media joke/meme, not from her testimony.

claim: Anthony Fauci the NIAID director is a democrat.
response_text: FALSE.  Anthony Fauci is a career civil servant who served under presidents of both parties. He has said he isn’t registered with any political party, and fact-checks have found no public record of him being a registered Democrat.

claim: CNN announces on social media that President Donald Trump dies from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Donald Trump did contract COVID-19 in October 2020 but recovered. He did not die from COVID-19, and CNN never issued such an announcement. Posts claiming CNN reported his death were hoaxes using doctored CNN-style graphics.

claim: 18-year-old man was recently killed by Trinamool Congress workers in West Bengal for supporting BJP
response_text: FALSE  Briefly: Viral posts claiming an 18-year-old was “recently” killed in West Bengal by Trinamool Congress workers for supporting the BJP relied on miscaptioned/old, unrelated images. No credible, independent reports or police confirmations substantiate such a politically motivated killing of an 18-year-old. Some fact-checks traced the circulated photos to unrelated incidents, and no verified source confirms the claim as stated. Uncertainty: Without a specific name/date, “recently” is vague, but available evidence does not support the claim.

claim: Fact check: Harris' statement on Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination misses key details
response_text: TRUE.  Harris suggested Lincoln declined to nominate a justice before the 1864 election on principle. In reality, Chief Justice Taney died Oct. 12, 1864, the Senate was out of session until December, and Lincoln could not realistically secure confirmation before the election. He then nominated Salmon P. Chase on Dec. 6, and the Senate confirmed him the same day. Harris’s account omits this context and overstates a precedent of principled delay.

claim: Daughters of President Muhammadu Buhari and Vice President Yemi Osinbajo brought about the dissolution of Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS).
response_text: FALSE.  The Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS) was dissolved on 11 October 2020 by the Inspector General of Police, following massive nationwide #EndSARS protests and public outcry over police abuses. While the daughters of President Buhari and Vice President Osinbajo publicly expressed support for the protests, they held no official roles and did not bring about the dissolution.

claim: The Median White Household Wealth In The US Is 81 Times that of The Black Median Household Wealth
response_text: FALSE.  Authoritative data (Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances) shows the median White family has about 6–10 times the median wealth of Black families, not 81 times. For example: - 2019: White $188,200 vs Black $24,100 (~7.8×) - 2022: White $285,000 vs Black $44,900 (~6.3×)  “81 times” is off by an order of magnitude.

claim: Congress MP Rahul Gandhi has been listed as the seventh most educated leader by Forbes.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no Forbes list ranking “most educated leaders,” and no Forbes article naming Rahul Gandhi as the 7th most educated leader. Multiple fact-checks have traced the claim to a fabricated graphic; neither Forbes nor Forbes India has published such a ranking.

claim: Donald Trump is facing a court case for raping a teen in 1994
response_text: FALSE.  A civil lawsuit was filed in 2016 alleging Trump raped a 13-year-old in 1994, but it was voluntarily dismissed before proceeding. There is no active court case against Trump for raping a teen in 1994.

claim: Joe Biden said “You know, we have to come together. That’s why I’m running. I’m running as a proud Democrat for the Senate. So vote! Vote!”
response_text: TRUE.  Joe Biden said those words at an Oct. 12, 2020 campaign event in Toledo, Ohio, while urging people to vote. He misspoke in saying he was “running … for the Senate” (he was running for president), but the quote is accurate. Reported by outlets including USA Today, PolitiFact, and Snopes.

claim: NASA always receives blessings from the Pope and that God’s permission must be sought before a space mission.
response_text: FALSE.  NASA is a secular U.S. government agency and does not seek or require religious approval for missions. While Popes have occasionally offered greetings or blessings to astronauts (e.g., Pope Paul VI during Apollo 11; Pope Francis speaking with ISS crews), there is no policy or practice of NASA “always” receiving papal blessings or having to obtain God’s permission before launches.

claim: Most Arab citizens support normalization with Israel.
response_text: FALSE.  Regional polling shows the opposite: large majorities of Arabs oppose normalization with Israel. The Arab Opinion Index (ACRPS) 2022–2023 found about 84% opposed their country recognizing Israel, and surveys conducted after the 2023 Gaza war put opposition near 90%. Arab Barometer likewise reports majorities against normalization in most surveyed countries (e.g., Jordan, Egypt, Tunisia, Lebanon, Algeria, Iraq), with only a few exceptions showing higher support (such as the UAE, and mixed views in Morocco).

claim: The PHE has began to combine Covid-19 and influenza statistics to make the numbers look worse.
response_text: FALSE.  Public Health England merged its weekly flu and COVID-19 surveillance into one report for convenience, but it did not lump the figures together to inflate totals. Within that report, COVID-19 and influenza metrics are presented separately and clearly labeled. Independent fact checks have also found no evidence that UK authorities combined flu and COVID deaths to make numbers look worse; where broader categories (like “influenza and pneumonia”) are used, overlaps are explained and COVID-19 is reported separately.

claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
response_text: FALSE.  - No Australian law called “the Flora and Fauna Act” ever classified Aboriginal people as animals. - The 1967 referendum removed Section 127 (which excluded Aboriginal people from the Commonwealth census) and amended Section 51(xxvi) to allow the federal government to make laws for Aboriginal people. It did not “reclassify” them from fauna. - The myth likely arose because some state departments once administered Aboriginal affairs alongside wildlife/parks, and due to discriminatory “protection” laws—but not legal classification as animals.

claim: Robert E. Lee, commander of the Confederate States Army during the American Civil War, was not a slave owner.
response_text: FALSE.  Robert E. Lee enslaved people. He personally owned enslaved individuals and, as executor of his father‑in‑law G. W. P. Custis’s estate, he controlled and managed nearly 200 enslaved people on the Custis plantations, formally signing their manumission only on December 29, 1862, as the will required. This is documented in the 1862 manumission deed and contemporary records from Arlington House.

claim: A BLM or antifa activist shot and killed a patriot at a protest in Denver, Colorado on October 10, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  On Oct. 10, 2020 in Denver, Lee Keltner, a right‑wing demonstrator, was shot and killed during dueling protests. The shooter was Matthew Dolloff, a private security guard contracted by local TV station 9News, not a BLM or antifa activist. Police said there was no known affiliation with BLM or antifa.

claim: From 8th October the UK government will combine weekly flu and covid reports.
response_text: TRUE.  Public Health England (now UKHSA) announced in 2020 that, from 8 October 2020 (week 41), it would publish a single combined weekly national surveillance report covering both influenza and COVID-19. This was a consolidation of the report format, not a merging of the underlying data or death counts.

claim: PTFE Sprayed On Blue Masks Causes Symptoms Similar To COVID-19
response_text: FALSE.  - Most blue surgical masks are made from polypropylene, not PTFE, and are not “sprayed” with Teflon. - PTFE is chemically inert at normal temperatures. Health effects (polymer fume fever with flu‑like symptoms) occur only when PTFE is overheated to high temperatures, not from wearing a mask. - No evidence shows PTFE in masks causes COVID‑like symptoms; fact-checks and health agencies report masks are safe when used as intended.  Minor uncertainty: some respirators use ePTFE membranes, but these are solid filter layers and not associated with such symptoms in normal use.

claim: The gross domestic product  (GDP) figure in Nigeria for 2020 has decreased from the figure for 2019.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria’s economy contracted in 2020. Real GDP growth was negative (about −1.8% to −1.9%), meaning the level of real GDP fell versus 2019. In current US dollars, World Bank data also show GDP declined from roughly $448 billion (2019) to about $432 billion (2020). Sources: Nigeria NBS; World Bank.

claim: Ulysses S. Grant, commander of the Union Army during the American Civil War, was a slave owner.
response_text: TRUE.  Before the Civil War, Grant married into a slaveholding family and personally owned at least one enslaved man, William Jones, whom he freed in St. Louis on March 29, 1859. He did not own slaves during the war, but the statement that he was a slave owner is accurate.

claim: Dr. Anthony Fauci said of Trump’s pandemic response, “I can’t imagine that … anybody could be doing more.”
response_text: FALSE.  Fauci did say “I can’t imagine that … anybody could be doing more” in March 2020, but he was referring to the broader federal task force/government response, not specifically praising Trump’s personal pandemic response. He later said the Trump campaign’s use of that line was taken out of context and did not represent an endorsement of Trump. Uncertainty: none about the context dispute.

claim: Joe Biden proposed a US wide 2% property tax increase.
response_text: FALSE.  - Property taxes in the U.S. are set by state and local governments, not the federal government; a president cannot impose a nationwide property tax rate. - Joe Biden has not proposed a U.S.-wide 2% property tax increase.  - The claim likely confuses this with other ideas (e.g., Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s proposed 2% annual wealth tax on fortunes over $50 million, or the federal stock buyback tax), neither of which is a property tax.

claim: US Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden was endorsed by Black Lives Matter and Antifa
response_text: FALSE.  - Black Lives Matter’s national organizations (e.g., Black Lives Matter Global Network Foundation, Movement for Black Lives) did not issue a formal endorsement of Joe Biden in 2020. Some local activists or unrelated PACs may have supported him, but there was no official BLM-wide endorsement. - “Antifa” is not a centralized organization; as noted by U.S. officials (e.g., FBI Director Christopher Wray), it’s a loosely organized ideology/movement, so it does not issue formal endorsements.

claim: Kirron Kher, BJP’s Chandigarh MP, said “Rape is part of Indian culture and tradition. We cannot stop it!”
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The quote has been circulated via fake quote cards but no credible report or record shows Kirron Kher saying “Rape is part of Indian culture and tradition.” Fact-checkers (e.g., Alt News, BOOM) have debunked it. Kher was criticized in 2017 for advising women to avoid getting into autos with men after a rape case, but she did not make the cited statement.

claim: We do not know where Covid-19 places among causes of death because the data is not published.
response_text: FALSE.  Cause-of-death data are routinely published by official agencies. For example, in the United States the CDC/NCHS publishes leading-cause rankings each year: COVID-19 was the 3rd leading cause of death in 2020–2022 and dropped to about 10th in 2023 (provisional). Similar data are published by other national statistics offices and the WHO. Rankings vary by year and country, but the data are publicly available.

claim: Swiss Squash player Ambre Allinckx’s refuses to play in India due to safety reasons
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: There are no credible reports or official statements showing Ambre Allinckx refused to play in India for “safety reasons.” The viral claim circulating online has been debunked, and Allinckx has not made such a statement. (Slight uncertainty only because social posts can be ephemeral, but no reliable source corroborates the claim.)

claim: Labour reversed the 4,400 health health worker cuts by the LNP.
response_text: TRUE (with minor caveats)  - In Queensland, the Newman LNP government (2012–2015) reduced Queensland Health staffing by roughly 4,000–4,400 FTE, largely in non‑clinical roles. - After Labor took office in 2015, Queensland Health staffing grew substantially (thousands of additional nurses, doctors and allied health staff), more than offsetting those reductions. - Caveat: figures vary by whether headcount or FTE and by which roles are counted, but on standard measures the cuts were effectively reversed.

claim: WHO ( World Health Organization) approved water, salt and vinegar remedy for coronavirus
response_text: FALSE.  WHO has not approved water, salt, or vinegar as a remedy for COVID-19. WHO’s myth-busters explicitly state that rinsing the nose or gargling with saline does not prevent COVID-19, and there is no evidence that vinegar cures or prevents it. Only evidence-based measures (vaccination, masks, ventilation, tested treatments like antivirals/steroids for specific cases) are recommended. Uncertainty: none.

claim: Forty percent of Iowa’s energy resources are from renewables.
response_text: FALSE.  “Iowa’s energy resources” is vague, but 40% doesn’t match the common metrics. Iowa now gets about two‑thirds of its electricity from wind alone (around 64% in 2023 per EIA), so 40% understates the electricity share. If instead you mean total energy use across all sectors (transportation, heating, etc.), renewables are below 40%.

claim: it is unknown whether a person under 20 can pass the disease to an older adult.
response_text: FALSE.  For common infectious diseases like COVID-19 and influenza, it is well established that people under 20 can transmit infection to older adults (e.g., documented child-to-adult household and school-related transmission). Note: slight uncertainty since “the disease” isn’t specified, but as a general claim this is false.

claim: Fly swatters are now available on Joe Biden's online store.
response_text: TRUE. After the October 2020 vice presidential debate (when a fly landed on Mike Pence), the Biden-Harris campaign added a “Truth Over Flies” fly swatter to its official online store, which sold out quickly.

claim: A campaign ad video for John Cornyn says that his plan would guarantee insurers must sell plans to any patient with preexisting conditions and will be covered in his plan.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In his 2020 campaign, John Cornyn aired ads stating his plan would protect people with preexisting conditions, asserting that insurers would be required to sell plans to them and that they would be covered. (Whether his proposal matched ACA-level protections was disputed, but the ad did make that claim.) Uncertain on exact wording, but the ad’s message conveyed this guarantee.

claim: Charlotta Bass was the first Black woman to run for vice president in 1952
response_text: TRUE.  Charlotta Bass, a newspaper publisher and civil-rights activist, was the Progressive Party’s vice-presidential nominee in 1952 alongside presidential candidate Vincent Hallinan. She is widely recognized as the first Black woman to run for vice president in U.S. history.

claim: China seek for court’s approval to kill the over 20,000 coronavirus patients to avoid further spread of the virus.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated from a hoax/fake-news website and was debunked by multiple fact-checkers. There were no credible reports or official statements that China sought court approval to kill COVID-19 patients. China’s response involved quarantines, lockdowns, testing, and treatment—not euthanizing patients, which would be illegal and unprecedented.

claim: Nigeria’s Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has been appointed the new and first female Director-General of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
response_text: TRUE. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala of Nigeria was appointed Director-General of the WTO on 15 February 2021, becoming the first woman (and first African) to lead the organization. She took office on 1 March 2021.

claim: When Joe Biden was US vice-president they took a month to act on information that might have saved Kayla Mueller, a humanitarian worker held hostage and sexually abused by the Islamic State terrorist group
response_text: FALSE.  - Timeline: Public reporting (NYT, Washington Post, AP) shows the Obama administration authorized and launched a Special Operations raid in early July 2014, soon after receiving sufficiently specific intelligence on the hostages’ location. The preceding weeks involved corroborating intel and planning, not inaction. The hostages, including Kayla Mueller, had been moved shortly before the raid. - The assertion that “they took a month to act” overstates or misstates the record, and the claim that quicker action “might have saved” her is speculative and unproven.  Note: Some critics and family members have alleged a month‑long delay, but contemporaneous reporting and official accounts do not substantiate that.

claim: Right after a time where we're going through a pandemic that lost 22 million jobs at the height, we've already added back 11.6 million jobs.
response_text: TRUE  - BLS data show U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by about 22 million from February to April 2020. - By early fall 2020, roughly 11.4–11.6 million of those jobs had been added back. Note: Exact figures vary by month, but the claim is consistent with BLS totals for that period.

claim: Because of a so-called trade war with China, America lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs.
response_text: FALSE.  - BLS data show U.S. manufacturing employment rose by roughly 450,000–500,000 from early 2017 to late 2019, during the tariff “trade war” period; there was no net loss of 300,000 manufacturing jobs then.  - Some research (e.g., Federal Reserve economists) finds the tariffs modestly reduced manufacturing employment relative to what it otherwise would have been, but on the order of tens of thousands, not 300,000. - The oft-cited “300,000 jobs lost” estimate (e.g., Moody’s Analytics, 2019) referred to total U.S. jobs across the economy, not specifically manufacturing.  Minor uncertainty: precise estimates of tariff effects vary, but none credible show a 300,000 manufacturing-job loss from the trade war.

claim: They [the Democrats] want to ... ban fracking.
response_text: FALSE.  The Democratic Party and President Biden have not called for a nationwide fracking ban. Biden repeatedly said he would not ban fracking and the 2020 Democratic platform did not propose one. Democrats have pushed for tighter methane rules and limits on new oil and gas leasing on federal lands, but not a blanket ban. Some individual Democrats support a ban, but it is not the party’s position.

claim: Zimbabwe gets more than half of the African Export Import Bank loans.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: Afreximbank’s loan book is spread across dozens of African countries and totals tens of billions of dollars. Zimbabwe’s outstanding facilities amount to only a small fraction of that (even with recent $1 billion–level facilities), nowhere near 50%. The bank has publicly refuted claims of such a concentration. (Exact percentages vary over time, but they are far below half.)

claim: The Democrats want to shut down U.S. churches permanently.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no Democratic Party platform, proposal, or evidence indicating a desire to shut down U.S. churches permanently. Democrats routinely affirm First Amendment religious freedom, and many Democratic leaders are themselves religious. Temporary COVID-19 public‑health restrictions on large gatherings (including religious services) were time-limited and often applied broadly; some were narrowed by courts, but none aimed at permanent church closures.

claim: Over thirty million people... in the last several months had to file for unemployment."
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: U.S. Department of Labor data show that during the early months of the COVID‑19 pandemic (roughly mid‑March to late April/early May 2020), cumulative initial unemployment claims exceeded 30 million—about 33 million by April 30 and around 36 million by mid‑May. Minor caveat: initial claims count filings, not unique individuals, so there can be some duplication.

claim: COVID-19 had caused zero deaths in people under 20.
response_text: FALSE.  COVID-19 deaths in people under 20, while rare compared with older adults, have occurred. For example, U.S. CDC mortality data show thousands of COVID-19 deaths among ages 0–19 (over 2,000 in ages 0–17 alone by 2024), and similar pediatric deaths have been recorded in other countries.

claim: Trump said 'there were fine people on both sides' in far-right protests.
response_text: TRUE — In an Aug. 15, 2017 press conference about the far-right “Unite the Right” events in Charlottesville, Trump said “you also had people that were very fine people, on both sides,” while adding he was not referring to neo-Nazis and white nationalists.

claim: Vice president of the U.S Mike Pence said “When Joe Biden was vice president of the United States, the FBI actually spied on President Trump and my campaign.”
response_text: TRUE  Explanation: Mike Pence has repeatedly claimed that, “when Joe Biden was vice president,” the FBI “spied” on the Trump campaign—e.g., during the Oct. 7, 2020 vice presidential debate and other 2020 remarks. He typically phrased it as spying on “President Trump’s” or “our” campaign; the “my campaign” wording may vary slightly, but the substance of the quote is accurate. Uncertainty: exact phrasing may have been “our campaign” rather than “my campaign.”

claim: Richard A. Rothschild filed a patent for novel coronavirus tests in 2015.
response_text: FALSE.  Richard A. Rothschild’s “System and Method for Testing for COVID‑19” was filed in 2020 and published in September 2020. The 2015 date seen online refers to an earlier, unrelated provisional application in the same patent family about biometric data, not a COVID-19 test. Multiple fact-checks (e.g., Reuters, AP) confirm this.

claim: US President Donald Trump following his positive diagnosis of COVID-19, was given treatment developed from the use of fetal tissue, made by the company Regeneron.
response_text: TRUE.  Trump received Regeneron’s experimental monoclonal antibody cocktail (casirivimab/imdevimab). In its development/testing, Regeneron used HEK293-derived cells, a lab cell line originally derived from fetal tissue in the 1970s. The therapy itself does not contain fetal tissue and is manufactured in non-human cells; no new or recent fetal tissue was used.

claim: U.S. mortalities this year are not materially different from the previous 5 years
response_text: FALSE  Reason: CDC/NCHS provisional data show 2025 all‑cause deaths are running well below the pandemic peaks of 2020–2022 (hundreds of thousands fewer on an annualized basis, i.e., >5% difference) and slightly below 2023–2024. Given that pre‑pandemic year‑to‑year changes were typically ~1–2%, the difference from the prior five-year period (2020–2024) is material.   Note: 2025 figures are provisional and the year isn’t complete, but the pattern is clear.

claim: President Donald  J Trump said it [coronavirus] was a hoax.
response_text: FALSE.  At a Feb. 28, 2020 rally in South Carolina, Trump said Democrats were “politicizing the coronavirus” and called that “their new hoax.” He did not say the virus itself was a hoax, and later clarified he was referring to Democrats’ actions. Fact-checkers (PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Snopes) concur.

claim: Documents show the CIA made a referral to the FBI documenting the allegation that U.S. Presidential candidate Hillary Clinton had approved a campaign plan to stir up a scandal against U.S. Presidential candidate Donald Trump by tying him to Putin and the Russians’ hacking of the Democratic National Committee.
The Democratic party has spent the last three and a half years trying to overturn the results of the last US election.
response_text: FALSE.  Democratic leaders conceded the 2016 result and participated in the transition; there was no party effort to nullify or reverse the certified election. Subsequent investigations (e.g., the Mueller probe) and the 2019 impeachment were constitutional oversight of a sitting president, not attempts to overturn the election result, and would not have installed the prior opponent. A few symbolic objections and short-lived recounts (largely led by the Green Party) do not amount to a years-long effort by the Democratic Party to overturn the election.

claim: The content of the conspiracy network, Radio Quebec, hosted by Alexis Cossette-Trudel is banned by Facebook.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In October 2020, Facebook implemented a platform-wide ban on QAnon-related content and removed pages, groups, and accounts tied to it. As part of this action, Facebook took down Alexis Cossette-Trudel’s Radio-Québec page and related accounts, effectively banning Radio-Québec content on the platform. Minor uncertainty: enforcement can fluctuate over time, but the ban and removals were explicitly reported.

claim: OPCW scenario of the Navalny case is a fantastic story and a planned conspiracy scenario
response_text: FALSE.  OPCW did not publish a “scenario” or conspiracy narrative about Navalny. It provided technical assistance and reported that biomedical samples from Navalny contained biomarkers of a Novichok-type cholinesterase inhibitor, confirmed by multiple independent OPCW-designated labs. These findings aligned with German, French, and Swedish lab results. No credible evidence has been presented that this was a planned conspiracy; the claim contradicts the documented technical findings.

claim: In 1977 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer had an affair with his daughter best friend from high school.
response_text: FALSE.  - In 1977, Chuck Schumer was a New York State Assemblyman, not Senate Minority Leader (he became Senate Minority Leader in 2017). - He didn’t marry until 1980, and his daughters were born in the 1980s, so he had no daughter in 1977. - There are no credible reports supporting this claim.

claim: 49 percent of Nigerians are in extreme poverty.
response_text: FALSE.  Recent, reputable estimates put Nigeria’s extreme-poverty rate well below half. World Bank data (international extreme-poverty line of $2.15/day, 2017 PPP) place Nigeria around roughly one-third of the population, and Nigeria’s 2018/19 national survey shows about 40% below the national (not “extreme”) poverty line. The “about 49%” figure reflects older or different measures (e.g., earlier World Poverty Clock snapshots), not current consensus. Uncertainty: precise rates vary by method and year, but they are not near 49% today.

claim: During the Obama/Biden administration, 18,000 people got clemency.
response_text: FALSE.  Barack Obama granted 1,927 acts of clemency (1,715 commutations and 212 pardons). That is far short of 18,000. The 18,000 figure may reflect the number of denied petitions or confusion with other sentence reductions, not clemency grants.

claim: People in the UK who are required to self-isolate due to having tested positive for the COVID-19 virus will receive a support payment of £500 per week
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In the UK, the main support was a one‑off £500 payment (e.g., England’s Test and Trace Support Payment) for eligible low‑income individuals asked to self‑isolate—not £500 per week. It was not universal and the schemes have since ended.

claim: A Congressman Just Introduced A Bill To Remove Nancy Pelosi From The House.
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: No U.S. Representative actually introduced and filed a legitimate bill that would “remove Nancy Pelosi from the House.” While a few Republicans at times proposed symbolic resolutions (e.g., to censure her or call for her resignation) and one member in 2019 publicly said he would introduce an expulsion resolution, there is no record of a formal, actionable bill or resolution to expel her being introduced and advancing. The claim stems from misleading headlines and social media posts. (Some uncertainty stems from sporadic announcements that were never formally filed.)

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump has departed Walter Reed hospital just a few days after testing positive for COVID-19.
response_text: TRUE.  Donald Trump announced a positive COVID-19 test on Oct 2, 2020, was admitted to Walter Reed that day, and was discharged on Oct 5, 2020—just a few days later.

claim: All students in India who had to switch to an online mode of education due to the coronavirus pandemic are being provided free Android smartphones by the government.
response_text: FALSE.  There has been no nationwide Government of India program to give all students free Android smartphones for online classes. PIB Fact Check repeatedly debunked such viral claims during the pandemic. While a few state governments ran limited schemes (e.g., distributing phones/tablets to certain grades or college students), these were not universal and did not cover all students across India. Many students continued to lack device access, with the Centre focusing on TV/radio/digital platforms (e.g., PM eVidya, DIKSHA) rather than universal smartphone distribution.

claim: Oxygen deprivation is caused by wearing face masks.
response_text: FALSE.  Face masks (cloth, surgical, N95) are designed to be breathable. Studies measuring oxygen saturation and carbon dioxide in healthy adults and children show no significant changes while wearing them at rest or with usual activity. Masks can feel stuffy and slightly increase breathing effort, but they do not cause oxygen deprivation. People with severe cardiopulmonary disease may find masks uncomfortable and should follow medical advice.

claim: Carbon dioxide intoxication is caused by wearing face masks.
response_text: FALSE.  Face masks (surgical, cloth, N95) are permeable to carbon dioxide and do not cause CO2 intoxication. Studies show no clinically significant rise in CO2 or drop in oxygen in healthy people wearing masks, even for extended periods. Hypercapnia occurs with exposure to high environmental CO2 or severe respiratory failure, not from normal mask use. At most, masks may cause discomfort or mild, safe increases in inhaled CO2; people with severe lung disease should seek medical advice.

claim: Wearing face masks leads to permanent neurological damage, especially in children.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that wearing face masks causes permanent neurological damage in children or adults. Studies and guidance from bodies like the CDC, WHO, and the American Academy of Pediatrics show that masks do not cause harmful CO2 buildup or oxygen deprivation in people over age 2; physiological measures remain within normal ranges. Masks can cause temporary discomfort (e.g., headaches) but not lasting neurological harm. Masks are not recommended for children under 2 due to suffocation risk, not neurological damage.

claim: “Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months.”
response_text: FALSE.  Republicans in the Wisconsin Legislature did pass bills within recent six‑month windows of the 2023–24 session (e.g., the new legislative maps approved in Feb. 2024, along with earlier measures like the 2023 budget and shared‑revenue law). While there were stretches with little or no floor action (especially after March 2024), the blanket claim that they “have not passed a single bill in 6 months” is not generally accurate. Uncertainty: depends on the exact six‑month period referenced.

claim: Tax avoidance costs £90 billion per year.
response_text: FALSE.  HMRC’s official estimates put the entire UK “tax gap” at roughly £35–40 billion a year in recent years, with tax avoidance accounting for only a small fraction of that (around £1–2 billion). The £90 billion figure comes from older, highly disputed campaign estimates that use much broader assumptions and are not accepted by HMRC.

claim: President Trump is not on supplemental oxygen.
response_text: FALSE (uncertain/context-dependent). During his October 2020 COVID-19 illness, Trump did receive supplemental oxygen on at least two occasions, per his physician, despite statements that he was not on oxygen at certain moments. Without a timestamp, the blanket present-tense claim is misleading.

claim: The PLAAF has shot down an Indian Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jet in Tibet.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible evidence from official sources or major media indicates the PLAAF shot down an Indian Su-30 over Tibet. Such an incident would be a major escalation and widely reported; recent Su‑30 losses have been accidents within India, and past social media claims of a Tibet shootdown have been debunked.

claim: Senate President Vicente Sotto III claimed that hardheaded Filipinos are to blame for the cases of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in the country
response_text: FALSE.  This quote was misattributed. Fact-checkers (e.g., VERA Files) found no record of Senate President Vicente “Tito” Sotto III saying hardheaded Filipinos are to blame for COVID-19 cases; Sotto also denied the quote. In public remarks, he had argued Filipinos were largely compliant and that hardship, not “pasaway” behavior, was driving many to go out.

claim: Dr. Ebeneezer, a medical doctor and a herbal practitioner at the Amuzu Hospital has instructed men to have sex at least 21 times a month to avoid prostate cancer.
response_text: FALSE.  - There’s no credible evidence that a real “Dr. Ebeneezer” at an “Amuzu Hospital” issued such an instruction; fact-checks have traced this to a viral social media hoax. - The “21 times a month” figure misinterprets a 2016 observational study that found an association between higher ejaculation frequency and lower prostate cancer risk. It did not prove causation, prescribe a monthly target, or claim sex prevents/“avoids” prostate cancer.

claim: The ex-Prime Minister of India Lal Bahadur Shastri took a loan to buy a car.
response_text: TRUE.  It’s widely documented that Lal Bahadur Shastri took a small loan (about Rs 5,000) from Punjab National Bank to buy a car (often cited as a Fiat) for his family in the mid-1960s. After his death in 1966, the remaining installments were reportedly paid by his widow, Lalita Shastri.

claim: President Trump announces  he has tested positive for Covid-19.
response_text: TRUE — On Oct 2, 2020, while serving as U.S. president, Donald Trump announced (via Twitter) that he and First Lady Melania Trump had tested positive for COVID-19.

claim: The wife of  Lal Bahadur Shastri (ex Prime minister of India) repaid his car loan after his death.
response_text: TRUE.  Lal Bahadur Shastri had taken a small bank loan (commonly cited as from Punjab National Bank) to buy a Fiat car. After his sudden death in 1966, his wife, Lalita Shastri, repaid the outstanding installments from the family pension. Multiple biographies and news features note this, though the exact loan amount varies across sources.

claim: President Trump's positive COVID-19 test result is a 'con'
response_text: FALSE.  Evidence strongly indicates Trump did contract COVID-19 in Oct. 2020: his physician and the White House announced positive tests; he was admitted to Walter Reed, required supplemental oxygen, and received therapies (Regeneron monoclonal antibodies, remdesivir, dexamethasone). Multiple close contacts in the same timeframe also tested positive, consistent with a White House outbreak. There is no credible evidence it was fabricated. (Public cannot see his lab results directly, but the weight of evidence contradicts the “con” claim.)

claim: US President Donald Trump's positive COVID-19 result is a false positive, which could allow an adversary in the White House to poison the president’s soda and later say that he suffered from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  - Trump’s COVID-19 infection in Oct. 2020 was corroborated by multiple positive tests, clear COVID-19 symptoms (fever, oxygen desaturation), hospitalization at Walter Reed, and COVID-specific treatments (monoclonal antibodies, remdesivir, dexamethasone). Several close contacts also tested positive around the same time, consistent with an outbreak, not a false positive. - PCR false positives are rare, and the combination of repeated positives plus clinical illness makes a false positive extremely unlikely. - The poisoning scenario is unfounded speculation with no evidence.

claim: The Democrats deliberately spread the COVID-19 virus to US President Donald Trump  during the first  US presidential debate on Sept. 29, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Democrats intentionally infected Donald Trump at the Sept. 29, 2020 debate. Public reporting and contact tracing tied the subsequent White House COVID-19 outbreak largely to the Sept. 26 Rose Garden event for Amy Coney Barrett, where numerous attendees later tested positive. Trump’s positive result was announced Oct. 2, consistent with exposure before the debate. No health authorities or reliable sources have found any deliberate infection or link to Democrats.

claim: During a speech on 2nd October 2020 Joe Biden said he would create 550 million new jobs.
response_text: FALSE.  In his Oct. 2, 2020 speech in Grand Rapids, Michigan, Biden talked about creating about 1 million auto-industry jobs and building roughly 500,000–550,000 electric-vehicle charging stations. Some posts miscaptioned or conflated “charging stations” with “jobs” and inflated the number to “550 million,” which he did not say.

claim: US President Donald Trump used a fabricated COVID-19 positive diagnosis to benefit his re election campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump fabricated his COVID-19 diagnosis. In October 2020 he was hospitalized at Walter Reed, received documented treatments (e.g., remdesivir, dexamethasone, monoclonal antibodies), and multiple White House aides and contacts also tested positive in a well-documented outbreak. Claims that it was staged for campaign benefit are speculative and unsupported; he did not gain an electoral advantage and ultimately lost the election. Uncertainty: none beyond unsubstantiated conspiracy theories.

claim: Flu shots lead to severe or life-threatening conditions making them unsafe.
response_text: FALSE.  Extensive safety monitoring shows flu vaccines are very safe. Serious reactions (like severe allergic reactions) are extremely rare, on the order of about 1 per million doses; a small increased risk of Guillain–Barré syndrome has been observed in some seasons but is also very rare and lower than the risk after influenza infection itself. Most side effects are mild and short-lived, and the benefits—preventing flu-related hospitalizations and deaths—far outweigh these rare risks.

claim: Two E-6B Mercury planes were deployed because of US President Trump's positive COVID-19 test.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: U.S. Strategic Command and the Navy said the E‑6B Mercury flights seen after Trump’s positive COVID-19 announcement were routine, preplanned training missions. There was no change in alert status and no deployment in response to his diagnosis.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria became independent in 1960, and UN/World Bank estimates put its 1960 population at about 45.1 million. While the 1963 census (later disputed) reported ~55.6 million, the best estimates for 1960 are roughly 45 million.

claim: Today, we grapple with multiple challenges with a population exceeding 200 million.
response_text: FALSE (uncertain). The claim doesn’t specify who “we” refers to. Only a few countries (e.g., India, China, US, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Brazil) have populations over 200 million; without context, it can’t be verified.

claim: Video shared to make misleading claim that Hathras victim’s family did her last rites
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple fact-checks found that a circulating video was misused to suggest the Hathras victim’s family performed her last rites. In reality, the UP Police cremated the victim at night without the family conducting the rites, and the video was unrelated/old, making the claim misleading.

claim: Trade relations between the United States and Africa have declined significantly while Donald Trump was president of the US.
response_text: FALSE.  U.S.–Africa goods trade did not “decline significantly” during most of Trump’s term. Two‑way trade was roughly flat to slightly up from 2016 through 2019 (e.g., sub‑Saharan Africa: ~$37B in 2016, ~$41B in 2018, ~$40B in 2019). The notable drop came in 2020, largely due to the global COVID‑19 shock, not a sustained Trump‑era shift. The major long-term decline from the 2008 peak occurred before 2017. (Minor uncertainty depends on whether one counts all Africa vs. sub‑Saharan and how “significant” is defined.)

claim: Today, Nigeria grapple has a population exceeding 200 million.
response_text: TRUE — Recent UN and World Bank estimates put Nigeria’s population well above 200 million (roughly 220–230+ million in 2023–2024), so saying it exceeds 200 million is correct.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of Nigeria's 60 years of existence as a nation, Nigeria has been under military rule.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria became independent in 1960. It was under military rule in two long stretches: Jan 1966–Oct 1979 (~13 years 8 months) and Dec 1983–May 1999 (~15 years 5 months; excluding the brief Aug–Nov 1993 interim government still yields ~28.9 years). That totals about 29 years out of its first 60 years. Minor uncertainty stems from whether to count the 1993 interim government, but it doesn’t change the ~29-year figure.

claim: Other Countries Have Proved that the U.S. FDA Was Wrong to Withdraw Approval Of Hydroxychloroquine as COVID Drug
response_text: FALSE.  Why: - The FDA did not “withdraw approval” of hydroxychloroquine overall; it revoked its Emergency Use Authorization for COVID-19 in June 2020 while the drug remained approved for malaria and certain autoimmune diseases. - Large, well-run trials in other countries found no benefit for COVID-19. The UK RECOVERY trial and WHO’s multinational SOLIDARITY trial both showed hydroxychloroquine did not reduce mortality or improve outcomes. Multiple randomized trials in outpatients and as prophylaxis also found no meaningful benefit and increased adverse effects (e.g., cardiac arrhythmias). - Many countries and regulators that initially permitted use later restricted or advised against it (e.g., France, UK, EMA, WHO), aligning with the FDA’s decision.  Thus, other countries did not prove the FDA “wrong”; international evidence largely supported the revocation.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, have tested positive for COVID-19
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: On October 2, 2020, President Donald Trump announced that he and First Lady Melania Trump tested positive for COVID-19. He was later hospitalized at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center and recovered.

claim: Potential voter fraud in the 2020 U.S Presidential Election is caused by mail-in ballots being sent in error to previous tenants in Washington DC.
response_text: FALSE.  While some DC residents reported receiving election mail for former tenants in 2020, these were often voter guides or applications, and even if an actual ballot was misdelivered, DC uses voter-specific barcodes and signature verification so a ballot cast by anyone else would be rejected. claim: Hindus are a minority in Kerala.

Hindus are a minority in some districts (e.g., Malappuram), but not statewide. Latest official figures are from 2011; no credible data shows a statewide shift since. claim: At independence in 1960  Nigeria had a population of 45 million.

claim: Judith Collins said, on Donald Trump, "actually, he's a damn sight better than any of the other Presidents that have been there before him, including those that you admire, Miss Arden,"
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no reliable record (Hansard or major NZ media) of Judith Collins saying that line. claim: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said ‘our job is to save cows, not women.’
response_text: FALSE.  No credible record shows Yogi Adityanath said this. The quote has circulated as a fake social‑media meme; multiple Indian fact-checkers (e.g., Alt News, BOOM, India Today AFWA) found no speech, interview, or report containing this statement.

claim: Kamala Harris called Joe Biden Trash.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports, transcripts, or verified recordings show Kamala Harris calling Joe Biden “trash.” During the 2019 primary she criticized some of his positions (e.g., on busing) but did not use that insult. The claim appears to stem from misattributed or satirical social media posts.

claim: In England You can get a £3,000 fine for not wearing a cloth over your face at the time of this claim.
response_text: FALSE.  In England during COVID rules, the fixed penalty for not wearing a required face covering was £100 (often £50 if paid early), doubling for repeat offences up to a maximum of £3,200 (and later up to £6,400 when rules returned in late 2021). There was no £3,000 fixed penalty for this offence.

claim: Covid 19 Will Go Away If You Stop Getting Tested, It's Just The Elderly Dying and People Are Being Intentionally Infected
response_text: FALSE.  - Testing doesn’t create or eliminate the virus; it only detects it. Stopping testing would hide cases, not stop transmission, and typically worsens outbreaks by delaying isolation and treatment (CDC/WHO guidance). - Severe illness and death are more common in older adults, but not exclusive to them. Significant numbers of younger and middle‑aged adults have been hospitalized and have died, and many across age groups experience long‑COVID. - There’s no credible evidence that populations are being intentionally infected. Aside from small, highly regulated research challenge trials with consenting participants, claims of deliberate mass infection are unfounded.

claim: The number of police decline when National Party leader Judith Collins’ was police minister.
response_text: FALSE.  Judith Collins was Police Minister twice (2008–2011 and 2015–2016). In her first term, sworn police numbers increased substantially—National delivered its pledge of about 600 additional sworn officers by 2011, taking the total to roughly 9,000. In her later brief stint, numbers were essentially flat (the per‑capita ratio fell as population grew), but not a clear decline.

claim: Judith Collins, the National Party leader stated that New Zealand was using more coal to generate electricity because of the oil and gas exploration ban.
response_text: FALSE.  Coal use for electricity did rise, but experts and official data attribute it to low hydro-lake levels and reduced gas supply from outages at existing fields (especially Pohokura), not the 2018 exploration ban. The ban applied only to new offshore exploration and has little to no short‑term impact on gas availability, so it’s not the reason for the recent increase in coal generation.

claim: Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden received the questions for the first presidential debate in advance.
response_text: FALSE.  For the Sept. 29, 2020 first presidential debate, moderator Chris Wallace said he did not share questions with either campaign. Only the broad topics were publicly announced in advance by the debate commission, which is standard. No credible evidence shows Biden received the specific questions beforehand. (Claims may be conflating this with a 2016 primary town hall where questions were leaked to Hillary Clinton.)

claim: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention downgrades COVID-19, rating it less fatal than seasonal flu
response_text: FALSE.  The CDC has not rated COVID-19 as less fatal than seasonal flu or “downgraded” it. In 2023–2024, COVID-19 continued to cause more hospitalizations and deaths in the U.S. than influenza, especially among older adults and high‑risk groups. CDC’s 2024 update aligned isolation guidance across respiratory viruses, but the agency explicitly noted COVID-19 still poses greater severe-illness risk than flu.

claim: Eating millets will protect you from Coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence that eating millets (or any specific food) can prevent or protect you from coronavirus infection. Millets are nutritious and support general health, but they don’t block or cure COVID-19. Proven protections include vaccination, well-fitting masks, ventilation, hand hygiene, and staying home when sick.

claim: Claims that there were links between Trumps 2016 election campaign and Russia were part of a hoax that Hilary Clinton was behind.
response_text: FALSE.  - U.S. investigations found real Russia–2016 activity and multiple Trump-campaign links. The Mueller Report documented extensive Russian interference to help Trump and numerous contacts between Trump associates and Russians (though it did not establish a criminal conspiracy). The bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee likewise detailed significant ties, including Paul Manafort’s sharing of internal polling data with a Russian intelligence associate. - The FBI’s Crossfire Hurricane probe was opened based on a tip about George Papadopoulos from Australia, not the Steele dossier. The DOJ Inspector General found serious FISA errors but no political bias in opening the case. - The Clinton campaign and DNC funded the Steele dossier, which had errors and was partly used in FISA applications; however, that does not make the broader Russia–Trump links a Clinton “hoax.” John Durham criticized the FBI’s handling but did not prove Clinton fabricated the Russia narrative; his prosecutions ended in acquittals.  Overall, evidence shows genuine Russia-related contacts and interference, not a hoax orchestrated by Hillary Clinton. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Potential voter fraud in the 2020 U.S Presidential Election is caused by mail-in ballots being sent to a mans  deceased parents in Mercer County in New Jersey.
response_text: FALSE.  Even if a New Jersey resident received mail-in ballots addressed to deceased parents (often due to lag in updating voter rolls), that is not evidence that it “caused” potential voter fraud. Ballots have unique identifiers and require signature verification; attempting to vote a dead person’s ballot is illegal and typically rejected. There’s no evidence such mailings led to fraud in the 2020 election. (Uncertainty: the specific Mercer County anecdote isn’t independently verified here, but it wouldn’t substantiate the claim regardless.)

claim: A “new virus” disease called Novel Bunya V!rus that is caused by ticks is diagnosed as severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is spreading in China.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: - Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is a known tick-borne illness caused by the SFTS virus (a banyangvirus in the order Bunyavirales) first identified in China around 2009–2011. It was initially described as a “novel bunyavirus” then, but it is not new now. - SFTS is endemic in parts of China (as well as Japan, Korea, etc.) with seasonal cases reported annually. Saying a “new virus” is spreading is misleading; it’s a long-recognized disease with ongoing, periodic cases. - Also, SFTS is the disease; “Novel Bunya virus” isn’t a current official disease name.

claim: There is more chance of an asteroid hitting Earth on 02/11/2020 than dying from COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  - The “Nov 2, 2020 asteroid” (2018 VP1) had only about a 0.41% chance of entering Earth’s atmosphere and was ~2 meters across—too small to pose danger (would burn up). - By that date, COVID-19 had already caused over 1 million deaths worldwide, and individual risk of dying from COVID-19 (given widespread transmission and infection-fatality rates around ~0.5–1% for many adults, higher for older people) was far greater than the risk from that asteroid. - If the date is Feb 11, 2020, there was no credible impact threat either.  The claim also compares a planet-level event to individual mortality risk, which is misleading.

claim: Sadiq Khan faked getting the flu jab as the plastic cap was still on the needle.
response_text: FALSE.  The photo being shared shows a safety guard/hub on the syringe, not a cap covering the needle. NHS flu jabs commonly use safety-engineered needles with a plastic shield that is rotated over the tip after injection to prevent needlestick injuries. Other images from the same session and statements from the clinic confirm Sadiq Khan did receive the flu jab.

claim: AARP endorsed President Biden and gave financial support to planned parenthood.
response_text: FALSE.  - AARP is a nonpartisan organization and has repeatedly stated it does not endorse or oppose candidates for public office, including in the 2020 and 2024 cycles (it specifically pushed back against materials implying a Biden endorsement). - AARP has also said it has no financial relationship with Planned Parenthood and does not fund it. Claims that it donates to Planned Parenthood have been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: Indian legendary singer Sripathi Panditaradhyula Balasubrahmanyam's family asked the Tamil Nadu government for help to pay the hospital bills after his death, but it was  Vice President Venkaiah Naidu's daughter who stepped in.
response_text: FALSE.  SP Balasubrahmanyam’s son, S. P. Charan, publicly stated after his father’s death that the family did not seek financial help from the Tamil Nadu government or anyone else and that rumors about Vice President M. Venkaiah Naidu’s daughter paying the hospital bills were untrue. Multiple fact-checks (e.g., BOOM, Factly, The News Minute) cited Charan’s clarification and debunked these claims.

claim: FAcebook meme shows real stats on Black v White Violence and Police shootings
response_text: FALSE  Reason: Widely shared Facebook memes about “Black vs. White” crime and police shootings have been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org). They typically cherry-pick or misread FBI/DOJ data, conflate arrests with offenses, misuse small or outdated samples, and ignore population-adjusted rates. Key points those memes get wrong include: - Most violent crime is intraracial, not interracial. - Sensational claims about interracial rape are unsupported by reliable data. - Police shootings: raw counts show more white victims, but per capita Black Americans are killed at significantly higher rates.  Without the exact meme, there’s slight uncertainty, but the common versions do not show “real” (accurate, contextualized) stats.

claim: New Zealand opposition leader Judith Collins is opposed to new environmental legislation because of her connection to Oravida, a local water and dairy company that exports produce to China.
response_text: FALSE.  Judith Collins did have past ties to Oravida (her husband was a director; she was censured in 2014 over meetings involving the company). However, there’s no credible reporting that links her later opposition to specific new environmental legislation to that connection. As Opposition leader (2020–2021), Collins and the National Party opposed parts of Labour’s freshwater regulations on policy grounds; attributing this stance “because of her connection to Oravida” is unsubstantiated. Uncertainty: motives are hard to prove, but no evidence supports this causal claim.

claim: The Nigerian government is donating $600 million to Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden’s campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  U.S. law prohibits foreign nationals and foreign governments from donating to U.S. political campaigns, and there are no FEC records or credible reports showing any such donation. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters, PolitiFact) have debunked this rumor; it originated from misleading posts, not real events.

claim: Olive Garden prohibits its employees from wearing face masks depicting the American flag.
response_text: FALSE.  Olive Garden stated in 2020 that it does not prohibit American flag face masks. The company’s policy allows patterned masks (including the U.S. flag) as long as they don’t contain words or logos. A viral claim stemmed from an isolated incident/miscommunication at a location, which the company corrected.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett has a written track record, disagreeing adamantly with the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to uphold the Affordable Care Act.
response_text: TRUE.  As a law professor, Barrett criticized the Supreme Court’s ACA rulings in writing. In a 2017 article, she said Chief Justice Roberts “pushed the Affordable Care Act beyond its plausible meaning to save the statute” in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012). She also wrote that the dissent “had the better of the legal argument” in King v. Burwell (2015), which upheld the subsidies. These show clear written disagreement with the Court’s decisions upholding the ACA, though her critiques focused on legal reasoning rather than policy.

claim: A child died in Germany from wearing a mask.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: In a widely cited 2020 case, a 13-year-old in Rhineland-Palatinate collapsed and died while wearing a mask on a school bus. Investigators and the public prosecutor said the autopsy did not establish a cause and found no evidence the mask was a factor. German authorities and fact-checkers reported no confirmed child deaths in Germany attributable to mask wearing. (Uncertainty: full medical details weren’t public, but available official findings do not support the claim.)

claim: A Maryland man was sentenced to a year in jail for throwing parties.
response_text: TRUE.  In October 2020, a Maryland man, Shawn Marshall Myers of Hughesville, was sentenced to one year in jail after repeatedly hosting large parties in March 2020 in violation of the state’s COVID-19 emergency orders. Note: some reports indicate part of the sentence was suspended, but the imposed sentence was one year.

claim: A Supreme Court nominee has never been nominated and installed while a presidential election is already underway.
response_text: FALSE.  Example: In 2020, Amy Coney Barrett was nominated (Sept 26), confirmed (Oct 26), and sworn in (Oct 27) while the presidential election was already underway—millions had already voted via mail and early voting ahead of Election Day (Nov 3).

claim: Jo Biden the U.S Democratic Presidential nominee calls Donald Trump supporters the "dregs of society".
response_text: FALSE.  Biden did use the phrase “dregs of society” in a 2018 speech at a Human Rights Campaign event, but he was referring to “forces of intolerance” (e.g., white supremacists/anti-LGBTQ extremists) he said were emboldened by Trump, not to Trump supporters generally. Also, he was not the Democratic presidential nominee at the time.

claim: Distance between Gandhi and Green thread can determine if Rs 500 note is genuine or fake
response_text: FALSE.  RBI does not specify any fixed “distance” between Mahatma Gandhi’s portrait and the (green/colour‑shifting) security thread as a test of authenticity. In genuine Rs 500 notes, the thread’s exact position can vary slightly due to printing tolerances and different presses. Authenticity should be checked using official security features (watermark with electrotype 500, windowed security thread with RBI/भारत/500 inscriptions and color shift, see‑through register, microlettering, intaglio features, etc.), not by measuring this distance.

claim: Nigeria performed poorly in Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the past five years.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: In recent Sustainable Development Reports (2020–2024), Nigeria has consistently ranked in the bottom tier of the SDG Index and is off track on most goals, with many indicators showing “major challenges” and stagnating or worsening trends. While exact ranks vary by year, the overall pattern over the past five years indicates poor SDG performance.

claim: No news coverage was given to US President Donald Trump's executive order on September 24, 2020 guaranteed health coverage protections for those with preexisting conditions.
response_text: FALSE.  There was extensive news coverage of Trump’s Sept. 24, 2020 executive order on preexisting condition protections. Examples include: - Reuters (Sept. 24, 2020) reported Trump signed orders on preexisting conditions and surprise billing. - NPR (Sept. 24, 2020) covered the order and noted it didn’t create new protections beyond the ACA. - Associated Press, Washington Post, New York Times, Politico and others also reported on it, often noting the order was largely symbolic.

claim: Donald Trump has not appoointed any black federal judges.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump appointed multiple Black federal district judges. Examples include: - Ada E. Brown (Northern District of Texas, 2019) - Terry F. Moorer (Southern District of Alabama, 2018) - Stephanie Dawkins Davis (Eastern District of Michigan, 2019; later elevated by Biden) - Rodney Smith (Southern District of Florida, 2019)  Note: He appointed no Black judges to the courts of appeals, but the claim that he appointed none at all is incorrect.

claim: A mail-in ballot application for voting in the US presidential election which was sent to a deceased grandfather in the State of New Mexico is evidence of potential widespread voter fraud via mail-in ballots.
response_text: FALSE.  A misaddressed mail-in ballot application—especially to a deceased person—is typically the result of outdated or third‑party mailing lists, not evidence of fraud. It’s an application, not a ballot, and can’t be used to vote unless the person is an eligible, registered voter who requests and returns a ballot with required verification (e.g., signature checks). New Mexico election officials routinely remove deceased voters and verify absentee ballots. A single anecdote does not indicate “potential widespread” fraud.

claim: Raveer Singh requested Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) to let him join anxiety-prone Actor Deepika Padukone during drug interrogation.
response_text: FALSE  NCB officials publicly clarified in September 2020 that they had received no request from Ranveer Singh to accompany Deepika Padukone during her questioning. Reports claiming he asked to join her because of “anxiety” were denied by the agency.

claim: Pennsylvania ballots will be rejected without outer and inner envelopes.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: For Pennsylvania mail-in/absentee voting, the ballot must be placed in the inner secrecy envelope and then sealed inside the official outer return envelope, which must be signed (and dated as required). Ballots missing the inner secrecy envelope (“naked ballots”) or not returned in the official outer envelope are not counted under Pennsylvania law. Note: This applies to mail/absentee ballots; in‑person ballots don’t use envelopes.

claim: US President Donald Trump's executive order on September 24, 2020 legally ensures health coverage protections for those with pre existing medical conditions.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump’s Sept. 24, 2020 “America-First Healthcare Plan” executive order only stated it is U.S. policy to protect people with pre‑existing conditions; it did not create any enforceable rights or requirements for insurers. Executive orders can’t replace or replicate the Affordable Care Act’s statutory protections, and the order provided no mechanism that would legally ensure such coverage if the ACA were struck down.

claim: House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said of US employers, “Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions.”
response_text: FALSE.  Pelosi did not praise employers cutting workers’ hours. In 2014, responding to a CBO report on the Affordable Care Act, she said it would be good if people were no longer “job-locked” to employer coverage and could choose to work fewer hours or pursue other goals. The meme reframes her point about worker choice as if she endorsed employers cutting hours. (She was also House Minority Leader then, not Speaker.)

claim: False Facebook posts claim Philippine vice president demanded multi-billion dollar budget for her office in 2021
response_text: TRUE. Reuters and other fact-checkers debunked viral Facebook posts claiming VP Leni Robredo demanded a multi‑billion dollar budget for her office in 2021. The OVP’s proposed 2021 budget was only in the hundreds of millions of Philippine pesos (roughly tens of millions of US dollars), not billions.

claim: The State of Massachusetts committed voter fraud by deleting over one million ballot images during the 2020 Presidential Election.
response_text: FALSE.  - Massachusetts’ official record is the paper ballot, which was preserved for the required 22 months.   - Most MA tabulators in 2020 did not create or store “ballot images” at all; officials said there were no images to delete.   - Multiple fact-checks and a related lawsuit found no evidence of deletion or voter fraud.

claim: George Soros connected to U-Haul operated by antifa activists distributed “shields, weapons & black bloc” to protesters in Louisville, Ky.
response_text: FALSE.  - A U-Haul did arrive at Louisville protests (Sept. 2020) and people took shields, signs, umbrellas and supplies. A local activist associated with The Bail Project was reported to have rented it. - There is no evidence that George Soros or his Open Society Foundations funded that U-Haul or The Bail Project’s action; OSF has said it did not fund The Bail Project. The Bail Project also said it did not direct or finance the truck. - No verified evidence shows “weapons” were distributed; videos show shields/signs, not arms. “Antifa” involvement was an allegation without substantiation.  Given the lack of evidence for Soros funding or weapons, the claim is false.

claim: Adani Logistics Limited has established a food silo in the aftermath of the three farm and agriculture-related bills passing Parliament.
response_text: FALSE.  - The grain silos linked to Adani are operated by Adani Agri Logistics Ltd (AALL), not Adani Logistics Ltd. - AALL has run modern food-grain silos under long-term contracts with the Food Corporation of India since 2007 (e.g., Moga, Kaithal), well before the 2020 farm bills. Viral photos claiming “new” silos after the bills are from 2018 or earlier. - No evidence shows a silo newly established by Adani Logistics Ltd specifically “in the aftermath” of the farm bills.  Sources: Fact-checks by Alt News (Sep 2020), BOOM (Sep 2020), India Today AFWA (Sep 2020), The Quint (Sep 2020).

claim: Shah Rukh Khan's Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) is acquiring a 1.28 per cent stake in Reliance Retail at Rs 5,500 crore
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The 1.28% stake in Reliance Retail for about Rs 5,550 crore was acquired in 2020 by KKR & Co. (Kohlberg Kravis Roberts), the global private equity firm—not Kolkata Knight Riders, the IPL team co-owned by Shah Rukh Khan. The claim confuses the two “KKR”s and also misstates the amount (Rs 5,500 crore vs Rs 5,550 crore).

claim: Due to coronavirus schools and colleges have been closed and because of this, the education of students has been affected. The government is providing free laptops to all the students so that they can complete their education and also give exams with the help of the internet
response_text: FALSE.  - While COVID-19 did cause widespread school and college closures and disrupted education, there was no universal government program giving free laptops to all students. - Some governments and local authorities provided devices or subsidies to certain groups (e.g., low-income or device-less students), but not to every student. - Such blanket claims are often used in scams; verify any offer through official government channels.

claim: New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio officially ordered all police and citizens to stop sharing the booking photo of his daughter caught up during rioting
response_text: FALSE.  De Blasio criticized the leak of his daughter’s arrest information during the 2020 protests and said it should be investigated, but there was no official order directing “all police and citizens” to stop sharing a booking photo. In fact, no credible record shows he issued such a directive, and mayors don’t have authority to order citizens not to share images. Uncertainty: low.

claim: The Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews of the state of Victoria in Australia accepted a multi-million dollar bribe from the IMF conditional on Andrews locking down the state of Victoria unnecessarily during the COVID-19 pandemic.
response_text: FALSE.  - No credible evidence supports this claim; multiple fact-checkers have debunked similar allegations. - The IMF does not pay bribes and deals with national governments’ treasuries/central banks, not individual state premiers. - Australia did not receive IMF financing during COVID-19, making such a payment implausible. - Victorian lockdown decisions were made by the state government based on public health advice; claims of IMF-linked bribery are baseless conspiracy theories.
