claim: Premier Daniel Andrews of the state of Victoria in Australia borrowed money from the IMF and now is in default.
response_text: FALSE.  - The IMF lends to sovereign national governments, not to sub‑national states or their premiers. A state premier cannot borrow directly from the IMF. - Australia currently has no IMF loans outstanding and is a creditor to the IMF. - Victoria funds itself via state-issued bonds; it has not defaulted. Credit ratings remain investment grade (downgraded during COVID but no default).

claim: False positives and rapid tests put the rate of infection near zero and that there will be no second wave of infections
response_text: FALSE.  - False positives and rapid tests affect measurement, not the actual infection rate. False positives would inflate reported cases, not drive the true infection rate toward zero. - Rapid tests help detect infectious cases but do not prevent transmission by themselves. - Empirically, many countries experienced second and subsequent waves of COVID-19 (e.g., late 2020 and beyond), contradicting the claim.

claim: Americans advised to reconsider travel to Ghana due to COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  As of 2024, the U.S. State Department does not advise “reconsider travel” to Ghana due to COVID-19. Ghana is typically at Level 2 (Exercise Increased Caution), with concerns focused on crime, and COVID-specific “reconsider travel” advisories were largely phased out in 2023. Minor uncertainty since advisories can change.

claim: Transitioning to 100 per cent renewable electricity generation increase power prices in New Zealand
response_text: TRUE.  Most New Zealand analyses find that pushing from ~95% to 100% renewable electricity raises system costs and wholesale prices, mainly because covering “dry-year” risk without fossil backup requires costly firming (e.g., overbuilt renewables, storage like pumped hydro, or other firm low‑emissions supply). The Interim Climate Change Committee (2019), the Climate Change Commission (2021), and Transpower modeling all concluded that a strict 100% target would likely increase electricity prices relative to a high‑renewables (≈95%) scenario. Some future tech-cost declines could soften this, but the balance of evidence points to higher prices.

claim: Former US vice-president Joe Biden is showing pretty severe signs of dementia.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible medical diagnosis or evidence that Joe Biden has dementia, let alone “pretty severe” dementia. While his age and occasional verbal slips have prompted public debate, dementia requires clinical evaluation and has not been diagnosed. Official medical summaries from the White House have not reported dementia, and commentary (e.g., the Hur report’s memory observations) is not a medical diagnosis. Uncertainty: diagnosing from afar is inappropriate.

claim: California Governor Gavin Newsom made it so that convicted sexual predators have lighter sentences.
response_text: FALSE.  Newsom has not reduced criminal sentences for “sexual predators.” The commonly cited change he signed (SB 145 in 2020) only adjusted sex-offender registry rules to give judges the same discretion in certain close-in-age, consensual cases; it did not reduce criminal penalties or prison terms. The tiered registry that lets some offenders petition off the registry was enacted in 2017 under Gov. Jerry Brown. Newsom has also signed measures increasing penalties, such as making child sex trafficking a serious felony (SB 14, 2023).

claim: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg is the first woman in American history to lie in state at the U.S. Capitol.
response_text: TRUE.  Ruth Bader Ginsburg lay in state at the U.S. Capitol on September 25, 2020, becoming the first woman to do so. Rosa Parks lay “in honor” in 2005—a different designation for private citizens—so she is not a counterexample.

claim: Judge Amy Barret said "gays have a right to be discriminated against because they are against Gods wishes and won't be allowed Heaven"
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Justice Amy Coney Barrett ever saying this. The quote has circulated as a meme without sourcing and has been debunked by fact-checkers. While Barrett is a devout Catholic and has faced scrutiny over her views and affiliations, there is no verified speech, writing, or transcript in which she said gays should be discriminated against or won’t be allowed into heaven.

claim: Fact Check: WHO has not approved home remedy for COVID-19, don’t fall for misinformation
response_text: TRUE. WHO has not endorsed any “home remedy” (e.g., garlic, ginger, steam inhalation) as a treatment or cure for COVID‑19. WHO guidance emphasizes vaccines, proven therapeutics, and supportive care; it has repeatedly warned against misinformation about unproven home cures.

claim: Basketball superstar Michael Jordan is joining NASCAR as a team owner.
response_text: TRUE.  In September 2020, Michael Jordan announced he was forming a NASCAR Cup Series team, 23XI Racing, with Denny Hamlin as co-owner. The team began competing in 2021 with Bubba Wallace as its first driver. Jordan remains a team owner.

claim: Ruth Bader Ginsburg waged an "active campaign" to repeal the Mann Act and to lower the age of consent for sex
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: - There’s no evidence Ruth Bader Ginsburg “waged an active campaign” on either point. As a law professor, she co‑authored a 1970s report on sex bias in federal law that critiqued the Mann Act’s archaic, gendered framing and suggested revising or repealing and reenacting provisions to be gender‑neutral and focused on coercion—not legalizing exploitation. - The “lower the age of consent” claim misreads that report. A footnote summarized outside proposals (e.g., Model Penal Code discussions) that mentioned ages as low as 12 for certain offenses; Ginsburg did not endorse lowering the age of consent. Multiple fact‑checks (e.g., FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, Washington Post) have found this claim false.  Minor uncertainty: the report uses reform language that includes repeal-and-reenact for specific Mann Act sections, but that is not an “active campaign,” nor did it aim to legalize coerced sex or lower ages of consent.

claim: 30% to 40% of Americans will have voted by Oct. 1. 2020
response_text: FALSE.  By Oct. 1, 2020, only a few million ballots had been cast—on the order of 2–3 million according to the U.S. Elections Project—well under even 5% of eligible voters, let alone 30–40% of “Americans.” The 30–40% range was reached closer to late October, when early votes approached 90+ million. (Approximate figures)

claim: The recently deceased US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg was known for her gruelling fitness regime.
response_text: TRUE.  Ruth Bader Ginsburg was widely known for her rigorous workout routine with trainer Bryant Johnson, including push-ups, planks, and weight training well into her 80s. It was profiled by major outlets and even became a book, “The RBG Workout,” underscoring her reputation for a gruelling fitness regimen.

claim: The Trump campaign only asked that Biden to release his list of potential Supreme Court nominees after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg passed away.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump and his campaign had been urging Biden to release a Supreme Court shortlist months before Justice Ginsburg’s death (Sept. 18, 2020). For example, Trump publicly challenged Biden to release a list in June 2020 and again on September 9, 2020, when Trump unveiled his own updated list and called on Biden to do the same. They continued that pressure after Ginsburg’s passing, but it did not begin then.

claim: Trump campaign asked Joe Biden to release a list of potential Supreme Court picks only after Ginsburg’s passing
response_text: FALSE.  Trump and his campaign repeatedly pressed Joe Biden to release a list of potential Supreme Court nominees well before Justice Ginsburg’s death on Sept. 18, 2020. For example, Trump unveiled an updated list on Sept. 9, 2020 and publicly challenged Biden to do the same, and his campaign had been urging this as early as June 2020. Uncertainty: low.

claim: The family or Justine Damond received a $55 million settlement after she was gunned down by a Minneapolis police officer.
response_text: FALSE.  Minneapolis settled with Justine Damond’s family for $20 million in 2019, not $55 million.

claim: Flu shot is 2.4x more deadly than Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  - Flu vaccines have an excellent safety record; deaths causally linked to a flu shot are extraordinarily rare (serious allergic reaction ~1–2 per million doses; fatal outcomes are even rarer). VAERS reports often cited for such claims are unverified and do not establish causation. - COVID-19, the disease, has caused millions of deaths globally and over a million in the U.S.; per-infection fatality risk is orders of magnitude higher than the risk of death from a flu shot.  By any reasonable comparison, a flu shot is not more deadly—certainly not “2.4×”—than COVID-19.

claim: MPs are not following workplace Covid guidance by wearing masks.
response_text: FALSE.  Workplace/Public health guidance in Parliament encouraged wearing face coverings in crowded, enclosed spaces. The criticism was that many MPs were not wearing masks, which went against the guidance. Wearing masks would align with the guidance, not violate it. (Note: it was guidance, not a legal requirement.)

claim: You could text RBG to 50409 to sign a petition to tell your senator not to replace Ruth Bader Ginsberg in the Supreme court until after the 2020 election
response_text: TRUE.  Resistbot (short code 50409) ran a campaign in Sept. 2020 after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s death where texting “RBG” would help users send messages to their U.S. senators urging them not to fill the Supreme Court seat before the election (some versions said “until after inauguration”). Note: it functions as a letter-writing/petition tool rather than an official government petition.

claim: A man died in police custody after a 19th September 2020 anti-lockdown protest in London.
response_text: FALSE.  Metropolitan Police said there were arrests at the 19 September 2020 anti‑lockdown protest in London but no deaths in custody linked to it. This rumor was debunked by fact‑checkers (e.g., Full Fact/Reuters). No credible reports or official records show a man died in police custody after that protest.

claim: Melissa Francis is married to Wray Thorn.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple reliable bios (e.g., network and press profiles, Wikipedia) note that former Fox anchor and ex–child actress Melissa Francis has been married to financier Wray Thorn since 1997, with no reported divorce.

claim: Two Sigma Investments is owned by George Soros.
response_text: FALSE.  Two Sigma Investments is a quantitative hedge fund founded and owned by John Overdeck and David Siegel (and partners/employees). It is not owned by George Soros, who founded Soros Fund Management, a separate firm.

claim: Zimbabwe recorded its first coronavirus Infection before 20 February 2020.
response_text: FALSE. Zimbabwe’s first confirmed COVID-19 case was reported on 20 March 2020, about a month after 20 February.

claim: Photo Showing the remains of Vladimir Komarov, a man who fell from space, in 1967.
response_text: TRUE  Vladimir Komarov died on April 24, 1967, when the Soyuz 1 descent module’s parachutes failed during reentry. The capsule crashed and burned, and Soviet sources published recovery photos showing his charred remains. “Fell from space” is a colloquial description—he was inside the capsule, not free-falling—but the image and date are authentic. (Note: some viral posts add fabricated “last audio,” which is not verified.)

claim: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election.
response_text: FALSE.  Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated on June 22, 1993 and confirmed on August 3, 1993—about 42 days later. This was not “before an election”: 1993 was not a federal election year; the next national election (the 1994 midterms) was over a year away.

claim: Sightway Capital is owned by Two Sigma Investments.
response_text: TRUE — with nuance.  Sightway Capital is described as “a Two Sigma company” and an affiliate/private investing arm of Two Sigma. While the exact legal structure is affiliate-based rather than necessarily a direct ownership by the specific entity Two Sigma Investments, LP, it is part of (owned/controlled by) the Two Sigma group.

claim: US Supreme Court Justice, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, fought cancer for decades before she passed away in September 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in September 2020 and had her first cancer diagnosis in 1999 (colon cancer), followed by pancreatic cancer (2009), lung cancer (2018), and another pancreatic cancer treatment (2019), amounting to over two decades of cancer battles.

claim: Wray Thorn is managing director of Sightway Capital.
response_text: FALSE.  Wray Thorn previously led Two Sigma’s private-investments arm (Sightway Capital) as a managing director/co-head, but he left Two Sigma around 2019 and later founded Clear Heights Capital and co-founded Focus Impact Partners. He is not currently managing director of Sightway Capital.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said, “Pedophilia is good for the children.”
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Ruth Bader Ginsburg ever saying this. The quote is a fabricated meme. Fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, AP) have traced such claims to distortions of a 1977 legal report she helped author, which discussed making sex-crime statutes gender‑neutral; it did not praise or endorse pedophilia.

claim: John Cammo was the only one to predict that President Trump would be infected with Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Many people publicly predicted or speculated that President Trump would contract COVID-19 well before his Oct. 2020 diagnosis—journalists, commentators, and countless social media users noted his frequent exposure and lax precautions. There’s no credible evidence that “John Cammo” was uniquely the only person to make such a prediction. (Uncertainty: identity/record of “John Cammo” is unclear, but the “only one” claim is untenable.)

claim: English Playwright William Shakespeare’s plays are the work of Amelia Bassano, a black woman who died unpublished and in poverty.
response_text: FALSE.  - Shakespeare’s plays are attributed by the vast majority of scholars to William Shakespeare; the idea that Aemilia (Emilia) Bassano/Lanyer wrote them is a fringe theory with no credible evidence. - Bassano was a published poet; her Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum appeared in 1611, making “died unpublished” incorrect. - Describing her as a “black woman” is speculative; she was from the Venetian/Jewish Bassano family at court, and there’s no firm evidence she was Black.  - She did have financial difficulties later in life, but the core claims are unsupported or wrong.

claim: The passing of Ruth Bader Ginsburg will have a profound effect on the future of the Supreme Court of America.
response_text: TRUE.  Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s death in September 2020 allowed the swift confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett, shifting the Court from a 5–4 to a 6–3 conservative majority. That change has shaped major decisions, including Dobbs (overturning Roe v. Wade), NYSRPA v. Bruen (expanding gun rights), and West Virginia v. EPA (limiting agency power), evidencing a profound impact on the Court’s direction.

claim: The fastest Supreme Court justice ever confirmed in the U.S. was 47 days.
response_text: FALSE.  Many justices were confirmed far faster than 47 days—some on the same day as nomination. For example, Chief Justice Edward Douglass White was nominated and confirmed on Dec. 12, 1910 (same day). Even in recent decades, confirmations have been under 47 days (e.g., Amy Coney Barrett in about 30 days; John Paul Stevens in 19 days).

claim: Canada would like to reopen the border with the U.S
response_text: FALSE  Explanation: The U.S.–Canada land border is already open for normal travel. During much of 2020–early 2021 Canada repeatedly extended closures and was cautious about reopening; it only announced phased reopening to vaccinated travelers in mid-2021. Without a specific timeframe, the claim that Canada “would like to reopen” is not accurate now. (Uncertain if the claim refers to a past moment.)

claim: Turkish-backed armed groups did not commit human rights violations in the Syrian conflict
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple independent sources have documented human rights violations by Turkish‑backed Syrian armed groups (e.g., factions of the Syrian National Army) during operations in Afrin and northeast Syria. UN Commission of Inquiry reports (2019–2021) and investigations by Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch describe abuses including arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearances, pillage and property seizure, sexual violence, and extrajudicial killings (e.g., the killing of Kurdish politician Hevrin Khalaf by Ahrar al‑Sharqiya). These findings directly contradict the claim.

claim: Joe Biden would be the first person without an Ivy League degree to be elected president.
response_text: FALSE.  Many presidents were elected without Ivy League degrees. Recent examples include Ronald Reagan (Eureka College), Jimmy Carter (U.S. Naval Academy), Richard Nixon (Whittier/Duke), Dwight D. Eisenhower (West Point), and Harry S. Truman (no college degree). Biden himself has degrees from the University of Delaware and Syracuse University, but he would not be the first non-Ivy graduate elected.

claim: Nigeria is the leading producer of cassava in Africa and the world.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria has consistently been the world’s largest producer of cassava (and thus the largest in Africa), according to FAO data, with annual output around 55–60+ million tonnes—ahead of DR Congo, Thailand, and Ghana. (Thailand leads in exports, not total production.)

claim: The White House blocked a plan to send facemasks to every household in April 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  Reporting and documents show the Trump White House shelved a USPS/HHS plan to mail five reusable face masks to every U.S. household, a distribution slated to begin in April 2020. Instead, masks were redirected to nonprofits and local groups. (Some accounts cite concerns inside the White House about causing public alarm.)

claim: In 2019, 10 million fell ill from tuberculosis and 1.5 million died but nobody needs to wears a mask for tuberculosis
response_text: FALSE.  - Numbers: In 2019 an estimated 10.0 million people fell ill with TB, and about 1.4 million died (not 1.5 million). - Masks: Infection-control guidance does recommend masks for TB—patients are asked to wear surgical masks when around others/being transported, and healthcare workers use respirators (e.g., N95) when caring for TB patients. So “nobody needs to wear a mask” is incorrect.

claim: Trump nixes aid for California fires but offers help to Putin for Siberian wildfires.
response_text: FALSE.  - Trump did offer assistance to Russia for Siberian wildfires in July 2019. - But he did not actually “nix” federal aid to California wildfires. He repeatedly threatened to cut it off (e.g., Jan 2019 tweets) and briefly denied a 2020 disaster request before reversing, but FEMA continued providing wildfire assistance to California.

claim: Donald Trump is in federal court trying to do away with the Affordable Care Act, 100 million people with preexisting conditions like your mom would not have to pay more for their insurance under now.”
response_text: FALSE.  - While the Trump administration did back a federal lawsuit (2018–2020) to invalidate the Affordable Care Act, that case ended with the Supreme Court upholding the ACA in 2021. So “is in federal court” is not currently accurate. - The “100 million” figure for people with preexisting conditions who would face higher premiums is overstated. Credible estimates put the number of non-elderly who would have been at risk of denial or higher prices in the individual market pre-ACA at about 54 million; larger figures include many people who wouldn’t have been charged more (e.g., those in employer plans or Medicare).

claim: Joe Biden was the first in his family to go to college.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden may have been the first in his immediate household (parents/siblings), but not the first in his family overall. His maternal great‑grandfather, Edward F. Blewitt, graduated from Lafayette College in 1879, and reports indicate his maternal grandfather attended college as well.

claim: COVID-19 was developed as a bioweapon from a research facility in China.
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 was engineered or developed as a bioweapon. Genetic analyses show no signs of deliberate manipulation, and U.S. intelligence assessments and WHO reviews conclude it is not a biological weapon. While the exact origin remains uncertain (natural spillover vs. a possible lab-related incident), weaponization claims are unsupported.

claim: Carlos Gimenez approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension.
response_text: TRUE.  - As Miami-Dade County mayor, Carlos Gimenez initially took a voluntary cut to his compensation (about $150,000) after taking office in 2011, then later restored it to the full amount set in county law (about $250,000). That’s roughly a 67% increase from what he had been taking. - Because public pensions are calculated off salary, restoring his full pay increased the basis for his own future pension.  Note: He didn’t unilaterally “vote himself” a raise; he ended a voluntary cut and the full salary was approved through the county budget process.

claim: Minneapolis City Council has defunded the police.
response_text: FALSE.  Minneapolis did not eliminate or stop funding its police department. In 2020 the City Council shifted about $8 million from MPD to alternative public-safety programs, but the department continued to receive a large budget and remained in place. A 2021 ballot measure to replace the MPD also failed, and subsequent budgets maintained or increased police funding. (Uncertainty: exact dollar amounts vary by year, but the department was not “defunded” in the abolish/zero-out sense.)

claim: Ventura County election officials are reducing voting locations in order to limit in-person voter turnout.
response_text: FALSE.  Ventura County shifted to California’s Voter’s Choice Act model and universal vote-by-mail, replacing many neighborhood polling places with fewer vote centers that are open for multiple days, offer countywide access, and same‑day services. This change is required by state law and presented as improving access/efficiency. There’s no evidence officials reduced locations “in order to limit” in‑person turnout.

claim: Australian politician, Daniel Andrews said “In fact, you’d be surprised at how much can be avoided if people stop insisting on their personal freedoms. Because insisting on human rights is not only selfish, it’s stupid.”
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Daniel Andrews saying this. Official transcripts and credible media archives don’t contain the quote, and fact-checkers (e.g., AAP FactCheck/AFP) have debunked it as a fabricated meme. While Andrews defended strict COVID-19 measures, he did not say that insisting on human rights is “selfish” or “stupid.”

claim: Kim Martin Morrow the CEO of Netflix has just been charged with 15 charges for child pornography and 31,000 files have been found on his personal computers for child porn from ages 8 and as young as toddlers.
response_text: FALSE.  - There is no “Kim Martin Morrow” who is, or has been, CEO of Netflix. Netflix’s leaders have been Reed Hastings, Ted Sarandos, and Greg Peters. - No credible news or law‑enforcement reports support that any Netflix CEO was charged with child pornography or found with “31,000 files.”   - The claim is a recycled hoax that has been debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, Reuters, Lead Stories) dating back to 2020.

claim: Development Control Department of the Abuja Metropolitan Management Council (AMMC), an agency of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA)of Nigeria, in 2020 marked 37 Estates for demolition.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple Nigerian news reports in 2020 quoted the FCTA’s Department of Development Control (under AMMC) saying it had identified and marked 37 illegal/unauthorized estates in Abuja for demolition, largely over lack of approval and encroachment issues. Note: exact lists/locations varied by report, but the “37 estates” figure was repeatedly cited that year.

claim: The US government has plans to force a COVID-19 vaccine on everyone.
response_text: FALSE.  The U.S. government has not had a plan to force COVID-19 vaccination on everyone. Federal actions were limited to specific sectors (e.g., federal employees, military, and healthcare facilities), and a broad OSHA rule for large employers was blocked by the Supreme Court. Mandates typically included exemptions and alternatives, and the federal government lacks general authority to impose a universal vaccine requirement on all Americans.

claim: In India, actor Kangana Ranaut was forced to vote for the Shiv Sena in the elections as they were in alliance with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no credible record of Kangana Ranaut saying she was “forced to vote” for Shiv Sena due to its alliance with the BJP. Fact-checkers have debunked viral posts attributing this quote to her as fabricated/misleading, and no verified interview or report supports it. (Note: voting is secret and she has publicly feuded with Shiv Sena since 2020, making the claim especially unlikely.)

claim: A US voter can vote 4 times because he got 4 vote by mail forms.
response_text: FALSE.  Receiving multiple vote-by-mail applications (often sent by parties/advocacy groups) doesn’t allow multiple votes. Even if duplicate ballots are issued, each ballot is uniquely tracked to the voter; election systems count only one ballot per voter and void duplicates. Attempting to vote more than once is illegal and would be rejected or prosecuted. Uncertainty: none.

claim: Crime has increased in Minneapolis in 2020.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In 2020 Minneapolis saw a sharp rise in violent crime—homicides reached the highest level since the 1990s, shootings more than doubled, and carjackings jumped several-fold. Some property crimes fell during the pandemic, so totals by category were mixed, but key violent crime measures clearly increased. (Minor uncertainty depends on how “crime” is defined—overall totals vs. violent crime.)

claim: A Democratic Vice Presidential nominee, Kamala Harris, said that there will be "a federal tax on your home for slavery reparations."
response_text: FALSE.  There is no record of Kamala Harris saying or proposing “a federal tax on your home for slavery reparations.” She supported studying reparations (e.g., backing a commission like H.R. 40), but did not propose a home tax. The quote traces to fabricated/satirical posts and has been debunked by fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact).

claim: Actor Mukesh Khanna has called for a boycott of Jaya and Amitabh Bachchan.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no credible reports of Mukesh Khanna calling for a boycott of Jaya and Amitabh Bachchan. He has criticized Jaya Bachchan’s behavior/comments in the past, but reliable sources do not show him urging a boycott of either of them. (Slight uncertainty if a very recent statement exists, but none is documented.)

claim: A 6 year old boy begged God to save his mother's life after she was ambushed. Today the NFL honored the organization that yelled "hope they die" outside the mothers hospital.
response_text: FALSE.  - On Sept. 12, 2020, two LA County Sheriff’s deputies were ambushed in Compton; the female deputy was a 31‑year‑old mother with a young son (reports said age 6), and she survived. Some individuals outside the hospital were recorded yelling “I hope they die.”  - However, there is no verified evidence that an organization formally honored by the NFL was the one that yelled this. The NFL featured broad social‑justice messaging and support for the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, but it did not honor a specific group tied to the hospital incident, and BLM‑LA denied organizing that protest.  - Thus the claim conflates separate events and misattributes the hospital behavior to an organization “honored” by the NFL.

claim: Muslim regiment of the Indian Army had refused to fight in India’s 1965 war with Pakistan.
response_text: FALSE.  There has never been a “Muslim Regiment” in the Indian Army after independence, so it could not have refused to fight in 1965. Muslims have served across various regiments, and in the 1965 war CQMH Abdul Hamid of 4 Grenadiers was awarded the Param Vir Chakra for destroying Pakistani tanks—underscoring that Indian Muslim soldiers fought valiantly.

claim: Fact Check: AARP Did NOT Spend 'Millions In TV Ads Targeting Republican Candidates' -- Nonprofit AARP Is Prohibited From Involvement In Any Political Campaigns
response_text: TRUE.  There’s no evidence AARP spent “millions” on TV ads targeting Republican candidates, and AARP says it does not endorse or oppose candidates or contribute to campaigns. Note: AARP is a 501(c)(4), which may do some advocacy; it is not absolutely barred by law from all political activity, but AARP’s policy is to stay nonpartisan and avoid candidate-focused campaigning.

claim: McDonald’s take down American flags at their fast-food restaurants in support of Black Lives Matter and antifa (an umbrella term for far-left anti-fascism groups).
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no evidence or company policy that McDonald’s removed American flags in support of Black Lives Matter, and certainly not in support of “antifa.” McDonald’s did issue statements and donations supporting racial justice in 2020, but fact-checkers and the company have said they did not instruct restaurants to take down U.S. flags. This claim originated from misleading social posts/rumors.

claim: A Rafale Aircraft crashed during training and two pilots are dead.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports indicate a Rafale crash killing two pilots. As of the latest verified records (through 2024), Rafale accidents have been rare; the only known fatal Rafale incident involved one pilot (2009 mid-air collision). Recent Rafale mishaps saw pilots eject safely. Claims of “two pilots dead” typically confuse Rafales with other aircraft (e.g., Mirage 2000).

claim: The Indian UPSC examination is discriminatory in favour of Muslim candidates.(Sudarshan News Editor-in-Chief, Suresh Chavhanke, 11 September, 2020, UPSC Jihad Par Ab Tak Ka Sabse Bada Khulasa (The Biggest Expose of All Time on UPSC Jihad)
response_text: FALSE.  - UPSC exams are merit-based with standardized, anonymized written tests and interviews; the application and selection processes do not include or favor any religion. There is no religion-based reservation or relaxation in UPSC. - Data on selections consistently shows Muslim candidates form a small fraction of those selected (generally far below their population share), not an overrepresentation. - The “UPSC jihad” claim aired by Sudarshan News was widely debunked by independent fact-checkers, and courts criticized the program’s communal insinuations; no evidence was presented that UPSC favors Muslim candidates.  Uncertainty: None significant; multiple official processes and public data contradict the claim.

claim: US state of Georgia has “almost 100,000 more COVID-19 cases, almost twice as many deaths and almost 600 more nursing home deaths than North Carolina, US.
response_text: TRUE (with timing caveat)  At the time this comparison was commonly made (late summer 2020), Georgia’s totals did fit those magnitudes: - Cases: roughly 240–250k in GA vs about 150k in NC — ≈100,000 more. - Deaths: ~4,800–5,000 in GA vs ~2,400–2,600 in NC — nearly double. - Nursing home deaths: GA’s long‑term care deaths were roughly ~600 higher than NC’s.  Exact counts varied by date and reporting source, but the claim’s scale was accurate for that period.

claim: Tourism, lockdown key to deep New Zealand recession.
response_text: TRUE.  New Zealand’s sharp 2020 recession was driven largely by strict COVID-19 lockdowns and border closures that crushed tourism. Stats NZ reported a record GDP fall in Q2 2020, with the biggest declines in accommodation, food services, transport, and retail—sectors heavily tied to tourism and restricted by lockdowns.

claim: Wildfires do not Affect Mexico And Canada
response_text: FALSE.  Both Canada and Mexico are affected by wildfires. Canada had a record fire season in 2023 with millions of hectares burned, mass evacuations, and smoke that degraded air quality across North America. Mexico experiences thousands of wildfires annually, with seasonal outbreaks causing air-quality alerts, ecological damage, and evacuations. Smoke from fires can also cross borders, affecting neighboring countries.

claim: Former FBI Director James Comey and former CIA Director John Brennan have been charged with multiple counts of treason.
response_text: FALSE.  There are no indictments or court records showing James Comey or John Brennan have been charged with treason. DOJ investigations (including the Durham probe) brought no charges against them, and treason is a narrowly defined, extremely rare charge that would be publicly documented if it occurred.

claim: Donald Trump tweeted that he was donating $500,000 each toward the expenses of the two Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies who were shot and critically injured on September 12, 2020.
response_text: FALSE.  Trump tweeted about the ambush and called for harsh punishment of the shooter, but there is no record of him tweeting a pledge to donate $500,000 each to the deputies. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) found the alleged tweet was fabricated and no credible reporting shows such a donation or pledge.

claim: Iran has stockpiled 10 times as much enriched uranium as it had in 2016.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: After the 2015 nuclear deal took effect in 2016, Iran was capped at about 300 kg of UF6 (≈203 kg of uranium) enriched up to 3.67%. Recent IAEA reports (2023–2024) put Iran’s total enriched uranium stockpile in the thousands of kilograms (roughly 5,000–7,000+ kg), i.e., well over 10 times the 2016 level. Minor uncertainty depends on the exact month referenced, but the order-of-magnitude comparison is clearly correct.

claim: Ignat Shchetinin And Sammy Scott Piatt, charged with arson connected to Clackamas County, Oregon wildfires.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible records or official releases show anyone named Ignat Shchetinin or Sammy Scott Piatt being charged with arson tied to Clackamas County wildfires. Fact-checkers and local authorities debunked circulating lists of “arsonists” from the 2020 Oregon fires, and Clackamas County did not report such charges for those names. (Minor uncertainty only because absence of records can’t prove impossibility.)

claim: Nigerian Government had placed a ban on alcohol in sachet and polythene.
response_text: TRUE.  Nigeria’s federal regulator NAFDAC (a government agency) has banned the production and sale of alcoholic beverages in sachets and small plastic containers (PET/polythene) of 200 ml or less, with enforcement beginning in early 2024. Note: it’s a packaging-size ban, not a blanket ban on alcohol.

claim: Edo State in Nigeria has a 19% unemployment rate.
response_text: TRUE.  According to Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics state-level unemployment data (2020 release, covering Q4 2020), Edo State’s unemployment rate was about 19%. Note: unemployment rates change over time and newer surveys use different methods, so the current rate may differ.

claim: Antifa is recruiting people to dress as President Trump supporters and police to riot on Election Day 2020 in the United States
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: This was a viral social‑media rumor before the 2020 election. Fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, AP, Reuters, Snopes) found no credible evidence that “antifa” was recruiting people to pose as Trump supporters or police to riot on Election Day. Law enforcement reported no such verified plots, and no organized antifa operation of this kind materialized.

claim: Netflix tweets that its content is "mostly pedophilia-free" in response to criticism over its streaming of "Cuties"
response_text: FALSE.  No verified Netflix account ever tweeted that its content was “mostly pedophilia-free.” The phrasing comes from satirical/fabricated posts circulating during the 2020 “Cuties” controversy (notably from satire sites like The Babylon Bee). Netflix apologized for an inappropriate poster for the film and defended carrying the movie, but did not use that wording.

claim: Joe Biden’s own chief of staff said that when Biden managed swine flu in 2009, they quote, “Did every possible thing wrong.”
response_text: TRUE.  Ron Klain—who was Joe Biden’s chief of staff when Biden was vice president in 2009 and later Biden’s White House chief of staff—said in a 2019 panel discussion about the 2009 H1N1 response: “We did every possible thing wrong… It is purely a fortuity that this isn’t one of the great mass casualty events in American history.” Context: Klain was criticizing the Obama administration’s overall response and crediting luck; he wasn’t saying Biden personally “managed” the swine flu response.

claim: Netflix CEO Reed Hastings was arrested by the FBI on child porn charges.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible news outlet or law enforcement record shows Reed Hastings was arrested on child pornography charges. The rumor traces to fabricated/satirical posts that circulated amid the 2020 “Cuties” controversy, when a Texas grand jury indicted Netflix (the company) on a content-related charge—not Hastings personally. This claim has been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: Antifa Admit to Igniting Fires All Over The Country To Draw Attention To Climate Change
response_text: FALSE.  This headline originated from disinformation sites (e.g., NewsPunch) and has been debunked by multiple fact-checkers. There is no credible evidence that “Antifa” admitted to setting fires; law enforcement and the FBI explicitly said rumors of antifa-started wildfires were false during the 2020 wildfire season. Some arson arrests occurred, but none substantiated ties to “Antifa,” and no such admissions exist.

claim: Netflix CEO Reed Hastings was arrested by the FBI after being caught with 13,000 files of child pornography.
response_text: FALSE.  This claim originated on a disinformation site (Conservative Beaver) in 2020 and has been debunked by multiple fact-checkers. The FBI and Netflix both said no such arrest occurred, and there are no credible reports or records supporting it.

claim: The eligibility criteria for applying to take the exam for the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) of India, differentiates depending on whether you are a Hindu or a Muslim.
response_text: FALSE.  UPSC exam eligibility does not differ by religion. Criteria are based on nationality, age limits, educational qualification, number of attempts, and category-based relaxations (General, OBC, SC/ST, EWS, PwBD). Religion (Hindu, Muslim, etc.) is not a factor. India’s Constitution (e.g., Article 16) prohibits discrimination in public employment on grounds of religion.

claim: Muslim candidates are allowed more attempts at the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam than others
response_text: FALSE.  UPSC attempt limits are based on category and age, not religion. As per the UPSC rules, General/EWS candidates get 6 attempts, OBC candidates get 9, and SC/ST candidates have no cap on attempts (within their higher age limits). Persons with Benchmark Disabilities have additional relaxations. Some Muslims may fall under OBC or ST categories and thus get the corresponding relaxations, but being Muslim per se does not confer extra attempts.

claim: Muslim candidates can qualify with lower marks than others in the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam
response_text: FALSE.  UPSC does not give any religion-based relaxation. Lower cutoffs/age/attempt relaxations apply only to reserved categories (SC, ST, OBC, EWS, Persons with Benchmark Disability). Some Muslim candidates may fall under OBC or ST and get those benefits, but being Muslim per se does not confer any lower qualifying marks.

claim: CDC announces that ordinary (non-N95) masks (which most people are wearing) will do nothing to protect you against wildfire smoke because they do not catch small particles
response_text: TRUE.  CDC guidance says cloth and typical surgical masks do not protect you from wildfire smoke because they don’t filter the small, harmful fine particles (PM2.5); protection requires a well‑fitting respirator like an N95 (or similar). Nuance: ordinary masks may block larger ash particles but not the dangerous fine smoke particles.

claim: The upper age-limit for Muslim candidates for the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam is relaxed to be higher than that of other applicants
response_text: FALSE.  UPSC age limits and relaxations are not based on religion. Relaxations apply to categories such as SC/ST (5 years), OBC-NCL (3 years), Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (10 years), ex‑servicemen, certain J&K domicile years, etc. A Muslim candidate gets relaxation only if they fall into one of these categories (e.g., OBC if listed), the same as any other applicant. There is no age relaxation solely for being Muslim.

claim: Greater number of Muslim aspirants are suddenly taking the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam
response_text: FALSE  Reason: UPSC does not publish religion-wise data for applicants or test-takers, so there is no official evidence to show a “sudden” rise in Muslim aspirants. Media counts sometimes track how many Muslim candidates qualified in a given year, but that doesn’t measure the number of aspirants and shows normal year-to-year fluctuation rather than a verified surge. Therefore the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: the Indian Government set up 5 coaching centres for UPSC exams, 4 of which were in Muslim universities.
response_text: FALSE.  Reason: The central government hasn’t created “only 5” UPSC coaching centres, nor are “4 in Muslim universities.” Government-supported coaching operates under multiple schemes (UGC Residential Coaching Academies and the Minority Affairs “Free Coaching” scheme) across many institutions nationwide. While notable centres exist in minority universities like Jamia Millia Islamia, AMU, and MANUU, several others are in non-minority institutions. The claim misstates both the number and distribution of centres. (Minor uncertainty on exact counts by year, but the “5 with 4 in Muslim universities” framing is incorrect.)

claim: Police: Political Activists Didn’t Cause Oregon’s Wildfires
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During the September 2020 Oregon wildfires, multiple law enforcement agencies—including FBI Portland and several Oregon sheriff and police departments—publicly stated there was no evidence that antifa, Proud Boys, or other political activists started the fires. They urged the public to stop spreading such rumors. While a few individuals were arrested for arson, authorities found no links to organized political activist groups.

claim: Clinical trials of a vaccine against COVID-19 were paused
response_text: TRUE.  Several COVID-19 vaccine trials were temporarily paused for safety reviews—for example, AstraZeneca/University of Oxford paused their trial in September 2020 after an unexplained illness in a participant, and Johnson & Johnson paused in October 2020. Both later resumed after investigation.

claim: Western Wildfires Are evidence Of A Coordinated Antifa Campaign To 'Burn The Country Down
response_text: FALSE.  There is no credible evidence that Western wildfires are part of a coordinated Antifa campaign. In 2020, the FBI and multiple law enforcement agencies in affected states publicly stated that rumors of organized extremist arson were false. Wildfires in the West are primarily driven by lightning, drought, high winds, and human activity (e.g., accidents, power lines); occasional arson cases have not been tied to an Antifa plot. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Kasab was fed biriyani.
response_text: FALSE.  The “biryani for Kasab” story was a myth. In 2015, special public prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam admitted he had fabricated the claim that Ajmal Kasab was served biryani in jail. Jail and state officials had also denied it at the time.

claim: US Congress voted 49-46 to add the repeal of Section 230 — legislation which shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content — into the country’s annual defense bill in December 2020
response_text: FALSE.  - No chamber voted 49–46 to add a Section 230 repeal to the 2020 National Defense Authorization Act.   - The NDAA passed the House 335–78 (Dec 8, 2020) and the Senate 84–13 (Dec 11, 2020) without any Section 230 repeal.   - President Trump vetoed the bill partly because it did not repeal Section 230; Congress overrode the veto (House 322–87 on Dec 28; Senate 81–13 on Jan 1, 2021).   - A 49–46 tally would be a Senate vote, not “US Congress,” and there is no record of such a vote to add a 230 repeal to the NDAA.

claim: Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden talk about how the Chevrolet Corvette is "one of the best cars in the world" while he was visiting a Ford plant.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden often mentions his 1967 Corvette and did so during Ford visits (e.g., Rawsonville in 2020 and the Ford Rouge EV Center in 2021), citing its 0–60 time and saying he’s a “car guy.” But there’s no credible transcript or video showing him saying the Corvette is “one of the best cars in the world” while at a Ford plant. The phrasing appears to be paraphrase or from other contexts, not from those Ford visits. (Some uncertainty due to the volume of appearances, but no reliable source confirms this quote in that setting.)

claim: Nita Ambani is to give Rs 200 crore for Kangana Ranaut’s new studio
response_text: FALSE. This claim circulated as a social media rumor in 2020 after the BMC demolition of Kangana Ranaut’s office. Fact-check outlets (e.g., BOOM, India Today) debunked it, and Reliance representatives denied any such Rs 200 crore funding by Nita Ambani. No credible announcement or report supports the claim.

claim: US Democratic Vice Presidential nominee Kamala Harris tweeted that she ‘filed a complaint’ to remove a specific Instagram account.
response_text: FALSE.  No record exists on Kamala Harris’s official Twitter/X account of such a statement, and fact-checks have shown the circulating “tweet” screenshot to be fabricated. If she had posted it, it would appear in archives and reputable coverage; it does not. (Slight uncertainty only because rumors referenced a generic “specific account,” but the claim lacks any verifiable source.)

claim: Asha Ranaut tweeted ‘you havent crushed my daughter’s office but Bal Thackeray’s soul.
response_text: FALSE.  This line was circulated from an impersonator account during the 2020 BMC demolition row. Fact-checks reported that Asha Ranaut is not on Twitter and did not post this; the “Asha Ranaut” handle sharing the quote was fake. (Multiple outlets, e.g., BOOM/India Today AFWA, debunked it.)

claim: Brazil preserves its native forests better than any other country in the world
response_text: FALSE.  Brazil has the largest area of tropical forest, but it is not the best at preserving native forests. In recent years it has often led the world in absolute loss of primary tropical forest (per Global Forest Watch/WRI), despite recent improvements. Several countries preserve a higher share of their native forests with very low loss—e.g., Suriname, Guyana, Gabon, and Bhutan—so Brazil is not the top preserver. Uncertainty: depends on metric, but on common ones (loss rates, share intact), the claim does not hold.

claim: $400,000 ... is more money than I’ve ever made” in a year
response_text: TRUE.  Context: Minnesota Gov. (and 2024 Democratic VP nominee) Tim Walz said this. His career earnings — teacher/coach, U.S. House member (~$174k/yr), and governor (~$130k–$175k/yr) — never approached $400,000. Public disclosures/tax records show no year in which his personal income exceeded $400k. Slight uncertainty only because full personal tax details for every year aren’t public, but available records align with the claim.

claim: The CDC has removed the “Covid-19 Pandemic” and replaced it with “Covid-19 Outbreak” on their website.
response_text: FALSE.  CDC has not “replaced” pandemic with outbreak across its site. The agency still refers to COVID-19 as a pandemic in multiple pages and materials. “Outbreak” is used in specific contexts (e.g., the initial 2019 Wuhan outbreak, training materials, or page headings for particular incidents). There’s no CDC announcement or site‑wide terminology change from “pandemic” to “outbreak.”

claim: In England only 69.4% of COVID-19 contacts are now reached and asked to self-isolate.
response_text: TRUE.  NHS Test and Trace statistics for England reported that about 69.4% of identified close contacts had been reached and asked to self-isolate (cumulative since launch at the time). Weekly figures fluctuate and were often around 60–70%, so the exact current week may differ slightly.

claim: Rhea Chakrabortys father Indrajit Chakraborty said ‘I Should Die, No Father Can Bear Injustice On His Daughter’.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible reports or interviews show Indrajit Chakraborty saying “I should die, no father can bear injustice on his daughter.” His documented statements during 2020 included the widely reported “Congratulations India, you arrested my son… my daughter is next… then me, then my wife,” and appeals about harassment, but not the quoted line. This appears to be a misattributed or fabricated social media quote. (Some uncertainty, but no reliable source corroborates it.)

claim: The NFL, NBA and MLB have Tax-Exempt status.
response_text: FALSE.  - NFL: Its league office was tax‑exempt under 501(c)(6) but voluntarily gave up that status in 2015. - MLB: The Commissioner’s Office previously had 501(c)(6) status but ended it in 2007. - NBA: Generally operated as a taxable entity (not a 501(c)(6)).  Note: Teams themselves are for‑profit and taxable; past exemptions applied only to certain league offices.

claim: Schools have resumed in New Brunswick, Canada despite the COVID-19 pandemic
response_text: TRUE.  After closing in spring 2020, New Brunswick implemented a return-to-school plan and reopened K–12 schools for in-person learning in September 2020 with health measures. There were intermittent closures later, but schools did resume despite the pandemic. Sources: Government of New Brunswick return-to-school plan (Aug–Sept 2020); CBC/CTV coverage of Sept. 2020 reopening.

claim: The sky has turned orange to blood red in several parts of the United States.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: During major wildfire smoke events, skies in multiple U.S. regions have taken on deep orange to red hues. Notable examples include the West Coast during the 2020 wildfires (California, Oregon, Washington) and much of the Northeast and Midwest during Canadian wildfire smoke in June 2023 (e.g., New York City, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Ohio). Smoke particles scatter shorter wavelengths, leaving the sky orange to red. Note: the claim lacks a specific date, but such occurrences are well-documented in recent years.

claim: 80 million ballots for the US November 3 2020 election will be mailed to US voters who didn’t request them.
response_text: FALSE.  About 44–45 million ballots were automatically mailed to voters in November 2020 (in universal mail-voting states like CA, CO, HI, NJ, NV, OR, UT, VT, WA, plus DC and many MT counties). The oft-cited ~80 million figure referred to the total number of mail ballots expected to be sent nationwide, most of which were sent only after voters requested them. Many other states mailed applications—not ballots—to all voters.

claim: PGA star Bubba Watson wrote a post that says, "I see signs all over saying black lives matter. I’m just trying to figure out which black lives matter.”
response_text: FALSE.  That “which black lives matter” text is a long-circulating chain post that has been misattributed to various people. There’s no record of it on Bubba Watson’s verified accounts, and fact-checks traced the wording to a different author (often credited to conservative activist Derrick Wilburn). The viral screenshot tying it to Watson is fabricated.

claim: Photo of three officers at the Indian Police Service who belong to the same family.
response_text: FALSE.  This viral photo is not of Indian Police Service officers. It shows officers from Pakistan’s Police Service; the cap badges and insignia display the Pakistani crescent-and-star rather than India’s Ashoka emblem, and there are no “IPS” shoulder tabs. (Noting slight uncertainty without the image, but this matches known fact-checks of the widely shared photo.)

claim: Wearing a face mask can cause pleurisy.
response_text: FALSE.  Pleurisy (pleuritis) is inflammation of the lining of the lungs, most commonly caused by viral or bacterial infections (e.g., pneumonia), pulmonary embolism, autoimmune disease, cancer, or chest trauma. There’s no evidence or plausible mechanism that wearing cloth, surgical, or N95 masks causes pleurisy. In fact, masks can lower the risk of respiratory infections that might lead to pleurisy. Uncertainty: none noted in medical guidance.

claim: The Indian government has launched an online health consultation scheme.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Government of India launched eSanjeevani, a national telemedicine/online health consultation service (including eSanjeevaniOPD) under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. It enables patient-to-doctor and doctor-to-doctor online consultations and has been widely used since 2019–2020.

claim: The Daily Trust news report about a UK judge ruling on how Nigerian Vice President Yemi Osinbajo detected the Process and Industrious Development Limited (P&ID) fraud against Nigeria is fake news.
response_text: TRUE.  Reason: In the UK High Court’s 2023 judgment on the P&ID case (Justice Robin Knowles), the court did not credit or describe Vice President Yemi Osinbajo as the person who “detected” the fraud. Osinbajo is not identified in that ruling as uncovering the scheme; the judgment instead lays out evidence of bribery and perjury and credits Nigeria’s investigations and litigation for exposing it. Claims that the judge “ruled how Osinbajo detected” the fraud misstate the judgment. (Earlier 2020 proceedings mention various Nigerian officials in background, but not Osinbajo as the detector of the fraud.)

claim: Math Mistake Caused U.S. Leaders To Panic And Order COVID Lockdowns
response_text: FALSE.  - U.S. stay‑at‑home orders were made by states, not from a single federal “lockdown,” and were based on multiple inputs: rapidly rising cases/hospitalizations (e.g., New York), experiences abroad (e.g., Italy), and several epidemiological models (Imperial College, IHME, CDC), none of which has been shown to contain a decisive arithmetic error that triggered the policies. - Claims that a “math mistake” (e.g., in early fatality estimates or modeling) caused lockdowns mischaracterize modeling uncertainty and the policy process; there is no evidence that a specific calculation error prompted U.S. leaders to order lockdowns.

claim: Video of a man blowing vape smoke through various face masks shows that they do not help prevent the spread of coronavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  A vape “smoke” demo isn’t a valid test of mask effectiveness. E‑cigarette aerosol particles are much smaller than most respiratory droplets and behave differently, so seeing vapor escape doesn’t mean masks fail to block the larger droplets that carry most virus. Laboratory and epidemiologic studies show well‑fitted masks (especially surgical and respirators) reduce emission and transmission of respiratory viruses, including SARS‑CoV‑2. The video mainly illustrates fit and extreme exhalation, not that masks “do not help.” Uncertainty: none significant.

claim: Spraying of Naira notes is an offence punishable by imprisonment in Nigeria.
response_text: TRUE.  Section 21 of the Central Bank of Nigeria Act, 2007 criminalizes abuse/mutilation of the Naira, which explicitly includes “spraying” notes at social events. On conviction, offenders are liable to imprisonment and/or a fine (commonly cited as a minimum of six months). Recent cases, such as the April 2024 conviction of Idris “Bobrisky” Okuneye for naira abuse, confirm courts do impose custodial sentences.

claim: 53 Johannes Ramokhoase street Pretoria is a human trafficking hotspot.
response_text: FALSE  Reason: There are no credible, widely reported sources identifying 53 Johannes Ramokhoase Street, Pretoria as a human trafficking “hotspot.” Public reporting typically refers to broader areas (e.g., parts of the CBD or certain neighborhoods) rather than a specific numbered address. Uncertainty: While isolated incidents anywhere can’t be ruled out, there’s no verifiable evidence for this precise claim.

claim: Tweet shows Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) president Raj Thackeray showing their support of Bollywood actress Kangana Ranaut.
response_text: FALSE.  Raj Thackeray did not tweet support for Kangana Ranaut; claims circulating used miscaptioned or fake/parody handles. In fact, MNS leaders publicly criticized her remarks about Mumbai at the time. (Some uncertainty without the specific tweet, but credible reports show no such endorsement from Raj Thackeray.)

claim: Willie Obiano, the Governor of Anambra State in Nigeria, procured over 100 SUVs as gifts for Anambra state traditional monarchs.
response_text: TRUE.  Multiple Nigerian outlets reported that during his tenure (2018–2019), Governor Willie Obiano procured and distributed about 179 Innoson SUVs to recognized Anambra traditional rulers, in batches. They were presented as official vehicles to aid their duties, but the quantity was well over 100.

claim: Donald Trump tweeted “THE NEXT 30 TO 60 DAYS WILL BE THE BIGGEST DRAINING OF THE SWAMP EVER”
response_text: FALSE. There’s no record of Trump ever tweeting that phrase. Searches of Trump’s tweet archives show nothing matching it, and fact-checkers have debunked circulating images of this quote as a fabricated tweet.

claim: Mark Zuckerberg Banned Richard Jewells Defence from raising money on Facebook.
response_text: FALSE.  Richard Jewell’s legal defense fundraising happened in 1996–1997, years before Facebook existed (launched in 2004). There’s no evidence Facebook or Mark Zuckerberg ever banned fundraising for Jewell. This claim likely confuses Jewell with later cases (e.g., Kyle Rittenhouse) where Facebook did restrict fundraising.

claim: Taiwan Shot down a Chinese SU-35 Jet.
response_text: FALSE.  This was a viral rumor (notably in September 2020) that both Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense and Chinese authorities denied. No credible evidence, wreckage, or official accident report ever surfaced, and videos used were misattributed from unrelated incidents.

claim: Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray has come forward in support of Bollywood actress Kangana Ranaut and would welcome her back to Mumbai, India.
response_text: FALSE.  In the 2020 row over Kangana Ranaut’s remarks about Mumbai and the Mumbai Police, the MNS did not back her. MNS leaders publicly criticized her and warned against her shooting in Mumbai unless she apologized. Offers to “welcome/protect” her in Mumbai came from BJP figures, not Raj Thackeray. I find no credible record of Raj Thackeray saying he would welcome her back. (Slight uncertainty due to the volume of statements at the time.)

claim: Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook declared Richard Jewell to be a Mass Murderer in 1996
response_text: FALSE.  Facebook didn’t exist in 1996 (launched in 2004), and Mark Zuckerberg was 12 years old then. In 1996, some news outlets wrongly identified security guard Richard Jewell as a suspect in the Atlanta Olympic bombing, but he was later exonerated; the bomber was Eric Rudolph.

claim: Taiwan claimed to have brought down a Chinese Air Force Su-35 that allegedly violated its airspace over Taiwan Strait.
response_text: FALSE  Taiwan made no such claim. In early September 2022, rumors spread online that Taiwan had shot down a Chinese Su‑35 near the Taiwan Strait, but Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense publicly denied it and said no Chinese aircraft had been shot down. No credible evidence or official confirmation supports the claim.

claim: Between 2010 and 2018, the Uighur population had the region’s highest birthrate, at about 12 newborns per 1,000 people in Xinjiang, China.
response_text: FALSE.  - Xinjiang’s overall crude birth rate was around 15–16 per 1,000 as late as 2017 (e.g., 15.9‰ in 2017), and Uyghur-majority southern prefectures historically had rates higher than the regional average (often well above 15–20‰ before 2017). So “about 12 per 1,000” would not have been the region’s highest during most of 2010–2018. - After 2017, birth rates in Uyghur areas fell sharply (regional overall dropped to ~10.7‰ in 2018), undermining the idea that Uyghurs held the highest rate then.  Thus the figure and characterization are not accurate for 2010–2018.

claim: Raj Thackeray tweeted "On 9 September, Hindu lioness Kangana Ranaut will be given a grand welcome in Maharashtra’s capital, Mumbai."
response_text: FALSE.  Raj Thackeray did not post such a tweet. In 2020 a viral screenshot claiming he wrote “On 9 September, Hindu lioness Kangana Ranaut will be given a grand welcome in Mumbai” was traced to a fake/impersonator account. Raj Thackeray did not have an official personal Twitter account then, and no authentic record shows he made this statement.

claim: US President Donald Trump plans to cut social security, resulting in social security becoming permanently depleted by the middle of calendar year 2023.
response_text: FALSE.  The “mid‑2023 depletion” date came from an SSA actuary’s hypothetical assuming payroll taxes were eliminated starting in 2021 with no replacement funding. Trump issued a temporary payroll tax deferral in 2020 and talked about ending the payroll tax if reelected but also said general revenues would backfill it; he had no enacted plan to cut Social Security benefits and could not unilaterally eliminate the tax. Social Security was not “permanently depleted” in 2023; trustees project OASI trust fund depletion around 2033 absent reforms.

claim: 450,000 people attended the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally in South Dakota, and there were only 88 positive Covid-19 tests, so a .02% infection rate.
response_text: FALSE.  The 450,000 attendance estimate is plausible, but “only 88 positive tests” was an early count limited to South Dakota residents soon after the rally. Many attendees were from out of state, not everyone was tested, and multiple states later reported cases linked to the event—hundreds in total, including at least one death (e.g., Minnesota alone documented 86 linked cases per CDC/Minnesota DOH). Using 88/450,000 to claim a 0.02% infection rate is therefore incorrect and misleading.

claim: People are trying to lower the legal age of consent to four years old in the U.S.
response_text: FALSE.  In the U.S., the legal age of consent is set by states and ranges from 16 to 18. There is no credible movement or legislation to lower it anywhere near four years old; sex with a 4-year-old is criminal in all jurisdictions. Claims suggesting efforts to lower the age to four are misinformation.

claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention fraudulently add deaths from poisoning, trauma, and unintentional injury to their tally of COVID-19 deaths.
response_text: FALSE.  CDC counts COVID-19 deaths from death certificates using ICD-10 code U07.1. For its primary COVID-19 death tally, COVID-19 must be the underlying cause of death. Deaths whose underlying cause is an external cause (poisoning, trauma, unintentional injury) are not reclassified as COVID-19 deaths. CDC also publishes a separate metric for “deaths involving COVID-19,” which includes cases where COVID-19 is listed anywhere on the certificate; in those data, other conditions (including some injuries/adverse events) can appear as contributing factors. That transparent reporting is not fraudulent, and there’s no evidence CDC “adds” accident or poisoning deaths to inflate the COVID-19 death count.

claim: Sturgis Motorcycle Rally resulted in no more positive Covid results than the rest of the state, South Dakota, average stating 88 positive tests to Sturgis Rally, 0.02% infection rate of attendees.
response_text: FALSE.  - South Dakota officials and CDC-linked reports documented far more than 88 cases tied to the 2020 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. For example, Minnesota alone reported 86 rally-associated cases (plus secondary spread and one death), and South Dakota’s Department of Health logged around 120+ cases among South Dakota residents. Other states also reported cases, bringing totals well above 88. - With hundreds of cases across multiple states, the implied 0.02% infection rate (88 out of ~460,000 attendees) substantially understates known infections. - The assertion that the rally produced “no more positive results than the rest of the state average” is not supported by public health data and uses a nonstandard comparison.  Uncertainty: Exact totals are hard to pin down due to incomplete contact tracing, but they clearly exceed 88.

claim: The CDC recommended wearing only certain beard styles to help prevent the spread of coronoavirus.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The widely shared “beard chart” came from a 2017 CDC/NIOSH graphic about how facial hair can interfere with the seal of tight-fitting respirators (e.g., N95) for workers. It was not a CDC recommendation for the general public to wear only certain beard styles to prevent COVID-19 spread. CDC guidance was about respirator fit for those who needed them, not about beard styles to stop coronavirus.

claim: Viral message claims that all Haldiram’s food products were banned in USA
response_text: FALSE.  No blanket U.S. ban exists on all Haldiram’s products. The FDA has not issued such an order, and Haldiram items continue to be sold in the U.S. An old 2015 FDA import alert affected certain products/shipments, which was misrepresented in recent viral posts as a total ban.

claim: Voters in North Carolina can send their Mail-in vote and then go to the polling place to vote again to check that their mail-in vote has been counted.
response_text: FALSE.  In North Carolina it is illegal to vote more than once in the same election (a felony). If you’ve mailed an absentee ballot, you cannot go to the polls to “vote again” to check it. You can track your absentee ballot’s status online. If you decide to vote in person instead, you must surrender your absentee ballot at the polling place or vote provisionally; only one vote will be counted.

claim: Fox News is unavailable in Canada because the Radio Act makes it a crime to lie to the public via airwaves.
response_text: FALSE.  - Fox News is available in Canada; the CRTC approved it for distribution in 2004 and major cable/satellite providers carry it. - Canada does not criminalize “lying on the air” via a “Radio Act.” The old Criminal Code “false news” offence was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1992. CRTC regulations do prohibit Canadian licensees from broadcasting false or misleading news, but that is a regulatory (not criminal) rule and hasn’t been used to bar Fox News.

claim: "Jihadists" attacked a Temple in West Bengal and charred the Hindu deity Kali
response_text: FALSE.  Multiple fact-checks and local police statements have clarified that a widely shared image/video of a charred Kali idol in West Bengal was the result of an accidental fire (likely from lamps/short circuit) at a small temple/mandap. Police found no evidence of any attack or a communal angle, and no “jihadists” were involved. Uncertainty: exact location/date details vary across reports, but all converge on an accidental cause.

claim: A Pakistani website was hacked by an Indian cyber group to wish Pawan Kalyan a Happy Birthday.
response_text: TRUE.  Reports in early September 2017 (around Pawan Kalyan’s Sep 2 birthday) noted that an Indian hacker/cyber group defaced a Pakistani website with a “Happy Birthday Pawan Kalyan” message. Screenshots circulated in Indian media at the time. Attribution in such hacks can be hard to verify, but the incident was widely reported.

claim: US President Trump opened a complaint platform to report censorship on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In May 2019, the Trump White House launched an online form on whitehouse.gov inviting people to report alleged political bias or “censorship” by social media platforms, including Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube (also Instagram). The tool was later re-upped in 2020.

claim: US President Trump issued an executive order for the White House to take over all electrical grids, which will include internet servers, broadcasting systems and electronic systems
response_text: FALSE.  Trump’s May 1, 2020 executive order (EO 13920) addressed securing the U.S. bulk-power system from foreign-adversary equipment. It restricts certain purchases and empowers the Energy Department to block risky transactions; it does not let the White House “take over” the electrical grid, nor does it cover internet servers, broadcasting systems, or all electronic systems. Fact-checkers (e.g., Reuters) debunked this claim.

claim: US President Trump canceled the Democrats’ HR6666 bill, known as the COVID-19 TRACE Act.
response_text: FALSE.  H.R. 6666 (the COVID-19 TRACE Act) was a House bill introduced in May 2020 to fund COVID testing and contact tracing. It never passed Congress and thus never reached the president. Presidents cannot “cancel” a bill; they can only veto one after it passes both chambers. The bill stalled in committee and expired at the end of the 116th Congress.

claim: US President Trump canceled Bill Gates’ project known as ID2020
response_text: FALSE.  ID2020 is an independent, nongovernmental alliance formed in 2016 to promote digital identity solutions. It is not “Bill Gates’ project,” though Microsoft (which Gates co-founded) has been a partner. As a private/global initiative, it isn’t something a U.S. president can “cancel,” and there is no credible record of President Trump canceling it. The alliance continued operating beyond his term.

claim: US President Trump issued an executive order to reopen states in lockdown during COVID-19 pandemic; governors who refuse will be sued
response_text: FALSE.  Trump did not issue an executive order forcing states to reopen. The White House released nonbinding “Opening Up America Again” guidelines (April 16, 2020), and while Trump claimed broad authority, states retained control over public health measures. There was no executive order mandating reopening or a policy to sue governors who refused.

claim: The US military will check purity and distribute COVID-19 vaccines in US.
response_text: FALSE.  - Vaccine “purity” and quality testing are handled by manufacturers under FDA oversight; FDA reviews data and controls lot release—not the U.S. military. - Distribution was coordinated by HHS/CDC using contracted private distributors (e.g., McKesson, with UPS/FedEx). The Department of Defense supported logistics planning under Operation Warp Speed but did not check purity or directly distribute vaccines to the public.

claim: A 21 year old can have sex with an 11-year-old, and not be listed on the sex registry as a sex offender
response_text: FALSE.  In all U.S. states (and other countries with sex‑offender registries), sexual activity with an 11‑year‑old is a serious crime (statutory rape/sexual assault of a child) and a conviction triggers mandatory sex‑offender registration, often for life. There are no close‑in‑age exceptions that would cover a 21‑year‑old with an 11‑year‑old. Only avoiding detection/conviction or being in a jurisdiction without any registry would avoid listing, but legally the claim is false.

claim: In Massachusetts, "anybody can go vote for anybody so long as they have their information. … They're not even checking IDs at the polling stations."
response_text: FALSE.  Massachusetts does not require every voter to show ID, but poll workers do require ID in several situations (e.g., first-time voters who registered by mail and didn’t provide ID, “inactive” voters, challenged voters, or provisional ballots). Voters must also be on the precinct list and state their name and address, and impersonation is illegal and subject to penalties. So it’s not true that “anybody can go vote for anybody,” nor that IDs are never checked.

claim: Economic damage caused by the pandemic shows United States GDP (gross domestic product) falling by 33 percent compared to India's 23.9 percent drop.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The “33%” U.S. figure refers to the annualized quarter‑to‑quarter drop in real GDP for Q2 2020 reported by the BEA. India’s 23.9% is a year‑over‑year drop for the same quarter. That comparison mixes different metrics. On a comparable basis, U.S. GDP fell about 9% year‑over‑year (or roughly 9% non‑annualized q/q) in Q2 2020, not 33%.

claim: In Belfast, the digital sector employs 26 per cent of the workforce.
response_text: FALSE.  Available estimates (e.g., Tech Nation and NI statistics) put Belfast’s digital tech employment at roughly 13,000–15,000 jobs out of well over 200,000 total jobs—around 6–8%, not 26%. The 26% figure likely refers to a broader “knowledge economy” category or to job adverts, not the digital sector’s share of the workforce. Uncertainty only in definitions, but 26% for digital is implausibly high.

claim: Hooligans from the Muslim community were behind the desecration of Goddess Kali Idol in a Bengal Temple in West Bengal's Murshidabad district by burning it.
response_text: FALSE.  Local police and temple/pandal organizers in Murshidabad said the idol was charred in an accidental fire (from diyas/electrical short-circuit). No evidence or arrests indicated “Muslim hooligans” were involved, and police found no communal angle. Multiple fact-checks cited these statements. Slight uncertainty always remains pending full investigations, but available official accounts contradict the claim.

claim: Bill Gates was involved in crafting the TRACE Act.
response_text: FALSE.  Explanation: The TRACE Act (H.R. 6666, “Testing, Reaching, And Contacting Everyone”), introduced in May 2020 by Rep. Bobby Rush, proposed grants for COVID-19 testing and contact tracing. There is no evidence Bill Gates or his foundation helped draft or craft the bill; fact-checkers (e.g., PolitiFact, Snopes) found the claim baseless. Gates publicly supported testing and tracing generally but had no role in writing the legislation.

claim: It's NOT a SECOND WAVE of COVID-19 coming soon. It's the NORMAL COLD / FLU SEASON
response_text: FALSE  COVID-19 surges (“waves”) were real and documented by testing, hospitalizations, and deaths attributable to SARS‑CoV‑2, a virus distinct from the common cold and influenza. In many places, influenza activity was historically low in 2020–21 due to mitigation measures, while COVID-19 still surged, confirming those increases were not just the “normal cold/flu season.”

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) says there is no proof that face masks protect against Covid-19.
response_text: FALSE.  WHO’s current guidance recognizes that masks help reduce COVID-19 transmission and recommends their use in appropriate settings. Early in 2020 WHO noted limited evidence for masking by healthy people in the community, but it updated its advice from June 2020 onward, citing growing evidence that masks lower infection risk as part of a broader set of measures.

claim: Masks lower immune systems.
response_text: FALSE.  Wearing masks does not weaken or “lower” the immune system. Evidence from clinical studies and decades of use in healthcare show masks do not cause harmful CO2 buildup or oxygen deprivation in healthy people, nor do they reduce immune competence. You’re still exposed to plenty of microbes in daily life; masks mainly reduce inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets, which prevents illness rather than impairing immunity.

claim: US President Trump made vaccines voluntary, not mandatory, in the US.
response_text: FALSE.  - The U.S. has never had a general federal vaccine mandate; vaccination rules are mostly set by states (e.g., for school entry) and employers. Those mandates existed before, during, and after Trump’s term. - Trump said he would not make the COVID-19 vaccine mandatory, but he did not pass any law or order “making vaccines voluntary.” - COVID vaccines in late 2020 were under Emergency Use Authorization, which by statute already allows individuals to accept or refuse unless a president issues a specific waiver (none was issued).

claim: A virus can easily pass through a mask.
response_text: FALSE.  Viruses in the air are typically carried in respiratory droplets/aerosols much larger than the virus itself. Well-fitted respirators (e.g., N95/FFP2) filter ≥95% of 0.3 μm particles and capture even smaller ones via diffusion and electrostatic effects; surgical and multilayer cloth masks also reduce particle emission and inhalation, though less effectively and fit-dependent. Leakage or poorly woven fabrics can reduce protection, but it is not accurate to say viruses “easily” pass through masks.

claim: Some US mayors are fining people for going to church during the COVID-19 pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  Example: In April 2020, Greenville, Mississippi police—enforcing the mayor’s emergency order—issued $500 citations to congregants attending a drive-in church service. Similar enforcement actions (citations/fines for church gatherings) occurred in other cities, such as Chicago citing churches for violating crowd limits. Some measures were later rescinded or blocked, but fines did occur.

claim: US President Trump declared places of worship as essential services during COVID-19 pandemic.
response_text: TRUE.  In a May 22, 2020 White House briefing, President Trump said he was designating houses of worship (churches, synagogues, mosques) as “essential places that provide essential services” and urged governors to allow them to reopen. Note: the legal authority to set such rules largely rested with states, and CDC issued guidance rather than a federal mandate.

claim: PEDOPHILIA is now LEGAL in CALIFORNIA
response_text: FALSE.  Sexual activity with minors remains illegal in California. A 2020 law (SB 145) did not legalize sex with minors; it only gave judges discretion over mandatory sex‑offender registration in limited cases involving 14–17-year-olds and partners less than 10 years older.
