All child sexual abuse, statutory rape, and exploitation offenses are still crimes.

claim: Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins said of President Donald Trump, “Yes, I said that I wouldn’t endorse him but that doesn’t mean I don’t fully support him.”
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Susan Collins saying this. In 2016 she wrote an op‑ed explaining why she could not support Trump, and in 2020 she said she would not endorse anyone for president and declined to say how she voted. The quote appears to be a fabricated/misattributed line circulating online, not something Collins actually said. Uncertainty: low.

claim: US President Trump instructed his administration to halt funding of the World Health Organization while a review was conducted to assess the World Health Organization’s role regarding the spread of coronavirus.
response_text: TRUE.  On April 14, 2020, President Donald Trump announced he had instructed his administration to suspend U.S. funding to the World Health Organization while conducting a review of the WHO’s handling of the COVID-19 outbreak, alleging mismanagement and a cover-up related to the virus’s spread.

claim: US Cable news channel Fox News is unavailable in Canada due to media legislation.
response_text: FALSE.  Fox News Channel is authorized by the Canadian regulator (CRTC) for distribution in Canada (approved in 2004) and is carried by major TV providers like Bell, Rogers, and Shaw. While there have been complaints urging the CRTC to reconsider, it has not been banned by Canadian media legislation.

claim: idol of goddess Kali was burnt in West bengals Murshidabad by the muslim community.
response_text: FALSE.  No credible news reports or police statements confirm that a Kali idol was burned in Murshidabad by “the Muslim community.” Similar viral posts have been debunked by fact-checkers as either old/unrelated videos or accidental fires with no communal angle. The sweeping attribution to an entire community is unsupported.

claim: In 2018, South African police service officers were accused of 217 cases of torture and 3,661 cases of assault.
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: The Independent Police Investigative Directorate’s 2018/19 annual report recorded 217 complaints of torture and 3,661 of assault against South African Police Service members. Note: these figures are for the 2018/19 financial year, not strictly the calendar year 2018.

claim: Since 2002, South Africa’s police force has grown by 50%.
response_text: TRUE.  SAPS headcount rose from roughly 120,000–130,000 in 2002/03 to about 195,000–200,000 by 2011/12—around a 50–60% increase. Numbers later declined, so the net increase by the early 2020s is closer to 40–45%, but the claim is accurate for the 2002→2011/12 period. (Source: SAPS annual reports; figures approximate.)

claim: All India Institute of Medical Sciences Nursing Officer Recruitment Common Eligibility Test 2020 was postponed.
response_text: TRUE.  AIIMS officially postponed the Nursing Officer Recruitment Common Eligibility Test (NORCET) 2020. The exam, initially slated for 1 September 2020, was rescheduled and conducted on 8 September 2020, as per AIIMS Exam Section notices issued around late August/early September 2020.

claim: US cable news channel Fox News is not available in Canada due to media legislation in the country.
response_text: FALSE.  Fox News Channel is authorized by Canada’s regulator (CRTC) and has been carried by major Canadian TV providers since 2004. While there have been calls to review or drop it (e.g., 2023 submissions to the CRTC), it has not been banned by Canadian media legislation and remains available in Canada.

claim: 558 people were killed by the police in 2018, while 201 people died in police custody
response_text: FALSE.  - The claim lacks a country. In major jurisdictions, the 2018 figures don’t match:   - United States: ~990 people were shot and killed by police in 2018 (Washington Post), and total killed by police across methods is ~1,100+ (Mapping Police Violence)—not 558. “Custody”/arrest‑related deaths were far higher than 201.   - England & Wales (2018/19): 3 fatal police shootings and 23 deaths in or following police custody (IOPC)—far below 558 and 201.   - South Africa (2018/19): ~440 deaths from police action and ~214 in custody (IPID)—not 558 and 201.  Given available official/credible sources, the stated numbers do not align. Uncertainty: exact intent/country unspecified.

claim: The number of North American bison has been reduced to only twenty-seven individuals due to colonizers.
response_text: FALSE  Euro-American commercial hunting and related policies nearly exterminated bison, but the species’ nadir was in the hundreds (often cited as fewer than ~1,000 by the late 1880s), not 27. A specific wild herd in Yellowstone fell to about 23 animals in 1902, which may be the source of confusion, but overall survivors across North America numbered several hundred.

claim: Jacob Blake raped a 14 year old teenage girl.
response_text: FALSE.  The felony charge against Jacob Blake in 2020 alleged third-degree sexual assault of an adult woman in Kenosha, not a 14-year-old. Multiple fact checks and the criminal complaint show no evidence he raped a minor. The sexual-assault charge was later dropped in a plea deal to lesser charges.

claim: Amber Alert Issued For License Plate Q72B381
response_text: FALSE  Reason: The claim is too vague (no date or location) and matches a common social-media hoax format. Amber Alerts are time- and location-specific and are listed on official state/federal alert pages; there’s no corroboration for a generic alert tied to plate Q72B381. If concerned, verify via your state’s official AMBER Alert site or local law enforcement channels. Uncertainty: Cannot live-check current alerts, but absent official notice, this is most likely false.

claim: Suresh Raina, the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) cricketer, has withdrawn from the upcoming 2020 edition of the IPL after testing positive for COVID-19.
response_text: FALSE.  Suresh Raina withdrew from IPL 2020 citing personal reasons and returned to India; he was not among the CSK members who tested positive for COVID-19. The players who tested positive included Deepak Chahar (and later Ruturaj Gaikwad), not Raina.

claim: Even with a voter ID card, you won’t be allowed to vote in Ghana on December 7 if your name is not found in the Register. So, people should take advantage of the exhibition exercise to verify their names.
response_text: TRUE.  In Ghana, you can only vote if your name appears on the voters register at your polling station. A voter ID card alone is not sufficient if your name is not on the register. The Electoral Commission runs a voters’ register exhibition before elections so people can verify and correct their details, which is exactly what the claim advises.

claim: A crowdfunding campaign on the Christian site GiveSendGo solicited donations to help Kyle Rittenhouse, a 17-year-old accused of killing two people at a protest in Kenosha, Wisconsin.
response_text: TRUE.  GiveSendGo, a Christian crowdfunding site, hosted campaigns soliciting donations for Kyle Rittenhouse’s legal defense after the August 2020 Kenosha protest shootings. At the time, Rittenhouse was 17 and charged with killing two people, which multiple news outlets reported alongside the GiveSendGo fundraising.

claim: Islamic study is a subject in UPSC exam
response_text: FALSE.  UPSC Civil Services exams do not offer “Islamic Studies” as a subject. The mains optional list includes disciplines like History, Political Science, Sociology, etc., and literature of languages (e.g., Arabic, Persian), but no dedicated Islamic Studies paper. Note: other exams like UGC-NET do have Islamic Studies, but not UPSC.

claim: The Trump RNC Acceptance Speech Was The First Time The White House Was Used For 'Purely Political Campaign Event'
response_text: FALSE.  While Trump’s 2020 RNC acceptance speech was an unusually large, convention-style event on the South Lawn, the White House has been used for overtly political purposes before. Notably, Franklin D. Roosevelt accepted the 1940 Democratic nomination with a radio address from the White House. Presidents have also hosted partisan fundraisers and other campaign-related activities at the White House (e.g., Clinton’s 1995–96 DNC “coffees”). So it wasn’t the first time the White House was used for a purely political campaign event.

claim: Donald trump said "We have already built 300 miles of border wall."
response_text: TRUE.  Trump repeatedly said this in 2020 as the project hit that milestone (e.g., late August–September 2020). CBP reported around 300 miles of “border wall system” completed at that time, largely replacing older barriers rather than creating new miles.

claim: Donald Trump says Biden "is even talking about taking the wall down."
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no record of Biden “talking about taking the wall down.” During the 2020 campaign and after taking office, Biden said he would stop building new wall (and did pause construction), but he did not propose tearing down existing sections. In fact, his administration later allowed some additional barrier work to proceed due to prior congressional funding.

claim: George Floyd died of drug overdose, not US police brutality
response_text: FALSE.  The official Hennepin County Medical Examiner ruled George Floyd’s death a homicide: “cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression.” Fentanyl and methamphetamine were present but listed as contributing conditions, not the cause of death. Multiple medical experts testified he did not die of a drug overdose. Derek Chauvin was convicted of murder and manslaughter in Floyd’s death. Uncertainty: low.

claim: Donald Trump said: Biden "has pledged a $4 trillion tax hike on almost all American families."
response_text: FALSE.  Biden proposed roughly $4 trillion in additional revenue over 10 years, mostly from raising corporate taxes and taxes on households earning over $400,000. He explicitly pledged not to raise taxes on those under that threshold. Independent analyses found the increases concentrated on high earners and corporations—not “almost all American families.” Any indirect effects from corporate taxes don’t turn this into a broad-based $4T hike on most families.

claim: Biden has promised to abolish the production of American oil, coal, shale, and natural gas.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden pledged to transition the U.S. away from fossil fuels over time—ending federal subsidies and stopping new oil and gas leasing on federal lands/offshore—not to abolish all production. He repeatedly said he would not ban fracking on private land, and under his presidency U.S. oil and gas output has reached record highs (and projects like Willow were approved). The claim overstates his position.

claim: Joe Biden had not condemned the violence and looting during protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin by 27th August 2020
response_text: FALSE.  By Aug. 26, 2020, Joe Biden had publicly condemned the violence in Kenosha, saying he condemned “violence of every kind” and calling for it to end. News reports at the time (e.g., Reuters, Aug. 26, 2020) and later fact-checks (e.g., PolitiFact, Aug. 31, 2020) documented his statements denouncing rioting/looting and arson around the Kenosha protests.

claim: Duterte has signed order to open nuclear power plant.
response_text: FALSE.  Duterte signed Executive Order No. 164 in March 2022 to adopt nuclear energy into the Philippines’ energy mix and to study/assess options (including possible rehabilitation of the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant). It did not order any nuclear plant to open, and the BNPP remains mothballed.

claim: Donald Trump said: "When asked if he supports cutting police funding, Joe Biden replied, ‘Yes, absolutely.’"
The Edo State government of Nigeria receives 600 million naira monthly as a security vote.
response_text: TRUE (with caveat)  Multiple credible reports, including the 2018 “Camouflaged Cash” report by Transparency International/CISLAC and media summaries (e.g., Premium Times, TheCable), list Edo State’s security vote at about N600 million per month. However, security votes are opaque, amounts can change, and Governor Godwin Obaseki has publicly claimed he does not take a security vote, so the exact current figure isn’t officially verified.

claim: Donald Trump said "Last month, I took on Big Pharma. You think that is easy? I signed orders that would massively lower the cost of your prescription drugs."
response_text: TRUE.  Trump used that line during remarks at the Republican National Convention in late August 2020, referencing four executive orders he had signed in July aimed at lowering prescription drug prices, saying he “took on Big Pharma” and signed orders that would “massively lower” costs.

claim: President Trump marshalled the full resources of our federal government to deal with the coronavirus from the outset. He directed the US to forge a seamless partnership with governors across America in both political parties.
response_text: FALSE.  - “From the outset” is inaccurate: early U.S. testing was botched and slow (faulty CDC test, regulatory delays), PPE and ventilator shortages persisted, and the Defense Production Act was invoked late and used sparingly at first. A national emergency wasn’t declared until March 13, 2020, and the government repeatedly framed itself as a “backup” to states rather than mobilizing all federal resources immediately.  - “Seamless partnership” is contradicted by public clashes with governors (e.g., Trump criticizing and withholding outreach to governors like Inslee and Whitmer, and states forced to bid against each other for supplies). Governors across parties reported competition and confusion rather than seamless coordination.  Overall, the claim overstates the speed, scope, and bipartisanship of the early federal response.

claim: Kyle Rittenhouse, shooter in the Kenosha shootings, was a white supremacist.
response_text: FALSE.  There’s no verified evidence that Kyle Rittenhouse was a white supremacist or belonged to a white supremacist group. Investigators and the court proceedings did not present such evidence. He was photographed months later with members of the Proud Boys and making an “OK” hand sign (which prosecutors flagged and a judge then restricted his associations while on bond), but that incident does not establish that he is a white supremacist. He has also publicly denied being racist.

claim: Mobs torched our cities while popular members of Congress promote the same socialism my father fought against in World War II.
response_text: FALSE.  - In World War II, the U.S. fought Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and Imperial Japan—not socialist regimes. The Soviet Union, a communist state, was actually a U.S. ally. So claiming WWII was fought “against socialism” is historically wrong. - Some members of Congress advocate democratic socialism, which is not “the same” as Nazism or Soviet-style communism. - “Mobs torched our cities” is hyperbolic; while some protests/riots involved arson in certain areas, U.S. cities were not broadly “torched.”  Some rhetorical ambiguity exists, but the core historical comparison is inaccurate.

claim: Kenosha police allowed Kyle Rittenhouse to walk away after he killed two protesters and injured a third with an AR-15-style rifle.
response_text: TRUE  Video from Aug. 25, 2020 shows Rittenhouse walking toward police with his rifle and hands up after shooting three people in Kenosha; officers drove past and told him to move away rather than detain him. He later turned himself in to police in Illinois. Police later said they did not realize he was the shooter at the time.

claim: EU Trade Commissioner resigned after being accused of violating COVID-19 health rules in Ireland
response_text: TRUE.  Explanation: In August 2020, EU Trade Commissioner Phil Hogan (from Ireland) resigned after public outcry over his attendance at an Irish golf society dinner (“Golfgate”) and related travel, which was accused of breaching Ireland’s COVID-19 restrictions.

claim: Joe Biden wants to end school choice.
response_text: FALSE.  Biden opposes private-school vouchers and for‑profit charter schools and has pushed for more oversight of charters, but he has not proposed eliminating school choice. He supports public school options such as accountable, non‑profit charter schools and magnet schools, and his administration continues funding the federal Charter Schools Program (with added guardrails).

claim: Where President Donald Trump achieved energy independence for the United States, Joe Biden would abolish fossil fuels and end fracking.
response_text: FALSE.  - “Energy independence” is vague. The U.S. did become a net exporter of total energy/petroleum in 2019–2020 (a long-running trend), but it still imported millions of barrels of crude oil and remained tied to global markets—so claiming Trump “achieved energy independence” is overstated. - Biden has not sought to abolish fossil fuels or end fracking. He repeatedly said he would not ban fracking, has targeted a long-term transition to clean energy (e.g., net-zero by 2050), and U.S. oil and gas production has hit record highs during his term.   Uncertainty: hinges on how “energy independence” is defined.

claim: Before the first case of the coronavirus spread within the United States, the president Donald Trump took unprecedented action and suspended all travel from China.
response_text: FALSE.  - Timeline: The first confirmed U.S. case was reported Jan 21, 2020. The China-related restrictions were announced Jan 31 and took effect Feb 2—after the first U.S. case (though before the first confirmed community spread in late February). - Scope: The policy did not “suspend all travel from China.” It barred most non‑U.S. citizens who had recently been in China but allowed U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and others to enter, with screening and quarantine; flights continued and thousands still arrived.  Note: If “spread within the United States” is taken to mean community transmission, the timing part could be read as roughly correct, but the “all travel” claim remains inaccurate.

claim: The Obama-Biden administration secretly launched a surveillance operation on the Trump campaign.
response_text: FALSE.  What happened: The FBI opened “Crossfire Hurricane” in 2016 to investigate possible Trump–Russia links. It used informants and obtained a FISA warrant to surveil former adviser Carter Page (in Oct. 2016, after he’d left the campaign). The DOJ inspector general found the probe was properly predicated (though riddled with FISA errors) and found no evidence it was politically directed by Obama or Biden or that the White House “launched” a surveillance operation on the Trump campaign itself. The Durham report later criticized the FBI’s judgment but likewise did not show an Obama/Biden-ordered spying operation.

claim: This Democratic Party of Joe Biden is pushing the so-called Green New Deal. If given power, they would essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars.
response_text: FALSE.  - Joe Biden has said he does not support the Green New Deal; his administration pursues its own climate plan. The Democratic Party platform does not adopt the Green New Deal as policy. - Neither Biden’s policies nor the Green New Deal resolution call for banning animal agriculture. They focus on reducing agricultural emissions and supporting farmers. - Federal policy does not ban gas-powered cars. Biden set targets (e.g., 50% of new sales being zero‑emission by 2030) and tougher emissions standards, but no prohibition on owning or selling gas cars. Some states plan future zero‑emission new‑sales mandates, which still are not bans on existing gas cars.  Uncertainty: None significant; no Democratic platform or Biden proposal “essentially” bans animal agriculture or eliminates gas cars.

claim: Nancy Pelosi says that China would prefer Joe Biden.
response_text: TRUE.  In August 2020, Pelosi referenced U.S. intelligence assessments that China preferred Joe Biden (and that Russia preferred Trump) in the 2020 election context. She acknowledged China “would prefer Joe Biden,” while stressing Russia’s more active efforts for Trump. Note: This referred to 2020, not necessarily current preferences.

claim: The first night of the US Republican National Convention had 128.4 million viewers
response_text: FALSE.  Nielsen-measured TV viewership for the first night of the 2024 Republican National Convention was around the low-20 millions (roughly 20–22 million during the 10–11 p.m. hour), not 128.4 million. Even including streaming and digital, credible totals don’t approach 128 million; that figure would far exceed typical convention audiences and likely reflects inflated “impressions,” not actual viewers.
